en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, O King, when Droṇa had been slain, the kings headed by Duryodhana,
their minds deeply agitated, approached the son of Droṇa—
who was clad in white garments, resembled Viṣṇu in complexion, and possessed four arms, like the moon itself.

One should meditate upon his serene face for the pacification of all obstacles. Then, grieving for Droṇa, their vigor struck down by dejection and afflicted with sorrow, they sat around the son of Śaradvatī.
Having consoled him for a moment with arguments consistent with the scriptures,
those lords of the earth retired to their own quarters at the arrival of night;
especially so the son of the Sūta and King Suyodhana.
Then Duḥśāsana and Śakuni found no sleep;
O Kauravya, even in their own dwellings, those lords of the earth obtained no comfort,
for as they contemplated that terrible destruction, they could not find sleep at all.
Together, during that night in Duryodhana’s residence,
out of extreme and fierce hatred for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
they brought Kṛṣṇā— who had been tormented by the gambling match— into the assembly hall.
Remembering that, they were consumed by intense remorse, their minds deeply agitated; and as they reflected upon those sufferings of the Pārthas caused by the gambling match,
O King, they passed the night with great difficulty, as if it were a hundred years long.

Then, at the clear dawn, remaining under the decree of destiny, they all performed their necessary duties according to the rites prescribed by rule. Having completed those obligatory tasks and having composed themselves, O Bhārata—
Having appointed Karṇa as their commander-in-chief, they issued orders for the formation of battle arrays and set forth for war.

Having performed the auspicious rites of consecration and having caused the best of the twice-born to recite blessings with vessels of curd, clarified butter, and unbroken grains of rice, they marched out.
Being honored with gold coins, cattle, gold, and costly garments,
and being celebrated with blessings of victory by bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists;
even so, O King, the Pāṇḍavas performed all their daily morning rites.
O King, having resolved upon battle, they emerged from their camps.
Then there commenced a tumultuous and hair-raising combat between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, each desiring the slaughter of the other.

For two days, O King, there was a battle between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, while Karṇa served as the commander-in-chief; it was a sight of wondrous marvel. Then, having caused a vast destruction of enemies in the fray, Vṛṣa—
While the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were looking on, he was struck down by Phalguna.
Then Sañjaya, having gone to the city named after the elephant,
related everything that had occurred in Kurujāṅgala to Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Janamejaya said:
Having heard that the son of the River (Bhīṣma) and Droṇa had been slain by the enemies in battle,
the aged king, the son of Ambikā, fell into the deepest distress.
O best of the twice-born, having heard that Karṇa, the well-wisher of Duryodhana, had been slain, how did that king, being so afflicted, sustain his life—
he upon whom the monarch had placed the hope of victory for his sons?

When he was slain, how did that descendant of Kuru sustain his life? Alas, I consider death to be difficult for men to attain, even when they are in the midst of great distress, since the king did not abandon his life upon hearing that Karṇa had been killed.
Likewise, O Brahmin, [he saw] the aged son of Śantanu and Bāhlīka,
as well as Droṇa, Somadatta, and Bhūriśravas;
and similarly, he saw his other friends, sons, and grandsons who had been struck down.
"O twice-born one, having heard this, that he did not abandon his life-breaths—I consider that a difficult feat. O you whose wealth is asceticism, tell me all of this in detail;
for I am never satiated by hearing the great deeds of my ancestors."
Vaiśampāyana said: O great king, when Karṇa had been slain, Gāvalgaṇi then,
dejected, went to Nāgapura at night on horses equal to the wind in speed.

Having gone to Hastinapura with a deeply distressed mind, he went to the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose kinsmen had been destroyed. Beholding the king, his vital energy struck down by dejection, he approached.

With palms joined in reverence, he bowed his head at the feet of the king; having honored Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth, according to custom, he uttered, "Alas, what misery! and then spoke these words.
"I am Sañjaya, O lord of the earth; I hope you are well?
Having met with this calamity through your own fault, I hope you do not despair today, even though beneficial words were spoken by Vidura, Droṇa, the son of Gaṅgā, and Keśava."
Do you not feel distress by recollecting those things that were not accepted? Do you not feel distress by recollecting the beneficial advice spoken in the assembly hall by Rāma, Nārada, and Kaṇva?
"Recalling those friends headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa, who were devoted to your welfare, but were slain by the enemies in battle— do you perhaps feel no distress?
To the son of the Sūta, who was speaking thus with palms joined in reverence, the king [replied]:
Sighing deeply and afflicted by grief, he spoke these words:
"O Sañjaya, now that the heroic son of Gaṅgā, who possessed divine weapons, has been slain,
and Droṇa, the supreme archer, my mind is deeply distressed."
He who, born of the Vasus, was a radiant warrior who day after day slew ten thousand armored chariot-warriors—
him, the son of Yajñasena, Śikhaṇḍin has slain here.
My mind is deeply distressed by him who is protected by the sons of Pāṇḍu—
he to whom Bhārgava gave the supreme weapon,
and who was personally instructed in the science of archery by Rāma himself in his youth.
Having heard that Drona— by whose grace the sons of Kunti, those princes of great strength,
as well as other lords of the earth, attained the status of great chariot-warriors (mahāratha)—
had been slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle, [the kings were overcome with grief].

My mind is deeply distressed upon hearing that Drona and Bhishma— those great archers true to their word, for whom there was no man equal in the world in the fourfold science of weapons— have been slain. My mind is deeply distressed.

Having heard that Droṇa— whom no man equal to him exists in the three worlds according to the scriptures— has been slain, what did my men do? And regarding the army of the Saṃśaptakas, what did the high-souled Pāṇḍava do?
When Dhananjaya, having displayed his prowess, had sent [the foe] to the abode of Yama,
and when the Nārāyaṇa weapon of the wise son of Droṇa had been neutralized,
what did my men do as their remaining armies were being slaughtered?
I think they have fled in all directions, submerged in an ocean of grief,
like those swimming upon the sea after their ship has been destroyed when Droṇa was slain—
Duryodhana, Karṇa, the Bhoja Kṛtavarman, and the others.
O Sañjaya, when the armies were scattered, what was the complexion on the faces of Śalya, the king of Madra, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, my remaining sons, and likewise those of the others?
"O son of Gavalgaṇa, relate all this exactly as it occurred in truth during the battle— the events concerning both the sons of Pāṇḍu and my own men in their entirety.
Saṃjaya said:

O noble one, having heard what was done by the sons of Pāṇḍu toward the Kauravas, do not give way to distress; for the mind of one who desires [the truth] is not shaken. This is because whatever purpose may come to pass for a man—whether it be destined to fail or destined to succeed—is beyond his control.
Whether that [state] is not attained or is attained, no wise person is distressed.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, no distress whatsoever exists for me as I listen."
"I believe this was ordained of old; speak as you wish.
Sañjaya said: "When the great archer Droṇa had been slain, your sons, those great car-warriors,"

O lord of the people, all those who bore weapons had their faces downcast; dejected and deprived of their senses, they were afflicted with grief and did not speak to one another. Their faces were pale and weary, and they could not look at each other.
O Bhārata, seeing them with such distressed appearances, your troops,
terrified by grief, looked upward repeatedly;
and their weapons, O Indra among kings, were entirely smeared with blood.
Seeing Droṇa struck down,
O Bhārata, the auspicious ornaments bound upon the tips of their fingers fell away;
they appeared, O great king, like stars hanging in the sky.

Seeing his own army thus distressed, motionless, and standing as if deprived of life, O great king, King Duryodhana said to them: "Relying indeed upon the strength of your arms in battle, I have [entered this fray]."
The sons of Pāṇḍu were summoned and this battle was set in motion;
now that Droṇa has been slain, it appears as if despondent.
And the warriors fighting in the encounter are being killed on all sides.
Whether there be victory or even death for one fighting in battle—what indeed is surprising in this? Fight, facing every direction!
And behold the high-souled Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, in combat.
As that great archer of immense strength moved about, employing divine weapons,
Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, would always turn back from him in battle out of sheer terror,
like a small animal before a lion.
By him, through a purely human battle, the mighty Bhīmasena, who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, was reduced to that state; by him,
the heroic Ghaṭotkaca, skilled in divine weapons and a master of illusion, was likewise overcome.
Slain by the infallible spear in battle while roaring a terrible roar,
you shall today behold in the conflict the inexhaustible power of the arms of that wise one, whose heroism is difficult to overcome and who is true to his promise.
You shall behold the prowess of both the high-souled son of Droṇa and the son of Rādhā among the armies of the Pāṇḍus and the Pañcālas;
let those sons of Pāṇḍu witness them like Viṣṇu and Vāsava.
All of you are indeed heroes, wise, and of noble birth;
why then, when united with your armies, would you not slay the sons of Pāṇḍu in battle?
Being virtuous and skilled in weapons, you shall behold one another today.
When this had been said, O Great King, Karṇa Vaikartana, the king,
then made him the commander-in-chief;
so did your son of great heroism, O sinless one, together with his brothers.
Then, having attained the command of the army,
that one of great strength let out a loud lion’s roar and fought,
while all the Sṛñjayas and Pañcālas looked on.
He wrought great slaughter among the Kekayas and the Videhas.
From his bow there issued forth hundreds of streams of arrows,
joined at their tips and nocks like rows of bees.
Having oppressed the Pañcālas and the swift Pāṇḍavas,
and having slain thousands of warriors, he was struck down by Arjuna.
O Bhārata, Sanjaya reached Hastināpura from the camp.
The highly wise Sūta, overwhelmed by grief, agitated and deeply distressed, entered the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra while reflecting upon the terrible slaughter of the son of the Sūta by the Pāṇḍavas.
Having entered the inner apartments, O best of kings, Sañjaya—
his throat choked with tears and deeply distressed— approached the king; and having stood before the king, the son of the Sūta sighed deeply.
O King, Saṃjaya, with a mind not at all joyful, spoke these words:
"I am Saṃjaya, O Great King; salutations to you, O bull of the Bharatas."
Karna Vaikartana has been slain after performing a most difficult feat; having wrought a carnage among the Cedis, Kāśis, Karūṣas, Matsyas, and Somakas,
he lies like a tree uprooted by the wind.
Like a bull in the midst of a cow-pen surrounded by herds of cattle,
he was slain by his enemies as if struck down by a serpent;
O King, he left the Pāṇḍavas, along with Sātyaki, hopeless regarding victory.
Having destroyed thousands of Pāñcāla chariots,
having slain heroic and great archers, and having routed [the enemy] in the ten directions,
Karṇa Vaikartana has been killed by the Pāṇḍava Kirīṭin.

O Great King, having slain Karṇa, the son of Pāṇḍu became free from the shafts that were difficult for the wicked-hearted to remove; he attained freedom from the debt of his enmity, which was as hard to traverse as the ocean. It is as impossible as the drying up of the seas or the falling of the moon and sun.
The shattering of the earth was just like the felling of Karṇa;
and many warriors there, O King, who were seekers of victory, were slain—
kings and princes, heroes with arms like iron clubs.
O King, multitudes of chariots and multitudes of men were slain by the thousands;
elephants and horses were struck down there in that great battle,
and Kṣatriyas from both armies were killed, O Great King.
Having looked at one another there, having committed offenses against each other,
and having reduced the enemy forces to a mere remnant, the bull-like Vaikartana was slain after crossing the Pāṇḍava host and reaching the very shore of Arjuna.
O King, the hope for victory of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the opening of this enmity—
O Great King, that which you did not previously perceive has now been crossed over by the Pāṇḍavas,
even as it was being proclaimed to you by your kinsmen who desired your welfare.
O King, this calamity and great terror has now come upon you because, though desiring the welfare of your sons and wishing for their sovereignty,
you have acted only to their detriment; the fruit of those deeds has now arrived.
O King, Duḥśāsana has been slain exactly as the Pāṇḍava had spoken; Bhīmasena has fulfilled his vow at the head of the army,
and he has drunk the blood of that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in battle.
"O Great King, having performed that most difficult deed by means of the Pāṇḍava," Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Great King, having heard this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā..."
Seeing no end to his grief and believing Suyodhana to be slain,
he fell to the ground overwhelmed, like an elephant that has lost its senses.
When that best of kings had fallen to the ground in such distress, [the others were likewise affected].
A great cry of lamentation arose from the women, O best of the Bharatas;
that sound filled the entire earth in every direction. The women of the Bharata lineage were submerged in a most terrible ocean of grief.
Afflicted by pain and grief, their minds deeply agitated, they wept,
filling their eyes with tears like rivers flowing into the ocean.
And having approached the king, O bull of the Bharatas, Gāndhārī likewise wept.
All the women of the inner apartments fell senseless upon the ground;
then, O King, Sañjaya comforted those distressed women,
who were fainting repeatedly and shedding tears from their eyes.
Those women, though comforted, were trembling again and again like plantain trees being shaken on all sides by the wind;
and Vidura likewise [comforted] the king, the lord whose wisdom was his eye.
Then, sprinkling him with water, he comforted the Kaurava. Having slowly regained consciousness and seeing those women, O King,
that monarch stood silent like one distracted, O lord of the people.
Then, having meditated for a long time and sighing again and again,
he censured his own sons and held the Pāṇḍavas in high regard. Having thus reproached his own intellect as well as that of Śakuni, the son of Subala, he said:
Having meditated for a very long time, trembling again and again,
the king, endowed with fortitude, steadied his mind once more and questioned the charioteer Sañjaya, the son of Gavalgaṇa.
"O Sañjaya, I have heard those words spoken by you.
O Sūta, has Duryodhana not indeed gone to the abode of Yama—
he who was ever desirous of victory, yet now hopeless of victory for my son?"
"Desiring the welfare of his sons, he should always speak with hopelessness. O Sañjaya, tell this story again in its true essence, even though it has already been told.
Having been addressed thus, O Janamejaya, the Sūta spoke to the king.
O King, Vaikartana has been slain along with his sons, who were great chariot-warriors,
and his brothers, those mighty archers and sons of the Sūta who were ready to lay down their lives;
and Duḥśāsana too has been killed by the illustrious Pāṇḍava.
And in the battle, Bhīmasena drank blood out of rage.
Having heard this, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, burning with grief, said to the charioteer: "Wait a moment, Sañjaya!"
"My mind is agitated, dear father; do not say anything for now.
Neither the king nor Sañjaya nor Vidura said anything;
thus the lord of the earth remained silent.
Janamejaya said:
O best of the twice-born, having heard that Karṇa had been slain in battle and that his sons had fled, what did Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the best of kings, say?
He experienced supreme and great suffering born of the calamity involving his son;
tell me truly what he said at that time.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this, O great king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā,
his mind agitated by grief, spoke to the charioteer Sañjaya:
"O dear one, because my own mind was overwhelmed by its own wicked resolve..."

Hearing that Vaikartana has been slain, grief cuts through my vital organs. Among the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas— who have reached the pinnacle of mastery in weapons and who now seek to cross to the further shore of their sorrow— who indeed still live, and who are dead?
"Tell me all of this, for you are indeed skilled, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, the son of Śantanu, invincible and majestic, has been slain."
Having slain one hundred million (an *arbuda*) of the Pāṇḍava warriors over ten days,
the great archer Droṇa— invincible in battle— was subsequently killed after he had destroyed the multitudes of Pāñcāla charioteers, O you of the golden chariot.
When half of the army had been slain by Bhīṣma and the high-souled Droṇa, Karṇa Vaikartana was killed. O great king, the mighty prince Vivimśati was also slain.
Having slain hundreds of Ānarta warriors, he was himself struck down in battle. Then your son Vikarṇa, the hero, remembering the vow of the Kṣatriyas,
stood facing his enemies even though his mounts and weapons were exhausted.
Remembering his vow, Bhīmasena struck down the two mighty princes of Avanti, Vinda and Anuvinda, after they had inflicted many terrible sufferings upon him at the hands of Duryodhana.
Having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, they have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata;
indeed, ten kingdoms here, headed by the kingdom of Sindhu,
remain under the control of that hero who stands under your command.
O King, having conquered eleven akṣauhiṇīs with his sharpened arrows,
Arjuna slew the immensely powerful Jayadratha;
likewise, he slew Duryodhana’s son, who was swift and fierce in battle.
While still following his father’s instructions, he was struck down by the son of Subhadrā;
likewise, the heroic son of Duḥśāsana, mighty-armed and fierce in battle,
was sent to the abode of Yama by the son of Draupadī through his prowess.
The lord of the Kirātas dwelling on the coastal marshlands of the ocean,
the virtuous Bhagadatta, was a dear and highly esteemed friend of the King of the Gods; that protector of the earth was ever devoted to the dharma of the Kṣatriyas.
Having displayed his prowess, Dhanañjaya sent him to the abode of Yama.
Likewise, O King, the highly illustrious Bhūriśravas, the son of Somadatta and scion of the Kuru lineage,
that hero was slain in battle by Sātyaki.
Śrutāyu, the Ambaṣṭha, a bowman among the Kṣatriyas,
was slain by Savyasācin while moving fearlessly in battle;
so too was your son, who was always skilled in weapons and fierce in combat.
O Great King, Duḥśāsana was struck down by Bhīmasena;
O King, Sudakṣiṇa, whose wonderful elephant division numbered many thousands,
was slain in battle by Savyasācin.

Having slain many hundreds of enemies, the lord of the Kosalas was sent to the abode of Yama by the prowess of Saubhadra; and that great car-warrior, having fought Bhīmasena many times, [was likewise slain].
Your son Citrasena has been struck down by Bhīmasena;
the heroic son of the King of Madra, who increased the fear of his enemies and bore a sword and shield, that illustrious one has been felled by the son of Subhadrā.
Equal to Karṇa in battle, while Karṇa looked on, Vṛṣasena— possessed of great energy, swift in the use of weapons, and firm in his resolve—
remembered the slaughter of Abhimanyu as well as his own vow.
Through his prowess, Dhanañjaya sent him to the abode of Yama—
that lord of the earth who was perpetually engaged in enmity with the Pāṇḍavas; having proclaimed his hostility, Śrutāyus was struck down by the son of Pṛthā.

O Sire, the valiant son of Śalya, Rukmaratha, was slain in battle by Sahadeva— your brother-in-law and maternal cousin, O King. Also slain were the aged King Bhagīratha and Bṛhatkṣatra of the Kekayas.
O King, exerting themselves with great prowess, those two most heroic warriors were slain; Bhagadatta’s son, wise and possessed of great strength,
was struck down in battle by Nakula, who moved like a hawk.
Likewise, O King, your grandfather Bāhlīka, along with the Bāhlīkas,
was sent to the abode of Yama by Bhīmasena through his prowess;
and so too was the mighty Jayatsena, the son of Jarāsaṃdha.
The King of Magadha, that hero bearing sword and shield who increased the fear of his enemies, was slain in battle by the high-souled son of Subhadrā;
whirling like a circle of fire, Somadatta was struck down.
"O King, your son Durmukha and the great car-warrior Duḥsaha,
both of whom considered themselves heroes, have been slain by Bhīmasena with his mace.
So too have Durmarṣaṇa, Durviṣaha, and the great car-warrior Durjaya."
Having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, they have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata;
both brothers, bulls among the Kaliṅgas, intoxicated by battle,
having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Your minister Vṛṣavarman and your charioteer, who possessed supreme heroism,
were sent to the abode of Yama by Bhīmasena through his prowess. The great king, who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, was likewise slain.
Together with his followers, he was slain by the son of Pāṇḍu, Savyasācin; O great king, two thousand Vasātis, skilled strikers,
and all the valiant Śūrasenas were struck down in battle.
The Abhīṣāhas, clad in armor and striking with force, intoxicated by pride;
and the Śibis, noble chariot-warriors together with the Kaliṅgas—have all been slain.
They were raised in Gokula from childhood and were supremely skilled in battle.
Those heroes who had turned back from flight were slain by Savyasācin;
the many thousands of ranks and the hosts of Saṃśaptakas—
all of them, having encountered Pārtha, went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
"O Great King, your two brothers-in-law, the kings Vṛṣaka and Ācala,
who were both valiant for your sake, have been slain by Savyasācin. Ugrakarmā was a great archer both by name and by his deeds."

O Great King, the king of Śālva was struck down by Bhīmasena; and O Great King, both Oghavān and Bṛhanta, exerting their prowess together for the sake of their ally, went to the abode of Vaivasvata in battle.
Likewise, O lord of the people, Kṣemadhūrti, the best of chariot-warriors,
was slain in battle by Bhīmasena with his mace, O King;
and so too was the king Jalasaṃdha, a great archer of immense strength.
Having caused a great slaughter in battle,
Alāyudha, the lord of the Rākṣasas, who rode upon a chariot drawn by donkeys, was slain by Sātyaki;
yet Ghaṭotkaca, exerting his prowess, dispatched him to the abode of Yama.
O Bhārata, the valiant and powerful brothers,
the sons of Rādhā, the sons of the Sūta, and the great car-warriors who were their brothers,
as well as all the Kekayas, have been slain by Savyasācin.
Having wrought the destruction of their enemies, they have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata:
the Mālavas, the Madrakas, and the Draviḍas of fierce prowess;
the Yaudheyas, the Lalitthas, the Kṣudrakas, and the Uśīnaras as well.
The Māvellakas, Tuṇḍikeras, Sāvitrīputrakas, and Añcalas—
those from the east, north, west, and south, O noble one—
along with multitudes of foot soldiers and tens of thousands of horses, were all slain.
The throngs of chariots were destroyed, and the excellent elephants were slain;
along with their banners, weapons, armor, garments, and ornaments, the heroes—
who had been diligently nurtured by their lineage over a long period of time— were all brought down by Time.

O King, those of immeasurable strength, who were intent on slaying one another, were slain in battle by Pārtha of unwearied deeds; other heroes likewise perished in that encounter as they met one another in combat.

"O King, these and many other kings along with their hosts have been slain by the thousands in battle— about whom you ask me. Thus did this destruction occur in the encounter between Karṇa and Arjuna."
Just as Vṛtra was slain by Mahendra, as Rāvaṇa was slain by Rāma, and as Mura was struck down in battle and killed by Kṛṣṇa,
and just as Kārtavīrya was killed by Rāma Bhārgava; so too [was he].

A hero accompanied by his kinsmen and relatives, fierce in battle and intoxicated with the passion for war, having waged a great and terrible combat in the field of battle renowned throughout the three worlds—
just as Mahiṣa was by Skanda, or Andhaka by Rudra.
Likewise, O King, Karṇa— the best among strikers, who was intoxicated with the pride of battle— was slain by Arjuna in a duel, along with his ministers and kinsmen;
he from whom the Dhārtarāṣṭras held their hope for victory and who was the very source of the enmity.
O King, that which you did not perceive before has now been crossed over by the Pāṇḍavas.
Though you were previously advised, O Great King, by your well-wishing kinsmen, you did not act; rather, it was by the force of destiny and fate.
This great calamity has now come upon you,

O King, as a result of those actions which, though intended for their benefit by you who desired their welfare, were in fact harmful to your sons who were greedy for the kingdom; the fruit of those deeds has now arrived.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear Sañjaya, you have told me of my own men slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas;
now tell me of those among the Pāṇḍavas who were slain by my men."
Saṃjaya said:
Those Kuntis, valiant in battle, possessed of great courage and great strength,
have been struck down in combat by Bhīṣma, along with their followers and ministers.
Men, horses, along with elephants and chariots by the hundreds,
as well as Nārāyaṇas, Ballavas, and other Rāmas by the hundreds—
those who were devoted to victory, were all slain in battle by Bhīṣma.
Equal to Kirīṭin in battle, both in heroism and in strength,
Satyajit was slain in combat by Droṇa, who is ever true to his promise;
and the Pāñcālas, those great archers, O King, were for the most part filled with indignation.
Having encountered Droṇa, they went to the abode of Vaivasvata;
likewise, the two aged kings Virāṭa and Drupada, along with their sons,
exerting their prowess for the sake of their ally, were slain by Droṇa in battle.
He who, even as a youth, was a match for Savyasācin in battle,
and who was as invincible as Keśava and superior in power to Baladeva—
he, skilled in the art of war, having wrought a great slaughter, [now lies here].

Surrounded by six great ministers on supreme chariots who were unable to overcome Bībhatsu, Abhimanyu was struck down. That hero, rendered carless and established in the duty of a Kṣatriya, was thus slain.
O Great King, the son of Duḥśāsana slew the son of Subhadrā in battle;
and the illustrious and valiant slayer of the Paṭaccaras, surrounded by a vast army and accompanied by the Ambaṣṭhas, fought for the sake of his allies.

Having encountered the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Duryodhana, in battle and having wrought a great slaughter, he went to the abode of Vaivasvata. Bṛhanta, however, was a great archer, skilled in weapons, and fierce in combat.
Maṇimān and Daṇḍadhāra, both kings intoxicated by battle, were sent to the abode of Yama by Duḥśāsana through his prowess;
exerting their valor for the sake of their friend, they were struck down by Droṇa.
The great car-warrior Aṃśumān, the king of the Bhojas, along with his army,
was sent to the abode of Yama by the son of Bharadvāja through his prowess.
O Bhārata, Sāmudra and Citrasena, together with their son, [were likewise slain].
Samudrasena was forcibly sent to the abode of Yama; likewise, Anūpavāsī, Nīla, and the heroic Vyāghradatta were sent to the abode of Yama by Aśvatthāman, O Great King.

Having wrought a great slaughter with his variegated weapons and fighting with diverse maneuvers, Citrāyudha, who was as firm in battle as Vṛkodara, was slain by Karṇa in the fight. The son of the Kekayas was likewise struck down in combat.
The powerful Janamejaya, a mountaineer and a warrior with the mace, was struck down by his own brother, the Kekaya prince, who displayed great prowess;
O Great King, he was felled by your son Durmukha.
O King, those two tigers among men, shining like two radiant planets,
were simultaneously sent to heaven by Droṇa with his arrows.
And other kings, fighting back with great prowess, O lord of the people, [were likewise struck down].
Having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, they have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Purujit Kuntibhoja, the maternal uncle of Savyasācin,
has been sent to the worlds won in battle by the arrows of Droṇa.
Abhibhū, the King of Kāśī, surrounded by many Kāśikas,
was made to lay down his body in battle by the son of Vasudāna;
as were Amitaujas, Yudhāmanyu, and the heroic Uttamaujas.
O King, O honorable one, Amitaujas, Jayatsena, the heroic Jayānīka, Amitaujas, Bṛhatkṣetra,
and Kṣatradeva the ruler of the earth were all slain by your grandson Lakṣmaṇa.
Bṛhatkṣatra, the great archer, and King Kṣatradeva, O sire,
having slain hundreds of heroes, were themselves struck down by their enemies in battle;
as were Kṣatradharman of the Pañcālas and Kṣatravarmā, O noble one.
O King,
O Bhārata, Śikhaṇḍin’s son Kṣatradeva, a lord of warriors and a supreme archer, was sent to the abode of Yama by Droṇa; he was slain in battle by Lakṣmaṇa, your grandson.
Sucitra and Citradharman, father and son, both great car-warriors of immense prowess who were roaming the field, were slain by Droṇa in battle; likewise,
O Great King, Vārdhakṣemi, having wrought a carnage in the fray, was killed.
Having encountered the exhaustion of his weapons and attained supreme peace after causing a carnage in battle, Purujit, the supreme king,
and Senābindu, the best of monarchs, scorched his enemies in combat.
O great king, Dhṛṣṭaketu, the preeminent chariot-warrior of the Cedis, was struck down by Bāhlika, the descendant of Kuru;
having performed a deed difficult to accomplish, O great king, he departed for the abode of Vaivasvata.
Likewise, O dear one, Satyadhṛti, having caused a carnage in battle and exerted his prowess for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas, was sent to the abode of Yama;
so too Senābindu, the best of the Kurus, having caused a carnage in battle.
O lord of the earth, Suketu, the son of Śiśupāla,
having slain his enemies in battle, was himself killed by Droṇa in the fray. Also,
Śaṅkha, the son of Virāṭa, and Uttara, the great car-warrior, [were slain].
Performing a most great deed, they went to the abode of Vaivasvata;
likewise, the heroic Satyadhṛti, the valiant Madirāśva,
and the courageous Sūryadatta were slain by the arrows of Droṇa.
The illustrious Śatānīka, the younger brother of Matsya,
has been struck down; and the valiant Śreṇimān, O great king, while fighting with prowess and having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, has gone to the abode of Vaivasvata.
In that same way, O King, the valiant Magadha, the slayer of enemy heroes,
skilled in supreme weapons,
was sent to the abode of Yama by Bhīṣma while he was fighting with great prowess.
And Vasudāna, while causing a great slaughter in the midst of battle,
was dispatched to the abode of Yama by the son of Bharadvāja through his prowess.
And the powerful King of Pāṇḍya, though valiant, was overcome by the one endowed with mighty arms.
There, he was struck down by Aśvatthāman and sent indeed to the abode of Yama.
These and many other great car-warriors (*mahāratha*) of the Pāṇḍavas were slain by Droṇa through his prowess— those concerning whom you ask me.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O best of speakers, since the heroes of this army of mine have been slain, tell me,
O Sūta, who among those here still live."
"Once these whom you have enumerated are slain today, even those whom you consider unslain shall be regarded as conquerors of heaven. Sañjaya said:
O King, in him were placed great weapons—
various, brilliant, of four kinds,
divine, and well-honored.
By Droṇa, the best of heroic brahmins,
he was made a great car-warrior— skillful, swift-handed,
with firm weapons, a firm grip, and firm arrows.
That energetic and powerful son of Droṇa stands firm, desiring to fight for your sake;
he is the son of Hṛdika, a resident of Ānarta.
The great chariot-warrior, the best among the Sātvatas, Kṛtavarman himself of the Bhojas, skilled in weapons,
stands ready, desiring to fight for your sake.
O King, Śāradvata Gautama was also there,
possessed of great strength and a warrior skilled in many wonderful weapons; he wielded a magnificent, massive bow capable of bearing a heavy burden.
The mighty son of the King of Kekaya, having taken up his position and being intent on battle,
stood with his chariot yoked to excellent horses and adorned with banners.
Having mounted his excellent chariot, O hero of the Kurus,
the son of Ārtāyani stands firm in battle, difficult to shake, desiring to fight for your sake.
The leader of your army, the foremost of your men,
being swift and desiring to make that word true, set aside his sister's sons, the Pāṇḍavas.
Having previously promised before Ajātaśatru to diminish the splendor of the Sūta’s son in battle,
he who is invincible and possesses prowess equal to Śakra—
Śalya stands here, desiring to fight for your sake,
with well-bred horses from Sindh, the mountains,
the river-lands, Kamboja, Vanāyu, and Bahlika.
The King of Gandhāra, joined by his own forces and desiring to fight for your sake, stands ready,
O King, along with his son.
O King, that gambler fond of strife, having been stationed by the leading Gāndhāras and Yavanas,
stands ready to fight for your sake.
Likewise, O lord of men, your son Kurumitra, that hero of the Kurus, having mounted a chariot with the brilliance of fire and the sun, stood firm.
Like the sun shining in a cloudless sky,
Duryodhana, possessed of great heroism, stood in the midst of the elephant host together with the foremost warriors of his army.
Stationed in his chariot adorned with Jāmbūnada gold,
that hero among men stood in the midst of the kings, desiring to fight in battle.
Clad in variegated armor of Jāmbūnada gold,
Padmaprabha shone like a fire with little smoke,
or like the radiant sun appearing amidst the clouds.
Likewise, Suṣeṇa, with sword and shield in hand,
and your heroic son Satyasena,
stood together with Citrasena.
With joyful hearts and desiring to fight in battle,
the Bharata princes— restrained by their sense of honor—
were Citrāyudha, Śrutakarman, and Jaya.
Ugrāyudha, Kṣaṇabhojin, Sudarśa, Jārāsaṃdhi, Prathama, Adṛḍha,
Śala, Satyavrata, and Duḥśala.
Stationed there, powerful and desiring to fight,
was the prince, the lord of the Kaitavyas, who considers himself a hero and is a slayer of enemies in every battle.
Patrin, Hayi, and Nāgarathaprayāyin are stationed there,
desiring to fight for your sake;
as are the heroes Śrutāyu and Śrutāyudha.
That hero Citrāṅgada, clad in variegated armor,
and those foremost of men who stood firm in the army— striking warriors, proud, and true to their word.
The high-souled Satyasena, the son of Karṇa,
stood firm in battle, desiring to fight;
then there were two other sons of Karṇa, worthy of the best honors.
O King, these two light-handed warriors,
stationed there with great and unbreakable strength that cannot be overcome by those of little fortitude,
have taken their stand and are ready to fight for your sake.
O King, stationed in the midst of the elephant host with these and other preeminent warriors of immeasurable power, he remained firm.
Just as Mahendra [is for victory], so was the Kuru king Dhṛtarāṣṭra; he said:
"Those who are alive among the others have been described by you exactly as they are."
"Thus I perceive this clearly from the attainment of the facts.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, was speaking thus, then—

Hearing that his own army— its foremost heroes slain, shattered, and with only a small remnant left— had fallen into such a state, he was overcome by confusion, his senses agitated by grief. While fainting, he spoke and said, "Wait a moment, Sañjaya!"

"My mind is agitated, O dear one, having heard this most grievous and unpleasant news; my heart faints and I am unable to support my limbs. Having spoken these words, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, [fell silent].
Then that lord of the earth became distraught in mind.
Janamejaya said:
"Having heard that Karṇa was slain in battle, as well as my sons who did not flee..."
O best of the twice-born, when the lord of men had somewhat recovered from the great and supreme sorrow born of his son's calamity, what did he say at that time? Tell me,
as I ask you, what he spoke on that occasion.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard of the death of Karṇa— an event as incredible and marvelous as it was, a terrifying delusion for all beings like the overturning of Mount Meru— [the king was struck with grief].
It was like the delusion of mind of the high-minded Bhārgava;
like the defeat of Indra, the performer of terrible deeds, by his enemies;
or like the falling from heaven to the earth of the sun of great splendor.
It was like the inconceivable drying up of the ocean of inexhaustible waters;
it was like the wondrous total destruction of the earth, the sky, and the lords of the quarters;
it was like the fruitlessness of both merit and sin.
Having reflected skillfully with his intellect, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men,
considered that this [destruction] would not happen; yet, reflecting upon the death of Karṇa,
he thought that such destruction might indeed occur because of the self-nature of living beings.
Burning with the fire of grief as if his very heart were being smelted,
his soul shattered, sighing piteously and crying out "Alas! Alas!",
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, lamented in great sorrow, O Great King.
And, extremely overwhelmed by doubt, he spoke these words again.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, that hero, the son of Adhiratha, possesses the prowess of a lion or an elephant."
With shoulders like a bull and possessing the eyes, gait, and voice of a bull,
he is a bull among men who never retreats in battle,
even against the enemy Mahendra himself; a youth with a body as firm as a thunderbolt.
At the sound of whose bowstring and the roar of whose shower of arrows,
chariots, horses, men, and elephants do not stand their ground in battle;
relying upon that mighty-armed and infallible slayer of enemy hosts—
Duryodhana instigated this enmity with the mighty sons of Pāṇḍu. How was that Karṇa— the best of chariot-warriors, a tiger among men, and one of unbearable prowess— slain by Pārtha in battle?
Relying on the strength of his own arms, he did not consider Acyuta, nor Dhanañjaya, nor those other Vṛṣṇis to be eternal; for he regarded the two—
Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa, armed with the Śārṅga and Gāṇḍīva bows— as invincible when united.
"I alone shall strike him down from his celestial chariot in battle"— thus did he,
deluded by greed, constantly speak in a weak voice to the distressed Duryodhana, who was afflicted by his longing for the kingdom.
And he who has conquered exceedingly powerful enemies, even those difficult to defeat—
the Gāndhāras, Madrakas, Matsyas, Trigartas, Taṅgaṇas, and Śakas;
the Pāñcālas, Videhas, Kuṇindas, and the people of Kāśi and Kosala.
In former times, that hero, having conquered in battle the Suhmas, Aṅgas, Puṇḍras, Niṣādas, Vaṅgas, Kīcakas, Vatsas, Kaliṅgas, Taralas, Aśmakas, and likewise the Ṛṣikas, made them payers of tribute.

Having conquered in battle the Śabaras, the Parahūṇas, the Saralas who face the east, as well as the lords of the Mleccha kingdoms, and those dwelling in forts and forests— the hero, with his exceedingly sharp arrows feathered with heron plumes— [subdued them].
Having thus conquered all his enemies, he caused [the enemy] to suffer;
with volleys of well-sharpened, extremely keen arrows feathered with heron plumes,
he acted for the sake of Duryodhana’s prosperity and for the sake of victory.
How was Senāgopa, that master of supreme weapons,
slain by the Pāṇḍavas— those heroes who were capable and endowed with great prowess?
Vṛṣa is Mahendra among the gods, and Karṇa is likewise a bull (vṛṣa) among men.
We have never heard of any other bull among men in the worlds like him;
Karna Vaikartana, the master of divine weapons and possessed of great splendor, is a bull.
Among horses, Uccaiḥśravas is the best; among kings, Vaiśravaṇa is the best.
Mahendra was the best among the gods, and Karṇa was the best among strikers;
joined by heroic kings who were capable and endowed with prowess,
he then conquered the entire earth for the sake of Duryodhana’s prosperity.
Having obtained him [as a minister], the King of Magadha— through conciliation, honor, wealth, and respect—
subjugated the circle of kings, with the exception of the Kauravas and the Yādavas.
Hearing that Karṇa had been slain by Savyasācin in single combat, [he was deeply affected].
I am submerged in an ocean of grief, like one whose boat has been wrecked at sea; having heard that the bull among men, the best of chariot-warriors, has been slain in single combat,
I am immersed in an ocean of sorrow, like a man without a raft upon the great deep.
"O Saṃjaya, if I do not perish despite such sorrows as these,
I consider my heart to be harder than a diamond and difficult to break,
having heard of this defeat of my kinsmen, relatives, and friends."
"O charioteer, what man other than I in this world would not give up his life? I would choose poison, fire, a fall from a mountain peak,
the departure on the Great Journey, drowning in water, or fasting unto death."
"For I shall not be able to endure these painful hardships, O Sañjaya;
as I reflect upon them, I sink down, and my mind is utterly bewildered.
Sañjaya said:
"In wealth, lineage, fame, asceticism, and sacred learning, the virtuous today regard you as equal to Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
O King, you are like a great seer in your Vedic knowledge; you have accomplished all that is to be done."
"Compose yourself; do not set your mind on despair.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I consider destiny alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort!"
Where Karna, who resembled Rama himself, was slain in battle—
having struck down Yudhiṣṭhira’s army and the multitudes of Pāñcāla chariots,
that great car-warrior having scorched all the directions with a rain of arrows.
Having bewildered the Pārthas in battle like the wielder of the thunderbolt against the Asuras,
how does he lie slain, like a tree uprooted by the wind?
I see no end to my grief, just as there is no end to the spray of the ocean.
My anxiety increases intensely, and even the desire for death arises within me,
having heard of the slaying of Karṇa and the victory of Phalguna. O Sañjaya, I consider the killing of Karṇa to be incredible.
"Surely my heart is made of the essence of adamant and is exceedingly firm,
since it does not shatter upon hearing that Karṇa, that tiger among men, has been slain.
Truly, a very long lifespan must have been ordained for me by the gods in the past."
"O Sañjaya, since I still live here in great misery having heard that Karṇa has been slain, shame on this life of mine today, now that I am bereft of my friend! O Sañjaya,
today I have reached this contemptible state."
"I shall live a miserable life, an object of pity for all, dull-witted as I am. Having previously been honored by the whole world,
O charioteer, how shall I be able to go on living, now that I have been humiliated?"
"O Sañjaya, I have fallen into a calamity that is more painful than pain itself.
Therefore, now that Bhīṣma has been slain and the high-souled Droṇa as well,
I see no remnant of my army left once the Sūtaputra has been killed in battle."
For he was indeed the great protector of my sons, O Sañjaya;
that hero, discharging many arrows, has been slain in battle.
What purpose, indeed, is there for my life without that bull among men?
Surely that great car-warrior, afflicted by arrows,
has fallen from his chariot like the peak of a mountain split apart by the stroke of a thunderbolt;
drenched in blood, he surely lies there adorning the earth.
Like an elephant struck down by a rutting elephant,
Karna— the very strength of the Dhartarashtras and the source of fear for the Pandavas,
the peerless standard for all archers— has been slain by Arjuna.
For that hero, the great archer who granted fearlessness to his sons,
lies slain like Bala struck down by Śakra;
he is like a journey on foot for the lame, or a desired object for the poor.
The intention of Duryodhana was like gnats to one who is parched with thirst; a task conceived in one way turns out quite another. Alas! Destiny is indeed powerful, and Time is difficult to overcome.
Fleeing in a piteous manner, dejected in spirit and lacking in manliness—
O Sūta, has my son Duḥśāsana not been slain?
O dear one, has he not committed some base act in the battle?
"O Sañjaya, my son Duryodhana has been slain in battle;
I hope that hero was not killed in a manner such as the other Kṣatriyas were.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having lamented thus, Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
deeply afflicted by grief and with eyes agitated by sorrow, spoke again to Sañjaya:
"He who conquered the Vatsas, Kāmbojas, and Ambaṣṭhas, along with the Kekayas..."

Having conquered the Gāndhāras and the Videhas in battle for the sake of his purpose, Duryodhana— being deluded— did not accept Yudhiṣṭhira’s words that there should always be no war, just as a fool refuses wholesome medicine.

While lying upon a bed of arrows, the high-souled Bhīṣma requested water from Pārtha; he, for his part, pierced the surface of the earth. Seeing that stream of water produced by the Pāṇḍava, [Bhīṣma was satisfied].
The mighty-armed one said, "O father, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas;
for through tranquility there will be peace, and let this war end. Enjoy the earth together with the sons of Pāṇḍu in a spirit of brotherhood."
"Surely my son grieves because he did not follow his words;
now those words of the far-sighted one have come to pass.
But I, O Sañjaya, am one whose ministers are slain and whose sons are killed."
Having fallen into distress because of the gambling, he is like a bird with its wings clipped.
For just as boys, O Sañjaya, having caught a bird and cut off its wings, release it joyfully while playing; so have I become.
Because its wings have been severed, its flight is no longer possible;
likewise, I too have become like a bird with clipped wings. I am exhausted, deprived of all resources, without kinsmen, and abandoned by my relatives.
"To which direction shall I go, wretched and fallen under the power of the enemy—
he who, as a lord, conquered the earth for the sake of Duryodhana’s prosperity,
has now been defeated by the heroic, capable, and valorous Pāṇḍavas?"
When that great archer Karṇa had been slain in battle by Kirīṭin, which heroes rallied around him? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
Was he not slain alone in the fight, abandoned by the Pāṇḍavas?
"O hero, you previously spoke of how those heroes were struck down—
how Śikhaṇḍin, with his finest arrows, felled Bhīṣma, the best among all wielders of weapons, in battle while he was not fighting back."
Likewise, when Draupadi’s son had dropped all his weapons in battle, the great archer Droṇa—
having heard the words of Dharmarāja that Aśvatthāman was slain—
became absorbed in yoga and was covered with many arrows.
O Sañjaya,

I have heard that Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been struck down; indeed, I heard that they were slain by Dhṛṣṭadyumna while he raised his sword, and that these two were killed through treachery in particular.
For even the wielder of the thunderbolt himself could not slay Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle while they were fighting according to the rules; this I tell you truly.
But Karna, when discharging many divine weapons—
How did death touch that hero in battle, who was like Indra himself—
he to whom Purandara gave, as a reward for his earrings, a divine spear adorned with gold, possessing the brilliance of lightning, and capable of slaying enemies?
He whose divine, gold-adorned, feathered arrow with a serpent’s head lay there,
slain upon sandalwood logs— O destroyer of enemies—
he who held in contempt the great car-warriors headed by Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
He learned the most terrible Brahma-weapon from the son of Jamadagni; and that mighty-armed one,
seeing Drona and the others turned away and afflicted by arrows,
shattered the bow of Subhadra’s son with his own shafts.
And he who, having deprived his brother Bhīmasena— who possessed the strength of ten thousand elephants, the speed of the wind, and was unshakable— of his chariot, mocked him; and who,
having conquered Sahadeva with straight-jointed arrows...
Out of compassion and because he knew the dharma, he did not kill him after having deprived him of his chariot;
and he, having destroyed thousands of illusions,
struck down Ghaṭotkaca, the lord of the Rākṣasas who was fierce in battle, with Śakra’s spear.

For all these days in battle, the heroic Dhanañjaya, being afraid, did not come for a single combat; how then was he slain in the fray? As for those warriors of the Saṃśaptakas who were always challenging him elsewhere—
"Having slain these, I shall afterwards slay the son of Vikartana in battle"—
proclaiming this and avoiding the Suta's son in the fray,
how was that hero slain by Pārtha in the great conflict?
If his chariot had not been stuck, or if his bow had not shattered,
or if his weapons had not failed him, how could he have been slain by his enemies?
For who indeed would be able [to defeat] Karṇa in battle as he brandished his great bow?
As he was discharging terrible arrows and celestial weapons in battle to conquer that tiger among men who was rushing forward like a tiger,
his bow must surely have been severed, or else his chariot has sunk into the earth.
Or perhaps my weapons have been lost, as you tell me he has been slain;
for I see no other cause for his destruction. As long as I have not slain Arjuna, I shall not wash my feet.
Such was the most formidable vow of that high-souled one,
of whom Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, that bull among men, being constantly afraid in the forest,
did not obtain sleep for thirteen years.
Relying upon the prowess of that heroic and high-souled one,
my son forcibly dragged my wife into the assembly hall in the presence of the Pāṇḍavas,
even as they looked on from within that very hall.
In the assembly of the Kurus, he addressed Pāñcālī as "the wife of a slave":
"O Kṛṣṇā, your husbands do not exist; they are all like sterile sesame seeds. O woman of excellent complexion, attend upon another husband."

How was that son of a Sūta slain by his enemies— he who formerly, out of rage, used to address harsh words to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly hall? [This would have been so] if Bhīṣma, who prided himself on battle, or Droṇa, who was indomitable in combat, had been present.
Out of partiality, Suyodhana will not slay the sons of Kuntī;
I shall slay them all. Let the fever of your mind depart.
What can the Gāṇḍīva bow or the two inexhaustible quivers do?
How indeed was that one with the shoulders of a bull slain by Arjuna as he charged forward,
smeared with smooth sandalwood paste and disregarding the fierce touch of arrows released from the *Gāṇḍīva*?

"O Sañjaya, he who had no fear even for a moment of the Pārthas, along with their sons and Janārdana, relying solely on the strength of his own arms— he, Kṛṣṇa, looked upon the Pārthas while saying, 'Indeed, you are without a protector.'"
I do not believe that his death could be brought about even by the gods together with Indra, should they rush against him in opposition; how much less so, my dear father, by the Pāṇḍavas?
For he does not even touch the bowstring while grasping his finger-guards.
No man whatsoever is able to stand before the son of Adhiratha;
even this earth might be deprived of the rays of the light of the moon and sun,
but the death of that lord of men, who never retreats in battles, is not possible.
If that dull-witted and evil-minded one, together with his brother Duḥśāsana as his companion, chose to reject Vāsudeva’s proposal,
it was surely because he saw Karna— whose shoulders were like those of a bull— already struck down.
I think my son is grieving that Duḥśāsana has been slain;
having heard that Vaikartana was killed by Savyasācin in single combat,
and seeing the Pāṇḍavas victorious, what indeed did Duryodhana say?
Having heard that Durmarṣaṇa and Vṛṣasena had been slain in battle,
and seeing his army broken and being slaughtered by the great car-warriors,
as well as the kings turning their backs and intent on flight—
Seeing the chariot-warriors fleeing, I think my son Duryodhana is grieving;
for he spoke something out of the turmoil of sorrow and suffering.
Inflated with pride, foolish-minded, and intolerant,
what did Duryodhana say upon seeing his army’s spirit destroyed—
he who had himself created this great enmity while being restrained by his circle of friends?
When the army was mostly struck down by Pradhāna, what did Duryodhana say?
Having seen his brother slain in battle by Bhīmasena while he himself was drinking blood,
what indeed did Duryodhana say?

What did Karṇa say when he was defeated in the assembly hall by the King of Gāndhāra, after having previously boasted that he would slay Arjuna in battle? Having once played at dice with joy and having deceived the Pāṇḍavas, what did he say now?
O dear one, when Karṇa had been slain, what did Śakuni Saubala say?
And seeing Karṇa struck down, what did the great archer Kṛtavarman, the great car-warrior of the Sātvatas and son of Hṛdika, say?
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas attend upon his instruction,
desiring to master the science of archery under the wise son of Drona.
He is young, endowed with beauty, handsome to behold, and possessed of great fame.
"O Sañjaya, when Karṇa was slain, what did Aśvatthāman say?
And Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, who has attained mastery in the science of archery and knows the supreme truth— what, my dear, did he say when Karṇa was killed?"

The king of Madra, the great archer Śalya, who graces the assembly— what did that powerful lord of the Madras, the ruler of the Sauviras, say regarding all that was ordained by him, namely, how Karṇa was struck down?
Having seen him slain, what did all those warriors— those elephants among men who were difficult to conquer— and whatever kings from across the earth had come to fight,
say upon seeing the son of Vaikartana killed, O Sañjaya?
When the hero Karṇa— the tiger among chariot-warriors and bull among men— had been slain,
O Sañjaya, what was the state of your respective divisions?
And how was Śalya, the king of the Madras and best of chariot-warriors, appointed [as his charioteer]?
Tell me that, O Sañjaya:
who protected the right wheel of Vaikartana’s chariot in the battle,
and who protected the left wheel, or who stood behind that hero?
Which heroes struck Karna, and which cowards fled in fear?
And how was the great chariot-warrior Karna slain while you were all assembled together?
And how did the heroic Pāṇḍavas advance against that great chariot-warrior?
Discharging showers of arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of rain—
that divine and supreme great arrow with a serpent's head—
how did it become useless? Tell me that, Saṃjaya.
O Sañjaya, now that the height of this army of mine has been struck down,
I see no remnant left once the peak has been crushed.
For those two heroes, the great archers and best of the Kurus, were fighting for my sake.
Having heard that Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been slain, what purpose indeed is there in my life? And I cannot endure that the son of Rādhā, the ornament of battle, has been killed—
he whose strength of arms was equal to ten thousand elephants.
Tell me, Sañjaya, what occurred when Droṇa was slain, regarding the battle between the Kauravas and their enemies, and concerning those heroic men;
and how Karṇa engaged in combat with the sons of Kuntī.
"And how it was that the slayer of his enemies became pacified in battle—let that be told.
Saṃjaya said:
"O Bhārata, when that great archer Droṇa had been slain on that day,"
When the son of Droṇa, that great car-warrior, had rendered his resolve futile,
and while the Kaurava army was thus fleeing, O Great King,
Pārtha, having arrayed his own troops, stood firm together with his brothers.
O bull of the Bharatas, perceiving him stationed there and seeing his own army fleeing, your son restrained them through his prowess;
establishing his own division, he stood firm upon the strength of his arms.
O Bhārata, after fighting for a very long time with the Pāṇḍavas—
who were joyful, had found their mark, and had been exerting themselves for a long duration—
he reached the hour of twilight and ordered a withdrawal.
Having stationed that formidable army— which was afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fear,
and exhausted by great toil as well as by the slaughter of Droṇa—
they performed terrible deeds on the battlefield throughout that dreadful night.
Having reached their encampment and rested, that army became joyful. Having withdrawn the troops and entered their own camps, the Kurus then deliberated upon a counsel for their own benefit.
Seated upon most excellent couches provided with costly coverlets and fine seats,
they were like the immortals reclining on comfortable beds. O Bhārata, when those princes had thus taken their seats...
Then King Duryodhana, having addressed those great archers with most beautiful conciliation, spoke words appropriate for the occasion:
"O best among the wise, all of you, declare your counsel without delay."
"O kings, since things have come to this pass, what action must be taken that will accomplish our purpose?
When the lord of men had spoken thus, those lions among men, eager for battle and seated upon their thrones, then made various gestures.
Having observed the gestures of those who were willing to sacrifice their lives in battle,
and having gazed upon the face of the king, which possessed the splendor of the rising sun,
the wise son of the preceptor, skilled in speech, took up his words.

Passion, application, skill, and policy—these are declared by the wise to be the means for accomplishing one's goals; yet all of them depend upon destiny. Those great car-warriors of ours, who are world-renowned heroes and equal to the gods, [depend on this as well].
Those who were wise, disciplined, skillful, and devoted have been slain;
yet we must certainly not despair regarding victory. For when all matters are managed with sound policy, even destiny is made favorable.

"O Bhārata, we shall consecrate Karṇa alone, the most excellent among men and endowed with every multitude of virtues, in the command of the army. Having made Karṇa our general, we shall crush our enemies."
"For he is exceedingly powerful, a hero skilled in weapons and fierce in battle;
like Vaivasvata himself, he is irresistible and capable of conquering his enemies in combat.
O King, having heard this from the preceptor’s son, your son—
O great king, Duryodhana, with a joyful heart and full of affection,
then placed his great hopes in Karṇa;
for he believed that once Bhīṣma and Droṇa were slain, Karṇa would surely defeat the Pāṇḍavas.
O Bhārata, having placed that hope in his heart and having taken heart,
Duryodhana was then delighted upon hearing those pleasant words— which were imbued with affection, truthful, beneficial to himself, and auspicious.
Having steadied his own mind and relying upon the strength of his arms,
O great king, Duryodhana spoke thus to the son of Rādhā:
"O Karṇa, I know your valor and your supreme friendship toward me."
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one, I shall speak these beneficial words to you;
having heard them, O hero, do as you wish—that which pleases you.
You are always the wisest of men, and you are indeed my supreme refuge.
"The two great car-warriors, Bhīṣma and Droṇa, my generals, have been slain.
May you become the general, for you are more powerful than they. Moreover, those two aged and great archers were partial toward Dhanañjaya."
O son of Rādhā, at your word, those two heroes were honored by me; yet,
O dear one, considering the status of the Grandfather, the sons of Pāṇḍu were protected by Bhīṣma for ten days in that great battle.
And when he had laid down his weapons, Bhīṣma, the grandfather,
was slain by Phalguna in the great battle after Śikhaṇḍin had been placed in front; when that illustrious one had been killed and lay upon the bed of arrows.
"O tiger among men, when you spoke, Drona was indeed our leader;
yet even he, though the sons of Pṛthā were protected by him here in battle because of his status as their teacher,
has been swiftly slain— though he was an elder— by Dhṛṣṭadyumna."
"O you of immeasurable prowess, now that those two foremost warriors have been slain, I see no other combatant equal to you when I reflect upon them in battle.
You alone are capable of securing victory for us; of this there is no doubt."
For that is indeed known to you—before, in the middle, and after;
as such, you ought to bear the burden in battle like a leader. Consecrate yourself as the commander-in-chief by your own self.
Just as Skanda is the imperishable lord and commander-in-chief of the gods,
so may you lead this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons for me;
slay all the hosts of enemies, just as Mahendra slew the Dānavas.
Knowing you, O great car-warrior, to be stationed in battle, the Pāṇḍavas along with the Pañcālas will flee like the Dānavas upon seeing Viṣṇu;
therefore, O tiger among men, you should draw forward this great army.
When you have stood firm, those Pāṇḍavas,
along with their ministers, the Pañcālas, and the Sṛñjayas, will lose their resolve,
just as the risen sun, scorching with its own brilliance, [overpowers all else].
Just as it dispels intense darkness, so may it drive away our enemies.
Saṃjaya said:
O King, the hope that your son possessed was indeed powerful.
"Once Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been slain, Karṇa will defeat the Pāṇḍavas. Holding this hope in his heart, he then spoke thus to Karṇa:
"O son of a Sūta, the son of Pṛthā does not wish to fight while you stand before him."
Saṃjaya said:
Thus addressed by King Duryodhana,
the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful son of Rādhā, with a joyful heart, spoke in the midst of the kings.
Gladdening him, Karṇa spoke these words to Duryodhana.
Karṇa said:
"O son of Gāndhārī, this was previously spoken by me in your presence."
"O King, I shall conquer the Pāṇḍavas along with their sons and Janārdana;
I will be your commander-in-chief, of this there is no doubt. Be firm, O Great King, and consider the Pāṇḍavas as already defeated."
"O all you Kurus, listen! I say that in this great battle, no one other than me can laugh at Arjuna, who is like a vessel of feverish decay."
Like death following in succession from supreme immortality.
Sañjaya said:
Thus addressed, O King, the highly energetic Duryodhana then—
He rose up together with the kings, like Śatakratu with the gods,
in order to honor Karṇa with the command of the army, as the immortals did for Skanda.
Then they quickly consecrated him according to the prescribed ritual.
O King, the kings headed by Duryodhana, desiring victory,
[performed the lustration] with jars made of gold and those made of earth consecrated with mantras,
filled with water, and with the horns of leopards, rhinoceroses, and great bulls.
Seated upon a throne made of udumbara wood, covered with fine linen, and adorned with jewels, pearls, other precious things, holy perfumes, and medicinal herbs,
he was consecrated according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures and with all the necessary materials duly prepared.

The esteemed Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras praised that high-souled one who had been consecrated upon the excellent throne. Then, O Indra among kings, he was consecrated with gold coins, cattle, and wealth.
The son of Rādhā, the slayer of enemy heroes, caused the foremost of Brahmins to recite [the praises];
then he honored those Brahmins, who were knowers of the Vedas, with garments. That son of Rādhā shone resplendent amidst the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards.
Like the sun at its rising being praised by those who discourse on Brahman,
there then arose a tumultuous roar from all sides, consisting of the proclamation of an auspicious day, the sounding of musical instruments, and the shouts of "Victory! from the heroes.
"Victory! all the kings gathered there cried out to the son of Rādhā:
"Conquer the Pārthas, along with Govinda and their followers, in this great battle! Thus did the panegyrists and the twice-born speak to him, O bull of the Bharatas.
"O son of Rādhā, slay the Pārthas along with the Pañcālas for our victory!
Just as the rising sun always destroys the darkness with its fierce rays, so too,
those men together with Keśava are not capable of enduring the arrows discharged by you."
Ungrateful as they are, like those who gaze upon blazing sunbeams,
the sons of Pṛthā along with the Pañcālas are not able to stand before you in battle when you have taken up your weapons, just as the Dānavas cannot stand before Mahendra.
Saṃjaya said:
Honored, being praised, and surrounded by a circle of friends, that bull among men,
Karṇa, smiling, spoke these pleasing words to Duryodhana.

"O Duryodhana, today, together with my hosts and the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, I shall slay Phalguna along with his kinsmen for the sake of your pleasure. Rule the earth, including its mountains, oceans, and islands, now that the Pāṇḍavas have been removed."
"You shall bring about stability for your sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
O subduer of enemies, nothing is impossible for me when it is for the sake of your pleasure,
just as success is certain for one who is self-possessed and devoted to truth and righteousness."
But once consecrated, that son of Rādhā, possessed of immeasurable splendor, surpassed all in beauty like a second sun. Having consecrated the son of Rādhā in the command of the army, your son—

Urged by time, he then considered himself to have achieved his purpose. O King, Karna too, the subduer of foes, having obtained the command of the army, ordered the troops to prepare for battle at the rising of the sun.
Surrounded by your sons, O Bhārata, Karṇa shone there like Skanda among the gods in the battle against Tāraka. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Then Karna Vaikartana, having obtained the command of the army and having been addressed by the king himself with affectionate words equal to those of a brother,
gave the order for the army to assemble as the sun rose.
"He was always well-disposed toward my son and desired his welfare;
what did that man of great wisdom do? Tell me that, Sañjaya.
Sañjaya said:
O bull of the Bharatas, having understood Karna’s intention, your son ordered the mobilization,
preceded by the sounding of festive musical instruments.
O honorable one, during the latter part of the night, your son [issued the command].
"Yoga! Yoga!"— a great roar suddenly arose,
O lord of the people, from the elephants as they were being prepared, from the chariots with their protective fenders,
and from the infantry and horses as they were being equipped.
As the warriors cried out to one another in their haste,
a tumultuous and immense sound arose that then reached the very heavens.
Then, [he advanced] on a chariot with white banners and horses having the appearance of the rising sun.
With a bow of golden back, with a banner bearing the emblem of an elephant’s girth,
with a quiver full of arrows, with a protective armor adorned with armlets, and carrying *śataghnīs*, small bells, spears, tridents, and lances.

Equipped with a bow possessing the splendor of the stainless sun, the Sūtaputra appeared upon a chariot adorned with many banners; O dear one, he was blowing his conch shell, which was decorated with nets of gold.
Seeing the great archer Karṇa, the best among chariot-warriors, standing upon his chariot and brandishing his massive bow adorned with gold—
resembling the rising sun that destroys darkness by the thousands.

O venerable one, O tiger among men, none of the Kauravas there thought of Bhīṣma’s calamity, nor that of Droṇa, nor that of the others. Then, O venerable one, he urged the warriors on with the sound of his conch shell.
Karna, the great archer and scorcher of enemies, drew out the army of the Kauravas; having formed the Makara array, the son of the Sun, clad in armor, took his stand within that Makara formation.
Then Karṇa advanced against the Pāṇḍavas with a desire for victory.
O King, Karṇa was stationed at the snout of the Makara formation;
the heroic Śakuni and the great car-warrior Ulūka were stationed at its two eyes.
The son of Droṇa was at the head, while all his brothers were on the neck;
King Duryodhana, surrounded by a great force, was in the middle.
And on the left foot, O Indra among kings, stood Kṛtavarman.
Endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa and intoxicated by battle, he stood at the right foot, O King, along with the cowherds; there Gautama, whose prowess is truth,
was surrounded by the Trigartas and the great archers from the south.
But on the left, O Great King, stood Anūpāda, with whom was stationed the stake Śalya together with a vast army raised from the Madra country;
while on the right was Suṣeṇa, true to his promise.
Surrounded by thousands of chariots and hundreds of elephants,
the two great heroic brothers,
the princes Citrasena and Citra, then took their positions at the tail, accompanied by a vast army.
Then, O king of kings, when Karṇa, the best among the foremost of men, had set forth,
Dharmarāja, beholding Dhananjaya, spoke these words:
"Behold, O Pārtha, the great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son in this encounter."
O hero, this great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons was formed by Karṇa and protected by great car-warriors; yet its finest heroes have been slain,
O mighty-armed one, and it remains as a mere remnant, which in my estimation is equal to straw.
For here stands alone that great archer, the son of the Sūta,
who is invincible to the three worlds— with their mobile and immobile beings, including gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— being the foremost of all chariot-warriors.
"O mighty-armed Phalguna, by slaying him today, victory shall be yours;
the thorn that has rankled me for twelve years will be extracted.
Knowing this, O mighty-armed one, form the battle array as you desire."
Having heard those words of his brother, the Pāṇḍava Śvetavāhana arrayed that army in a crescent formation (*ardhacandra*). O King, Bhīmasena stood stationed on the left flank.
And on the right was the great archer, the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
in the very center of the array was the Pāṇḍava with Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer,
while Nakula, Sahadeva, and Dharmarāja followed behind.
The two Pāñcāla wheel-protectors, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas,
did not abandon Arjuna in battle, being protected by the Diademed One (Kiritin). The remaining heroic kings stood armored at the front of the formation.
O Bhārata, according to their respective status, according to their enthusiasm, and according to their strength,
the Pāṇḍavas and your own great archers, having thus formed this great array, O Bhārata,
set their minds solely upon battle.
Having seen your army arrayed for battle by the Sūtaputra,
your son, along with his followers, considered the Pāṇḍavas already slain.
Likewise, Yudhiṣṭhira, having seen the Pāṇḍava army drawn up in formation, [considered the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as already defeated].
O lord of men, he considered the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, including Karṇa, as already slain.
Then conchs, kettledrums, cymbals, drums,
and horns were suddenly sounded together with a great clamor on all sides.
O King, loud sounds were raised by both armies;
the lion-roars of the heroes, greedy for victory, broke forth,
along with the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants.
O lord of men, the fierce sounds of chariot wheels arose;
O bull of the Bharatas, no one perceived the calamity that had befallen Droṇa upon seeing the great archer Karṇa, clad in armor, at the head of the battle array.
Both armies, O King, consisting of great beings and joyful men and elephants,
stood eager for battle, desiring to slay one another directly. Seeing each other stationed there, they became alert and highly incensed.
In the midst of the army, O Indra among kings, Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava shone forth. As those two armies danced toward one another,
their wings and sub-wings marched out, eager for battle.
Then, O great king, a fierce battle commenced between men, elephants, horses, and chariot-warriors as they struck one another down. Saṃjaya said:
Those two vast armies, consisting of horses, men, and elephants, having encountered one another, fought with great joy like the hosts of gods and asuras; then,
in that great battle, there were elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry.
They engaged in a supreme combat that destroys both the body and its sins;
with their heads— equal in beauty to the full moon, in brilliance to the sun, and in fragrance to the lotus—
the lions among men covered the earth.
With crescent-headed arrows, bhallas, razor-sharp shafts, swords, paṭṭiśas,
and battle-axes, they lopped off the heads of those fighting with long,
outstretched arms by means of other long, outstretched arms.
Their outstretched arms fell, their fists, weapons, and armlets severed;
with those quivering limbs and hands with reddened fingers, the earth then shone as if strewn with fierce five-headed serpents struck down by Garuḍa.
Slain by their enemies, the heroes fell from horses, chariots, and elephants,
just as the inhabitants of heaven fall from their celestial palaces when their merit is exhausted;
some were struck down by heavy maces, others by iron clubs and pestles.
In that supreme tumult, heroes were struck down by even more heroic warriors by the hundreds;
chariots were destroyed by chariots, intoxicated elephants by intoxicated elephants,
and horsemen likewise by horsemen.
Chariots were struck down by excellent chariots, and elephant-riders along with horsemen and foot-soldiers;
horsemen and foot-soldiers lay slain in battle.
Chariots, horses, and foot-soldiers were destroyed by elephants, and elephants and foot-soldiers were destroyed by chariots.
Chariots, infantry, and elephants were joined by horses and men;
horses, chariots, and elephants were joined by men; and men, horses, elephants, and chariots were joined together.
Thus, a chaotic melee of horses, men, and elephants appeared as they clashed with one another.
With hands, feet, weapons, and chariots, a great slaughter was wrought;
while that army was thus being struck down and slain by the heroes,
the Pārthas, led by Vṛkodara, advanced against us.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, the sons of Draupadī, and the Prabhadrakas;
Sātyaki and Cekitāna, together with Dravidian soldiers,
as well as the Pāṇḍyas, the Auḍras, and the Keralas— all maintained by great wealth.
Broad-chested, long-armed, tall, and pleasing to behold; wearing head-garlands, with red teeth, possessing the prowess of elephants in rut,
dressed in garments of various colors, and dusted with fragrant powders.
With their inner intent fixed, holding nooses in their hands, and acting as both defenders and adversaries,
O King, those standing in the ranks regarded one another as equal to death;
wearing quivers, with bows in hand, long-haired, they were lovers of battle.
The Andhra foot-soldiers of Sātyaki, possessing terrible forms and prowess, as well as other heroes— the Cedis, Pañcālas, Kekayas,
Karūṣas, Kosalas, Kāśis, and Māgadhas— also rushed forward.
Their chariots, elephants, and excellent foot-soldiers,
filled with joy, danced and laughed amidst various kinds of sounds.
Surrounded by the foremost of great ministers, he stood at the head of that vast army.
Vṛkodara, mounted upon your elephant, approached the center.
That most formidable and excellent elephant, equipped according to ritual, shone like the peak of the mountain of sunrise with the sun risen upon it.
His excellent iron armor, adorned with the finest jewels,
possessed a brilliance equal to the autumnal sky illuminated by stars.
With a beautiful crown and well-adorned, he held a *tomara* and a spear in his hands.
Moving about like the midday sun, he scorched his enemies with his splendor.
Seeing that elephant from afar, Kṣemadhūrti, mounted upon his own elephant, being himself highly elated,
rushed toward him with even greater joy, challenging him to combat.
A battle took place between those two elephants of fierce appearance,
like that between two great mountains covered with trees by chance. Those two heroes, their elephants locked together, struck one another with javelins.
Resounding with a roar, they pierced each other again and again with arrows as powerful as the rays of the sun; then,
withdrawing from their elephants, they moved in circles and,
seizing their bows, struck one another.
With the sounds of their roars and the slapping of their arms, and with the whizzing of arrows on all sides,
the two of them gladdened the people and let out lion-like cries;
both were skilled and stood upon their elephants with trunks raised high.
With banners fluttering in the wind, the two mighty warriors fought;
having severed each other’s bows,
they roared at one another like clouds in the rainy season pouring down showers of spears and lances.
Then Kṣemadhūrti, roaring, violently pierced Bhīma in the middle of the chest with a lance,
and struck him again with six others.
Adorned by those lances fixed in his body, Bhīmasena shone resplendently.
His body blazing with wrath like the sun behind its clouds,
the formidable Bhīma then, exerting himself against his adversary, hurled an iron *tomara* that was straight-flying and radiant as the sun.
Then the lord of Kulūta, having drawn his bow,
severed the lance with ten arrows and pierced the Pāṇḍava with a spear.
Then he took up a bow that sounded like a great rain-cloud.
The intoxicated Pāṇḍava, assailing his enemy’s elephant with arrows,
struck it down in battle; tormented by that flood of shafts from Bhīmasena, the elephant could not stand its ground, like a cloud scattered by the wind.
The king of elephants rushed toward Bhīmasena’s elephant,
like a cloud driven by a great wind charging against a cloud tossed by the wind;
Kṣemadhūrti, however, with great effort, turned his own elephant back.
He pierced Bhīmasena and his elephant with arrows as they charged forward.
Then, with a well-aimed razor-headed arrow (kṣura), that bull among men severed the enemy’s bow and struck the hostile elephant.
Then, O Bhārata, Kṣemadhūrti struck Bhīma with a mace and slew his elephant with iron shafts in all its vital parts;
