that great beast fell down, O Bhārata.
Before the elephant could fall, Bhīmasena leaped down and stood upon the earth; with his mace, he crushed the enemy's elephant to pieces. From that mangled elephant, Kṣemadhūrti fled away.
Drawing his sharp sword, he rushed toward the son of Pāṇḍu;
as he approached with his blade raised, Vṛkodara struck him with his mace.
Slain, he fell lifeless with his sword beside his own elephant.

O bull of the Bharatas, seeing the illustrious king of the Kulūtas slain— immovable like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt, like a lion struck down by a bolt of lightning— your army fled in distress.
Saṃjaya said:
Then the heroic Karṇa, that great archer, struck the army of the Pāṇḍavas in battle with straight-jointed arrows.
In the same way, O King, those great car-warriors, the Pāṇḍavas, furiously struck down your son's army at the front of Karṇa. O King,
the mighty-armed Karṇa slaughtered the Pāṇḍava host.
O Bhārata, there the elephants, struck by Karṇa with iron arrows (*nārāca*) polished by smiths and shining like the rays of the sun,
shrieked, collapsed, fainted, and wandered in the ten directions.
O noble one, while that army was being slaughtered by the Sūtaputra,
Nakula swiftly rushed toward the Sūtaputra in that great battle,
and Bhīmasena likewise rushed toward the son of Droṇa as he performed difficult feats.
Sātyaki held back Vinda and Anuvinda, the two Kaikeyas;
King Citrasena opposed Śrutakarman as he approached,
and likewise Citra, whose banner and bow were variegated, opposed Prativindhya.
While King Duryodhana was [occupied] with Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma,
the enraged Dhanañjaya rushed against the hosts of Saṃśaptakas; and then, during that slaughter of the best of heroes, Dhṛṣṭadyumna attacked Kṛpa.
Śikhaṇḍin encountered the steadfast Kṛtavarman; likewise,
Śrutakīrti [encountered] Śalya, and the powerful Sahadeva, O great king, [encountered] your son Duḥśāsana.
The two Kekayas covered Sātyaki in battle with a radiant shower of arrows,
O Bhārata, and Sātyaki likewise covered the two Kekayas.
Those two brothers struck that hero deeply in the heart.
Like two elephants with their tusks against a rival elephant in a great battle, O King,
those two brothers, their armor pierced by arrows,
struck Satyaki of truthful deeds with shafts in that conflict.

O great king, O Bhārata, Sātyaki, laughing, covered them in every direction with a shower of arrows and held them back. Then, those two were warded off by the showers of arrows from the descendant of Śini.
They quickly covered the chariot of Śaineya with arrows.
But in that great battle, Śauri, having severed their two variegated bows,
then covered them both with sharp and unbearable shafts.
Then, grasping two polished bows and great arrows,
those two moved with lightness and skill, filling Satyaki [with their shafts].
The great arrows released by them were fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks.
Illuminating all directions, those adorned with golden ornaments rushed forward;
O King, a darkness of arrows arose in that great battle between them,
and those great car-warriors cut each other’s bows asunder.
In that battle, both [warriors] cut through the bow of the Sātvata hero.
Then, O great king, the Sātvata, enraged and difficult to vanquish in combat,
took up another bow and strung it in the fray.
O Indra among kings, having wiped that bow capable of bearing great weight,
he struck off Anuvinda’s head with an exceedingly sharp razor-headed arrow.
That large head, adorned with earrings, fell to the earth.
Like the head of Śambara when he was slain in the great battle,
[the arrow] quickly reached the earth, drying up all the Kekayas.
Seeing that hero slain, his brother, a great chariot-warrior, [beheld him].
Having strung another bow, he warded off the descendant of Śini.
Piercing Sātyaki with gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone, he let out a powerful roar and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"

Then that great car-warrior of the Kekayas, filled with rage, struck Sātyaki again in the arms and chest with arrows resembling tongues of fire. With all his limbs mangled by those shafts, the Sātvata hero, skilled in courage, [remained steadfast].
O King, pierced in battle by the high-souled Kekaya, Sātyaki shone like a *kiṃśuka* tree with its leaves intact;
laughing as it were, he pierced the Kekaya in return with twenty-five arrows.
In that battle, those two great chariot-warriors, the best among car-fighters, having severed each other’s bows and swiftly slain each other’s charioteers and horses,
approached one another in the fray for a sword-duel, now deprived of their chariots.

Grasping shields adorned with a hundred moons, those two mighty-armed warriors, wielding excellent swords, shone resplendent upon the great stage like the immensely powerful Jambha and Śakra in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Then, moving in circles during that great battle,
those two quickly struck each other with their swords in the fray;
they both exerted the utmost effort to slay one another.
Then the Sātvata cut the shield of the Kaikeya king in two; likewise, that monarch also cut through the shield of Sātyaki.
Having sliced through the shield, the Kaikeya [wielded one] adorned with hundreds of clusters of stars.
He moved through various circular maneuvers, advancing and retreating.
As he was thus performing on the great stage, wielding his excellent sword,
the descendant of Śini, filled with haste, cut him down with a single blow of his hand.
O King, the Kekaya prince, clad in armor and a great archer, fell in that great battle, cut in two like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Having slain him in combat, the heroic grandson of Śini, the best of chariot-warriors—
Yudhāmanyu, the scorcher of foes, swiftly ascended another chariot;
then, mounting yet another chariot duly equipped,
Sātyaki scattered the great army of the Kekayas with his arrows.
Being slaughtered in battle, that great army of the Kekayas abandoned their chariot and their enemy, and fled in the ten directions. Saṃjaya said:
O great king, the enraged Śrutakarman struck Citrasena, the lord of the earth, in battle with fifty stone-tipped arrows.
King Abhisāra, however, [struck him] with nine sharpened shafts.
Having struck Śrutakarman, he pierced the Sūta with five arrows.
Then Śrutakarman, enraged at Citrasena at the head of the army,
struck him in a vital spot with an exceedingly sharp iron shaft (nārāca).
O Great King, having been deeply pierced by that great-souled iron shaft,
the hero fell into a swoon and was overcome by a state of fainting. In that interval, the highly illustrious Śrutakīrti [approached him].

With ninety feathered shafts, he covered the protector of the earth. Then, regaining his composure, the great car-warrior Citrasena cut his bow with a broad-headed arrow and pierced him with seven more.
Taking up another bow, which was gold-adorned, capable of checking the enemy's speed,
and exceedingly beautiful in form, he covered Citrasena with waves of arrows.
O King, that youth, variegated by those arrows, appeared like one wearing a garland of diverse flowers.

Well-adorned, he shone like a youth in the midst of a social gathering. Then, in that battle, the enraged [warrior] pierced Śrutakarman between the breasts with an iron shaft and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
Śrutakarman also, pierced in battle by an iron shaft,
shed copious blood like a mountain discharging streams of red chalk-water.
Then, his limbs smeared with blood and his complexion transformed by the gore, he stood there.
O King, he shone in battle like a *kiṃśuka* tree in full bloom. Then, O King, Śrutakarman, having charged against his enemies,
warded off the foe's attack and cut his bow in two.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the highly illustrious Śrutakarman pierced him whose bow had been severed with three hundred iron arrows;
he covered the protector of the earth with ninety straight-knotted shafts.
Then, with another extremely sharp broad-headed arrow,
he swiftly struck off the head of that great-souled one, including its helmet.
That massive head of Citravarman fell to the earth.
O noble one, seeing the king slain and Abhimanyu as well, Citrasena’s soldiers rushed forward with speed, like the moon fallen from heaven to the earth by chance.
Then the great archer, enraged, pursued that army with his arrows,
just as the King of the Dead, filled with wrath at the time of universal destruction, pursues all living beings.
Being slaughtered in battle by your grandson, the bowman, [the soldiers fled].
They fled swiftly in all directions like elephants scorched by a forest fire;
seeing them fleeing, devoid of enthusiasm for victory over the enemy,
Śrutakarman shone brightly as he quickly pursued them with his arrows.
Then Prativindhya, having pierced Citra with five swift arrows,
struck his charioteer with three and his standard with a single shaft. Thereupon,
Citra struck him in the arms and chest with nine broad-headed arrows.
O Bhārata, having severed his bow with arrows gold-feathered, whetted on stone, and fletched with the plumes of herons and peacocks,
Prativindhya then struck him with five sharpened shafts.
Then, O great king, he hurled at your son a formidable spear with a golden shaft, as fierce as a flame of fire. As that spear came rushing suddenly like a meteor from the sky—
In that battle, Prativindhya, as if smiling, cut it into two pieces;
severed by Prativindhya’s sharp arrows,
it then fell like a thunderbolt at the end of an eon, terrifying all living beings.
Seeing that spear destroyed, Citra seized a great mace adorned with a network of gold and hurled it at Prativindhya;
in that great battle, it struck down his horses and his charioteer.
Having crushed the chariot with its speed, it fell to the earth.
At that very moment, O Bhārata, leaping down from his chariot,
he hurled a spear adorned with golden bells at Citra.
O King, as it was falling toward him, the high-minded Citra seized it;
then, O Bhārata, he hurled that very same [weapon] back at Prativindhya.
Having reached the heroic Prativindhya in battle, that weapon of great luster—
Having pierced through his right arm, it fell to the surface of the earth;
falling, it illuminated that region like a thunderbolt.
Then, O King, Prativindhya [hurled] a gold-adorned lance.
Enraged and desiring the slaughter of Citra, he dispatched it;
having pierced through his divine armor and his very heart,
it quickly entered the earth like a great serpent entering its lair.
O King, struck by that lance, he then fell down,
stretching out his two massive, thick arms which resembled iron clubs.
Seeing Citra slain, your warriors, the ornaments of the battlefield, were filled with wonder.
They rushed with speed toward Prativindhya from all sides,
discharging various kinds of arrows and *śataghnīs* equipped with small bells;
they covered him just as masses of clouds shroud the sun.
Having warded them off with a network of arrows in the encounter, the mighty-armed one put your army to flight, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt routed the host of the Asuras.
O King, your men were being slaughtered in battle by the Pāṇḍavas.
Scattered suddenly like clouds driven by the wind,
when that army had fled and was being slaughtered on all sides,
the son of Droṇa alone rushed swiftly toward the mighty Bhīmasena.
Then a terrible encounter suddenly took place between those two,
like that which occurred between Vṛtra and Vāsava in the war between the gods and the asuras.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, endowed with supreme haste and displaying his lightness of hand in weaponry, pierced Bhīmasena with a feathered shaft;
he then struck him again with ninety sharpened arrows.
Having observed all his vital points, Bhīmasena, who was skilled in the vital points and possessed of a light hand, though overwhelmed by the son of Droṇa with sharpened arrows,
shone in battle, O King, like the sun with its rays.
Then, having covered the son of Droṇa with a thousand well-aimed arrows, the Pāṇḍava let out a lion’s roar. Thereupon,
the son of Droṇa, having warded off those arrows with his own in the battle, [assailed] the Pāṇḍava with arrows.
O King, as if smiling, he struck him on the forehead with an iron shaft;
then the Pāṇḍava bore that arrow fixed in his forehead,
O monarch, just as a proud rhinoceros in the forest bears its horn.

Then the valiant Bhīma, as if in wonder, pierced the striving son of Droṇa in the forehead with three iron shafts (nārācas) in that battle. With those arrows fixed in his forehead, that Brahmin shone resplendently.
Like the highest mountain with its three peaks when drenched by the rainy season,
the Pāṇḍava then afflicted the son of Droṇa with hundreds of arrows;
yet he could not shake him, just as the wind cannot shake a mountain.

In that very same way, the son of Droṇa, exulting in battle, could not shake the Pāṇḍava with his hundreds of sharp arrows, just as a torrent of water cannot move a mountain. Those two great car-warriors continued to cover each other with terrible shafts.
Moving along the path of their chariots, those two heroes, fierce in battle,
shone like two blazing suns capable of destroying the world,
scorching one another with their excellent arrows as if with their own rays.
Making every effort to strike and counterstrike in that great battle, those two acted fearlessly, exerting themselves in deed and counter-deed;
like two tigers, those two great chariot-warriors moved about in the fray.
With arrows for their tusks, difficult to assail, with bows drawn into terrifying curves,
those two became invisible on all sides by the nets of their shafts,
like the sun and moon in the sky shrouded by masses of clouds.
And in a mere moment, those two subduers of enemies became radiant right there,
like the moon and the sun in the sky when released from a mass of clouds.
Then, while that most terrible battle was still raging on that very spot—
Then the son of Droṇa moved to the left of Vṛkodara there,
scattering hundreds of fierce arrows upon him like torrents of rain upon a mountain.
But Bhīma could not endure that sign of his enemy’s victory.
And the Pāṇḍava, O King, also countered him by moving to the right;
as they moved through the various divisions of their circles, advancing and retreating,
a tumultuous battle took place between those two in that great conflict.
Having performed various maneuvers on the paths and in the circular positions,
those two great chariot-warriors struck each other with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch; they exerted every effort to slay one another.
In that battle, they both strove to deprive each other of their chariots;
then the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, manifested mighty celestial weapons,
which the Pāṇḍava countered in the encounter with his own weapons.
Then, O great king, a terrible battle of missiles ensued,
as fierce as the planetary conflict that occurs at the destruction of all beings.
Those arrows, O Bhārata, were discharged by the two of them and collided with one another.
Illumining all directions and that entire army on every side,
O King, the sky became filled with terrible masses of arrows, like the portents of meteors that appear at the destruction of living beings.
O Bhārata, from the impact of the arrows, fire was produced there, with sparks and blazing flames; it consumed both armies. There, O great king, the Siddhas, gathering together, spoke these words:
This battle surpasses all other battles; it is greater than them.
All other battles are not worth even a sixteenth part of this one.
A battle such as this has never occurred before, nor will it ever happen again.
"Oh, how both are endowed with wisdom and possess fierce prowess! Oh, how both the Brahmin and the Pāṇḍava are perfected in heroism!
Oh, how terrible is the strength in Bhīma, and how great is their mastery of weapons!"
"Oh, the essence of their heroism! Oh, the excellence of these two! For they stand in battle like Yama, the Ender of Time at the end of an aeon;
they are like two Rudras manifested, or like two suns."
Then, the words of the Siddhas were heard repeatedly: "These two tigers among men, the twins of terrible form, are in battle!
And a lion-like roar arose from the assembled dwellers of heaven.
Beholding that wondrous and inconceivable feat performed by the two in battle,
the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas were filled with amazement;
then the gods, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis offered their praise.
"Excellent, O mighty-armed son of Droṇa! Excellent, Bhīma! they cried out.
O King, those two heroes, having inflicted injuries upon one another in battle, glared at each other with eyes rolling in rage.
With eyes red with rage, their lips quivering from anger,
and their teeth and lips bitten together in fury,
those two great chariot-warriors covered one another with showers of arrows.
In that battle, those two great car-warriors, who resembled clouds raining arrows and flashing with the lightning of their weapons,
pierced each other’s banners and charioteers; then,
having struck one another’s horses, they tore into each other.
Then, O great king, enraged in that great battle, both of them, desiring each other's death, quickly took up two arrows and hurled them at one another.
Those two arrows, O great king, shone brightly at the front of the armies.
Having encountered one another, those two invincible warriors, possessing the speed of thunderbolts, struck each other. Severely wounded by their mutual force and by their arrows,
those two great heroes then collapsed onto the floors of their respective chariots.
Then, O King, the charioteer, perceiving that the son of Droṇa was unconscious, bore him away from the battlefield while all the kṣatriyas looked on;
likewise, O King, he carried away the Pāṇḍava as he repeatedly fainted.
The charioteer bore away that scorcher of enemies from the field of battle in his chariot.
Sañjaya said:
Then Śrutakīrti approached, scattering sharpened arrows.
O great king, the King of Madra cheerfully resisted him;
then the great car-warrior Śrutakīrti, having encountered the King of Madra,
pierced him with thirty broad-headed arrows adorned with gold.
Śalya quickly pierced him in return with three straight-flying arrows,
O Bhārata, and with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) he deeply struck his charioteer as well.
He then covered Śalya with a shower of arrows in that encounter.
He released sharpened arrows toward the chariot of the King of Madra.
Then, O Great King, Śalya cut down those arrows discharged from the arms of Śrutakīrti in that battle with his own straight-knotted shafts.
Then Śrutakīrti, having pierced Śalya with nine iron arrows,
struck his charioteer with three and Śalya again with five. Śalya, for his part, cut off his bow and lopped off his hand-guard.
In that battle, he quickly pierced him with seven excellent arrows.
Then, taking up another bow, the great car-warrior Śrutakīrti struck the Lord of Madra in the arms and chest with sixty-four shafts.
Then, O King, having been pierced by him in that battle with stone-tipped arrows,
he in turn pierced him back with ninety sharpened shafts;
and the Lord of Madra, O noble one, once more cut his bow asunder.
His bow severed in the encounter, O Bhārata, he quickly hurled a mace that was bound with bands of Jāmbūnada gold and silver bands;
it shone like a woman adorned with celestial garments.
As it came rushing suddenly with the brilliance of a blazing thunderbolt,
the King of Madra checked it with many thousands of arrows;
having checked it, the hero brought his mace down upon the ground.
Then, O King, Ayata pierced Śrutakīrti with five arrows;
he further hurled at him in battle a spear resembling a serpent,
which Śalya cut in two, and it fell shattered upon the earth.
O best of men, Śalya struck off the head of his charioteer from his body with a razor-sharp arrow, just as a hawk snatches meat from the hand of a child;
O Bhārata, that charioteer fell from the seat of the chariot.
Then, O Great King, those horses of that high-souled one bolted away in the battle;
being carried off from the field of combat by those fleeing steeds,
Śrutakīrti was removed from the fray while all the warriors looked on.
Then King Madra, filled with joy, plunged into the army of the Pāṇḍavas like an elephant into a lotus pond; he agitated that force as a lion agitates herds of beasts.
In that great arena, Śalya, having slain the Pāṇḍavas and the Pāñcālas among the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, stood firm amidst the armies;
in battle, Śalya shone like a blazing fire free from smoke.
Having burned down the vast camp like a fire that has arisen in a forest thicket,
he stood resplendent in battle like Śaṅkara after burning a city.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Just as the battle took place between Arjuna and the Saṃśaptakas,
how did the combat proceed between the Sūta’s son and the Pāñcālas?
And as for the battle between Aśvatthāman and Arjuna, O Saṃjaya— tell me.
"And tell me also of the others who were mine, as they were slain by the Pāṇḍavas.
Saṃjaya said:
"Listen, O King, as I describe the battle exactly as it occurred."

It was the destroyer of the bodies and sins of heroes in their conflict with enemies. Pārtha, the slayer of foes, having entered the host of Saṃśaptakas which resembled an ocean, agitated it like a great wind agitates the sea.

Having severed the heads of the heroes with sharp broad-headed arrows, Dhanañjaya quickly covered the earth with those faces— resembling the full moon and possessing beautiful eyes, brows, and teeth— as if with lotuses stripped of their stalks.

In that battle, Arjuna severed with razor-sharp blades the arms of his enemies— arms that were well-formed, long, and muscular, adorned with sandalwood and aloe paste, equipped with weapons and finger-guards, and resembling five-headed serpents.
The son of Pāṇḍu repeatedly severed with broad-headed arrows the draft-animals, the more noble steeds, the charioteers, the banners, the bows, the shafts, the hands, and the forearms.
In that battle, Arjuna likewise struck down elephants, horses, and chariots along with their riders.
O King, with many thousands of arrows, he sent him to the abode of Yama.
Like roaring bulls, those great heroes rushed toward that preeminent warrior, and like cows enraged for the sake of a cow in heat, they charged at him, uttering cries of "hum."
As he was striking them down, they struck him back with arrows, like bulls with their horns.
That battle between him and them was hair-raising,
like the one between the Daityas and the wielder of the thunderbolt during the conquest of the three worlds.

Having warded off the weapons of his enemies from all sides with his own weapons, Arjuna quickly pierced them with many arrows and took their lives. Their triple-bamboo poles, wheels, and axles were shattered; their warriors, horses, and charioteers were slain.
Their weapons and quivers were shattered, their banners torn away;
their thongs and reins were severed, their triple-pole frames and chariot-boxes destroyed;
their axles and yokes were ruined, and the circles of their weapons were hacked to pieces.
Shattering chariots like the wind dispersing great clouds,
Arjuna performed deeds equal to those of a thousand great car-warriors— a sight that caused amazement and increased the fear of his enemies.
The hosts of Siddhas and celestial rishis, as well as the Cāraṇas, offered hymns of praise;
divine drums resounded and showers of flowers fell upon the heads of Keśava and Arjuna, while an incorporeal voice spoke.
Those two heroes, Keśava and Arjuna, who always possess the luster, brilliance, strength, and splendor of the moon, the sun, the wind, and the fire—
those two invincible heroes standing upon a single chariot are like Brahmā and Īśāna.
"O Bhārata, having seen and heard of this great marvel— that both heroes, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, are the best among all beings—
Aśvatthāman, fully prepared, rushed toward the two Kṛṣṇas in battle."
Then, as the son of Pāṇḍu was discharging arrows that were like Yama, the Ender of Time,
the son of Droṇa, smiling, challenged him with his hand still holding the shafts and said:
"O hero, if you consider me to have arrived here like a guest worthy of honor..."
"Therefore, with all your soul, grant me today the hospitality of battle.
Thus challenged by the preceptor’s son, who desired to fight,
Arjuna held himself in high esteem and said this to Janārdana:
"The Saṃśaptakas must be slain by me, yet the son of Droṇa also challenges me. O mighty-armed one, command what should be done next;
if you think it right, let the rites of hospitality be offered as he rises to meet me."
Thus addressed, Kṛṣṇa bore Pārtha to the presence of Droṇa’s son,
who had been summoned according to the rules of victory, just as Vāyu bore Indra to the sacrifice.
Having taken leave of him with a focused mind, Keśava spoke to the son of Droṇa.
"O Aśvatthāman, stand firm, strike quickly, and prevail!
For this is the time for dependents to repay the sustenance provided by their master.
Subtle is the dispute among Brahmins; victory and defeat for Kshatriyas are manifest."
"Since you cannot endure out of delusion this divine hospitality shown by Pārtha,
fight the son of Pāṇḍu today, becoming firm in your resolve and desiring to attain that [hospitality].
Having been addressed thus by Vāsudeva, the best of the twice-born replied, "So be it."

He pierced Keśava with sixty iron shafts and Arjuna with three. At this, Arjuna, highly incensed, cut his bow with three broad-headed arrows; thereupon the son of Droṇa took up another, even more terrible, bow.
Having strung it in the blink of an eye, he pierced both Arjuna and Keśava with three arrows and Vāsudeva with a thousand;
then he loosed thousands, millions, and billions of arrows.
Exerting himself and steadying Arjuna in battle, the son of Droṇa,
O noble one, discharged [arrows] from his quiver, from his bow, from the bowstring, from his fingers,
from his arms, from his hands, from his chest, and from his mouth, nose, and eyes.
From his ears, from his head, from his limbs, and even from the pores of his skin,
as well as from the chariot and the banner, arrows flew forth from that proclaimer of the Veda.
Having pierced Keśava and the Pāṇḍava with a great net of arrows, he [stood there].
The son of Droṇa, joyful and with a voice like the roar of a great mass of clouds, let out a shout.
Hearing him shouting, the Pāṇḍava said to Acyuta:
"Behold, O Mādhava, the wickedness of Droṇa’s son toward me."
"Thinking that we have fallen into his power, he intends to cast us into a house of arrows;
I shall destroy this resolve of his through my skill and strength. Having spoken thus, he cut [the enemy's weapons] with straight-knotted *bhalla* arrows.

Having severed each of Aśvatthāman’s discharged arrows into three pieces, that best of the Bharatas destroyed his variegated bow, banner, chariot, spear, and auspicious mace, just as the wind disperses the mist.
Then the Pāṇḍava once again pierced the Saṃśaptakas— along with their horses, drivers, chariots, and elephants, and the throngs of their banners and infantry— with fierce arrows;
whatever form each individual was seen in there, and in whatever manner, [he struck them].
They each perceived themselves as being completely covered by those various arrows;
those winged shafts of diverse forms, impelled from the Gāṇḍīva bow,
struck down elephants and men standing within a distance of more than a krośa on the battlefield.
Severed by broad-headed arrows, the trunks of the elephants— drinking in rut—
fell down like full-grown trees cut by axes in autumn;
thereafter, those elephants fell along with their riders like mountains.
Just as masses of mountains are shattered by the thunderbolt of the wielder of the vajra,
so too were the chariots— constructed according to rule with the appearance of celestial cities, yoked to well-trained, swift horses, and occupied by warriors intoxicated for battle— crushed.
Shattering his enemies with arrows, he rained them down;
those arrows, resembling the sun as they fell in every direction,
struck the decorated horsemen and foot soldiers, O Dhanañjaya.
Dhanañjaya, like the sun at the end of an eon, dried up the great ocean of the Saṃśaptakas—
which was otherwise difficult to dry— with the fierce rays of his arrows;
then, with iron shafts resembling the sun, he [assailed] the great mountain that was the son of Droṇa.
With great speed, he pierced him as the wielder of the thunderbolt swiftly cleaves a mountain.
Enraged, the preceptor’s son, desiring to fight, was unable to combat him along with his horses and charioteer; Pārtha cut those arrows down in mid-air.

Then, exceedingly enraged, he discharged arrows from his quivers as Aśvatthāman did for a handsome guest arriving at his home. Thereupon, the Pāṇḍava abandoned the Saṃśaptakas and advanced against the son of Droṇa.
"O King, having seen the battle between those two great-souled ones, the Saṃśaptakas stood aside like a donor who, seeing a worthy recipient, abandons one who is unworthy of the row.
Then there occurred a battle between those two who possessed the splendor of Śukra and Aṅgiras."
Like the two planets Śukra and Aṅgiras on either side of a constellation in the sky,
they scorched one another with the blazing rays of their arrows;
like two planets straying from their courses, they became a source of terror to the world.
Then Arjuna pierced him deeply between the eyebrows with a steel-tipped arrow (nārāca).
With that wound, the son of Droṇa shone like the sun with its rays pointing upward.
Then the two Kṛṣṇas were severely afflicted by Aśvatthāman with hundreds of arrows.
With their masses of radiating rays, they appeared like two suns at the end of an eon.
Then Arjuna, protected by Vāsudeva, released a weapon that discharged its edge in every direction.
And he struck the son of Droṇa with arrows resembling the thunderbolt, fire, and the staff of Yama;
that one of exceeding splendor [struck] both Keśava and Arjuna.
He of exceedingly fierce deeds pierced him in his vital organs with well-aimed arrows of extreme velocity—
arrows by which even Death himself would be pained when struck.
Arjuna, having warded off the arrows of the son of Droṇa as he exerted himself, struck that peerless hero— along with his horses, charioteer, and standard— with twice as many well-feathered shafts.
Having surrounded the army of the Saṃśaptakas, he struck them—
[severing] their bows, arrows, quivers, bowstrings,
hands, arms, and the weapons held in their hands.
Their umbrellas, banners, horses,
as well as their garments, garlands, and ornaments;
their shields, armor, and even their chariots— [he took them all].
With arrows released from his bow, Pārtha severed all the beloved heads of his enemies as they stood facing him and did not turn their backs.
Well-equipped chariots, horses, and elephants, mounted by heroic men who had exerted themselves,
were struck down by the multitudes of arrows discharged by the son of Pṛthā.
Together with those very best of men, they fell—
those whose faces were like lotuses, suns, and full moons,
and who were resplendent with crowns, garlands, and diadems.
Mangled by *bhallas*, crescent-headed arrows, and razor-sharp shafts,
the heads of men fell incessantly upon the earth; meanwhile, elephants resembling the elephant of the Lord of the Gods [rushed forward].
With pride swelling from their intense anger at the enemy of the gods,
the heroic warriors of Kaliṅga, Vaṅga, Aṅga,
and Niṣāda rushed toward the Pāṇḍava, desiring to slay him.
Pārtha cut through the armor, the vital organs, the trunks, and the drivers of those elephants;
then their banners and pennants fell down.
When those peaks of the mountain had been shattered like [rocks] struck by a thunderbolt,
Kirīṭin pierced the preceptor’s son with arrows having the hue of the newly risen sun.
He covered him with masses of great clouds, like the wind obscuring the sun when it has risen; then, having warded off Arjuna’s arrows with his own shafts, he—
Having shrouded Arjuna and Vāsudeva in the sky with his arrows like the moon and the sun, the son of Droṇa roared like a cloud at the end of the summer heat.
Arjuna,
though pressed by them with their unsharpened weapons,
suddenly created a darkness of arrows against him and those of your side.
He pierced them all with well-feathered arrows;
Savyasācin was not seen in battle taking up, aiming, or even releasing his shafts.
They beheld slain elephants, horses,
and foot soldiers, as well as chariots with their bodies pierced through;
having quickly fixed ten excellent iron shafts [to his bow].
The son of Droṇa, acting with haste, discharged as if it were a single shaft;
five of these well-aimed arrows pierced Arjuna,
and five others pierced Acyuta.
Struck by them, those two foremost of all men—
resembling Kubera and Indra— streamed with blood,
utterly overwhelmed by one who had completed his mastery of the sciences.
"Or did the others think that these two were already slain?
Then the Lord of the Daśārhas said to Arjuna:
"Why are you being negligent? Slay this warrior!"
"For if neglected, this [fault] will surely cause harm;
it would become as painful as a disease left untreated.
Having said "So be it" to Acyuta, the vigilant one—
With great effort, he mangled the son of Droṇa with arrows—
his two excellent arms smeared with the essence of sandalwood,
his chest, his head, and likewise his peerless thighs.
Enraged, he pierced the son of Droṇa in battle with sharp arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow;
having severed the horse-reins, he struck the steeds.
They carried him away from the battle to an exceedingly great distance; borne by those horses swift as the wind,
the son of Droṇa was thoroughly overwhelmed by the arrows of Pārtha.
Having reflected, the wise one did not desire to engage in battle again with Pārtha,
knowing that victory was certain for the Vṛṣṇi hero.
And when Dhanañjaya had entered the army of Karṇa, that powerful one— the best of the Aṅgirases—
was shattered in his resolve, his supply of arrows exhausted, and his application of weapons spent.
Having restrained his horses and regained his composure, O Sire, the son of Droṇa entered Karṇa’s army, which was crowded with chariots, horses,
and men, while Aśvatthāman was being carried away from the battle by his horses against his will.
Just as a disease is extracted from the body by means of mantras, medicinal herbs, rituals, and gifts,
so did Keśava and Arjuna advance toward the Saṃśaptakas on a chariot whose banners were fluttered by the wind and which thundered like a torrential flood.
08,013.001 Saṃjaya said: 08,013.001a Then, from the north, a clamor arose within the army of the Pāṇḍavas,
08,013.001c as the chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry were being slaughtered by Daṇḍadhāra.
Having turned the chariot back, Keśava spoke to Arjuna while driving the horses,
which possessed the speed of Garuḍa and the wind: "The King of Magadha has already passed us with his crushing elephant."
"Inferior to none in training and in strength even to Bhagadatta—
having slain him, you shall then slay the Saṃśaptakas. At the conclusion of these words, he brought Pārtha toward Daṇḍadhāra.
That preeminent wielder of the goad among the Magadhas was as irresistible as a planet among the planets when it is out of its orbit;
fierce, he crushed the army of his enemies.
Like a comet [sweeping] across the entire earth,
he— well-equipped, resembling a Dānava or a Nāga,
with a roar like a great cloud— crushed his enemies.
Mounted upon thousands of multitudes of chariots, horses,
and elephants, he slays even the elephants with his arrows; having ascended his chariot together with its horses and charioteer, he strikes down the enemy.
He swiftly crushed chariots with his feet; standing upon his elephant, he struck down other elephants with his feet and trunk like the wheel of Time.
In that battle, the valiant hero struck down the elephant-drivers, great car-warriors, hosts of foot-soldiers, horses with their riders,
and elephants with his arrows.
Striking out in every direction like the wheel of Time,
he felled men adorned with armor of black iron,
along with their horses and foot-soldiers.
With his powerful, excellent elephant, he crushed them with a great noise, just as one might crush thick reeds;
then Arjuna [raised] the sound of his bowstring, palms, and wheel-rims.
Amidst the sounding of many mṛdaṅga drums, bherī kettledrums, and conchs,
and the clamor of thousands of men, horses,
and elephants, he assailed that preeminent elephant with his most excellent chariot.
Then he struck Arjuna with twelve excellent arrows and Janārdana with sixteen;
Daṇḍadhāra struck the horses with three arrows each.
Then he roared and laughed repeatedly;
then Pārtha, with broad-headed arrows, cut down his bow along with its string and arrow, as well as his decorated standard.
Then he again [attacked] the drivers along with the foot-guards;
thereupon the lord of Girivraja became enraged.
Then [he struck] Arjuna with an elephant whose temples were split open.
With a mallet possessing a speed equal to the wind,
he, desiring to greatly agitate Janārdana,
struck Dhanañjaya with javelins.
Then the Pāṇḍava, with three razor-sharp arrows, simultaneously severed his two arms, which resembled the trunks of elephants, and his head, whose face was like the full moon.
Then he struck the elephant with hundreds of arrows;
that elephant, wearing golden armor, was set ablaze by Pārtha’s arrows adorned with refined gold.
Thus did that mountain shine in the night,
like one whose herbs and trees are set ablaze by a forest fire; afflicted by pain, he roared with a sound like the thundering of clouds.
Trembling, reeling, stumbling, and distressed as he ran,
he fell down broken along with his driver,
like a mountain pulverized by the strike of a thunderbolt.
When his brother had been slain in battle by that elephant— which was as white as snow, adorned with a golden garland, and resembled a peak of the Himālaya mountains— Daṇḍa rushed forward.
Desiring to slay Dhanañjaya, the younger brother of Indra, he struck Janārdana with three *tomaras* as radiant as the rays of the sun,
and Arjuna with five.
Having delivered [the weapon], he let out a roar and struck him;
then the Pāṇḍava severed his two arms,
which were well-equipped with clubs and fashioned like razor-edged arrows.
The two arms, adorned with fallen armlets and smeared with sandalwood paste,
shone as they fell simultaneously from the elephant like two great serpents falling from a mountain peak.
Then, struck by the crescent-shaped arrow of Kirīṭin,
Daṇḍa’s head fell from the elephant to the earth;
shining with blood as it fell, it gleamed brilliantly.
Then, with his supreme arrows resembling the rays of the sun, he struck the elephant— which resembled the peak of a white mountain— as the sun sinks toward the western quarter.
Pārtha pierced it, and it fell down roaring,
like a peak of the Himālaya mountains struck by a thunderbolt.
Then other excellent elephants, resembling those, [advanced].
Seeking victory in battle against Savyasācin,
those two elephants were treated by him in such a manner that the vast army of the enemy was then utterly broken.
Elephants, chariots, horses, and men fell in heaps upon one another in the battle,
striking and stumbling against each other.
Those who spoke harshly against their own kin were slain;
then the soldiers, surrounding Arjuna on all sides,
spoke to him as the hosts of gods speak to Purandara.
O hero, by good fortune that enemy has been slain by you— he from whom we were as terrified as living beings are of death;
had he not protected these people from fear.
If they were thus oppressed by powerful enemies,
it would have been a cause for the joy of those foes,
just as it would be if these enemies here were slain by you.
Having heard these words spoken by his friends once again, Arjuna, being well-disposed,
then honored those people in a fitting manner.
The slayer of the Saṃśaptaka hosts went forth again.
Sañjaya said:
Having returned once more, Jiṣṇu slaughtered many Saṃśaptakas.
Like the planet Mars moving in its direct and retrograde courses,
O King, men, horses, chariots, and elephants struck by the arrows of Pārtha wavered, wandered aimlessly, shrieked, fell, and fainted, O noble one.

The son of Pāṇḍu, using broad-headed arrows, razor-sharp shafts, crescent-shaped arrows, and calf-tooth-headed bolts, struck down the draft animals, the most excellent charioteers, and the chariots themselves, as well as hands, weapons held in the hands, arms, and heads.
In that battle, he cut down the heroic enemies who were fighting against him. Your foremost warriors, roaring,
rushed toward him like bulls desiring a cow in heat, eager to fight another bull.
Hundreds and thousands of heroes rushed toward Arjuna;
the battle between them and him was hair-raising,
like that which occurred when the Daityas fought the wielder of the thunderbolt for the conquest of the three worlds.
Ugrāyudha pierced him with three arrows like venomous serpents,
and then he struck off his head from his body. Enraged, they showered Arjuna from all sides with various weapons.
Like clouds driven by the Maruts against the Himavat at the end of the hot season,
Arjuna, having warded off the weapons of his enemies with his own weapons from every side,
struck down all those many assembled foes with his well-aimed arrows.

With their triple-pole shafts and yokes broken, their side-horses and charioteers slain, their weapons and quivers shattered, their wheels, chariot-banners, and standards destroyed, and their reins, fastenings, axles, undercarriages,
and yokes severed— the chariots lay in ruins.

Arjuna, acting with haste, shattered all their armor with his arrows. Those chariots there, though utterly destroyed, shone in their many hundreds like the mansions of the wealthy ruined by fire, wind, and water.
Elephants, their vital organs pierced by arrows equal to thunderbolts and lightning,
fell like mountain peaks and palaces struck by vajra-winds and fire.
Many horses, along with their riders, fell, struck down by Arjuna.
With tongues and entrails protruding, wasted away on the earth, drenched in blood, and most hideous to behold— men,
horses, and elephants pierced by the iron shafts of Savyasācin wandered, stumbled, fell, shrieked, and fainted, O noble one.
With arrows that were whetted on stone, unerring, and like thunderbolts or poison, Pārtha struck them down just as Mahendra strikes down the Dānavas;
they, adorned with costly armor and ornaments, and equipped with various kinds of garments and weapons.
The heroes, together with their charioteers and banners, lie slain by Pārtha;
though they were victors of meritorious deeds, distinguished by noble birth and sacred learning,
they have gone to the earth with their bodies, while by their powerful deeds they have reached heaven.
Then your heroic warriors, the lords of various realms, accompanied by their hosts and filled with wrath, rushed toward Arjuna’s chariot;
borne on chariots and horses, as well as on foot, they sought to slay him.
They rushed forward together, swiftly hurling various weapons. Then,
the wind that was Arjuna quickly dispersed with his sharp arrows that great rain of weapons cast by the great clouds that were the warriors.

Then Vāsudeva said to Pārtha, who was suddenly seeking to cross over that flood of great weapons— devoid of boats and consisting of horses, infantry, elephants, and chariots— by means of a bridge of missiles and weapons: "O sinless one, why do you play?"
"O Pārtha, these powerful ones have been overcome; why do you delay, O sinless one?
Having crushed these Saṃśaptakas, hasten then to the slaying of Karṇa. Having said, "So be it," Arjuna then quickly [attacked] the remaining Saṃśaptakas.
Having struck down the Daityas with his weapon by force, he slew them like Indra. Arjuna was seen by some in battle as he took up and fixed his arrows,
yet he was seen by others as he released his shafts with such speed.
"Marvelous! Govinda exclaimed, as he urged on the horses;
those steeds, white as the breast of a swan, entered the army like swans entering a lake.
Then those horses, resembling swans and possessing the speed of the wind—
They entered that army joyfully, like swans entering a great lake. Then, while that slaughter of men was underway on the field of battle,
Govinda, looking toward Savyasācin, spoke to him.
"O Pārtha, this great and terrible destruction of the Bharatas is now unfolding—
a vast slaughter of the kings upon the earth caused by Duryodhana.
Behold, O Bhārata, the gold-backed bows of the archers!"
He saw discarded quivers and bow-cases belonging to great warriors,
as well as straight-knotted arrows with shafts made of gold,
and iron-tipped shafts polished with oil, resembling snakes that have just cast their skins.
The battlefields were strewn with swords having ivory hilts adorned with gold, with spears, and with variegated bows decorated with gold;
they were also covered with staffs variegated with gold. Thus did the grounds of war become overspread.
O Bhārata, there were discarded armors with gold-backed surfaces, spears fashioned with gold,
javelins adorned with gold,
and massive maces bound with bands of Jāmbūnada gold.
He saw spears made of gold, pattishas adorned with gold,
battle-axes scattered about with handles variegated by gold, as well as iron clubs, bhindipalas, bhusundis, and kunapas.
Behold the iron hooks with their points broken, the fallen heavy maces, the *śataghnīs*, the variegated and massive clubs,
the discarded wheels, and the many hammers left on the battlefield.
Grasping various kinds of weapons and greedy for victory, those swift warriors, though their vital strength had departed, appeared as if they were still alive,
with limbs crushed by maces and heads split by clubs.
Behold thousands of warriors crushed by elephants, horses, and chariots;
[behold] men, elephants, and horses [slain] by arrows, spears, double-edged swords, lances, and tomara-javelins,
as well as by scimitars, sharp-edged spears, barbed missiles, claws, and even clubs.
O slayer of enemies, the battlefields were covered with bodies severed in many ways and drenched in floods of blood, their life-breaths departed;
they lay there with arms smeared with sandalwood paste, adorned with armlets and beautiful ornaments.
O Bhārata, the earth shines with hundreds of thousands of armlets and bracelets,
with decorated forearms still wearing finger-guards,
and with the severed thighs of the swift warriors, which resemble the trunks of elephants.
The earth shines with the severed heads of bull-eyed warriors— heads adorned with excellent crest-jewels and earrings—
and with headless trunks smeared with blood, their limbs and necks mangled.
O best of the Bharatas, the earth shines as if with fires whose flames have been extinguished. Behold the various kinds of beautiful chariots, broken and adorned with golden bells,
and the horses drenched in blood in many ways.
He saw the chariot-poles, quivers, various banners and standards,
the great conch shells of the warriors, and white yak-tail fans;
as well as elephants resembling mountains, lying there with their tongues protruding.
He saw the variegated Vaijayantī banners and slain elephant-warriors, as well as the housings of the elephants adorned with fine cloth and woolen blankets,
and likewise various torn and colorfully decorated rugs.
Bells were shattered in many ways and crushed by falling elephants; there lay on the ground elephant goads with handles of lapis lazuli,
as well as horses' yoke-straps, head-ornaments, and breastplates variegated with jewels.
Whips adorned with gold were tied to the tops of the riders' standards; and variegated horse-blankets, decorated with jewels and embellished with gold,
as well as woolen rugs from the Rāṅku deer, lay fallen upon the earth.
The crest-jewels of kings, variegated golden garlands, discarded parasols, and yak-tail fans; and faces radiant as the moon or stars, adorned with beautiful earrings.
Behold the earth, mired in the mud of blood, completely covered by the faces of heroes— faces beautifully adorned and with well-trimmed beards—
just as a lake is covered by clusters of blooming white and blue lotus petals.

Likewise, behold the earth, adorned with the faces of kings resembling white and blue lotuses, which is equal to the sky, variegated by clusters of stars and radiant with the luster of the stainless moon, garlanded by planets and constellations.
O lord of the people, behold the living men all around,
crying out and being attended by many kinsmen who have laid down their weapons and are weeping again and again.
Having covered other swift warriors who had broken through the ranks,
those furious men, greedy for victory, returned once more to the fight;
others there, full of pride, rushed hither and thither.
O Arjuna, while being entreated for water by their fallen kinsmen and heroes,
many who had gone there for the sake of water returned lifeless;
and upon seeing them, those heroes were themselves deprived of their senses.
Seeing water, they run toward it while crying out to one another;
behold, O Bhārata, those who have died after drinking water, and others as they drink. Others, O lover of kinsmen, abandon their dear relatives.
In that great battle, they were seen here and there leaping across [the field];
behold others, O best of men, with their lips bitten again and again,
looking all around with faces contorted by frowns.
Speaking thus, Kṛṣṇa then proceeded toward Yudhiṣṭhira;
and Arjuna also, for the sake of seeing the king in that great battle, urged Govinda again and again, saying, "Go! Go!"
Having shown that battlefield of Pārtha to Mādhava, he said:
"O Arjuna, this deed performed by you in the great battle is worthy of you alone,
just as [that] which was done by the King of the Gods in heaven during his combat."
While thus showing the battlefield to the Diademed One (Arjuna), Kṛṣṇa,
as he proceeded, heard a great noise in Duryodhana’s army—
the resounding blasts of conchs and kettledrums mingled with the sounds of drums and cymbals.
Hearing the sounds of chariots, horses, and elephants, as well as the dreadful clashing of weapons,
Kṛṣṇa entered that army on horses swift as the wind;
having seen your army being hard-pressed by the Pāṇḍya king, he took his stand.
For that preeminent archer, with various kinds of arrows in battle,
struck down the hosts of his enemies like Death himself taking away their lives;
he pierced the bodies of elephants, horses, and men with his sharp shafts.
Having pierced through them, that best of strikers deprived the Videhas of their lives; having shattered with his arrows the various weapons hurled by the enemy heroes,
the Pāṇḍya king slew those foes just as Śakra slew the Asuras.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"You have already previously described him as a pre-eminent hero renowned throughout the world;
yet, O Sañjaya, his deeds in battle have not been recounted by you."
"Tell me now in detail of that great hero’s prowess— his training, his power, his valor, his stature, and his pride. Sañjaya said:
Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, Arjuna, and Janārdana—
those whom you consider the foremost in battle, masters of weaponry and perfected in their knowledge;
indeed, he who by his prowess surpasses all these great chariot-warriors.
He did not consider any lord of men to be his equal;
he could not see anyone who was equal to himself in the eyes of Karṇa and Bhīṣma,
nor did he admit any inferiority in himself before Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
That Pāṇḍya, the best of kings and the foremost among all wielders of weapons,
slaughtered Karṇa’s army like Death himself when provoked;
that host consisting of exalted chariots, horses, elite foot-soldiers, and elephants.
Like a potter’s wheel whirling, the army was presided over by Pāṇḍya;
with well-aimed arrows, Pāṇḍya scattered his enemies— deprived of horses, charioteers, banners, and chariots, and with their weapons cast aside— just as the wind disperses the clouds.
The slayer of enemies destroyed the elephants— whose trunks were struck down and whose banners, standards, and weapons were cast off—
along with their foot-guards, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt destroys his foes;
he likewise destroyed the horsemen and their horses, together with their spears, lances, and quivers.
Having stripped the Pulindas, Khaśas, Bāhlīkas, Niṣādas, Dhrukas, Taṅgaṇas,
the southerners, and the Bhojas— those cruel ones fierce in battle—
of their weapons and armor with his arrows, the Pāṇḍya king deprived them of life.

Seeing Pāṇḍya slaying the fourfold army with his arrows in battle, the son of Droṇa, remaining unperturbed himself, advanced even more calmly; addressing him sweetly, he rushed forward as if dancing and free from fear.
The best among strikers, summoning him with a smile, said:
"O King, lotus-petal-eyed one, you who possess preeminent weapons and mounts,
whose frame is like a thunderbolt, and who are endowed with supreme strength and prowess!"
With your two outstretched arms, gripping weapons firmly in your fists,
you shine intensely like a massive rain-cloud as you draw your great bow and shower your enemies with volleys of arrows of great velocity.
I see no other hero besides me who can withstand you in battle;
alone, you crush many chariots, elephants, infantry,
and horses, like a fearless lion of terrifying strength destroys herds of deer in the forest.
Making heaven and earth resound with the great roar of his chariot,
like a parching wind at the end of the rainy season filling the land with its rays,
he drew sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents from his quiver.
"Fight with me alone, as Andhaka did with Tryambaka.
Thus addressed, Malayadhvaja replied, "So be it," and having said, "Strike! he struck him; then, with a barbed arrow, he pierced the son of Droṇa.
Smiling, the son of Droṇa, that best of teachers, struck Pāṇḍya with extremely fierce arrows resembling flames of fire that pierced his vital organs;
then he [fired] nine other sharp iron shafts feathered with heron plumes.
Aśvatthāman discharged those [arrows] joined with the tenth course;
Pāṇḍya cut them down with five sharpened shafts.
Four [of his arrows] struck the horses, and they quickly became lifeless.
Then, having cut those arrows of Droṇa’s son with his own sharp shafts,
Pāṇḍya, who possessed the splendor of the sun, severed the stretched bowstring. Thereupon, the son of Droṇa, the slayer of enemies, strung his bow which had been unstrung.
Seeing that other excellent horses had been quickly yoked to his chariot by men,
he then dispatched thousands of arrows at the Pāṇḍya king;
he filled the sky and the very quarters of the horizon with a dense mass of shafts.
Then, O bull among men, although he knew them to be inexhaustible, Pāṇḍya, that best of men, struck down all those arrows being discharged by the high-souled son of Droṇa;
having severed with great effort those shafts sent forth by the son of Droṇa, the enemy [remained unshaken].
Then, with sharpened arrows, he [Aśvatthāman] struck down his two wheel-protectors. Then,
beholding the lightness of hand of his enemy,
the son of Droṇa drew his bow into a circle and loosed a rain of arrows, like the younger brother of Pūṣan (Yama).
O noble one, the son of Droṇa discharged in a single eighth-part of a day as many weapons as eight carts drawn by eight oxen each could carry;
he was like the enraged God of Death himself, resembling the Destroyer at the end of time.
Whoever beheld him there mostly lost their senses;
like Parjanya at the end of the summer heat drenching the earth with its mountains and trees by means of rain,
the preceptor’s son showered that army with a rain of arrows.
Having quickly checked with the Vāyavya weapon that unbearable shower of arrows released by Droṇa’s son, who was like a rain-cloud, the Pāṇḍya-wind roared. As he roared,
[he struck] his banner, which was adorned with sandalwood and aloe.
The son of Droṇa, having cut through [Draupada’s] bow which resembled Mount Malaya, slew his four horses; then,
having killed the charioteer— who possessed a voice like the roar of a great rain-cloud— with a single arrow,
he severed the bow with a crescent-headed shaft and shattered the chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
Having warded off weapons with his own weapons and having cut down all his [opponent's] arms,
the son of Droṇa did not slay his enemy even when he was within reach, out of a desire for further combat.
In that interval, Karṇa rushed toward the elephant division.
At that time, he caused the great army of the Pāṇḍavas to flee;
O Bhārata, he deprived the chariot-warriors of their chariots and struck down the elephants and horses.
He pierced many elephants with numerous straight-jointed arrows.
Then the son of Droṇa, that great archer, did not slay Pāṇḍya— the destroyer of enemies and the best among chariot-warriors—
who had been deprived of his chariot, out of a desire for further combat. That excellent elephant, well-equipped, had its rider slain.
Urged on with haste, the powerful Pratiśarmaga rushed toward him; struck by the son of Droṇa’s arrows,
he quickly roared like a rival elephant as he charged with speed.
The great lord of Malaya mounted that elephant, the best of tuskers, which resembled a mountain peak and for which he was skilled in the art of elephant warfare.
Just as a roaring lion [leaps] upon a mountain peak,
so did he [launch] that lance, which resembled the rays of the sun,
with the force of his strength, the excellence of his weapon, his effort, and his fury.
The lord of mountains, roaring, swiftly released [the weapon] while pressing down upon the elephant, for the sake of his preceptor’s son,
with [arrows] adorned with excellent diamonds, gold, and clusters of jewels.
Adorned with fine silks, garlands, and pearls,
he repeatedly cried out in joy, "You are slain!
and struck down the excellent ornaments from the body of Droṇa’s son.
That [mountain], possessing the brilliance of the sun, moon, planets, and fire,
fell shattered by the violent impact,
like a great forest struck down by the thunderbolt of Mahendra.
Just as a mountain peak stands upon the surface of the earth,
so he blazed with supreme fury,
like the lord of serpents when struck by a foot.
He took up fourteen arrows, which resembled the staff of Death and were capable of ending his enemies;
with five of them, he struck the elephant’s forefeet and trunk.
With three arrows he struck the king’s two arms and his head, and with six more— possessing the brilliance of the six supreme seasons— he slew the great chariot-warriors who followed the Pāṇḍya king.
Those two arms of the king— long in their reach, smeared with excellent sandalwood paste,
and adorned with gold, pearls, gems, and diamonds—
lay fallen upon the earth.
They writhed like two serpents struck by Tārkṣya;
and that head, with a face possessing the luster of the full moon,
with large eyes copper-red with rage, and a prominent nose—
Adorned with earrings, it shone upon the earth as it fell like the moon situated between the two Viśākhā stars; meanwhile,
that elephant was struck by five excellent arrows.
The king took a sixth part for himself, while four parts were set aside by the three [allies]; thus,
through his skillful fighting, he secured a tenth share,
just as the sacrificial oblation belongs to ten deities.
Having offered many horses, men, and elephants, limb by limb, as food for the Rākṣasas,
the Pāṇḍya king attained his own abode like the fire dear to the ancestors.
Then, once the flow of water had subsided,
the king approached his son, who had completed his studies under the guru and finished his ritual duties. Your son [approached him].
Surrounded by his friends, he honored him exceedingly with joy,
just as the Lord of the Immortals honored Viṣṇu when Bali had been conquered.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, when Pāṇḍya had been slain, what did Arjuna do in battle,
while the enemies were being put to flight by the peerless hero Karṇa?
For the Pāṇḍava is one who has completed his studies, is powerful, disciplined, and a true hero."
"Permitted by the high-souled Śaṅkara among all beings,
there is therefore a great and intense fear of Dhananjaya, the slayer of enemies.
Tell me, Saṃjaya, what Pārtha did there."
Saṃjaya said:
When the Pāṇḍya king had been slain, Kṛṣṇa spoke these beneficial words to Arjuna with haste:
"Behold the highly esteemed king and the Pāṇḍavas who have retreated."
"By the mere resolve of Aśvatthāman, the Sṛñjayas were slain by Karṇa;
likewise, a great slaughter of horses, men, and elephants was wrought.
Thus spoke the invincible Vāsudeva to the Diademed One (Arjuna).
Having heard this and having seen the terrible, great danger facing his brother, the Pāṇḍava said, "O Hṛṣīkeśa, drive the horses quickly! Thereupon,
Hṛṣīkeśa set forth on the chariot that was invincible in combat.
Then, once again, dust arose there in that great battle,
and once more a terrible encounter took place.
Thereupon, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, undaunted, came together once again.
The Pārthas, headed by Bhīmasena, and we, headed by the Sūta’s son— then,
O best of kings, there once again commenced a battle between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍavas, which increased the population of Yama’s realm.
Bows, arrows, iron clubs, black spears, and sharp-edged pikes;
maces, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, javelins, double-edged swords, battle-axes;
bludgeons, lances, scimitars, spikes, and great hooks.
Grasping their weapons, they quickly rushed forward, desiring to conquer one another.

With the sound of arrows, bowstrings, and palms, and with the roar of wheel-rims, they advanced against the enemies, making the heavens, the cardinal directions, the intermediate points, the sky, and the earth resound.
At that great sound, the heroes were filled with joy and engaged in a most terrible battle, desiring to reach the end of the conflict; there arose the sounds of bowstrings,
arm-guards, and bows, along with the trumpeting of elephants.
A tremendous clamor arose from those who were being struck down and falling;
and hearing the various sounds of arrows and the shouts of the roaring heroes, O Bhārata, they trembled violently, struck one another, and fainted.
As they were crying out and discharging a rain of weapons,
Karṇa, the son of Adhiratha, crushed many of them in battle with his arrows—
five, ten, and five chariot-warriors among the Pāñcāla heroes.
Karna sent those, along with their horses, charioteers, and banners, to the abode of Yama with his arrows.
The chief warriors of the Pandavas, possessed of great heroism and swift in the use of weapons, surrounded Karna from all sides in the battle, covering the very heavens.
Then Karṇa, agitating the enemy army with showers of arrows,
plunged into it like a leader of a herd entering a lotus pond filled with birds.
Having leaped into the midst of the foes, the son of Rādhā took up his excellent bow.
Shaking his sharp arrows, he struck off and felled heads;
he brought down elephants with their great mahouts, horses along with their riders,
and even chariot-warriors as they whirled about, with a single arrow each.
Having sliced through shields and armor as if extinguishing the fires of embodied beings,
they could not endure contact with his second feathered shaft,
for by means of arrows released from his bow that crush armor, bodies, and lives, [he struck them down].
With his leather finger-guards and bowstring, he struck them as one strikes horses with a whip;
he brought the Pāṇḍus, Sṛñjayas, and Pāñcālas within the range of his arrows,
crushing them with force like a lion among herds of deer.
Then, O Sire, the sons of the Pāñcāla king, the sons of Draupadī,
the twins, and Yuyudhāna, joined together, advanced against Karṇa;
the Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and Sṛñjayas exerted themselves with great intensity.
Having abandoned their dear lives in battle, the warriors rushed at one another;
well-armored, clad in mail, and adorned with helmets,
other great car-warriors [attacked] with maces, clubs, and iron bludgeons.
O noble one, they rushed forward violently like gods with uplifted staffs, shouting, challenging, and leaping about;
then they struck one another and fell, mangled in the combat.
Vomiting blood from their limbs, with brains and eyes crushed in battle,
they stood as if still alive, bolstered by their weapons, their mouths filled with teeth and smeared with blood like pomegranate seeds.
Others, moreover, [attacked] one another with spears, swords, as well as javelins, slings, claws, barbed darts,
and lances; some hacked, others cut, some pierced, and others likewise hurled [their weapons].
Enraged, they hacked, struck, and pierced one another;
slain by each other, they fell lifeless,
drenched in blood like sandalwood trees exuding their own resin.
Chariots were struck down by chariots, and elephants likewise by elephants;
men fell by the hands of the best of men, and horses by the thousands at the hands of horses. Banners, heads, umbrellas, the trunks of elephants, and the arms of men lay scattered about.

Cut by razors, bhallas, and crescent-shaped arrows, they dropped their weapons. A terrible sound arose from those being slain, as well as from men, horses, elephants, and chariots falling and groaning amidst other men, horses, elephants, and chariots at that time.
In that battle, they crushed men, elephants, chariots, and horses;
likewise, slain chariots fell by the thousands along with their horse-riders.
Heroes were killed by horse-riders, and elephants had their trunks severed.
Banners and standards fell like shattered mountains;
and foot-soldiers having surged forward, as well as elephants and chariots,
were struck down, slaughtered, and fallen in every direction.
Horsemen, having encountered foot soldiers, were swiftly slain;
and throngs of foot soldiers, struck down by horsemen,
lay upon the battlefield like crushed lotuses or withered garlands.
O Great-minded One, O King, the faces and limbs of the slain elephants,
horses, and men— though their forms were exceedingly desirable—
became utterly unsightly, like garments that have been soiled.
In that very same way, the facial complexion of some there was seen to be like that of those who have fallen asleep from intoxication, with their ornaments and garlands disarrayed. Sañjaya said:
Urged on by your son, the high-ranking elephant-riders,
filled with rage and desiring to slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata, advanced against him;
these were the foremost heroes from the east and the south, skilled in fighting from elephants.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, Māgadhas, and Tāmraliptakas;
the Mekalas, Kośalas, Madras, Daśārṇas, and Niṣadhas— these,
O Bhārata, along with the Kaliṅgas, are skilled in elephant warfare.
Like rain-bearing clouds, they all then showered that mountain-like Pāñcāla with arrows, tomara-spears, and iron shafts in battle;
yet he violently crushed those elephants with his heels, toes, and goads.
O Bhārata,
the son of Pṛṣata showered those elephants— each resembling a mountain— with iron shafts and arrows, piercing them one by one with ten, six, or even eight discharged arrows.
Being shrouded by elephants like the sun by clouds,
the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas, roaring and brandishing sharpened weapons,
rained upon those elephants with the sounds of bowstrings as their lutes and arrows as their music.
Dancing a heroic dance, impelled by the rhythm of their valor,
Nakula, Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas,
Sātyaki, Śikhaṇḍin, and the heroic Cekitāna [advanced].
The heroes showered [them] from all sides, just as clouds drench mountains with water.
Those elephants, dispatched by the Mlecchas and filled with great fury, seized men, horses, and even chariots with their trunks and crushed them with their feet.

They pierced him with the tips of their tusks, and having seized him, they hurled him about; others, clinging to the tusks, fell down in a terrifying manner. But Sātyaki [encountered] the elephant of Vaṅga as it stood before him.

Having pierced his vital organs with a steel arrow of fierce velocity, he struck him down as that elephant-riders was about to leap from his mount after it had been turned aside; Satyaki’s chest was split open by the steel arrow, and he fell to the earth.
As Puṇḍra rushed forward with his elephant, which was like a moving mountain,
Sahadeva struck it with three iron shafts (nārācas) with great effort,
depriving it of its banner, its driver, its armor, its standard, and its life.
Having fashioned that elephant, Sahadeva then advanced against Aṅga.
But Nakula, having restrained Sahadeva,
struck Aṅga with three iron shafts resembling the staff of Yama, and [struck] the elephant with a hundred.
Aṅga hurled eight hundred lances, each as brilliant as the rays of the sun, at Nakula; but he cut each one into three pieces. Then, with a crescent-headed arrow, the Pāṇḍava severed his head.
Slain, that Mleccha fell along with his very elephant. When the preceptor’s son, who was highly skilled in the science of elephants, had been killed,
the enraged elephant-riders of Aṅga advanced against Nakula with their great elephants.
With their banners fluttering and their golden girths and armor gleaming, they rushed forward like blazing mountains, crushing their enemies— the Mekalas, Utkalas,
Kalingas, Niṣādas, and Tāmraliptakas.
Discharging showers of arrows and *tomaras* with the intent to slay him,
Nakula was covered by them as the sun is by clouds;
then the Pāṇḍus, Pañcālas, and Somakas, highly incensed, rushed forward to his aid.
Then that battle took place between the chariot-warriors and the elephants,
as they discharged showers of arrows and *tomaras* by the thousands;
the frontal globes and various vital organs of the elephants burst open.

The teeth and ornaments of those who were deeply pierced by iron shafts [were shattered]. Sahadeva swiftly struck eight great elephants with sixty-four well-sharpened arrows; they fell down together with their riders.
Drawing that supreme bow with effort and straight movements,
Nakula, the joy of the Kurus, struck down the elephants with iron arrows.
Then the grandson of Śini, the Pāñcālya, the sons of Draupadī, and the Prabhadrakas [advanced].

And Śikhaṇḍin drenched the great elephants with showers of arrows. Those mountain-like enemy elephants, struck by the rain of shafts from the Pāṇḍava warriors who were like clouds, fell down like mountains struck by a rain of thunderbolts.

Having thus slain your elephants, those elephant-like warriors of the Pāṇḍavas quickly beheld your army like a river whose banks have been breached. Beholding that army, the soldiers of the son of Pāṇḍu—
Having thrown them into agitation, they then rushed back toward Karṇa himself.
Then, O Great King, Duḥśāsana advanced against his brother Sahadeva, who was enraged and consuming your army.
Seeing those two joined together in that great battle,
the lords of men there let out lion-like roars and waved their garments.
Then, O Bhārata, by your son, the enraged archer—
Struck in the chest with three arrows by the powerful son of Pāṇḍu,
O King, Sahadeva then pierced your son with a steel shaft (nārāca) and struck his charioteer with seventy arrows, along with three more for each of them.
Then, O King, Duḥśāsana, having severed his bow in that great battle,
struck Sahadeva in the arms and chest with seventy-three arrows.
Thereupon, the enraged Sahadeva seized a sword in that great battle.
The illustrious best of warriors brandished [his weapon] against your son;
having severed his bow along with its clusters of arrows,
that great sword then fell to the earth like a snake fallen from the sky.
Then the powerful Sahadeva, taking up another bow,
discharged a death-dealing arrow at Duḥśāsana.
As that shaft approached, it possessed a brilliance like the staff of Yama.
With a sharp-edged sword, the Kaurava cut it in two.
Then, quickly brandishing that whetted sword in battle,
the valiant one took up another bow and seized an arrow.
As that sword was suddenly falling upon him,
Sahadeva, as if smiling, caused it to fall in battle with his sharpened arrows.
Then, in that great battle, your son [discharged] sixty-four arrows.
O Bhārata, he swiftly caused them to fall upon Sahadeva’s chariot;
O King, as those many arrows fell with great force in that battle,
Sahadeva cut each one down with five shafts.
Having warded off the great arrows dispatched by your son,
the son of Mādrī then loosed a vast multitude of shafts at him in that battle.
Your son, too, having cut each of those arrows with three shafts of his own,
let out a tremendous roar that seemed to rend the earth.
Then, O King, Duḥśāsana pierced the son of Pāṇḍu in battle.
Then,
O great king, the powerful Sahadeva, filled with rage,
struck the charioteer with nine arrows and fixed a terrible shaft upon his bow that resembled Death himself at the end of time.
Drawing his bow with great force, he discharged [an arrow] at your son; O King,
having pierced him with speed and shattered his great armor,
it entered the earth like a serpent into an anthill.
Then, O King, your son, that great car-warrior,
lost consciousness; and seeing him thus bewildered, his charioteer, greatly terrified and being struck by sharp arrows, quickly drove the chariot away.
There was indeed a tremendous roar that made the earth resound;
having defeated him in battle, O elder brother of Pāṇḍu,
the son of Pāṇḍu joyfully crushed Duryodhana’s army on all sides.
O King, O Bhārata, just as a man might angrily crush an anthill, so was that Kaurava army crushed by him. Nakula, impetuous in battle, was tearing through the ranks of the army.
Then, O King, Karṇa Vaikartana indeed held Nakula at bay;
and Nakula, laughing, then said this to Karṇa:
"Ah, after a long time at last I have been beheld by the gods with a favorable eye!"
O wicked one, since you have come within the range of my vision in battle,
you are indeed the root of all misfortunes, of enmity, and of strife.
It is through your fault that the Kurus have been destroyed, having encountered one another.
"Having slain you today in battle, I shall have accomplished my purpose and be free from my fever.
Thus addressed, the son of the Sūta replied to Nakula with words befitting a prince, and especially one skilled in the bow.
"Strike in battle, O child! Let us see your prowess.
O hero, it is only after performing deeds in battle that you ought to boast. For heroes, my dear, fight to the best of their ability without speaking in the midst of combat."

"Fight with me to the best of your power; today I shall humble your pride. Having said this, the son of the Sūta quickly struck the son of Pāṇḍu and pierced him in battle with seventy-three stone-tipped arrows.
Then Nakula, pierced by the Sūtaputra, O Bhārata,
struck the Sūtaputra in return with eighty arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Karna, having cut his bow with gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone, [pierced him].
With thirty arrows, that supreme archer struck the Pāṇḍava.
Having pierced his armor, they drank his blood in the battle,
just as venomous serpents, having pierced the earth, drink water.
Then, taking up another formidable bow with a golden back,
he pierced Karṇa with twenty arrows and his charioteer with three.
Thereupon, O great king, Nakula, the slayer of enemy heroes, was filled with rage.
With an exceedingly sharp razor-headed arrow, he severed Karna’s bow. Then, laughing, that hero struck the great chariot-warrior of all the worlds— now deprived of his bow— with three hundred shafts.
O noble one, seeing Karṇa thus afflicted by the son of Pāṇḍu, the chariot-warriors along with the gods were struck with supreme wonder. Then, taking up another bow, Vaikartana Karṇa—

He struck Nakula in the region of the collarbone with five arrows. With those arrows fixed in his chest, the son of Mādrī shone like the sun scattering its radiance throughout the world with its own rays.
Then Nakula, having pierced Karna with seven iron arrows,
once more cut the tip of his bow, O Sire.
Taking up another bow that was even more powerful in battle, [Karna...]
Then, with his arrows, he blocked all directions around Nakula.
Suddenly covered by the shafts released from Karna’s bow,
that great car-warrior swiftly cut those arrows down with his own arrows.
Then a net consisting of arrows was seen spread across the sky,
like the heavens filled with swarms of falling fireflies;
the firmament was then covered by those hundreds of arrows released by them.
It was as crowded as a swarm of locusts;
those arrows, adorned with gold, falling again and again,
shone like rows of swans flying in formation.
When the sky was covered by a net of arrows and the sun was obscured,
O lord of the people, some kind of being then began to creep forward;
for that path was blocked on all sides by a multitude of shafts.
Those two highly fortunate ones shone like two young suns that have just risen.
But the Somakas, being struck by arrows released from Karna’s bow,
O king of kings, cowered in pain, afflicted by the shafts and tormented by agony.

O King, as your army was being slaughtered by Nakula’s arrows, it scattered in all directions like clouds driven by the wind. While those two armies were being struck down by those two with their divine, great shafts, [the battle continued].
Having retreated to the distance of an arrow-shot, they then stood like spectators;
while that crowd was being driven back by the arrows of Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava,
those two great-souled ones pierced each other with showers of shafts.
Displaying divine weapons at the forefront of the battle and suddenly shrouding one another while seeking each other's death,
Nakula released arrows feathered with the plumes of herons and peacocks.

Having covered Karna, those arrows remained suspended in the sky just as the enemy [stood]; likewise, dispatched by the Sūtaputra in that great battle, the arrows covered the son of Pāṇḍu and remained suspended in the air.
Having entered the house of arrows, those two could not be seen by anyone,
O King, like the sun and the moon obscured at the onset of the rainy season.
Then, enraged in battle, Karṇa assumed a most terrible form.
He covered the Pāṇḍava from all sides with showers of arrows. Though being thus shrouded in battle by the Sūta’s son, O King, the Pāṇḍava felt no distress, just as the sun is not troubled by clouds.
Then, O noble one, the son of Adhiratha laughed and loosed nets of arrows by the hundreds and thousands in that battle;
everything became a single expanse of shadow due to the shafts of that great-souled warrior.
A shadow like that of clouds was produced by those falling, excellent arrows.
Then, O great king, Karna, having severed the bow of that high-souled one,
struck down his charioteer from the seat of the chariot as if laughing.
Likewise, O Bhārata, with four sharpened arrows, he swiftly dispatched his four horses to the abode of Yama; then, with his shafts,
he quickly shattered that chariot of his into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
O noble one, [he took] the banner, the two wheel-protectors, the standard, and the sword;
then the shield marked with a hundred moons, all the equipment,
and that bow adorned with gold along with its arrows in the battle.
O lord of the people, his horses slain, his chariot lost, and his armor stripped away,
he quickly descended from the chariot and stood firm, grasping a club.
Seeing that most terrible club raised by him, the son of the Sūta—
O King, he struck him with arrows by the hundreds and thousands;
