and observing that he was deprived of his weapons, Karṇa afflicted him repeatedly with straight-knotted shafts, yet he did not crush him.
Being struck in battle by that more powerful warrior skilled in weapons,
O King, Nakula fled suddenly with his senses overwhelmed. Pursuing him, the son of Rādhā laughed again and again.
O Bhārata, he placed that strung bow around his neck;
then, O King, with the great bow fastened to his neck,
he shone like the moon in the sky when it has entered a halo.
And just as a white cloud adorned with Indra’s bow shines,
O great king, so did the son of Pāṇḍu shine in battle.
Then Karṇa said to him, "You have spoken in vain."
"Now, being joyful, you speak to me again and again as if I were one to be slain:
'O Pāṇḍava, do not fight with those who are superior and more powerful;
O dear one, fight with your equals! Do not feel shame, O Pāṇḍava.'"
"Go home, O son of Mādrī, or go wherever Kṛṣṇa and Phalguna are.
Having spoken thus, O great king, he then dismissed him.
But though he was within his power to kill him, O king, the son of the Sūta did not slay him.

O King, remembering the words of Kuntī, he then dismissed him. Once dismissed by the bow-wielding son of the Sūta, O King, the Pāṇḍava then departed toward Yudhiṣṭhira’s chariot as if filled with shame.
Tormented by the son of the Sūta, he ascended his chariot,
sighing and consumed by grief like a serpent cast into a jar;
having abandoned him in battle, Karṇa quickly proceeded toward the Pāñcālas.
With his chariot bearing a towering banner and drawn by horses the color of the moon,
a great outcry arose among the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of the people,
upon seeing the commander-in-chief advancing toward the throngs of Pāñcāla chariots.
There, O Great King, the son of the Sūta wrought a great slaughter,
moving like a wheel as the lord advanced when the sun had reached its meridian.
Some [warriors] were left with chariots whose wheels were shattered and whose banners and flags were torn away.

O noble one, we beheld the throngs of Pāñcāla chariots being dragged away— some with their drivers slain, some with their drivers killed, and others with their axles broken. And here and there, intoxicated elephants wandered about in utter confusion.
O noble one, they were like elephants in a great forest whose limbs are enveloped by a forest fire—
elephants with shattered temples,
covered in blood, with severed trunks, their excellent bodies mangled, and their tails lopped off.
Being struck down by the high-souled one, they fell like scattered clouds;
other elephants, terrified by hundreds of iron shafts and lances,
rushed toward him alone like moths into a fire.
Other great elephants were seen groaning, shedding blood from their limbs like mountains discharging waterfalls; and the horses were seen with their breastplates cast off and their manes unbound.
They were deprived of ornaments made of silver, bronze, and gold;
they were lacking in rugs and devoid of bits;
and their fly-whisks, saddle-cloths, and quivers had also fallen away.
With the slain horsemen— heroes who graced the field of battle—
we suddenly beheld the finest steeds galloping like the wind;
we saw those excellent horses wandering about there on the battlefield.

O lord of men, O Bhārata, we beheld horse-riders wearing tunics and turbans, pierced by spears, swords, and double-edged blades— some already slain, some being struck down, and others trembling with fear.

O Bhārata, there he saw chariots with their various parts and limbs missing here and there, as well as those still yoked to horses, all rolling about in every direction; and he saw chariots adorned with gold, well-harnessed to swift steeds.
We saw them wandering swiftly among the slain chariot-warriors,
O noble one— some with broken axles and poles, some with shattered wheels,
others with their banners and standards fallen, and still others with their shafts, yokes, and frames cut to pieces.
O lord of the people, we beheld the chariot-warriors there deprived of their vehicles and fleeing in every direction;
we saw the chariots there shattered into pieces as small as sesame seeds by the prowess of Karṇa,
and we saw them terrified by the arrows of the Sun’s son.
He saw many of your men slain— some weaponless and others still clutching their weapons— covered in nets and adorned with breast-plates and bells,
and decorated with banners of various colors and diverse patterns.
We beheld foot-soldiers running in every direction;
and heads, arms, thighs, and other limbs severed in battle— arms, thighs, bows, and more, O lord of men, cut down by arrows.
With severed heads, arms, and variegated thighs,
we beheld men deprived of life by arrows shot from the bows and ears [of warriors].
A great and terrible carnage of the combatants was witnessed.
Pierced by Karna’s arrows and struck down by his sharpened shafts,
those Sṛñjayas, being slaughtered in battle by the son of the Sūta,
rushed toward him alone like moths into a fire.
As that great car-warrior scorched the ranks here and there,
the Kṣatriyas avoided him as if he were the fierce fire at the end of an eon.
Those heroes among the Pāñcālas who remained after the slaughter were likewise great car-warriors.
As they were broken and fleeing with their armor and banners shattered, the radiant Karṇa pursued them from behind, scattering them with his arrows;
that great car-warrior, the son of a Sūta, scorched them with his shafts.
He reached midday like the sun that dispels the darkness of all beings.
Saṃjaya said:
But your son Yuyutsu fled from that great army.
The owl swooped down swiftly and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Thereupon, O King, Yuyutsu struck the owl with a sharp-edged feathered shaft, just as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
Then Ulūka, enraged in that battle, cut your son’s bow with a razor-headed arrow and struck him with a barbed shaft. Casting aside that severed bow, Yuyutsu took up another of even greater speed.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he took up another massive bow;
then, O bull of the Bharatas, he pierced Śakuni with sixty arrows,
struck his charioteer with three, and pierced him yet again.
Ulūka, however, having pierced him with twenty gold-adorned arrows,
then, enraged in that battle, cut down his golden standard.
With its staff severed, that great and magnificent banner began to crumble.
O King, that gold-bright [standard] fell before Yuyutsu.
Seeing his standard shattered, Yuyutsu, overwhelmed with rage,
struck Ulūka in the center of the chest with five arrows.
O worthy one, O best of the Bharatas, with a broad-headed arrow cleansed in oil, Ulūka suddenly severed the head of Yuyutsu’s charioteer. That severed head then fell to the ground.
Like a variegated star-form, it fell upon the surface of the earth.
Filled with rage, he severed the driver’s head in battle,
struck down the four horses, and pierced him with five arrows.
Pierced by that powerful warrior, he retreated from his chariot to another;
having vanquished him in battle, O King, Ulūka proceeded swiftly,
slaughtering the Pāñcālas and the Sṛñjayas with sharpened arrows.

O great king, your son Śrutakarman, without any agitation, deprived Śatānīka of his horses, charioteer, and chariot within half a blink of an eye. Standing upon that chariot whose horses had been slain, the mighty Śatānīka—
O noble one, filled with rage, he hurled a mace at your son.
Having reduced the chariot to ashes along with the horses and the charioteer,
O Bhārata, it fell swiftly to the earth as if tearing it asunder.
Both those heroes, the enhancers of the Kurus' fame, being deprived of their chariots and distressed by the battle, withdrew while glancing at one another; meanwhile,
your son, greatly agitated, mounted the chariot of Vivitsu.
Śatānīka also quickly went to Prativindhya’s chariot;
Sutasoma, however, pierced Śakuni with sharpened arrows,
yet he could not make him waver, even though enraged, just as a torrent of water cannot shake a mountain.
But Sutasoma, O Bhārata, seeing him— the extreme enemy of his father— covered him with many thousands of arrows. Śakuni swiftly cut those arrows down with other winged shafts.
Light-handed in the use of weapons, a versatile fighter, and appearing victorious in combat,
he warded off those arrows in battle with his own sharpened shafts; then,
highly incensed, he struck Sutasoma with three arrows.
With his arrows, your immensely powerful brother-in-law shattered his horses, standard, and charioteer into pieces as small as sesame seeds; then, O noble one, the people cried out,
for he was now deprived of his horses, his chariot, and his bow.
Taking up his excellent bow, the archer descended from the chariot to the ground;
he then discharged arrows with golden feathers, sharpened on stone,
which completely covered that chariot of your brother-in-law.
Like swarms of locusts, the volleys of arrows [fell upon] the great car-warrior; yet even upon seeing those [arrows] from the seat of his chariot, the son of Subala did not waver at all,
and that highly illustrious one crushed each of those arrows with his own volleys of shafts.
There, the warriors and even the Siddhas stationed in heaven were filled with wonder upon seeing that incredible and marvelous feat of Sutasoma;
for on foot, he fought against that king who was mounted upon his chariot.
With sharp, high-velocity, straight-knotted *bhalla* arrows,
the king completely shattered his bow and quiver in every part.
With his bow broken in the battle, he raised his sword and let out a roar.
With the luster of lapis lazuli and blue lotuses, its hilt made of ivory,
and shining like the clear sky as it was being whirled about,
that sword appeared to them like Death itself before the wise Sutasoma.
Equipped with the strength of his training, O Great King, he who possessed the sword moved suddenly through thousands of circular maneuvers— twenty-four in all:
whirling, leaping upward, brandishing, bounding, leaping sideways, and rushing forward.
In that battle, he displayed both his swiftness and his power; then the valiant son of Subala discharged arrows at him,
which he swiftly cut down with his supreme sword as they were still falling.

Then, O great king, the son of Subala, the slayer of enemy heroes, being enraged, dispatched arrows resembling venomous serpents at Sutasoma. But with his sword, through both skill and strength, he cut them down.
Displaying agility in battle, he who possessed a splendor equal to the prowess of Tārkṣya,
O King, as he was then moving in circular maneuvers,
cut his brilliantly shining sword with an extremely sharp razor-edged arrow.
That great sword, severed, suddenly fell to the ground; yet at that moment, the hilt remained in the hand of the helpless man. Realizing his blade was broken, he leaped back six paces.

Then Sutasoma, the great car-warrior, took up another bow that was very firm and more powerful, and from there he hurled the remainder [of his weapons] at him. Having severed the bow along with its string in battle, he struck down the weapon of that high-souled one.
Adorned with gold and diamonds, it fell swiftly to the earth;
then Sutasoma proceeded toward the great chariot of Śrutakīrti.
Saubala, for his part, also took up another formidable and most difficult-to-withstand bow.
He advanced against the Pāṇḍava army, slaughtering many hosts of enemies.
A great roar arose there among the Pāṇḍavas, O lord of the people,
upon seeing the son of Subala roaming fearlessly in battle.
Those proud, well-armed,
and vast divisions were seen being routed by the high-souled son of Subala,
O King, just as the king of the gods crushed the army of the Daityas.
In that very manner, the son of Subala destroyed the Pāṇḍava army.
O King, Kṛpa held back Dhṛṣṭadyumna in the encounter,
just as a śarabha might hold back a proud elephant in the forest during a fight.

O Bhārata, having been checked by that powerful Gautama, the son of Pṛṣata was unable to move even a single step from his position there. Upon seeing the form of Gautama facing Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s chariot, [he stood firm].
All beings were terrified and believed that destruction had arrived.
There, the chariot-warriors and horsemen, despondent, said:
"Surely the best of men is enraged at the death of Droṇa."
Will there be well-being today for Dhṛṣṭadyumna against Gautama— the son of Śaradvat, possessed of great splendor, skilled in divine weapons, and noble-minded?
Will this entire army be delivered from this great danger?
"Could this brahmin not slay all of us gathered here? For the form he displays is exceedingly like that of the God of Death himself;
today in battle, he will follow the path of Bhāradvāja."
The preceptor is swift-handed and always victorious in battle;
he is equipped with celestial weapons, endowed with heroism, and filled with wrath.
Yet even now, the son of Pṛṣata is seen to be utterly averse to fighting in the fray.
O Great King, such various words were heard there in that encounter between your men and the enemies; and in that battle, portents foreboding fear for Gautama’s side spread abroad.
Then, O King, sighing in anger, Kṛpa Śāradvata covered the son of Pṛṣata— who remained motionless— with arrows in all his vital parts. Thus was he struck in battle by the high-souled Gautama.
Deluded in that supreme battle, he did not know what ought to be done.
Then his charioteer said to him, "O son of Pṛṣata, is all well?
Never before have I seen such a calamity in battle."
Yet, by the power of fate, those arrows capable of piercing the vital organs,
though discharged in every direction by that foremost of the twice-born aiming at my vitals, did not penetrate me.
At that moment, I turned the chariot away from him, as one turns back the current of a river from the ocean.
"I consider the Brāhmaṇa to be unslayable, by whom your prowess has been struck down.
Then, O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna spoke these words softly:
"O father, my mind is bewildered and sweat is breaking out upon my limbs."
Behold the trembling in my body and the bristling of my hair;
O charioteer, avoiding the Brāhmaṇa in battle, proceed slowly toward where Acyuta is,
or toward Arjuna or Bhīmasena in the encounter.
"It would be safe for you today, O driver"— this was my firm conviction.
Thereupon, O great king, the charioteer proceeded,
urging the horses toward where the great archer Bhīma was fighting with your soldiers.
O noble one, seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s chariot fleeing,
Gautama then pursued it, scattering hundreds of arrows;
that subduer of foes repeatedly blew his conch shell.
He rushed toward the son of Pṛṣata as he advanced, like Mahendra against Śambara.
But in that battle, the son of Hṛdika, as if smiling again and again, checked the unassailable Śikhaṇḍin, who was the very death of Bhīṣma.
And Śikhaṇḍin, having encountered the great car-warrior of the Hṛdikas,
struck him in the region of the collarbone with five sharpened broad-headed arrows.
But Kṛtavarman, enraged, pierced him in return with sixty swift shafts.
Laughing, O King, that great car-warrior cut down the bow with a single shaft.
Then the powerful son of Drupada, taking up another bow, addressed the son of Hṛdika in a rage, saying, "Stay! Stay!"

Then, O king of kings, he dispatched ninety well-sharpened arrows with golden shafts; however, they struck his armor and fell away from it. Observing that they were rendered futile and seeing them fallen upon the earth, [he acted].
With an extremely sharp razor-edged arrow, the mighty one severed his bow.
Then, as he stood with his bow broken like a bull with shattered horns,
the enraged warrior struck him in the arms and chest with eighty shafts.
But Kṛtavarman, enraged and mangled by arrows,
vomited blood from his limbs like water from the mouth of a jar;
drenched in blood, Kṛtavarman shone resplendent.
O King, like a mountain of red chalk drenched by rain,
he took up another bow along with a multitude of arrows, O Lord,
and struck Śikhaṇḍin in the shoulder region with excellent shafts.
With arrows lodged in his shoulder,
Śikhaṇḍin shone like a great tree with its pure, spreading branches;
having pierced each other deeply, they were both drenched in blood.
For like two great elephants wallowing in a lake of blood,
those two heroes shone, drenched in gore;
they were like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom when the month of Puṣya has arrived.
With all their limbs drenched in blood and smeared with red sandalwood paste,
those two best of men shone like two enraged serpents;
both had their bodies pierced by arrows and were wounded by each other’s shafts.
Striking each other with their horns like two bulls,
those two great car-warriors, striving for one another's slaughter,
moved in thousands of circular maneuvers upon their chariots.
O great king, Kṛtavarman pierced the son of Pṛṣata in battle with seventy sharp arrows, gold-tufted and whetted on stone.
Then, in that encounter, Bhoja, the best among strikers, [discharged] an arrow at him.
Filled with haste, he discharged that terrible, life-ending weapon. Struck by it, O King, he quickly fell into a swoon; overcome by faintness, he suddenly leaned against his flagpole for support.
The charioteer then bore that best of car-warriors away from the battle—
him who was tormented by the arrows of Hārdikya and sighing again and again—
once the heroic son of Drupada had been defeated, O Lord.
The Pāṇḍava army fled, being slaughtered on all sides.
Sañjaya said:
"O great king, even he of the white horses (Arjuna) scattered your forces."
Just as the wind, having encountered a heap of cotton from all sides, drives it away,
so did the Trigartas, the Śibis along with the Kauravas,
the Śālvas, the Saṃśaptakas, and that Nārāyaṇa force advance against him.
Satyasena, Satyakīrti, Mitradeva, Śrutañjaya,
Sauśruti, Citrasena, Mitravarmā, O Bhārata,
as well as Suśarman, Sudharman, and Suvarman, O Bhārata.
The King of Trigarta, surrounded in battle by his brothers and by his sons— all great archers bearing various weapons in the fray—
discharged volleys of arrows, scattering them over Arjuna in the combat.
They rushed forward in battle like torrents of water toward the ocean;
but upon reaching Arjuna, those warriors by the hundreds of thousands all met their destruction, just as serpents perish at the sight of Tārkṣya.
Though being struck down in battle, they did not abandon the son of Pāṇḍu at that time,
O King, just as moths, though being consumed, do not leave a fire.
Satyasena pierced the Pāṇḍava in combat with three arrows.
Mitradeva pierced him with sixty-three arrows, Candradeva with seven; Mitravarmā with seventy-three, Sauśruti also with five;
Śatruñjaya with twenty, and Suśarmā with nine shafts.
Pierced by many in the battle, he pierced those kings in return;
having struck the son of Śrutāyus with seven arrows and Satyasena with three,
he struck the son of Śrutāyus again with twenty-five and Candradeva with eight.
He struck Śatruñjaya with twenty arrows, Candradeva with eight, Mitradeva with a hundred, Śrutasena with three shafts,
Mitravarmā with nine, and Suśarmā likewise with eight.
In that battle, he struck Suvarman with a hundred arrows and Suśarman with five;
furthermore, he struck Suśarman and Suvarman again with eight,
and having slain King Śatruñjaya there with arrows sharpened on stone.
Sauśruti struck off the head, complete with its helmet, from the body,
and swiftly sent Candradeva to the abode of Yama with his arrows.
Then, O great king, he [attacked] the other great car-warriors who were striving [to resist].
With five arrows each, he warded off each of them. But Satyasena, filled with rage, hurled a great lance at Kṛṣṇa in the battle and let out a lion’s roar.
Having pierced the left arm of the high-souled Mādhava,
that great and fierce iron shaft then entered the earth. Thus was Mādhava pierced by the *tomara* in that great battle.
O lord of the people, the whip and the reins fell from his hand.
Seeing Vāsudeva with his limbs pierced, Pārtha Dhanañjaya summoned a fierce rage and spoke thus to Kṛṣṇa.
"O mighty-armed lord, drive the horses toward Satyasena,
so that with my sharp arrows I may send him to the abode of Yama.
Then he urged the chariot toward Satyasena's vehicle.
Then the heroic Dhanañjaya, skilled in divine weapons, his anger aroused,
took up the whip and the reins once more; and that highly illustrious one drove those horses toward the chariot of Satyasena.
Seeing Viṣvaksena pierced through, the mighty Pārtha Dhananjaya,
having torn Satyasena with sharp arrows,
then [struck] that king’s great head with well-sharpened shafts.
In the midst of the army, he cut from his body the ear-rings that adorned it;
having struck him down with sharp arrows, he felled Mitravarmā,
O noble one, and with a sharp calf-toothed shaft, he struck down his charioteer.

Then, the self-controlled one, filled with rage, once more brought down the hosts of Saṃśaptakas by the hundreds and thousands with hundreds of arrows. Thereafter, with a silver-feathered shaft, he struck off the head of the high-souled king.
The highly illustrious one cut off Mitradeva with a razor-sharp arrow;
and, filled with rage, he struck Suśarman in the region of the collarbone with a well-aimed,
exceedingly sharp iron shaft.
Then all the Saṃśaptakas, having surrounded Dhanañjaya,
furiously assailed him with floods of weapons, making the ten directions resound.
But Jiṣṇu, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra, though oppressed by them, [remained steadfast].
The great car-warrior of immeasurable soul manifested the Aindra weapon;
then, O lord of the people, thousands of arrows issued forth from the bow of Pārtha, the son of Pāṇḍu, who possesses boundless splendor.
In that battle, there was the sound of standards being severed, as well as bows,
chariots with their banners, quivers along with arrows, axles, yokes,
wheels, and reins.
In that battle, there was the sound of chariot-poles, fenders, and arrows;
of falling stones along with spears and double-edged swords;
and of maces, iron clubs, javelins, and lances.
O noble one, there were *śataghnīs* together with their wheels, along with arms and thighs; and of neck-threads, armlets, bracelets,
necklaces, golden coins, and body armor, O Bhārata.
O lord of the people, a great clamor was heard here and there from umbrellas and fans, along with heads adorned with crowns;
[heads] that possessed earrings, beautiful eyes, and were like the full moon.
Their heads were seen upon the earth like clusters of stars in the sky;
their bodies, adorned with beautiful garlands, fine garments, and anointed with sandalwood paste,
were seen lying dead upon the surface of the ground.
At that time, O Great King, that terrible battlefield, appearing like a city of the Gandharvas,
was strewn here and there in that great conflict with slain princes and mighty Kṣatriyas by Arjuna.
With fallen elephants and horses,
the earth in that battle became impassable, as if covered by shattered mountains;
there was not even a path for the chariot wheels of the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
O noble one, as he struck down his enemies with broad-headed arrows and slaughtered immeasurable hosts of elephants and horses,
the chariot wheels sank up to their hubs, O King,
lord of the people. Then, having been overtaken, the chariot wheel became stuck, O ruler of men.
As he moved about in battle within that mire of blood,
his sinking wheels were vigorously pulled by the horses, which,
though joined with great exhaustion, possessed the speed of thought and the wind.
As that army was being slaughtered by the archer, the son of Pāṇḍu,
almost all of them turned their backs and would not stand firm in the battle.
Having conquered those numerous hosts of Saṃśaptakas in combat, Jiṣṇu—
O great king, he shone like a blazing fire without smoke;
O great king,
King Duryodhana himself, undaunted, received Yudhiṣṭhira as he discharged many arrows.
As your mighty son was suddenly rushing toward him, Dharmarāja quickly pierced him and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
And she, in turn, pierced him with nine sharpened arrows.
And, being violently enraged, he struck his charioteer with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla).
Thereupon, King Yudhiṣṭhira fearlessly received the stone-tipped arrows feathered with gold.
Driven by supreme haste,
he hurled thirteen stone-sharpened arrows at Duryodhana;
having slain his four horses with four of them, that great car-warrior—
With the fifth [arrow], he struck the head from the body of the charioteer;
with the sixth, the king's banner; and with the seventh, his bow;
likewise, with the eighth, he caused his sword to fall to the ground.
And with five arrows, Dharmarāja struck the king severely. Then, leaping down from that chariot whose horses had been slain, your son,
having fallen into extreme distress, stood upon the very ground.
Seeing him fallen into such distress, Karṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, and the others advanced together, desiring to rescue the lord of men. Then all the sons of Pāṇḍu surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira.
They advanced in battle, O King, and then the combat commenced;
then, in that great conflict, thousands of trumpets were sounded,
and shouts of defiance and cries of joy arose, O lord of the earth.
When the Pāñcālas encountered the Kauravas in battle,
all those heroes were destroyed here and there in that conflict;
men clashed with men, and elephants with choice elephants.

Chariots with their chariot-warriors and horses with their horse-riders, O great king, formed duels in the battle that were a sight to behold— wondrous and formidable, belonging both to your men and to the enemy.
They were all heroes who, possessing great speed and seeking to slay one another, fought in battle with weapons that were marvelous, swift, and excellent— causing wonder, inconceivable, and supreme.
Observing the vow of warriors, they struck one another in battle;
indeed, they did not turn their backs on the fight in any way whatsoever.
For only a brief moment was that combat pleasant to behold.
Then, O King, it proceeded without restraint like a scene of madness;
a chariot-warrior, encountering an elephant while roaming at the forefront of the battle,
dispatched it to Death with straight-jointed arrows.
Then those exceedingly fierce elephants, having encountered the horses, scattered many of them and put them to flight here and there at various times;
and many horsemen, surrounding the best of the elephants, [attacked].
Falling from all sides, they made a thunderous sound like the clapping of palms; as those great elephants ran and fled hither and thither,
the horsemen struck them from their flanks and from behind.
O King, having put many horses to flight, those elephants, fierce in their strength,
struck others with their tusks and trampled others violently.
In that battle, they pierced horses along with their riders with their tusks.
Seizing others, those of exceeding strength likewise hurled them with force;
struck on all sides by the foot-soldiers in their vulnerable spots, the elephants let out a terrible cry of distress and fled in the ten directions.
As the foot soldiers fled suddenly in that great battle,
the mighty elephants, disregarding the ornaments they had dropped, quickly leaped down onto the field of combat and turned back, regarding them as omens.
They seized and even tore apart the various ornaments.
But the foot soldiers, surrounding those elephant-riders who were thus preoccupied there, slaughtered them— men of great speed and fierce strength.
In that great battle, others were tossed into the air by the trunks of elephants;
falling down, they were pierced deeply by the tips of the tusks of those well-trained beasts.
Others, seized suddenly by the very tusks, were slaughtered.
O Great King, having encountered the enemy host, some there had their limbs crushed by massive elephants; being tossed about again and again,
others were slain in the battle like whirling fans.
O lord of the people, other elephants that were leading the way had their bodies pierced here and there on the field of battle— some in their frontal globes,
some in their temples, and others in the gums surrounding their tusks.
The elephants were severely struck down by spears, javelins,
and darts; some, having been seized by the extremely fierce men standing at their sides with maces,
and hundreds of other elephants, O King, pierced through, sank into the earth.
There, chariots, horses, and riders, shattered [by weapons], fell to the earth; meanwhile,
other great elephants crushed on the ground with force a rider together with his chariot, his armor, and his banner.
Likewise, O lord of the people, in various places there, some elephants with their riders encountered chariots; having seized them by the pole, O noble one,
they suddenly dragged them away in that terrible great battle.
Struck by iron arrows, the great elephant fell to the earth like a mountain peak shattered by a thunderbolt. Warriors,
encountering other warriors in battle, struck them down with their fists.
Seizing one another by the hair, they tore and mangled each other together;
raising their arms, one threw the other down upon the earth,
and treading with his foot upon the quivering body, he struck off the head.
O Great King, at that time one struck a dead man with his feet;
another, O King, severed the head of one who was falling with a sword;
and likewise, another plunged a weapon into the body of one who was still alive.
O Bhārata, there was a great fist-fight among the warriors there,
as well as fierce seizing by the hair and pure wrestling with the arms; while one was engaged with another, yet another remained unnoticed.
In that battle, he took away their lives in many ways with various weapons;
and as the warriors were locked in combat and the tumultuous fray proceeded,
headless trunks rose up by the hundreds and thousands.
The weapons and armor, being drenched with blood,
shone like garments dyed in the colors of a great stage. Thus did that great battle unfold— terrible and exceedingly tumultuous.
Resembling a mad stage, it filled the world with sound;
O King, neither one's own nor the enemy could be distinguished, for all were afflicted by arrows.
Greedy for victory, the kings fought on, thinking only, "We must fight."
O great king, those on their own side struck down their own kin, as well as the enemies who had encountered them;
the field became chaotic with the heroes of both armies.
O great king, it was filled with shattered chariots and fallen elephants.
With horses fallen there and men struck down,
O Great King, the earth became impassable in an instant, mired in mud of flesh and blood and flowing with torrents of gore.
Generating joy for the brave and increasing the fear of the timid,
Karṇa slew the Pāñcālas, and Dhanañjaya slew the Trigartas;
Bhīmasena, O King, slaughtered the Kurus and the entire elephant division on all sides.
"Thus did this destruction occur between the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas in the afternoon, O great king, as both sides desired vast victory. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O Sañjaya, I have heard from you of many exceedingly intense and unbearable sufferings, and of the destruction of my sons;
indeed, you describe to me exactly how the battle is proceeding.
"O Sūta, it is my firm conviction that the Kauravas no longer exist;
for Duryodhana was deprived of his chariot there in that great battle. How did the son of Dharma act then, or how did the king [Duryodhana] fare?"
"How did that hair-raising battle take place in the afternoon?
Tell me that in truth, for you, Saṃjaya, are indeed skilled.
Saṃjaya said:
While the armies were locked in combat, fighting in their respective divisions,
O lord of the people, your son mounted another chariot,
possessed by a great rage like a venomous serpent.
Gazing upon his entire army with eyes rolling in rage,
and seeing the son of Dharma stationed in the midst of the troops—
the son of Kuntī blazing with splendor like the wielder of the thunderbolt in battle— [he spoke].
But Duryodhana, having seen Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira,
said, "O Sūta, go quickly, go quickly! O Bhārata,
"O charioteer, take me swiftly to where that Pāṇḍava is."
With the royal umbrella held over him, the king shone resplendent in his armor.
Urged by the king, the charioteer drove that excellent chariot toward Yudhiṣṭhira in the battle.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, enraged like a bull out of rut,
urged his charioteer, "Go where Suyodhana is!
Those two heroes, brothers and the best of chariot-warriors, then encountered one another.
Having come together, those two of great heroism, armored and fierce in battle,
those two mighty archers mangled one another with arrows in the fray.
Then, O Sire, King Duryodhana [attacked] the virtuous-souled one.
With a stone-sharpened crescent-headed arrow, he cut through the bow in that encounter. O Kauravya, O sire, Yudhiṣṭhira could not tolerate that resolve of your son Duryodhana in battle.
Casting aside his broken bow, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
the son of Dharma took up another bow at the head of the army and cut down Duryodhana’s standard and his bow as well.
Then, taking up another bow, he pierced the Pāṇḍava in return;
he discharged at Yudhiṣṭhira arrows adorned with gold,
with golden shafts and bright points, like venomous serpents.
Highly enraged with one another, the two released showers of arrows like two lions fiercely incensed by a desire to conquer each other;
and they struck one another, bellowing like two bulls.

Gazing at one another, those two great car-warriors moved about; there, King Suyodhana could find no opening against him. Then, with arrows released from bows drawn to their full stretch, they wounded each other well.
O great king, they shone like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom. Then,
O king, in that great battle, there arose repeatedly the terrifying lion-roars [of the warriors], as well as the sounds of their palms and their bows.
Those two excellent chariots produced the sounds of conch shells,
O great king, and they both severely afflicted one another.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira [struck] your son with three arrows.
Enraged, Vajravega, who was difficult to approach, struck him in the chest;
your son, the lord of the earth, swiftly pierced him in return with five sharp arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone.

Then, O Bhārata, King Duryodhana hurled a sharp spear made entirely of iron, resembling a great meteor. As it came rushing suddenly toward him, Dharmarāja [Arjuna] [struck it] with arrows whetted on stone.
With three arrows he suddenly cut it down and pierced him with seven;
then that great mace with its golden staff fell,
and as it descended, it shone like a great meteor resembling a flame.
O lord of the people, seeing his spear destroyed, your son struck Yudhiṣṭhira with nine sharpened broad-headed arrows. That foremost of the powerful, the scorcher of his enemies, was deeply pierced.
Aiming at Duryodhana, he quickly seized an arrow;
the mighty one fixed that fierce shaft upon his bow and,
filled with rage, the powerful king then discharged it at the monarch.
But that arrow, having reached your son, the great car-warrior,
bewildered the king and then entered the earth.
Thereupon, Duryodhana, enraged and impetuous, raised his mace.
Desirous of bringing an end to the quarrel, he rushed toward the Pāṇḍava.
Seeing him with his mace raised like Death himself with staff in hand,
Dharmarāja hurled a great spear at your son.

In that great battle, standing upon his chariot, he was pierced by that blazing, high-velocity great meteor, which was like a flaming torch, resembling the staff of Yama, and as terrible as another Night of Doom. It shattered his armor.
With his heart deeply agitated, he fell down and fainted.
Then Bhīma, reflecting upon his vow, said to him,
"O King, this man is not to be slain by you," and having been thus addressed, he desisted.
Then Kṛtavarman, arriving in haste, approached your son,
the king who was indeed submerged in an ocean of calamity.
Bhīma, for his part, seized a massive mace adorned with gold.
With great speed, he rushed toward Kṛtavarman in the battle;
taking Duryodhana with him, he became intent on flight.
Thus did that battle between your men and the enemies unfold.
O tiger among men, O great king, in the afternoon, as those enraged warriors sought victory in battle, they slaughtered one another,
causing the destruction of men, horses, and elephants, which increased the population of Yama’s kingdom.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, placing Karṇa at their head, your warriors, intoxicated with the frenzy of battle,
turned back once more and engaged in a combat resembling that between the gods and the asuras.
With the sounds of elephants, chariots, men, horses, and conchs,
and with various discharges of weapons, the caravans of elephants, chariots, and infantrymen were greatly delighted.
Rushing forward face-to-face, they struck with arrows, excellent axes, swords, and spears; and being struck down by various kinds of shafts, they fell.
In that great battle, elephants, chariots,
and horses— along with excellent men and their mounts—
resembled lotuses, suns, and moons.
The earth shone, strewn with human heads that possessed beautiful faces, eyes, and noses, and were adorned with lovely crowns and earrings.
By means of iron clubs, maces, spears, and javelins,
and by hundreds of claws, *bhuśuṇḍi* weapons, and bludgeons, thousands of elephants, men, and horses were swiftly struck down.
Then rivers of blood began to flow;
with slain men, chariots, horses, and elephants,
that scene was terrifying to behold and exceedingly fierce.
That army, struck down by that [weapon], shone like the kingdom of the Lord of the Ancestors when its subjects have perished;
then, O god among men, your soldiers—
And your sons, resembling the sons of the gods,
those bulls among the Kurus, preceded by armies of immeasurable strength, advanced in battle against the son of Śini.
That army,
crowded with excellent men, horses, chariots, and elephants,
shone with intense brilliance and a formidable splendor, its roar rising up like the surging sound of the salt-water ocean.
Then, possessing prowess equal to the Lord of the Gods, he displayed a strength comparable to the armies of the immortals and asuras,
like the younger brother of the foremost of the thirty gods in battle.
With arrows possessing the brilliance of the sun's rays,
the son of the Sun struck the hero of the Śinīs,
along with his chariot, horses, and charioteer.
Then Śini’s bull, acting with haste in battle, covered that best of men with various arrows possessing a luster like the venom of serpents.
O bull among men, afflicted by the arrows of Śini,
your friends— the foremost of great car-warriors— quickly approached Vasuṣeṇa, that bull among chariot-fighters.
The powerful one rushed toward him, who resembled the ocean, together with elephants, chariots, horses, and foot soldiers;
yet he was swiftly assailed by his enemies who charged forward with even greater speed.
The friend of Drupada’s son then wrought great destruction among the men, chariots, horses, and elephants;
then those two best of men completed their daily rites.
Having worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rites,
Arjuna and Keśava, having swiftly resolved upon the slaughter of their enemy, rushed against your army.
The chariot, with its banner and standard fluttering in the wind, sounding like the roar of a rain-cloud, and drawn by white horses,
approached nearby.
Then his enemies, with their minds captivated, beheld him whose hand was like the trunk of a lordly elephant,
as he repeatedly drew arrows from the mouth of his quiver.
O lord of men, like the wielder of the thunderbolt entering the army of the Dānavas with his bow drawn,
Bhīma’s younger brother plunged into your host;
then Arjuna, as if dancing in battle, stretched his Gāṇḍīva bow.
He made the sky, the cardinal directions, and the intermediate quarters crowded with arrows.

Then, with his shafts, he struck down the chariots— which resembled celestial palaces and were equipped with machines, weapons, and banners— along with their charioteers, just as the wind scatters the clouds.
With his arrows, he sent elephants and their riders, along with their Vaijayantī banners, weapons, and standards; he sent horsemen, horses, and foot soldiers to the abode of Yama.
He was like the enraged God of Death himself—an irresistible great chariot-warrior.
Duryodhana advanced alone, striking with various kinds of arrows;
Arjuna, having slain his bow, charioteer, standard, and horses— one by one— with seven shafts, cut down his umbrella with a feathered arrow.

And having reached the ninth [arrow], he discharged that destructive, excellent arrow at Duryodhana; the son of Droṇa cut it into seven pieces. Then, having severed the bow of the son of Droṇa and slain his excellent horses with arrows, [he struck him].
In that same manner, the Pāṇḍava cut through Kṛpa’s exceedingly fierce bow;
having severed the bow of Hārdikya, he likewise slew his standard and his horses;
and having cut through Duḥśāsana’s excellent arrow, he advanced against the son of Rādhā.
Then, leaving Sātyaki and acting with haste, Karṇa pierced Arjuna with three arrows,
struck Kṛṣṇa with twenty, and again hit Pārtha with three;
there was no fatigue in Karṇa as he discharged so many shafts.
As Karna, enraged like Śatakratu, struck down his enemies in battle,
his bow— shooting arrows with extreme force— roared,
striking terror into all beings and bringing an end to his foes.
Then Sātyaki, having arrived, pierced Karṇa with ninety-nine sharp arrows, and again struck him with a hundred fierce shafts. Thereupon,
all the foremost heroes of the Pāṇḍavas tormented Karṇa.
Yudhāmanyu, Śikhaṇḍin, the sons of Draupadī, the Prabhadrakas,
Uttamaujas, Yuyutsu, the twins, and the son of Pṛṣata,
as well as the forces of the Cedis, Kārūṣas, Matsyas, and Kekayas— [all these stood against him].
The powerful Cekitāna and the virtuous Dharmarāja—
these [heroes], surrounding Karṇa in battle with chariots, horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers of fierce prowess, overwhelmed him with various weapons.
Speaking with fierce words, they all rushed toward the slaughter of Karṇa;
but Karṇa, having cut that shower of weapons into many pieces with his sharp arrows,
drove them all back, just as the wind blows away trees after breaking them.
Enraged, Karna was seen slaughtering chariot-warriors along with their mahāmātras, elephants, horses with their riders, and volleys of arrows;
thus was the Pandava army being struck down by the fiery energy of Karna’s weapons.
With his body mangled by wounds from weapons, he was for the most part turned away from the fight.
Then Arjuna himself, having neutralized Karṇa’s weapon with his own weapon,
covered the quarters, the sky, and the earth with showers of arrows.
Like pestles, like iron clubs, and like arrows, others fell like *śataghnīs*, while still others were like fierce thunderbolts;
by these, that army— along with its infantry, horses, chariots, and elephants— was being slaughtered.

With their eyes closed in extreme distress, they wandered aimlessly in every direction; then the horses, men, and elephants entered into a total melee. Being struck by arrows, others, overcome with fear, fled away.
Thus, while they were thus engaged in battle, each desiring victory,
the sun reached the western mountain and set.
And by darkness, O great king, and especially by dust, [the world was enveloped].
O Bhārata, seeing nothing at all— whether auspicious or inauspicious— and trembling at the prospect of a night-battle,
those great archers then made their retreat together with all their horses.
O King, when the Kauravas had departed at the close of day,
the Pārthas, having attained victory and being high-spirited, went to their own camp amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and the roaring of lions.
Mocking their enemies and praising Acyuta and Arjuna,
all those heroic warriors and lords of men, once the withdrawal had been made by them,
offered blessings upon the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Then, when the withdrawal had been made, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, being greatly delighted,
went to their camps at night and those lords of men settled down,
comfortably recounting the events that had occurred during the day in battle.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and beasts of prey went in great throngs to that terrible battlefield, which resembled the dance of Rudra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Clearly Arjuna did not slay us all out of his own free will;
for even Death himself, were he an assailant, could not escape him in battle.
For Pārtha alone carried off Bhadrā, and alone he gratified the Fire-god."
Having conquered this earth alone, he made the kings payers of tribute;
alone, wielding his divine bow, he slew the Nivātakavacas, and indeed,
he destroyed thirty million of those Nivātakavacas.
One fought Śarva while he stood in the form of a Kirāta;
one protected the Bharatas, and one gratified Bhava. By that one alone were all my sons of fierce energy defeated.
"They are neither to be censured nor praised; tell us what they did.
"Then, O Sūta, what did Duryodhana do after that?
Saṃjaya said:
Wounded, struck down, and shattered, stripped of their armor, weapons, and mounts,
the proud Kauravas— vanquished by their enemies, wailing in piteous tones and consumed by grief— convened once more in council while staying in their camp.
Like serpents whose fangs are broken, whose venom is spent, and who have been trampled by a foot,
Karna then spoke to them, hissing like an enraged snake,
pressing one hand against the other as he glared at your son.
Diligent, firm, skillful, and always steadfast, Arjuna is ever-vigilant; yet Adhokṣaja awakens him only when the time is right.
By that sudden discharge of weapons, we have been deceived today.
"Tomorrow, O Lord of the Earth, I shall destroy his entire resolve.
Having been addressed thus, he replied, "So be it," and gave leave to those best of kings. Permitted by him, all those kings returned to their own abodes.
Having spent that night happily, they set forth for battle with joyful hearts.
They beheld the invincible array formed by Dharmarāja,
the leader of the Kurus, through great effort and according to the doctrines of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas.
Then Duryodhana remembered Karṇa, whose shoulders were like those of a bull, who was the constant adversary of those who have conquered their own selves;
he who is equal to Purandara in battle and equal to the host of Maruts in strength.
The king’s mind turned toward Karṇa, whose valor was equal to that of Kārtavīrya;
indeed, the minds of all the troops turned toward Karṇa alone,
as they would toward a kinsman in times of great peril, for he was a son of a Sūta and a mighty archer.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dull-witted ones, since your minds then turned toward Karṇa Vaikartana,
did you not see him, as those afflicted by cold [long for] the sun?"
When the withdrawal of the armies had been completed and battle was joined once more,
how did Vaikartana Karṇa fight there, O Sañjaya?
And how did all the Pāṇḍavas fight the Sūta’s son there?
For the mighty-armed Karṇa alone could slay the Pārthas along with the Somakas; the prowess of Karṇa’s two arms is considered equal to that of Śakra and Viṣṇu,
as are the most terrible weapons and the valor of that high-souled one.
And that dull-witted man always used to praise them before me;
meanwhile, Karna, seeing Duryodhana then severely afflicted by the son of Pāṇḍu, [praised] those great archers, the sons of Pāṇḍu, who are mighty chariot-warriors.
Having seen the sons of Pāṇḍu exerting their prowess in that great battle,
Duryodhana’s pride was restored as he relied upon Karṇa in the conflict;
he again ventured to conquer the Pārthas, along with their sons and Keśava.
Alas! What great sorrow it is that Karna, acting with such impetuosity, could not overcome the sons of Pandu in battle; surely destiny is the ultimate resort.
Alas! This terrible conclusion of the gambling match is now unfolding.
"Alas, O Sañjaya, I shall have to endure these most terrible and intense sufferings caused by Duryodhana, which are like thorns piercing me! And likewise,
my son, the son of Subala is considered by him to be wise in policy."
Karna is always impetuous and devoted to the king;
he considers Karna— who is peerless in battle and difficult even for the gods to withstand—
to be superior to Partha, and fate dwells within his heart.
O Sañjaya, while those divine battles were indeed taking place,
I heard that my sons were being constantly slain and utterly defeated;
there was no one in battle who could hold back the Pāṇḍavas.
"They plunge as if into the midst of women; for destiny is indeed most powerful.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, reflect upon these signs that precede [the event], which are consistent with righteousness."
"For that task which has already passed and one reflects upon later—
that task will not be accomplished for him, and he is destroyed by such reflection.
But this task of yours has reached its critical point, O wise one."
O King, lord of the people, that which you previously failed to do when considering what was attainable and unattainable— that you were told many times, "Do not fight with the Pāṇḍavas"—
you did not accept because of your delusion regarding the Pāṇḍavas.
Terrible sins were committed by you against the Pāṇḍavas;
because of your deeds, this horrific destruction of kings now proceeds.
Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, do not grieve, having now transcended that.
"Listen, O Acyuta, to everything that occurred regarding that terrible slaughter.
When the night had turned to dawn, Karṇa approached the king;
having met with him, the mighty-armed one spoke to Duryodhana."
"O King, today I shall encounter the illustrious Pāṇḍava;
I shall slay that hero, or he will slay me.
O Ruler of the Earth, this is because of the great number of my duties as well as those of the son of Pṛthā."
"O King, there has been no encounter between myself and Arjuna.
However, O Lord of the People, listen to these words of mine according to my wisdom:
O Bhārata, I shall not return from this battle without having slain Pārtha."
"When the heroes of this army have been slain and I alone remain standing in battle, Pārtha will attack me, deprived of Śakra’s spear. Therefore,
O lord of men, learn that which is for your own welfare."
Regarding the prowess of weapons, the efficacy of materials, and that of Arjuna himself—
in piercing massive bodies, in lightness of hand, in long-range striking, and in both the elegance of form and the application of celestial weapons— Savyasācin is not my equal.
O Bhārata, in vital breath, heroism, discernment, and even in prowess,
as well as in the yoga of knowledge of omens, Savyasācin is not my equal.
That bow named Vijaya is the greatest among all weapons.
Desiring it for the sake of Indra, it was fashioned by Viśvakarman;
by means of it, O King, Śatakratu indeed conquered the hosts of Daityas,
and at its roar, the ten directions of the Daityas were utterly bewildered.
Śakra gave that highly esteemed [bow] to Bhārgava;
Bhārgava then gave that divine and supreme bow to me,
with which I shall fight the mighty-armed Arjuna, the best among victors.
Just as Indra slew all the assembled Daityas in battle, so shall I conquer all the Pāṇḍavas in combat. That terrible bow given by Rāma is superior even to the Gāṇḍīva.
The earth was conquered twenty-one times by that very bow;
Bhārgava has proclaimed its divine deeds. Rāma indeed gave that bow to me, with which I shall fight the Pāṇḍava.

Today, O Duryodhana, having slain in battle the hero Arjuna, the foremost of victors, I shall gladden you along with your kinsmen. Having destroyed the enemy, the earth— with its mountains, forests, islands, and oceans— shall be mine.
"O King, today you shall have a firm foundation in sons and grandsons.
For my sake, especially for the sake of what is dear to you, nothing remains impossible for me today—
just as success is certain for one who is self-possessed and perfectly devoted to dharma."
For he is not able to withstand me in battle, just as a tree cannot withstand fire;
yet I must certainly state that in which I am inferior to Phalguna:
his bowstring is divine, and likewise his two great quivers are inexhaustible.
Govinda is his charioteer; such a one as he does not exist for me.
His is the supreme, divine, and undecaying bow Gāṇḍīva in battle;
and mine also is the great, divine, and excellent bow Vijaya.
"In that regard, O King, I am superior to Pārtha by virtue of that bow;
and understand from me that the heroic Pāṇḍava is superior to me,
for the charioteer who holds the reins is the descendant of Daśārha, who is honored by all the worlds."
O hero, there is also the divine chariot given by Agni, adorned with gold, impenetrable from all sides, and drawn by horses swift as thought;
and there is the divine, radiant banner featuring a monkey that inspires wonder.
And Kṛṣṇa, the creator of the world, protects that chariot.
Deprived of these resources, I yet desire to fight the Pāṇḍava.
But this hero Śalya, who graces the assembly, is his equal.
"If he would act as my charioteer, your victory would be certain. Let Śalya, who is difficult for enemies to overcome, be my charioteer;
let carts carry for me iron arrows and those feathered with vulture plumes."
"O Indra among kings, let the finest chariots, yoked with the most excellent horses,
follow me constantly from behind, O bull of the Bharatas.
In this way, I shall become superior to Pārtha in my qualities."
For Śalya is indeed superior to Kṛṣṇa, and I am indeed superior to Arjuna.
Just as the descendant of Daśārha, the slayer of enemy heroes, knows the heart of horses,
so too does the great car-warrior Śalya know the nature of steeds.

There is no one equal to the King of Madra in the strength of his arms; likewise, there is no archer at all equal to me in the use of weapons. Similarly, there is no one at all equal to Śalya in the management of horses.
In terms of vigor, essence, application, action, and purpose,
this chariot of mine will be superior to that of Pārtha;
even the gods, together with Vāsava, will not be able to advance against it.
"O best of the Kurus, if this is done, standing upon such a chariot, I shall be superior to Arjuna in my qualities; I shall conquer Phalguna in battle,
O joy of the Kurus, and I shall utterly defeat Phalguna in the fray."
"O Great King, O scorcher of foes, I desire that this be done by you. Let this wish of mine be fulfilled; let not this time pass you by.
When this is accomplished, it will be as if all my desires have been realized."
Then, O Bhārata, you shall see what I will do in battle;
today I shall utterly defeat all the assembled Pāṇḍavas. Indeed, neither gods nor asuras are capable of advancing against me in combat.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, what then can the sons of Pāṇḍu achieve in battle, being merely of human origin? Thus was your son addressed by Karṇa, who shines in the theater of war.
Having honored him, with a heart full of joy, he then spoke to the son of Rādhā.
Duryodhana said:
"O Karṇa, I shall do all this exactly as you intend."
O son of a charioteer, let chariots equipped with quivers and yoked with horses follow you;
let wagons carry for you iron arrows and those winged with vulture feathers. We and all these kings shall follow after you, O Karṇa.
08,022.061 Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus, O great king, your powerful son,
the king, approached the King of Madra and addressed him with these words.
08,023.001 Saṃjaya said:
08,023.001a O great king, your son spoke these words to the King of Madra.
08,023.001b Thus addressed, O great king, your powerful son—
08,023.001b*0205_02 Toward the Lord of Madra, who struck terror into the enemy armies in battle,
08,023.001b*0205_03 the son of Rādhā quickly did everything exactly as he had said;
08,023.001b*0205_04 and having bowed down to the great car-warrior, the King of Madra, in the midst of the fray.
Approaching with humility, he spoke these words out of affection:
"O Satyavrata, O highly fortunate one, you who increase the misfortune of your enemies!
O Lord of Madra, hero in battle, you who strike fear into the enemy forces!"
O best among speakers, you have heard what Karṇa said when he chose you from among these lions among kings; therefore,
O you of matchless prowess, come today to bring about the destruction of the enemy faction.
O Lord of Madra, I entreat you with my head bowed in humility:
protect Karṇa in every way, as Bhava protects Brahmā, O observer of noble vows.
Therefore, for the sake of destroying the son of Pṛthā and for my own welfare, [act accordingly].
"O best of chariot-warriors, you ought to act as my charioteer with a well-disposed mind. With you as his driver, the son of Rādhā will conquer my enemies;
for there is no one else to be found who can grasp the reins of Karṇa."
In this world, there is no other grasper of the reins equal to you;
for, O highly fortunate one, apart from you, there is none equal to Vāsudeva in battle. May you protect Karṇa on all sides, just as Brahmā protects Śaṅkara.
Just as Kṛṣṇa, the best of those who hold the reins, is the counselor of Pārtha,
so too must you protect the son of Rādhā from all sides;
and just as the descendant of Vṛṣṇi protects the Pāṇḍava in every kind of calamity.
Therefore, O Lord of Madra, from this day forward, you must protect the son of Rādhā.
Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, yourself, the heroic Bhoja, Śakuni the son of Subala, the son of Droṇa, and I myself— these constitute our strength.
"O Lord of Armies, these very [troops] were divided into nine parts;
yet there was no share here for Bhīṣma or the high-souled Droṇa.
Having bypassed those two shares, my enemies have been slain by them."
For those two tigers among men, having grown old and having performed deeds difficult to accomplish, were slain by deceit; O sinless one, they have gone from here to heaven.
Likewise, other tigers among men have been struck down by their enemies in battle.
And many of our own men have gone to heaven in battle,
having cast off their lives and exerted themselves to the full extent of their power;
O lord of men, this army of mine is now mostly slain.
Even in the past, they were slain by a few sons of Pṛthā; how much more so now?
The sons of Kuntī are powerful, high-souled, and possess true prowess;
O King, act in such a way that they do not destroy the remainder of my forces.
"O Lord, this army has had its heroes slain by the Pāṇḍavas in battle;
for Karna alone— the mighty-armed one who is devoted to our pleasure and welfare—
and you yourself, O tiger among men and great chariot-warrior of all the worlds, remain."
O Śalya, Karṇa desires to fight with Arjuna in battle today;
in him, O Lord of the Madras, I have great hope for victory,
for there is no one else on earth who is his equal in holding the reins.
Therefore, O hero, you ought to act as my charioteer for my victory,
just as Kṛṣṇa was the holder of the excellent reins for Pārtha in battle. O King, be the holder of the reins on Karṇa’s chariot in that same manner.
O King, joined by him and protected in battle, the deeds that Pārtha performs are evident to you;
for previously in combat, Arjuna did not slay his enemies in such a manner.
Now indeed, his prowess is joined with that of Kṛṣṇa;
accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha is seen day after day in battle, O Lord of Madra, putting the great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons to flight.
O you of great splendor, this remaining portion belongs to Karṇa and to you alike;
destroy that portion together with Karṇa simultaneously in battle,
just as the sun dispels darkness along with the dawn.

Thus, joined with Karṇa, slay Pārtha in the great battle! Seeing Karṇa and Śalya in the fray— resembling two rising suns, possessing a radiance like the morning sun— let the great car-warriors flee in all directions.
O noble one, just as darkness perishes upon seeing the sun and the dawn,
so may the sons of Kuntī perish along with the Pañcālas and the Sṛñjayas.
Karṇa is the foremost of chariot-warriors, and you are the foremost of drivers.
In this world, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a union such as yours;
there is no one else in the world whose meeting is so perfectly matched.
Just as the scion of the Vṛṣṇis protects the son of Pāṇḍu in all circumstances, so too is your alliance.
"Likewise, may you protect Karṇa Vaikartana in battle;
let the charioteership be performed for him as he fights in the fray,
just as Kṛṣṇa protects Arjuna from all sides in combat."
"Likewise, O Rādhēya, protect him in the great battle;
for with you as his charioteer, he will be invincible even in combat against the gods themselves, including Śakra, O lord of the earth."
"Do not entertain any doubt regarding my words concerning the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Having heard these words of Duryodhana, Śalya, filled with rage and licking the corners of his mouth,
then spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Thus addressed, like a serpent touched by a foot, he became enraged;
knitting his brows into three furrows and wringing his hands again and again,
the mighty-armed one rolled his great eyes, which were blood-red with fury.
Arrogant on account of his lineage, sovereignty, learning, and strength, Śalya said this:
"O son of Gāndhārī, you hold me in contempt; you surely suspect me, since you speak to me so confidently, saying, 'Let the charioteership be performed.'"
"Thinking Karna to be superior to us, you praise him;
yet I do not consider the son of Rādhā to be my equal in battle.
O Lord of the Earth, let a greater portion than mine be assigned to him."
"Having slain him in battle, I shall depart as I came;
or else, O joy of the Kurus, I alone shall fight. Behold today my prowess as I consume the enemies in combat."

"O Kauravya, a man like me would never act by harboring lustful desires in his heart; do not suspect me of such a thing. Furthermore, you must not show me any contempt in battle under any circumstances."
Behold these two arms of mine, resembling the adamantine thunderbolt;
behold my wonderful bow and my arrows like venomous serpents;
and behold my chariot equipped with excellent horses swift as the wind.
"And behold this mace, O Gāndhārī, adorned with bands of gold;
in my wrath, O King, I could split the earth, scatter the mountains,
and dry up the oceans by my own splendor."

Knowing me to be such as this, capable of subduing my enemies, O King, why do you appoint me to the charioteership of an inferior warrior? Furthermore, the son of Rādhā does not deserve even a sixteenth part of me.
O King, if the three worlds, including Karṇa, Arjuna, and Janārdana,
were all bound together in battle, I would not be released from them by any means;
yet even so, O Kauravya, you have abandoned me, though I am capable, out of your heart.
I am no ordinary man, nor have I attained [this state] on my own; therefore,
O Indra among kings, you should not subject me to such humiliation in any way, nor should you deign to employ me here in this burden.

For one who has become superior should not endure servitude to a worse person. Indeed, he who places under the control of a worse man a superior person who has submitted out of affection— that is a sin which inverts the natural order.
"Brahmins were created by Brahmā from his mouth, and the Kṣatriyas from his chest;

he created the Vaiśyas from his thighs and the Śūdras from his feet—so says the Śruti. From these [four], the various specific castes (varṇa) born in the inverse and direct orders [of marriage] arose."
Furthermore, O Bhārata, through their mutual association with the four social orders,
Kṣatriyas are traditionally regarded as the protectors, the gatherers [of taxes], and the givers;
while Brāhmaṇas are defined by officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving pure gifts.
For the sake of favoring the world, these were established on earth by Brahmā:
protection of the subjects, giving, and warfare were ordained for the Kṣatriyas;
while agriculture, cattle-rearing, and giving in every way were ordained for the Vaiśyas.
Śūdras are ordained as attendants for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
Sūtas are ordained as attendants specifically for the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. They are not [ordained] for the Vaiśyas and Śūdras—listen to my words on this matter, O sinless one.

Thus, being an anointed king born of a lineage of royal sages, I am renowned as a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha), one to be served and praised by bards. Having become such as this, I am here, O crusher of enemy clans.
"I am willing to act as charioteer for the Sūta’s son in battle;
however, having suffered such humiliation, I will not fight under any circumstances.
Having taken my leave of you today, O son of Gāndhārī, I shall depart as I came."
"And I did not become the charioteer of the Suta's son.
Having spoken thus, Śalya, that tiger among men and ornament of the assembly,
rose up and departed swiftly from the midst of the kings in indignation.
Out of affection and great respect, your son restrained him and spoke these sweet words, which were conciliatory and capable of accomplishing every purpose:
"O Śalya, exactly as you have said this, so it is, without a doubt."
"But I have a certain intention; listen to it, O lord of men. I do not suspect Karna to be superior to you in any way whatsoever, for the King of Madra would never do anything that is false."
For indeed, those former best of men carried out only the *ṛta*;
for indeed, O best of royal seers, you have previously known the path.
Therefore, it is my conviction that you are called Ārtāyani.
"O giver of honor, O lord of the earth, because you are like a thorn to your enemies upon this earth, therefore your name is called Śalya.
This is exactly what was previously uttered by you, O giver of abundant sacrificial fees."
"O knower of dharma, do exactly as you are told for my sake.
Neither the son of Rādhā nor even I am more heroic than you.
We choose you to be the driver of these foremost horses in battle."
"For just as this world considers Karṇa to be superior to Dhanañjaya in his qualities, O dear one, and even superior to Vāsudeva and yourself, so too,
O bull among men, Karṇa is indeed superior to Pārtha in the matter of weapons."
"You too are superior to Kṛṣṇa in the management of horses and in strength;
just as the high-minded Vāsudeva knows the heart of horses,
you know it twice as well, O King of Madra— of this there is no doubt."
Śalya said: "O son of Gāndhārī, O Kaurava, as for what you say to me in the midst of the army—
that I am superior to the son of Devakī— I am indeed pleased with you."

"O hero, I shall undertake the charioteership for the illustrious son of Rādhā as he fights with the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, just as you desire. For there is a certain condition of mine, O hero, regarding the son of Vikartana."
"I would release my words according to my faith in his presence.
Sañjaya said:
"So be it, O King," replied your son, O Bhārata, together with Karṇa.
O best of the Bharatas, he spoke to the son of the King of Madra.
Duryodhana said:
"O Lord of Madra, listen further to that which I shall say to you."
O Lord, O best of royal sages, as the great seer Mārkaṇḍeya related this ancient account of the battle between the gods and the asuras to my father, so shall I relate it to you in its entirety.
Understand this, and let there be no further deliberation on your part:
it is certain that kings arise from delusion;
yet, having done so, they all resolve upon determinations of dharma and artha.

There was a great encounter between the gods and the asuras. Then the sons of Siṃhikā, having become arrogant, began to slaughter the gods. Those Dānavas, proud of their strength, were driven away by the gods.
O King, there occurred the first great battle known as the Tārakāmaya;
we have heard that at that time the Daityas were utterly defeated by the gods.
Their pride shattered and their enthusiasm extinguished, they then entered the netherworld of Pātāla.
When the Daityas had been defeated, O King, three sons of Tāraka— Tārākṣa, Kamalākṣa, and Vidyunmālī—
along with a certain formidable Prajāpati, joined together with that great-souled one.
A most terrible battle took place between the gods and the others; so it is heard.
In that conflict, the Asuras, together with the Dānavas, were utterly defeated.
Thus cast down by the gods, the Asuras, sighing in indignation, departed thereafter.
O scorcher of enemies, having undertaken fierce austerity and remaining fixed in supreme discipline, they emaciated their own bodies through penance,
O King, by means of self-restraint, asceticism, and religious observances.

The Grandsire, pleased with them and being the granter of boons, bestowed those boons upon them. O King, they together requested from the Grandsire of all the worlds the boon of being unslayable at all times by any living beings.
Then the god, the lord and master of the worlds, said to them:
"Indeed, there is no such thing as immortality for all; therefore, O Asuras, desist from this.
Choose another boon, whatever you may desire."
Then, O King, having deliberated together many times,
they bowed down to that Lord of All Worlds and spoke these words:
"We desire to build a beautiful city that moves at will."
For the sake of fulfilling all desires, it is indestructible by gods or dānavas,
by hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and uragas, as well as by various other species;
nor can it be overcome by magical spells, weapons, or curses for those who speak the Veda.
"O God, when you are pleased with us, Tripura may be destroyed;
O Grandfather, O God, grant us this boon:
that we, having established ourselves upon these three cities, [shall rule] this earth."
"Preceded by your grace, we shall wander throughout this world;
then, after a thousand years have passed, we shall meet one another again.
Brahmā said:
"At the end of its time, there is dissolution; at the end of life, there is death.
Reflecting thus, consider some means of slaying him.
O sinless one, these cities will soon fall into a state of unity.
"O Blessed One, when these have gathered together, he who shall slay them with a single arrow,
O best of gods, he will be our death.
Having heard those words of the Dānavas, the highly illustrious one—
"So be it," the god replied to them and entered heaven. Having obtained the boon, they were delighted and, after deliberating among themselves,
chose the great asura Maya for the purpose of constructing the three cities.
To Viśvakarman, the undecaying one worshipped by the Daityas and Dānavas,
the wise Maya then built three cities through his own ascetic power:
one of gold, one of silver, and likewise one of black iron.
O lord of the earth, there was a golden wheel in the sky, a silver one in the intermediate space, and an iron one upon the ground;
each measured a hundred yojanas in both width and length.
It was filled with houses, watchtowers, and palatial turrets, with massive walls and arched gateways; crowded with the abundance of its virtues, it was spacious and free from affliction,
adorned with various mansions and gates.
O King, there were indeed separate kings in the cities;
O best of monarchs, those Daityas wore celestial garlands and garments.
The great-souled Tārakākṣa’s chariot was variegated with gold.
The silver [palace] belonged to Kamalākṣa, and that of Vidyunmālin was made of iron.
Those three kings of the Daityas, having swiftly overrun the three worlds with their splendor, remained there for many series of years, as if they were the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis).
Millions, hundreds of millions, and tens of millions of those chief Dānavas—
invincible heroes who were meat-eaters, exceedingly arrogant, and likewise oppressed by the gods— gathered there from every direction.
Desiring great sovereignty, they took refuge in the fortress of Tripura. Moreover, Maya, who provides all means of union (*yoga*), was the supporter of them all;
for relying upon him, they all lived free from fear from any quarter.
For whatever desire one dwelling in Tripura meditated upon with his mind,
Maya then provided that very desire for him through his illusory power (*māyā*).
And the son of Tārakākṣa was a mighty being named Hari.

He performed supreme austerity by which the Grandfather was pleased. He chose a boon from the gratified god: "Let there be a pond in our city where those slain by weapons, when cast therein, shall become even more powerful."
O Lord, having obtained that boon, the heroic Hari, son of Tārakākṣa,
created there a pond that restores the dead to life—
a pond filled with divine water resembling nectar.

In whatever form and in whatever attire the Daitya had died, he was conceived in that very same way when cast into her. O King, he was endowed with complete strength and heroism, and possessed of valor.
Thus endowed with such vigor by that Great-Souled One,
they reached the city of Tripura and oppressed all the worlds.
Hari himself, possessing supreme splendor, dwelt in the world of the gods.
Having provided for the welfare and well-being of all the worlds, and having acted for their benefit,
that benefactor toward your own people was thereafter utterly dispassionate;
through great asceticism, they became perfected ones who increased the fear of the gods.
When one Daitya was slain, they would create ten asuras;
O King, there was no way for them to suffer depletion in battle by any means.
Then, overcome by greed and delusion, they became deprived of their senses.
Lacking all sense of shame, they utterly destroyed the established order that had been ordained.
Having driven away the gods along with their hosts here and there at various times, they roamed about according to their own will, arrogant due to the granting of the boon.

The Dānavas of wicked conduct destroyed all the divine forests beloved by the inhabitants of heaven, as well as the holy hermitages of the ṛṣis, the sacrificial posts, and the inhabited regions; they overthrew all established boundaries.
The gods, along with the sages and the ancestors, were driven to their final extremities;
indeed, the three worlds were assailed by those three types of Daityas, the enemies of the gods.
While the worlds were thus being oppressed, Śakra, surrounded by the Maruts, [set out].

He waged war against those ancient cities with thunderbolt strikes from all sides; O lord of men, when Purandara was unable to break through those impenetrable cities, which had been granted boons by the Creator, [he desisted].
Then the Lord of the Gods, terrified, abandoned those cities; thereafter,
O subduer of enemies, all those gods together approached the Grandfather to report the mistreatment by the non-gods.
Having explained all that truth and having bowed their heads in prostration,
they asked the blessed Grandfather for the means of their destruction.
Having heard that, the blessed Lord spoke thus to the gods.
"He who acts unkindly toward you commits an offense against me as well.
Listen, all you gods, to this weighty word:
even those evil-minded Asuras, the enemies of the wise ones."
Those who constantly offend you and even afflict you—
I do not consider them to be truly offending me,
for I am equal toward all beings; of this there is no doubt.
"But those who are unrighteous must be slain," I tell you; "those fortresses are to be pierced by a single arrow and not otherwise.
And no one is able to pierce a city with a single arrow except for Sthāṇu."

"O Ādityas, choose him as your warrior—Sthāṇu, the Lord, the Victorious One who acts without effort; he shall slay those who are not gods. Having heard these words of his, the gods, led by Śakra, [chose him].
Urged by those words, those gods stood bowed down;
having performed austerities for a thousand divine years, those bulls among the gods—
pure-souled and high-minded— went indeed to the one whose banner is the bull.
Placing Brahmā at their head, they sought refuge with the bull-bannered Lord;
knowing the Dharma, they performed supreme austerity together with the sages, chanting the eternal Veda and having approached Bhava with their whole being.
They praised with meaningful words the God of gods, the supreme Sthāṇu, the boon-granter, the three-eyed Śiva,
Śarva, the one worthy of praise, the unborn Rudra, whose hair is marked by the crescent moon—
the greatest bestower of fearlessness in times of danger.
He who is the self of all, the Great Self, by whom everything has been attained through his own being;
he who knows through manifold specific austerities the yoga of the self;
he who knows the Sāṃkhya of the self, and whose self is always under his own control.
With supreme effort, those thirty gods beheld that Lord, the Master of Umā, a mass of splendor— Bhava, Śarva, the Sovereign,
peerless in the world, observant of his vows, and stainless.
And they perceived the single Blessed One in various forms; then,
seeing within that Great Soul forms corresponding to their own selves,
and seeing one another [in those same forms], they were all utterly amazed.
To that Lord, who consists of all beings, who is unborn, and the master of the world—
the gods and the celestial sages prostrated themselves with their heads upon the earth.
Having honored them with words of blessing and raised them up, Śaṅkara spoke.
"Speak! Speak! the Blessed One said, smiling.
Then, permitted by Tryambaka, they, with restless minds, spoke to Bhava: "O Lord, let there be salutation after salutation unto you."
Homage to the god beyond gods, to the wielder of the bow, and to the one of exceeding wrath; homage to the slayer of Prajāpati and the sacrifice, who is praised by the Prajāpatis.
Homage to the one already lauded, to the one worthy of praise, to the one being praised, and to Death.
To the deep-red Rudra, the blue-throated one, the wielder of the trident;
to the unerring one, the deer-eyed one, the warrior who fights with the most excellent weapons; and to the Worthy One, the Pure One, the Destroyer, and the Slaughterer.
To the one who is difficult to restrain, to the pure, to the Brahman, to the student of sacred knowledge;
to the Sovereign, the immeasurable, the Controller, the one clothed in a hide;
to the one eternally devoted to austerity, the tawny-hued, the observer of vows, the one clad in an animal skin.
Salutations to the father of Kumāra, the three-eyed one who wields supreme weapons;
to the destroyer of the suffering of those who seek refuge, the slayer of the hosts of those who hate the Vedas;
salutations to the Lord of the lords of the forest, the Lord of men.
Salutations always to the Lord of cattle and to the Lord of sacrifices;
let there be homage to you, Tryambaka, who possess an army and fierce splendor. O God, favor us who have sought refuge in you through our thoughts, words, and deeds.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, greeted them with a welcome and said:
"Let your fear depart; tell me, what may I do for you?
Having heard Śarva’s words, the gods were filled with joy.
When the boon had been granted by the Great-Souled One to the hosts of the ancestors, gods, and sages,
Brahmā, having honored Śaṅkara, spoke these words for the welfare of the world:
"These fortresses of the Asuras invade the three worlds."

And who is Prajāpati? Slay all those terrible ones without delay. O Lord of Gods, because of your permission, while I was presiding over this station of Prajāpati, a great boon was granted to the Dānavas.
"We have heard that there is indeed no other slayer of them in battle;
none other than you is capable of destroying those who have transgressed the bounds of propriety,
O Lord of the past and the future, for you alone are their adversary in death."
