Therefore, O God, Lord of Devas, wielder of the trident, show favor to us who have sought refuge and to the gods who implore you; slay the Dānavas. Through your grace, O giver of honor, the entire world prospers in happiness.
"For you are the one worthy of refuge in this world, O Lord of the World; we have come to you for refuge.
The Blessed One said:
"It is my intention that all your enemies must be slain."
"I alone am indeed not capable of slaying those enemies of the gods;
therefore, all of you together, by means of the power of my weapons,
conquer those foes in battle, for a united force is exceedingly powerful."
The gods said:
"We consider that their energy and strength are twice as great as our own;
for we have indeed witnessed their energy and strength."
The Blessed One said:
"Those wicked ones who have offended against you must be slain by all means. By half of my own splendor and power, slay all those enemies."
The gods said:
"O Maheśvara, we shall not be able to bear half of your splendor;
you yourself, with half the strength of us all, slay the enemies."
"O Lord, we too must be protected by you in every way;
therefore, O Mahādeva, protect us and slay our enemies yourself.
The Blessed One said:
"If you have no power whatsoever to sustain my army,
I shall slay these [enemies], strengthened by half of your energy.
Duryodhana said:

Then, O best of kings, having been told "So be it" by them, the Lord of the Gods took half from each of them and became superior to all in splendor; that god was indeed more powerful than all others in strength.
From that time forth, Śaṅkara became known as Mahādeva. Then Mahādeva said, "Bearing my bow and arrows,
I shall indeed slay those enemies of the dwellers of heaven in battle from my chariot."
"Behold my chariot, as well as my bow and arrows,
while I cast these down upon the surface of the earth this very day!
The gods said:
"O Lord of Gods, having gathered the entire substance of the forms from here and there throughout the three worlds, we shall fashion for you a chariot of great majesty;
it will be fashioned by Viśvakarman and designed with such wisdom that it is auspicious."
Then those tigers among the gods prepared that chariot;
they made Viṣṇu, Soma, and Agni its arrow, O lord of the people. Fire became its shaft, and Soma its barb.
Then, upon that excellent arrow, Viṣṇu became the flower-bud;
they then made the goddess Earth— the supporter of all beings, adorned with garlands of vast cities, together with her mountains, forests, and islands— into the curved surface of the bow.
Mount Mandara was its axle, and the great rivers were its poles;
the cardinal and intermediate directions were indeed the retinue of that chariot. The lineage of the stars was its shaft, and the Kṛta Yuga became its yoke.
Vāsuki, the best of serpents, became the pole of the chariot;
Himavat and the Vindhya mountain served as the axle-stand;
and the foremost of gods made the Udaya and Asta mountains the two side-pieces of the stand.
They released the ocean, the supreme abode of the Dānavas, as its axle;
the constellation of the Seven Sages served as the ornamentation of the chariot,
while the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, and the sky itself formed its pole.
The equipment of the chariot was the waters and all the rivers;
day and night, the *kalās*, the *kāṣṭhās*, and likewise the seasons were its parts.
The blazing planets were its undercarriage, and the stars were its fender.
The excellent chariot was joined with the three shafts of dharma, artha, and kāma, and was beautiful;
there were various medicinal herbs there, yielding diverse flowers and fruits.
Having made the sun and the moon its two wheels, he mounted that best of supreme chariots.
There, they made the auspicious day and night the two fore and aft sails;
they made the ten lords of the *nāgas*, headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the sturdy keel,
and the hissing great serpents the lashings.
The *yuga*, the *yugacarma*, and the *saṃvartaka* clouds were [the ornaments];
then Kālapṛṣṭha, Nahuṣa, Karkoṭaka, Dhanañjaya,
and other *nāgas* became the tail-tassels for the horses.
The cardinal directions and the intermediate directions were the reins of the chariot horses;
the four Vedas, adorned with the ancillary sciences (*vedāṅga*) and the Purāṇas, were the horses.
*Śamyā*, *dhṛti*, *medhā*, *sthiti*, and *saṃnati* likewise [were the chariot parts].
The vault of heaven was variegated with planets, lunar mansions, and stars; [he saw] the lords of the world, the masters of gods, waters, spirits, and wealth, as well as the horses [of the sun];
and Sinīvālī, Anumati, Kuhū, and the virtuous Rākā.
They made the yokes for the draft animals, and Rohaka and Kaṇṭhaka were also prepared;
truth, ritual action, austerity, and wealth were ordained there as the reins;
the mind was the seat, and Sarasvatī was the chariot-fender.
Various and variegated banners, stirred by the wind,
illuminated the blazing chariot, which was further adorned with lightning and Indra’s bow;
the *vaṣaṭ*-call became the whip, and the *gāyatrī* verse served as the head-stall.
That which was previously ordained for the sacrifice of the high-souled Īśāna—
the year itself was his bow, and the great-sounding Sāvitrī was its string;
and a divine, highly precious armor, adorned with jewels, was provided.
Impenetrable, stainless, and indeed beyond the reach of the wheel of time,
the majestic golden mountain Meru became the flagpole;
and the clouds, adorned with flashes of lightning, became the banners.

Standing in the midst of the *adhvaryu* priests, they shone like blazing fires. Seeing that chariot thus prepared, O noble one, the deities were struck with wonder upon beholding the splendors of all the worlds gathered in a single place.
The gods presented [the chariot] to that Great-Souled One.
O great king, when that best of chariots had been thus prepared by the gods for the crushing of his enemies, O tiger among men—
Śaṅkara placed his own principal weapons upon the chariot;
he fixed the chariot-pole, drawn through the air, as a bull,
and likewise established the Staff of Brahmā, the Staff of Time, the Staff of Rudra, and Fever.
His attendants were raised up on all sides around this chariot;
Atharvan and Aṅgiras were the protectors of the wheels of that high-souled one,
while the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Purāṇa were his precursors.
The Itihāsas and the Yajurveda became his rear-guards;
the divine speeches and the sciences were made his attendants;
and, O king of kings, the *tottra* and other such implements, as well as the *vaṣaṭkāra*, likewise accompanied him.
And the syllable *oṃ*, O King, was at its tip, making it exceedingly beautiful.
Having fashioned the year— divided by the six seasons— into a bow,
he made his own shadow the inexhaustible string for that bow in battle.
For the Lord Rudra is Time; his bow is the year.
Therefore, the Night of Time (Kālarātri) was made the undecaying string of that bow.
Viṣṇu became the arrow, as did Agni and Soma.
"If all of you gods, even when united, are not able to withstand half of my strength in battle, then I tell you this: all of you,
both the Dānavas and the immortals, are equal to me."

"I am auspicious (*śiva*) toward all beings; therefore, O gods, my nature is auspiciousness (*śivatva*). However, because those enemies of the gods act with unrighteousness (*adharma*), they must be slain by me as well, out of a desire for your welfare."

To you who have come for refuge and who desire to conquer through righteousness, I shall provide assistance; I will slay your enemies. Let half of your army be given to me, by all of you individually.

"May all the worlds, even though they are oppressed, be subject to my state as a sacrificial animal; O dwellers of heaven, let me today become the lord of those animals. In this way, I shall not incur sin by slaying the enemies of the gods."
"Prepare for me a divine chariot and horses swift as thought;
[prepare] a bow, an arrow, and a charioteer, and then I shall conquer your enemies. Having heard these words of the God of gods, O King, the gods—

They all fell into despondency, fearing they were about to become cattle. Then, perceiving their state of mind, the god spoke this to them: "O best of the wise, let there be no fear in you regarding this state of being cattle."
"Listen! Let the liberation from the state of being a *paśu* be brought about.
He among you who shall practice the conduct (*caryā*) of Paśupati will be liberated from the condition of a *paśu*. I promise this truly to you all in this assembly."
And those others who shall practice this vow will also be liberated— whether for a lifetime,
or for twelve years, or for one year, or for half a year, or for three seasons,
or for a month, or for twelve nights; such a person is released from the state of being a beast.
"Therefore, you shall practice this supreme, divine, and secret vow. "So be it," the gods replied to him who is saluted by the gods of gods. And they said to the Lord, "Accept half of our splendor."
"‘So be it,’ replied the wielder of the trident, O best of kings. Then they all gave half of their splendor to that high-souled one;
taking all of it, he gathered half of the splendor of all the inhabitants of heaven."
Having become superior even in splendor, he became once more exceedingly powerful. From that time forth, Bhava became the God of gods among the gods;
and he then became the Lord of all beings and of all creatures.

Therefore, he is called Paśupati because he is the lord of creatures (*paśu*), and he is indeed called Bhava because he causes beings to come into existence (*bhū*). Taking half of the splendor of them all, as if blazing with brilliance,
the God of gods, possessed of great luster, illuminated them all.
Then all the gods consecrated Rudra, the enemy of Tripura.
For Mahādeva, the god of gods, Maheśvara, was indeed known as Duryodhana.
Having given half of their splendor to the high-souled Śaṅkara,
and even having assumed the state of sacrificial animals, they all addressed the imperishable Viśvakarman and said, "Let a chariot be fashioned."
Viśvakarman, having reflected, fashioned a divine chariot;
he made the goddess Earth— the vast supporter of all beings, garlanded with cities, together with her mountains, forests, and islands— into that chariot.
The pole, the lineage of the constellations, the parasol, and the great mountain Meru;
the unsurpassed ocean, filled with many trees and a treasury of jewels;
and the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, teeming with various trees and creepers.
At that time,

the blessed Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned Mount Asta as the foundation for the chariot’s axle-box and Mount Udaya as its pole. He established the mountain of excrement as its base, which was filled with various flocks of birds.

He made the ocean his axle, adorned with cities and mines, a supreme abode of *dānavas* and a dwelling place for fish, crocodiles, and large sea-monsters; he fashioned the moon as his wheel, encircled by the host of stars.
The imperishable Creator made the sun the other wheel, garlanded with rays; he made the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī his two quivers. Furthermore, the rivers and streams became the ornaments of the chariot.
He fashioned the three sacred fires according to the mantras for the triple-pole of the chariot;
he made the blazing planets its undercarriages, the stars its fenders,
and the radiant clusters of herbs and creepers its network of bells.
The Lord adorned the chariot with months, fortnights, and seasons;
likewise with days and nights, *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, and solstices;
as well as the heavens, the *yugas*, the joints of the *yugas*, and the clouds of universal destruction.
He fashioned *śamyā*, *dhṛti*, *medhā*, *sthiti*, and *saṃnati*; he appointed the *Ṛgveda* and the *Sāmaveda* as the two lead horses,
while the *Yajurveda* and the *Atharvaveda* were likewise made the two flanking horses.
He also fashioned a collection of ornaments for the horses;
he made Sinīvālī, Anumati, Kuhū, Rākā,
and Suprabhā the yokes for the horses, and he made the Kūṣmāṇḍas the serpents [for the reins].
Then Kālapṛṣṭha, Nahuṣa, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya,
as well as other *nāgas*, became the hair-tassels for the horses;
O lord of the earth, the reins and the six parts [of the harness] were thus prepared.
The syllable *oṃ* was fashioned as its goad by Viśvakarman;
all sacrifices were separately fashioned as the various parts of the chariot,
and the mind became the seat while Sarasvatī became the fender.
Clouds of various colors and banners stirred by the wind,
together with lightning and Indra’s bow, illuminated the chariot with their brilliance; and the sky, crowded with hosts of planets, became the armor ordained for the warrior.

Impenetrable, radiant, and variegated, it was adorned with the wheel of time. Seeing that chariot thus fashioned, O noble one, the deities were struck with wonder upon beholding the splendors of all the worlds gathered in a single place.
The gods reported this to that Great-Souled One.
O tiger among men, O great king, when that best of chariots had thus been fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, it became a source of increasing fear for his enemies.
Śaṅkara deposited his own divine weapons upon the chariot;
having raised the flagpole toward the sky, he stationed the bull there.
The Staff of Brahmā, the Staff of Time, and the Staff of Rudra—these were the fevers.
The ornaments of the chariot were raised up toward every direction. Having fashioned the year into a bow by means of the six seasons as its variegated decorations,
he made his own shadow the eternal and firm string of that bow.

For Time is the Lord Rudra, and that year is the bow; therefore, the Night of Time (Kālarātri), belonging to Rudra, was made the undecaying string of the bow. Then the sages yoked those chariot-horses to the chariot.
Taking them up one by one, those of firm vows, being greatly delighted,
placed the *Ṛgveda* at the right yoke-pole by those who had mastered the mantras; and on the left, O King, the *Sāmaveda* was yoked by the great seers.

On the right flank was joined the Yajurveda by the gods and the twice-born; likewise, O King, on the other flank was joined the Atharvaveda. Thus were those steeds yoked to the chariot at that time by the knowers of sacrifice.
Thus equipped, they shone as if they were standing in the midst of a sacrifice. Having fashioned the divine chariot, he then prepared the arrow;
having meditated upon Hari Viṣṇu, the imperishable one whose vehicle is the sacrifice.
The high-minded Viśvakarman then resolved to fashion an arrow; O King, best of monarchs, he then fashioned its shaft and its feathers, employing the wind that carries auspicious fragrances.
At that time, he indeed fashioned Agni and Soma at the tip of the arrow;
for Agni and Soma are said to be the entire world, and the world is said to belong to Viṣṇu. And Viṣṇu is the self of the Lord Bhava, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
Therefore, they could not endure the touch of Hara’s bowstring;
upon that arrow, the Lord, his wrath sharpened,
released the unbearable fire of his anger, born from the fury of Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Manyu, which was exceedingly difficult to withstand.
He was dark blue and red, smoke-colored, clad in a skin, and terrifying;
resembling ten thousand suns, he blazed, enveloped in flames of splendor.
He was difficult to dislodge, yet the dislodger; the conqueror, the slayer of those who hate the Brahman, Hara.
He is the eternal protector and destroyer of people who rely on righteousness and unrighteousness. Resolved in his self-control, he obtained power through violent and impetuous means;
surrounded by hosts of terrible form, fierce and formidable, who cause great distress.

The Blessed Lord Sthāṇu shines forth, encompassed by those very qualities of his own self. Having taken refuge in his limbs, this entire world— both moving and unmoving, O King— stands established, radiant with a wondrous appearance.
Having seen that divine chariot, he, clad in armor and armed with a bow,
took up that celestial arrow born of Soma, Viṣṇu, and Agni;
then the gods fashioned the feathers for that lordly shaft.
O King, O best of monarchs, Mahādeva mounted that wind which carries sacred fragrances,
terrifying even the gods; and mounting it with great effort, he seemed to make heaven and earth tremble.
As the Lord of Gods desired to ascend, the supreme ṛṣis praised him,
as did the gandharvas, the hosts of gods, and likewise the throngs of apsaras.
Being lauded by the great ṛṣis and honored by the bards, he proceeded.
Accompanied by throngs of Apsarases skilled in the dance,
that boon-granting god, shining resplendent and equipped with sword, arrow, and bow,
spoke as if smiling: "Who shall be my charioteer?"
The hosts of gods said to him, "O Lord of the Gods, whoever you shall appoint, he will become your charioteer; of this there is no doubt.
The god spoke to them again, "He who is indeed superior to me—"
"Reflecting upon it yourselves, do not delay, but appoint him as my charioteer.
Having heard these words spoken by the high-souled one, the gods then went to the god Pitāmaha, and having propitiated him, spoke these words.

"O Lord, this destruction of the enemies of the thirty gods has been described by you, and we have acted accordingly; the Bull-bannered One is well-pleased. And a chariot, equipped with various weapons, has been prepared by us."

"But we do not know who might be the charioteer for that supreme chariot. Therefore, O best of gods, let someone be appointed as the charioteer; O Lord, O All-pervading One, you ought to make our words bear fruit."
"O Blessed One, you have indeed said this to us in the past:
'I shall do what is beneficial for you. You ought to fulfill that promise.
O Lord, let that best of chariots be yoked for us."
Difficult to withstand and the router of enemies,
he who holds the Pināka bow in hand has been appointed as the warrior here; prepared for battle, he stands there terrifying the Dānavas.
Likewise, the four Vedas were his excellent horses,
and the great-souled one’s chariot was the earth with its mountains; the host of stars followed as his protective fender.
In a situation where the warrior must be protected by the charioteer, a charioteer distinguished by all these qualities must be sought;
for upon him depend the chariot, O Lord, as well as the horses and the warrior.
"O Grandfather, regarding the armor, weapons, and the bow,
we see no one other than you there who can serve as the charioteer. For you, O Lord, are endowed with all virtues and are superior even to the gods."
O Lord, you alone are capable of restraining these runaway horses of the Vedas along with the Upaniṣads in this world; therefore, become our charioteer yourself,
for you are able to fight with strength, courage, youth, and discipline.
A charioteer must be superior; there is no one else who is more excellent than you. May you, the imperishable one, deliver us; exercise the role of charioteer.
You are indeed superior; there shall be no other like you here.
"For you indeed, O Lord of Gods, best among speakers, are superior to all. Ascending that chariot, do you restrain the supreme horses.
By your grace, O God, may the thorns of the gods be slain."
O mighty-armed one, protect us from this great fear of the Daityas;
for you, O undistracted one of great vows, are our refuge and our protector.
By your grace, O Lord, all the gods are honored in the third heaven.
"Quickly mount the charioteer's seat and restrain the supreme horses for the victory of the lords of the three heavens and for the slaying of the enemies of the gods.
Having thus bowed his head to the Grandfather, the lord of the three worlds, [he did as commanded].
"The gods propitiated him for the sake of charioteership; so we have heard.
Brahmā said: "O gods, this is indeed the truth; there is no one else superior to you."
"I shall serve as the charioteer for the high-souled Śaṅkara.
In every respect, the charioteer must be made superior to the warrior in the chariot.
Therefore, having understood this according to its true nature, and knowing that you are all assembled here—"
"O gods, I shall restrain these horses for Kālamardin;
there is not a single word of falsehood in what has been said to you, O denizens of heaven. I am indeed holding back the horses of the matted-haired one as he fights."
Having spoken thus, the great-grandfather bound his mass of matted hair,
put on a deerskin tightly, and set down his water-pot.
Then the Blessed One, with a goad in his hand, mounted the chariot.
Thereupon that Blessed Lord, the Creator of the World, the Grandfather,
was appointed by the gods to the office of charioteer for the high-souled Īśāna.
As he swiftly ascended that chariot honored by the world,
those horses, possessing the speed of the wind, quickly lowered their heads;
then the Blessed Lord, the god blazing with his own splendor, mounted it.
The Grandfather indeed took hold of the reins and the goad;
as Maheśvara ascended, the earth sank down upon its knees. That most excellent chariot was mounted by both lords of the worlds.
The Veda-horses were unable to bear the load and fell to the earth on their knees; then the Great-Grandfather, the Lord of the Three Worlds, grasping the reins,
urged those horses on, which possessed the speed of thought and the wind.
Then the Lord, the omnipresent Master, having raised up the horses with the reins,
urged on the chariot, saying, "May there be vigor and heroism for the horses of the Vedas," he, the imperishable Lord of the gods.
Then, having raised up those horses that were like the wind, the Blessed One, the best of gods, spoke to Sthāṇu: "Mount [this chariot]. Thereupon, he took up that arrow born of Viṣṇu, Soma, and Agni.
Then Sthāṇu ascended [the chariot], making his enemies tremble with his bow.
When the Lord of Gods had ascended, the supreme ṛṣis,
the gandharvas, the hosts of gods, and likewise the throngs of apsarases praised him.

Shining, the granter of boons, armed with a sword, arrows, and a bow, he stood upon his chariot, illuminating the three worlds with his own splendor. Then the god spoke once more to the gods, headed by Indra.
"You must not feel grief for them in any way, thinking 'they have been slain.
Know rather that by this arrow the Asuras have already been killed. The gods said, "It is true," and they declared, "They are indeed slain."
"And that word which the Lord, the Master, has spoken is not false"—
reflecting thus, the gods indeed attained supreme satisfaction.
Then the Lord of the Gods departed, surrounded by all the hosts of deities.
O King, there was no comparison for his great chariot;
the highly illustrious god was being honored by his own attendants,
as well as by other flesh-eating beings who were difficult to approach and were dancing.
Running about on all sides and threatening one another,
the highly fortunate ṛṣis, endowed with ascetic power and great virtues,
wished for victory in every way for the gods and Mahādeva.
When the Lord of Gods, the granter of fearlessness to the worlds, had thus departed,
O best of men, the entire world and the deities were filled with joy;
and there the sages praised the Lord of Gods with many hymns.
O King, thousands, millions, and billions of Gandharvas repeatedly increased his splendor;
and during his departure, they played various kinds of musical instruments.
Then, when the Giver of Boons had mounted and set out toward the Asuras, the Lord of All, smiling, addressed him: "Excellent, excellent!
Go, O God, to where the Daityas are; urge on the horses without weariness."
"Behold today the strength of my arms as I slay the enemies in battle! Then he urged those swift steeds, equal to the wind in speed,
toward the cities situated in the sky belonging to the powerful Dānavas.
O King, by means of that [bow], the three cities protected by the Daityas and Dānavas were [attacked].
Then those horses of the chariot named Veda, suddenly leaping up,
brought the Lord to those cities of the Daityas in an instant.
As if drinking up the sky with those horses honored by the world,
the Blessed One proceeded swiftly for the victory of the dwellers of the triple heaven;
when Bhava had mounted his chariot and set forth toward Tripura.
The bull let out a tremendous roar, filling the quarters of the sky.
Hearing that great and terrifying bellow of the bull,
the Tārakas, the enemies of the gods, met their destruction there.
Others stood there at that time, facing forward for battle.
Then, O great king, Sthāṇu, the wielder of the trident, was overcome with wrath;
all beings were terrified, and the three worlds and the earth trembled.
And as he fixed that arrow there, terrible omens appeared;
due to the agitation of Soma, Agni, and Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā and Rudra,
that chariot sank down excessively from the strain upon the bow.
Then Nārāyaṇa emerged from that portion of Śarabha;
assuming the form of a bull, he lifted up the great chariot while the vehicle was sinking and the enemies were roaring.
Out of agitation, the immensely powerful Lord let out a roar while standing upon the head of the bull and on the back of the horse, O giver of honor;
then that Lord Rudra gazed upon the city of the Dānava.
O best of men, Rudra, standing upon a bull and a horse,
then struck their flanks and split their hooves in two.
From that time forth, may you be blessed, the hooves of cattle have been divided in two.
O King, from that time forward, horses no longer had udders,
having been afflicted by Rudra of wondrous deeds with his powerful [missile].
Then Śarva, having strung his bow and fixed that arrow upon it—

Having equipped himself with the Pāśupata weapon, he meditated upon Tripura. O King, while he stood there enraged with his bow drawn, those three cities then became united as one through the power of time.
When the three cities had indeed become one and were brought together,
a tumultuous joy arose among the high-souled deities.
Then all the hosts of gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis—
"Victory! they cried out, praising him with joy.
Then, as he was about to strike down the Asuras, Tripura appeared before the god of indescribable and fierce form and unbearable splendor.
Then, seeing the three ancient cities standing as one, the Lord who wields the Pināka bow,
the Sovereign of the World, drew that divine bow and released that arrow— the very essence of the three worlds— toward Tripura.
O highly fortunate one, when that supreme arrow was released,
there arose a great cry of distress from the ancient cities as they fell to the earth;
thus did the Supreme Lord, the God, destroy Tripura with a single shaft.
Maheśvara, the God of gods, struck down the host of Asuras;
scorched by the fire of Bāṇa’s splendor, that army shattered into a thousand pieces and,
uttering a great cry of distress, perished without a remnant remaining.
Having incinerated that host of Asuras, he cast them into the western ocean.
Thus was Tripura burnt, along with the Dānavas without exception,
by the enraged Maheśvara, who desires the welfare of the three worlds.
And that fire born of his own anger was extinguished by him crying out "Hā hā!
yet it proceeded once more to burn the three worlds without exception,
rising again and again like the fire of cosmic destruction to consume all.
"Do not reduce the worlds to ashes," the Three-Eyed One said to him. Thereupon,
the gods, the worlds, and likewise the ṛṣis returned to their natural state and praised Sthāṇu, who possesses incomparable power, with meaningful words.

Permitted by the Blessed One, all those gods, led by Prajāpati, having accomplished their purpose and being filled with serene joy, departed as they had come. Thus is that Blessed Lord, the creator of the world, Maheśvara.
The lord of the hosts of gods and asuras brought about the welfare of the worlds,
just as the Blessed Brahmā, the creator and grandfather of the world-systems, acted as the charioteer there for Rudra, the supreme and imperishable one.
In that same way, may you also quickly become, like the Grandfather [Brahmā] for Rudra,
the creator of the three worlds yourself out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; therefore,
restrain the horses of this high-souled son of Rādhā.
For you, O protector of the earth, surpass Kṛṣṇa, Karṇa, and especially Phalguna in strength, appearance, skill, and the perfection of weapons; therefore,
bestow upon me that which I desire for my own welfare.
O tiger among kings, there is no doubt that he is superior;
for in battle, this one is like Rudra, while you, O sinless one, are equal to Brahmā.
Therefore, you two are capable of conquering my enemies, just as [the gods conquered] those Asuras.

O Śalya, act quickly today so that this Karṇa may strike down the son of Kuntī, who has white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer, after having overwhelmed him. O Lord of Madra, upon you rests the hope for the kingdom as well as the hope for life itself.
And likewise today, victory has been achieved through Karna acting as your deputy; O protector of the earth,
secure for yourself the kingdom, happiness, life, and victory, which are all dependent upon you— do what is beneficial and desired by me.
"O King, O scorcher of foes, restrain his horses for my sake;
for upon you depend Karṇa, the kingdom, and we ourselves, as well as victory in battle. Therefore, restrain the excellent horses today."
Furthermore, listen again to this other ancient history from me,
which a brahmin learned in dharma spoke in the presence of my father.
Having heard these wondrous words, which are consistent with reason, action, and purpose—
O Śalya, having reached a firm decision, act; let there be no further hesitation in this matter.
In the lineage of the Bhṛgus was born Jamadagni, a man of great asceticism;
his son, endowed with the quality of splendor, is renowned as Rāma.

Having undertaken intense austerity, he— pure in soul, disciplined, and with senses restrained— sought to propitiate Bhava for the sake of the weapon. Mahādeva was pleased with him because of his devotion and his tranquility.
Having understood what was in his heart, Śaṅkara, the Great God who brings welfare to all, revealed his own form directly to him. The Lord said:
"O Rāma, I am pleased; may prosperity be yours! Your desire is known to me. Purify yourself, and you shall obtain all of this.
I will grant you those weapons once you have become purified."
"O Bhārgava, weapons consume one who is an unworthy recipient and one who is incapable.
Having been addressed thus by the trident-bearing God of gods, the son of Jamadagni,
bowing his head, replied to the high-souled Lord.
"O Lord of the Gods, when you know me to be a worthy vessel for bearing weapons, then,
as I am desirous of hearing them, you ought to grant me those weapons.
Duryodhana said:
Then, through asceticism, self-restraint, and religious observances, as well as by means of worship, offerings, and oblations accompanied by burnt sacrifices and mantras,
he propitiated Śarva for many groups of years.
And Mahādeva, being pleased with the high-souled Bhārgava,
spoke of his many virtues in the presence of the Goddess:
"This Rāma, firm in his vows, is constantly devoted to me."
Thus the Lord, the slayer of enemies, joyfully recounted his virtues many times in the presence of the gods and the ancestors. At that very time, however, there were Daityas of great strength.
Then, blinded by pride and delusion, they oppressed the inhabitants of heaven.
Thereupon, the gods, having assembled and resolved to slay them,
made an effort to destroy their enemies, yet they were unable to conquer them.
Then the gods, having approached Maheśvara, spoke to him, propitiating him with devotion: "Slay the hosts of our enemies.
Thereupon, the god promised the destruction of the enemies of the deities.
Having summoned Rāma Bhārgava, Śaṅkara addressed him:
"O Bhārgava, slay all the assembled enemies of the gods,
for the sake of desiring the welfare of the worlds and likewise for the sake of my own pleasure."
Thus addressed, he replied to the three-eyed Lord, the giver of boons.
Having been thus spoken to by the god, the highly illustrious Bhārgava then replied to Śaṅkara, the lord of gods, with palms joined in reverence.
Rāma said: "O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, what power do I have, being unskilled in weapons,
to slay all the Dānavas who are skilled in weapons and intoxicated with battle?"
The Lord said:
"Go; by my grace you shall slay the Dānavas.
Having conquered all your enemies, you shall attain abundant virtues."
Duryodhana said:
Having heard these words and having accepted them in their entirety,
Rāma, for whom the rites for success had been performed, set out toward the Dānavas.
He slew those enemies of the gods who were endowed with intoxication, pride, and strength.
"O Daityas, you who are fierce with the intoxication of battle, give me battle! O great Asuras, I have been sent by the God of Gods to conquer you."

Having been addressed thus by Bhārgava, the Daityas then commenced the battle. Having struck down those Daityas in combat with blows whose touch was like that of the thunderbolt, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the son of Bhārgava, [prevailed].
That son of Jamadagni, the best of the twice-born, whose body had been wounded by the Dānavas,
was immediately made free of wounds upon being touched by Sthāṇu;
and the blessed Lord was truly pleased with that deed of his.
He granted boons to the high-souled Bhārgava, the knower of Brahman;
and the trident-bearing God of gods, filled with affection, said to him:
"Whatever pain has arisen in your body from the falling of weapons..."
"By that [act], O descendant of Bhṛgu, your human karma has been cast off.
Accept from my presence whatever divine weapons you desire. Then he bestowed upon him all the weapons and boons desired by his mind.
Having obtained various boons and bowed his head to Śiva, Rāma,
that great ascetic, departed from the Lord of Gods after receiving his permission;
thus did the Ṛṣi relate this ancient event of old.
Bhārgava also, O tiger among men, with a deeply gratified heart, bestowed the entire science of archery upon that high-souled Karṇa.
For if there were any deficiency whatsoever in Karṇa, O King, it would have been a source of reproach.

For the descendant of Bhṛgu would not have bestowed the divine weapons upon him had he been a Śūdra constantly nurtured by a charioteer; rather, having recognized his pure lineage, the Lord gave him the celestial weapons. He was indeed a king, not a Śūdra.
Nor do I think in any way that Karṇa was born in the family of a charioteer;
I consider him a son of the gods, born into a lineage of Kṣatriyas.
It is my conviction that he was born into such a distinguished family for the sake of its awakening.
O Śalya, in no way indeed is this Karṇa born of a Sūta lineage;
how could a doe give birth to a tiger such as this— one with earrings and armor, long-armed, a great chariot-warrior, and resembling the sun?
Behold his two thick arms, resembling the trunks of the king of serpents;
behold his broad chest, the destroyer of all enemies. This Karṇa Vaikartana, the bull-like hero, is by no means an ordinary man.
"For he is a great-souled one, O Indra among kings, a powerful disciple of Rāma.
Duryodhana said:
"In this way, that blessed Lord is the Grandfather of all the worlds."
He acted as the charioteer there where Rudra was the warrior;
for a hero superior to the warrior must be appointed as the chariot-driver.
Therefore, O tiger among men, do you restrain the horses in battle.
Just as the Grandfather was chosen there with great effort by the hosts of gods, so have you, who are superior even to Karṇa, been chosen by us with great effort;
just as the Great King was chosen by the gods as one superior to Īśvara.
"Likewise, may you also quickly [attain success], just as the Grandfather [Brahmā] did for Rudra.
Śalya said:
"O you of great splendor, restrain the horses of the son of Rādhā in battle!"
O best of men, I too have heard this divine and superhuman narrative told many times regarding those two lions among men;
and how the Great-Grandfather acted as the charioteer for Bhava.
O Bhārata, just as the Asuras were slain by a single arrow,
all this was already known to Kṛṣṇa long ago,
as well as how the Lord Grandfather then became the charioteer.
Kṛṣṇa knows the future and the past in their true essence;
even though he understood this,
O Bhārata, he undertook the role of charioteer for Pārtha, just as Svayambhū did for Rudra.
If the Sūtaputra should somehow slay the son of Kuntī,
Keśava himself, having seen Pārtha slain, will fight;
with conch, discus, and mace in hand, he will consume your army.
"And not even a single king among your opposing forces will stand before that high-souled Vārṣṇeya when he is enraged.
Sañjaya said:
"None of your kings here shall remain in the enemy ranks."
To the King of Madra who was speaking thus,
your son, the subduer of enemies, the mighty-armed and undaunted one, replied:
"O mighty-armed one, do not despise Karṇa Vaikartana in battle."
The best among all wielders of weapons, who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures—
upon hearing whose great and terrifying sound of the bowstring,
the armies of the Pāṇḍavas flee in the ten directions.
O mighty-armed one, you have witnessed with your own eyes how Ghaṭotkaca,
though employing hundreds of illusions and relying on his powers of deception, was slain;
and yet Bibhatsu did not stand firm against the enemy force in any way whatsoever.
Throughout all these days, O King, he was enveloped by great fear;
and the powerful Bhīmasena, urged on by the tip of his bow, addressed him with a sign, saying, "O fool, you are as gluttonous as a beast!"
Likewise, O noble one, those two heroic sons of Mādrī were not slain in battle by him who, having conquered them in the great fray for some specific purpose, [left them behind];
nor was Sātyaki, the foremost of the Vṛṣṇis and the best of the Sātvatas, slain by him.
Having been defeated in battle, the hero was deprived of his chariot and overpowered by force;
likewise, all the other Sṛñjayas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
were repeatedly vanquished in the encounter by him who smiled during the fray.
How will the Pāṇḍavas defeat that great chariot-warrior in battle—
he who, when enraged in combat, could slay even Purandara, the wielder of the thunderbolt?
And you, O hero, are a knower of all weapons, having reached the further shore of all sciences and arms.
There is no one on earth equal to you in the strength of arms; you are like a dart to your enemies, irresistible in prowess. Therefore, O King, slayer of foes, you are called Śalya.
Having encountered the strength of your arms, all the Sātvatas were unable [to prevail].
O King, is Kṛṣṇa indeed superior in strength because of the power of your arms? For it was by Kṛṣṇa that strength had to be maintained once Phalguna was slain.
Likewise, when Karṇa has passed away, you must maintain this great force.
For what reason did Vāsudeva restrain the army in battle?
And for what reason, O noble one, will you not slay the army?
"O noble one, for your sake I wish to follow in your footsteps in battle.
Śalya said:
"Among all my heroic brothers and all the rulers of the earth..."

"O son of Gāndhārī, O giver of honor, since you speak of me before this army as being superior to the son of Devakī, I am pleased with you; I shall undertake the charioteership for the illustrious son of Rādhā."
"O hero, fight as you see fit against the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas;
for I have a certain agreement, O hero, regarding Vaikartana.
Sañjaya said:
"I shall utter whatever words I desire in his presence.
"So be it," O King, replied your son, O honorable one, together with Karṇa,
to the King of Madra in the presence of all the kṣatriyas.
Then, comforted by Śalya’s acceptance of the role of charioteer,
Duryodhana was filled with joy and embraced Karṇa;
and being praised, your son spoke again to Karṇa.
"Slay all the Pārthas in battle, as Mahendra slew the Dānavas! When Śalya had thus agreed to the task of restraining the horses,
Karṇa, with a joyful heart, spoke again to Duryodhana.
"For this King of Madra speaks with a mind that is not at all joyful;
O King, speak to him once more with sweet words.
Then the wise and powerful king, skilled in all weapons, [spoke].
Duryodhana spoke to Śalya, the king of Madra and lord of the earth,
filling the air as it were with his roar, in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"Śalya, Karṇa believes that he must fight Arjuna today."
O tiger among men, restrain his horses in battle;
having slain all others, Karṇa desires to kill Phalguna.
O King, I entreat you again and again to take up the reins for him.
"Just as Kṛṣṇa is the excellent holder of the reins for Pārtha,
so too must you protect Rādheya from all sides.
Saṃjaya said:
Then Śalya, the lord of Madra and slayer of enemies, being pleased, embraced your son Duryodhana and spoke these words:
"O King, O handsome son of Gandhārī, if you think thus," he said.
Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, I shall perform whatever is pleasing to you; whenever I am capable of any task, I will bear the burden of your duty with my whole soul.
"Whatever I may say to Karṇa, whether pleasant or unpleasant, out of a desire for his welfare,
may you and Karṇa forgive all of that entirely.
Karṇa said:
"O King of Madra, just as Brahmā is devoted to the welfare of Īśāna, and as Keśava is to Pārtha, so do you always devote yourself to our welfare. Śalya said:

Self-reproach and self-praise, as well as the reproach of others and the praise of others— these four kinds of conduct are not practiced by the noble ones. However, O learned one, that which I shall declare for the sake of your conviction—
"Understand this, exactly as it is, which concerns my own praise:
O Lord, I am as fit for the office of charioteer to Śakra as Mātali,
by virtue of my unwearied application and my knowledge, sciences, and medical arts."
"Then, O sinless one, while you are fighting Pārtha in battle, I shall drive your horses; be free from anxiety, O son of a Sūta.
Duryodhana said:
"O Karṇa, this King of Madra shall act as your charioteer;
he is a driver superior even to Kṛṣṇa, just as Mātali is for the Lord of the Gods.
Just as that Mātali restrains the chariot yoked with bay horses,"
"O Śalya, so too is this man today the driver of your chariot-horses.
With you as the warrior standing on the chariot and the King of Madra as the charioteer,
that best of car-warriors, Pārtha, will certainly not prevail over you in battle."
Saṃjaya said:
Then, O King, Duryodhana again spoke to the swift king of Madra,
who was restraining the excellent horses in the midst of battle.
When the battle has arrived and is at hand, bestow [your protection] upon Karṇa in the fray;
guarded by you, the son of Rādhā will conquer Dhanañjaya.
Having been addressed thus, O Bhārata, he mounted his chariot and said, "So be it.
When Śalya had accepted, Karṇa, being well-pleased, spoke repeatedly and with haste to his charioteer: "O Sūta, prepare my own chariot for me!"

Then, having said "Victory! to his master, he presented that excellent, victorious chariot—which resembled a city of the Gandharvas and had been prepared according to ritual rules. Karṇa, the best among chariot-warriors, honored that chariot in accordance with the prescribed rites.
The priest, a knower of Brahman, had already prepared everything;
having carefully circumambulated and worshipped the sun,
he placed the King of Madra, who was standing nearby, at the front of the procession.
Then the highly energetic Śalya, like a lion ascending a mountain, mounted Karna’s great and invincible, preeminent chariot. O King,
once Śalya was seated upon that excellent chariot of his own, Karna—
Just as the sun presides over a cloud charged with lightning,
those two, possessing splendor equal to the sun and fire, mounted a single chariot and shone like the sun and fire together in the sky upon a cloud.
Being thus praised, those two heroes then appeared most resplendent,
like Indra and Agni being invoked by the officiating priests and members of the assembly at a sacrifice,
while Karṇa stood upon that chariot whose horses were held by Śalya.
Drawing his terrible bow like the sun encircled by a halo,
Karna— standing upon that best of chariots,
that tiger among men with arrows for his rays— shone like the sun atop Mount Mandara.
To that great hero of immeasurable splendor, who was standing on his chariot and advancing,
Duryodhana spoke these words to the son of Rādhā:
"That difficult task which could not be accomplished by Droṇa and Bhīṣma in battle— "
"O hero, act against the son of Adhiratha while all the archers look on!
For this was my firm conviction: that the two great car-warriors Bhīṣma and Droṇa would surely slay Arjuna and Bhīmasena."
O hero, perform that heroic deed in the great battle which has not yet been accomplished by those two; O son of Rādhā, act like a second wielder of the thunderbolt.
Either seize the King of Dharma, or slay Dhanañjaya yourself.
O son of Rādhā, [protect] Bhīmasena and the twin sons of Mādrī as well. May you have victory and prosperity; set forth, O bull among men, and reduce all the armies of Pāṇḍu’s son to ashes.
Then thousands of musical instruments and tens of thousands of kettledrums, being sounded,
resounded like the roar of clouds in the sky.
Having accepted those words, that best of chariot-warriors stood upon his chariot.
The son of Rādhā addressed Śalya, who was skilled in battle:
"O mighty-armed one, urge on the horses so that I may strike down Dhanañjaya,
Bhīmasena, both the twins, and King Yudhiṣṭhira."
"Today, O Śalya, let Dhanañjaya behold the strength of my arms as I discharge hundreds and thousands of heron-feathered arrows.
Today, O Śalya, I shall hurl arrows of supreme sharpness."
O Śalya, I shall join the Pāṇḍavas along with Janārdana in battle for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas and for the victory of Duryodhana.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard these words of his, Śalya spoke these words to Karṇa.
Śalya said:
O son of a Sūta, how can you hold the Pāṇḍavas in such contempt—
those who are masters of all weapons, great archers, all of whom are indeed great car-warriors (mahārathas),
never-retreating, highly fortunate, unconquerable, and possessed of true prowess?

Even those who would inspire fear in Śatakratu himself will be struck with terror when you hear the roar of Gāṇḍīva in battle, O Rādheya, sounding like the crash of a thunderbolt; then you will no longer speak in this manner.
When you behold Bhīma in battle against the elephant division,
with its tusks shattered and its leader slain, then you will not speak thus. When you behold the son of Dharma and likewise the twins in the midst of combat—
When you see those light-handed and unassailable warriors discharging sharp arrows that create, as it were, a cloud-shade in the sky, piercing and slaying their enemies—
even other kings— you will not speak in such a manner.
08,026.030 Saṃjaya said:
08,026.030a But disregarding those words spoken by the King of Madra,
08,026.030c Karṇa indeed said to Śalya, "O lord of men, you shall see [today]."
O scorcher of foes, seeing the great archer Karṇa standing there eager for battle, all the Kurus cried out, filled with joy. Then, there arose the sound of kettledrums and the roar of war-drums.
Amidst the various sounds of arrows and the roars of the swift warriors,
your men went forth to battle, making death their only means of retreat.
But when Karṇa had set out and the warriors were filled with joy...
O King, the earth trembled and let out a terrible roar;
the seven great planets were seen emerging from the sun,
and there was a falling of meteors as well as a burning of the quarters of the sky.
Likewise, meteors fell and fierce winds blew;
and hosts of beasts and birds repeatedly kept your army to their left, portending a great danger.
As Karṇa set forth, his horses stumbled upon the ground,
and a terrifying rain of bones fell from the sky;
his weapons blazed and his banners trembled.
And the mounts shed tears, O lord of the people.
These and many other most dreadful portents, O honorable one, arose there for the destruction of the Kauravas.
Deluded by fate, they all failed to take them into account;
and seeing Karṇa, the ornament of battle, accompanied by Śalya, the men on earth cried out, "Victory! to the son of the Sūta as he set forth.
Your Kauravas then believed that the Pāṇḍavas had already been conquered. Then, standing upon his chariot, the slayer of enemy heroes beheld Bhīṣma and Droṇa, whose prowess had been restored.
O Bhārata, that bull among men, Vaikartana, a tusker among chariot-warriors, blazed like a fire;
addressing Śalya, he spoke these words.
Having witnessed the incomparable feat of Pārtha,
burning with pride and arrogance,
and sighing as if blazing with wrath;
I do not fear even Mahendra himself, nor Vajrapāṇi with his thunderbolt, though he be enraged, standing on his chariot with bow in hand; yet having seen those led by Bhīṣma lying prostrate;
Yet steadfastness does not abandon me at all—
those two blameless ones, who resemble Mahendra and Viṣṇu,
and who crush the foremost of chariots, horses, and elephants.
When those two who were nearly invincible were slain by the enemies,
even now I feel trepidation in battle upon seeing those exceedingly powerful ones [slain] by the lords of men in the fray.
Why did the preceptor, that bull among brahmins and master of great weapons, not slay all those enemies in battle— men, horses, elephants, and chariots— already struck down by his arrows?
Remembering that encounter with Droṇa in the great battle, I speak the truth; listen, O Kurus!
No one other than me could withstand Arjuna in combat.
Like death itself appearing in a terrible form as it arrives in due course,
Drona possesses instruction and grace, strength and fortitude, great weapons and humility.
If that great-souled one has gone under the power of death,
I consider all other afflicted beings today to be likewise;
nothing whatsoever here should be considered certain.
In this world, people know that actions are subject to impermanence;
for who, free from doubt, would harbor pride today when the sun has risen and the preceptor has been struck down?
Surely neither weapons, nor strength, nor prowess,
nor skillful action, nor supreme missiles are sufficient for a man to live in happiness.
For thus was my preceptor slain by his enemies in battle—
he who possessed a splendor equal to fire and the sun,
and who was like Viṣṇu and Purandara in prowess.
He was always equal to Bṛhaspati or Uśanas in policy;
yet that weapon, so difficult to endure, did not fail him even as the women and children cried out in lamentation.
O Śalya, I know that when the prowess of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son has been defeated, my task must be performed;
therefore, advance against the army of the enemies.
Where the Pāṇḍava king, true to his promise,
stands firm, along with Bhīmasena and Arjuna,
Vāsudeva, the Sṛñjayas, and Sātyaki;
And who other than me could withstand the twins?
Therefore, O Lord of Madra, proceed quickly to the Pāñcālas, the Pāṇḍavas, and the Sṛñjayas in battle.
Either I shall slay them all upon meeting them in battle, or I shall go to the front led by Droṇa;
I think that I will certainly not fail to enter their midst.
O Śalya, know this: for those heroes, this betrayal of a friend is not to be tolerated by me;
having cast off my life-breaths, I shall follow after Droṇa.
For both the wise man and the fool, at the end of life,
there is the release of breath as they enter the mouth of Death.
Therefore, O learned one, I shall advance against Pārtha.
"O King, it is indeed impossible to transcend what is ordained by fate;
for he was always of virtuous conduct and was the son of Vicitravīrya’s son, my own [son]."
For the sake of accomplishing his purpose, I shall renounce my dear enjoyments and even my life, which is so difficult to give up—
clad in a tiger skin, with eyes that do not blink.
Indeed, Rāma gave this to me: a preeminent chariot with a golden triple-bow and a silver triple-pole, yoked with the finest horses.
O Śalya, having beheld the variegated bows,
the banner, the mace, the arrows of fierce form,
the flaming sword, and that supreme weapon;
The high-souled one gave him a bright, resonant, and formidable conch shell, as well as divine weapons,
along with a bannered chariot that sounded like the crash of a thunderbolt.
In battle, I shall slay Arjuna by force,
even if Death, the destroyer of all,
should protect that son of Pāṇḍu in combat, remaining ever vigilant.
Either I shall slay him by encountering him in battle,
or I shall go to Yama with Bhīṣma at my head; or else Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Vāsava [shall come for me].
If all the hosts together were to come here in this great battle desiring to protect the Pāṇḍava,
what need is there to say more? With them, I shall conquer him.
While he was thus boasting in his impetuousness for battle,
the powerful King of Madra heard those words and laughed in derision.
He forbade him and spoke this reply:
"Desist, desist, O Karṇa, from your boasting! You are too impetuous and speak what is improper."
Where indeed is Dhanañjaya, the best of men,
and where are you here, O fool, having come to rest?
[Go to] the abode of the Yadus, protected by Upendra.
Having beheld her here by force— who else could carry off this younger sister of the best of men, except for Arjuna— anyone other than him, like the celestial realm guarded by the king of the gods?
Who here, other than Arjuna, would challenge Bhava— the creator of the three worlds and the Lord of lords— in battle, save for the slaughter of a deer?
By virtue of a majestic power equal to that of the Lord of the Gods,
[he subdued] the asuras, gods, great serpents, and humans;
the garuḍas, piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
Out of respect for Agni, he conquered with arrows;
and the victorious one offered the oblation he himself desired.
Do you not remember when he was carried away by his enemies?
And that son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was liberated by those best of men, the sons of the Sun,
after he had slain many of those enemies in the desert.
Even when you first fled,
do you not remember how the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who were fond of quarreling, were released by you?
Having previously defeated the hosts of sky-dwellers with their assembled forces and mounts,
you were conquered once again by that best of men during the cattle-raid.
"O Arjuna, why was he not conquered by you then, along with his preceptor, his preceptor’s son, and Bhīṣma?
Now this other [enemy] has again appeared."
Today, indeed, you shall have a well-fought battle for your own destruction,
provided you do not flee out of fear of the enemy; having gone to the field of battle today, O son of a Sūta, you are as good as slain.
Sañjaya said:
Thus, while the lord of the Madras was speaking many harsh words with a distracted mind, his enemy praised him.
Greatly incensed, the bull-like leader of the Kuru army spoke to the Madra king:
"Enough, enough! Why do you boast?"
"Surely a battle between me and him is imminent; if he conquers me in this great conflict,
then let these words of yours be well-spoken."
"So be it," said the Lord of Madra, and he offered no further reply.
"Go, O Lord of Madra! Karna said to him, desiring to fight.
Then that chariot, with its white horses and Śalya as its charioteer, set forth toward the enemies.
Slaying his enemies in battle like Savitṛ dispelling the darkness,
Karṇa then set forth joyfully on a chariot covered with tiger-skin and yoked with white horses.
And having beheld the army of the Pāṇḍavas,
he inquired urgently about Dhanañjaya.
Sañjaya said:
Then, as Karna advanced, gladdening your army,
he saw each Pāṇḍava one by one in battle and asked about him:
"Who among you can show me today that high-souled one with white horses?"
I would grant him whatever desired boon he wishes for in his mind;
if he should so desire it, I would further give to him a cart filled with jewels to whoever tells me of Dhanañjaya.
Alternatively, suppose there were a cart filled with jewels, yoked to six large, capable oxen, ready for immediate use; if a man who had seen Arjuna were to desire that [cart].
I would give him a hundred cows, each with a bronze milking vessel for daily use;
I would even give a hundred of the best villages to the one who shows me Arjuna.
Likewise, I would further give him a chariot drawn by white mules.
It would be fitting for one with eyes like collyrium to tell me where Dhanañjaya is;
or else, I shall grant him another boon as he desires. [The chariot] is yoked with the finest Kamboja steeds, victorious and well-trained.
If that man who has seen Arjuna should think highly of that [gift], I would further give him another golden chariot yoked with six bulls as large as elephants;
likewise, I would further give him a hundred adorned women.

To that man who points out Arjuna, if he should consider it acceptable, I shall give a hundred elephants, a hundred villages, and a hundred chariots— [to him] among those dark-complexioned women with golden neck-ornaments, who are experts in song and instrumental music.
And of the finest gold, there were hundreds upon hundreds of the most excellent horses;
they were well-trained, capable of bearing the yoke, and perfectly subdued through their supernatural power and virtues.
Likewise, there were four hundred milch-cows with horns tipped in gold.
"I would give him cows with their calves who could tell me of Dhanañjaya. If that man who has seen Arjuna should desire that, I would give him another boon: five hundred white horses."
I would give him eight hundred excellent horses, covered with golden trappings and adorned with polished jeweled earrings, all perfectly tamed;
or else, for him, those with variegated limbs and decorated with diverse gems.
I would give him eighteen chariots yoked with noble horses;
I would grant him another boon: four hundred well-trained draft oxen, and four hundred red cows, endowed with beauty and having horns adorned with gold.
I would give milch cows to him who would tell me of Dhanañjaya;
and I would give him a bright, golden chariot, well-adorned and yoked with the finest Kamboja horses, to him who would tell me of Dhanañjaya.
If that man who has seen Arjuna should desire it,
I would grant him another boon: six hundred elephants covered with various golden trappings and adorned with golden garlands.
If a man who has seen Arjuna were to think highly of those horses born in the western regions and trained by elephant trainers,
he would give a hundred of the finest steeds for every single color.
If a man who has seen Arjuna should consider those excellent, well-tamed draft-oxen trained by the best of men as being like that,
I would give him a hundred villages, a hundred elephants, and a hundred horses.
If that man who has seen Arjuna should so desire it,
I would grant him another boon: fourteen prosperous Vaiśya villages,
endowed with wealth and situated near forests and water.

To him who tells me of Dhanañjaya, I shall give fourteen types of food fit for kings, all excellent and free from fear from any quarter; likewise, I shall give a hundred Māgadha slave-girls from Magadha, adorned with golden neck-ornaments and in the prime of their youth.
If that man who has seen Arjuna should think highly of that,
I would grant him another boon, whatever he himself might desire—
sons, wives, pleasure-groves, or whatever other wealth I possess.
And I would further give him whatever he desires in his mind;
and having slain the two Kṛṣṇas together, I would bestow all their wealth upon that person who would tell me where Keśava and Arjuna are.

Uttering these words many times in the battle, Karṇa blew his excellent, sweet-sounding conch shell born of the ocean. Having heard those words of the Sūta’s son, so full of resolve, [the warriors were moved].
O great king, Duryodhana and his followers became filled with joy. Then, from all sides, there arose the sound of kettledrums and mṛdaṅga drums,
along with lion-like roars, the music of instruments, and the trumpeting of elephants.
Then, O King, bull of the Bharatas,
there arose in your army the sound of warriors who were greatly rejoicing;
and while the troops were thus exultant, they beheld that great car-warrior leaping forward.
As the son of Rādhā, the crusher of enemies, was boasting in battle,
the King of Madra laughed and addressed him with these words:
"O Sūtaputra, do not, out of pride, [boast of] this golden chariot yoked with six bulls."
"Give it to the man today, and you shall see Dhanañjaya!
Like Vaiśravaṇa, you are giving away wealth as if out of childishness;
O son of Rādhā, you shall behold Dhanañjaya this very day without even an effort."
Why do you bestow [gifts] falsely, and why do you act so much like a fool? You do not perceive, out of delusion, those faults that arise from giving to an unworthy recipient,
even though you proclaim your wealth to be vast indeed.
"O Sūta, it is possible to sacrifice with many kinds of offerings; therefore, perform those sacrifices.
As for your desire to slay the two Kṛṣṇas out of delusion, that is surely in vain;
for we have never heard of two lions being struck down by a jackal in a conflict."
"You seek that which should not be sought; indeed, you have no friends who do not quickly restrain you as you are falling headlong into the fire.
You do not recognize the work of Time; without a doubt, you have been ripened by Time."

Who that wishes to live would utter such much that is nonsensical and unworthy of being heard? Your intended action is like attempting to cross the ocean with one's arms after tying a stone to one's neck, or like leaping from the summit of a mountain.
Accompanied by all your warriors and well-protected by your battle arrays,
fight with Dhanañjaya if you wish to attain what is beneficial.
I speak to you for the sake of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s welfare, not out of a desire to harm you.
"Have faith in what I have spoken, if you have any desire to live.
Karṇa said:
"Relying on my own prowess, I shall seek out Arjuna in battle."
But you, an enemy with the face of a friend, wish to terrify me. No one today can turn me back from this intention—not even Indra raising his thunderbolt; what indeed could a mortal do?
08,027.030 Saṃjaya said:
At the conclusion of Karna’s speech, Śalya,
the lord of Madra, spoke these words in reply once more, desiring to provoke Karna excessively.
When indeed those sharp-pointed arrows, fletched with heron feathers, impelled by the force of Phalguna and released from the bowstring by his skilled hand, shall pursue you;
Then you will grieve because of Arjuna’s assault,
when Pārtha Savyasācin, taking up his divine bow, causes the army to tremble with his brilliance.
If he were to afflict you with sharpened arrows, then, O son of a Sūta, you would later regret it—
just as a child lying on his mother’s lap [regrets] the moon.
Just as someone might strive to seize [something] from another,
so do you, standing in your chariot, out of delusion strive today to conquer Arjuna.
Just as an expert would dig for a sharp-edged sword well-whetted and buried in the earth, so today you shall dig for your sharpened arrows.
O Arjuna, you who seek battle here,
having embraced a trident with an extremely sharp edge,
you rub all your limbs against it.
O Karṇa, you who desire to fight today with Arjuna, whose deeds are like a blade of extremely sharp edge— you seek to challenge a great,
maned lion that has already achieved its goal.
Just as a foolish, deluded, and impetuous small deer might challenge [a lion], so too is this challenge of Arjuna to the Sūta’s son today.
Do not address the prince,
who possesses great heroism, as "son of a charioteer," just as a jackal, satiated with meat, would not address a lion in the forest.

Do not perish by encountering the son of Pṛthā; O Karṇa, you are challenging Dhanañjaya, the son of Pṛthā, to battle— like a hare challenging a great elephant with tusks as long as plow-poles and temples flowing with rut.
Out of childishness, you poke with a stick a black cobra dwelling in its hole— a highly venomous serpent with its hood fully expanded— when you wish to fight Pārtha;
you roar in defiance, having overstepped a furious maned lion.

O Karna, out of folly you challenge the son of Pāṇḍu, that lion among men, like a jackal; you challenge Dhanañjaya, the son of Pṛthā, like a small bird challenging the swift Vainateya, the best of winged creatures, Suparṇa, at the moment of his swoop.
Without a boat, you wish to cross the formidable ocean, the abode of all waters, surging with waves and teeming with fish, as it tosses about at the rising of the moon;
[and you face] the bull with a neck like a drum, possessing sharp horns and a striking nature.
O child Karna, you challenge Dhananjaya Partha to battle,
just as a young calf, having grown a powerful hump,
might desire a fight with the lord of bulls; even so do you desire a contest with the Diademed One.
Like a frog croaking in response to a great cloud of thunderous sound, you roar against Arjuna, who is like a rain-cloud to the world, bestowing the water of his will.
And just as a dog staying in its own house might bark at a tiger roaming in the forest, so do you challenge him.
In that same way, O Karṇa, you bark at Dhananjaya, that tiger among men.
Even a jackal living in the forest, surrounded by hares, O Karṇa,
considers himself a lion as long as he does not see a lion.
In the same way, O Rādheya, you consider yourself a lion while failing to see Dhananjaya, that tiger among men and subduer of enemies;
you regard yourself as a tiger only so long as you do not behold the two Kṛṣṇas.
Mounted upon a single chariot like the sun and the moon,
as long as you do not hear the roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow in that great battle,
so long, O Karṇa, are you able to say whatever you wish.
Seeing him making the ten directions resound with the noise of chariots and the twang of bows, roaring like a tiger, you will become a jackal;
you are eternally a jackal, while Dhanañjaya is eternally a lion.
"O fool, because of your hatred for heroes, you are always seen as a jackal;
just as a rat is to a cat, or a dog to a tiger, in terms of strength and weakness; just as a jackal is to a lion, or a hare to an elephant."
"Just as falsehood and truth, and likewise poison and nectar,
so too are you and Pārtha renowned for their own deeds.
Sañjaya said:
Thus insulted by Śalya of immeasurable splendor, the son of Rādhā, filled with great rage and feeling the sting of those words, said to Śalya:
"O Śalya, one who possesses virtues knows the virtues of another; one devoid of virtue does not."
But you are eternally devoid of virtues; how can you, being meritless, understand virtues—Arjuna’s great weapons, his wrath, his prowess, his bow, and his arrows?
I, Śalya, know these things, whereas you do not know them in that way.
O Śalya, I know the prowess of that high-souled one, as well as the majesty of Kṛṣṇa and of Ṛṣabha, the lord of the earth.
"O Śalya, knowing full well my own prowess and the prowess of the Pāṇḍava, I nevertheless challenge him to battle; I do not fly like a moth into a fire.
Moreover, O Śalya, here is this arrow, well-feathered and blood-drinking."
Lying alone in its quiver, this well-polished and finely adorned feathered shaft has rested there for many years;
yet it remains a serpent-like weapon, full of virulent poison, fierce, and the slayer of multitudes of men, horses, and elephants.
A lone hero, most fierce, who rends armor and bones— with him, when enraged, I could shatter even the great mountain Meru;
yet I would never discharge that [arrow] at anyone other than Phalguna.
Or rather, from Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī—listen now to my truth regarding this:
O Śalya, with that very arrow, I shall fight Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya in a state of supreme fury; such an act is worthy of me.
The fortune of all the Vāsudevas is established in Kṛṣṇa;
the victory of all the sons of Pāṇḍu is established in Pārtha. Having encountered both of these, who would be able to overcome them?
"O Śalya, behold my well-born self as these two tigers among men, standing together upon their chariot, have both come against me alone—
those two undefeated brothers, born of my father’s sister and her husband."
Like two gems strung upon a thread, you shall see them both struck down by me:
Arjuna with the Gāṇḍīva bow and Kṛṣṇa with the discus, those who bear the banners of Tārkṣya and the ape— those who inspire terror in cowards and bring joy to me, O Śalya.
But you, being of evil nature and a fool, unskilled in great battles, have descended into fear; out of sheer terror, you speak much that is incoherent.
For some reason, O man born in a wretched land, you praise those two.
"Having slain those two in battle, the slayer will surely kill you along with your kinsmen,
O evil-minded one born in a wicked land, O base defiler of the Kṣatriyas!
Having been a friend, why do you now act as an enemy, threatening me with the two Kṛṣṇas?"
Either they two shall slay me today while I stand in battle, or I shall slay them both;
I do not fear the two Kṛṣṇas, knowing my own strength.
Even if there were a thousand Vāsudevas or hundreds of Phalgunas, [I would face them].
"I alone shall slay them; remain silent, you low-born one!
Women, children, the elderly, and people generally engaged in play—those who sing these verses as if they were reciting their studies."
O Śalya, listen to those verses concerning the wicked-souled Madrakas,
as they were formerly recited by Brahmins in the presence of kings exactly as they occurred.
Having heard them with a focused mind, O fool, either endure them or offer a reply.
The Madraka is always a betrayer of friends; whoever hates us, he is a Madraka.
There is no true alliance with a Madraka, that lowest of men, who speaks mean words. The Madraka is eternally evil-minded, eternally untruthful, and crooked.
We have heard that wickedness among the Madrakas extends to the very end.
Father, mother, son, mother-in-law, father-in-law, maternal uncle,
son-in-law, daughter, brother, grandson, and all those various kinsmen— [all these may be slain by them].
Other friends have arrived, as well as male and female servants gathered together;
and women, mingled with men, known and unknown, according to their own desire—
[all this occurs] in the houses of those refined people who always eat parched grain and flour-mash.
Having drunk liquor along with beef, they roar and laugh; whatever unrestrained acts they perform out of desire, speaking amorous words to one another— how can there be any dharma among them?
When the Madrakas— who are notorious for their evil deeds—
have been ruined, one should practice neither enmity nor friendship toward them;
there is no true association with a Madraka, for the Madraka is indeed fickle.
Among the Madrakas, purity is difficult to find, as is the case among the Gandhārakas.
An oblation offered by one who has a king as his officiating priest becomes lost;
just as a Brahmin who performs the sacraments for a Śūdra meets with downfall.
Likewise, those who constantly hate the Brahmins meet with defeat here in this world;
in the same way, a man falls by forming an alliance with the Madrakas.
Indeed, no such alliance as that found among the Madrakas exists here.
"There is no remedy for one bitten by a Madraka; it is like the venom of a scorpio.
By the Atharvan mantra, all peace shall be established.
Thus [is the treatment] for one bitten by a scorpio and for one afflicted by various poisons.
"The wise prepare medicine, and that is indeed seen to be effective.
Knowing this, O learned one, remain silent and listen to these further words:
women who are deluded by wine cast off their garments and dance."

In the state of *mithuna*, they are unrestrained and act according to their own desires; how can a Madraka, who is the son of such women— who stand while urinating just like a female camel in the desert— be fit to speak of dharma?
Of those shameless women who have cast off their modesty, wandering here and there— you, their son, indeed wish to speak of dharma in this world!
When being asked for a *suvīraka* (a small vessel), the Madraka woman scratches her buttocks.
Unwilling to give it, she spoke these harsh words:
"Let no one beg my beloved *suvīraka* from me; I would give away my son at any time, but I would not give away the *suvīraka*."
We have heard that, for the most part, the women of the Madras are shameless, large-bodied, and wrapped in blankets; they are gluttonous, devoid of purity, and having urinated,
they drag their buttocks along the ground without performing any cleansing.
"Even by touching them with words and not with mud, they indeed remain perpetually impure.
Such things— and many more could be said by me or others—
regarding the evil paths that must be described, starting from the tips of the hair down to the tips of the nails."
"How indeed could the Madrakas and the Sindhu-Sauviras know the dharma here,
they who are Mlecchas born in sinful lands and unacquainted with the principles of dharma? We have heard that this is the foremost duty of a Kshatriya."
That I should lie slain in battle, honored by the virtuous— were I to be released from that [duty] in the midst of weapons, it would not be my primary wish for death while desiring heaven.
"I am the dear friend of the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
for his sake indeed are my life-breaths and whatever wealth I possess.
It is evident, O man born in a sinful land, that you too have been won over by the Pāṇḍavas."
For you treat us all as if we were enemies; indeed,
O knower of dharma, it is not possible for even hundreds of people like you to turn me away from battle, just as it is impossible for atheists to turn a righteous man from his path.
"Like a deer distressed by the heat, you may lament at will and wither away;
yet I cannot be intimidated, for I am established in the conduct of a Kṣatriya,
among those lions among men who cast off their bodies and never retreat in battle."

"Remember that destination which was previously described to me by my elder brother Rāma. Know that I have adopted the supreme conduct of Purūravas, being intent on protecting my own people and also on the destruction of my enemies."
"O Madraka, I do not perceive anyone in the three worlds who could turn me back from this intention; such is my resolve. Knowing this, remain silent; why do you speak so much out of fear?"
"O lowest of Madrakas, having killed you, I shall not hand you over to the flesh-eaters;
O Śalya, it is out of regard for both my friendship and the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
and because of your endurance of insults— that these three things cause you to live."
"O King of Madra, if you speak such words again,
I shall strike down your head with my mace, which is like a thunderbolt.
O man born of a wretched land, those who hear this here today shall be its witnesses."
"Either the two Kṛṣṇas will slay Karṇa, or Karṇa will slay them both.
Having spoken thus, O lord of the people, the son of Rādhā once more addressed the King of Madra without any agitation: "Proceed! Proceed!"
Saṃjaya said:
O noble one, having heard the words of the son of Adhiratha who rejoiced in battle,
Śalya spoke again to Karṇa, citing an illustrative example.
I was born into a lineage of performers of sacrifices, kings who never retreat in battle,
consecrated monarchs who were themselves devoted to righteousness;
yet you are not like me, or perhaps you are just as intoxicated by liquor as I am.
Thus, out of friendship, I treat you who are acting with negligence;
O Karna, listen to this parable of the crow as it is being told by me.
Having heard it, do as you wish, you wretch who brings disgrace upon your lineage.
"O mighty-armed Karṇa, I do not recall having committed even the slightest offense against you for which you wish to kill me, who am innocent. Nevertheless,
since I perceive what is for your benefit, I must certainly speak."
Especially by one standing upon a chariot who desires the welfare of the king,
[he must know] the even and the uneven terrain, as well as the strength and weakness of the chariot-warrior,
along with the constant fatigue and exhaustion of the horses together with the charioteer.
The thorough knowledge of weapons, the cries of beasts and birds, what constitutes a burden and what an excessive burden, the treatment of arrow-wounds,
the application of missiles, combat, and likewise the interpretation of omens.
"All this must be known by me as the master of this chariot;
therefore, O Karṇa, I shall relate this illustrative story to you once more.
It is said that there was a Vaiśya on the shore of the ocean who possessed abundant wealth and grain."
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, patient, established in his own duty, and pure; having many sons, beloved by his children, and compassionate toward all beings—
he dwelt without fear in the kingdom of that king who was preeminent in righteousness.
Of his many sons— those young and illustrious princes— a crow became the one who fed on their leftovers. Indeed,
the young sons of the Vaiśya always gave him food.
Meat, rice, curd, milk, milk-rice, honey, and clarified butter—
having been fed on these leftovers by the young sons of Vaiśyas,
that crow became arrogant and began to despise birds both his equals and his superiors.

Then, once upon a time, some swans— birds marked with circles on their wings, equal in speed to Garuḍa, and joyful in heart— flew toward the edge of the ocean. Seeing those swans, the young boys then spoke to a crow:
"O bird, you alone are indeed superior to these winged creatures;
look at them, falling together while remaining in the sky. Why is it that you, who are capable of overcoming them, have not brought him back?"
Being thus deceived by those small-minded creatures, that bird,
out of both folly and pride, believed their words to be true.
Desiring to know which among them possessed the greatest power, he flew toward them.
Proud of his leftovers, a crow challenged that best of birds among those swans capable of long-distance flight, thinking himself superior; the evil-minded one called out to the bird, "Let us fly!"
Hearing those words of the crow as he spoke so much, the swans who were assembled there laughed; and those birds, the best of flyers, the cakravākas, addressed these words to the crow:
08,028.019a Having heard that, the swans who had gathered there laughed, 08,028.019c at the crow speaking so much, they who are the strongest among birds.
08,028.019e And these words the wheel-footed birds spoke to the crow:
"We are swans who roam this earth, dwelling in Lake Mānasa;
among birds, we are always honored for our long-distance flight.
How then [could you capture] a powerful swan, whose body is like a thunderbolt and who flies great distances?"
"Having become a crow, you challenge us to a flight, O evil-minded one!
How can you, a crow, speak of such a flight along with us? Thus did the fool, having repeatedly reviled the words of the swans,"
The boastful crow, due to his inherent lack of dignity, uttered this reply:
"I shall fly a hundred and one descents, without a doubt;
each one for a hundred *yojanas*, wonderful and diverse."
Flying upward, flying downward, flying forward, and simply flying;
flying out, flying together, moving crosswise, and moving beyond;
flying apart, flying around, flying away, and flying well.
The *atiḍīna*, the *mahāḍīna*, the *niḍīna*, and the *pariḍīnaka*;
the *saṃpāta*, the *samudīṣa*, and that which is distinct from them; the *avaḍīna*, the *praḍīna*, the *saṃḍīna*, and the *ḍīnaḍīnaka*.
