I shall perform today, while you look on, the maneuvers of diving, soaring, and flying, as well as flying back and forth and various downward swoops; then you shall witness my power.
"Among these, I shall fly through the sky with whichever one you choose.
O swans, designate according to the rule with which one I am to fly.
Having reached a firm decision, you must indeed fly along with me."
"Indeed, by these very steps, birds fly through the supportless sky.
When this was said by the crow, one bird—a swan—laughed and spoke these words to that crow; listen to them from me.
"O crow, you have surely flown one hundred and one different ways of flight;
yet, O crow, I have flown only that single way which all birds know, and I know no other whatsoever."
"Fly away, Red-Eye, by whatever path you deem best! Then the crows who had gathered there laughed aloud,
saying, "How can a single flight of a swan defeat a hundred flights?"
With a single flight alone, he will overcome a hundred;
like a crow, I shall conquer a hundred flights of swans with but one flight.
"O swan, you shall fly here with but a single flight. Then,
the powerful crow of swift prowess challenged the swan's flight,
and so those two, the swan and the crow, flew forth in rivalry.
The one-legged Cakrāṅga and the crow,
both swift and vying with each other, quickly took to the sky together;
yet the crow was the first to begin his rapid flight.
Then the crow, displaying his swiftness through restlessness to the swan,
repeatedly overtook him with great speed and force, only to fall back again and again; and calling out his name from the right, he struck him with his beak.
And crying out repeatedly, "Rorūyan! he indeed called out to him again and again.
Then the wheel-marked bird flew away, and then the crow flew away, wishing to cause amazement by his flights and proclaiming his own deed.
Then, seeing the various beautiful and other [ordinary] flights of the crow,
the other crows were delighted and cried out with those sounds;
they mocked the swans and spoke unpleasant words to them.
Leaping up again and again, they cried out "A moment! A moment!
They fell from the tops of trees and from the ground, and leaped up once more, uttering various cries while then proclaiming their victory.
But the swan began to advance with great gentleness;
for a moment, O noble one, he seemed to fall behind the crow. Disregarding the speed of the swans, he spoke these words:
"That swan who has flown away is indeed being abandoned. Then that swan,
the best of birds, having heard those words, flew toward the western direction.
Having plunged into and agitated the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, the swan moved with great speed higher and higher above it—
an ocean crowded with many creatures and terrifying to behold with its waves.
Then, O son of Rādhā, in a short time the crow fell behind due to his speed;
thereafter, being utterly exhausted, he somehow managed to follow the swan.
Then fear entered the crow, who was at that moment bewildered.
Seeing the islands and trees falling away as he was overcome by exhaustion,
and looking back again and again at that agitated crow,
he thought, "Where indeed shall I alight, weary as I am, upon this ocean of water?"
Indeed, the ocean is insurmountable, a dwelling place for multitudes of living beings;
resplendent with hundreds of great creatures, it excels even the sky.
For in its profundity, O lowest of your lineage, there is no difference between the ocean and the sky.
"O Karṇa, those who dwell in the ocean are indeed difficult to conquer with water that is as vast as the sky;
how much more so, O Karṇa, for a crow in the midst of such a vast expanse of water? Then the swan, having bypassed it in a moment, here and there—"
Gazing at that crow, he was unable to move away;
and having passed him by, the swan looked back at the crow,
thinking, "How far this crow must go before he falls upon me."
Then the crow, being utterly exhausted, approached the swan; seeing him gradually failing, completely fatigued, and unconscious,
the swan then laughed at the crow of slow gait.
Seeing him thus sinking, the swan, desiring to rescue him who was drowning and remembering the vow of the virtuous, spoke these words:
"You have repeatedly described many modes of flight."
"You fly about without uttering a word, yet you do not speak of our secret.
What indeed is this 'flying' (patana), O crow, that you are flying now? You touch the water again and again with both your wings and your beak."

"Tell me, crow, on which of those falls do you rest? Come, come quickly, O crow! Here I am waiting for you. Thus he spoke, as the bird, distressed, touched the waters of the ocean with his wings and his beak.
"O evil-minded one, I have been seen by the swan! Then,
not seeing the far shore of the water and falling down overcome with exhaustion,
the crow, distressed by the force of his descent, said this to the swan:

"We are crows; how indeed could we travel upon the path of a crow? O swan, I seek refuge in you with my very life; take me to the other shore. Distressed, he touched the great ocean with both his wings and his beak.
Exhausted and utterly weary, the crow suddenly fell down into the waters of the ocean. Seeing him fallen there with a dejected mind,
on the verge of death, the swan spoke these words to the crow:
The Haṃsa said:
"O crow, as for the one hundred and one ways of flight that you have spoken of,
praising yourself, O crow, you have indeed uttered them."
"You, who were flying with a hundred and one beats of your wings, surpassing me—
how is it that you have fallen into the great ocean so exhausted? Then the crow, sinking down, replied with these words:
Then, beholding the swan above and seeking to appease him, the crow said:
"Various kinds [of falsehoods] were previously uttered by me here; those were untrue, but today they are yours. The crow spoke thus.
O swan, arrogant from eating leftovers, I considered myself equal to Suparṇa; having held in contempt many other crows and birds, O swan,
I now seek refuge in you with my very life— please carry me to another island.

Nourished by leftover food, I, a wicked crow, became arrogant and haughty; through my own lack of discernment, I came to think of myself as a *suparṇa*. Now, having sought refuge in you, may I reach the edge of the water.
O swan, now rescue me who am exhausted by calamities!
O swan, if I should reach my own country again in safety, I shall never again hold anyone in contempt; therefore, rescue me from this distress!
"Even if I were to return alive to my own home,
I would never again cast down even a lowly creature wandering in the sky.
To him who spoke thus, wretched, lamenting, and senseless—
Seeing the crow crying out "Caw! Caw! as he was sinking into the great ocean, the swan, overcome with compassion, felt pity for that wicked-souled one;
thus approaching the crow, who was drenched in water and in a most wretched state, the swan acted.
Lifting the trembling bird with his feet, he slowly placed him upon his back; having mounted that crow upon his back, O Karṇa, the swan,
remaining unperturbed, then brought him back again, O Karṇa, while the crow was deprived of his senses.
He returned again to the island from which they had flown in rivalry;
releasing him, he said, "Do not act thus again.
Having thus restrained that sky-traveler and comforted him once more, he departed.
Like a swift-moving swan or the mind, he went to his desired destination.
Thus, Karna, that crow nourished on leftovers, having been defeated by the swan,
abandoned his great strength and prowess and resorted to patience.

Just as a crow [subsists] on leftovers in the house of a Vaiśya, so too have you been sustained by the leftovers of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; of this there is no doubt. O Karṇa, you hold yourself in contempt for all those who are your equals or even your superiors.
Protected as you were by Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, Kṛpa, Bhīṣma, and other Kauravas,
why did you not slay Pārtha while he was alone in the city of Virāṭa? There,
when you were all together and united, you were utterly defeated by Kirīṭin.
Like jackals before a lion, where was your prowess then?
Having seen your brother slain and yourself defeated by Savyasācin,
you were the first to flee while the Kuru heroes looked on.
Likewise, O Karṇa, when you were pursued by the Gandharvas in the Dvaitavana forest,
you first fled, abandoning all the Kurus;
yet after you had slain and conquered the Gandharvas led by Citrasena in battle—
O Karna, Pārtha liberated Duryodhana along with his wife;
furthermore, O Karna, the ancient power of both Pārtha and Keśava was recounted by Rāma in the assembly before the gathering of kings.
And you constantly heard those words of Droṇa and Bhīṣma as they declared that the two Kṛṣṇas were unslayable in the presence of the lords of the earth.
How much more shall I say there concerning Dhananjaya by means of this or that?
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is superior to all beings,
so shall you see him today standing upon his chariot in battle—
Vasudeva’s son and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya.
Just as a crow, relying on its intelligence, took refuge with the wheel-marked goose,
so too should you rely upon the Vārṣṇeya and the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya.
When you face Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, who are both valiant in battle—
O Karṇa, when you behold Arjuna on his single chariot, you will no longer speak thus;
for when Pārtha destroys your pride with hundreds of arrows,
you will then perceive the difference between yourself and Arjuna.
"O Vārṣṇeya, you must quickly [confront] the Pāṇḍava Dhanañjaya—
those two bulls among men renowned among gods, asuras, and humans.
Do not, out of folly, despise them, like a firefly [disregarding] the sun."
Just as the sun and the moon, so too are Arjuna and Keśava renowned for their brilliance; you, however, are like a firefly among men.
Knowing this, do not hold in contempt the son of a charioteer, Acyuta, and Arjuna.
"Those two are Nṛsiṃhas, while you are a mere man-tiger; therefore, O boaster, sit silent!
Sañjaya said:
At that very moment, the son of Adhiratha [Kṛṣṇa] spoke thus to the lord of the Madras.
Hearing these unpleasant words, he was displeased and said to Śalya: "This is already known to me—
what kind of men Arjuna and Vāsudeva are."
I know today, exactly as it is, the strength of Arjuna, the son of Śūra, as he drives his chariot, and the great weapons of the Pāṇḍava.
O Śalya, although that [encounter] was out of my sight,
those two invincible ones, the best among wielders of weapons,
I shall fight against the two Kṛṣṇas, free from fear.
O Śalya, in the past, on the magnificent Mahendra mountain,
you approached the ascetic Rāma and said,
"Accept me today as your disciple, for I seek the divine weapons."
Then, under the guise of a brahmin, I spoke; though not a true brahmin, I dwelt there as one, having lied out of greed for the Brahma-weapon.
That supreme great weapon, accompanied by its mantras, had been prepared for me by the son of Jamadagni;
when that weapon was known to me, [it was ready].
Then that great ṛṣi, the brahmin, said to me:
"When you have fallen into calamity and go forth to battle, you must employ this weapon; accomplish your purpose."
The curse from Rāma, and especially that from the best of Brahmins, torments me exceedingly today. Indeed,
I lived there under the guise of a Brahmin.
O Śalya, in former times when Rāma desired to create a divine weapon,
even there my effort was obstructed by the King of the Gods,
who acted for the benefit of Phalguna.
Having approached Mamoru,
he pierced him with a split; having entered the body of a worm, the worm, having approached Mamoru, pierced him.
While my guru was asleep there with his head resting [on my lap],
a great torrent of thick blood issued from my body due to the piercing of my thigh.
Out of fear of my preceptor, I did not move;
and that brahmin, having perceived me,
beheld me endowed with such fortitude.
"O Brahmin, you are not a brahmin; who are you? Speak the truth!
To him, O Śalya, I then related my identity exactly as it was, saying, "I am a *sūta*."
When questioned, I said to that great seer,
"I am a charioteer," and he cursed me.
Having heard me, that man of great asceticism then [pronounced his curse].
With his mind overcome by rage, he swore an oath:
"O charioteer, this weapon was obtained by you through deceit;
it shall not manifest for you at the time of action."
Except for the time of your own death,
for the Brahman is not established in one who is no Brahmin; therefore,
this weapon is now more than sufficient.
In this tumultuous and terrible battle, O dear one,
he who has appeared among the Bharatas, O Śalya,
is a most fearsome destroyer who drags everything away.
I consider him a powerful crusher who has indeed scorched the foremost heroes among the Kṣatriyas; Śalya is the most excellent of fierce bowmen.
I shall lead Dhananjaya, the son of Pandu— that swift and terrible warrior of irresistible valor, whose promise is true— to the jaws of death in battle.
For today I have obtained that weapon with which I shall strike down the hosts of enemies in battle—
the powerful, valiant, and skilled-in-weapons foe.
I shall slay in battle that Dhananjaya, who wields a formidable bow, possesses immeasurable energy, is cruel, heroic, fierce, a subduer of enemies, and a conqueror of wealth.
Surely this is the time of the Kurus' end,
a great terror that flows with floods of blood;
the destruction of the bulls among the Kṣatriyas is certain.
A great terror has arisen today;
indeed, no weapon occurs to my mind by which I might bring the hosts of enemies to destruction.
Therefore, O King of Madra, attack him—
he who possesses a celestial bow and great arrows,
and in whom there exist divine weapons.
Drive the chariot there quickly today;
let them hear this wonderful tale being told as long as there shall be men upon the earth.
The peerless hero Karṇa slew the two Kṛṣṇas,
yet the two Kṛṣṇas likewise slew Karṇa;
[so too did] the impetuous and immeasurable Lord of Waters.
He who would submerge the multitudes of living beings into the great ocean—
only the shoreline can restrain that immeasurable force.
I shall fight in battle against the son of Kuntī, who releases volleys of unfailing arrows— feathered shafts that pierce the vital organs and slay heroes.
Today, he is the best among those who draw the bowstring in this world—
a great weapon of exceeding strength,
like the ocean itself, difficult to attain, and fierce.
Like the shore withstanding the ocean, I shall withstand Pārtha with my arrows as he submerges the kings with his showers of shafts;
today in battle there is no other equal to him.
I consider that man who, taking up his bow, might indeed conquer the gods and asuras in battle; with him,
behold today my most terrible combat.
The son of Pāṇḍu is overweening in pride and eager for battle;
he will come against me with superhuman great weapons. Having struck down his weapons with my own weapons in combat, [I shall prevail].
With my finest arrows, I shall strike down Pārtha,
who blazes with glory like the sun itself, scorching all and endowed with its full rays.
Resembling the thousand-rayed sun,
blazing and fiercely scorching all directions,
he was like a massive cloud dispelling the darkness.
I shall shroud Dhanañjaya with my arrows—
him who is like the blazing Vaiśvānara fire with its crest of smoke, radiant and consuming this world.
Having become a cloud, I shall extinguish Pārtha in battle with showers of arrows, just as one extinguishes fire;
[I shall quell] that unassailable and immeasurable venomous serpent.
With my broad-headed arrows, I shall quell the son of Kuntī— that great adversary who possesses sharp fangs, the brilliance of fire, and is ablaze with wrath.
I shall endure in battle that fierce one, the powerful striker,
the shatterer Mātariśvan,
like the immovable Himavat mountain.
Dhanañjaya, enraged and intolerant,
skilled in the paths of chariots, unattached,
a leader ever-preeminent among heroes in battles;
In this world, I shall withstand Dhananjaya, the best among all wielders of the bow in combat,
for whom there is no other equal today in battle.
He who could withstand this entire earth when it took up a bow of medium human size—
I, knowing him to be such, shall fight with him.
Who, indeed, desiring to preserve their life, would fight with him who, as Savyasācin, conquered all beings including the gods at the Khāṇḍava forest?
No other human besides me desires to fight him— he who is proud, skilled in weapons, possessed of manual dexterity,
an expert in divine missiles, mounted on white horses, and a destroyer of foes.
"O Śalya, today I shall take the head from the body of that Atiratha with my sharp arrows; indeed,
I will fight this Dhananjaya."
Placing death before him or victory in battle,
for no other mortal indeed could fight on a single chariot against the son of Pāṇḍu, who is like Indra himself.
"I would gladly proclaim the prowess of that Pāṇḍava in the assembly of Kṣatriyas.
Why do you, a fool of deluded mind, speak thus?"
"You spoke to me of Arjuna’s manliness—
he who is unpleasant, harsh, and cruel, a base reviler who lacks patience toward one who is patient."
I could slay hundreds of such as you,
yet I forgive you out of patience due to the exigencies of time;
you have spoken unpleasant words for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas.
O evil-doer, attacking me like a fool—
you who move crookedly toward one who is upright— you are slain; for friendship is formed by walking seven steps together.
But this time was exceedingly terrible, consisting of death itself,
since Duryodhana approached for battle; desiring the accomplishment of his own purpose, he [approached].
I shall go to that place where there is no certainty;
nevertheless, I will fight in battle against the Pāṇḍavas and Vāsudeva, for such is the duty of one like me.
An ordinary man would never indeed venture against those two, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya;
for a "friend" (*mitra*) is so called from the roots *mīd*, *nand*, or *prī*.
That which protects, O giver of honor, that which gladdens, that which causes one to perish, and that which bestows— whatever such a friend may be,
all of that exists in Duryodhana for me.
A friend is gladdened or pleased by friends; one who bestows honor protects and rejoices;
and he speaks that which is preceded by the learned.
And all of that is present in my Duryodhana.
[The word] *śatru* is derived from the root *śad*, or *śās*, or *śāy*,
or from *śṛ* or even *śvi* in the sense of destruction (*sarga*).
And from the root *sūd* with various prefixes;
for the most part, all that belongs to me is in you.
When the enemy is pacified, the lord of the Kauravas shall rule.
O Śalya, O lord of men, you likely know the power of my entire army, which is enriched with every prosperity,
as I fight for the sake of Duryodhana.
Whether for the sake of fame, for the sake of wealth, or for some other purpose,
it was therefore for the sake of Duryodhana and for your own displeasure that I [acted] against the Pāṇḍavas and Vāsudeva.
Whether for the sake of fame, for my own sake, or even for the sake of the Lord,
therefore I shall fight with all effort against the Pāṇḍavas and Vāsudeva; behold that deed of mine today.
Go; having united with the Pāṇḍava,
I shall lead Dhanañjaya to the world of death,
and through her, I too shall go to the world of death.
Since I have received this multitude of weapons from Bhārgava, I shall discharge these weapons upon the host of enemies;
for I am joined with Śalya and the other Pāṇḍavas.
If I should somehow be released while still alive,
may I forever be of an invincible form, O Death; thus,
I shall clearly be liberated from that battle.
Behold today my supreme weapons—
those of Brahmā, the divine, and those of humans;
I shall employ them against him of fierce valor.
Like one intoxicated against an intoxicated elephant, the best of steeds,
I shall mentally discharge that invincible Brahmā weapon,
peerless for victory, against the son of Pṛthā.
Even by him I would not be released in battle,
unless my wheel should sink today into uneven ground—
before Vaivasvata with staff in hand, or even Varuṇa with his noose.
"O Śalya, know this: we do not fear even the Lord of Wealth with his mace, nor Vāsava with his thunderbolt, nor any other assailant whatsoever; thus, being fearless, I have no fear."
Therefore, O Pārtha, I have no fear of you, nor indeed of Janārdana;
for today I shall have a battle with them both in this conflict.
Once, O King, while I was wandering for the sake of weapons, I encountered Vijaya.
"Indeed, because of his ignorance, that Brahmin said to me: 'Though you discharge arrows of terrible and fearsome form,
your wheel shall fall into a chasm when you are fighting in battle and have encountered danger on a narrow path.'"
Therefore, I am greatly afraid of the utterance of a Brahmin;
for these men, whose king is Soma, are masters over happiness and suffering.
I gave him a thousand cows and six hundred bulls.
O Śalya, lord of the Madrakas, I could find no favor with the Brahmins. Once, O King, while I was unaware, I discharged a terrible and fearsome arrow at the sacrificial cow of a Brahmin.
"O Śalya, while wandering in a lonely place, I, being heedless, struck with an arrow the calf of this sacrificial cow belonging to a Brahmin— a treasury of ascetic power—
because you, in your negligence, had killed her offspring."
"O child, because you have killed the calf of this sacrificial cow,
therefore, O son of Rādhā, you too shall receive a great arrow of words; your wheel shall fall into a pit."
While you were fighting with the enemy, when the time had come for a single-file passage— a moment shared by all who face death— you vied with him in battle, for whose sake you strove incessantly.
"O charioteer, you will certainly meet your death in battle right there. I then propitiated that Brahmin of rigid vows with a gift of one thousand cows, wealth, and six hundred oxen.
At that time, I offered to the Brahmin whatever he desired as a gift:
a hundred female slaves with golden neck-ornaments, a hundred chariots drawn by mules,
and a thousand well-adorned maidens with golden neck-ornaments.
To extract the dart,
he arrived with seven hundred elephants with tusks like plow-poles, hundreds of male and female slaves,
and sixty-year-old elephants.
When I gave two thousand horses to that foremost of the twice-born, he did not show me favor;
nor did he accept fourteen thousand black cows with white calves.
Because I did not obtain favor from that best of the twice-born despite my efforts,
I offered him my prosperous home with all its objects of desire and whatever wealth I possessed, honoring him; yet he did not wish for it.
"Whatever wealth I possess, I place it at your disposal"—
when I made this request, O Śalya, the brahmin restrained me,
his eyes blazing with anger as if burning me with his gaze.
Then, as I was earnestly entreating him for forgiveness after my transgression, he said to me:
"O Sūta, that which has been uttered by me is so and not otherwise.
A false word would destroy living beings; therefore, one incurs sin."
"Therefore, for the sake of protecting dharma, I cannot bring myself to speak a falsehood. Do not destroy the path of Brahman; you have already performed the expiation.
O son of a Sūta, even the whole world would not do what has been spoken here."
"O son of a charioteer, go without delay!"— thus that best of the twice-born spoke to me repeatedly in anger when I had spoken with wrath.
For these kings, whose sovereign is Soma, are the masters of happiness and misery.
I do not fear Bībhatsu, nor Śalya, nor Madhusūdana;
I fear only that curse, and by that truth I swear to you.
Today, this battle with those two together has arrived.

"O Śalya, in this battle, my life today has come to a state of uncertainty. Even Śakra, the king of the immortals, having approached those two in combat, would fall into the greatest peril; what do you think of this?"

"No one in this world would ever make my word false; therefore, fulfill it. This which I have spoken to you was said out of friendship, even though I am insulted. I know that you are reviling me; be silent and hear the reply.
08,030.001 Saṃjaya said: 08,030.001a Then once more, O great king, the son of Rādhā, having warded off further words, addressed the King of Madra, the subduer of enemies.
"O Śalya, as for what you have spoken to me for the sake of illustration:
I cannot be intimidated by your words in battle,
even if all the gods, together with Vāsava, were to fight against me."
Even from any other immeasurable assassin, I would have no fear; how much less so from Pārtha together with Keśava? I cannot be intimidated by mere words in any way whatsoever.
Know someone else who can be intimidated by you in battle; for base men, burning with the sharp fire of another's glory,
are unable to reach that same station and therefore resort to slander.
"The strength of a base man is merely this harshness that you speak to me; O evil-minded one, being unable to attain our virtues, you boast excessively.
For Karna was not born here, O noble sir, for the sake of fear."
I was born for the sake of valor and likewise for the sake of glory;
indeed, O Śalya, it is because of these three reasons— friendship, affection, and the bond of a friend— that you live at present.

A very great task has been undertaken by King Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, and that was directed against me, O Śalya; it is for that reason that you live for a moment longer. Furthermore, an agreement was made previously: "Your unpleasantness must be forgiven."
"O Madraka, my agreement must be honored; it is because of that you still live.
Without a thousand Śalyas, I could have conquered the enemies; but because treachery toward a friend is the most heinous sin, you live for now."
Śalya said:
"Are these not merely idle boasts, Karṇa, which you utter regarding your enemies?
Saṃjaya said:
"Without a thousand Karṇas, it is impossible to defeat the enemies in battle.
To him who was speaking thus harshly, Karṇa then addressed the ruler of Madra,
who was unpleasant to behold, with words twice as harsh.
But listen to this from me with one-pointed attention, O lord of the Madras,
as it was heard by me while being recounted in the presence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
concerning various wonderful lands and kings of former times.
Brāhmaṇas were conversing as they sat in attendance upon Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
There, a certain elderly and eminent twice-born man, recounting stories of the past,
spoke these words while censuring the Bāhlīka country and the Madras.
Those who are excluded by the Himavat and set aside by the Gaṅgā,
as well as those situated between the Sarasvatī, the Yamunā, Kurukṣetra,
and the five rivers of which the Sindhu is the sixth.
One should avoid those Bāhlīkas who are impure and outside the bounds of dharma.
There is the banyan tree named Govardhana and the square named Subhāṇḍa;
I remember this gateway to the royal palace from my childhood.
"Because of an exceedingly urgent matter, I lived among the Bāhlīkas;
through that residence, their customs became known to me. There is a city named Śākala and a river named Āpagā."
The Bāhlīkas known as the Jartikas have a most censurable conduct:
having drunk parched grain with molasses liquor and *āsava*, they eat beef along with garlic,
and they consume cakes, meat, and *vāṭya* while being devoid of virtuous character.
Intoxicated by wine and stripped of their garments, they laugh, sing, and dance upon the ramparts of the city houses and outside, adorned with garlands and ointments,
to various drunken songs that resemble the braying of donkeys and camels.
Unrestrained in sexual intercourse and acting according to their every desire, they speak to one another, shouting out while intoxicated with passion:
"Alas, he is slain! Alas, he is slain! He has been killed by his own master!"

At the sacred festivals, those dull-witted and unrestrained men would shout and dance about. While residing in Kurujāṅgala among those arrogant people, a certain man among the leaders of the Bāhlīkas, with a rather cheerless mind, sang this song: 08,030.018c Shouting and dancing, the dull-witted and unrestrained ones [behave] at the sacred festivals.
08,030.019a While dwelling in Kurujāṅgala among those indeed who were conceited, a certain one among the chiefs of the Bāhlīkas sang with a not-very-joyful heart.
Surely that noble Gaurī, clad in fine woolen blankets,
lies there remembering me as I dwell among the Kurus in Bāhlīka;
she who crossed the river Śatadru and that lovely Irāvatī.

Having gone to my own country, I shall see auspicious women with large conch-like breasts, their outer corners of the eyes brightened by red arsenic, fair-complexioned, adorned with collyrium from Mount Trikakuda,
clad solely in deerskins, leaping about, and lovely to behold.

To the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, ānakas, conchs, and mardalas, and amidst the cries of asses, camels, and mules, we shall proceed happily and intoxicated through the forests of śamī, pīlu, and karīra trees along pleasant paths.
Eating cakes and balls of parched grain mixed with curds,
having become powerful on the roads, when shall we, while making offerings at threshing floors, strike down many more upon the path that has not yet been trodden?
"Indeed, what man of discernment would dwell even for a moment among such base Vātyas and wicked-souled Bāhlīkas?
Thus were the Bāhlīkas, who wander in vain, described by the Brāhmaṇa."
"You are the one who takes a sixth share of both their merit and their sin.
Having said this, the virtuous brahmin spoke further:
"Listen to what is being said regarding the undisciplined Bāhlīkas."
There, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a rākṣasī used to sing in the prosperous city of Śākala, having beaten a drum at night:
"When will the Ghoṣikā songs be sung again in Śākala?"
Satiated with beef and having drunk the great liquor made from molasses,
they— well-adorned women of the Gaurī class, large in stature—
took mouthfuls of onions and ate many sheep.
"The birth of those who do not eat the meat of boar, fowl, cow, donkey, camel, or sheep is useless"—
so sing the intoxicated followers of Śākala, who are drunk on *śīdhu* liquor.
How can there be righteous conduct among those who leap about together with the young and the old,
where Kṛṣṇa— the Lord of the World, God of gods, and Janārdana— is forgotten by fierce men? How can there be dharma for them?
"Know this, O Śalya; indeed, I shall speak further to you that which another Brāhmaṇa also spoke to us in the assembly of the Kurus:
'There flow these five rivers and there are forests of Pilu trees.'"
The Śatadru, the Vipāśā, and thirdly the Irāvatī, the Candrabhāgā, the Vitastā, and the Sindhu as the sixth—these rivers flow beyond [the boundary];
those regions are called Āraṭṭas, where dharma has perished; one should not go there.

The gods, the ancestors, and likewise the brahmins do not accept [the offerings] of those who are outcasts (vrātyas), those born of slaves (dāsamīyas), the Videhas, or those who do not perform sacrifices—
provided that those brahmins are present at the rites of the śrāddha and the libations (tarpaṇa).
"All that has become fruitless," so says the Veda; "of those Bāhlikas whose dharma has perished," so says the Veda—
thus was it declared by a learned Brāhmaṇa in an assembly of the virtuous.
The pitiless Bāhlīkas eat from wooden bowls and earthenware vessels that are smeared with barley-meal porridge and licked by dogs;
they consume the milk of sheep, camels, and even donkeys.

The Bāhlīkas eat and drink those very transformations; these wretched men, who cause the confusion of offspring, consume all kinds of food and milk. The Bāhlīkas known as Āraṭṭas are to be avoided by the wise.
Furthermore, O Śalya, understand this; indeed, I shall speak to you further that which another learned Brāhmaṇa spoke in the assembly of the Kurus:
"Having drunk milk at Yugandhara and having stayed at Acyutasthala..."
In the same way, having bathed at Bhūtilaya, how could one not go to heaven?
Five rivers flow from that mountain;
where there are those called Āraṭṭas and Bāhlīkas, a noble man should not dwell among them for even two days.
Furthermore, Bahiṣ and Hlīka were two Piśācas born from the Vipāśā;
their offspring are the Bāhlīkas. This creation is not from Prajāpati.
How then shall those of low birth understand the various forms of dharma?
"One should avoid the Kāraskaras, Mahiṣakas, Kaliṅgas, Kīkaṭas, Aṭavis, Karkoṭakas, Vīrakas, and those of wicked conduct.
Thus spoke a certain Rākṣasī to one who was visiting sacred fords.
For one night she stayed in the house of Śamī, girdled with a great mortar.
Those regions are named Āraṭṭas, and those people are named Bāhlīkas;
they are outcasts among Brāhmaṇas, existing from the very time of Prajāpati.
The Vedas, their objects of knowledge, the sacrifices, and the act of sacrificing—none of these belong to them.
The gods do not consume the food of the *vrātyas*, those born of the tenth [intercourse].
The Prasthalas, Madras, Gāndhāras, Āraṭṭas, and by name the Khaśas—[these are excluded].
The Vasātis, Sindhus, and Sauviras are generally despised;
O Śalya, understand this well. Come now, I shall speak further to you;
listen with a one-pointed mind as I explain it correctly.
A brahmin, a guest from another city, went to the house of an artisan.
Observing the conduct there, he was pleased and said to the artisan:
"I have dwelt for a long time alone upon a peak of the Himalayas."

I have seen many countries filled with various laws, yet these subjects do not conflict with one another in their adherence to any particular law; for all of them declare that dharma is exactly as it has been described by those who have mastered the Vedas.
O Great King, while wandering constantly through various lands filled with diverse dharmas, I observed this among the Bāhlikas:
having been a Brāhmaṇa right there, one then becomes a Kṣatriya.
The Vaiśya and the Śūdra become Bāhlikas, and from them the barber arises;
having been a barber, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa again;
and having become a twice-born man, he is born once more as a slave in that very same place.

"In a family there is but one learned Brahmin, while the others act according to their own whims; such is the case with the Gandhāras, the Madrakas, and the Bāhlīkas, who are for the most part devoid of sense. This is what I heard there, which causes the confusion of dharma."
Having wandered over the entire earth, I found this reversal of conduct among the Bāhlikas. Know this well, O Śalya; indeed, I shall tell you more.
Even another person has spoken words that are highly censurable regarding the Bāhlikas.
In former times, it is said, a certain virtuous woman from Āraṭṭa was abducted by bandits;
having been approached unrighteously, she then cursed them:
"Since you have approached me, a young girl who has kinsmen, with injustice..."
"Therefore, women shall become harlots within your families;
and you, O lowest of men, shall not be released from this terrible sin.
Consequently, their inheritors shall be their sisters' sons, and not their own sons."
The Kurus along with the Pāñcālas, the Śālvas, Matsyas, and those of Naimiṣa;
the Kosalas, Kāśis, Aṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Magadhas;
as well as the highly blessed Cedis—all these know the eternal Dharma.
In various lands, the virtuous are generally devoid of absorption [in worldly matters],
from the people of the Matsya, Kuru,
and Pañcāla regions up to those of Naimiṣa and the Cedis who are distinguished.
The virtuous live according to the ancient dharma,
except for the Madrakas and the crooked people of the Five Rivers;
O King, knowing this, listen to these discourses on dharma.
O Śalya, may you become as one who is silent like a fool;
for you are the protector of those people and their king,
taking a sixth share of both their merit and their evil deeds.

"Or rather, you are the remover of their misdeeds and not their protector; a king who protects his subjects shares in their merit, yet you share in their demerit. Formerly, when the eternal Dharma was honored in all lands,"
Having seen the Dharma of the Pañcanadas, the Grandfather said, "Fie!
Even for the sake of the Vratyas, the sons of Daśa who perform inauspicious deeds,
and for that Dharma censured by Brahmā— what did you say to them in this world?
"Thus the Grandfather (Bhīṣma) held the dharma of the Pañcanada in contempt;
even he would not honor this [dharma] while the social orders remained established in their own duties.
Know this, O Śalya! Come now, I shall tell you more."
As he was submerging himself in the lake, the Rākṣasa Kalmāṣapāda said:
"Begging is the stain of a Kṣatriya; falsehood is the stain of a Brāhmaṇa. The Bāhlīkas are the stain of the earth; women of Madra are the stain of women."
Having rescued a night-stalker who was sinking [into the water], a certain king questioned him;
listen now to what was told by him in response.
"The Mlecchas are the dregs of human beings, and the boxers (mauṣṭikas) are the dregs of the Mlecchas."
The impurity of boxers is the eunuchs; the impurity of eunuchs is those who sacrifice for kings.
Whatever impurity belongs to those for whom kings’ priests sacrifice, and to the Madrakas—that indeed shall be your impurity if you do not release us.
Thus, for those possessed by *rākṣasas* and those struck by the potency of poison,
this proven *rākṣasa* medicine has been declared as the supreme instruction. The Pāñcālas follow the *brāhma* [dharma], while the Kauraveyas follow their own specific duty (*svadharma*).
The Matsyas and Śūrasenas are truthful, as is sacrifice;
the Dāsas of the East, the Vṛṣalas of the South,
the Bāhlīkas are thieves, and the Surāṣṭras are indeed of mixed caste.
Ungratefulness, stealing the wealth of others,
drinking intoxicants, violating the teacher’s wife,
verbal cruelty, killing a cow, and wandering about at night.
Using another's clothing outside of one's own home—
there is no unrighteousness toward those for whom this is their dharma; fie upon the Āraṭṭakas and the people of the Five Rivers!
From the Pañcālas to the Kurus and the Naimiṣas,
as well as the Matsyas, they know the Dharma; so too do the Kaliṅgas, the Aṅgas, and the Māgadhas.
The elders live according to the remaining duties;
the gods, led by Jātavedas, have taken refuge in the eastern direction,
while the ancestors, protected by Yama of auspicious deeds, occupy the southern.
The mighty Varuṇa protects the western quarter, guarding the Asuras;
the blessed Soma, devoted to sacred knowledge, protects the northern quarter along with the Brāhmaṇas.
Himavat protects the Rākṣasas and Piśācas, while Gandhamādana protects the Guhyakas.
Likewise, O Great King, the *rakṣasas* and *piśācas* [dwell] on Himavat, the best of mountains; and the *guhyakas* [dwell] on Mount Gandhamādana.
Viṣṇu Janārdana is the constant sustainer of all beings and of the worlds.
No one at all protects the wicked people of the Pañcanada region even when they are united.
The Magadhas understand by a mere gesture, the Kosalas by a glance,
the Kurus and Pañcālas by half-spoken words, and the Śālvas require full instructions.
The mountaineers are as rugged as their mountains; the Yavanas, O King, are all-knowing and especially heroic;
the Mlecchas are restricted by their own conventions, unlike other people who do not speak thus.
The Bāhlikas have been subdued, yet none of the Madrakas have been so;
such as you are, O Śalya, you ought not to speak further.
Among all the regions on earth, the Madraka is said to be the very dregs.
Likewise, among all women, Madrikā is said to be the stain;
the drinking of *sīdhu*, violating the teacher’s bed,
the killing of an embryo, and the theft of another’s wealth.
Knowing this, remain silent; do not act in opposition.
Having first slain you, I shall slay Keshava and Arjuna. Knowing this, remain silent; do not act in opposition.
Do not be angry, O foremost among the evildoers; having previously slain you along with your sons and your forces,
I shall afterwards slay both Vāsudeva and Arjuna.
Śalya said:
"O Karṇa, the abandonment of the afflicted and the sale of one's own wife and children prevail among the Aṅgas, over whom you are the sovereign."

Regarding that which Bhīṣma said to you at the time of the enumeration of chariot-warriors and great chariot-warriors—having recognized those faults of your own, be free from resentment and do not be angry. Brahmins exist everywhere; Kṣatriyas exist everywhere.
O Karṇa, Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as well as virtuous women of firm vows,
take delight in mockery; and in various regions, men sport with one another, carving each other up while engaging in sexual union.

Everyone is always skillful in criticizing the speech of others, but they do not know their own faults; even if they do know them, they become deluded. Everywhere there are kings who are devoted to their respective duties.
They restrain wicked men; there are righteous people everywhere. O Karṇa, it is not because of the commonality of region that everyone practices evil.
Sañjaya said:
Even the gods are not like him by their very nature.
Then King Duryodhana restrained Karṇa and Śalya;
he addressed the son of Rādhā with the affection of a friend, and Śalya with a respectful salutation.
Then, O noble one, Karṇa was restrained by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Sañjaya said:
Karṇa did not utter a reply, and Śalya also faced the enemies.
Laughing once more, the son of Rādhā urged him again, saying, "Go! "This has been told to you by me out of anger, and not from a lack of friendship.
Then, as the son of Rādhā was departing, the King of Madra spoke as if smiling.
Having uttered this speech in the presence of the Kurus, he spoke these words:
"This vast and prosperous army of yours,
countless and teeming with horses and men— "
Likewise, Dhanañjaya will enter the battle like a blazing fire consuming dry grass;
O hero, those two most excellent warriors stand upon their chariot in the fray.
Today you shall behold, without effort, those with lion-like shoulders and eyes like red lotuses;
for thus do my omens inform me.
08,031.001 Saṃjaya said:
Then Karna, having observed that incomparable array of the Pārthas— which shattered the enemy forces and was protected by Dhṛṣṭadyumna— [proceeded].
He set forth with the roar of chariots, the sound of lion-like shouts,
and the blaring of musical instruments, as if making the earth tremble;
that scorcher of foes, skilled in battle, seemed to quiver with rage.
Having arrayed his forces in formation, O bull of the Bharatas, that one of great splendor duly scattered the Pāṇḍava army like Maghavan scattering the host of Asuras;
and overwhelming Yudhiṣṭhira, he deprived him of his left flank.
At the roar of Karṇa’s chariot, by the friction of his bowstring, and by the clenching of his reins,
the Sṛñjayas trembled;
all those armies, O lord of men, shook upon seeing Karṇa.
Your troops became filled with great joy, eager for battle. Then, O lord of the people, the voices of your men were heard:
"Today this great battle between Karṇa and Arjuna shall take place."
Today King Duryodhana will have his enemies slain;
today, upon seeing Karṇa in battle, Phalguna will flee;
today, for that very reason, he shall follow after Karṇa’s chariot in the fray.
Today we shall behold a terrible battle in this conflict, consisting of ears and arrows;
this which has been prepared for a long time shall now come to pass.
Today we shall witness a fierce combat resembling that between the gods and the asuras.

Now at this time, a great and terrifying battle will take place; now at this time, victory in the fray will surely belong to one side or the other. It is said that Rādheya will slay Arjuna in the great battle.
"Or rather, what man in this world is not touched by desires? Having spoken these various words, O joy of the Kurus,
the Kurus beat thousands of kettledrums and trumpets.
O noble one, they sounded various kettledrums and conchs, let out abundant lion-roars,
and produced the great sounds of *muraja* drums and the auspicious resonance of *ānaka* drums,
while many danced and brandished their threats.
Men who had entered the arena of battle rushed at one another in the fray.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, how did the son of Rādhā array his forces against the Pāṇḍavas?"
O Sañjaya, who were those heroes led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, protected by Bhīmasena—
all of them great archers, invincible even to the gods—
who served as my army's wings or its flanks?
Having divided them according to the rules, how were they stationed?
And how did the sons of Pāṇḍu counter-array themselves against my men?
And how did this great and most terrible battle commence?
And where was Bībhatsu when Karṇa went against Yudhiṣṭhira? For who indeed would be capable of approaching Yudhiṣṭhira in the presence of Arjuna—
he who alone formerly conquered all beings at Khāṇḍava?
"Who, desiring to live, would fight against him other than the son of Rādhā?
Sañjaya said:
"Listen to the formation of the battle array and how Arjuna departed."
Having entrusted the king to them, a battle ensued;
O King, Kṛpa Śāradvata, the swift Māgadha,
and the Sātvata Kṛtavarman took their positions on the right wing.
On their wings were the bird-bannered Śakuni and the great car-warrior Ulūka;
with riders armed with spotless spears, they protected your army along with the undaunted Gāndhāris and the invincible mountaineers.
Like swarms of locusts, or like Piśācas difficult to behold,
thirty-four thousand chariots that never retreat—
the Saṃśaptakas, experts in battle— protected the left flank.
Gathered by your sons, they were intent on slaying Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna; their advanced wing consisted of the Kambojas, Śakas, and Yavanas,
along with chariots, horses, and infantry, acting under the command of the Sūta’s son.
Challenging Arjuna and the mighty Keśava, they stood their ground; in the midst of the front of the army, Karṇa, clad in armor,
adorned with variegated mail, armlets, and garlands, stationed himself protecting the vanguard of the host.
Protected by his sons who were highly enraged, that hero, the best among wielders of weapons,
shone as he led the vanguard of the army;
the mighty-armed Ayoratni possessed the splendor of the sun and the fire.
Mounted upon the shoulders of a great elephant, the tawny and handsome Duḥśāsana stood at the rear of the formation, surrounded by his troops;
O Great King, King Duryodhana himself followed behind him.
Protected by his uterine brothers with variegated horses and colorful armor,
and guarded by the immensely powerful Madrakas and Kekayas acting in concert,
he shone, O great king, like Śatakratu among the gods.
Aśvatthāman and those who were the preeminent great chariot-warriors among the Kurus, as well as elephants ever-intoxicated and mounted by brave Mlecchas,
accompanied by their riders and mahouts holding spears and goads in their hands.
That army followed after him like clouds pouring down rain;
with their banners, victory-flags, blazing supreme weapons,
and mounted cavalry, they shone like mountains covered in trees.
The foot-guards of those infantrymen and elephants numbered in the thousands;
they were brave warriors who never retreated,
bearing sharp-edged spears and swords, as well as slings, tridents in their hands, and excellent discuses.
Their encounter was terrible, like the battle between the gods and the asuras;
with horsemen, chariots, and highly adorned elephants,
that king of battle arrays shone like the armies of the gods and the asuras.
Well-arranged by the wise leader, the son of Bṛhaspati,
this great military array seems to dance, instilling fear in the enemies;
from its wings and sub-wings, warriors eager for battle rush forth.
Foot soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants were like clouds in the rainy season.
Then, seeing Karṇa at the head of the army, King Yudhiṣṭhira spoke to Dhananjaya, the slayer of enemies and peerless hero.
"Behold, O Arjuna, this great array formed by Karṇa in battle; equipped with wings and sub-wings, the army shines forth. Having observed this great force of the enemy, [act accordingly]."
"Let such a policy be enacted so that he does not overcome us.
Thus addressed by the king, Arjuna, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the monarch:
"Everything shall be exactly as you have said; it shall not be otherwise."
"O Bhārata, I shall carry out that which has been ordained for his slaughter;
indeed, the destruction of this man lies in the killing of his chief, and that I shall accomplish.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Therefore, let Bhīmasena himself encounter Rādheya;
let Nakula face Suyodhana; let Sahadeva face Vṛṣasena; let Śatānīka face the son of Subala; and let the bull of the Śinis face the son of Hṛdika.
"Let Dhṛṣṭadyumna go against the son of Droṇa, and I myself shall go against Kṛpa;
let the sons of Draupadī, together with Śikhaṇḍin, face the remaining sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Let those men of mine slay their respective enemies."
08,031.036 Saṃjaya said:
Having been thus addressed by the King of Dharma, Dhanañjaya replied, "So be it," and he gave orders to his own troops while he himself went to the front of the army.
Resembling the sun and Vaiśvānara, with banners raised high—Agni Vaiśvānara was indeed the first; Brahmā became the moon and attained the state of a steed.
Therefore, the gods and the Brahmins know him as the one who was born first.
Having mounted that primordial chariot, which was first created by Brahmā, the creator of the world,
and which in ancient times successively bore Brahmā, Īśāna, Indra, and Varuṇa,
Keśava and Arjuna set forth.
O great king, Dhanañjaya took his position on the right wing;
the mighty-armed Bhīmasena took his place on the left wing;
and likewise Sātyaki, the sons of Draupadī, and the Pāṇḍava king himself.

Surrounded by their own division, they stood at the head of the array. Having stationed that enemy force with his own troops, the Pāṇḍava drew up his counter-array, placing Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin at its forefront.

That mighty military array, teeming with cavalry and elephants, crowded with foot soldiers and chariots, and headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, shone resplendently. Then, seeing that approaching chariot of most wondrous appearance, [he was struck with amazement].
Śalya spoke again to that son of Adhiratha, who was maddened by battle, as he stood there; the King of Madra, as if smiling, uttered these words:
"There comes that chariot with white horses and Kṛṣṇa as its charioteer."
Irresistible to all armies like the ripening of karmic fruits,
the son of Kuntī slays your enemies— whomever you inquire about—
a tumultuous sound is heard, the great roar of chariot wheels.
"Surely these two great-souled ones are Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya;
for this dust has arisen and stands enveloping the heavens,
and the earth, O Karṇa, trembles, struck by the rims of their chariot wheels."
The unconquered Dhanañjaya will surely enter this vast and prosperous army of yours, which is countless and filled with the sounds of weeping.
How is it that these horses, colored like moonbeams, though being pricked by the black goad, do not burn like a blazing fire consuming its own fuel?
Noble beings carry Bibhatsu,
who possesses white radiance, like masses of clouds carrying their own reflection;
this great wind blows from all sides against your army.
"These flesh-eaters are crying out; these beasts are making a terrible noise.
Behold, Karṇa, that most horrific, fear-inducing, and hair-raising headless trunk (kabandha), resembling a cloud, standing there having shrouded the sun."
Behold, in every direction, the sun is being gazed upon by various herds of animals and by powerful, proud tigers;
and [the monkey] with his flaming tail stood facing the sun and let out a roar.
Behold the thousands of *kaṅka* vultures and *gṛdhra* eagles gathered together; O Karṇa, these inauspicious birds are looking intently at the sun with great haste,
standing face to face and speaking to one another in a terrifying manner.
O Karna, great car-warrior, these white horses yoked to your chariot are shedding tears;
these wheels are glowing with fire, and even your banner is trembling. Behold the horses being urged forward—huge-bodied and possessed of great speed.
Gliding through the sky like beautiful Garuḍas,
it is certain that upon these omens, kings by the hundreds and thousands will fall slain upon the earth, O Karṇa, covering the ground as they sleep.
O Rādheya, the tumultuous and hair-raising sound of conchs is heard on all sides, along with that of kettledrums and clay drums,
as well as the various sounds of arrows and the noise of men, horses, and chariots.
O Karṇa, hear the sounds of the bowstrings, arm-guards, and arrows of those great-souled men; fashioned by craftsmen from cloth polished with gold and silver,
they shine in various colors upon the chariot as it is shaken by the wind.
"Behold, O Karṇa, these banners of Arjuna, adorned with golden moons, stars, and suns, and equipped with tinkling bells; they appear like flashes of lightning amidst a cloud,
making a 'kaṇakaṇa' sound as they are stirred by the wind."
O Karṇa, the chariots of the high-souled Pāñcālas, adorned with banners, shine in battle like deities in their celestial vehicles. Behold the heroic Bībhatsu, the son of Kuntī, who is unconquered.
Behold this terrifying monkey,
the increaser of his enemies' misfortune, who is seen at the tip of Partha’s banner as he surveys all directions while approaching to assail him whose standard bears the foremost of monkeys.
This discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and conch belong to the wise Kṛṣṇa;
moreover, the Kaustubha gem shines exceedingly upon Kṛṣṇa.
Here is Vāsudeva, possessed of great heroism, with the Śārṅga bow and mace in his hands.
He comes driving white horses, swift as the wind;
this is the twang of the Gāṇḍīva bow drawn by Savyasācin;
these sharp arrows, released by that dexterous hand, are slaying the enemies.
With their large, long, copper-hued eyes and faces resembling the full moon,
this earth is strewn with the heads of kings who did not flee;
these [heads] have the appearance of great door-bolts and are anointed with sacred perfumes.
The arms of those intoxicated by their raised weapons, still clutching their arms,
were severed; horses, with their eyes and tongues protruding, fell along with their riders— already fallen, being struck down, or lying there spent upon the earth.

These elephants, resembling mountain peaks, have been slain by Pārtha; mangled and torn apart, they fall like mountains. The chariots, with their lords of men slain, resemble cities of the Gandharvas.
Like the meritorious celestial chariots of the denizens of heaven falling down,
behold this army being utterly thrown into confusion by Kirīṭin,
like a herd of thousands of various deer by a lion.
These heroic Pāṇḍavas, rushing forward together,
are slaying the kings and the vast multitudes of your elephants, horses, chariots,
and infantry; yet the tip of his banner is visible and the sound of his bowstring is heard.

"Today, O Karna, you shall behold that hero whom you inquire about— he who possesses white horses and has Krishna as his charioteer, and who slaughters the enemies in battle. Today, you shall see those two tigers among men, red-eyed and scorchers of foes."
O Karṇa, you shall see Vāsudeva and Arjuna standing together upon a single chariot—where Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World, is present; where King Yudhiṣṭhira is present;
and where Pārtha, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, is present—how can you destroy that army?
O Rādheya, if you can slay him whose charioteer is the Vārṣṇeya and whose bow is the Gāṇḍīva, you shall become our king;
for the sound of his chariot wheels in battle is like the thundering roar of a cloud.
Indeed, it is clearly heard that these two, Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya,
are present; this powerful one, summoned by the Saṃśaptakas, has gone directly toward them and is causing a slaughter of those enemies in battle.
To the Lord of Madra who was speaking thus, Karṇa, filled with great indignation, said:
"Behold! Surrounded on all sides by the enraged Saṃśaptakas, this son of Pṛthā is no longer visible, shrouded like the sun by clouds."
"O Śalya, Arjuna has reached this end, submerged in an ocean of grief.
Śalya said:
"Who could slay Varuṇa with water, or fire with fuel?"
Who indeed could restrain the wind, or who could drink up the great ocean?
I consider the subduing of Pārtha in battle to be of such a nature;
for Arjuna cannot be conquered even by all the gods and asuras together with Indra.
If this is your satisfaction, then speak these words and be of good cheer;
he cannot be conquered in battle, so set your heart on another desire. He could lift up the earth with his two arms, and in his wrath, he could consume all these creatures.
He who could defeat Arjuna in battle might cast down the gods from the third heaven. Behold the heroic son of Kuntī, Bhīma, the doer of effortless deeds,
shining with splendor, mighty-armed, standing firm like Mount Meru.
"Impatient, ever-agitated, and long remembering his enmity,
this heroic Bhīma stands in battle, desiring victory.
This is Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, the best among the upholders of righteousness."
That conqueror of enemy cities stands in battle, difficult for others to overcome;
and these two tigers among men, Nakula and Sahadeva, who are like the twin Aśvins, stand in the fight, invincible.
These five sons of Kṛṣṇā are seen standing like five mountains,
all prepared for battle and equal to Arjuna in combat.
And here are the sons of Drupada, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Deprived of Satyajit, these heroes of supreme prowess stand ready;
this Sātyaki, the best of the Sātvatas, is as irresistible as Indra himself. Yuyutsu advances against us from the front, like the enraged God of Death.
"Where the heroes Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna are, where King Yudhiṣṭhira is, there is righteousness and truth; where there is righteousness, there is victory.
While those two lions among men were thus conversing, [the sun set].
Those two armies clashed violently like the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
Then, not perceiving that the great force of the enemy stood firm before him,
Arjuna failed to form a counter-array against your son’s invincible formation.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, when the armies had been thus arrayed and were engaged in combat,
how did Pārtha proceed against the Saṃśaptakas, and how did Karṇa proceed against the Pāṇḍavas?"
"Tell me this battle in detail, for you are indeed skilled;
I am not yet satiated by hearing of the heroic exploits of these warriors in combat.
Sañjaya said:
Having stationed that mighty enemy force in its proper place,
Arjuna did not form a counter-array against the array of your son due to his misconduct.
That army was thick with cavalry and elephants, and crowded with infantry and chariots.
That great army, arrayed with Dhṛṣṭadyumna at its head,
shone resplendent; the son of Pṛṣata, whose horses were the color of pigeons and who possessed a splendor equal to the moon and sun, appeared as a bowman like Time incarnate.
The sons of Draupadī, eager for battle,
clad in celestial armor and bearing weapons, possessing the prowess of tigers and formidable forms with their followers, surrounded the son of Pṛṣata like hosts of stars surrounding the moon.
Then, seeing the Saṃśaptakas arrayed in battle formations on the field,
the enraged Arjuna rushed toward them, brandishing his bow Gāṇḍīva. Thereupon, the Saṃśaptakas, desiring his death, charged against Pārtha.
Having resolved upon victory and making death their only retreat,
that host— abounding in throngs of horses, crowded with rutting elephants and chariots,
surging forward and filled with fury— rushed toward Dhanañjaya.
That great army, raised up and resembling the surge of the ocean in its speed,
was seen standing still upon reaching the shore of Pārtha; then,
with throngs of heroic warriors on foot, it swiftly rushed toward Arjuna.
That tumultuous battle between them and Kirīṭin was just like the one we have heard of him with the Nivātakavacas;
[it involved] chariots, horses, banners, elephants, infantry, and even chariot-lords.
Pārtha severed the arrows, bows, swords, discuses, and axes; he cut down the arms raised with weapons and the uplifted weapons themselves, as well as the heads of his enemies by the thousands.

Thinking that their chariot had sunk into that great whirlpool of the army, which resembled a vortex in the netherworld (pātāla), the Saṃśaptakas shouted with joy. Having slain the enemies in front, he [Arjuna] also struck them from the rear and the left flank.

And to the south, Bībhatsu, enraged like Rudra over his sacrificial animals, [fell upon them]. Then, O noble one, a most terrible battle took place between the Pāñcālas, Cedis, and Sṛñjayas on one side, and your men on the other.
Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and Śakuni the son of Subala—
these strikers with their chariot-divisions, accompanied by joyful and highly incensed armies,
together with the Kosalas, the Kāśis, the Matsyas, the Kārūṣas, and the Kekayas.
The Śūrasenas, heroic warriors intoxicated by battle, fought [with them].
That battle was the end-maker for them, destroying the bodies and sins of the Śūdra, Vaiśya, and Kṣatriya heroes; it was righteous, leading to heaven, and bringing glory.
O bull of the Bharatas, Duryodhana also, accompanied by his brothers and protected by the foremost heroes of the Kurus and the great chariot-warriors of the Madras,
[fought] against the Pāṇḍavas along with the Pañcālas, the Cedis, and Sātyaki.
While Karna was fighting in the battle, the Kuru hero protected him;
and Karna, having struck down the great army with sharp arrows and crushed the best of chariot-warriors, afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having deprived thousands of enemies of their feathers, weapons, bodies,
and lives, and having united them with heaven and glory, he brought joy to his own people.
Thus, O noble one, was that battle, which caused the destruction of men, horses, and elephants.
The battle between the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas became equal to that between the gods and the asuras.
Having plunged into that array of chariots, the great car-warrior, the son of the Sūta,
set flowing a river with waves of surging blood.
[He saw] a river with blood for its water, teeming with small fish and crocodiles in the form of *nāgas*, difficult to cross;
it had flesh and marrow for its mud, wheels for its tortoises, and chariots for its rafts;
and it was strewn here and there with fallen great elephants resembling clouds.
O King, the earth shone as if devastated by thunderbolts;
it was filled with waves of arrows and great whirlpools, crowded with umbrellas like swans,
strewn with the heaps of armor and turbans, and thick with elephants like boulders.
O Great King, [cross] that river which has no further shore and no near shore, resounding with the sounds of conchs and drums, fierce, shrouded on all sides by dust,
extremely sharp, filled with crocodiles, and flowing toward the end-maker (Death).
Equal and yet uneven, bringing great terror, it came along;
there, O King, men sank up to their ankles in the mire of blood,
surrounded on all sides by other men like great trees.
Then, O King, as they continued to advance here and there, those warriors roamed everywhere across the great river with their boats, elephants, and great chariots;
the ground all around was made level with blood.
"O Lord of the People, the earth was like that [land] by the force of river currents.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"When he had entered the army of the Pārthas, causing the destruction of men—"
Karna rushed toward the king; tell me that, O Sañjaya!
And which of the Pārtha heroes resisted Karna in battle? And whom did the son of Adhiratha crush before he afflicted Yudhiṣṭhira?
Saṃjaya said:
Seeing the Pārthas led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna standing in their positions, Karṇa,
the crusher of enemies, swiftly charged toward the Pañcālas.
O great king, as he rushed forward swiftly, the Pāñcālas, appearing victorious,
advanced against him like swans toward the great ocean.
Then there arose the heart-stirring sound of thousands of conchs.
A terrible sound of kettledrums arose from both sides,
along with the noise of various musical instruments and the clamor of elephants, horses, and chariots;
and then there was the fierce lion-roar of the heroes.
The earth with its mountains, trees, and oceans; the sky with its winds and clouds; and the heavens with the sun, moon, planets, and stars—all visibly shook.
All living beings considered that sound to be excessive and were deeply distressed by it.
And those aquatic creatures for the most part perished;
then Karṇa, becoming violently enraged, swiftly invoking his weapons,
struck down the Pāṇḍava army as Maghavan struck the army of the Asuras.
Quickly entering the ranks of the Pāṇḍava chariots and discharging his arrows,
he slew seventy-seven of the foremost Prabhadrakas.
Then, with well-feathered and sharpened shafts from his excellent chariot, that best of car-warriors struck them down.
With twenty-five gold-feathered iron shafts capable of rending the bodies of enemies, he slew twenty-five Pāñcālas;
then that hero killed the Cedis by the hundreds and thousands.
O great king, as he was thus performing superhuman deeds in battle, the throngs of Pāñcāla chariots surrounded him. Then, O Bhārata, having fixed five unbearable arrows, he—
Karna Vaikartana, the bull-like hero, slew five Pāñcālas, O Bhārata:
Bhānudeva, Citrasena, Senābindu, Tapana, and Śūrasena; he killed those Pāñcālas in battle.
As the heroic Pāñcālas were being slaughtered by his arrows, a great cry of "Alas! arose among the Pāñcālas in that great battle;
O Great King, ten chariots of the Pāñcālas surrounded him.
As they were being overwhelmed, the quarters of the sky were filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!
And Karna once again swiftly struck them down with his feathered arrows, O noble one;
for Karna’s two sons, the protectors of his chariot wheels, were difficult to conquer.
Suṣeṇa and Satyasena fought while disregarding their own lives. Vṛṣasena, the eldest son of Karṇa and a great car-warrior (*mahāratha*), himself protected Karṇa from behind as his rear-guard.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, the sons of Draupadī, Vṛkodara,
Nakula, Sahadeva, the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
Janamejaya, Śikhaṇḍin, and the heroic Prabhadrakas.
The Cedis, Kaikeyas, Pañcālas, the twins, and the Matsyas, all clad in armor,
rushed toward the son of Rādhā, seeking to slay him with their weapons. They assailed him with various missiles and showers of arrows.
They rained down [arrows] while crushing [the enemy], like clouds raining upon a mountain during the monsoon.
But the sons of Karṇa, those strikers, seeking to protect their father,
and other heroes on your side, O King, held back the enemy heroes.

Suṣeṇa, having severed Bhīmasena’s bow with a broad-headed arrow and having pierced Bhīma in the heart with seven iron shafts, let out a roar. Then, he of terrible prowess took up another very firm bow.
Having strung his bow, Vṛkodara severed Suṣeṇa’s bow and,
as if dancing, struck him in fury with nine arrows.
He also swiftly pierced Karṇa with seventy-three sharp shafts.
And with ten arrows, he struck Satyasena— along with his horses, charioteer, standard, and weapons—
and felled the son of Karṇa in the midst of his watching friends;
that head of his, with a face like the moon, was severed by a razor-headed arrow.
He appeared truly beautiful, like a lotus fallen from a cloudless sky.
Having slain the son of Karṇa, Bhīma again afflicted your troops; having severed the bows of Kṛpa and the son of Hṛdika, he then afflicted them as well.
Having pierced Duḥśāsana with three iron arrows and Śakuni with six, he rendered both Ulūka and Patatri carless. Crying out, "O Suṣeṇa, you are slain! he took up an arrow.

Karna cut off his [Bhima’s] hand with an arrow and struck him with three more. Then Bhima seized another well-jointed and sharp-pointed shaft and discharged it at Suṣeṇa; but Vṛṣa (Karna) cut that one down as well.

Again, Karṇa, desiring to protect his son, pierced the cruel Bhīmasena with seventy-three cruel shafts from his chariot, seeking to slay him. Suṣeṇa, however, took up an excellent bow capable of bearing a great burden.
With five arrows, he struck Nakula in the arms and chest;
but Nakula, having pierced him with twenty firm shafts capable of bearing great weight,
uttered a powerful roar, instilling fear in Karṇa.
O great king, having pierced him with ten swift arrows, the great car-warrior Suṣeṇa quickly cut his bow with a razor-headed shaft. Then Nakula, overwhelmed with rage, took up another bow.

With many arrows, he warded off Suṣeṇa in the encounter. O King, that slayer of enemy heroes, having covered the quarters with his shafts, then struck his charioteer and Suṣeṇa himself with three arrows.
And with three broad-headed arrows, he cut his very firm bow into three pieces. Then Suṣeṇa, overwhelmed with rage, took up another bow and pierced Nakula with sixty arrows and Sahadeva with seven.
That battle was exceedingly great and terrible, like the conflict between the gods and the asuras,
as they swiftly struck one another with arrows, each seeking the other's death.
Satyaki, having pierced Vṛṣasena with seven swift-flying shafts, [continued the fray].
He pierced him again with seventy arrows and his charioteer with three; then,
O great king, Vṛṣasena struck the great car-warrior Śaineya in the region of the temple with a straight-knotted shaft.
O great king, being severely afflicted by Vṛṣasena with a feathered shaft, the descendant of Śini became enraged; filled with fury,
he unleashed a terrible impetus and quickly seized fifteen excellent arrows.
Sātyaki, having slain Vṛṣasena’s charioteer with three arrows,
cut his bow with a broad-headed shaft and killed his horses with seven; then,
having struck down the standard with a single arrow, he pierced him in the heart with three.
Then, having collapsed upon his own chariot, he rose up again after a moment;
deprived of his charioteer, horses, chariot, and standard by Yuyudhāna in that battle,
he approached, bearing sword and shield, desiring to slay the descendant of Śini.
As Vṛṣasena was swiftly swimming away, Sātyaki pierced him with ten boar-eared arrows through his sword and shield.
But Duḥśāsana, seeing him deprived of his chariot and his weapons, [intervened].
Having quickly placed him upon his own chariot, he bore him away to another chariot.
Then, mounting a different chariot, the great car-warrior Vṛṣasena struck the sons of Draupadī with seventy-three arrows and Yuyudhāna with five.
He struck Bhīmasena with sixty-four arrows, Sahadeva with five, Nakula with thirty shafts, Śatānīka with seven,
Śikhaṇḍin with ten, and Dharmarāja with a hundred.
O lord of the people, O king of kings, the son of Karṇa— the great archer, invincible in battle— pressed upon these and other pre-eminent heroes who were greedy for victory,
while he himself protected the rear of Karṇa once again.

But the grandson of Śini, having deprived Duḥśāsana of his chariot, horses, and driver with nine fresh, swift arrows, struck him on the forehead with three more. He, however, mounting another chariot that had been duly prepared, [returned].
He fought together with the Pāṇḍavas, augmenting the strength of Karṇa.
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna pierced Karṇa with ten arrows;
the sons of Draupadī pierced him with seventy-three, and Yuyudhāna with seven.
Bhīmasena struck him with sixty-four arrows, Sahadeva with five, Nakula with thirty shafts, Śatānīka with seven,
the heroic Śikhaṇḍin with ten, and Dharmarāja with a hundred.
O Indra among kings, these and other preeminent heroes, greedy for victory,
assailed that great archer, the Sūta’s son, in the great battle. The Sūta’s son [struck] them with ten sharp arrows each.
Moving gracefully on his chariot, that heroic subduer of enemies pierced Satyaki, Bhīmasena, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin,
and the sons of Draupadī— all those great car-warriors who were enraged and striving with all their might.
While all the troops were looking on, the son of the charioteer deprived those foremost of car-warriors of their chariots within half a blink of an eye;
and because of the infallibility of his arrows, the hosts of beings were filled with wonder.

There, O great king, we beheld the power of Karṇa’s weapons and the lightness of hand of that high-souled one; it was as if a marvel. For they did not see him taking up his arrows nor fixing them to the string.
They beheld that great car-warrior discharging [arrows] with fury;
having seen him in the western quarter, they saw him in the eastern quarter due to his swiftness,
yet we could not see, O king of kings, where Karṇa was stationed.
O King, we saw him indeed scattering arrows in every direction, covering the quarters like swarms of locusts; by those thousands of sharp arrows of his falling upon us, [the sky was obscured].
O King, all the directions were then seen by the warriors to be pervaded by those sharp, straight-jointed arrows, like the rays of the hot-rayed sun;
the sky, covered with shafts, became as if filled with clouds.
The sky, the firmament, the earth, and the quarters were swiftly driven away by his sharpened arrows;
in that region, the atmosphere shone as if enveloped by crimson clouds.
Then once more, O King, the immeasurable-souled Karna, that great car-warrior—
Observing the vow of a warrior, he struck down the combatants in battle. Indeed, the powerful son of Rādhā, bow in hand, seemed as if he were dancing;
pierced by those [enemies], he pierced each one of them back with threefold arrows.

Piercing them again with ten arrows each, he let out a roar; then they, along with their horses, charioteers, standards, and umbrellas, gave way. Being slaughtered by Karṇa, they fled in the ten directions.
Making all the directions resound, they were terrified and deprived of their senses by the sound; crushing those great archers with showers of arrows, the son of Rādhā,
the crusher of enemies, entered the royal army without hindrance.
Having slain three hundred chariots of the Cedis who never retreat,
the son of Rādhā, with his sharpened arrows, then advanced toward Yudhiṣṭhira.
Thereupon those heroes, deprived of their chariots, mounted other chariots.
O Great King, they surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
Then, O King, those Pāṇḍavas— Śikhaṇḍin and Sātyaki as well—
surrounded the king, protecting him from the son of Rādhā.
Discharging various arrows with golden feathers sharpened on stone,
all those great bowmen of your army, remaining vigilant, protected Karna— who was difficult to restrain in battle— from every side.
O lord of the people, the sounds of various musical instruments arose,
and the lion-roars of the brave warriors who do not retreat were produced.
Then once again, the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas, free from fear, came together once more.
"The sons of Pṛthā, headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, and we, headed by the Sūta’s son.
Saṃjaya said:
"Having torn through that army, Karṇa rushed toward the King of Dharma."
Surrounded by thousands of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantrymen,
Vṛṣa— without any agitation— cut down the thousands of various weapons hurled by his enemies and pierced them with hundreds of fierce arrows.
He severed their heads, arms, and thighs on all sides—
some who were desiring to strike,
others with arrows already fixed to their bows, and the outstretched arms of yet others as they rushed forward with weapons grasped.
In that battle, Karṇa struck down those who were equipped with various weapons;
they fell to the earth slain, while others, broken, fled away.
Then the Draviḍas, Āndhras, and Niṣādas, urged on once more by Sātyaki, [rushed forward].
Desiring to strike and seeking to kill Karna in the battle, the foot-soldiers pressed forward;
struck down by Karna’s arrows, they fell upon the earth simultaneously with their arms and helmets severed, like a forest of *śāla* trees cut down at once.
In this way, hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of warriors were slain in battle;
they reached the earth with their bodies and filled the quarters of the sky with their fame.
Then [he beheld] Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana, who was like the enraged God of Death on the battlefield.
The Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas checked him, as one checks a disease with mantras and medicines; yet,
crushing them, he rushed again toward Yudhiṣṭhira,
like a most violent disease that has transcended the efficacy of mantras, medicines, and medical treatments.
Obstructed by those greedy for the kingdom— the Pāṇḍus, Pāñcālas, and Kekayas—
he was unable to overcome them, just as death cannot overcome those who know the Brahman.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira [beheld] Karṇa, who had been held back and was not far away.
Seeing the hero before them, those warriors pierced him with arrows;
Karna, pierced by the shafts of Pārtha like an elephant tormented by a goad,
crushed the assembled heroes and oppressed Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the slayer of enemy heroes, his eyes bloodshot with rage, approached Karṇa—the best among victors—and spoke these words:
"Karṇa! Karṇa! You of vain vision, son of a Sūta, listen to my words!"

You always vie in battle with the illustrious Phalguna; likewise, abiding by the will of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, you constantly oppress us. Whatever strength and whatever prowess you possess, as well as your hatred for the Pāṇḍavas—[all this is directed against us].
"Display all that today, relying upon your great manliness!
I shall today quell your desire for battle in this great conflict.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the son of Pāṇḍu then addressed Karṇa.
With ten sharp, iron-tipped arrows feathered with gold,
he pierced him; then the son of the Sūta, that subduer of foes and great archer, struck him back with nine calf-tooth-headed shafts as if smiling, O Bhārata.
O noble one, having been thus disregarded and pierced by the Sūta’s son,
he then blazed up with rage like a fire fed with oblations. Then, drawing his massive bow adorned with gold, he—
He fixed a cold arrow capable of splitting even mountains; then,
drawing it back to his full ear, the king swiftly released that sharp shaft, which resembled the staff of Yama, with the intent to slay the Suta’s son.
Released with great force by him, that arrow, sounding like a thunderbolt,
suddenly entered the great car-warrior Karṇa in his left side.
Afflicted by that blow, he indeed fell into a swoon.
With his limbs collapsing, the mighty-armed one cast aside his bow upon the chariot;
then the entire great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons raised a cry of "Alas!
seeing Karṇa in such a state, their faces for the most part pale with distress.
O great king, upon seeing the prowess of the king, the roar of lions, as well as shouts and cries of joy, arose from the Pāṇḍavas; meanwhile,
the son of Rādhā regained consciousness almost immediately.
He of cruel prowess set his mind upon the destruction of the king;
drawing his great, gold-adorned bow, Vijaya,
that one of immeasurable soul covered the Pāṇḍava with sharpened arrows.
Then, with two razor-sharp arrows, that hero slew the two Pāñcālya wheel-protectors of the high-souled one in battle with his straight-knotted shafts;
those two great warriors stood at both sides of Dharmarāja.
Near the chariot, they shone like the two Punarvasu stars beside the moon. Yudhiṣṭhira again pierced Karṇa with thirty arrows,
and struck Suṣeṇa and Satyasena each with three.
He pierced Śalya with ninety arrows and the son of the Sūta with seventy-three;
he also pierced those protectors of his with three straight-flying shafts each.
