Then, laughing, the son of Adhiratha shook his bow.
Having pierced the king with a broad-headed arrow and struck him with sixty more, he roared with joy.
Then the preeminent heroes of the Pāṇḍavas rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira,
seeking to rescue him from the Sūta’s son and afflicting Karṇa with their arrows.
Enraged, Karṇa pierced Sātyaki, Cekitāna, Yuyutsu, and Pāṇḍya,
as well as the Cōla, the Ceraka, and the inhabitant of Siṃhaladvīpa—
those Southerners from every side.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, the sons of Draupadī, and the Prabhadrakas;
the twins, Bhīmasena, and the son of Śiśupāla;
the Kārūṣas, the remnants of the Matsyas, the Kekayas, and the Kāśis and Kosalas.
And these swift heroes held Vasuṣeṇa in check;
and Janamejaya the Pāñcālya pierced Karṇa with arrows— boar-eared shafts, iron bolts, nālīkas, and sharpened darts.
With calf-toothed arrows, vipāṭhas, kṣurapras, and caṭakāmukhas,
and with various other fierce weapons, the chariot-fighters, elephant-riders,
and horsemen surrounded Karṇa on all sides, rushing at him with the intent to kill.
Then, though assailed from all sides by the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas,
who covered him with sharp arrows engraved with their own names,
Karṇa did not waver in battle, like Mahendra amidst the Dānavas.
Discharging arrows that filled the quarters of the sky, he unleashed the Brahma weapon;
Saṃjaya said:
he struck down twenty-one great bowmen among the Pāñcālas.
Then again, O best of the Bharatas, Karna Vaikartana, immeasurable in soul, slew ten of the foremost Cedis at that time;
thousands of his arrows fell, O noble one.
In all directions, they appeared like swarms of locusts;
arrows marked with the name of Karṇa, gold-feathered and well-sharpened,
having pierced through the bodies of men and horses, fell upon the earth on every side.
By Karna alone in battle, the preeminent chariot-warriors of the Cedis and all the Srinjayas were slain by the hundreds in combat;
a vast darkness, thick with Karna’s arrows, enveloped them.
Then, when that darkness had become terrifying to the kṣatriyas, nothing could be discerned— neither of others nor even of oneself—
and the mighty-armed one roamed about, consuming many kṣatriyas.
Then, O great king, the fire that was Karṇa— blazing with arrows as its great flames and possessing the heat of his prowess—
roamed beautifully through the battle, consuming the forest of the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, O great king, the great chariot-warriors of those Pāṇḍavas...

And all the Sṛñjayas, by the hundreds and thousands, surrounded the great archer Karṇa on all sides with their weapons. Having warded off the great weapons of those high-souled ones, that great archer—
Laughing, he cut the bow of that lord of men with his arrows; then,
having aimed ninety straight-knotted shafts,
Karṇa pierced the king’s armor in battle with those sharp arrows.
That armor, wrought of gold, shone as it fell,
like a fragment of a cloud from the sun’s orb, struck by the wind and accompanied by lightning.
Deprived of its armor, that limb of the lord of men gleamed brilliantly.
Adorned with divine jewels, he was like the cloudless sky at night;
though deprived of his armor and drenched in blood by arrows, Pārtha,
that best of men, shone like the rising sun.
With all his limbs pierced by arrows and his armor shattered in that encounter,
he nevertheless stood firm in the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*) and let out a lion’s roar. Having roared for a long time, the impetuous Pāṇḍava [continued] in the battle.
Enraged, he hurled an iron spear at the son of Adhiratha;
with seven arrows, he cut that spear— which was as if blazing in the sky—
as it fell to the earth, severed by the shafts of that great archer.

Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having struck Karṇa on his two arms, his forehead, and his chest with four iron darts, he roared with joy. With blood gushing forth, Karṇa became enraged and hissed like a serpent.
With nine arrows he struck Pārtha’s charioteer and his rear-guard;
with a broad-headed shaft (bhalla) he cut down the banner, and with three more he pierced the Pāṇḍava.
Having slain Pārtha’s charioteer and his protector of the rear with his arrows—
He cut through his two quivers and shattered his chariot into pieces as small as sesame seeds. Then,
mounting a chariot yoked with those horses of the color of ivory that bore Pārtha— horses with black manes— the king fled with his back turned.
In the meantime, O Bhārata, the heroic great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas showered volleys of arrows upon the son of Rādhā;
Sātyaki with twenty-five and Śikhaṇḍin with nine arrows.

O Great King, he did not rain [arrows] upon Karṇa, the son of Rādhā and crusher of enemies; but then, O King, the enraged Karṇa pierced the descendant of Śini in battle with five iron shafts and three other stone-tipped arrows.
Karṇa pierced his right arm with three arrows,
his left with sixteen, and his charioteer with seven;
then he struck his four horses with four sharpened shafts.
The son of the Sūta quickly led him toward the abode of Yama. Then,
with another broad-headed arrow, that great car-warrior severed the bow and struck off the charioteer’s head, complete with its helmet, from his body.
But that bull among the Śinis, standing on a chariot whose horses and charioteer had been slain,
hurled at Karṇa a spear adorned with lapis lazuli gems;
as it came rushing toward him, O Bhārata, he suddenly cut it in two.
Karna, the best among archers, held them all back;
then that one of immeasurable soul, through both his training and his strength, warded off those great car-warriors of the Pandavas with sharpened arrows.
Having afflicted them with arrows like a lion attacking small deer,
the son of Rādhā, afflicting the King of Dharma with straight-knotted shafts,
rushed at the son of Dharma with sharp arrows.
Thus Pārtha departed, his rear-guard charioteer having been slain;
dejected and unable to stand before Karṇa,
Rādheya pursued him and touched him on the shoulder with his hand.
With his hand, which was endowed with the auspicious marks of the thunderbolt, the parasol, the goad, the fish, the banner, the tortoise, the lotus, and so forth,
he touched the shoulder of the son of Pāṇḍu in order to purify himself.
Desiring to seize him by force, he recalled Kuntī’s words.
Śalya said to him, "O Karṇa, do not seize this best of kings;
as soon as you have seized him, he will kill you and reduce you to ashes."
Laughing, O King, as if censuring the Pāṇḍava, he said:
"How indeed could one born in such a lineage and established in the duty of a Kṣatriya abandon his enemies in battle while protecting his own life in this great conflict?"
"It is my opinion that you are not skilled in the duties of a Kṣatriya;
you are devoted to Brahmanic strength, to Vedic study, and to the performance of sacrifices. Do not fight, O son of Kuntī, and do not encounter these heroes."

Do not speak unpleasant words to them, nor enter into a great battle with them. O worthy one, others may be addressed [harshly], but those like me should not be addressed so; for by speaking thus to those like me in battle, you will receive this and more.
"Go to your own home, O son of Kuntī, or wherever Keśava and Arjuna may be.
For Karṇa shall not slay you in battle by any means whatsoever, O King."—
Sañjaya.

Remembering the boon granted by Kuntī, the great chariot-warrior Karṇa did not slay the son of Kuntī, that best of men, even though he had him within his power. Having spoken thus and released the son of Pṛthā, the mighty one—
He struck down the Pāṇḍava army like the wielder of the thunderbolt striking the host of Asuras.
Then, O King, that lord of men departed swiftly as if filled with shame.
And as the king was thus departing, they then followed after that infallible one.
The Cedis, Pāṇḍavas, and Pāñcālas, the great car-warrior Sātyaki,
the heroic sons of Draupadī, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī—
then Karna, seeing Yudhiṣṭhira’s army with its faces turned away, [advanced].
Accompanied by the heroic Kurus following behind him, he pursued from the rear;
then, with the blare of conchs and kettledrums, and the twanging of bows,
there arose the roar of lions from the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, O Kauravya, having quickly mounted his chariot,
O great king, witnessed the prowess of Karṇa against Śrutakīrti; seeing his army being driven away, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira [acted].
Enraged, he said to those warriors, "Slay him indeed by the thousands!
Then, authorized by the king, all the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
led by Bhīmasena, rushed against your sons.
O Bhārata, a tumultuous noise arose there from the warriors,
from the elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry,
and from the weapons being hurled and brandished here and there.
"Arise! Strike! Advance! Attack!"—shouting thus, the warriors struck one another on the field of battle. There, the sky was covered by showers of arrows as if by the shadow of clouds.

As those best of men, having returned from their studies, struck one another down in battle, they fell upon the earth—deprived of banners, standards, and umbrellas; stripped of horses, charioteers, and weapons;
with limbs and body-parts mangled; exhausted and their lords slain.
Like the preeminent peaks of mountains, those best of elephants, O hero,
having leaped down from the mountain summits—
those elephant-like creatures— fell slain along with their riders like mountains shattered by a thunderbolt.
With their armor, ornaments, and bodies cut, shattered,
and overturned, horses fell by the thousands along with their riders, their heroes slain;
and elephants, struck down by other elephants, horses, and chariots, lay there with their weapons and limbs scattered.
In the clash with rival warriors,
the earth was strewn on all sides with the heads of those intoxicated by battle— heads belonging to thousands of foot-soldiers, whose large, long, copper-hued eyes resembled lotuses and moons.
Thus, as the sky was spread wide, the people heard a sound from the celestial chariots of the throngs of Apsarases, with the resonance of songs and musical instruments,
[proclaiming] the thousands of heroes slain by heroes— slain and mangled while facing their foes.
The hosts of Apsarases, repeatedly lifting him up, carry him away in celestial palaces;
embraced by women standing above him, he perceives his beloved with the thought, "This is yours, this is not yours alone, this is mine."
Thus, having bound the throngs of Apsarases with nooses made of their vine-like arms, those beings of divine form departed for heaven in various celestial vehicles.
Having witnessed that great marvel before his very eyes, he desired to attain heaven himself.
With joyful hearts, those heroes quickly rushed at one another;
chariot-warriors fought wondrously with chariot-warriors in the battle,
as did foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, elephants with elephants, and horses with horses.
When the battle had thus proceeded, causing the destruction of elephants, horses,
and men, and when the army was shrouded in dust, one's own men struck their own and the enemies struck their enemies;
the combat shone with hair-to-hair tugging, tusks-to-tusks grating, and nail-to-nail tearing.
Fists and wrestling— both of which destroy the impurities of the body—
proceed thus in that battle where elephants, horses, and men are being destroyed;
from the bodies of men, horses, and elephants, a river of blood flows forth.
She carried away many fallen bodies of men, horses, and elephants; in that dense throng of men,
horses, and elephants, there arose a most terrible river with blood for its water and red mud for its silt, flowing from those men, horses, elephants, and their riders.
Carrying the bodies of men, horses, and elephants, that river was terrifying to the timid;
yet those seeking victory crossed to its further shore,
some by wading, others leaping, and still others by repeatedly sinking and surfacing.
With their limbs smeared with blood, their armor, weapons, and garments dyed red,
they bathed in that [blood], drank it, and grew faint, O bull of the Bharatas—
[bathing] in the chariots, horses, men, elephants, and weapons and ornaments.
Then, seeing garments and armor, those being slain and those already killed,
we mostly beheld blood upon the earth, in the sky, in heaven, and in all directions;
indeed, by the scent, the touch, and the taste of that blood—
O Bhārata, with his surpassing form and his spreading roar, a very great despondency took hold of the army for the most part. That army of yours was then utterly shattered by those led by Bhīmasena.
Once again, the heroic car-warriors led by Sātyaki rushed forward.
O King, unable to withstand the force of those high-souled warriors as they charged,
your sons' great army turned its back in retreat.
With its chariots, horses, and elephants scattered, crowded with men and steeds, its shields and armor shattered, and its weapons and bows cast aside,
your army fled, being churned from every side.
"Just like a herd of elephants in the great forest tormented by a lion," Sañjaya said:
"Seeing the Pāṇḍavas rushing toward them, your army..."
O great king, Duryodhana restrained his warriors and his own army from all sides; yet, O bull of the Bharatas,
despite your son crying out, they did not turn back, O King.
Then, from the wings, the flanks, and even from the right flanks,
the Kurus, with weapons raised, rushed against Bhīma in battle.
Karna, too, saw the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fleeing with their backs turned.
He spoke these words to the King of Madra: "Go toward Bhīmaratha.
Thus addressed by Karṇa, Śalya, the lord of the Madras, then urged those foremost steeds, white as swans, toward where Vṛkodara was.
O great king, those horses, urged on by Śalya who shines in battle, reached Bhīmasena’s chariot and drew it to a halt. Seeing Karṇa approaching, Bhīma was filled with rage.
O bull of the Bharatas, he set his mind upon the destruction of Karṇa.
He then spoke to the hero Sātyaki and to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata:
"Protect this king, the righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira."
While I was looking on, somehow freed from great danger,
that king was placed before me with all his retinue stripped away by the evil-souled son of Rādhā for the sake of pleasing Duryodhana.
"O son of Pṛṣata, today I shall bring an end to that suffering;
either I shall slay Karṇa in battle, or he shall slay me.
In this most terrible conflict, I tell you this as the truth."
"Today I give this king to you as a trust;
all of you, free from anxiety, strive to protect him.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed one set out toward the son of Adhiratha.
Making all the directions resound with a great lion’s roar,
the powerful lord of the Madras, seeing Bhīma approaching swiftly and delighting in battle, then spoke to the son of the Sūta.
"Behold, O Karṇa, the mighty-armed son of the Pāṇḍavas, enraged;
he surely desires to release upon you the anger he has accumulated over a long period. Never before have I seen his form appear in such a manner."
O Karṇa, when Abhimanyu was slain, or even when the Rākṣasa Ghaṭotkaca was killed,
he who was capable of resisting all the three worlds in his wrath assumed such a formidable form, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
O King, while the lord of the Madras was speaking thus to the son of Rādhā,
Vṛkodara, blazing with rage, rushed toward Karṇa;
and seeing Bhīma approaching in that manner, eager for battle, [the king spoke].
The son of Rādhā, as if laughing, spoke these words to Śalya:
"O Lord of the Madra people, O powerful one, that which you have said to me today regarding Bhīmasena is true; there is no doubt in this matter."
This Vṛkodara is both a hero and a warrior, yet prone to anger;
he is indifferent toward his own body and life, and possesses superior strength.
This was while he was living in concealment in the city of Virāṭa at that time.
Desiring to do what was pleasing to Draupadī, Kīcaka, relying solely on the strength of his arms and adopting a hidden purpose, was slain along with his followers;
yet today, he stands at the head of the battle, armored and frantic with rage.
One might even go to battle against Death himself, with his staff raised by his servants;
yet this has been my long-cherished desire:
that I should slay Arjuna in combat, or that Dhanañjaya should slay me.

"O Śalya, that very great doubt of mine might perhaps be resolved this very day through an encounter with Bhīma; for having encountered Bhīma, the tamer of foes, [my fate is uncertain]. Whether Bhīmasena be slain or rendered carless,"
"If Pārtha advances against me, it will be well for me;
therefore, quickly determine what you deem appropriate in this matter.
Having encountered Bhīmasena, I shall be able to turn back."
I consider Māruti to be the personified lord of the Maruts;
here, I am able to withstand Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma,
the twins, and likewise Yama, the wielder of the staff who possesses the splendor of Yama.
"Let this battle be a source of happiness for us through them alone;
I shall go against Bībhatsu, who wields the mace. Having heard these words of the high-souled son of Rādhā, [he departed].
Śalya spoke these words to the son of the Sūta who stood before him:
"O mighty-armed one, advance against the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena;
having repelled Bhīmasena, you shall then reach Phalguna."
Fight without hesitation, displaying your full prowess!
O Karṇa, that desire which has long been cherished in your heart shall surely be fulfilled; I tell you this truly.
When this had been said, Karṇa then spoke again to Śalya:
"I shall slay Arjuna in battle, or Dhanañjaya shall slay me.
Having spoken thus, O King, Rādheya, the best of chariot-warriors, [proceeded].
"Fixing your mind on battle, go! Go! he urged. Then, O lord of the people, Śalya quickly set out with his chariot to where the great archer Bhīma was putting the army to flight.
Then, O Indra among kings, at the encounter between Karṇa and Bhīma, the sound of trumpets and the great roar of kettledrums arose. Then Bhīmasena, filled with rage, [assailed] your invincible army.
With bright and sharp iron arrows, the mighty one put the quarters of the sky to flight.
O lord of the people, that tumultuous encounter between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava in battle was fierce and terrible in form, O great king.
Then, O Indra among kings, after a mere moment, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena, the son of Pāṇḍu, rushed toward Karṇa as if laughing, without much difficulty.
Seeing him rushing toward him, Karṇa Vaikartana, the bull among men,
struck him in the chest between the breasts with an iron shaft (nārāca) in his wrath; then,
that one of immeasurable soul again covered him with showers of arrows.
Pierced by the son of the Sūta, he covered him with feathered shafts;
he struck Karna with nine sharp, straight-knotted arrows.
Then Karna cut his bow in two at the middle with a winged shaft.
Then, he pierced that man whose bow was broken between the breasts with a very sharp iron shaft capable of piercing all armor. Taking up another bow, Vṛkodara [struck] the son of the Sūta.

O King, having pierced the vital spots with well-sharpened arrows, he who was skilled in the knowledge of the vital spots uttered a powerful roar, as if making heaven and earth tremble. Karṇa struck him in return with twenty-five iron shafts.
Like an elephant intoxicated with rut and arrogant in the forest [struck] by firebrands,
the Pāṇḍava, his limbs pierced by arrows, was then overwhelmed with rage;
his eyes copper-red with fury and indignation, he desired the slaughter of the Sūta’s son.
He fixed upon his bow an excellent arrow of great velocity, capable of achieving a heavy task and able to pierce even mountains;
then the son of Māruta, having drawn the powerful bow back as far as his ear, released it.
The great archer, enraged and desiring to slay Karṇa, released it.
That arrow, discharged by the powerful one with a sound like a thunderbolt,
tore through Karṇa in battle like the force of a thunderbolt splitting a mountain.
O best of the Kurus, struck by Bhīmasena, that son of a Sūta,
the commander of the army and subduer of foes, sat down on the floor of his chariot unconscious,
his limbs drenched in blood as if his life had departed.
In the meantime, seeing Vṛkodara approaching to cut out his tongue, the King of Madra spoke these words to him consolingly:
"O mighty-armed Bhīmasena, listen to what I shall say to you."
"Having heard these words, which are endowed with reason, act accordingly. Arjuna has vowed the slaughter of the powerful Karṇa.
Bhīma said:
Act accordingly, may you be blessed, regarding that vow of Savyasācin;
O best of kings, I know the firmness of Pārtha’s resolve.
Yet that wicked man has committed an insult against the king in my very presence.
Then, overcome by anger, I paid no heed to the consequences; even when Rādheya had fallen, my wrath did not subside. In my view, the time had come for him to have his tongue torn out.
But while we were present among the assembled kings, O uncle, this cruel and base man made us hear many words addressed to Kṛṣṇā that were utterly unbearable.
"O King, even though you were far away, you surely understood that;
the cutting off of his tongue was exactly what I desired. Out of a wish to do what was pleasing to the king, this time has been waited for."

But as for the words spoken by you, O Great King, which were endowed with reason and purpose, they were received by me like a bitter medicine; for Bibhatsu, having failed in his vow, would never live.
If he is destroyed, we are all destroyed, including Keśava.
And today, that cruel-souled, sinful wretch, the foremost of evildoers,
shall meet his downfall the moment he is beheld by Kirīṭin.
Previously consumed by the wrath of Yudhiṣṭhira,
that perpetrator of cruelty has today been protected by you through skillful means from my presence.
Then the lord of Madra, seeing the son of the Sūta unconscious, [acted].
He carried Karna, the ornament of the battlefield, away from the fray in his chariot. Then,
once Karna had been defeated, Bhimasena put to flight the great army of Dhritarashtra’s sons, just as Indra routed the host of the Danavas.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Sañjaya, this deed performed by Bhīma is exceedingly difficult to accomplish,
by which the mighty-armed Karṇa was struck down upon the seat of his chariot."
"O Sūta, Duryodhana said to me again and again: 'Karna alone shall slay the Sṛñjayas along with the Pāṇḍavas in battle.
But having seen the son of Rādhā defeated by Bhīma in the encounter,"
"What did my son Duryodhana do after that?
Sanjaya said:
"Having seen the son of Radha, the Suta's son, bewildered in that great battle..."
O King, with a great army, he addressed his brothers:
"Go quickly, may prosperity be yours; protect the son of Rādhā as he sinks into a fathomless ocean of calamity through fear of Bhīmasena."
Commanded by the king and desiring to slay Bhīmasena, they advanced in great rage like moths into a fire— Śrutāyu, Durdhara, Krātha, Vivitsu, Vikaṭa, and Sama.
Niṣaṅgin, Kavacin, Pāśin, as well as Nanda and Upanandaka;
Duṣpradharṣa, Subāhu, Vātavega, Suvarcas,
Dhanurgrāha, Durmada, as well as Sattvasama and Saha.
These heroic and mighty warriors, surrounded by chariots,
approached Bhīmasena and hemmed him in from all sides;
they discharged volleys of arrows of various kinds in every direction.
O lord of men, while being thus assailed by them, the immensely powerful Bhīmasena swiftly slew fifty chariot-warriors with fifty chariots as your sons were charging forward.
Then, enraged at Vivitsu, he struck off his head with a broad-headed arrow;
that head, adorned with earrings and a helmet, resembling the full moon,
shone, O great king, like the full moon in the sky.
And by Bhīma, O great king, he fell slain upon the earth. Seeing that hero struck down, O Lord, his brothers rushed from all sides in battle toward Bhīma of terrible prowess.
Then, with two other broad-headed arrows in that great battle, Bhīma of terrible prowess took the lives of your two sons in the encounter;
they fell to the earth like two trees uprooted by the wind.
O King, both Vikaṭa and Sama were like the offspring of gods;
then Bhīma, acting with haste, dispatched Krātha to the abode of Yama,
and struck down by a very sharp iron arrow (nārāca), he fell to the earth.
Then, O lord of men, a fierce cry of "Alas!
Alas! arose as those archers, your sons, were being slain, O King;
while their army was thus thrown into confusion, the mighty Bhimasena [advanced].
He sent Nanda and Upananda to the abode of Yama in battle.
Then your sons, terrified and overwhelmed, fled,
seeing Bhīmasena in the fray resembling Kāla, Antaka, and Yama.
Seeing your sons slain, the high-minded son of the Sūta once again urged his swan-colored horses toward where the Pāṇḍava was. O great king, those horses were dispatched by the King of Madra.

Having reached Bhīmasena’s chariot, they impetuously engaged him in combat. O lord of the people, that tumultuous encounter between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava in battle was fierce and terrible in form, O great king.
O Great King, seeing those two great chariot-warriors come together, the thought occurred to me: "How indeed will this turn out today?
He struck him with many arrows and struck down his standard with a single shaft.
And with a broad-headed arrow, he dispatched his charioteer to death;
then, having swiftly severed the Pāṇḍava’s bow with a feathered shaft,
Bhīma, who delights in battle, covered him with arrows.
O great king, while your sons were looking on in the battle,
Karna— well-versed in supreme weapons— then became violently enraged and pierced Bhima with nine iron, straight-knotted *bhalla* arrows.
Struck thus, the mighty-armed Bhīma of terrible prowess pierced Karṇa with seven arrows drawn back to his ear.
Then, O great king, Karṇa hissed like a venomous serpent.
With a great shower of arrows, he covered the Pāṇḍava; Bhīma also, having covered that great car-warrior with volleys of arrows while the Kauravas looked on, roared aloud, O one of great strength.
Then Karṇa, becoming violently enraged, took up a firm bow and pierced Bhīma with ten heron-feathered arrows sharpened on stone;
he also cut through his bow with a whetted broad-headed shaft.

Then the mighty-armed Bhīma, desiring the death of Karṇa, took up a terrible iron club adorned with golden bands— resembling a second staff of Death— and, roaring, hurled it, for he was possessed of exceeding strength.
As that iron club, sounding like a thunderbolt or lightning, came rushing toward him,
Karṇa shattered it into many pieces with arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then Bhīma took up an even more formidable bow.
He covered Karṇa, the crusher of enemy forces, with his arrows.
Then a terrible battle took place between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava on the field,
like that between two leaders of monkeys who repeatedly sought each other's death.
Then, O great king, Karna, having drawn his bow firmly to his ear, pierced Bhimasena with three arrows right up to the root of his hair.
Thus deeply pierced by Karna, that great archer, the best among the strong, [stood firm].
He took up a terrible arrow capable of rending Karna’s body;
having pierced through his armor and his body,
O King, that shaft entered the earth like a serpent entering an anthill.
Afflicted by that severe blow and as if overwhelmed,
Karṇa trembled on his chariot like a mountain during an earthquake.
Then, O great king, Karṇa was filled with rage and indignation.
He struck the Pāṇḍava with twenty-five iron shafts;
then, O Indra among kings, after a mere moment and without much difficulty,
Karna— smiling as it were— deprived Bhima of terrible deeds of his chariot.
Deprived of his chariot, O best of the Bharatas, that man who was like the wind laughed aloud; then, indignant and possessed of great splendor, that foremost of car-warriors,
the mighty-armed one, fell from his excellent chariot with mace in hand.
O lord of the people, having leaped with speed upon your army,
Bhīma scattered it with his mace, just as the wind disperses clouds of autumn.
And with his mace, O great king, he struck the pole of Karṇa’s chariot.
Enraged in battle, that scorcher of enemies struck him down;
the powerful son of Pāṇḍu, having fallen under the sway of wrath,
that hero drove back your sons with his mace in the great conflict.
As if laughing, he struck Karṇa and Śalya simultaneously with his mace and felled them onto the floorboards of their chariots; having slain them, he let out a great roar.
O King, he also destroyed seven hundred attacking elephants with tusks as long as plow-poles.
Bhīma, the scorcher of foes, assuming a wrathful form, suddenly struck him violently;
knowing the vital spots, he roared and struck him fiercely in the gums, the eyes, the temples, the cheeks, and even in his other vulnerable parts.
Afflicted by the son of the Wind-god and crying out in extreme distress,
they fled in fear; yet, being driven back again,
they were hemmed in by the elephant-keepers like clouds surrounding the sun.
Standing on the ground, he struck those seven hundred elephants— along with their riders, weapons, and banners— with his mace, just as the wind scatters autumnal clouds.
Then, [he attacked] the exceedingly powerful elephants of Subala’s son once again.
The son of Kuntī crushed fifty-two [warriors] in battle;
likewise, the Pāṇḍava slew more than a hundred chariots and hundreds of other foot soldiers in the fight, scorching your army.
Scorched by the sun and by the high-souled Bhīma,
your army shriveled up like a piece of leather placed in a fire.
O bull of the Bharatas, your men were utterly terrified by the fear of Bhīma.
Abandoning Bhīma in the battle, they fled in the ten directions;
five hundred other rattling chariots, their warriors clad in shields and armor,
swiftly rushed toward Bhīma from all sides with volleys of arrows.

Bhīma crushed all of them— along with their charioteers, chariots, banners, standards, and weapons— with his mace, just as Viṣṇu destroyed the Asuras. Then, the horsemen designated by Śakuni, who were esteemed as heroes, [rushed forward].
Three thousand [Yavanas], with spears, double-edged swords, and darts in their hands, advanced toward Bhīma.
Rushing out to meet those Yavana horsemen,
the slayer of foremost enemies moved through various maneuvers, striking them down and crushing them.
A great sound arose from them all as they were struck,
O Bhārata, like that of reeds being cut down by swords;
thus did the son of Subala [slay] three thousand excellent horses.
Having slain the other [charioteer], he mounted another chariot and, filled with rage, rushed toward the son of Rādhā.
O King, Karṇa also, in that battle, covered the subduer of enemies, the son of Dharma,
with arrows and struck down his charioteer as well.
Then, seeing the chariot fleeing in battle, that great car-warrior pursued it,
scattering straight-flying arrows feathered with heron plumes;
he covered the king as he rushed forward, filling both heaven and earth with his shafts.
Enraged, the son of the Wind-god covered him with a net of arrows. Then Rādheya, the crusher of enemies, quickly turned back and covered Bhīma on all sides with sharpened shafts.
O Bhārata, while Karṇa was preoccupied with Bhīmasena’s chariot, the immeasurable-souled Sātyaki attacked him in order to seize his rear;
though he was severely afflicted by arrows, Karṇa turned back against him.
Those two high-minded bulls among all archers, having encountered one another, shone brilliantly as they discharged variegated arrows.
O king of kings, by those two, a terrifying sight was spread across the sky.

A fierce mass of arrows, as red as the back of a *krauñca* bird, was seen; we could no longer perceive the light of the sun, nor the sky, nor the cardinal or intermediate directions— how much less anything else—
for by those two, thousands of arrows were discharged.
O King, at midday, as the sun blazed with great radiance,
all its rays were then seized by the showers of arrows from Karṇa and the descendant of Madhu.
[They struck] the son of Subala, Kṛtavarman, the son of Droṇa, the son of Adhiratha, and Kṛpa.
Seeing the Kurus engaged in combat with the Pāṇḍavas, they turned back once more;
O lord of the people, the sound of those charging forward was as fierce and terrifying as that of oceans tossed by rain.
Seeing each other in that great battle, those two armies, though deeply agitated,
were filled with great joy as they grappled one another; then,
when the sun had reached the meridian, the combat commenced.
Indeed, such a sight had never been seen before, nor even heard of; yet,
having encountered that flood of force in battle,
this flood of force suddenly approached with speed, like a torrent of water rushing toward the ocean.
A truly great clamor arose from the masses of troops as they roared at one another,
like the immense sound of the surging waves of the ocean. Those two armies, possessing great momentum, having encountered each other, [rushed forward].
O lord of men, they rushed forward with speed against one another; having attained a state of union like two rivers at their confluence,
O ruler of the people, a battle of terrible form then commenced.
Filled with great joy, the soldiers of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas—
both Kurus and Pāṇḍavas seeking great glory—
uttered continuous shouts as they roared there.
O King, descendant of Bharata, various [names] are heard being uttered in reference to individuals;
for whatever defect a man may have— whether on his father's side, his mother's side, or even regarding his actions or character— he causes that very thing to be proclaimed in battle.

Seeing those heroes in battle threatening one another, O King, the thought occurred to me: "There is no life left for them. Indeed, I beheld the forms of those enraged warriors of immeasurable splendor.
"A fierce fear arose within me: 'How will this come to pass?
Then, O King, those Pāṇḍavas and the great car-warriors among the Kauravas hacked at one another with sharp arrows, intent on slaying each other.
Saṃjaya said:
O great king, those kṣatriyas, harboring mutual enmity and desiring to slay one another,
struck each other down in battle.
O great king, multitudes of chariots, multitudes of horses, multitudes of men, and multitudes of elephants were locked in combat with one another on all sides;
and maces, iron clubs, and *kaṇapas* were being hurled.
In that exceedingly terrible battle, we beheld the falling of lances, *bhiṇḍipālas*, and *bhuśuṇḍīs* from every side; showers of arrows fell on all sides like swarms of locusts.
Elephants, having encountered elephants, struck one another;
likewise, horses against horses, chariot-warriors against chariot-warriors in that battle,
and foot-soldiers against groups of foot-soldiers, and horses against groups of horses.
O King, foot soldiers crushed chariots, elephants, and chariots with horses; likewise,
elephants, horses, and chariots—
those swift-moving creatures— crushed the three-fold army in battle.
O noble one, the horses crushed three divisions,
and the men likewise crushed three divisions; O noble one, the chariots also crushed three divisions,
with arrows, tomara-spears, iron shafts, maces, javelins, and battle-axes.
As those heroes fell there and cried out to one another,
the battlefield became as terrible as a slaughter of animals;
O Bhārata, the earth shone, strewn all over with blood.

The earth was like the ground in the rainy season strewn with swarms of *śakragopa* insects, or like a youthful, dark-complexioned woman wearing two white garments dyed with saffron; such was the appearance of the Vasundharā.
The earth shone with the heads of those bull-eyed men, adorned with beautiful earrings and excellent crest-jewels,
which had been cast down; it appeared as if variegated with flesh and blood, yet as if made of gold.
O best of the Bharatas, the earth shone as if with fires whose flames had been extinguished,
strewn with severed heads, arms along with thighs,
and scattered earrings and ornaments, O Bhārata.
There, heaps of gold coins, necklaces, bodies of archers,
and armor with banners fell upon the earth;
the ground became almost impassable and extremely difficult to traverse on all sides.
Elephants, having encountered other elephants, tore them apart with the tips of their tusks;
struck by those tusks, they shone like elephants with blood-drenched limbs,
resembling streams of red chalk.
Just as mountains adorned with minerals shine as they move,
so did the elephants gleam in battle, drenched in blood.
They encountered many lances released by the elephants, which were aimed directly at them.
Those elephants moved about with their trunks, while others likewise broke [the enemy] apart;
with their armor pierced by iron shafts, O Great King, those excellent elephants shone like cloudless mountains at the onset of winter.
O noble one, the best of elephants, covered with gold-feathered arrows,
shone like mountains whose peaks are set ablaze by meteors;
some mountain-like elephants were struck down upon the earth by other elephants.
In that battle, they fell like winged mountains;
other elephants fled, afflicted by darts and tormented by wounds,
falling upon the earth with their frontal globes and temples in that great conflict.
Others sat down like lions, uttering terrible roars;
many grew faint, O King, while others likewise cried out in distress.
And horses, adorned with golden trappings and ornaments, were struck down by arrows.
They sat down, fainted, and wandered in the ten directions;
others, being dragged along, writhed upon the surface of the earth and assumed many different postures as they were struck by arrows and *tomaras*.
O noble one, men were slain upon the ground, groaning there;
others, O Bhārata, saw their kinsmen, some their fathers, and others their grandfathers,
while others there saw their enemies fleeing.
They called out to one another, proclaiming their clan names.
O Great King, their arms, adorned with golden ornaments, were severed;
they writhed, twisted, fell down, and leaped up again.
They fell upon the ground and quivered by the thousands;
others in that battle displayed such speed as serpents hissing.
O lord of the people, those arms, smeared with sandalwood paste, resembled the coils of snakes.
Drenched in blood, they trembled violently like golden banners. As that terrible and chaotic battle raged in every direction,
they fought on without being recognized, slaughtering one another.
Covered by the dust raised by the earth and thick with the clashing of weapons, O King, neither one's own men nor the enemy could be distinguished, as everything was shrouded in darkness;
thus did that battle become terrible in form and fearsome.
There, great rivers with blood for their waters flowed repeatedly;
they were covered with heads for stones, hair for moss and grass,
strewn with heaps of bones, and filled with excellent bows and arrows.
With mud of flesh and most dreadful floods of blood,
they set flowing rivers that increase the realm of Yama—
causing terror to the timid and increasing the joy of the brave.
Those rivers of terrible form, leading [souls] to the abode of Yama,
deep and submerging, produced fear among the kṣatriyas;
O tiger among men, there, in various places, the flesh-eating beasts were roaring.
The terrible battlefield became like the city of the King of the Dead;
countless headless trunks (kabandhas) rose up on all sides,
and throngs of spirits, satiated with flesh and blood, were indeed dancing.
Having drunk blood there, O Bhārata, and having drunk fat,
they were indeed satiated with marrow, fat,
and flesh; and flocks of crows, vultures, and cranes were seen running about.
But the heroes in that battle, O King, having cast off fear— which is so difficult to abandon—
and being renowned for their warrior's vow, performed their deeds fearlessly amidst the carnage strewn with arrows and spears and teeming with throngs of flesh-eating beasts.
The heroes moved about with their troops, proclaiming their own prowess;
O Bhārata, they made known to one another their names and lineages,
as well as the names of their fathers and their ancestral clans throughout the battle.

O lord of the people, while that battle was proceeding— terrible in form and exceedingly cruel— the many warriors there cried out to one another as they crushed each other with spears, lances, and sharp-edged clubs.
The Kaurava army despaired like a shattered ship in the ocean.
Sañjaya said:
While that battle was then proceeding, which caused the submersion of the kṣatriyas...
O noble one, the great roar of the Gāṇḍīva was heard in battle where the Pāṇḍava wrought slaughter among the Saṃśaptakas,
as well as among the Kosalas and the Nārāyaṇa force, O King.

But the Saṃśaptakas, greedy for victory and filled with fury, let fall a shower of arrows from all sides upon the head of Pārtha in that battle. O King, the lord [Arjuna] suddenly held back that shower by his own power.
Pārtha, the best among chariot-warriors, plunged into the battle, slaughtering his foes;
having checked the division of chariots with stone-sharpened arrows feathered with heron plumes,
Pārtha encountered the great car-warrior Suśarman in the fray.
That best of chariot-warriors showered him with volleys of arrows,
as did the Saṃśaptakas stationed in battle against Pārtha;
then Suśarman pierced Pārtha with nine swift shafts.
O noble one, Suśarman, overwhelmed with rage, struck Janārdana in the right arm with three arrows;
then, O King, with another broad-headed shaft,
he pierced his standard in that battle.
O King, that great and excellent monkey, fashioned by Viśvakarman, let out a tremendous roar and bellowed, terrifying them indeed. Upon hearing the cry of the ape, your army was struck with terror.
Taking up immense fear, she became motionless.
Then, O King, that army, standing still and motionless,
shone like the Caitraratha forest strewn with various flowers.
Then, O best of the Kurus, having regained their senses,
those warriors showered Arjuna with arrows like clouds drenching a mountain;
they all then surrounded that great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍava.
Having seized him, they cried out while being struck by sharp arrows;
overcome with rage, they rushed forward from all sides to capture him. Having seized his chariot, those thousands of warriors [surrounded him].
They indeed formed a circular array (*rathabandha*) against the Pāṇḍava of immeasurable prowess;
some mounted their chariots, desiring to seize both Pārtha and Kṛṣṇa,
while those warriors of the Saṃśaptakas let out lion-like roars.
That chariot of the high-souled Pāṇḍava was seized by them, yet it continued to move forward;
that was indeed like a marvel.
Then the mighty-armed Pārtha remained surrounded by those great car-warriors.
Seeing the chariot held fast and those many [enemies] rushing toward it,
they all cried out for the destruction of the chariot in that great battle,
O Bhārata, as they struck at the horses, the chariot wheels, and the chariot poles.
Having seized him with great force, they quickly let out lion-like roars;
others, O Great King, joyfully seized the mighty arms of Keśava, while still others seized Pārtha as he stood upon his chariot.
Then Keśava, shaking his arms at the head of the battle,
struck them all down like a rogue elephant striking other elephants.
Thereupon, Pārtha, surrounded by those great chariot-warriors, became enraged in the fray.
Seeing the chariot checked and Keśava also rushing forward,
he struck down many who were mounted on chariots as well as those on foot;
then, with arrows suited for close combat, he felled the warriors who had drawn near.
Having scorched them in battle, Pārtha, the conqueror of enemy cities,
caused them to fall in the encounter and spoke thus to Keśava:
"Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, the hosts of Saṃśaptakas by me!"
"O bull among the Yadus, while they perform such cruel deeds and are being slain by the thousands,
there is no man whatsoever on this earth who could withstand this terrible array of chariots, other than myself."
"Behold them today in battle,
O Kṛṣṇa, being struck down in the fray by my well-sharpened arrows, which are like venomous serpents,"—
having spoken thus, Bībhatsu blew his conch, Devadatta.
The immeasurable-souled one caused Devadatta to resound in the great battle.
Hearing the sound of Devadatta, the highly illustrious Keśava,
Kṛṣṇa, likewise blew the Pāñcajanya conch, as if filling both heaven and earth.
O great king, hearing that sound of the conch, the army of the Saṃśaptakas trembled and became utterly terrified;
then the Pāṇḍava, the slayer of enemy heroes, laid a trap for their feet.
O Great King, having repeatedly unleashed the Nāga weapon,
Pārtha, as if smiling, then manifested the Nāga weapon;
for he, the knower of great weapons, bound their feet with it.
O King, those whom Pārtha targeted in battle with the "foot-binding" maneuver were bound by that high-souled Pāṇḍava;
rendered motionless, they became like they were made of solid stone.
Then the son of Pāṇḍu slew those motionless warriors,
just as Indra of old slew the Daityas in battle during the slaughter of Tāraka.
As they were being slaughtered in the fray, they abandoned that excellent chariot.
They began to cast away all their weapons,
but being bound by the foot-fetter, O King, they were unable to move;
then Pārtha struck them down with straight-knotted arrows.
Indeed, all the warriors in that battle were enveloped by serpents.
Then, O king of kings, seeing his army seized, the great car-warrior Suśarman quickly invoked the Sāuparṇa weapon.
Then the Suparṇas swooped down, devouring the serpents;
seeing those sky-rangers, O King, the Nāgas fled in all directions. Released from their fetters, O lord of the people, that army shone brightly.
Like the sun released from a mass of clouds, scorching all creatures,
those warriors, once liberated, discharged volleys of arrows and multitudes of weapons toward Phalguna’s chariot, O noble one.
Various weapons were hurled from all sides;
having cut down that rain of great missiles with his own showers of arrows,
the son of Vāsava, the slayer of enemy heroes, then stood firm against the warriors.
Then, O King, Suśarman, having pierced Arjuna in the heart with a straight-knotted arrow, struck him with three other shafts.
That great archer, deeply pierced by those arrows resembling venomous serpents, [remained firm].
O great king, the great car-warrior Pārtha, overcome with rage, then covered Suśarman in that battle with hundreds of arrows in an instant; there,
the master of great weapons obstructed all directions with his shafts.
Having turned Suśarman away in battle, Dhanañjaya [struck him];
deeply pierced and pained, he sat down upon the floor of his chariot.
Then everyone cried out, "Pārtha has been slain!"
Then there arose the blaring of conchs and the resonant sounds of kettledrums,
the clamor of various musical instruments, and lion-like roars. Then, having regained consciousness, he whose horses are white and whose charioteer is Kṛṣṇa—
The one of immeasurable soul, acting with haste, manifested the Aindra weapon. Then, O noble king, thousands of arrows appeared in all directions, slaughtering the elephants, O monarch.
With weapons, O King, he struck horses and chariots by the hundreds of thousands in that battle;
he shone in the fray like Śakra slaying the Asuras.
Then, as the army was being slaughtered, a vast terror took hold of them.
O Bhārata, among the hosts of Saṃśaptakas and the Gopālas,
there was not a single man there who could fight against Arjuna; while those heroes looked on, that great army was slaughtered.

Seeing him being struck down, we were rendered motionless in our prowess. Having slain ten thousand warriors there in battle, O King, the son of Pāṇḍu shone resplendent in the fray like a blazing fire without smoke.
O Bhārata, of those remaining fourteen thousand chariots,
ten thousand and three thousand elephants,
the Saṃśaptakas then once again surrounded Dhanañjaya.
Having resolved that they must either die or achieve victory and retreat,
O lord of the people, a great battle took place there between your men and the heroic,
powerful Pāṇḍava Kirīṭin.
Having conquered them, Pārtha struck down those enemies as Śakra struck down the Asuras.
Saṃjaya said:
O noble one, Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and the Sūta’s son—
Seeing the army sinking, afflicted by fear of the sons of Pāṇḍu, Ulūka, the son of Subala, and the king along with his brothers,
rushed forward with speed, desiring to rescue it like a shattered boat in the ocean.
Then, O Bhārata, for a mere moment there was a battle that was exceedingly fierce—
instilling terror in the timid and increasing the joy of the brave.
[It involved] Bhīmasena, together with the Pañcālas, surrounded by the Cedis and the Kaikeyas.
Vaikartana himself, fighting with his bows, held them back;
then, while Bhīmasena looked on, the enraged Karṇa struck down the great car-warriors of the Cedis, Karūṣas, and Sṛñjayas.
The showers of arrows released by Kṛpa in that battle were felled by the Sṛñjayas like swarms of locusts;
then Śikhaṇḍin, filled with rage, quickly advanced against Gautama.
He rained showers of arrows from every side upon the Brahmin;
at that moment, for a brief instant, a great and terrible battle ensued,
O King, like the encounter between the enraged Rāma and Rāvaṇa in combat.
But Kṛpa, an expert in great weapons, having warded off that shower of arrows,
angrily pierced Śikhaṇḍin in battle with ten shafts.
Then Śikhaṇḍin, enraged, [pierced him] in the combat with seven arrows.
He pierced Kṛpa very deeply with straight-flying arrows feathered with heron plumes.
Then that great car-warrior Kṛpa, having been deeply pierced by those sharp arrows,
[was struck] further by whetted, keen, gold-adorned razor-headed shafts.
The best of the twice-born deprived the son of Pṛṣata of his horses, charioteer,
and chariot. Then, leaping down from that vehicle whose horses had been slain, the great car-warrior seized a shield and a sword and quickly rushed toward the brahmin.
As he was rushing forward suddenly, [Arjuna] covered him in battle with straight-jointed arrows; it was like a marvel. There we beheld a wonder, as if stones were floating.
O King, when Śikhaṇḍin stood motionless in battle,
O best of monarchs, having seen Śikhaṇḍin covered by Kṛpa,
the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna quickly advanced against Kṛpa.
Then, as Dhṛṣṭadyumna advanced toward the chariot of Śaradvat’s son,
the great car-warrior Kṛtavarman impetuously opposed him;
likewise, he encountered Yudhiṣṭhira as he approached the chariot of Śaradvat’s son.
The son of Droṇa held back [Yudhiṣṭhira] along with his sons and his army;
and your son, warding them off with a shower of arrows, received the two great car-warriors Nakula and Sahadeva as they rushed forward.
O Bhārata, Karṇa Vaikartana held back Bhīmasena, the Karūṣas, the Kekayas, and the Sṛñjayas in battle. Then,
in that conflict, Kṛpa Śāradvata [fired] arrows at Śikhaṇḍin.
O noble one, filled with haste and as if desiring to consume him,
he dispatched those arrows; but [the opponent], brandishing and whirling his sword again and again, cut down those gold-adorned shafts sent by him from all sides.
Then Gautama quickly pierced the shield of the son of Pṛṣata, which was adorned with a hundred moons, with his arrows; thereupon the people raised a great shout.
Deprived of his shield, O Great King, he rushed forward with sword in hand.

O King, Suketu, the son of Citraketu, quickly advanced toward the mighty warrior who had fallen under Kṛpa’s power like a sick man into the jaws of death, and who was being tormented and seized by the arrows of Śāradvata.
Scattering the Brāhmaṇa in battle with many sharpened arrows,
he of immeasurable soul rushed toward Gautama’s chariot. Seeing that Brāhmaṇa, who was firm in his vows, to be irresistible in combat, [he attacked].
Then, O best of kings, Śikhaṇḍin quickly retreated. Thereupon,
O King, Suketu pierced Gautama with nine arrows,
and having struck him, he pierced him again with seventy and once more with three arrows.
Then, O noble one, he again cut his bow along with the arrow,
and struck his charioteer violently in a vital spot with an arrow.
Thereupon, Gautama, filled with rage, took up a new and sturdy bow.
He struck Suketu in all his vital parts with thirty arrows;
with all his limbs overwhelmed, he trembled upon his excellent chariot,
just as a tree shakes violently when shaken during an earthquake.
From that moving body, he struck off the head— blazing with earrings,
complete with turban and helmet— using a razor-edged arrow.
That head fell to the ground like a piece of meat snatched by a hawk.
Then, having fallen, his body reached the earth;
when he was slain, O Great King, his followers were terrified and,
abandoning Gautama in the battle, fled in the ten directions.
Having checked Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle, the mighty Kṛtavarman, filled with courage, said to the son of Pṛṣata, "Stay! Stay!
Then a tumultuous battle took place between the Vṛṣṇi and the Pārṣata in that conflict.
O King, just as two hawks or two vultures fight for the sake of meat,
so did Dhṛṣṭadyumna, enraged in battle, strike the son of Hṛdika in the chest with nine arrows, afflicting that scion of the Hṛdika clan.
But Kṛtavarman, having been struck hard by the son of Pṛṣata in battle,
covered the son of Pṛṣata— along with his chariot and horses— with arrows.
O King, being thus covered along with his chariot, Dhṛṣṭadyumna could no longer be seen.
Like the sun shrouded by clouds at the onset of the rainy season,
O King, Dhṛṣṭadyumna— though wounded in battle— shone forth after dispersing that multitude of arrows with his own gold-adorned shafts.
Then the son of Pṛṣata, the commander of the army, filled with rage, approached Kṛtavarman and unleashed a most terrible shower of weapons. That dense shower of weapons fell upon him suddenly.
With many thousands of arrows, the son of Hṛdika scattered them in battle;
just as one with a golden chariot might mingle the horses with horses in combat,
even so, O King, did the Sātvata mingle the horses with horses.
Taking up his shield and sword, he leaped onto the chariot of that [prince]. Then,
as the horses were mingled together and the son of Pṛṣata was close at hand,
the Sātvata, beholding his feat, quickly seized his mace.
Then, O King, the mace-bearer quickly leaped down from his chariot;
not seeing him there, he struck the charioteer on the seat of the chariot with a sharp-edged sword, and being slain, he fell from the chariot.
Then Kṛtavarman, filled with joy, made a sound by slapping his palms;
O King, he called out to the son of Pṛṣata again and again, "Come! Come!
He could not endure that sound of the palms being struck in the midst of battle.
Like an elephant always in rut at the sound of a palm-clap, he leaped from that chariot and mounted his own chariot once more;
he then rushed toward him swiftly and cried out, "Stay! Stay!"
Highly incensed, like a fire desiring to consume,
Kṛtavarman surrounded all the Pāṇḍavas, headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Then, O King, the great archer [Śalya] quickly [assisted] Kṛtavarman.
Seizing his mace once more with great force, he struck Kṛtavarman.
Severely pierced by that powerful man and overcome by fainting, he fell down.
Then, O King, [he quickly struck] the great archer Kṛtavarman.
Śrutavān, having placed him upon his chariot, carried him away from the field of battle. But seeing that shower of weapons, so difficult to withstand, shattered in the fight,
the son of Pṛṣata approached Kṛtavarman and checked him.
The son of Pṛṣata covered Hārdikya with sharpened arrows and swiftly dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama;
struck by a sharp-edged bhalla-arrow, he fell from his chariot.
The powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna, having conquered his great chariot-warrior enemy,
quickly checked the Kauravas in battle with his arrows.
Then those warriors of yours rushed toward Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
Having let out a lion’s roar, the battle then commenced.
Sañjaya said:
Seeing Yudhiṣṭhira protected by the grandson of Śini (Sātyaki), the son of Droṇa (Aśvatthāman) [advanced].
He advanced joyfully against the heroic sons of Draupadī,
scattering terrible swarms of gold-feathered arrows sharpened on stone,
displaying various maneuvers with light-handed skill for the sake of exhibition.

Then, that expert in weapons filled the sky with arrows consecrated by divine mantras and surrounded Yudhiṣṭhira in battle. Enveloped by the arrows of the son of Droṇa, nothing at all could be discerned.
Indeed, that entire head of the battlefield became composed of arrows;
that net of arrows situated in the sky, adorned with golden mesh,
shone, O best of the Bharatas, like a canopy spread aloft.
O King, by that shining web of arrows in that covered battle,
a shadow like that of clouds was produced when the vault of heaven was obstructed by shafts.
There, we beheld a marvel in that state where everything had become composed of arrows.
Seeing the prowess of Droṇa’s son, O great king, those great car-warriors did not even stand upon the ground; beholding the lightness of hand of Drona’s son there,
they were filled with wonder and could not even look at him.

All those kings were unable [to withstand him], who was like the scorching sun; yet Sātyaki, striving with effort, as well as the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja and the other troops, could not display their prowess.
Then, as the army was being slaughtered, the great car-warriors— the sons of Draupadī, Sātyaki, Dharmarāja, and the Pāñcālas— united and,
casting aside the terrible fear of death, rushed against the son of Droṇa.
Sātyaki, having pierced the son of Droṇa with twenty-five stone-tipped arrows,
struck him again with seven gold-adorned iron shafts;
Yudhiṣṭhira did so with seventy-three, and Prativindhya with seven.
Śrutakarman pierced him with three arrows, Śrutakīrti with seven,
Sutasoma with nine, and Śatānīka with seven;
many other heroes as well struck him from all sides.
O King, then, exceedingly enraged and hissing like a venomous serpent,
he pierced Sātyaki with twenty-five arrows whetted on stone;
he struck Śrutakīrti with nine and Sutasoma with five.
With eight arrows he struck Śrutakarman, Prativindhya with three,
Śatānīka with nine, and the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira) with seven;
then he struck the other heroes with two arrows each.
Likewise, he cut through Śrutakīrti’s bow with sharpened arrows.
Then the great car-warrior Śrutakīrti, taking up another bow,
pierced the son of Droṇa with three shafts and struck him again with other sharp arrows.
Then, O great king, descendant of Bharata, the son of Droṇa covered that army with a shower of arrows and, from all sides, struck the kings with shafts.
Thereafter, that one of immeasurable soul [struck] the bow of Dharmarāja.
Laughing, the son of Droṇa cut [the bow] and pierced him with three arrows. Then, O King, the son of Dharma, seizing another great bow,
pierced the son of Droṇa with seventy arrows and struck him in the arms and chest.
Then Sātyaki, enraged as the son of Droṇa struck him in battle,
severed his bow with a sharp crescent-headed arrow and roared loudly.
Thereupon, the son of Droṇa, the best among the powerful, being deprived of his bow, [hurled] a spear.
He swiftly struck down the charioteer of Śini’s grandson from his chariot. Then, O Bhārata, the powerful son of Droṇa, taking up another bow, covered Śini’s grandson with a shower of arrows.
O Bhārata, when the charioteer had fallen in battle, his horses bolted and were seen running hither and thither; meanwhile,
those warriors led by Yudhiṣṭhira [advanced against] the son of Droṇa, the foremost of weapon-bearers.
They rained down with force, discharging sharp arrows.
Seeing those approaching forms so terrible, the scorcher of foes,
the son of Droṇa, received them with a laugh in that great battle.

Then, like a fire consuming dry wood in a forest, the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, whose arrows blazed like a hundred fires, consumed the army of the son of Pāṇḍu in battle. That force of the son of Pāṇḍu was scorched by the prowess of Droṇa’s son.
O best of the Bharatas, that army at the very front of the host was agitated like the mouth of a river by a great fish;
for that force of the son of Pāṇḍu was consumed by the flame-like arrows of Droṇa’s son.
O best of the Bharatas, scorching [the enemy] with his shafts like the sun with its rays,
that army of the Pāṇḍavas was agitated as it was tormented by the sharp-pointed arrows of the Brāhmaṇa.
O Great King, seeing that [chariot] being shattered by the arrows of the Brahmin,
and witnessing the prowess of Droṇa’s son,
they all considered the Pāṇḍavas to have been already slain by the son of Droṇa.
But Yudhiṣṭhira, quickly embracing the great car-warrior,
the son of Droṇa, spoke to him while filled with rage and indignation:
"I know you to be the best in battle, endowed with heroism and strength."
If you, O son of Pṛṣata, were to display all this strength— being skilled in weapons, proficient, and likewise swift in prowess— then we would know you to be truly powerful and of accomplished valor.

Indeed, having seen that son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemies, in battle, your strength would become something [real]; yet I do not speak thus to you, O twice-born one. Truly, there is no affection in you, nor indeed any gratitude.
"Since you, O tiger among men, desire to kill me this very day—[know that] a Brahmin should practice austerity, charity, and study;
a Kshatriya should bend the bow. You, however, are merely one who calls himself a Brahmin."
"O mighty-armed one, while you look on, I shall defeat the Kauravas in battle! Perform your duty in the fray; you are surely a mere Brahmin by name.
O great king, having been addressed thus, the son of Droṇa spoke as if smiling.
Reflecting upon that state of being joined in battle, he did not utter any reply;
and having said nothing, he then covered the Pāṇḍava in the encounter with a shower of arrows,
like the enraged Antaka covering all creatures.
O Sire, being thus overwhelmed by the son of Droṇa,
Pārtha then quickly withdrew, leaving behind his vast army. When Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, had thus retreated, [the battle continued].
O King, the son of Droṇa stood firm because of the command of that high-souled one.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having left the son of Droṇa behind in that great battle,
advanced against your army, intent upon a cruel deed.
Saṃjaya said:
Vaikartana himself, having personally checked Bhīmasena— who was surrounded by the Pāñcālas, Cedis,
and Kekayas— held him back with his arrows.
Then, while Bhīmasena looked on, the enraged Karṇa struck down the Cedis, the Kārūṣas, and the Sṛñjayas, all great car-warriors.
Thereupon, Bhīmasena left Karṇa, that best of chariot-fighters.
The Kaurava army advanced like a blazing fire through dry grass;
and the Suta’s son also, in that battle, slaughtered the Pāñcālas, the Kekayas,
and the great bowmen of the Sṛñjayas by the thousands.
Pārtha among the Saṃśaptakas, Vṛkodara among the Kauravas,
and Karṇa among the Pāñcālas— those great car-warriors caused a destruction. Those kṣatriyas were scorched by those three, who were like fires.
O King, they met their destruction in battle due to your evil counsel.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, the enraged Duryodhana pierced Nakula with nine arrows and struck his four horses as well.
Then again, O lord of men, your son of immeasurable soul cut down Sahadeva’s golden standard with a razor-headed arrow.
Thereupon Nakula, filled with rage, struck your son with twenty-one arrows.
O King, Sahadeva struck him in the battle with five arrows. Then,
filled with rage, he pierced both of those foremost of the Bharatas— the best among all archers— in the chest with five arrows each.
Then, O King, laughing, he severed the bows of the twins with two other broad-headed arrows (bhallas), and pierced them each with seven more. They,
in turn, took up two other excellent and beautiful bows that resembled the bow of Indra.
Seizing their weapons, those two heroes, equal to the sons of gods in battle,
trembled with rage; then, O King, those two impetuous brothers showered their brother with terrible arrows in the fight, like two great clouds raining upon a mountain.
Then, O great king, your son, that great car-warrior, filled with rage,
checked the two sons of Pāṇḍu, those mighty archers, with his feathered shafts.
O Bhārata, in that battle, only the circular motion of his bow was visible.
Arrows were seen issuing forth from all sides;
and the two Pāṇḍavas, covered by his shafts,
shone like the sun and moon in the sky, their luster eclipsed when shrouded by clouds.
O great king, those arrows, gold-feathered and whetted on stone,
then shrouded all the directions like the rays of the sun. When the sky was thus covered and turned into a mass of arrows, [the battle continued].
Nakula and Sahadeva, filled with intense rage,
both covered that shower of arrows from the king with hundreds of thousands of shafts,
shrouding your son with floods of arrows.
Then, O Great King, as those two discharged arrows incessantly,
their appearance was seen to be like that of Yama, the Ender of Time at the end of an aeon.
And seeing that prowess of your son, the great car-warriors—
Assuming a supreme wrath and hissing like a serpent,
your son then released a darkness of arrows; at that moment,
the two sons of Mādrī thought they had reached the very jaws of death.
Then, O King, the commander-in-chief of the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
the son of Pṛṣata, advanced to where King Suyodhana was;
he then bypassed the two heroic sons of Mādrī, those great car-warriors.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna struck your son with arrows;
then your son, of immeasurable soul and great indignation,
laughing, pierced that prince of the Pañcālas, O bull among men, with twenty-five shafts.
Then once more, O lord of the earth, your son of immeasurable soul,
having pierced the Pāñcālya with sixty and five arrows, uttered a roar. Then,
O honorable one, he [struck] his bow with an arrow fixed to it and his hand-guard.
In that battle, the king cut it asunder with an exceedingly sharp razor-headed arrow.
Casting aside that severed bow, the prince of the Pañcālas, the crusher of his enemies,
swiftly took up another new bow capable of bearing a great strain.
Blazing as if with impetuous fury, his eyes bloodshot from agitation,
the great archer Dhṛṣṭadyumna, though wounded, shone resplendent;
he [discharged] fifteen iron shafts that were like hissing serpents.
Desiring to slay the best of the Bharatas, Dhṛṣṭadyumna released [those arrows].
Sharpened on stone and fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks, they pierced the king’s gold-adorned armor and entered the earth with great force.

O Great King, deeply pierced, your son shone most brilliantly, like a *kiṃśuka* tree in springtime, variegated with blossoms and covered in flowers. His armor shattered by iron arrows, his skin mangled by the blows.
Enraged, he severed Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s bow with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla). Then, O King, the lord of the earth, acting with haste toward him whose bow was broken,
struck him between the eyebrows with ten shafts.
He pierced him with various arrows resembling Kāla, Antaka,
and Yama; polished by the smith, those shafts beautified his face like honey-seeking bees upon a blossoming campaka flower.
Casting aside that broken bow, the high-minded Dhṛṣṭadyumna swiftly took up another bow and sixteen broad-headed arrows. Then,
having slain Duryodhana’s horses and his charioteer with five [arrows], he...
With a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he cut through the gold-adorned bow;
with nine broad-headed arrows, the son of Pṛṣata cut down your son’s chariot along with its equipment, his umbrella, spear, sword, mace, and standard.

All the kings beheld the severed banner of the Kuru lord, adorned with golden armlets, variegated, and featuring an auspicious elephant made of jewels. Duryodhana, however, stood in the battle deprived of his chariot and with all his weapons shattered.
O bull of the Bharatas, his uterine brothers protected him;
O King, having placed that lord of men upon his chariot, Daṇḍadhāra carried him away in great haste while Dhṛṣṭadyumna looked on.
But the mighty Karna, desirous of victory for the king, having defeated Sātyaki,
rushed in battle toward the slayer of Droṇa, who possessed fierce arrows. The grandson of Śini quickly pursued him from behind, piercing him with shafts.
Like an elephant repelling another with its tusks at the rear of its haunches,
O Bhārata, there occurred a great battle between Karna and the son of Pṛṣata in the midst of your high-souled warriors. This was a truly massive conflict among your troops.
Not a single warrior among the Pāṇḍavas nor among ourselves was seen with his back turned when Karṇa rushed swiftly toward the Pañcālas;
at that moment, O best of men, there occurred a destruction of elephants, horses, and men.
O King, at midday, it appeared from both sides;
then, O great king, the Pāñcālas, desiring victory, swiftly rushed toward Karṇa from all directions like birds toward a tree.
The son of Adhiratha, enraged, encountered those high-minded warriors as they strove against him;
piercing them with the tips of his arrows,
he confronted Vyāghraketu, Suśarman, Śaṅku, and the fierce Dhanañjaya right before him.
Śukla, Rocamāna, Siṃhasena, and Durjaya—
those heroes, with the speed of their chariots, surrounded that best of men,
the enraged Karṇa, the ornament of battle, as he discharged his arrows.
As those heroes were fighting, the powerful lord of men,
Rādheya, struck eight of them with eight sharpened arrows.
Then, O great king, the powerful son of the Sūta struck others as well.
Skilled in battle, he slew many thousands of warriors, O King,
including Viṣṇu, Viṣṇukarman, Devāpi, Bhadra,
Daṇḍa, Citra, Citrāyudha, and Hari in that encounter.
Highly incensed, he struck down Siṃhaketu, Rocamāna, and the great car-warrior Śalabha, as well as the great car-warriors of the Cedis;
the form of Ādhiratha’s son was like one devouring their very lives.

With his limbs drenched in blood, he possessed a great and formidable majesty like that of Rudra. There, O Bhārata, the elephants struck by Karṇa’s arrows fled in all directions out of fear, creating a great tumult.
Afflicted by Karṇa’s arrows, they fell upon the earth in battle, uttering various cries like mountains struck by thunderbolts;
and with elephants, horses, and men falling on all sides, [the field was covered].
The earth was strewn along the path with overturned chariots;
neither Bhīṣma, nor Droṇa, nor any other warriors on your side performed such a feat in battle as that which was accomplished there in the fray.
O tiger among men, the son of the Sūta wrought a great slaughter among the elephants, chariots, horses,
and men; he was seen moving about fearlessly like a lion in the midst of a herd of deer.
Likewise, Karna moved fearlessly in the midst of the Pañcālas;
just as a lion drives terrified herds of deer in all directions,
so did Karna drive away the throngs of the Pañcāla chariot-warriors.
Just as deer never survive once they have encountered a lion’s mouth, so too do great car-warriors not survive once they have encountered Karṇa. Indeed,
just as people are consumed when they encounter a blazing fire, so it is with them.

O Bhārata, in that same way, the Sṛñjayas were consumed by the fire of Karṇa’s arrows in battle. O Bhārata, among the Cedis and the Pañcālas, many who were esteemed as heroes were slain by Karṇa alone after he had proclaimed his name.
And it occurred to me, O lord of men, upon seeing the prowess of Karṇa:
"Not even a single Pāñcālya shall escape alive from the son of Adhiratha in battle.
As the powerful son of the Sūta scatters the Pāñcālas in the fray, he is like a fire consuming a forest.
Then, seeing Karṇa slaughtering the Pañcālas in that great battle,
he rushed in a rage toward Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma;
and so too did Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the sons of Draupadī, O sire.
Hundreds of other men surrounded the slayer of enemies;
likewise, Śikhaṇḍin, Sahadeva, Nakula, the son of Nakula,
Janamejaya, the grandson of Śini, and many Prabhadrakas [surrounded him].
Having become the leaders of Dhṛṣṭadyumna in that battle, those warriors of immeasurable prowess moved about, discharging their arrows and missiles at Karṇa.
There in the fray, the son of Adhiratha [encountered] those Cedis, Pāñcālas, and Pāṇḍavas.
And O great king, he did not spare Sātyaki in the encounter;
alone, he fell upon many like Garuḍa upon serpents.
O lord of the people, the battle between them and Karṇa was terrible in form.
Just as in the past it occurred between the gods and the dānavas,
that single hero, undisturbed, overcame those assembled great archers who were raining down floods of arrows, just as the sun dispels the darkness.
But Bhīmasena, filled with rage, struck the Kurus, Madras,
and Kekayas from all sides with arrows resembling the staff of Yama;
he assailed the Bāhlikas, Kekayas, Matsyas, Vāsātyas, Madras, and Saindhavas.
That lone great archer, fighting in the fray, shone resplendently. There, elephants struck in their vital organs by Bhīma with iron shafts fell down with their riders slain, making the earth tremble.
Horses with their riders slain and foot-soldiers deprived of life lay upon the battlefield, pierced and vomiting much blood;
O noble one, the elephants were suddenly struck down by Bhīmasena.
They fell with great force, like mountains shattered by thunderbolts.
O Great King, with those powerful, mighty elephants slain and scattered across the earth,
the ground shone, O King, as if strewn with mountains.
And by the thousands, chariot-warriors fell with their weapons fallen; though they appeared uninjured, they were seen to have lost their lives, terrified by Bhīma.
Likewise, there were charioteers, horses, drivers, foot-soldiers, and elephants [in the same state].
The earth became strewn with the limbs severed by Bhīmasena’s arrows; O King, Duryodhana’s army, afflicted by Bhīmasena’s might, stood as if paralyzed, its vigor gone and its warriors wounded.

Motionless and dejected in that tumultuous great battle, O King, your army stood perfectly still, like the ocean with its waters calm at the proper time. Thus indeed did your force remain, fixed and unmoving.
Endowed with wrath, heroism,
and strength, that army of your son was then forcibly cast down by his arrows; O best of the Bharatas, that force was being slaughtered by one another.
Drenched by a flood of blood, it became soaked in gore,
O best of the Bharatas, as they slaughtered one another. Then the son of the Sūta, enraged in battle, advanced against the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
Bhīmasena also shone brilliantly as he put the Kurus to flight; while that fierce battle of wondrous sight was thus proceeding,
he slaughtered many hosts of Saṃśaptakas in the midst of the army.
Arjuna, the best among victors, then spoke to Vāsudeva:
"O Janārdana, this army, though prepared for battle, has indeed been broken;
here these great car-warriors of the Saṃśaptakas are fleeing along with their hosts."
Indeed, they are invincible in battle even by the gods led by Indra;
unable to withstand my arrows, like deer at the roar of a lion,
the Kurus flee, tormented by the fear of Bhīmasena.
The great army of the Sṛñjayas is being torn asunder in this great battle;
for that elephant-girth banner of the wise Karṇa, O Kṛṣṇa,
is seen moving repeatedly in the midst of the royal host.
Other great chariot-warriors are not capable of defeating Karṇa in battle;
for he is difficult to conquer in combat even by gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas. Indeed, you yourself know Karṇa to be possessed of great heroism and prowess.
"Go there, for Karna is putting our army to flight. Avoid him and go toward the great chariot-warrior, the son of the Suta, O Kṛṣṇa; let not fatigue overcome you, or do as it pleases you."
Having heard this, O great king, Govinda, as if smiling, quickly said to Arjuna: "Slay the Kauravas, O Pāṇḍava! Then the horses, urged on by Govinda, [rushed] against your vast army.
Bearing the two Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, horses the color of swans, adorned with gold and sent by Keśava,
entered; as they entered, your army was broken apart in the four directions.

Resounding with the roar of thunderclouds and bearing the monkey-banner, that chariot with its fluttering pennants entered that army like a celestial vehicle entering the sky. Having pierced through that great host, Keśava and Arjuna entered.
Enraged, their eyes red with fury, those two of great splendor shone brilliantly;
intoxicated by battle and summoned by their enemies to the sacrifice of war,
they were like the two Aśvin deities invoked according to ritual by sacrificers at a sacrifice.

With eyes copper-red with rage, those two heroes of great strength shone like two elephants intoxicated with rut, moving about with the flickering of their glances; enraged, those two tigers among men became possessed of immense speed.
Enraged by the sound of the palm-clapping, like two serpents in a great battle,
Phalguna plunged into the array of chariots and the throngs of horses;
he moved through the midst of the army like Death himself with a noose in hand.
O Bhārata, seeing him displaying such prowess in battle against your army,
your son once again urged on the hosts of Saṃśaptakas.
Then, with a thousand chariots and three hundred elephants...
In that great battle, there were fourteen thousand horses,
two hundred thousand foot soldiers who were archers,
and heroes whose names were renowned and known everywhere.
O great king, those great car-warriors, impetuous on all sides along with Duryodhana,
rushed toward those two heroes,
covering the son of Pāṇḍu from every direction with showers of arrows.
Being covered by arrows in that battle,
that crusher of enemy forces— Partha— displaying his fierce nature like Death with noose in hand, became even more formidable to behold as he struck down the Saṃśaptakas.
Then, by the arrows discharged by Kirīṭin— flashing like lightning and adorned with gold— the sky became as if without any gaps.
As those great shafts released from Kirīṭin’s arms fell upon him, they filled the air.
O Lord, everything appeared completely covered, as if by the sons of Kadrū;
the Pāṇḍava of immeasurable soul displayed his gold-feathered, sharp-pointed, and straight-knotted arrows in all directions.
From the thundering sound of Pārtha’s palms, people perceived that the earth, the sky, all the quarters, as well as the oceans and mountains, were splitting apart;
for that great chariot-warrior had slain ten thousand kings.

The son of Kuntī swiftly advanced against the flank of the Saṃśaptakas; having reached that flank protected by the Kambojas, Pārtha crushed them with his arrows by force, just as Vāsava crushes the Dānavas.
With broad-headed arrows, he swiftly severed the arms—
still grasping weapons— and likewise the heads of his attacking enemies; with their limbs and members thus mangled, they fell to the earth, divested of their arms.
Like trees with many branches shattered on all sides by a whirlwind,
[the enemy forces were struck down]. Then the King of Kamboja, enraged upon seeing the great car-warrior Pārtha—
Arjuna— slaughtering the multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, [rushed forward].
"Urge the driver forward; carry me straight to Arjuna!
Then the charioteer quickly brought that best of car-warriors, who gives profuse sacrificial fees, to Arjuna's chariot in the battle.
Then, O King, having pierced Arjuna in battle with three arrows capable of bearing great weight,
