he struck Keśava on the arms and chest with nine.
Thereupon, O Great King, the Pāṇḍava, the slayer of enemy heroes, became enraged.
The younger brother of Sudakṣiṇa rained down a shower of arrows upon him.
With two crescent-shaped arrows, he struck off his arms, which were like iron maces, as he was shooting; and with a razor-sharp arrow, he struck off his head, whose face resembled the full moon.
Then he fell from his vehicle, streaming with his own blood,
like a peak of a mountain of red arsenic split apart by a thunderbolt.
They beheld the younger brother of Sudakṣiṇa, the Kāmboja, slain.
Tall, with eyes like lotus petals, exceedingly pleasing to behold,
resembling a pillar of gold like a split mountain of gold;
then there occurred again a battle, terrible and wonderful to behold.
And there, among those fighting, the warriors fell into various states;
O lord of the people, with the Kambojas, Yavanas, and Śakas having turned back their horses,
which were then smeared with blood, everything became red.

O Great King, with chariots, horses, and charioteers whose riders had been slain; with steeds whose riders had perished; and with elephants whose riders were killed and whose drivers were slain—there was a terrible destruction of men wrought by one another.
While that wing and the flank were being slaughtered by the high-souled one,
the son of Droṇa quickly advanced against Arjuna, the best among victors,
shaking his great bow adorned with gold.
Taking up his terrible arrows like the sun its own rays,
the mighty one, his mouth wide open with rage and impatience and his eyes bloodshot,
shone like the wrathful Death bearing his staff at the time of the world's end.
Then he discharged fierce showers of arrows in great numbers;
by those arrows released, O Great King, the Pāṇḍava army fled.
But upon seeing the descendant of Daśārha stationed upon his chariot, O Lord of the People, [he was struck with fear].
O noble one, he again released fierce showers of arrows;
between those two brothers in dharma, there occurred a great battle that was far from reaching its conclusion,
as they both desired to cause wonder in the world and sought supreme glory.
Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, slaughtered the Saṃśaptakas and the Kurus,
while the Sūta’s son repeatedly struck down the Pāñcālas with swift arrows;
thus, O great king, occurred this destruction of the lords of the earth.
When Arjuna was enraged, and Karṇa and the terrible Bhīmasena were likewise incensed,

a horrific battle then took place at the front of the army, which had split into three divisions. O great king, as those arrows released by the son of Droṇa fell on all sides, [the field was covered].
Both Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya, standing upon their chariot, were completely covered.
Then the powerful son of Bharadvāja, with hundreds of sharp arrows,
rendered both Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava motionless in battle.
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from all that is mobile and immobile;
seeing the two protectors of the moving and the unmoving covered with arrows, the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas indeed flew up from every side.
"Thinking thus, I pray today for the welfare of the worlds," he said. "O King, such prowess as that of the son of Droṇa, who was about to shroud the two Kṛṣṇas, has never been seen by me before."

O King, I heard the sound of the son of Droṇa’s bow in battle many times— terrifying to his enemies— like the roar of a lion. And as he moved about in combat, shooting with both his left and right hands, the twang of his bowstring was heard.
Standing in the midst of the clouds, she became as if blazing like lightning.
Then that Pāṇḍava, who was so swift in action and firm of hand,
having fallen into a state of extreme confusion, gazed upon the son of Droṇa.

O King, as that great battle between the son of Droṇa and the Pāṇḍava proceeded in this manner, he considered his own prowess to have been eclipsed by that high-souled one; likewise, his form in that combat became very difficult to behold.

O Indra among kings, as the mighty son of Droṇa was waxing strong and the son of Kuntī was waning, wrath assailed Kṛṣṇa. Heaving sighs in rage, O King, he seemed to consume everything with his very eyes.
For he repeatedly beheld the son of Droṇa and Phalguna in the battle;
then Kṛṣṇa, filled with wrath, spoke to Pārtha with affection:
"O Pārtha, I behold this most wonderful thing in your combat."
"O Bhārata, since the son of Droṇa now surpasses you in this matter,
I wonder if the heroism in your arms or your strength remains as it was before?
O Arjuna, I hope the Gāṇḍīva bow is still in your hand and that you remain standing upon your chariot."
"Are your arms well, and is that same vigor still yours?
For I see the son of Droṇa exerting himself in the battle,
O bull of the Bharatas, out of respect for him as the son of my preceptor."

"Be equanimous, O Pārtha; this is not the time for equanimity. Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, he quickly cast fourteen broad-headed arrows and, acting with haste at a time requiring haste, severed the bow of Droṇa’s son.

With his calf-toothed arrows, he struck the standard, the umbrella, the banner, the chariot, the spear, and likewise the mace, hitting them all very forcefully in the region of the collarbone; having fallen into a state of extreme unconsciousness, he leaned against the flagpole for support.
O great king, while he was unconscious and oppressed by the fear of Kirīṭin,
his charioteer bore him away from the battlefield, protecting him from Dhanañjaya.
At that very moment, however, Vijaya, the scorcher of his enemies—
O Bhārata, while your son— that hero— looked on, he slaughtered your army by the hundreds and thousands;
thus did this destruction of your men occur at the hands of the enemies.

O King, due to your evil counsel, Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, became cruel, a slaughterer, and terrible; and the Pāñcāla prince completely destroyed the Saṃśaptakas, the Kurus, and Vasuṣeṇa in battle.
O King, while that fierce slaughter of the best of heroes was thus proceeding,
countless headless trunks (kabandhas) rose up on all sides;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, too, suffered intense pain from the blows in the battle.
Having retreated a distance of one *krośa*, O best of the Bharatas, he stood still;
thus spoke Saṃjaya.
Then Duryodhana, O bull of the Bharatas, approached Karṇa.
He spoke thus to the King of Madra and to the other great car-warriors:
"O Karṇa, happy are those Kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle, which has arrived by chance like an open gateway to heaven."
O son of Rādhā, that which is desired by brave Kṣatriyas when fighting other brave warriors in battle has now arrived before you:
either by slaying the Pāṇḍavas in combat, you shall obtain the prosperous earth.
"Either slain by others in battle, you shall attain the world of heroes.
Having heard those words of Duryodhana, those bulls among kṣatriyas shouted with joy and sounded their musical instruments on all sides.
Then, while that army of Duryodhana was thus exultant,
the son of Droṇa spoke these words to gladden your warriors,
in the presence of all the troops and even as you were looking on.

"My father, having laid down his weapons, was struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna. Out of that indignation, and for the sake of my friends as well, O kings, I swear this truth to you; listen to these words of mine."
"Without slaying Dhṛṣṭadyumna, I shall not remove my armor;
if my vow remains unfulfilled, I shall not attain heaven.
Arjuna, Bhīmasena, and whoever else shall advance against me—"
"I shall crush them all; of this I have no doubt.
When this was said, the entire Bharata army together then charged at the sons of Kuntī, and the Pāṇḍavas likewise charged back.
O Bhārata, that gathering of the leaders of chariot-divisions, those great-souled ones, was bewildering;
it was a destruction of men resembling the end of an eon at the close of a Yuga.
It first unfolded among the Kurus and Sṛñjayas;
then, when that violent clash had begun in battle, all beings, together with the gods, [were struck with wonder].
Together with the Apsarases, they gathered there,
desiring to behold those foremost of men,
adorned with celestial garlands and various fragrances.
And with various divine jewels, the delighted Apsarases showered those foremost of men— those great heroes who were bearing their own karmic burden in battle.
Having enjoyed those fragrances, the wind attended upon all the leaders of the warriors;
and the warriors, being attended by the wind, [were refreshed].
Striking one another, they fell to the earth;
that ground was strewn with celestial flowers and with various arrows possessing golden shafts.
Variegated by the excellent warriors standing upon the earth, the ground shone like the sky adorned with clusters of stars;
then, from the sky as well, there arose shouts of "Well done! (sādhuvāda).
Amplified by the sounds of musical instruments, variegated by the twang of bowstrings and the roar of wheel-rims,
that battle became utterly tumultuous.
While that tumultuous battle was thus raging, Duryodhana, unable to endure his wrath,
approached the powerful Bhima as the strongest of men.
Duḥśāsana and the heroic Citrasena, as well as the gambler Saubala, presented themselves with a hundred minor warriors.
Then, seeing Bhīmasena thus engaged on all sides by the elephant divisions, they suddenly rushed toward him; and beholding that elephant force attacking, Vṛkodara—
The mighty-armed one covered Duryodhana with showers of arrows; likewise, the powerful Pāṇḍava Bhīma, having turned Duryodhana back with hundreds of sharp shafts, rushed toward the elephants.

Then, with straight-flying arrows resembling fire, the Pāṇḍava Bhīma tormented those elephants like swarms of locusts. Thereafter, the exceedingly powerful Bhīmasena [assailed] the herds of elephants.
Like the wind dispersing great clouds, he scattered [the enemy] with sharpened arrows;
elephants, shining like silver and gold and adorned with garlands of razors, followed that array of chariots with their networks of jewels.
O King, those elephants being struck by Bhīmasena’s arrows—
with their hearts pierced— some fell right there upon the earth along with those falling,
high-velocity steeds adorned with golden trappings.
O Great King, that battlefield shone like mountains variegated with minerals,
strewn with elephants fallen from their backs and adorned with glittering ornaments; it appeared, O King,
like the gods whose merit has been exhausted.

They beheld the two arms of Bhīmasena as he brandished his bow— arms resembling great iron clubs and smeared with sandalwood and aloe-wood— and they heard the thunderous sound of his bowstring as he discharged arrows from both the left and the right.
Hearing this, O King, the elephants, afflicted by fear, rushed toward Bhīmasena;
we beheld that feat of that single, wise Bhīma, O great king, which was truly like a marvel.
Saṃjaya said:
Thus did this great battle of the rulers of the earth take place when Arjuna, Karṇa, and the Pāṇḍava Bhīmasena were all enraged.
Having defeated the son of Droṇa and having conquered other great car-warriors,
O King, Arjuna spoke these words to Vāsudeva:
"Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, the Pāṇḍava army fleeing!"
Behold Karṇa in battle, driving away the great chariot-warriors;
yet, O descendant of Daśārha, I do not see Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira,
nor is the banner of Dharmarāja visible, O best among warriors.
"O Janārdana, only one-third of this day remains;
yet not a single one among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra fights me in battle. Therefore, doing what is pleasing to me, go to where Yudhiṣṭhira is."
"O Vārṣṇeya, having seen the son of Dharma safe in battle along with his younger brother, I shall once again fight with the enemies in the fray. Then,
at the word of Bībhatsu, Hari quickly departed on the chariot.
Since King Yudhiṣṭhira and the great car-warriors of the Sṛñjayas fought with your men, making death their only means of retreat,
Sañjaya said:
Hurrying again, Kṛṣṇa spoke softly to Pārtha:
"Behold the king, O Kauravya, and the Pāṇḍavas in retreat;
behold Karṇa in the great arena, like a blazing fire."
That formidable and great archer has turned back toward the battle;
following him return these warriors, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna—
the vanguard of the Pañcālas, the Sṛñjayas, and the Pāṇḍavas.
O Pārtha, the great army of the enemy has been shattered by you who have turned back;
indeed, O Arjuna, Karna is holding back these fleeing Kauravas—
he who is like the Destroyer in his speed and equal to Śakra in prowess.
O Kauravya, there goes the son of Droṇa, the best among wielders of weapons;
the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna is pursuing him as he flees in battle. Behold the Sṛñjayas being slaughtered in the fray!
The invincible Vāsudeva explained everything to the wearer of the diadem.
Then, O King, a most terrible great battle broke out,
and amidst that encounter, the sounds of lion-like roars arose.
O King, making death the only means of retreat, this destruction occurred on the earth for both armies— of your own men and those of the enemy— O Lord of the Earth, due to your evil counsel.
Saṃjaya said:
Then once again the Kurus and Sṛñjayas, fearless, came together—
the Pārthas headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, and we, headed by Vaikartana.
Then there commenced a terrible battle, hair-raising,
between Karṇa and the Pāṇḍavas, which increased the population of Yama’s realm.
As that tumultuous battle proceeded, with blood for its water, it was truly fearsome.
O Bhārata, when only a few of the heroic Saṃśaptakas remained, O great king,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, together with all the kings and the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, rushed against Karṇa alone.
As they approached in battle, joyful and seeking victory,
Karna alone held them back in the fray like a mountain against torrents of water.
But upon reaching Karna, those great car-warriors were shattered.
Just as masses of water, having encountered a mountain, scatter in every direction, so too,
O great king, occurred that hair-raising battle between those two powerful warriors, who, desiring victory, contended upon the great stage of combat.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, filled with rage, struck the son of Rādhā with a straight-knotted arrow and cried out, "Stay! Stay!
Meanwhile, that great car-warrior brandished his Vijaya, the best of bows.
Like a cloud pouring down showers of water,
he rained down showers of arrows; having severed the bow of the son of Pṛṣata, he, filled with rage, struck the son of Pṛṣata with nine arrows resembling venomous serpents.
O sinless one, having pierced the gold-adorned armor of that high-souled warrior, those arrows, smeared with blood, shone like *śakragopa* insects.
Then, casting aside that severed bow, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna—
Taking up another bow and arrows resembling venomous serpents,
he pierced Karṇa with seventy straight-knotted shafts.
In the same way, O King, Karṇa also [struck] the son of Pṛṣata, the scorcher of his enemies.
In that battle, he covered [his opponent] with arrows resembling venomous serpents;
the great archer Drona pierced the enemy with sharpened shafts.
O great king, Karna [then loosed] at him an arrow adorned with gold.
Enraged, he hurled it like a second rod of Death.
As it came rushing suddenly toward him with a terrifying form, O lord of the people,
the descendant of Śini, O King, cut it into seven pieces with the skill of a practiced hand.
O lord of the people, seeing that his arrow had been warded off by [Satyaki’s] shafts,
Karna surrounded Satyaki on all sides with a shower of arrows and pierced him in that battle with seven iron bolts (nārācas).
Śaineya pierced him in return with arrows adorned with gold.
Then, O King, there occurred a battle that was exceedingly terrifying to the eyes and ears— fierce, wonderful, and a sight to behold on all sides.
O King, seeing that feat of Karṇa and Śaineya in battle, the hair of all living beings there stood on end. In the meantime,
the son of Droṇa rushed toward the one of great strength.
Seeing Karṇa and the great car-warrior, the son of Pṛṣata— the subduer of enemies and the destroyer of the life-force and valor of his foes— in that battle,
the son of Droṇa, filled with rage while Dhanañjaya was still far away, addressed him.
Crushing chariot against chariot, that destroyer of the enemy's prowess said:
"Stay! Stay today, O slayer of Brahmins! You shall not escape from me alive!
Having spoken thus, the hero, acting with speed, [struck him] with sharpened arrows.
The great car-warrior, striving with all his might, covered the son of Pṛṣata— who was himself striving to the utmost— with fiercely shaped,
well-sharpened arrows in that battle.
O lord of the people, with supreme effort and all his might, he fought Dhṛṣṭadyumna in that great battle, assuming a wrathful form in the encounter;
for just as the son of Droṇa, O noble one, beheld the son of Pṛṣata in the fray.
Likewise, seeing the son of Droṇa in battle, the son of Pṛṣata, the slayer of enemy heroes,
became dejected in mind and considered his own death;
for he knew that in combat he was truly incapable of being slain by weapons.
With great speed, he rushed toward the son of Droṇa, like Time itself rushing toward Time at the end of an eon.
But seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna stationed in battle, O king of kings, the heroic son of Droṇa,
sighing in rage, charged at the son of Pṛṣata.
Upon seeing one another, they both immediately fell into a state of extreme fury.
Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, his soul overwhelmed with rage and unable to endure it,
that scorcher of foes, spoke impetuously to the son of Droṇa.
O lord of the people, having grasped his great bow which shone with its string,
the powerful son of Droṇa then spoke in haste to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who stood nearby, O great king.
"O lowest of the Pāñcālas, today I shall send you to death.
For that sinful deed which was committed by you in the past when you slew Droṇa— that very act shall surely consume you today, just as an evil deed consumes its perpetrator."
Today, by this vision of the sun, the perception [of darkness] is dispelled;
by the mere remembrance of the moon, the lineages [of darkness] are cast away.
O son of Pṛṣata, you are to be slain by me with the slaughter of a sacrificial animal.
"Today, tomorrow, or the day after— this shall surely come to pass:
if you remain in battle unguarded by Pārtha,
or if you do not flee, O fool— I tell you this as the truth."
Thus addressed, the powerful Dhṛṣṭadyumna replied:
"That very sword of mine shall give you an answer,
the same one by which it was given to your father as he strove in battle."
"This sword of mine shall indeed give you an answer,
by which the head of your father was severed while he was striving [to protect it]. Even though Drona, that so-called Brahmin, was slain by me."
"How shall I not now slay you in battle by my prowess?
Having spoken thus, O Great King, the indignant commander-in-chief,
the son of Pṛṣata, then pierced the son of Droṇa with a sharpened arrow.
Then, O King, the son of Droṇa, highly incensed, covered all directions with straight-jointed arrows in the encounter against Dhṛṣṭadyumna;
neither the sky, nor the quarters, nor the warriors on any side could be seen.
O great king, thousands were indeed seen covered by arrows;
likewise, O king, the son of Pṛṣata covered the son of Droṇa, who graces the battlefield,
with arrows while the Sūta’s son looked on.
O great king, the son of Rādhā alone, appearing magnificent on all sides, held back the Pāñcālas along with the Pāṇḍavas, the sons of Draupadī, Yudhāmanyu, and the great car-warrior Sātyaki.
O great king, Dhrishtadyumna also severed the bow of Drona’s son in battle with an extremely sharp razor-headed arrow, while Satyaki and thousands of other warriors looked on.

Casting aside that broken bow, he took up another formidable bow in the battle, one endowed with great speed, as well as arrows resembling venomous serpents. O king of kings, he [then struck] the bow, the spear, the mace, and the standard of the son of Pṛṣata.
He hurled a spear at him, but the son of Droṇa shattered it with his arrows.
Seeing that spear cut down by the son of Droṇa in battle, the powerful son of Pṛṣata took up a terrible iron club adorned with gold.
In former times, the son of Pṛṣata, roaring with the strength of his arms,
hurled that iron club; but as it came flying toward him, O King, the son of Droṇa, a great car-warrior, cut it into many pieces in the battle with his arrows through his great agility.
In the twinkling of an eye, he destroyed the horses, the charioteer, and the chariot itself with his arrows.
Then, the son of Droṇa, that scorcher of foes, became enraged at the son of Pṛṣata;
with his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, [he stood there].
He took up a massive sword and a radiant shield marked with a hundred moons;
but even that, O king of kings, the heroic son of Droṇa— a great car-warrior, swift-handed and firm in his weapons— quickly cut apart in battle with broad-headed arrows.
As he remained unseated from his chariot,
it was like a marvel to all the troops as they watched that mighty archer, powerful-armed.

But though that great car-warrior exerted himself, O best of the Bharatas, he could not overcome Dhṛṣṭadyumna, who was deprived of his chariot, whose horses were slain, whose bow was broken, who was pierced in many places by arrows, and whose body was mangled by celestial weapons.
O King, when the son of Droṇa could not reach his end with arrows,
the hero then cast aside his bow and swiftly pursued the son of Pṛṣata,
grasping a massive sword adorned with gold.
O King, the speed of that great-souled one as he rushed forward was like that of Garuḍa swooping down, desiring to seize the best of serpents. At that very moment, however, Mādhava spoke to Arjuna.
"Behold, O Pārtha, how the son of Droṇa is intent upon the slaughter of the son of Pṛṣata.
At that very moment, Keśava, the slayer of enemy heroes,
spoke to Arjuna, the best of the Bharatas and foremost among victors.
Behold the son of Droṇa striving for the slaughter of the son of Pṛṣata;
he exerts great effort and would undoubtedly slay him.
O mighty-armed one, deliver that son of Pṛṣata, the scorcher of his enemies!

"Having reached the mouth of the son of Droṇa like one who has entered the jaws of Death," having spoken thus, O great king, the powerful Vāsudeva urged the horses toward the place where the son of Droṇa was stationed.

Those horses, resembling the moon, urged on by Keśava, went toward the chariot of Droṇa’s son as if drinking up the sky. Seeing both Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya approaching, those two of great prowess, [the warriors were filled with anxiety].
O King, that one of great strength made an effort to slay Dhṛṣṭadyumna.
O lord of men, as soon as he saw Dhṛṣṭadyumna being dragged away,
the mighty son of Pṛthā discharged arrows toward the son of Droṇa.
Those arrows, fashioned of gold and impelled forcefully from the Gāṇḍīva,
reached the son of Droṇa and entered him like serpents into an anthill.
With those terrible arrows shattered, the powerful son of Droṇa—
O King, having abandoned the Pāñcālya of immeasurable prowess in battle,
the hero, afflicted by the arrows of Dhanañjaya, mounted his chariot;
and seizing his excellent bow, he pierced the son of Pṛthā with shafts.
In that interval, O lord of men, the hero Sahadeva carried away the son of Pṛṣata, the scorcher of enemies, from the battle on his chariot.
Arjuna also, O great king, pierced the son of Droṇa with feathered arrows.

The son of Droṇa, filled with rage, struck him on the arms and chest. Enraged in battle, Pārtha discharged at the son of Droṇa an iron shaft (nārāca) equal to Time itself, like a second staff of Death.
That arrow of great luster fell upon the shoulder of the Brahmin.
O Great King, overwhelmed by the force of the shaft in that battle,
he sat down on the floor of his chariot and fell into a state of extreme distress.
Then, O great king, Karna, filled with rage and looking repeatedly at Arjuna in the battle, drew his bow Vijaya,
desiring a single combat with Pārtha in that great conflict.

But leaving that slain hero, the slayer of enemies, the charioteer quickly bore him away from the field of battle on his chariot. Then, O great king, a loud shout was raised by the Pāñcālas, who appeared victorious.
Seeing the son of Pṛṣata rescued and the son of Droṇa afflicted,
thousands of celestial musical instruments were sounded,
and a lion’s roar arose upon witnessing that terrible and great marvel.
Having done this, Dhananjaya, the son of Pṛthā, said to Vāsudeva:
"Go toward the Saṃśaptakas, O Kṛṣṇa; this is my highest task.
Then, having heard the words of the Pāṇḍava, the descendant of Daśārha set forth.
On a chariot with towering banners and the speed of thought or the wind,
Sañjaya said:
"When that vast battle had commenced, in which blood was the water..."
The earth, drenched and stained in many ways by copious amounts of blood, shone intensely red.
Then, when the dust had subsided and the blood had settled on all sides,
Kṛṣṇa, beholding Pārtha, spoke these words.
In the meantime, Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to Pārtha,
as if pointing out Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī:
"O Pāṇḍava, here is your brother [besieged] by the mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
The great archers, desiring to slay him, are swiftly pursuing the son of Pṛthā; likewise, the Pāñcālas, enraged and intoxicated by battle, follow with great speed,
seeking to protect the high-souled Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O Pārtha, here is Duryodhana, the king of the entire world, clad in armor with his division of chariots;
accompanied by his brothers, that mighty one pursues the tiger among men, desiring to slay him."
With a touch like that of venomous serpents and skilled in every form of warfare,
these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— are advancing with the desire to seize Yudhiṣṭhira, just as seekers strive for the most precious of jewels.
Behold the Lord, held in check and stationed by the two Sātvatas and Bhīma; like Daityas rendered powerless by Śakra and Agni when they sought to seize the nectar, these [enemies],
despite their great numbers, are now retreating in haste toward the Pāṇḍava.
Like torrents of water flowing into the ocean during the rainy season, those great car-warriors—
mighty archers of great strength— roared lion-roars, blew their conchs, and shook their bows.
"I consider Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, to have entered the jaws of Death;
he has fallen under the power of Duryodhana and is as good as offered as an oblation into the fire— blessings be upon you,
O Pāṇḍava— for the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son is indeed arrayed according to plan."
Even Śakra himself could not escape once he had come within the range of the arrows of the heroic Duryodhana, of the son of Droṇa, of the son of Śaradvat,
and of Karṇa; indeed, the velocity of their shafts could split even mountains.

Who could withstand in battle the impetuosity of the heroic Duryodhana as he swiftly looses floods of arrows, like the enraged God of Death himself? And by Karṇa, the king— that scorcher of his enemies— was forced to turn away from the fight.
Strong, light-handed, skilled, and an expert in battle,
the son of Rādhā, together with the high-souled heroic sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, is capable of afflicting the best of the Pāṇḍavas in combat.
While he was thus fighting in battle with self-restraint,
the armor of that son of Pṛthā was stripped away by other great car-warriors as well;
the king, O best of the Bharatas, was exceedingly emaciated from fasting.
For he, O Lord, stands firm in Brahmanic power, not in the exceedingly great Kṣatriya power;
having performed his duty toward his son, this scorcher of enemies has established his kingdom and secured his life through constant fasting in battle, his resolve in his vow being complete.
This king Yudhiṣṭhira,
the son of Pāṇḍu and scorcher of his enemies, who was especially attacked by King Karṇa during the Vatsodayika festival, has indeed fallen into a state of peril.
"O Pārtha Yudhiṣṭhira, I think the great king does not live,
since Bhīmasena, though impatient,
endures the lion-like roars of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as they cry out again and again, O subduer of enemies."
O bull of the Bharatas, while blowing his great conch shell, Karna— appearing victorious in battle—
urges on those mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, saying, "Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, has been slain!"
O Pārtha, in that battle, the Kaurava great-chariot warriors followed the king, shrouding him with various and diverse weapons, including the Sthūṇākarṇa, the Indrajāla, and the Pāśupata.
"O Bhārata, I consider the king to be afflicted, yet he must be attended to;
for the Pāñcālas together with the Pāṇḍavas,
those best among all wielders of weapons, are hastening at this time of haste to follow his lead."

O Pārtha, while the twins, Sātyaki, and Śikhaṇḍin looked on, the banner of King Karṇa— though his forces were powerful and eager to rescue it as he seemed to be sinking into the underworld— was not seen, having been struck down by Karna’s arrows.
O Lord, O Bhārata, this Karṇa is [advancing] against the army of the Pāṇḍavas in battle— against Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Bhīma, or Śatānīka, and indeed against all the Pañcālas and the Cedis, O Pārtha.
Like an elephant destroying a lotus pond with its tusks, he is indeed shattering [the enemy] with his arrows.
O son of Pāṇḍu, these chariot-warriors of yours are fleeing;
they are being driven away in battle by Karṇa of immeasurable splendor, O Pārtha.
"Behold, behold, O Pārtha, how these great car-warriors are fleeing!
O Bhārata, these elephants, struck by Karṇa in battle,
are scattering in the ten directions, uttering cries of distress."
"O Pārtha, behold from all sides this multitude of chariots rushing about;
see how they are being driven away in battle by Karṇa, the crusher of enemies. And behold the elephant-girths moving here and there on the field."
O best among those who possess banners, that banner of the Suta’s son stationed upon his chariot—
that Rādheya— is rushing toward Bhīmasena’s chariot,
scattering hundreds of arrows as he slaughters your army.
Behold these Pāñcālas being driven away by that great-souled one,
like the Daityas being struck down by Śakra in a great battle. Here is Karṇa, having conquered the Pāñcālas, Pāṇḍavas, and Sṛñjayas in combat.
"It is my conviction that he gazes in all directions for your sake;
behold, O Pārtha, how he shines as he draws his excellent bow,
like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of gods after conquering his enemies."
08,043.034a These Kauravas are roaring upon seeing the prowess of Karṇa,
08,043.034c terrifying the Pārthas and the Sṛñjayas by the thousands in battle.
08,043.035a Having terrified the Pāṇḍus with his whole soul in this great battle—
Having terrified [the enemy] in battle, O Pārtha, Rādheya, the best of chariot-warriors, addresses all the troops, that giver of honor:
"Attack! Go! Rush forward quickly, O Kauravas!"
"O Sṛñjayas, act with such diligence that not one of you escapes alive in battle; we shall follow behind. Having spoken thus, he proceeded from behind, scattering arrows.
O son of Pṛthā, behold Karṇa in battle, resplendent with his white umbrella, protecting the Kaurava army on all sides like the sun beautifying the mountain of sunrise.
O Bhārata, with a hundred ribs, this umbrella resembling the full moon being held over his head in battle—
this Karṇa, O lord of the people, gazes at you with a sidelong glance.

Exerting the utmost effort, he will certainly prevail in battle. Behold him, O mighty-armed one, as he brandishes his great bow and discharges arrows resembling venomous serpents, endowed with great strength.
O Pārtha, scorcher of enemies, that son of Rādhā is seen returning with the monkey-bannered chariot, seeking battle with you;
he approaches for his own destruction, like a moth into a lamp.
For this man is impatient and brave, devoted to the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son;
O Pārtha, that one of very dull intellect can never tolerate you.
And seeing him alone on the field of battle, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son—
And seeing you, O Pārtha, enraged against the great car-warrior Karṇa,
and seeing Karṇa alone, O Bhārata,
that Duryodhana, clad in armor, has advanced with his division of chariots in a fit of wrath.
Desiring to protect [himself], the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra advances with great vigilance;
this evil-minded one must be slain with all effort by all of you together. As you two, renowned and undaunted, prepare for battle, [he stands before you].
O Pārtha, let all the Kauravas behold your prowess in this battle between gods and asuras, like that between the Devas and Dānavas;
for they shall see you, O bull of the Bharatas, exceedingly enraged, and Karṇa as well.
"O bull of the Bharatas, that Duryodhana, being enraged, finds no reply; yet you, desiring fame, sovereignty, and supreme happiness, and considering yourself a man of self-mastery, [should respond]."
And while the virtuous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira has forgiven the transgression of the son of Rādhā,
that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra advances against him with his followers.
O Bhārata, he alone must be slain, for he is the root of this enmity.
Just as the certain destruction of branches occurs when the root is cut,
so too, O Pārtha, when Duryodhana is slain, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— along with their servants, ministers, and kinsmen— will be destroyed, O mighty-armed one.
Behold how all the warriors advance toward Bhīma’s chariot;
Bhīma too, his eyes copper-red with fury, slays the enemies without exception.
This King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, is protected by the two Yamas.
Duryodhana, too, is protected by Karṇa and his son;
while Kṛtavarman, Kṛpa, and the son of Droṇa—those supreme warriors—protect one another; and both Kulūka and Śakuni stand there, having provided mutual protection.
"O son of Rādhā, adopt immediately the course of action appropriate for the occasion;
setting your mind on noble combat, advance against that leader of chariot-divisions. For these five, O best of chariot-warriors, are the foremost of chariot-fighters."
Hundreds of warriors of great strength and terrifying splendor are advancing with speed;
five thousand elephants, twice as many horses,
and millions of foot soldiers have gathered together, O son of Kuntī.

"O Hero, this army, protected by one another, is advancing against you; placing the son of Droṇa at their head, destroy it quickly. Having cut through this division of chariots, which is powerful and world-renowned..."

"O bull of the Bharatas, exerting the utmost effort, show yourself by your own power against that great archer, the son of a Sūta; confront him! And let all beings—the Kurus, Pañcālas, and Sṛñjayas—behold you."
"O scorcher of foes, look! That Karṇa, highly incensed, is charging against the Pāñcālas; for I see his banner directed toward Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s chariot. I believe he will utterly destroy the Pāñcālas."
"I tell you this pleasant news, O Pārtha, bull of the Bharatas:
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma and descendant of Kuru, is alive.
There is that mighty-armed Bhīma, who has returned to the front of the army."
Surrounded by the army of the Sṛñjayas and by Sātyaki, O Bhārata,
these Kauravas are being slain in battle with sharpened arrows by Bhīmasena, O son of Kuntī, and by the high-souled Pañcālas.
For the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son turned its back on the battle;
slaughtered by Bhīma’s arrows, it fled in haste.
Drenched in blood, it resembled the earth when its crops have perished.
O best of the Bharatas, this army of the Bharatas looks miserable. O son of Kuntī, behold Bhīmasena, the lord of warriors, who has returned;
like an enraged venomous serpent, the host flees from him.
O Arjuna, yellow, red, black, and white banners, adorned with stars, moons, and suns, are being scattered about; these various kinds of umbrellas are made of gold,
silver, and other metals.
The banners are being cast down, and the elephants and horses are scattered;
these chariot-warriors fall from their chariots, deprived of life,
slain by the arrows of various colors from the Pāñcālas who do not flee.
O Dhanañjaya, the powerful Pāñcālas are charging against the Dhārtarāṣṭras, who have deprived the elephants, horses, and chariots of their men;
and those tigers among men, relying on Bhīmasena, are crushing them.
O subduer of enemies, having abandoned your life and disregarding the invincible strength of your foes,
these Pāñcālas are roaring and blowing their conchs;
they charge forward in battle, striking down the enemy with their arrows.
Behold the majesty of heaven, O scorcher of foes! For the Pāñcālas, filled with wrath, are slaying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra like lions slaying elephants;
they do so by seizing the weapons of their armed enemies while remaining unarmed themselves.
With those very [weapons], these unfailing missiles strike them down and roar;
these heads of the enemies are felled, as are their arms,
along with their chariots, elephants, horses, and all those heroic men who bring glory.
This great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons is being overwhelmed on all sides;
the warriors have been led to the abode of Yama by the Pāñcālas and the Māgadhas.
Having cast away their lives, they are being slaughtered by the great archers of the Pāñcālas.
Having come from Lake Mānasa with the Pāñcālas, like swift swans upon the Gaṅgā,
the heroes Kṛpa, Karṇa, and the others— bulls among men— exerted themselves with great prowess to hold back the Pāñcālas.
O Lord, O scorcher of foes, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and other great archers— your valiant friends— tried to restrain the Pāñcālas;
yet the great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side were deeply submerged by Bhīma’s weapons.
The heroes, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, are slaying their enemies by the thousands.
When the Pāñcālas have been overwhelmed by their foes, the son of the Wind-god (Bhīmasena), roaring fearlessly,
leaps upon the enemy host and hurls his arrows.
When the bull of the Bharatas turned back, all the chariots turned back as well;
the great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, with the majority of its chariot-warriors despondent,
and these charioteers utterly terrified and afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena, retreated.
Behold, these elephants, severed by Bhīma with iron shafts, are falling;
these various elephants, struck down by Bhīma’s arrows,
are falling like the peaks of mountains shattered by the thunderbolt of Indra.
By Bhīmasena, the elephants were sent to the abode of Yama;
O bull among men, they fell like the peaks of mountains,
pierced by Bhīmasena’s straight-jointed arrows.
Crushing their own ranks, these great elephants are fleeing;
these Kurus are running away, afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena,
abandoning their chariots, elephants, and horses by the thousands.
Hear the roar of the rushing elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
hear the cry of Bhīmasena as he puts the Kauravas to flight. You do not recognize the unbearable lion-roar of Bhīma.
"O Arjuna, as this hero, appearing victorious, roars in battle— this Nishada approaches the Pandava on a preeminent elephant,
desiring to slay him with his lances like the enraged Antaka bearing the staff."
His two arms, still clutching his maces, were severed by Bhīma as he roared;
struck by ten sharp iron arrows resembling tongues of fire, he was slain. Having killed him, Bhīma returned once more to strike down other attacking elephants.
Behold him, resembling a dark blue cloud, stationed upon great elephants that look like spears and lances; he is striking down Vṛkodara along with seven elephants and their banners and standards.
Having been struck down by the sharp arrows of the elder brother of Pārtha, those elephants were cut apart;
one elephant after another was slain with ten iron shafts each. And that roar of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was no longer heard.
When that bull of the Bharatas, equal to Purandara, turned back in his wrath,
those three united Akṣauhiṇīs of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son were held in check by the enraged Bhīmasena, that lion among men.
Indeed, O Pārtha, the kings are unable even to look upon him,
just as those with weak eyes cannot gaze at the sun when it has reached midday;
terrified of Bhīma, they are like other animals before a lion.
Terrified by arrows in battle, they find no peace anywhere;
filled with wrath, they afflict the mighty-armed king.
This son of Rādhā advances with great speed, accompanied by many.
But having avoided that timid one, he brought his bow to his side;
protecting that great king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stood there endowed with strength.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard this from Vāsudeva,
and having witnessed that most difficult feat performed by Bhīmasena,
the mighty-armed Dhanañjaya scattered the remaining enemies with his sharpened arrows.
O Lord, those hosts of Saṃśaptakas, being slaughtered in battle,
were broken and fled in fear toward the ten directions; though they possessed great strength,
they attained the state of guests in Indra’s realm and became free from sorrow through joy.
Having become the guests of Śakra, they became free from fever; having come into the presence of Śakra, they became free from grief. But the son of Pāṇḍu destroyed the Nārāyaṇa cowherds.
Assuming the highest speed, like a fierce wind scattering the clouds,
they were scattered here and there in terror, O Bhārata;
and then that Supreme among Men struck down those shaken heroes.
And Pārtha, that tiger among men, with his straight-jointed arrows,
struck down the fourfold army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
When Bhīmasena and the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira had turned back,
and while my own army was being slaughtered by the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas,
that flood of troops fled again and again, crying out in distress.
"O Sañjaya, I see no remnant left among my armies.
Alas! Having reached such a state, I shall surely not survive. O Sūta, how can I, who desire victory, endure this regarding my sons who never retreat?"
"How shall I live, having heard that my soldiers have been slain? What is the use of saying much today? Destiny is their ultimate resort.
Tell me, Saṃjaya, what did the Kurus do?"
Saṃjaya said:
O King, a great destruction has occurred among them due to your evil counsel;
for having seen the mighty-armed Bhīma, the powerful son of the Sūta [Karna]—
With eyes red with rage, O King, he rushed toward Bhīmasena, saying:
"Stay! Stay, son of Pṛthā! Behold my prowess today!
Today I shall send you to the abode of Yama."
Having spoken thus, he departed swiftly to where Bhīma was stationed.
And seeing your army turning its back in retreat from Bhīmasena,
O King, the mighty one rallied the forces with great effort.
Having arrayed your son’s army,
the mighty-armed Karna then advanced against the Pāṇḍavas, who were fierce in battle;
and the great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas advanced against the son of Rādhā.
Brandishing their bows in battle and scattering their arrows— Bhīmasena, the grandson of Śini, Śikhaṇḍin, Janamejaya,
the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and all the Prabhadrakas as well.

And the Pāñcālas, those tigers among men, filled with rage and appearing victorious in battle, rushed from all sides against your army. Likewise, O King, your men charged against the host of the Pāṇḍavas.

The great car-warriors rushed forward in haste, desiring to slay him. O tiger among men, that army— thick with chariots, elephants, and horses, and crowded with foot-soldiers and banners— was a sight of wonder to behold.
Śikhaṇḍin went against Karṇa, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O great king, went against your son Duḥśāsana, who was surrounded by a vast army;
Nakula went against Vṛṣasena, and Yudhiṣṭhira against Citrasena.
O King, in that battle, Sahadeva advanced against Ulūka;
Sātyaki against Śakuni; Bhīmasena against the Kauravas;
and the great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, against Arjuna who was exerting himself in the fray.
In the battle, Gautama rushed against Yudhāmanyu, the great archer;
and the powerful Kṛtavarman charged at Uttamaujas.
O King, in that combat, Kṛpa also attacked Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas.
The great archer Kṛtavarman hemmed him in in the battle;
O noble one, the mighty-armed Bhīmasena alone held back all the Kurus and your sons, along with their armies.
Then, O great king, Śikhaṇḍin, the slayer of Bhīṣma, checked Karna with feathered arrows as he was roaming about fearlessly. Thereupon,
his lip quivering with rage, Karna was obstructed by him.
With three arrows, he struck Śikhaṇḍin between the eyebrows;
yet bearing those arrows, Śikhaṇḍin shone greatly,
like a silver mountain endowed with three peaks.

Deeply pierced in battle by the Sūta’s son, that great archer struck Karṇa in the encounter with ninety sharpened arrows. Karṇa, having slain his horses and his charioteer with three arrows, [continued the fight].

Then that great car-warrior, with a razor-sharp arrow, shattered his standard. O King, having had his bow cut by the Sūta’s son in that encounter, the great car-warrior leaped down from that chariot whose horses had been slain.
Enraged, that scorcher of enemies hurled a spear at Karṇa. Having cut it down in battle with three arrows, O Bhārata,
Karṇa then struck Śikhaṇḍin with nine sharpened shafts.
Avoiding the arrows discharged from Karna’s bow, Śikhaṇḍin, the best among men and foremost of victors, quickly withdrew from there. Then,
O great king, Karna began to slaughter the Pāṇḍava armies.
O great king, just as a wind of great velocity encounters a heap of cotton,
so Dhṛṣṭadyumna, though afflicted by your son,
pierced Duḥśāsana in the middle of the chest with three arrows.
O noble one, Duḥśāsana pierced his left arm with a sharp,
gold-feathered, straight-knotted *bhalla* arrow.
But Dhṛṣṭadyumna, being thus pierced, became incensed and [discharged] a terrible shaft.
Enraged at Duḥśāsana, O Bhārata, he swiftly dispatched an arrow resembling a venomous serpent and possessing the speed of the wind (8.44.27). That arrow,
impelled by Dhṛṣṭadyumna, was rushing toward him with great velocity (8.44.28).
O lord of the people, your son cut [Dhrishtadyumna's bow] with three arrows; then,
approaching Dhrishtadyumna with seventeen other gold-adorned broad-headed shafts, he struck him in the arms and chest.

Then, O noble one, the son of Pṛṣata, filled with rage, cut his bow apart with an exceedingly sharp razor-headed arrow, and the people raised a loud shout. Thereupon, O bull of the Bharatas, your son took up another bow.
He surrounded Dhṛṣṭadyumna on all sides with volleys of arrows.
Seeing that prowess of your high-souled son,
the warriors in battle, as well as the Siddhas and hosts of Apsarases, laughed aloud.

"O elder brother of the Pāṇḍus, we do not see the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna as he strives in battle, held in check by Duḥśāsana like a great elephant by a lion. Therefore, [let] the Pāñcālas, along with their chariots, elephants, and horses, [advance]."
Desiring to rescue the commander-in-chief, they besieged your son;
then, O scorcher of foes, a battle commenced between your men and the enemies—
a terrible conflict, fierce in form, occurring at the time of destruction for all living beings.
Vṛṣasena, having pierced Nakula with five iron arrows,
struck him with three others as he stood near his father.
Then Nakula, filled with rage, [attacked] Vṛṣasena as if smiling.
With an exceedingly sharp iron shaft, he pierced him firmly in the heart.
Deeply pierced by his powerful enemy,
that crusher of foes struck his adversary with twenty arrows, and the latter in turn struck him with five shafts.
Then, with a thousand arrows, those two bulls among men covered each other, and the army was broken. Seeing the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son thus fleeing, the Sūta’s son [Karna]—
O lord of the people, having rushed forward, he forcibly checked him.
In that interval, O lord of the people, a bitter battle took place.
When Karṇa had turned back, Nakula then advanced against the Kauravas.
O lord of the people, Vṛṣasena, the son of Karṇa, having abandoned Nakula in battle along with his father the Pāñcāla king,
quickly protected the chariot wheel of the son of Rādhā, O honorable one.
But Ulūka, enraged in battle, was held in check by Sahadeva;
having been restrained at the head of the fray with hundreds of arrows by the furious warrior,
the powerful Sahadeva slew his four horses.
He dispatched his charioteer toward the abode of Yama. Then, O lord of the people, Ulūka leaped down from the vehicle and quickly retreated from the front of the battle.
The delighter of his father went forth against the full army of the Trigartas;
mounting another chariot, he proceeded into the presence of his father.
Sātyaki, having pierced Śakuni with twenty sharpened arrows, [continued the fray].
As if laughing, he cut down the standard of Saubala with a broad-headed arrow.
O King, the powerful Saubala, enraged in that battle,
dispatched his charioteer toward the abode of Yama.
Having torn through his armor, he further cut down his golden standard;
then Satyaki pierced him with sharpened arrows and,
O great king, struck his charioteer with three shafts.
Then, with swift arrows, he sent his horses to the abode of Yama. Thereupon, O bull of the Bharatas, the great car-warrior Śakuni suddenly leaped down and quickly mounted the chariot of Ulūka.
Then, O King, he quickly bore him away from the son of Śini, who was skilled in battle;
he carried that warrior, seated upon his chariot, out from the ocean of Sātyaki’s army.
But Sātyaki, O King, [rushed] against the host of your troops in the fray.
He rushed forward with great speed, and then that army was broken; O lord of the people, driven by the arrows of Śini’s descendant,
the host quickly fled in the ten directions and fell down as if lifeless.
Your son restrained Bhīmasena in the encounter;
but in a moment, Bhīma deprived him of his horses, charioteer, chariot, and standard,
O lord of the world, and at that, the Cāraṇas were gratified.
O bull among great men, perceiving that he had been defeated by his enemy, the king then fled out of fear from Bhīmasena’s reach toward the regions of misfortune; thereupon,
the entire Kuru army rushed toward Bhīmasena.
A great roar arose there from those who desired to slay Bhīma alone.
Yudhāmanyu, having pierced Kṛpa, quickly cut his bow asunder;
then Kṛpa, the best among wielders of weapons, took up another bow.
He brought down Yudhāmanyu’s standard, charioteer, and umbrella to the ground;
then the great car-warrior Yudhāmanyu departed on his very chariot.
Uttamaujas, however, [assailed] the son of Hṛdika, who possessed terrible prowess, with arrows.

Suddenly he covered him with arrows, just as a cloud covers a mountain with rain. That battle, O scorcher of foes, was exceedingly great and terrible in form, such as I have never seen before, O lord of the people.
Then, O King, Kṛtavarman pierced Uttamaujas in the heart during that battle; he then sank down upon the seat of his chariot.
His charioteer carried away that best of car-warriors on the chariot.
Then, O King, the Kuru army quickly rushed against the Pandava host;
thereafter, the entire Kuru force charged at Bhimasena.
Yudhiṣṭhira, for his part, overwhelmed Citrasena with a shower of arrows.
Citrasena also, filled with rage, opposed the son of Kuntī;
but after turning Citrasena away for a moment, that King of Dharma struck your army on all sides with sharpened arrows.
When that tumultuous slaughter of heroic men had commenced,
Duryodhana was overcome by intense anger;
burning with the fire of his rage, he—
Quickly approaching another chariot,
Citrasena pierced Bhīma with arrows of variegated feathers; even now, Duḥśāsana [remains there].
The gambler addicted to foul play, the son of Subala,
suddenly rushed toward Bhīmasena, who was being assailed from all sides by divisions of elephants.
And your men, O mighty-armed one, led by Duryodhana,
desiring to capture Yudhiṣṭhira, threw their entire army against him; Duḥśāsana and the son of Subala [assailed] the Pāṇḍava with a division of elephants.
Surrounding him with a vast multitude, he struck him with small arrows.
Then Bhīma, having swiftly turned the impatient Duryodhana away with hundreds of shafts, rushed toward the elephant division.
Seeing that elephant division suddenly charging toward him, Vṛkodara became violently incensed and invoked a divine weapon;
he struck elephants with elephants, just as Indra struck the Asuras with his thunderbolt.
Then, in that battle, Vṛkodara, slaughtering the elephants, covered the sky with floods of arrows as locusts cover a tree. Then, thousands of elephant herds gathered together.

Bhīma swiftly scattered them like the wind dispersing masses of clouds. Covered with nets of gold and clusters of jewels, those elephants shone exceedingly in the battle like rain-clouds charged with lightning.
O King, being slaughtered by Bhīma, those elephants fled in all directions;
some elephants, their hearts pierced,
fell to the earth amidst other elephants already fallen or falling, adorned with golden ornaments.
The earth there shone with the fallen elephant-warriors, radiant and adorned with jewels, like shattered mountains; the ground gleamed with those who had fallen,
resembling celestial bodies whose merit has been exhausted.
Then, struck by Bhīmasena’s arrows in that battle, hundreds of elephants fled with their temples split and their frontal globes shattered;
some, resembling mountains, were afflicted by fear and vomited blood.
With their limbs pierced by arrows, they fled like mountains streaked with various minerals;
I beheld the two arms of Bhīmasena as he brandished his bow, resembling great serpents and smeared with sandalwood and aloe paste.

O King, hearing the sound of Bhīmasena’s bowstring, which resembled the roar of a thunderbolt, the elephants fled in great haste, discharging excrement and urine; such was the deed of that single, wise hero.
As he struck down all beings, it shone like that of Rudra.
Sañjaya said:
Then, [the chariot] yoked with white horses and concentrated upon Nārāyaṇa...
Standing upon his excellent chariot, the glorious Arjuna prevailed; O best of kings, Vijaya agitated that army of yours in battle,
like fire agitating the great ocean with its surging waves.
While the one with white horses was distracted, your son Duryodhana,
filled with rage and surrounded by half the army,
suddenly approached and hemmed in the indignant Yudhiṣṭhira as he advanced.
Then, with seventy-three razor-sharp arrows, he pierced the son of Pāṇḍu.
Thereupon, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, became exceedingly enraged;
he swiftly discharged three hundred broad-headed shafts (bhalla) at your son.

Then the Kauravas rushed forward, desiring to seize Yudhiṣṭhira; but perceiving those of evil intent to be their enemies, the assembled great car-warriors came together, seeking to protect Kuntī’s son, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Nakula, Sahadeva, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī, rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira;
and Bhīmasena, crushing your great car-warriors in battle.
Desiring to reach the king who was surrounded by his enemies,
he rushed forward; but Karna Vaikartana, O King, held back all those great archers as they approached with a mighty shower of arrows.
Discharging showers of arrows and hurling iron javelins,
they were unable even to look at the son of Rādhā, despite their efforts;
for he was one who had reached the further shore of all weapons and missiles, [overpowering] all those great archers.
With a great shower of arrows, the son of Rādhā warded him off;
but the high-minded Sahadeva, quickly discharging his weapons, approached and swiftly pierced Duryodhana with twenty shafts.
Pierced by Sahadeva, he shone like a mountain,
resembling an elephant in rut drenched in blood;
seeing your son there, deeply pierced by those well-sharpened shafts.
Highly enraged, Rādheya, the best of chariot-warriors, rushed forward;
seeing Duryodhana in that state, he swiftly discharged his weapon and with it slaughtered Yudhiṣṭhira’s army as well as the son of Pṛṣata.
Then, O King, Yudhiṣṭhira’s army, being slaughtered by that high-souled one and afflicted by the arrows of the Sūta’s son, suddenly fled;
various shafts there fell upon one another.
The feathered shafts released from the bow of the Sūta’s son struck one another in the sky; O Great King, from their friction as those floods of arrows fell against each other,
fire was produced.
Then, O King, Karṇa swiftly struck out in the ten directions with arrows that pierced the bodies of others, like swarms of locusts on the move.
His two arms, smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with jewels and gold, [appeared radiant].
Displaying his supreme weapons, Karṇa crossed his arms;
then, O King, bewildering all directions with his arrows,
Karṇa severely oppressed Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma.
Then, O great king, the righteous son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, enraged,
struck Karṇa with fifty sharpened arrows. That battle became terrible to behold, shrouded in the darkness of arrows.

A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among your men, O lord of the people, as the army was being slaughtered at that time by the son of Dharma, O honorable one, with various sharp arrows feathered with vulture plumes and whetted on stone.
With numerous various arrows, as well as spears, double-edged swords, and maces—
wherever that righteous-souled one cast his fierce gaze,
O bull of the Bharatas, there your men were shattered to pieces.

Karna, also violently enraged, being impatient and wrathful with his face quivering in fury, struck Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, in battle with iron shafts, crescent-headed arrows, and calf-tooth-headed bolts.
The one of immeasurable soul rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira with arrows;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, as if laughing, [struck] that Karṇa with a hundred sharp, gold-feathered shafts whetted on stone and fletched with heron feathers.
He pierced the king, the Pāṇḍava, in the chest with three broad-headed arrows.
Severely afflicted by him, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
sat down on the seat of his chariot and urged the charioteer, "Go!"
Then all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with the kings, cried out;
they rushed from every side toward the king, shouting, "Seize him!
Then there were seventeen hundred Kekaya strikers.
O King, accompanied by the Pāñcālas, they held back the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. While that tumultuous battle, which caused the destruction of men, was raging,
the mighty Duryodhana and Bhīma encountered one another.
Then Karṇa, with a multitude of arrows, struck down the great car-warriors of the Kekayas— those supreme archers who stood arrayed before him—
even as they strove to repel the son of Rādhā.
Karna sent five hundred chariots to the abode of Yama.
Then, seeing the son of Radha to be irresistible in battle, the warriors,
afflicted by Karna’s arrows, approached Bhimasena.
Having torn apart the chariot-array in many ways with his nets of arrows,
Karṇa, on a single chariot alone, rushed toward Yudhiṣṭhira,
who was wounded and mangled by his shafts as he approached the military camp.
Approaching the hero who was moving slowly between the twins and was deprived of his senses,
the Sūta’s son, desiring the welfare of Duryodhana, pierced the king with three sharp and excellent arrows.
In the same manner, the king pierced the son of Rādhā between the breasts;
with three arrows he struck the charioteer, and with four, the four horses.
As for the two protectors of Pārtha’s wheels, they were the two sons of Mādrī, the subduers of foes.
Those two also rushed toward Karṇa, crying, "Do not kill the king! Nakula and Sahadeva, exerting the utmost effort, showered the son of Rādhā with separate volleys of arrows.
In that very same way, the powerful son of the Suta pierced those two high-souled subduers of enemies with two sharp-edged broad-headed arrows; meanwhile,
Rādheya struck down the ivory-colored horses, swift as thought.

Then, with another broad-headed arrow, the son of the Sūta, that great archer, as if laughing, struck down the helmet of Yudhiṣṭhira’s excellent horse Kālavāla in the midst of the battle. The son of Kuntī’s [Yudhiṣṭhira] great bowman [was thus struck].
In the same manner, the powerful one, having slain Nakula’s horses,
cut through the pole and the bow of the wise son of Mādrī. Those two Pāṇḍavas, their horses slain and their chariots destroyed, were severely wounded.

Then the two brothers ascended the chariot of Sahadeva. Seeing them there deprived of their chariots, their maternal uncle, the King of Madra and slayer of enemy heroes, spoke out of compassion to the son of Rādhā.
"Today you must fight with Phalguna, the son of Pṛthā.
For what reason, being so violently incensed, do you fight with Dharmarāja? Your weapons, missiles, and armor are exhausted; your arrows are spent and your quiver is empty."
"Exhausted in both your charioteer and your horses, and likewise covered by the weapons of your enemies,
O son of Rādhā, you will become an object of ridicule when you encounter Pārtha.
Though addressed in this way by the King of Madra in the battle, Karṇa—
In that very same way, the enraged Karṇa struck Yudhiṣṭhira;
having pierced the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī with sharp arrows,
Karṇa, laughing in the midst of battle, turned them away with his shafts.
Then Śalya, laughing, spoke again to Karṇa,
who was standing upon his chariot, highly agitated and intent on the slaughter of Yudhiṣṭhira—
he for whose sake you have been constantly honored by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"O son of Rādhā, slay that Pārtha! What is the use of killing Yudhiṣṭhira?
This is the very great sound of the two Kṛṣṇas blowing their conchs, and this roar of their bows is heard like the thundering of a cloud in the rainy season."

"O Karṇa, behold him in battle— this Arjuna, who, striking down the noble chariot-warriors with showers of arrows, devours our entire army. And Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas are the protectors of that hero's rear."
The heroic Sātyaki protects his northern wheel,
while Dhṛṣṭadyumna likewise protects his southern wheel;
and Bhīmasena indeed fights against King Dhārtarāṣṭra.
O son of Rādhā, act in such a way that Bhīma does not slay him today while we all look on, so that our king may be released;
behold him, the ornament of battle, seized by Bhīmasena!

If, however, he should be released after being captured, it would be a source of very great astonishment. Come and rescue him before he falls into the ultimate peril! What indeed is the point of killing the two sons of Mādrī and King Yudhiṣṭhira?
O lord of the earth, having heard these words of Śalya and seeing Duryodhana himself seized by Bhīma in that great battle, the son of Rādhā—
being intensely devoted to the king and urged by the speech of Śalya— [acted].
Leaving behind Ajātaśatru and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī,
that heroic warrior rushed forward to protect your son,
drawn by the Madra king’s horses which moved as if through the sky.
When Karṇa had departed, O noble one, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu and Kuntī,
fled away with the swift horses of Sahadeva;
accompanied by those two, that lord of men proceeded quickly as if filled with shame.
Having reached the military camp, wounded and mangled by arrows,
he quickly descended from his chariot and entered a splendid bedchamber;
though the shafts had been extracted, he was still intensely tormented by the dart in his heart.
The king spoke to his two brothers, the sons of Mādrī, those great car-warriors: "O Pāṇḍavas, go quickly to Bhīmasena’s army;
that Vṛkodara fights while roaring like a thundercloud."
Then Nakula, that bull among chariot-warriors, and the radiant Sahadeva— those two brothers who crush their enemies— mounted another chariot and,
with horses of supreme speed, proceeded toward the powerful Bhima.
The two brothers stood there together, having surrounded that division.
Sañjaya said:
But the son of Droṇa was surrounded by a great multitude of chariots.
O King, he rushed suddenly toward the place where the king was stationed;
as he came charging forward with such force, the heroic Pārtha, aided by Śauri, suddenly held him back, just as the shore holds back the ocean.
Then, O great king, the powerful son of Droṇa, filled with rage,
covered both Arjuna and Vāsudeva with feathered shafts.
Seeing the two Kṛṣṇas thus shrouded there, the great car-warriors—
Then the Kurus, overcome with supreme amazement, gazed on;
but Arjuna, as if smiling, then invoked a divine weapon,
which the Brahmin warded off in battle, O Bhārata.
Whatever weapon the Pāṇḍava discharged in battle with the intent to slay, that very weapon the great archer, the son of Droṇa, neutralized. Thus,
O King, as that terrifying battle of weapons proceeded, [the conflict continued].
In the battle, we beheld the son of Droṇa like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Having covered the cardinal and intermediate directions with his straight-flying arrows,
he pierced Vāsudeva in the right arm with three shafts.
Then Arjuna, having slain all the horses of that high-souled one,
made the ground in battle flow with waves of streams of blood—
a fierce river carrying all beings to the other world.

They beheld all the charioteers and warriors slain in battle by the arrows discharged from Pārtha’s bow; and the son of Droṇa likewise caused that most terrible river, which carried away his enemies, to flow forth.
In that chaotic and fierce battle between the son of Droṇa and the son of Pṛthā,
the warriors fought without restraint, rushing hither and thither on chariots whose horses and drivers were slain, and on steeds whose riders had been killed.
O King, a terrible destruction of men was wrought in battle by Pārtha; with elephants whose riders were slain and with elephant-drivers whose elephants had been killed,
chariot-warriors fell, struck down by arrows released from Pārtha’s bow.
The horses, their traces loosened, ran hither and thither;
seeing that feat of Pārtha, who shines in battle,
the valiant son of Droṇa quickly approached Arjuna, the foremost of victors.
Shaking his great bow adorned with gold,
he covered Kṛṣṇa from all sides in battle with sharpened arrows.
Then, O great king, the son of Droṇa, having drawn back [his bow], struck Arjuna with a feathered shaft.
Having reached his chest in the encounter, he struck him in battle.
O Bhārata, being deeply pierced in that combat by the son of Droṇa,
the noble-minded wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow violently assailed him with showers of arrows.

Having completely shrouded the son of Droṇa in battle, he cut off his bow. With his bow severed, he took up in the fight a terrible iron club whose touch was like that of a thunderbolt, and hurled it at the son of Droṇa.
Then the son of Droṇa took it up and hurled it at the wearer of the diadem. As that iron club, adorned with gold and embellished with refined *jāmbūnada* gold, came flying toward him—
O King, the Pāṇḍava, as if laughing, suddenly cut [the bow];
then the son of Droṇa suddenly cut [his arrows], and the people raised a loud cry.
It fell to the earth in many pieces from the arrows of Bhāradvāja’s son.
O King, he was shattered like a mountain by the wind;
then, O great king, the enraged son of Droṇa, that great car-warrior,
overwhelmed Bibhatsu with the force of the Aindra weapon.
O King, seeing that net spread out like Indra’s illusion,
the powerful Pārtha took up his Gāṇḍīva bow and struck down that net of Indra.
Taking up that excellent weapon released by Mahendra, Pārtha then tore apart that net discharged by Indra,
and in an instant [reached] the chariot of Droṇa’s son.
Then the son of Droṇa, overwhelmed by the arrows of Pārtha,
approached and covered [him] by plunging into that rain of Pāṇḍava shafts.
Then, having revealed his supreme name with arrows,
he suddenly pierced Kṛṣṇa with a hundred and Arjuna with three hundred small shafts.
Then Arjuna, with a hundred arrows,
pierced the preceptor’s son in his vital organs,
as well as his horses, his charioteer, and his bowstring.
While your men were looking on, he covered him with arrows;
then Arjuna pierced the son of Droṇa in battle with ten shafts. Having pierced the vital organs of the son of Droṇa, that Pāṇḍava, the slayer of enemy heroes—
And with a broad-headed arrow (bhalla), he struck his charioteer down from the seat of the chariot. Taking up the reins himself, he covered the two Kṛṣṇas with arrows;
there we beheld the wonderful and swift prowess of Droṇa’s son.
O King, all the warriors praised him in that battle for restraining his horses and for fighting Phalguna;
because of this, O King, all the soldiers in the encounter offered him their acclaim.
Then, laughing in that battle, Bībhatsu [Arjuna]—
when Phalguna was being overwhelmed by the son of Droṇa in the fray—
then Jayasena cut the reins of the chariot horses with razor-sharp arrows.
Afflicted by the force of the arrows, those horses fled;
then, O Bhārata, a great clamor arose once more from your army.
But the Pāṇḍavas, having achieved victory, rushed upon your troops.
Discharging sharp arrows from all sides, they sought victory; yet,
O great king, the vast army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons was repeatedly broken by the heroic Pāṇḍavas, who were exultant in their triumph.
O great king, lord of men, while your sons— those warriors of diverse skills— along with Śakuni Saubaleya and the high-souled Karṇa looked on,
that vast army was being held back by your sons.
Being struck from all sides, it did not stand firm in battle;
then, O great king, as your sons' vast army fled here and there in fear, it became utterly chaotic.
"Stay! Stay! cried the son of the Sūta incessantly, yet that army did not halt as it was being slaughtered by those high-souled warriors.
Then, O great king, a loud shout was raised by the Pāṇḍavas, who appeared radiant with victory.
Seeing the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons fleeing in every direction,
Duryodhana then spoke to Karṇa as if out of affection:
"Behold, Karṇa, how the army is being severely afflicted by the Pāṇḍavas."
"While you stand here, they flee in every direction out of sheer terror;
knowing this, O mighty-armed subduer of foes, do what must be done. And thousands of warriors, O bull among men, [seek refuge] in you alone."
"O hero, they cry out in battle as they are being routed by the Pāṇḍavas.
Having heard these significant words of Duryodhana, Rādheya,
the son of the Sūta, spoke this speech to the King of Madra:
"Behold, O lord of men, the prowess of my arms and my weapons!
Today in battle I shall slay all the Pāñcālas along with the Pāṇḍus.
Drive the horses, O tiger among men, with auspicious speed, O lord of men!"
Having spoken thus, O great king, the powerful son of the Sūta,
that hero, took up the ancient and excellent bow Vijaya;
having strung it, O great king, he polished it again and again.
Having restrained his own warriors with oaths of truth,
that one of immeasurable soul and great strength invoked the Bhārgava weapon.
Then, O King, there appeared thousands, millions, and billions [of arrows].
And in that great battle, sharp arrows issued forth by the millions;
covered by those blazing and most terrible shafts, fletched with the feathers of herons and peacocks,
the Pāṇḍava army could not be discerned at all.
O lord of the people, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Pāñcālas as they were afflicted in battle by the powerful Bhārgava weapon;
O King, [the field was covered] with thousands of falling elephants and men.
O King, O tiger among men, with those chariots and horses slain here and there on all sides, the earth trembled;
the entire great army of the Pāṇḍavas became utterly disordered.
But Karṇa alone, the best among warriors, like a smokeless fire,
shone brilliantly as that scorcher of foes, O tiger among men, consumed his enemies.
Being slaughtered by Karṇa, the Pāñcālas together with the Cedis—
In various places they became bewildered, like elephants in a forest fire;
those tigers among men, O best of men, cried out as they had done before. Hearing the cries of those who were terrified at the front of the battle, [he acted].
O King, as they fled in all directions, terrified on every side,
a great cry of distress arose there like that of hungry ghosts (preta) during the dissolution of the world.
O noble one, seeing them being slaughtered by the Suta's son, [the warriors...]
All beings, even those belonging to the animal realm, were terrified.
As they were being slaughtered in battle by the Sūtaputra,
the Sṛñjayas cried out repeatedly toward Arjuna and Vāsudeva.
Having heard the cries of those being slain by Karṇa’s arrows—
like the bewildered inhabitants of the King of the Dead’s city crying out to the King of the Dead—
the mighty-armed Arjuna, the best among all wielders of weapons, [acted].
Having defeated the son of his preceptor— who was difficult even for the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) to overcome in battle—
Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, then spoke to Vāsudeva,
having seen that most terrible Bhārgava weapon being employed there with great fear.
"Behold, O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, the prowess of Bhārgava’s weapon!
Indeed, this weapon cannot be destroyed in battle by any means whatsoever.
And behold the son of the Sūta, filled with fury, in this great conflict, O Kṛṣṇa!"
That hero, resembling Death itself, performing dreadful deeds and urging on his exceedingly swift horses, looks at me again and again;
yet I do not see Karna fleeing from the battle.
"While living, a man may experience both victory and defeat in battle;
but for one who is conquered, O Hṛṣīkeśa, there is only death—how can there be victory?
Having been addressed thus by Pārtha, Kṛṣṇa, the best among the wise, [replied].

He spoke these words, appropriate for the occasion, to Dhanañjaya, the subduer of enemies: "For King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, has been severely wounded by Karṇa. Having seen him and comforted him, O Pārtha, you shall then slay Karṇa."
"O Kaunteya, proceed immediately with what the occasion demands.
O Bhārata, having slain Karṇa alone with your division of chariots,
he— this Karṇa— shines in battle like the sun at midday."
"O Kṛṣṇa, turn back the chariot; one who lives sees auspicious things.
Then Janārdana proceeded, desiring to see Yudhiṣṭhira.
Sañjaya said:
Then, O lord of the people, having heard his words, Janārdana quickly departed from the battle by chariot, O Bhārata,
leaving behind Bhīma of terrible prowess as the counter-force.
"Indeed, he is capable of enduring this as the Kurus advance;
O noble one, he will cause Karṇa to be won over by the toil of battle. And in the encounter, O King, he will cause Karṇa to experience exhaustion."
O Kauravya, for the sake of resting the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
and also to see the king, the hero withdrew from the battle. And Kṛṣṇa spoke to Arjuna, who was severely wounded by the king.
"O best of the Kurus, after you have comforted him, you shall then slay Karṇa. Then Dhananjaya, desiring to see the king afflicted by arrows, repeatedly urged Vāsudeva, saying, "Go! Go!"
"O Vārṣṇeya, my mind is deeply distressed regarding the king. Thus urged by Pārtha, Keśihā, the joy of the Vṛṣṇis,
set out swiftly on his chariot at the command of Keśava for the battle."
While proceeding with the desire to see Dharmarāja, the son of Kuntī surveyed the army but did not see his elder brother there. O Bhārata, having fought with the son of Droṇa, the son of Kuntī—
Having defeated the son of Bhrigu, who was difficult even for the wielder of the thunderbolt to withstand in battle, that fierce archer,
having performed a great and difficult noble deed, vanquished the son of Droṇa.
Then Dhanañjaya, invincible by his enemies, surveyed his own army as he fought against those stationed at the front of the host.
Gladdening the heroes with his own heroism, Savyasācin praised them by recounting their celebrated past deeds and steadied his own chariot-warriors in the army.
But not seeing his eldest brother, the descendant of Ajamidha, the one adorned with a diadem and garland approached Bhima with speed and spoke.
"O King, what is the news here regarding the king?
Bhīma replied:
"The king Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, has departed from here."
"If his limbs are mangled by Karna’s arrows, he might somehow survive.
Arjuna said:
"Therefore, may you depart from here quickly."
Surely that king, having been deeply pierced by Karna’s arrows, has gone to his camp for the sake of recovering from the wound of the best of the Kurus.
He who, when the nocturnal battle had commenced,
was pierced deeply by Droṇa,
remained there nonetheless, full of vigor and awaiting victory.
That foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, who was previously brought to a state of uncertainty by Droṇa before he was slain,
has today been brought to that same condition by Karṇa in battle, O high-souled one.
"O Bhīma, go quickly today to find him;
I shall remain here, holding back the hosts of our enemies.
Bhīma said:
"O you of great power, you yourself must know the news concerning the king, that bull among the Bharatas;
for if I were to go there, O Arjuna,"
"The great heroes will say of me, 'He was afraid';
therefore, Arjuna said to Bhīmasena,
'The Saṃśaptakas stand arrayed as my adversaries.'"
"Without slaying these men, I am unable to depart from this assembly of enemy hosts.
Then Bhīmasena spoke to Arjuna:
"Relying on my own prowess, O hero of the Kurus,
I shall fight against the Saṃśaptakas in battle; go, Dhananjaya, against all of them!"
Having heard those words of Bhīmasena—
so difficult to utter in the midst of his enemies— that single warrior [approached] the irresistible army of the Saṃśaptakas.
"It is most difficult to bear," said Pārtha, whose banner bears the ape,
to the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa,
who possesses true prowess.
Having heard the words of his brother Adīnasattva, that high-souled one, whose word is truth, then set out to see the best of the Kurus and to go toward that battle.
Then he spoke to the best of the Vṛṣṇis:
"O descendant of Vṛṣṇi, my mind is deeply distressed regarding the king.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, urge on the horses and plunge into this ocean of chariots."
"O Keśava, I wish to see King Ajātaśatru.
At these words of Bībhatsu, Hari urged on that chariot. Then the foremost of all the Dāśārhas [drove] the horses;
He urged Bhīma and said this to him:
"O hero, this deed of yours today is not surprising;
we shall go—slay the hosts of our enemies!"
Then, O King, Hṛṣīkeśa proceeded with horses as swift as Garuḍa, moving faster and faster than before, toward where King Yudhiṣṭhira was,
having stationed Bhīmasena, the tamer of foes, at the front of the opposing army.
And having thus instructed Vṛkodara for the battle, O Indra among kings,
those two subduers of enemies reached the king in an instant.
Then, having gone there, those two heroes among men—
Having approached the king as he lay alone,
both of them descended from the chariot and paid homage at the feet of the King of Dharma.
Having gone with speed, that foremost of the Daśārhas saw the King of the Kurus lying alone;
both of them had their minds impelled by a surge of great joy.
Having approached the king whose wound was still bleeding, they both stood with palms joined in reverence; O Great King, they were drenched in blood from their wounds inflicted by weapons.
Having struck down your army, those two have retreated from the field of battle.
O bull among men, seeing those two tigers among men safe and sound,
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna approached them with joy, like the Aśvins approaching Vāsava.
King Vivasvat indeed rejoiced at that, like the two Aśvins;
and when the great Asura Jambha was slain, he was like the preceptor Śakra-Viṣṇu.
Thinking that Karṇa had been killed, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira likewise rejoiced.
Delighted, that conqueror of enemy cities,
