having become those two tigers among men,
spoke with a voice faltering with joy, being pleased with those two subduers of foes.
Saṃjaya said:
Then those two broad-eyed men of blood-red hue arrived,
their limbs covered with arrows and smeared with blood.
Seeing those two heroes among men, who were like Mahendra himself, arrive there announcing pleasant news to Yudhiṣṭhira, they then beheld them.
King Yudhiṣṭhira, his mind overwhelmed with grief,
regained consciousness with great difficulty and then once more became joyful in heart.
Having observed those two foremost heroes at the head of the army,
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these words,
seeing the two of great being, Keśava and Arjuna, together.

He considered the son of Adhiratha already slain in battle by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow. O bull of the Bharatas, that slayer of enemies, the son of Kuntī, honored them with a smile and with words of supreme sweetness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Welcome, O son of Devakī; welcome to you, Dhanañjaya. Indeed, the sight of both of you, O Acyuta and Arjuna, is most pleasing to me."
How can you fight that great car-warrior who is unhurt and unharmed,
who is like a venomous serpent in battle, skilled in all weapons,
the leader of all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and their refuge and armor?
He was protected by Vṛṣasena and the archer Suṣeṇa;
he was permitted [to train] by the highly heroic Rāma, who is difficult to defeat in weapons; he was authorized by the illustrious Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
The foremost leader of the entire world, renowned throughout the world as a charioteer,
the protector of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, one who goes to the front of the army,
the slayer of enemy forces, and the crusher of the hosts of foes.
Devoted to the welfare of Duryodhana and exerting himself for our battle,
he is invincible in great combat even by the gods led by Indra;
he is equal to fire and wind in both splendor and strength.
Having slain Karṇa in the great battle— him who was as deep as the netherworld (pātāla), who increased the joy of his friends, and who appeared like Death to his enemies—
it is by good fortune that you two have arrived here, like two immortals after conquering an Asura.
O mighty-armed one, today I, undaunted, have waged a terrible battle against Acyuta and Arjuna while Dhṛṣṭadyumna looked on,
like the enraged God of Death seeking to destroy all living beings.
By him my banner was cut down and my two flank-drivers slain; I was deprived of my horses while Yuyudhāna looked on,
as well as Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the twins, and the heroic Śikhaṇḍin.
While the sons of Draupadī and all the Pāñcālas were looking on,
Karna— having conquered these many hosts of highly heroic enemies—
defeated me, O mighty-armed one, as I exerted myself in that great battle.
Having pursued me in battle, that best of warriors, having undoubtedly insulted me at every turn, spoke many harsh words; yet,
O Dhanañjaya, it is solely through the power of Bhīmasena that I still live.
What is the use of saying more here? I am not able to endure that, O Dhanañjaya, because for thirteen years I have been afraid;
I found no sleep at night, nor did I find happiness anywhere during the day.
"O Dhanañjaya, filled with hatred for him,
I am consumed by anguish, knowing my own death to be near, like an elephant struck by a *vādhrīṇasa* bird—
a winged creature with a black neck, red veins, and white wings."
"O Lord, that [animal] is indeed called a *vādhrīṇasa* by the ritualists in the rites for the ancestors;
yet this time has come upon me as I reflect:
how might Karṇa be slain by me in battle?"
Whether waking or sleeping, O son of Kuntī, I always see Karṇa everywhere; indeed, this entire world has become Karṇa for me.
For wherever I go, O Dhanañjaya, I am terrified of Karṇa.
"Indeed, wherever I looked, I saw Karṇa standing right before me.
Therefore, O Pārtha, having been defeated by that very hero who never retreats in battle, I have been released alive along with my horses and my chariot."
"What purpose, indeed, is there for me in life, or what use is there in sovereignty,
since I have been thus insulted here by Karṇa, who shines in battle? That which was never before encountered from Bhīṣma, Kṛpa, or Droṇa in combat [has now been suffered]."
"That which was to be attained by me today in battle from the son of a Sūta, that great car-warrior—
that I ask you about, O Kaunteya, as one who is unskilled;
tell it to me in its entirety, how Karṇa was slain by you."
Equal to Śakra in valor in battle, with prowess like that of Yama, and likewise equal to Rāma in the use of weapons— how indeed was he,
who was proclaimed a great chariot-warrior (*mahāratha*) and skilled in all forms of combat, slain?

O lord of the people, how was that son of Rādhā— who was the foremost of all archers, the peerless hero among men, and who was always honored by Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with his sons for your sake— slain by you?
O Arjuna, O bull among men, Dhṛtarāṣṭra— among all the warriors—
regarded Karṇa as your own death in battle;
how then was he slain by you in combat, O tiger among men?
Tell me that, O Bībhatsu, how Karṇa was slain by you,
so that his head, along with its swelling flesh, may be seen taken away by you, O tiger among men, like a deer by a tiger, while his friends look on.
The son of a Sūta, Karṇa, who sat waiting upon you from every direction and quarter, desiring to protect you in battle and wishing to give you multitudes of elephants in the fray;
Since he was now desiring to give men a chariot filled with jewels using his very sharp, heron-feathered arrows,
how was that Karṇa slain by you today?
"The Sūtaputra was slain by you in battle;
does that evil-souled one lie upon the surface of the earth? Have you today accomplished for me my greatest desire?"
Having slain the Sūtaputra in battle,
he who had been intoxicated with pride and roamed about in every direction for your sake— that haughty son of a charioteer— has been struck down.
Having encountered him in battle, was that one who considers himself a hero slain by you today in the fray—
he who possessed a golden chariot yoked with the finest of elephants?
O dear one, has that wicked man— who, desiring to give a chariot to his enemies for your sake, always challenges you in battle—
been slain by you in the fight?
He who, ever intoxicated by the pride of his own valor, used to boast in the assembly of the Kauravas—
he was exceedingly dear to that Suyodhana.
Has that wicked man been slain by you today? Has he been encountered by the birds sent forth by you, seeking blood and dispatched with arrows released from your bow?
Today that wicked man lies with his limbs shattered;
has the arm of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son been broken— he who always boasted in the midst of kings?
Delighting Duryodhana and filled with pride,
he said out of delusion, "I shall be the slayer of Phalguna";
has his chariot not indeed been destroyed in that manner?
I trust you have not made false that speech which Karna, dear to me, spoke to you in harsh and various ways in the midst of the assembly?
"Shame on the Pāṇḍavas! For you, O Kṛṣṇā, are now without a husband. Is it certain that this great-souled one was indeed your enemy, he who supported you for twelve years?"
Karna, the subduer of enemies, whose mind was fixed on the welfare of Duryodhana, undertook a terrible vow:
"I shall never wash my feet."
"As long as Pārtha remains, he is of little intelligence"—
this has always been the vow of that son of Śakra;
has that Karṇa been slain by you today?
"I shall not wash my feet until I have slain Dhanañjaya, who possesses such fierce impetuosity in battles. Having struck him down in combat, O Phalguna— "
I hope that vow has not been broken today by you—
that wicked-minded Karṇa who spoke to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly hall in the midst of the Kuru heroes?
"O Kṛṣṇā, why do you not abandon the Pāṇḍavas,
who are so extremely weak, fallen, and deprived of their strength—
those for whose sake Karṇa made that vow?"
"That evil-minded one thought: 'I, a mighty slayer of enemies, shall not return here from the battle without having slain Pārtha along with Kṛṣṇa.'"
I hope that his body was not pierced by arrows while he was still conscious during this encounter between the Sṛñjayas and the Kauravas in battle?
"Has he whom I have brought to such a state been slain by you today upon encountering him? Has he,
that man of very dull intellect, been killed by you?"
By the blazing arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, Savyasācin severed the radiant head, adorned with earrings,
from the body in battle.
O hero, since you were meditated upon by me as I discharged my arrow for the sake of Karṇa’s slaughter,
has that [meditation] of mine today been made fruitful by you?
That Suyodhana, filled with pride, looks upon us by relying on Karṇa— that has been meditated upon and accomplished by the piercing of Karṇa’s ear.
"Has that refuge of Suyodhana been broken by you today through your prowess— that refuge which formerly called us 'barren sesame seeds'?"
Has that evil-minded son of a Sūta, who was so intolerant, been slain by you in battle after approaching the kings in the midst of the assembly?
That wicked-souled son of a charioteer, who formerly spoke with derision when she had been defeated by the son of Subala, said:
"Bring Yājñasenī here yourself by force!"
I hope that you have slain here today that evil-souled son of a charioteer who sent Kṛṣṇā away after she had been won by the son of Subala, saying, "Bring her."
That man of dull intellect was slain by force;
but today, O Great-souled One, has Vaikartana perhaps attained that which was unattainable, desiring the inconceivable?

In this battle of terrifying form today,
O Pārtha, you have broken the vow of the Sūta’s son;
did you perhaps recall those wicked words spoken at the time of the gambling match?
And that which he spoke so excessively harshly to Vāsudeva in the assembly— though he was one who always acted for the welfare of the Kurus.
I hope that Karṇa has been slain today in battle—
he who, protecting the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the fray,
was alone and constantly withering my army.
Desiring to bestow the prosperity of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son upon all the Pāñcālas and Kekayas, that Karṇa— have you perhaps struck back at me today?
Then jackals, vultures,
and birds tore at the flesh from the body of him who was the most excellent wielder of weapons on earth.
That small-minded man insulted the Grandfather. Is that Adhiratha’s son, that wicked-souled one who was reckoned as only half a chariot-warrior, slain by you today?
"O Kirīṭin, that which was promised by you to me in the midst of the assembly— that here, once again in a single combat of chariots,
I shall slay Karṇa along with his son— [that I shall fulfill]."
Having performed that deed, are you perhaps free from debt? This fire of indignation, fanned by the wind of deceit, dwells constantly within my heart.
"Having encountered that evil-minded one today, he shall be slain by me;
O Phalguna, pacify my grief as you speak these words to me today, for this is difficult to obtain."
"How was the Sūtaputra slain by you? O great hero, I meditate upon you constantly,
like the blessed Indra after Vṛtra was killed."
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard those words of the righteous king who was filled with rage, the high-souled son of Adhiratha [replied].
Jiṣṇu, of infinite prowess, spoke to the invincible Yudhiṣṭhira of undaunted spirit:
"O Pārtha, Karṇa has learned that Droṇa has been slain."
Perceiving the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to be as bewildered as those in a shattered boat upon the bottomless deep,
and seeing that they lacked the will to conquer their enemies, [he spoke].
Like a brother,
the high-souled son of Adhiratha, possessed of immeasurable prowess, hurried on his chariot in battle, desiring to rescue the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Then, O King, he rushed toward me with great speed while I was fighting the Saṃśaptakas today,
for he is the leader of the vanguard of the Kuru army.
Releasing birds that resembled venomous serpents,
the son of Droṇa suddenly stationed himself in front of me;
having seen this chariot of mine resembling a cloud, he stood his ground.
The army of Ambaṣṭhas stood firm in the face of death;
having slain five hundred of them, O foremost of kings, I then approached the son of Droṇa.
Seeing that, the most heroic one commanded many hosts of chariots from the tip of his banner;
having slain five hundred of them, I—
He encountered the son of Droṇa as he was roaring; that high-souled son of Droṇa likewise obstructed me, who am his equal, in the midst of that army.
Scattering multiform and variegated showers of arrows,
he advanced like the planet Śukra pouring down rain;
he [discharged] at me from all sides arrows fletched with heron feathers.
He indeed discharged those arrows, radiant as the earth,
swiftly warding them off in the midst of that supreme battle;
then he struck me with multitudes of shafts.
Whether drawn back or released after being pulled,
no gap was seen in that great car-warrior; having reached me, O lord of men, he remained alert.
Like a lion attacking the lord of elephants,
he charged forward; O Great King, he desired to rescue the chariot-warriors while the Kauravas were being slaughtered.
Then, O Bhārata, in that battle, the son of the Preceptor— the most eminent of the Kurus, who was difficult to shake—
afflicted me with sharp arrows.
And even Janārdana [could not withstand] his eight hundred arrows, which were like poison and fire, as he fought with me. Those arrows carried him away.
I destroyed those arrows released by him with my own shafts,
just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds;
then I loosed many other multitudes of arrows.
With the skill, weapons, strength, and effort [required], he released arrows drawn back as far as his ear,
just as a dark cloud pours rain during the monsoon.
Neither taking up nor joining [the arrow],
we do not know by which side he shoots—
whether by the left or by the right.
That son of Droṇa moved about in battle,
neither aiming, nor taking up [an arrow], nor drawing back, nor pulling forth, nor releasing.
Whether with the left hand or with the right,
it was not known which one he would shoot;
like his teacher, he moved about in battle.
A great marvel was seen on all sides;
his gaze was a poison difficult for others to endure,
as he filled all directions with floods of arrows.
The bow of that great-souled one, who was a kinsman of Brahmā, was always bent like a circle of fire from a whirling brand; its circle remained perpetually drawn and strung.
The bow of Droṇa’s son was clearly visible. Piercing me with five arrows, the son of Droṇa struck Vāsudeva with five sharp shafts.
I, however, struck him with thirty thunderbolt-like arrows within the blink of an eye;
I smote him with those well-sharpened shafts.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, by means of gold-feathered arrows,
he was instantly transformed into the likeness of a dog,
being struck down by the shafts discharged by me.
Streaming blood from all his limbs,
he entered the chariot-force of the Suta’s son,
having overwhelmed the foremost of the soldiers by my power.
Seeing them smeared with blood,
the son of Droṇa, himself pierced and streaming with gore,
entered the chariot division of the great car-warriors.
Seeing his own excellent chariots overwhelmed by me,
and seeing his weapon smeared with blood,
he then beheld his army defeated in battle.
With fifty preeminent chariot-warriors, the destructive Karna, having destroyed the warriors and put the horses and elephants to flight,
approached me in haste.
Having slain them and spared Karṇa,
I have come here in haste to see you;
for all the Pāñcālas tremble before Karṇa.
Just as bulls run toward a scent, or as lions toward it, or as those who have entered the mouth of a great fish,
the Prabhadrakas are rushing toward Karṇa.
O King, having encountered Karṇa, the Prabhadrakas entered what was like the gaping mouth of Death;
desiring to cross over those floods of troops, I shall go toward them.
"By good fortune, O Pārtha, you have been seen safe and sound!
At that time, Karṇa dispatched those seven hundred chariots, which were submerged [in the water], to the abode of Death."
Nor did he become weary in spirit, O King,
as long as the Sūta’s son had not seen us;
but having heard that you had been seen by him together [with us], [he became dejected].
O King, I consider it the time for your retreat from this cruel Karṇa of inconceivable deeds, especially since you have already been wounded by Aśvatthāman.
O Pāṇḍava, this weapon of wonderful form has never before been seen by me in battle against Karṇa;
indeed, there is no other warrior among the Sṛñjayas who possesses it.
O King, let Śiniputra Sātyaki and Dhṛṣṭadyumna likewise be the wheel-protectors for Karna, that great car-warrior whom none could withstand today.
And let the two heroic princes, Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas, protect me from behind,
O high-souled one, you who are a preeminent car-warrior.
"Come today and behold me, who am difficult to overcome while stationed in the midst of the enemy host, desiring to fight for victory against both you and the Suta's son."
Six thousand princes, O Bhārata,
have sunk their chariots for the sake of the heavenly world;
today I shall go to release them from the battle.
O high-souled one, with his whole being he sought to slay the son of the charioteer,
while that preeminent car-warrior extensively consumed the enemy host.
O foremost of kings, having encountered the Sūta’s son in battle like the wielder of the thunderbolt encountering Vṛtra,
what can possibly be done by me now that things have come to this?
To accomplish the task of subduing the son of the Sūta,
as well as King Suyodhana,
and those who have gathered here desiring to fight me.
"O Bhārata, I shall fight most fiercely against the Sūta’s son in this battle if he is indeed seen today;
O King, if I do not slay Karṇa this very day," so he said.
O lion among kings, may I go to that miserable state which awaits those who, having promised to fight alongside their kinsmen, fail to fulfill it by force.
"I address you: speak of victory for me in battle!
Before the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra can devour Bhīma, O lion among kings, I shall slay the son of the Sūta."
Having heard that Karṇa was ready and possessed of noble prowess, Saṃjaya said: "The army and all the hosts of enemies likewise...
(8.48.1). Saṃjaya said:
"Having heard that Karṇa was ready and possessed of noble prowess... (8.48.1a).
Enraged and tormented by the arrows of Karṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, whose energy was immeasurable, spoke these words to Dhanañjaya, the son of Pṛthā.
"O dear one, your army has fled in all directions;
today it has been disgraced in a most improper manner.
Just as you were terrified and abandoned Bhīma, so too have you now fled."
Since you were unable to destroy Karna,
O Pārtha, this theft was committed by you against Pṛthā,
having entered her womb, which was not at all right.
O Sūta’s son, he who possesses a fierce prowess that is difficult to withstand in battle cannot be slain by you today,
since he has fled from the field, leaving Bhīma behind.
That you were unable to slay the son of a charioteer—
that speech which you uttered in the Dvaitavana forest,
"I shall truly slay Karṇa with a single chariot"— [is now proven].
Having abandoned him, how indeed have you departed today,
leaving Bhīmasena out of fear of Karṇa? Oppressed by Karṇa, you have come to this dwelling out of fear.
I, you, Bhīmasena, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī—
accompanied by Vāsudeva— we have been utterly defeated by Karṇa;
having returned once again to the forest, we are practicing austerities.
"Or else, let us perform service for the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having spoken thus to Bībhatsu, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, spoke once more.
"If you had said this in the Dvaitavana forest—
that you would not venture to fight Karṇa, O King—
then we would all have acted according to the circumstances of the time."
O Pārtha, O hero, having promised the slaughter of that man and likewise of his trusted army, we shall indeed attain our goals at that very time.
Having brought us into the midst of our enemies, why did you lift us up and dash us down upon the bare ground?
O Arjuna, we have placed our hopes in you.
O Prince, all that great merit we desired for those wishing to depart has become fruitless for us,
like a nicula tree in full bloom to one seeking its fruit.
O Pārtha, that truth which you uttered while sitting beside Vāsudeva, swearing an oath of truth together with him—
that truth you have rendered fruitless for us.
Like one who cuts down a flowering tree at the very time of its fruit,
like a hook concealed by bait,
or like a wild ox hidden by a deceptive cry.
"You have shown me something useless;
to me, who desired the kingdom, you have shown the destruction of the kingdom. You, O fool, are obscured by infamy."
O Arjuna, this speech of yours is not at all beneficial;
having abandoned Bhīma, who is the most terrifying among all things that inspire fear,
you have instead joined forces with the son of a Sūta to slay him.
For these thirteen years we have always lived following you, O Dhanañjaya, with the hope for wealth,
just as sown seed awaits rain from the god at the proper time.
Therefore, you have submerged us all in hell,
because that voice spoke from the sky when you were but seven days old and possessed of dull intellect, O Pṛthā.
"This son born here, possessing the prowess of Vāsava,
will conquer all heroic enemies;
this one born of Kuntī is not inferior to Vāsava."
He alone shall be the victor in many battles; he,
possessed of supreme energy, shall conquer the hosts of gods in the Khāṇḍava forest, as well as all living beings.
This conqueror slays the Madras, Kalingas, and Kekayas; he strikes down the Kurus in the midst of kings,
as well as the assembled Daityas and Rakshasas.
The Conqueror has completely subdued the entire earth;
there shall be no archer superior to him,
nor indeed has there ever been anyone who could conquer him.
The noble one, having mastered all branches of knowledge, being self-controlled and desiring it, could bring all beings under his power;
he would be like the moon in beauty and like the wind in speed.
In steadfastness like Mount Meru, in forbearance like the Earth,
in brilliance like the Sun, in prosperity like Kubera,
in heroism like Śakra, and in strength like Viṣṇu.
O Kuntī, this high-souled son of yours is equal to Viṣṇu born of Aditi as the slayer of enemies;
he is born for the victory of his own people and for the destruction of his foes.
"Renowned as Amitaujas, the continuer of the lineage,"—
thus did a voice speak in the sky upon the summit of Śataśṛṅga, while the ascetics were listening.
"Such as you were, that has not become so for you today;
surely even the gods speak untruth,
as do those other most excellent sages."
Having always honored those who speak such words,
I do not bow down to Suyodhana;
nor do I recognize you as one afflicted by fear of the son of Adhiratha.
Having mounted that beautiful chariot made by Tvaṣṭṛ, whose axle was noiseless, and bearing the monkey-banner,
you took up a flaming sword adorned with gold.
O Pārtha, how is it that you, carrying this Gāṇḍīva bow which is as tall as a palm tree, fled in fear from Karṇa while being carried away by Keśava?
Indeed, that which was previously stated by Suyodhana—
that Phalguna would not stand before the mighty Karna in battle— [has now been proven otherwise].
But because of my folly, that was not understood by me; therefore,
today I shall suffer immeasurable and intense remorse, since the circle of my friends has entered hell.
At that very moment, I was surely told by you:
"I will not fight the son of a Sūta under any circumstances; therefore, I shall not [fight] the Sṛñjayas or the Kekayas."
I would have gathered my friends for battle;
things having come to this pass, what can be done by me today to effect the subjugation of the Suta’s son?
Likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, shame upon my life today, in the presence of King Suyodhana and all those who have gathered here desiring to fight me!
I, who have fallen under the power of the Sūta’s son in the midst of the Kurus and Suyodhana,
as well as among those others who have assembled desiring to fight.
But today Bhīmasena alone is my protector,
by whom I was rescued from this great terror in battle after he had been assailed, even though he was filled with wrath.
Having abandoned his life-breaths in the battle, Bhīmasena pierced Karṇa with a sharp arrow and fought against the assembled leaders of the Kurus.
With mace in hand and his limbs drenched in blood, moving through the battlefield like Death at the time of universal destruction—
this indeed is the great roar of Bhīma.
The sound of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s men is heard again and again:
"If only that slayer of great car-warriors, that best of men, were still alive in battle!"
"O Pārtha, today Abhimanyu is your son;
I shall not suffer defeat in battle.
Moreover, let Ghaṭotkaca live through this battle."
Nevertheless, I shall not turn my back in battle; for I am the son of Bhīma, a leader at the forefront of combat,
skilled in great weapons, and worthy of you.
Having exerted effort against the enemy's force,
it became closed-eyed and overwhelmed by fear;
yet he alone waged battle during the night.
If that high-souled one, having encountered Karṇa in battle and bewildered him with multitudes of arrows, should then— after Karṇa has fled from the field out of fear— encounter him again...
Even though the charioteer remained steadfast in his composure,
he was struck by that Vāsavadattā with her spear;
this was surely due to my own past misfortunes.
Surely evil deeds bear fruit in battle;
for having treated you as mere straw in the fray,
I have thus been deceived by that wicked-souled one.
I have been treated here by the son of Vikartana just as one who is helpless and without kin is treated;
for he who would liberate a man fallen into calamity—
"He is indeed a kinsman, full of affection, and a true friend"—
thus the ancient seers declare,
and thus is dharma always practiced by the virtuous.
O evil-minded one, had you become the charioteer in battle after giving this bow to Keśava,
then Keśava would have slain the fierce Karṇa.
Just as the Lord of the Maruts, having taken up his thunderbolt, [slew] Vṛtra, so too, if you are unable to awaken this fierce son of Rādhā as he moves about, [you shall suffer].
"O King, give this Gāṇḍīva bow today to another— that monarch who is superior to you in weapons— so that we,
deprived of our sons and wives, may not suffer in this way."
O son of Pāṇḍu, the world will see them fallen even into a bottomless hell, frequented by the wicked, having been deprived of happiness and further ruined by the loss of their kingdom.
O Phalguna, standing in the chariot with Keśava, take up the reins and advance into battle; having encountered Karṇa, slay him this very day!
Just as Keśava [protected] the King of Cedi in the midst of kings,
had you not fallen into this great hardship in the fifth month,
you would not even have become Pṛthā’s child.
"O prince, that would have resulted only in exhaustion for you;
it is not right to retreat from battle, O evil-souled one! Shame on the Gāṇḍīva bow, and shame on the strength of your arms!"
Fie on you for those countless volleys of arrows!
Fie on you! Fie on your banner bearing the son of a lion; and fie on your chariot bestowed by Agni!
08,049.001 Saṃjaya said: Thus addressed by Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, whose horses are white,
seized his sword in a rage, desiring to slay that bull of the Bharatas.
Perceiving his anger, Keśava, who knows the hearts of others, then said:
"What is this, O Pārtha? Why have you grasped your sword?
I see nothing here with which you must fight, O Dhanañjaya."
Indeed, all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been destroyed by the wise Bhīma. You departed, O son of Kuntī, thinking that the king must be seen;
you have seen that King Yudhiṣṭhira, and he is well.
Seeing that tiger among kings, whose prowess is equal to a tiger’s,
why has anger taken possession of you now that a time for joy has arrived?
O son of Kuntī, I do not see anyone here who ought to be slain by you.
"Why do you wish to strike? Or is there some delusion in your mind? Why do you grasp your great sword so hastily?
Therefore I ask you, O son of Kuntī: what is it that you intend to do?"
"O you of wondrous prowess, why do you, enraged, grasp your sword?
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa,
Arjuna, looking toward Yudhiṣṭhira, spoke to Govinda, hissing like an angry serpent.
"Whoever should urge me, saying, 'Give the Gāṇḍīva to another,' I would cut off his head— this is my secret vow. And by that Yudhiṣṭhira, O Janārdana, was I addressed."

"O Govinda of undepressed soul and immeasurable prowess, I was addressed thus by the king in your very presence; I cannot endure that here. Therefore, I shall slay this king who is so fearful of violating dharma."
"I shall fulfill my vow by slaying this best of men;
it was for this purpose, O delighter of the Yadus, that I took up this sword.
Having slain Yudhiṣṭhira in battle, I shall attain freedom from debt regarding my truth."
"O Janārdana, I shall become free from sorrow and free from fever.
Or rather, what do you consider appropriate now that this time has arisen? O dear one, you know all the comings and goings of this world."
"For from you indeed Dharma and Adharma were born; such is the supreme Vedic revelation.
I shall act accordingly, just as you tell me.
Sañjaya said:
"Shame, shame! Govinda said to Pārtha, and then spoke again.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"Now, O Pārtha, I know that you have not served the elders."

"O tiger among men, O Dhanañjaya, one who knows the distinctions of dharma would never act with such impetuousity at an improper time as you have done here today, O Pāṇḍava, for you are fearful of dharma yet unwise."

O Pārtha, he who indeed brings about the union of things that ought not to be done with those that ought to be done, and of actions with non-actions, is the lowest of men. But those sages who have approached and followed the path of dharma...
"You do not know the certainty of those who understand both the concise and the detailed;
for a man who lacks knowledge of certainty regarding what ought and ought not to be done,
O Pārtha, becomes helpless and deluded, just as you are now deluded."
For it is not possible in any way to know whether an action is to be done or not to be done simply by means of pleasure;
all of that is known through sacred learning (*śruta*), yet you do not comprehend it. And as for the fact that you, though a knower of dharma, protect dharma out of ignorance—[that too is not right].
For a righteous person, O Pārtha, does not perceive the killing of living beings as acceptable. The non-killing of living beings, my dear, is in my view the highest of all virtues;
yet one may speak an untruth, but one must never, under any circumstances, commit violence.
O best of men, how could you slay your eldest brother, a king learned in dharma, like some other common man? O Bhārata, [how could you kill] one who was not fighting and was without weapons?
The wise do not approve of killing one who has turned his back, one who is fleeing, one who seeks refuge, one who joins his palms in supplication, one who has surrendered,
or likewise one who is distracted.

"Killing is not honored by the virtuous, and all of that [is present] in your teacher; furthermore, O Pārtha, this vow was undertaken by you long ago while you were still a child. Therefore, out of folly, you are resolving upon an act joined with unrighteousness."
O Pārtha, remembering the Dharma, why would you slay your guru? You have not yet considered the subtle course of dharmas, which is difficult to follow;
therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, I shall explain this secret of the Dharma.
Whatever Bhīṣma might say, or Yudhiṣṭhira, who knows the dharma,
or Vidura the steward, or the illustrious Kuntī—
O best of the Bharatas, whether it be Kuntī or the illustrious Draupadī.
I shall tell that to you in its true essence; understand it, O Dhanañjaya.
The speaking of truth is excellent; there is nothing superior to truth. This is difficult to comprehend in its true nature by one for whom truth is not practiced.
Truth may be something that should not be spoken, and falsehood may be something that should be spoken;
when one's entire property is being seized, falsehood should be spoken.
In a life-threatening emergency and at a marriage, falsehood should be spoken.
Where untruth would become truth, and truth would likewise become untruth—
at the time of marriage, during sexual union,
when life is at stake, and when all one's wealth is being seized.
One may indeed speak untruth for the sake of a Brahmin;
they say there are five kinds of untruth that do not constitute a sin.
A fool perceives such [untruth] as truth when it is practiced by one who has established himself in truth.
If that which is true were inexpressible, then what is practiced would not be expressible;
having distinguished between truth and falsehood, one thereby becomes a knower of dharma.
What wonder is there if even a man of sharp intellect is extremely cruel?
One may obtain very great merit from the killing of a blind *balāka* crane,
just as [the hunter did]. What wonder is it, then, that a fool who desires dharma but lacks wisdom may incur very great sin, like Kauśika [killing] the river [creature]?
Arjuna said:
"O Blessed One, explain this to me so that I may understand it—
the connection between Balāka and Andha, and [the account] of the rivers and Kauśika."
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Bhārata, there was once a certain hunter named Balāka;
for the sake of providing for his wife and children, he killed deer, not out of mere whim."
He supported his blind parents as well as others who were dependent on him; he was constantly devoted to his own duty, truthful in speech, and free from malice.
Once, though striving diligently, he could not find any deer to hunt.
Then he saw a beast of prey that drank only water and used its sense of smell as its eyes;
although that creature had never been seen before, it was then slain by him. Immediately thereafter, a rain of flowers fell from the sky.
Resounding with the songs and instrumental music of Apsarases,
that delightful celestial chariot arrived from heaven with the intent of carrying away the hunter Mṛgavyādha.
That being, O Arjuna, was indeed for the destruction of all living beings.
Having performed austerities, a boon was obtained by the Self-born One that Kṛta would be made blind;
having destroyed him—who was determined to bring about the non-existence of all beings—Balāka then ascended to heaven. Thus, Dharma is very difficult to understand.
There was also a Brahmin named Kauśika, an ascetic who was not very learned;
he lived, it is said, not far from a village at the confluence of rivers.
He had taken a vow that he must always speak the truth.
O Dhanañjaya, he was then renowned as a speaker of truth. At that time, some people entered that forest out of fear of bandits;
yet even those cruel bandits arrived and searched for them with great effort.
Then, approaching Kauśika, they spoke to that speaker of truth:
"O Blessed One, by which path have the many people gone?
Being asked with sincerity, tell us if you know of them; speak to us."
Being thus questioned, Kauśika spoke these truthful words to them; though he himself did not understand the distinctions within truth, he proclaimed the truth to them:
"We have taken refuge in this forest, which is filled with many trees, creepers, and shrubs."
Thus did Kauśika announce them to them, O Pārtha;
then, having encountered them, those cruel ones killed them—so it is heard.
By that great unrighteousness, through those ill-spoken words, Kauśika...

One who has not mastered the subtle dharmas has gone to a most painful hell; being dull-witted and lacking extensive learning, he does not understand the distinctions between dharmas. Without having questioned his elders regarding his doubts, he deserves a great abyss from this world.
In that regard, there will be for you only a brief indication of the characteristics.
Supreme knowledge is difficult to attain; one attempts to determine it here through logic.
For many people say, "Scripture is the Dharma."
But I do not find fault with this, for not everything is prescribed;
many people say that the Veda should be upheld,
and I do not find fault with them, O Pārtha, nor do they teach everything.
"Mindfulness should be maintained"—thus say many people;
yet I do not feel resentment toward them, for not everything is prescribed therein. The proclamation of the Dharma was made for the sake of the welfare of all beings.

O Hero, such a course of dharma is exceedingly difficult to perceive; for who is capable of declaring the entire dharma of Manu and the others without having studied under those who are advanced in knowledge, conduct, and age?
Great merit arises even from unrighteousness,
just as it did for Vyāḍa and Kauśika despite their opposing natures;
for the virtuous have declared that the Veda is indeed the root of all dharmas.
For one who knows the truth indeed seeks the means for the various branches of knowledge.
O scorcher of foes, having approached a Vedic Brahmin, he understands merit and demerit;
he knows the supreme dharma, O Bhārata, and he knows non-violence.
That which is joined with non-violence is Dharma; this is the certainty.
The proclamation of Dharma was made for the sake of the non-violence of all beings. They say it is called Dharma because it sustains; Dharma sustains all creatures.
"He who is endowed with the power of retention—that is Dharma; such is the certainty.
If people ever desire to seize [something] by unjust means, and if release were possible through silence, one should not cry out at all in this situation.
"One must certainly utter a cry, or else they might suspect one of not crying out; in such a case, it has been deliberated that it is better to speak a falsehood than the truth.
He who, having undertaken a vow for the sake of certain tasks, does not fulfill it through action [is at fault]."
"The wise have said that one does not obtain that fruit [of giving] in such a case;
when there is truth, wealth must never be given to those who are wicked,
except in a life-threatening emergency, at a wedding, or when all one's kinsmen and wealth are being destroyed."
When a jest is underway, what is spoken may be false;
those who perceive the true meaning of the principles of Dharma see no unrighteousness in this.
For a wise person should always speak in such a way that he does not become a liar.

He who is freed from association with thieves even by means of oaths—in that case, it is better to speak a falsehood; that is considered the truth without hesitation. And wealth must not be given to them under any circumstances, even if one is able to do so.
For wealth given to the wicked may even bring suffering upon the giver;
therefore, by speaking a falsehood for the sake of dharma, one does not become a liar.
This summary of the characteristics has been declared to you according to the rule.
"O Pārtha, I have requested this of you according to the Dharma and according to my understanding.
Having heard this, O Pārtha, tell me: is Yudhiṣṭhira to be slain?
Arjuna said:

Just as one of great wisdom would speak, just as one of great intelligence would speak— just as that which is truly beneficial for us, so are these words of yours. You are like a mother to us, and likewise, you are like a father.
And your destination is supreme, O Kṛṣṇa; therefore your word is wonderful. For there is nothing anywhere in the three worlds that is unknown to you.
Therefore, you know the highest dharma entirely as it truly is.

I consider the Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, to be invincible; therefore, at this juncture of our agreement, grant me some favor. Furthermore, hear now this other thing that dwells in my heart which I wish to speak.
O descendant of Daśārha, you know my vow:
that if anyone among mortals should say to me,
"O Pārtha, give the Gāṇḍīva to another," [I must grant it].
"O Keśava, I would forcibly slay whoever might become superior to you in weapons;
for Bhīma was told, 'You shall slay Tūbaraka.'"
O lion of the Vṛṣṇis, the king spoke to me in your presence, saying repeatedly, "Give him the bow.
O Keśava, if he were slain, [what would become] of him in the world of the living?
I shall not remain for even the slightest amount of time;
thus you know me fully, O Kṛṣṇa,
for one whose dharma is inferior lives only for a moment in this world.
Falling from the truth, I would abandon this world;
therefore, out of anger, I would reject the Son of Dharma. Having reflected thus, I am surely now liberated from that transgression.
Deprived of his prowess and bewildered, he shall face execution at the king's hands.
And that vow of mine, known throughout the world,
shall become true, O best among the upholders of dharma.
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to grant such counsel today as will ensure that both the Pāṇḍava and I may live;
having understood this, do what is always for my welfare.
08,049.063f *0707_02 Thus you ought to understand it as well.
Vāsudeva said:
"The king is exhausted and wounded from the world [of battle];"
Afflicted by the son of the Sūta with multitudes of sharpened arrows in battle,
O hero, he was constantly tormented by the Sūtaputra.
Being struck violently by arrows while fighting,
you were addressed with anger by him;
for one who is beset by suffering, this is not an improper thing to do.
"For if he had not been provoked in battle,
he would surely have slain Karṇa," so he spoke;
and this son of Pāṇḍu also knows that.
O Pārtha, a wicked deed in this world is unbearable to others;
therefore, you were addressed with harsh words by the king, who was greatly incensed, in your very presence.
Though greatly afflicted,
the high-minded one spoke harsh words to you, O Pārtha,
for today the game of dice has been bound to Karna in battle.
"If he were slain, the Kurus would be defeated";
such was the thought of the king, the son of Dharma.
Therefore, the son of Dharma does not deserve death.
O Arjuna, you must fulfill your vow;
for that by which this man, though living, becomes as if dead—
that which is worthy of you, listen to it from me here.
When one who is worthy of honor receives honor,
then indeed he truly lives in the world of the living;
but when he receives great dishonor;
Then he is said to be dead while living. This king is always honored by you, along with Bhīma and likewise by the two Yamas.
"Apply even a slight insult toward him by the elders and the preeminent men in this world;
for this is the meaning of the treatises on dharma and the illustration found in the Vedas."
Listen, O Pārtha, how your preceptor might be slain eternally: when that venerable one,
the best among wielders of weapons, is addressed by you with the words "Kill him," then,
O Pārtha, say to Yudhiṣṭhira, "It is you."
"For when one is addressed as 'You' [in such a manner], O Bhārata, the elder is indeed slain.
Act thus toward Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, O son of Kuntī; in this way, O upholder of the Kurus, enter into an alliance that is free from unrighteousness."
For this is the Atharva-Angirasa, the supreme scripture among all scriptures. Those men who desire their own welfare must always act upon it without hesitation.
When a master says, "You are my guru," that is declared to be a killing without a weapon.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, tell me what I have said regarding the King of Dharma;
for this execution of the King of Dharma is appropriate from you,
and he himself will understand it thus.
Then, having saluted his feet,
you should afterwards speak words of peace and consolation to the son of Pṛthā,
saying: "Your wise brother will never [act] out of anger."
O son of Pāṇḍu,
may that king be released from falsehood and from the slaughter of his brothers; O Pārtha,
joyfully slay Karṇa, the son of a Sūta!
08,049.072 Sañjaya said:
Having been addressed in this manner by Janārdana,
Pārtha then praised that slaughter of his kinsmen.
Then Arjuna spoke harsh words, never before uttered, with force to the King of Dharma:
"O King, do not speak while others are speaking!"
You do not stay even a *krośa* away from the midst of battle;
O King, do not say anything here today,
you who stand here having abandoned the fight.
But Bhīma,
that foremost hero among all warriors,
who oppresses his enemies in battle at the proper time, deserves to reproach me.
And having slain those heroic lords of the earth—
those preeminent chariot-warriors, the foremost of elephant-riders, and immeasurable, elite heroes— [he departed].
Having slain more than a thousand elephants, he let out a tumultuous lion’s roar;
[he also slew] ten thousand mountain-dwellers from Kamboja.
Just as a lion slays deer in battle,
the hero performs a most difficult deed—
one that you could never possibly perform.
Leaping down from his chariot and seizing his mace,
he struck down horses, men, and elephants in battle with it;
with his excellent sword, he [slaughtered] horses, chariots, steeds, and elephants.
Likewise, with his chariot wheels and his bow he slays his enemies; having trampled his foes with his feet,
he who possesses the prowess of Indra strikes them down again with his two arms.
Possessing great strength like Vaiśravaṇa or Antaka, he is one who forcibly slays his enemies as they deserve;
that Bhīmasena deserves my censure.
You, who were once protected by your friends after having crushed great chariot-warriors, excellent elephants, horses,
and even the foremost of foot soldiers, are no longer protected.
Bhīma alone has plunged into the Dhārtarāṣṭras;
that subduer of enemies deserves to reproach me.
[He has overcome] the Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Aṅgas, Niṣādas, and Māgadhas.
He who repeatedly slays hosts of enemies, who are like ever-intoxicated dark clouds—
he is capable of speaking to me, though I am innocent.
Having mounted his well-yoked chariot at the proper time,
that hero, drawing his bow with a fist full of arrows, releases showers of shafts.
In that great battle, like clouds pouring down torrents of rain,
I beheld eight hundred elephants with their frontal globes, trunks, and tusks shattered to pieces.
"Today Bhīma has slain [them] in battle with his arrows;
that slayer of enemies ought not to speak so cruelly to me regarding those full ten thousand great chariot-warriors."
Then, having crushed many throngs of foot soldiers and slain hundreds of heroes, he, remaining vigilant, [slaughtered] sixty thousand horses.
Bhīmasena, who in the midst of battle gave up his life— so difficult to relinquish— in combat with his enemies;
Bhīmasena, who has struck down the hosts of his foes.
That subduer of enemies deserves to reproach me:
"O King, chariots, elephants,
and horses have been slain today by Bhīma in battle by the hundreds."
And many kings of great power,
as well as the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra who are strong— by whom that subduer of enemies deserves to reproach me.
The mighty ones have for the most part been slain;
he is a hero whose prowess is irresistible in battles.
That subduer of enemies deserves to reproach me.
That hero of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side, who in battle possessed irresistible prowess and, assuming a fierce form, alone could withstand that army while scorching it with his majesty.
Therefore, you must never speak against me;
wherever those great chariot-warriors break through your army today in battle according to their will, [you shall follow].
In that very battle, in that very place, the high-souled Bhīma crushed the enemy hosts with great force;
therefore, you should never speak against me.
Do not speak such cruel words here today, O Pārtha;
one like me should certainly not be addressed by you in the same way that you are addressed by everyone in the world.
O Lord of Men, if you speak thus, how is it that your tongue does not split into a hundred pieces today?
Alas! This is truly a most cruel form of conduct.
For even you, O best of the twice-born, fear Karṇa in this matter; yet the wise declare that the strength of the foremost brahmins lies in speech,
while the strength of the kṣatriya lies in the power of the arm.
O Bhārata, you are powerful in speech and cruel;
you alone know me as I truly am.
O King, by means of Nakula, the elephants, horses, and warriors [were subdued].
Having encountered brave warriors who were suddenly slain,
that subduer of enemies, desiring battle and having cast away his life in the fray, deserves to reproach me.
A difficult deed was performed by Sahadeva,
who, as a crusher of enemy armies, fought while remaining silent; even when he had arrived here, that powerful one said nothing at all.
Behold the difference between him and yourself:
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Sātyaki, the sons of Draupadī,
Yudhāmanyu, Uttamaujas, and Śikhaṇḍī.
"All these have been utterly crushed in battle today;
they are the ones who ought to reproach me, and not you. For it is because of you that this enmity has come upon us."
Likewise, this most terrible calamity has been encountered;
you have repeatedly acted with negligence in gambling.
Why, then, do you deserve to be reproached here?
O King, you alone have been perpetually heedless;
you alone are the fool and the unrighteous one among the Bharatas.
Having obtained you, this kingdom has come to ruin.
The Pāṇḍavas have fallen into great servitude because of you;
for your sake, there would be the misery of forest exile,
the destruction of the kingdom, and the terrible death of Abhimanyu.
"O hero, having recognized yourself as being of such a cruel nature, for what reason do you reproach me today? O King, feel shame if you have any sense of shame."
"Be silent and behold all that we have accomplished.
Bhīma is always a doer in battle;
he is likewise ever the shatterer of pride."
O lord of men, when a man is himself incapable of fighting in battle,
he must always practice forbearance;
I constantly strive to do what is pleasing to you.
With my wives, sons, life, and even myself—
thus you strike me with the arrows of your words;
we do not know any happiness at all from you.
"Seated upon Draupadī’s bed, you disregarded me when I said,
'I shall strike down the great car-warriors for your sake. Because of that, O Bhārata, you are full of suspicion and cruel."
"O god among men, I have never known any happiness other than from you; O lord of men, Death himself has been declared by that one true to his promise to come for your sake in battle."
That heroic and high-souled Śikhaṇḍin, the son of Drupada,
was slain by me while I was protected by him; and Droṇa, who had always been my benefactor, was also slain by him.
Having been dragged from his chariot by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
the high-souled son of Droṇa, though enraged and accompanied by his followers,
nevertheless spoke those words like a cruel man.
O god among men, you would rather do what is painful than that which I, indeed, must do for your sake; for no man is ever truly released from this, whether in heaven or here on earth.
If anyone other than I were to act unpleasantly toward you,
I would not welcome your sovereignty;
for you are addicted to dice to your own detriment.
Having yourself committed a sin practiced by the ignoble,
you now wish to overcome your enemies in battle through these [dice];
yet there are many faults and unrighteous rules in dice.
You have heard those paths which Sahadeva spoke of, which you do not wish to cross— paths frequented by the unrighteous, by which we all would have fallen into hell.
"We have known no happiness from you at all,
since you yourself, O Pāṇḍava, having acted harshly, have proceeded to gamble with the dice."
Furthermore, today you make us hear even harsher words:
"The enemy army lies slain by us,
groaning upon the surface of the earth with its limbs severed."
For you indeed committed that cruel deed,
because of which there is this fault and the slaughter of the Kauravas;
the northerners have been killed and the westerners struck down.
The easterners have perished and the southerners have been slaughtered;
a great and improper deed has been committed by their warriors and our own in battle.
"You are the gambler, and for your sake the kingdom was lost;
O lord of men, this calamity has arisen from you.
Do not pierce us with the cruel goads of your words."
O King, further inciting those of little fortune with these harsh words, Savyasācin caused them to hear [them] and struck at him whose wisdom is firm.

Having thus committed some transgression, that wise man became dejected, fearing for his dharma; sighing deeply after having spoken such an undesirable thing to his elder brother, he remained troubled.
Then he drew his sword from its scabbard; that one of noble deeds raised his sword to slay himself, for he was a conqueror of his enemies.
Then the son of the king of the gods felt remorse;
sighing deeply, he drew his sword.
Kṛṣṇa said to him, "What is this that you are doing again?"
He draws his sword, which is unsheathed and resembles the sky.
Speak the truth once more as a response to the command;
I shall speak further words for the sake of accomplishing your purpose.
Thus questioned by Puruṣottama,
he, deeply distressed, spoke these words to Keśava:
"I shall destroy my own body."
Having heard those words of Pārtha, he who was the best among the upholders of dharma spoke thus to Dhanañjaya regarding that which had indeed been done by him through forceful violence.
"O Pārtha, slayer of foes, having said this to the king, why did you fall into such a terrible dejection, and why do you wish to kill yourself?"
O Kirīṭin, this is certainly not practiced by the virtuous;
O hero among men, if you were to slay your eldest brother today with a sword, he who is righteous in soul— this would be a great transgression.
Since you are afraid of dharma, how indeed could it be yours? Moreover, what answer will you yourself give?
For dharma, O Pārtha, is subtle and difficult to discern.
Understand specifically what is being said by the ignorant:
by killing yourself through your own hand,
you would incur the most terrible hell for the murder of your brother.
"Speak here, O Pārtha, of your own qualities and of your inner heart;
thus it shall be accomplished for you immediately.
"So be it, O Kṛṣṇa," he replied, welcoming those words.
Bending his bow, Dhanañjaya, the son of Śakra, spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost of the upholders of dharma: "Listen, O King," said the son of Indra.
"O god among men, there exists no other archer like me, except for the divine wielder of the Pināka bow;
for I have been authorized by that high-souled one."
In an instant, I could destroy the world with all its moving and unmoving beings.
For, O King, having conquered all the quarters along with their presiding deities, I have brought them under your control.
That Rājasūya sacrifice was completed with its full sacrificial fees,
and this divine assembly hall exists through my own power;
moreover, these arrows are engraved upon my palms.
My bow is drawn with an arrow in battle, my feet are equipped with shafts along with my banner;
those who have entered combat do not defeat one such as I.
The northerners were slain, the westerners struck down;
the easterners were driven off, and the southerners were slaughtered;
of the Saṃśaptakas, only a very small remnant remained.
Half of the entire army has been slain by me; O King, this Bharata host, which resembled the celestial army, lies prostrate, struck down by me.
"Those who are unskilled in weapons, them I slay with my own arms;
therefore, I do not reduce this world to ashes here,
O Kṛṣṇa, while mounted upon my formidable, victorious chariot."
Advance quickly to slay the son of the charioteer!
Let this king be well-comforted today;
I shall destroy Karṇa in battle with my arrows.
Having spoken thus, Pārtha spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira, the most excellent among the upholders of dharma,
after he had cast aside his weapons, missiles, and bow.
Having quickly placed his sword in its sheath,
the diadem-wearing Arjuna, with his head bowed in shame and palms joined in reverence, addressed Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O King, know this to be the truth: by that act, Rādhā shall remain childless, or else Kuntī shall be;
I speak the truth today, that I will not leave Karṇa in battle."
Without piercing the armor with arrows, I shall not release it.
Be gracious, O King, and forgive what I have said; you will understand its meaning in due time. Salutations to you!
Having propitiated the king, the subduer of enemies,
he stood before him with a humble supplication and said:
"I am going now to rescue Bhīma from the battle."
I would slay the Sūta’s son with my whole being for the sake of your pleasure; indeed, my life is for that purpose.
Know this as the truth I speak, O King.
Having thus grasped his feet, he departed;
the diadem-wearing one, blazing with splendor, rose up, saying, "This will not take long; this shall happen quickly."
"He turns back and attacks me!
Having heard these harsh words of his brother Phalguna, the Pāṇḍava Dharmarāja—
Rising from that bed, his mind overwhelmed with grief, he then said to Pārtha:
"O Pārtha, I have done what was not right."
Therefore, cut off this head of mine today— of me, the lowest of men and the destroyer of my lineage— from whom this most terrible calamity has been brought upon you.
Of one who is sinful and beset by the calamities of evil, whose intellect is deluded, who is indolent and cowardly,
who insults his elders, and who is indeed harsh;
Why do you follow me for so long with such harshness?
I, a sinner, shall go to the forest this very day;
may you live in happiness, deprived of my company.
The high-souled Bhīmasena is a fit king; what use is the business of kingship to me, a eunuch? Nor am I able to endure harsh words.
Furthermore,
O hero, let Bhīma be king even at the cost of my life; for what purpose is there now for one who has been so insulted?
Having spoken thus, he suddenly sprang up;
then the king, leaving that bed,
desired to depart for the forest.
Bowing down, Vāsudeva addressed him:
"O King, this is known to you: the vow concerning the Gāṇḍīva bow, which is famous, made by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, who is true to his promise."
"If anyone should say, 'Give the Gāṇḍīva to another,' that man would deserve to be slain by him in this world; yet you have spoken such words. Therefore, Pārtha must protect his vow of truth."
"O lord of the earth, this insult has been committed against you out of my own desire;
for it is said that an insult to one's elders is equivalent to their death.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, [act] for the sake of both myself and Pārtha."
"O King, please forgive this transgression toward Arjuna.
O Great King, we have both come to you for refuge. O King, you ought to forgive me, who am bowed before you and entreating you."
"Today the earth shall drink the blood of that wicked son of Rādhā;
I promise you this truly—know that the Sūta's son is slain today.
For whomever you desire his death, his life has already departed."
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
then hurriedly raised up Hṛṣīkeśa as he stood bowed with palms joined in reverence, and immediately spoke these words.
"It is exactly as you have said; this transgression of mine exists.
I am consoled by you, O Govinda, and I have been rescued today, O Mādhava.
We have been liberated from this terrible calamity today by you, O Acyuta."
Having obtained you as our protector,
we two— both formerly deluded by ignorance— have today crossed over the terrible ocean of calamity; having obtained the raft of your wisdom, we have emerged from the sea of suffering and grief.
"O Acyuta, we have crossed over [the ocean of distress] along with our ministers; we have found a protector in you.
Sanjaya said:
Having heard those words of Dharmarāja, which were filled with joy, [he then spoke].
The righteous Govinda, the joy of the Yadus, spoke thus to Pārtha. Having repeated those words of Kṛṣṇa to Yudhiṣṭhira,
Pārtha became somewhat dejected in mind, as if he had committed some sin.
Then Vāsudeva, as if smiling, said to the Pāṇḍava:
"O Pārtha, how indeed could this be possible— that you should slay with a sharp-edged sword the son of Dharma, who stands firmly established in righteousness?"
"Having merely said 'You' to the king, you have thus fallen into such dejection. But had you killed the monarch, O Pārtha, what would you have done after that?
Thus, dharma is extremely difficult to discern, especially by those of dull intellect."

Out of fear of violating dharma, you would certainly have fallen into a most terrible hell because of the murder of your eldest brother. Therefore, [protect] that king, the best among the upholders of dharma, who is firmly established in righteousness.

"Propitiate the best of the Kurus; this is my opinion in this matter. Having propitiated King Yudhiṣṭhira with devotion and having made him well-disposed, let us proceed swiftly to fight against the chariot of the Sūta’s son."
"O giver of honor, having slain the most difficult-to-conquer Karṇa today with your sharpened arrows,
bestow great joy upon the son of Dharma. O mighty-armed one, this is my opinion as to what is appropriate for the occasion."
"When this has been done, your task will indeed be accomplished.
Then, O great king, Arjuna, filled with shame,
prostrated his head at the feet of Dharmarāja, O sinless one.
"O best of the Bharatas, he said again and again, 'Be gracious!
O King, forgive what was spoken by me, who am fearful and desirous of dharma. Seeing him fallen at his feet, the Dharma-king Yudhiṣṭhira—"
O bull of the Bharata race,
having raised up his brother Dhanañjaya, the slayer of enemies who was weeping, King Dharmarāja, the lord of the earth, embraced Dhanañjaya with affection and wept aloud.
Having wept for a long time, the two brothers of great splendor,
those tigers among men, performed their purificatory rites and became filled with joy.
Then, embracing the Pāṇḍava with affection, he smelled the crown of his head.
Filled with supreme joy and smiling, he spoke to Jaya.
Dharmarāja then addressed that great archer Dhanañjaya:
"O mighty-armed one, while all the troops were looking on, [Karna struck] me by Karna."
The armor, the standard, the bow, the spear, the horses, and the mace—[all were destroyed].
The charioteer was slain, as were the bow, the chariot, the spear, the standard, and the arrows;
they were cut down by arrows while that great archer was striving in the battle.
"O Phalguna, having understood this and having witnessed his deed in battle, I am sinking in sorrow; life is no longer dear to me.
O hero, if you do not slay that son of the Suta today—"
"I shall surely give up my very life; for what purpose of living is there for me?
Thus addressed, O bull of the Bharatas, Vijaya replied:
"I swear to you by truth, O King, and by your very grace."
O best of men, O lord of the earth, by Bhīma and by the two Yamas as well—
O best of men, O lord of the earth— I shall today in battle either slay this Karṇa along with his ministers, or else be slain myself.
"I shall fall upon the surface of the earth; by this truth, I swear upon my weapon.
Having addressed the king thus, he spoke these words to Mādhava:
"Today, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall slay Karṇa in battle; of this there is no doubt."
"Reflect upon this, may prosperity be yours: the slaying of that evil-minded one.
Thus addressed, Keśava spoke to Pārtha, O best of kings:
"O best of the Bharatas, I am capable of making an effort according to my strength."
"O great chariot-warrior, this has indeed always been my wish:
how you might slay Karṇa in battle; such was my thought.
Having been addressed thus, O King, Pārtha then spoke these words.
Furthermore, the wise Mādhava spoke again to Yudhiṣṭhira, the delighter of Dharma:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, you ought to console this Bībhatsu and grant him permission today for the slaughter of the evil-minded Karṇa."

"O joy of the Pāṇḍavas, having heard that you were afflicted by Karṇa’s arrows, both he and I have come here to learn of your condition. By good fortune, O King, you are free from pain; by good fortune, you have not been captured."
"Console Bibhatsu and grant him hope for victory, O sinless one.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Come, come, O Pārtha Bibhatsu! Embrace me, O son of Pāṇḍu!"
"You have spoken what is harmful to me, yet I have forgiven it. I give you my permission, O Dhanañjaya; slay Karṇa. Do not harbor resentment, O Pārtha, because of the harsh words I spoke to you."
08,050.028 Saṃjaya said:
08,050.028a Then, O King, Dhananjaya, bowing with his head,
08,050.028c grasped the feet of his eldest brother with both hands, O honorable one.
Then the king, having raised him up and embraced him while he was still in pain,
and having smelled the crown of his head, spoke this once more:
"O Dhananjaya, O mighty-armed one, I have been deeply honored by you."
"May you further attain eternal greatness and victory.
Arjuna said:
"Today, with my arrows in battle, [I shall strike] that evildoer along with his followers."
"Having encountered the son of Rādhā, who is arrogant in his strength, I shall bring him to his end—
he by whom you were so severely afflicted with arrows as he drew his bow firmly. Today, Karṇa shall reap the terrible fruit of that deed."

"O lord of the earth, today I shall come to you after slaying Karṇa, to honor you at your cry of distress; I tell you this truly. I shall not return from the field of battle today without having slain Karṇa."
"By this truth, O Lord of the World, I touch your feet.
Sañjaya said:
Thus spoke the well-disposed one to the Diademed One.
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke these most exalted words:
"May you have imperishable fame, the life you desire, constant victory, and the prowess that destroys your enemies."
May the deities grant you prosperity;
may that which I desire for you come to pass exactly so. Depart quickly and slay Karṇa in battle!
O Phalguna, let Keśava, standing upon the chariot like Puraṃdara [Indra] for the sake of his own victory over Vṛtra,
take up the reins and advance into battle.
"Go now, O King, and having encountered Karṇa this very day, slay him in the midst of the kings, just as Keśava slew the Daitya.
Sañjaya said:
Having propitiated the King of Dharma with a joyful inner soul,
Pārtha, intent on the slaughter of the Sūta’s son, spoke to Govinda:
“Let the chariot be prepared once more, and let the excellent horses be yoked.”
"Let all weapons be readied for the great chariot;
let the well-trained horses be brought forward, and let the skilled horsemen approach with haste, accompanied by all the equipment for the chariot."
"O Govinda, today we two set out with the desire to slay the son of the Sūta.
When this was said by the high-souled Phalguna, O great king, Kṛṣṇa spoke to Dāruka: "Do everything exactly as he has commanded."

O best of kings, having been thus commanded by Kṛṣṇa, Dāruka then yoked the chariot covered in tiger-skin, which scorched the enemies— the Arjuna who is the best of the Bharatas and the foremost of all archers.
He announced that everything was ready for the high-souled Pāṇḍava. Then, having mounted the yoked chariot with the high-souled Dāruka,
Padmanābha, the ender of battles, saw the chariot standing before him.
Having taken leave of the King of Dharma and having had the Brahmins recite benedictions,
he ascended that most excellent chariot, accompanied by auspicious rites and prayers for well-being.
For him, the highly wise King Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [prepared the way].
He invoked the most powerful blessings directed toward the slaughter of Karṇa.
O Bhārata, seeing that great archer departing,
all living beings considered Karṇa already slain by the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
O King, all the directions became pure on every side;
and the blue jays, the woodpeckers, and the cranes, O lord of men,
then circumambulated the son of Pāṇḍu from left to right.
O King, many auspicious and favorable birds with masculine names,
appearing joyful, cried out in haste, urging Arjuna on in battle;
so too did the kaṅkas, vultures, vaḍas, and crows, O lord of the people.
Terrifying creatures went before him for the sake of devouring [his enemies],
and auspicious omens foretold the destruction of the enemy forces as well as the slaying of Karṇa.
Auspicious omens appeared, as did the cries of beasts and birds;
yet as Pārtha set forth, great perspiration broke out upon him, and a profound anxiety arose: "How indeed will this turn out?"
Then, perceiving that Savyasācin was despondent, the radiant Acyuta, the slayer of Madhu, urged on him whose banner bears the monkey. Thereupon, Madhusūdana spoke to the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Seeing Pārtha then thus distressed and overcome with anxiety, [Arjuna said]:
"O wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, among those whom you have conquered in battle with your bow,
no human victor other than yourself is found here."
Indeed, many heroes have been seen whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra;
having encountered you, O hero, they have attained the supreme goal in battle.
For who, O noble one, [could withstand] Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Bhagadatta?
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, Sudakṣiṇa of Kamboja,
the highly heroic Śrutāyus, and Acyutāyus—
he who goes out to meet them would find safety, provided he were not as patient as you.
For yours indeed, O Arjuna, are divine weapons, as well as dexterity and strength; your piercing, your aim, your target, and your application,
as well as your lack of confusion in battles and the mastery of your knowledge.
"You could slay all the gods and asuras, along with all that is mobile and immobile.
For on this earth, O Pārtha, there is no man who is your equal in battle.
Yet, you must not be addressed by me with these words in my presence."
O Arjuna, one who is honored will surely become greatly arrogant in battle;
since this must certainly be said, I am telling you this:
by means of that [honor], one's own self must never be regarded with excessive pride.
While Karṇa, the son of a Sūta and a great chariot-warrior, is still alive on the battlefield—what is the use of much speaking here? Listen briefly, O Pāṇḍava:
I consider Karṇa to be either your equal or even superior to you as a great chariot-warrior.
Exerting the utmost effort, you must slay him in the great battle; for even Purandara himself, O Pārtha, would not be able to return safely after encountering Karṇa in combat—
such is his prowess.

But having encountered you on the great stage of battle, O Bhārata, even one who is diligent, O Karṇa, would turn back from the fight; such is the conviction in my mind. For whatever Kṣatriyas there may be who grasp the bow and are intoxicated with war, [they would all fail].

"O Pārtha, among those gods, I see or hear of no one equal to you; for by Brahmā were created both the subjects and the most wonderful Gāṇḍīva bow with which you fight— therefore, there is none equal to you."
"O Pāṇḍava, I must certainly speak that which is beneficial for you:
do not disregard Karṇa, O mighty-armed one, who shines in battle.
For Karṇa is powerful, bold, skilled in weapons, and a great chariot-warrior."
Skilled and a versatile combatant, he was proficient in both place and time;
in brilliance he was like fire, equal to the wind in speed,
resembling the Ender (Yama) in wrath, and as powerful as a lion in his physical frame.
Ayoratni is mighty-armed, broad-chested, and exceedingly difficult to conquer;
he is highly esteemed, heroic, a pre-eminent warrior, and pleasing to behold. Endowed with all the qualities of a soldier, he grants fearlessness to his friends.
"O Pārtha, I do not intend to frighten you; rather, I am generating joy in you. Rādheya is constantly hostile toward the Pāṇḍavas and devoted to the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's sons;
he cannot be slain by anyone, even by all the gods led by Indra."
"Except for you, such is my conviction; therefore, slay the son of the Sūta today!
For even by the gods themselves, though united and bearing flesh and blood, he cannot be conquered in battle, even by all of them eager for combat."
I consider him impossible to defeat in battle even by the gods themselves, though they be enraged, or by all the lords of the worlds, even if they all desire to fight—
him who is evil-minded, wicked, and cruel.
Having slain Karṇa— who was always possessed of wicked wisdom toward the Pāṇḍavas and who had lost his own purpose through hostility with them— be one who has today established his true aim.
Today, bring that son of a Sūta, the best among chariot-warriors, who wears golden ornaments,
under the power of Time. Today,
bring that son of a Sūta, the best among chariot-warriors, [under the power of Time].
Having slain [him], show your affection for the King of Dharma;
O Pārtha, I know your prowess exactly as it is,
which cannot be resisted even by the gods and the asuras.
For that evil-souled son of a charioteer always despises the sons of Pāṇḍu out of pride;
it is by him that the wicked Suyodhana considers himself a hero.

O Dhanañjaya, conquer today that son of Sūti, the root of all evils! O Dhanañjaya, slay Karṇa— that proud tiger among men, swift of action, with his sword for a tongue, his bow for a mouth, and his arrows for teeth.
"I authorize you by my own heroism and strength;
slay the heroic Karṇa in battle, as a lion slays an elephant—
he whose prowess causes the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to disregard yours."
"O Pārtha, slay that Karṇa Vaikartana today in battle!
Saṃjaya said:
Then Keśava, of immeasurable soul, spoke again to Arjuna.
O Bhārata, today marks the seventeenth day since he resolved with all his might to slay Karṇa,
and since this most terrible destruction of men, elephants, and horses has been unfolding.

O lord of the people, having once been a vast army of yours facing the enemies in battle, only a small remnant remains after they have encountered one another in combat. O Pārtha, the Kauravas indeed once possessed an abundance of elephants and horses.
Having encountered you as their enemy at the forefront of the battle, they have indeed perished;
and all these Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas, along with their kinsmen,
as well as the Pāṇḍavas, stand firm having encountered you, O invincible one.
O slayer of foes, protected by you, the Pāñcālas, Pāṇḍavas, Matsyas, Kārūṣas, Cedis, Kekayas, Māgadhas, Pārijātas, Southerners, and Keralas have brought about the destruction of the hosts of enemies.
"Who indeed, O dear one, is able to defeat the assembled Kauravas in battle,
except for the great car-warriors, the Pāṇḍavas, when they are protected by you in combat?
For you alone are capable of conquering in battle even the gods, asuras, and humans."

When even the three worlds together would be no match for him when he is fully prepared, how much less so the Kaurava army? For who else besides you, O tiger among men, would be capable of defeating King Bhagadatta— even one who might be equal to Vāsava himself?
Likewise, O sinless Pārtha, all the kings were unable even to look upon this vast army protected by you with their eyes;
for it was thus constantly guarded by you in battle, O Pārtha.
Having crushed the forces in the great battle, Bhīṣma and Droṇa were struck down by Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin;
for who indeed, O Pārtha, would be able [to withstand] those two great chariot-warriors of the Pañcālas in battle?
Who indeed is able to conquer Bhīṣma and Droṇa— who possess prowess equal to that of Śakra—
in battle? [Who can defeat] the son of Śantanu in combat, Droṇa, Vaikartana, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, the son of Somadatta, and Kṛtavarman as well?
[Saṃjaya said: "The king of the Sindhus, the King of the Madras, and King Suyodhana—
those heroes skilled in weapons, all of whom follow him in battle,
fierce lords of an akṣauhiṇī, enraged and intoxicated with the pride of war."
"O tiger among men, there is no man here capable of conquering you except for yourself. Countless guilds have been decimated, their horses, chariots, and elephants shattered;
and many fierce kṣatriyas from various lands, full of indignation, have perished."
O Bhārata, having encountered you, O Bībhatsu, the Govāsas, Dāsamīyas, Vasātīs,
and those originating from various other lands,
as well as numerous elephants, have been slain in battle.
O Bhārata, the exalted great armies of the Vrātyas, the Vāṭadhānas, and the proud Bhojas— belonging to the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya orders—
having encountered you, have met their destruction along with their horses, chariots, and elephants.
The fierce Tukhāras of cruel deeds, the Yavanas, the Khaśas, the Dārvābhisāras, the Daradas, the Śakas, the Ramaṭhas, the Taṅgaṇas,
the Andhrakas, the Pulindas, and the Kirātas of formidable prowess— [all these were subdued].
The Mlecchas, the mountaineers, and those dwelling on the coastal marshlands— impetuous, skilled in war, powerful, and with hands firm in grasp— these,
together with the Kurus, are enraged for the sake of Suyodhana.
"O scorcher of the foe, having seen that great army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons drawn up in battle array and possessing immense strength, no man other than you could possibly conquer them in war;
for what mortal indeed would venture forward if you were not his protector?"

O Lord, that army, which was like the surging ocean and shrouded in dust, was torn asunder by the enraged Pāṇḍavas protected by you and slaughtered. Jayatsena, the mighty ruler of the Māgadhas, [was also slain].
It has been exactly seven days since Abhimanyu was slain in battle. Then Bhīma, with his mace, destroyed ten thousand elephants of fearsome deeds that formed the retinue of that king.
Then other elephants and hundreds of chariots were also slain by force.
Thus, O dear one, while that battle of great terror was raging,
the Kauravas encountered Bhīmasena and you, O Pāṇḍava.
O noble one, with their horses, chariots, and elephants, they departed from here for the world of death;
likewise, O Pārtha, when the vanguard of the army had been slain there by the Pāṇḍavas,
Bhīṣma released fierce showers of arrows, O sire.
Skilled in harsh weapons, he covered the Ikṣvākus, Pañcālas, Karūṣas, Matsyas,
and Kekayas with his arrows and brought them to their destruction;
by the body-piercing shafts released from his bow, [the enemy was overwhelmed].
The sky became filled with straight-flying arrows feathered with gold.
With a single fistful alone, he could have slain thousands of chariot-warriors;
having struck down a hundred thousand men and elephants gathered together, all possessed of great strength.

"Having slain ten thousand [enemies], he shall cast off his armor from his own body; 'I shall drive [the enemy] away,' such was the vow of that son of Gaṅgā. Having struck down various kings, he would discard his weapons in battle."
Tens of thousands of arrows were released by that powerful hero;
having traveled with the tenth motion, they struck down horses, chariots, and elephants.
Having abandoned the nine faulty motions, he discharged those arrows with full extension.
For ten days Bhīṣma struck down your army;
the seats of the chariots were emptied, and elephants and horses were slain.
When the tenth day arrived, he displayed terrible prowess.
Having displayed his own form, equal to Rudra or Upendra in battle,
he plunged into the armies of the Pāṇḍavas and slaughtered them,
striking down the lords of the earth— the Cedis, Pañcālas, and Kekayas.
He scorched the Pāṇḍava army, crowded with men, horses, and elephants;
