he was like the sun scorching as it moved through the battle, desiring to rescue the dull-witted Suyodhana who was sinking like a fool in a place without a boat.
Thousands of millions of foot soldiers, with excellent weapons in their hands,
as well as other lords of the earth, were unable even to look at him as he moved about in battle, appearing victorious.
With all their effort, the Pāṇḍavas suddenly rushed forward;
yet Bhīṣma alone, having routed both the Pāṇḍavas and the Sṛñjayas in battle, attained the status of a peerless hero on the field.
Having encountered that great car-warrior, that tiger among men, Śikhaṇḍin— protected by you—
struck him with straight-jointed arrows;
for Death himself had been born to slay Bhīṣma, felling him from his chariot with floods of shafts.
This very grandfather lies fallen upon a bed of arrows,
O tiger among men, having encountered you like a vulture encountering a crow.
Drona, the fierce one, having for five days scattered the armies of his enemies—
Having formed a battle array for the great conflict and struck down the great chariot-warriors,
that great car-warrior, having provided protection for Jayadratha in the encounter,
fought through the fierce night like the Destroyer himself and consumed all creatures.
For two days, the heroic and powerful Bhāradvāja,
having encountered Dhṛṣṭadyumna, attained the supreme goal.
And if he had indeed [faced] the enemy chariot-warriors in battle, headed by the Sūta’s son—
If you had not restrained him in battle, Droṇa would not have perished. But by you, the entire force of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son was held back;
therefore, O Dhanañjaya, Droṇa was slain in battle by the son of Pṛṣata.
Who else but you, O Kṣatriya, could have performed such a deed in battle? And what other man claiming to be a man would be capable of achieving in combat what you have done,
O Pārtha, regarding the slaying of Jayadratha?
Having repulsed the great army and slain the heroic kings,
the ruler of the Sindhus has been struck down by you through the power and splendor of your weapons.
The kings recognize the slaughter of the King of Sindhu as a marvel.
"It is no marvel from you, for you, O Pārtha, are indeed a great car-warrior (*mahāratha*).
Having encountered you in battle, O Bhārata, it is my conviction that the Kṣatriya host would not remain unscorched for even a single day."
O Pārtha, this terrible army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son has been destroyed in battle along with all its heroes, now that Bhīṣma and Droṇa have been slain;
today its foremost warriors are shattered, and its horses, men, and elephants are killed.
Deprived of the sun, moon, and stars, the Bharata host appears like the sky; for this army of Pārtha has been shattered in battle by Bhīma’s prowess,
just as the Asura host of old was destroyed by the valor of Śakra.
Of those, five great car-warriors remain as survivors of the slaughter:
Aśvatthāman, Kṛtavarman, Karṇa, the lord of Madra, and Kṛpa.
O tiger among men, having slain those five great car-warriors today—
Having slain his enemies, he bestowed the earth, along with its islands and cities, upon the king;
and having likewise slain these tigers among men—Droṇa’s son, Kṛpa, Śalya, Bhoja, and the son of Adhiratha—he [gave it away]. These were indeed heroes and great chariot-warriors.
May Pārtha, endowed with immeasurable heroism and glory, today obtain the earth— along with its sky, waters, and subterranean realms, its mountains and great forests—
just as Viṣṇu in former times did after slaying the Daityas and Dānavas.
"Give the earth back to the king, just as Hari gave it to Śakra.
Today let the Pāñcālas rejoice when their enemies have been slain by you,
just as the gods rejoiced when the Dānavas were slain by Viṣṇu."
Or perhaps, O best of bipeds, because you honor your preceptor Droṇa,
you feel compassion for Aśvatthāman, and out of respect for your teacher toward Kṛpa;
or else, because you hold in high esteem your brothers and kinsmen who have long been cherished by you.
"Having encountered Kṛtavarman, you shall not lead him to the abode of Yama.
O Pārtha, having fought today with those two enraged assailants,
and having encountered his maternal uncle Śalya, the lord of the Madra people— "
O lotus-eyed one, if you are compassionate and do not wish to slay him,
then today, O best of men, quickly kill this base and evil-minded Karna with your sharpened arrows for his extreme hostility toward the Pāṇḍavas.
"This deed of yours is well-done; nothing here is improper.
We too recognize this, and there is no fault whatsoever in it, O sinless one, regarding what happened to your mother and her son during the night while they were being burned."
And as for that which Suyodhana directed against you for the sake of the gambling match—
O Arjuna, in all those instances, the evil-minded Karṇa was the root cause here;
for Suyodhana always considers his protection to lie in Karṇa alone.
Then, being provoked, he proceeded to seize me as well;
Suyodhana, acting without restraint, would have destroyed you all,
O giver of honor, for the resolve of that king, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, is firm.
"Karna will undoubtedly defeat all the sons of Pritha in battle.
O son of Kunti, relying upon Karna, the son of Dhritarashtra has chosen war with you,
even though he knows your strength."

For Karna always says: "I shall defeat the assembled sons of Pṛthā, along with Vāsudeva and all the kings, in the great battle. Thus the evil-minded one encourages the wicked-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
O Bhārata, slay today that Karṇa who roars in the assembly;
he who, being crooked and unwise, formerly relied upon Karṇa and committed every kind of evil against you on behalf of the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
In all those instances, the evil-minded Karna was the leader;
and as for that hero, the bull-eyed son of Subhadrā, who was slain by the six cruel great chariot-warriors of the Dhartarāṣṭras, I beheld him fallen.
Making the heroic great chariot-warriors Droṇa, Aśvatthāman, and Kṛpa tremble, they—
terrified of Abhimanyu— fled in all directions in battle, leaving elephants riderless and great chariot-warriors deprived of their vehicles.
He deprived horsemen of their horses and foot-soldiers of their weapons and lives; he, whose shoulders were like those of a bull and who brought glory to the Kurus and Vṛṣṇis,
was scattering the armies and afflicting the great car-warriors.

O friend, I swear to you by the truth that my limbs burn with grief as I think of the son of Subhadrā, who, exerting himself, was sending men, horses, and elephants to the abode of Yama with his arrows, as if consuming the entire army.
And there, O Lord, the evil-minded Karṇa acted with malice;
yet Karṇa was unable to stand before Abhimanyu in battle,
pierced by the arrows of Subhadrā’s son, unconscious, and drenched in blood.
Sighing, inflamed with rage, turned away and afflicted by arrows,
his resolve set on retreat and despairing even of life,
he looked repeatedly at Duryodhana in the battle, feeling deep shame.
Then Pārtha did not flee from that great battle;
having seen Droṇa, he asked him for the means to slay Abhimanyu,
but he stood there utterly overwhelmed, exhausted by the blows received in the fray.
Then, having heard those cruel words of Droṇa in battle, which were appropriate for that moment, Karṇa cut his bow asunder. Thereupon,
with his weapon thus severed by him in the fray, five great car-warriors [attacked].
And that one of deceitful intellect struck him with showers of arrows.
When that hero was slain, grief entered all;
yet that evil-minded Karṇa and Suyodhana laughed aloud.
And as for those harsh words that Karṇa spoke to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly hall, like a cruel man, in the presence of the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus:
"The Pāṇḍavas are ruined, O Kṛṣṇā; they have gone to eternal hell."
"O lady of broad hips, O woman of measured speech, choose another husband! O you with arched brows and long-lashed eyes, enter the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as his slave; for you have no husbands."
"O Kṛṣṇā, the Pāṇḍavas have no power over you in any way whatsoever.
O beautiful Pāñcālī, you are the wife of slaves, and you yourself are a slave. Indeed, today Duryodhana alone is recognized as the sovereign on earth."
And all those rulers of the earth attend to his security and well-being.
Now behold, O blessed lady, how the Pāṇḍavas have been utterly destroyed;
they gaze at one another through the splendor of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son.
"Clearly these are like sterile sesame seeds, for they have sunk into hell;
yet they shall serve the Kuru king like slaves.
Thus spoke that man of supreme wickedness, who was ignorant of righteousness.
O Bhārata, as that wicked Karṇa utters evil words while you listen,
let these life-cutting arrows— sharpened on stone and adorned with gold— which are discharged by you, quench those sinful words of his.
Today, let the Kurus behold Karṇa seized by you in battle,
like the scorching sun standing at the gateway to heaven.
Today, let the Kuru warriors witness your prowess in combat.

O Pārtha, now that the Sūtaputra has been slain, let the great chariot-warriors know you for what you are! O Bhārata, today let the kankas, vultures, eagles, crows, and jackals tear apart the limbs of the Sūtaputra.
Today, this Atiratha, having been challenged and slain by you in battle,
has brought grief to the Kurus and likewise joy to the Pāṇḍavas.
Today, let the Pañcālas, together with the Pāṇḍavas, rejoice in you.
Just as all the gods were [joyful] when the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred,
O Pārtha, having slain Karṇa in battle today and attained supreme glory, become free from sorrow, free from fever, and honored by your kinsmen.
Just as the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by the powerful Viṣṇu after he had assumed the form of a man-lion (nārasiṃha),
so too, O son of Rādhā, you must assume a great and terrible form [to slay him].
O mighty-armed one, slay him in battle and protect your own people from fear!
Let your arrows today extinguish those other evils which that evil-minded one committed against you, as well as his very life.
O scorcher of enemies, bring an end to the suffering of Kṛṣṇā;
having slain in battle that boastful and exceedingly manly foe who is unworthy of praise,
today the son of Adhiratha has been pierced on all sides by your arrows.
O tiger among men, let them consider you the foremost of all archers;
today, let Pārtha encounter Karṇa in battle like a porcupine struck by the terrible arrows discharged from the Gāṇḍīva, as those shafts touch his limbs.
Today, as he feels with his limbs the terrible arrows discharged from the Gāṇḍīva,
let the evil-minded Karṇa remember the words of Droṇa and Bhīṣma.
These gold-feathered iron shafts, slayers of enemies, possess the brilliance of lightning.
Released by your arms,
those fierce and sharp arrows, having pierced his vital organs with great velocity, shall drink his blood today and send Karṇa to the abode of Yama.
If Rādheya does not remember the words of Droṇa and Bhīṣma, he shall have his armor shattered by the sharp, broad-headed arrows discharged from the Gāṇḍīva;
for those gold-feathered, enemy-slaying iron shafts possess the brilliance of lightning.

If fierce arrows released from your arms— capable of piercing vital organs— do not pierce the armor of Adhiratha’s son and drink his blood, then today those high-velocity shafts shall send Karṇa to the abode of Yama.

Today, let the lords of the earth behold Karna—distressed, dejected, and afflicted by your arrows, crying out "Alas! Alas!", fallen from his chariot, wretched and despondent. Let them see him as he falls, crying out in grief, miserable and overwhelmed by your shafts.
"Today let Karna’s own friends behold him fallen upon the earth, lying immersed in his own blood with his weapons cast aside;
and today let them see that great armor [pierced] by arrows dispatched from the Gāṇḍīva."
In the seat of his chariot, they shall scatter like a cluster of stars from the sky;
and today in this great battle, as his arrows fall swiftly,
let their tips be severed by your shafts and shatter upon the surface of the earth.
O bull among the Bharatas, when his prowess has been struck down by you today,
let all the kings turn their faces away as if their lives have departed; and when the son of Adhiratha has gone, let the Kurus flee in all directions.
Considering you, O best of chariot-warriors, to be the foremost archer among all the worlds,
let Duryodhana, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— now terrified and agitated by fear— abandon his great army today and flee toward his own city.
Likewise, hearing today that he has been slain, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s son, the lord of men,
will fall to the ground in a swoon, for that ruler of the earth will indeed lose consciousness.
Today, O Pārtha, let all the archers know your prowess.
O Bhārata, those harsh words which Hastikakṣya spoke to you in the midst of the assembly— let his great banner, now shattered by your broad-headed arrow,
fall trembling to the earth.

O Pārtha, if Śalya, terrified, had not fled— abandoning his gold-adorned chariot which you had shattered with hundreds of arrows and whose warriors were slain— while the son of the Sūta looked on at the son of Karṇa.
To fulfill his vow, you shall strike him down with your arrows.
O giver of honor, when that evil-minded Karṇa sees his beloved son slain,
he will remember the words of Droṇa, Bhīṣma, and Vidura.
Then, O Dhanañjaya, having seen the son of Adhiratha slain by you, Suyodhana has today become hopeless regarding both his life and his kingdom;
for that Karṇa, O Pārtha, was slaughtering your men in battle.
"Equal to Śakra in strength through his vigor, or even comparable to Śaṅkara himself—
these Pāñcālas flee while being struck by sharp arrows,
O best of the Bharatas, as Karṇa seeks to rescue the Pāṇḍavas."
[He struck] the Pāñcālas and the sons of Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, the sons of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śatānīka the son of Nakula,
Nakula, Sahadeva, Durmukha, and Janamejaya.

"Know that Suvarmāṇa and Sātyaki have fallen under Karna's power. O scorcher of foes, the terrible roar of your kinsmen, the Pāñcālas, as they are being struck down by Karna in this great battle, is heard."
The Pāñcālas, though terrified, will by no means turn their backs in retreat;
for those great car-warriors and mighty archers do not take death into account.
He who alone enveloped the Pāṇḍava army with floods of arrows—[that Drona is now slain].
Having encountered Bhīṣma, the Pāñcālas did not turn their backs;
how then could those mighty warriors flee upon encountering Karṇa—
he who alone, day after day, was destroying all the Pāñcālas?
The hero moves like Time itself amidst the throng of Pāñcāla chariots;
even having encountered him in battle, those who are devoted to their allies will [perish] for the sake of their friends—
him who blazes with the fire of weapons and is the preceptor of all archers.
They ascended the invincible Droṇa, who was consuming [the enemy] by his might;
those subduers of foes, ever intent on conquering their enemies in battle,
the Pāñcālas would never turn their backs out of fear of the son of Adhiratha.

As those swift Pāñcāla warriors were charging forward, the heroic Karṇa took away their lives with his arrows, just as fire consumes moths. These Pāñcālas are fleeing; they are being swiftly driven away by the combatants.
"Behold, O best of the Bharatas, behold them thus made by Karṇa—
those heroes facing him who have renounced their lives for the sake of their friends.
Rādheya is bringing the Pāñcālas to destruction by the hundreds in battle."
O mighty-armed one, rescue us from the weapon of Karṇa, which is like a blazing fire!
O Bhārata, since these great archers are sinking without a raft in the fathomless ocean of Karṇa,
you ought to become a boat to save the Pāñcālas.
Indeed, the form of that terrible weapon— which was formerly acquired by Karṇa from Rāma, the son of Bhṛgu and best of sages— is now being manifested;
it scorches all the armies and is of a horrific and most dreadful nature.
Having rallied his great army, he blazes with his own splendor;
these arrows discharged from Karna’s bow move through the battle like swarms of bees, afflicting your men.
Like bees, O Lord, they strike down the men of the enemies;
these Pāñcālas, O Bhārata, roam in all directions,
having encountered Karna’s weapon in battle— a weapon that cannot be resisted by those lacking self-control.
O Pārtha, this Bhīma, firm in his wrath and surrounded on all sides by the Sṛñjayas, is afflicting Karṇa while fighting him with sharp arrows;
[and likewise] the Pāṇḍavas, the Sṛñjayas, and the Pāñcālas, O Bhārata.
If neglected, Karṇa would destroy [the army] just as a spreading disease destroys the body.
I see no other warrior in Yudhiṣṭhira’s force besides you who,
having encountered the son of Rādhā, might return home in safety.
O bull of the Bharatas, having slain him today with sharpened arrows,
O Pārtha, fulfill your vow and attain glory;
for you are indeed capable of conquering even the Kauravas along with Karṇa in battle.

"O best of warriors, there is no other [who could do this] in battle; I tell you this truly. Having performed this great deed and having slain the great car-warrior Karṇa, O Pārtha, O best of men, be successful, fulfilled, and happy."
08,052.001 Saṃjaya said: O Bhārata, having heard those words of Keśava,
Bībhatsu became free from grief and was filled with joy in an instant.
Then, quickly wiping the bowstring, he drew back the Gāṇḍīva bow;
aiming for the destruction of Karṇa, he addressed Keśava:
"O Govinda, with you as my protector, this victory of mine is certain."
Since you, the Lord of the past, the future, and the present, are pleased with me today,
O Kṛṣṇa, with you as my ally, I could indeed send even the three worlds assembled together to the supreme realm;
how much more so Karṇa in this great battle?
"O Janārdana, I see the army of the Pāñcālas fleeing;
I see Karṇa moving about fearlessly in battle;
and I see the Bhārgava weapon coursing everywhere."
"O Vārṣṇeya, this was discharged by Karṇa like the great thunderbolt by Śakra. Indeed,
O Kṛṣṇa, this is that very battle in which I have repeatedly defeated the warriors, who were intent on flight."
Beings will speak of this as long as the earth endures: "Today, O Kṛṣṇa, my arrows, released from the Gāṇḍīva and impelled by my hand, shall bring Karṇa to his death, piercing through his ears."
Today King Dhṛtarāṣṭra will despise his own intellect,
by which he consecrated Duryodhana— who is unworthy of sovereignty— in the kingdom;
for he who, having abandoned one possessed of virtues, makes a meritless man his lord.
O Kṛṣṇa, that king grieves as soon as his destruction has arrived,
just like a certain dull-witted man who, having cut down a great mango grove, sets his mind on watering *palāśa* trees and then laments.

Having seen the flower, one greedy for the fruit grieves upon seeing the fruit; likewise, O giver of honor, Janārdana, this Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was greedy for the flower, will experience intense suffering upon seeing the fruit.
Now that the Sūta’s son has been slain, the lord will today become hopeless;
O mighty-armed one, Dhṛtarāṣṭra will today be separated from his kingdom, his happiness, his fortune, his realm, his city, and his sons.
Today, O Kṛṣṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra will be deprived of his kingdom, his sons, his royal splendor, and his vast happiness, having lost all hope. Today, King Duryodhana will lose all hope for his life.
"O Kṛṣṇa, once Karṇa is slain, this shall come to pass; I tell you the truth.
Today, having seen Karṇa shattered by my arrows, he will be like Vṛtra in the ancient war between the gods and asuras, struck down by the slayer of Bala."
O Kṛṣṇa, let that son of Subala, the lord of men, remembering your words regarding peace, recognize today the arrows as the stake,
the Gāṇḍīva bow as the gambling board, and my chariot as the circle of the dice.

O Govinda, today, by slaying Karṇa with my sharp arrows, I shall dispel the deep sleeplessness of King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī. Today, when the Sūta’s son has been slain by me, the son of Kuntī will be king.
With a mind full of great joy and delight, he shall obtain happiness for a long time.
And today, I shall discharge here that invincible, peerless arrow of Keśava,
which will deprive Karṇa of his life.
"O Madhusūdana, this was the vow he made regarding my slaying of that wicked-souled one: 'I shall not wash my feet until I have slain Phalguna. Having rendered that vow of that sinful man false,"
"I shall strike down his body from the chariot with straight-jointed arrows—
he who considers no other man on earth his equal in battle. Today,
the earth shall drink the blood of that son of a Sūta."
"Since the son of a charioteer said, 'O Kṛṣṇa, you are indeed without a master,' and since Karṇa, acting under Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s counsel, has boasted of his own virtues—
my sharpened arrows shall make those words false."
Like enraged venomous serpents, they shall drink his blood.
Released by my skillful hand, iron shafts with the brilliance of lightning,
discharged from the Gāṇḍīva, shall send Karṇa to the supreme destination.
Today the son of Rādhā shall suffer for those cruel words he spoke toward the Pāñcālī in the midst of the assembly, when he reviled the Pāṇḍavas; indeed,
those who were like sterile sesame seeds there shall today become actual sesame seeds.
When the evil-minded Sūtaputra Karṇa, the son of Vaikartana,
had been slain, he had said, "I shall protect you from the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Thus did Karṇa boast of his own virtues to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"My sharpened arrows shall make that [promise] false;
today the sin of the sons of Pāṇḍu shall reach its end—
for he who said, 'I shall slay all the Pāṇḍavas along with their sons.'"
Today, while all the archers look on, I shall slay that Karṇa,
relying upon whose prowess the high-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— that evil-souled and wicked-minded one— has always held us in contempt.
Having slain Karṇa in battle, I shall indeed satisfy my brother;
by discharging various kinds of arrows, I shall terrify the enemies with shafts drawn back to the ear, which increase the population of Yama’s kingdom.
I shall beautify the earth with the fallen chariots and elephants in that great battle where warriors intoxicated by war are joined in combat;
I shall destroy his army, consisting of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry.
"Today, O Madhusūdana, I shall slay that Karṇa, the son of Rādhā.
Today, O Kṛṣṇa, when Karṇa is slain, let the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with the kings,
flee in all directions in fear, like deer terrified by a lion."
Today, let King Duryodhana look upon the earth,
now that Karṇa has been slain by me in battle along with his sons and his circle of friends.
Today, seeing Karṇa slain, let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who is so intolerant of others' success, behold the truth.
O Kṛṣṇa, let him know me in battle as the foremost of all archers; let the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that lord of men,
be rendered hopeless— deprived of his sons, grandsons, ministers, and servants,
and devoid of hope for his ancestral kingdom.
"Today, O Keśava, I shall install Dhṛtarāṣṭra as the lord of men in the kingdom;
today, the wheel-marked birds and various kinds of carnivorous creatures will roam over Karna’s limbs,
severed by my arrows."
"O Madhusūdana, today in battle I shall sever the head of Karṇa, the son of Rādhā, while all the archers look on;
today, O Madhusūdana, with sharp *vipāṭhas* and razor-headed arrows."
In battle, I shall sever the limbs of the evil-minded son of Rādhā;
today, King Yudhiṣṭhira will cast off his great distress,
O hero, and the mental anguish he has long harbored within himself.
O Keśava, having slain the son of Rādhā along with his kinsmen today,
I shall gladden King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
Today, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall [slay] the wretched followers of Karṇa in battle.
"Alas! O Govinda, today I shall cover the earth with lords of the earth who resemble blazing fire, whose arrows are like the venom of serpents, and who wear golden armor and jeweled earrings."
O Madhusūdana, today I shall crush the limbs and heads of all the enemies of Abhimanyu with my sharp arrows;
today I shall give the earth, cleansed of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, to my brother.
O Keśava, you shall traverse a earth devoid of Arjuna;
today King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, will have his enemies slain;
today Duryodhana shall lose his blazing prosperity and his kingdom.

When Karṇa, the son of Vikartana, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa have been slain in battle, O Kṛṣṇa, which of those armies will enter and be liberated? From this day forward, [let us serve] King Yudhiṣṭhira, who is devoted to righteousness.
Let my friends and the Brahmins who have known me for a long time rejoice;
having heard today that Karṇa Vaikartana has been slain by me,
let them perform the worship of the deities' shrines accompanied by the sounding of drums.

O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, now that Karṇa has been slain today, let the long-prepared sacrifice for the gods be performed according to the prescribed rites. Today, both Ambā and Kṛṣṇā will hasten toward one another.
O Hṛṣīkeśa, when this desire is fulfilled,
let them embrace you; today, O Kṛṣṇa, let the eldest Pāṇḍava and the noble Vṛkodara look upon you with gentle eyes once Karṇa has been slain.
Having saluted my elders today and being saluted by my younger brothers,
and embracing them with both my arms, I shall indeed attain vast fame.
O Kṛṣṇa, when Karṇa has been slain today, the gods will praise Arjuna.
"Let the ascetics, gathered together, go joyfully to the third heaven.
O Kṛṣṇa, let the three worlds know today my prowess upon seeing Karṇa slain in single combat by Savyasācin."
"Today, O Kṛṣṇa, I shall become free from debt to the wielders of the bow,
to my wrath, to the Kurus, to my arrows, and to the Gāṇḍīva. Today I shall release the sorrow accumulated over thirteen years."
O Kṛṣṇa, having slain Karṇa in battle like Maghavan slaying Śambara,
let the great car-warriors of the Somakas today, desiring to accomplish the task of their allies in combat, consider their purpose fulfilled once Karṇa has been killed in the fray.
"O Mādhava, I do not know how Śaineya will feel joy today when Karṇa has been slain and I have achieved even greater victory. Having killed Karṇa and his great car-warrior son in battle..."
O Mādhava, I shall grant satisfaction to Bhīma, to the twins, and to Sātyaki;
likewise to Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Śikhaṇḍin, and to the Pāñcālas.
[I shall grant it] to the hero Dhṛṣṭadyumna and likewise to Śikhaṇḍin.
"O Vārṣṇeya, having heard the mutual oath sworn by Dharmarāja, I shall attain freedom from my debt by slaying Karṇa in this great battle.
Today, let them behold Dhananjaya, full of indignation, in the midst of the fray."
"Seeing him fighting the Kauravas in battle and striking down the Sūta's son,
I shall once again speak of my own praise in your presence. Thus,
even today, I shall slay that foremost of enemies, the Sūta's son."
"In the science of archery, there is no one equal to me in the world; who is my equal in prowess?
Or who else is my equal in forbearance?"
Likewise, there is no one equal to me in wrath;
armed with my bow, I [confront] the Asuras, the Suras,
and all beings gathered together.
"By the strength of my own arms, I shall cause his defeat;
know that my prowess surpasses even the most superior.
Alone, with the Gāṇḍīva bow and the flame-like arrows, I [shall overcome him]."
Having attacked all the Kurus and the Bāhlikas,
I shall forcibly consume them along with their hosts, just as a fire situated in dry grass burns at the end of winter.
These arrows are drawn upon my hand;
the bow, together with an arrow, is placed in my left; and my two feet are depicted along with the chariot and the banner.
"Those who have gone to battle do not defeat one such as me," having spoken thus to Acyuta, that peerless hero, whose eyes were like blood, swiftly [attacked] the enemy-slayer.
Desirous of releasing Bhīma, he advanced into the battle,
seeking to sever the head from Karna’s body.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
O dear one, when Dhananjaya had gone forth to battle amidst the great peril of the Pandavas and Srinjayas, and the bottomless danger facing my own men.
"What was that battle like?
Sañjaya said:
"Their armies possessed great banners."
In the battle, they have gathered together in full force and roar, facing the sound of the kettledrums,
like masses of clouds amidst other clouds at the end of the summer heat.
Resounding with the blasts of kettledrums,
those [armies] roared like clouds driven by the winds during the rainy season;
the water of their weapons was agitated by great elephants that resembled clouds.
It was like the sound of musical instruments and the rattling of chariot wheels;
it possessed the brilliance of lightning from variegated golden weapons;
and it was filled with the roar of great chariots.
That [river] flowed with a terrible current, carrying floods of blood,
filled with swords, and sweeping away the lives of kṣatriyas; it was out of season, cruel, and brought about an undesirable rain.
That destruction of living beings took place;
many chariots, having come together, surrounded a single chariot and led it toward death.
Likewise, one [warrior] struck down a single chariot-fighter among the foremost of car-warriors;
and likewise, a chariot also destroyed many other chariots,
as well as a certain chariot together with its driver and horses.
One charioteer brought [his enemies] under the power of death;
another, with a single elephant,
likewise brought many chariots and horses under the power of death.
With floods of arrows, he brought all the enemies— chariots with their charioteers and horses, as well as elephants— to the power of death;
likewise, he sent the horses along with their riders to the same fate.
And likewise Pārtha led away the hosts of foot-soldiers; Pārtha, whose eyes were proud with strength,
carried them off like the mighty Antaka, the destroyer of all.
Kṛpa and Śikhaṇḍin met together in battle,
while Sātyaki advanced against Duryodhana;
and Śrutaśravas engaged with the son of Droṇa.
Yudhāmanyu also encountered Citrasena, while Karṇa’s son, the chariot-warrior Uttamaujas, engaged with Suṣeṇa and the Sṛñjayas.
Sahadeva, afflicted by hunger, rushed at the king of Gandhāra like a lion at a great bull;
and Śatānīka, the son of Nakula, [rushed] at the son of Karṇa.
The youthful hero, the son of Karṇa, afflicted the youthful Vṛṣasena with showers of arrows, and likewise struck the Pāñcālya prince with many volleys of shafts.
Ratharṣabha attacked Kṛtavarman;
Nakula, the son of Mādrī, a versatile warrior,
[attacked] the lord of the Pañcālas, the son of Yājñasenī.
O Bhārata, Duḥśāsana and the Bhārata host encountered the commander Karṇa along with his army,
as did the vast force of the Saṃśaptakas.
Then he, with mouth wide open like the cruel Destroyer, assailed Bhīma— the best among weapon-bearers in battle— who possessed unbearable speed.
O Bhārata, the hero Uttamaujas then forcefully struck Karna’s son there and slew him with Bhīmasena. He likewise cut him down with great force.
His head fell to the ground,
making the earth and the sky resound with its roar;
Suṣeṇa’s head lay fallen upon the earth.
Then, beholding him in such a state of distress, Karṇa,
out of rage, cut down his horses, chariot,
and banner with sharp, well-edged arrows.
But Uttamaujas,
having struck Kṛpa’s flank and his horses with sharpened arrows and with his radiant sword, slew them.
Then the impetuous son of the Pāñcāla king mounted the chariot of Śikhaṇḍin; indeed,
Śikhaṇḍin deprived Kṛpa of his chariot.
But seeing Kṛpa deprived of his chariot while Śikhaṇḍin remained on his own,
the son of Droṇa, having intercepted him with his chariot, did not wish to strike Kṛpa with arrows.
Just as one might rescue a cow stuck in the mud,
the son of Anila indeed rescued your sons with his sharp arrows, O Hiraṇyavarman.
The exceedingly terrible Bhīma scorched the army,
like the sun situated in the meridian during the summer season.
Sañjaya said:
Then, in that tumultuous conflict,
surrounded by many enemies in a time of great danger, he spoke thus to his charioteer: "Alone and hemmed in by many foes..."
Bhīma, holding back the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, said:
"O charioteer, drive the horses with speed;
I shall lead these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra to Yama."
Thus urged by Bhīmasena,
that charioteer then drove toward your son's army with fierce speed.
When Bhīma desired to advance against that force,
the other Kurus then rushed at him from all sides with elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry.
They struck Bhīma’s foremost steed, which possessed noble speed,
from all sides with multitudes of arrows;
then the high-souled one [encountered] the arrows falling upon him.
He cut them with gold-feathered arrows; indeed,
those gold-feathered shafts fell down,
severed into two or three pieces by Bhīma’s arrows.
Then, O King, amidst your royal ranks, a terrible clamor arose from the elephants, chariots, and young horses struck down by Bhīma, O lord of men.
Like mountains struck by thunderbolts,
those foremost of kings were slaughtered and pierced through by the preeminent warriors led by Bhīmasena.
They ascended Bhīma from all sides in that battle,
like birds upon a tree for the sake of its blossoms;
then they fell upon the midst of your army.
He manifested his power as if he had assumed great speed,
like Time at the end of an eon, desiring to consume and destroy all beings with uplifted staff.
Your warriors were unable to withstand that extreme speed in battle,
just as one cannot resist a creature with its mouth wide open as it charges toward them.
O Bhārata, as Time was thus carrying away the subjects at its appointed hour, the strength of the Bhāratas was being consumed in battle by that Great-Souled One.
Terrified and driven by Bhīma,
the army scattered in all directions like a mass of clouds dispersed by a great wind; thus was the Bharata host scattered, O Bhārata.
And again, as Bhīma surrounded him in battle,
the wise and powerful one, Bhīmasena, being once more delighted, spoke thus to his charioteer.
"Hurry, hurry now, O Viśoka!
Quickly behold these tips of banners and chariots. O charioteer, distinguish whether they belong to the enemy or to our own."
As chariots and banners fall together in combat, I am not aware of anything at all;
let me not shroud my own army with my arrows.
Seeing my enemies on all sides free from sorrow,
anxiety burns intensely within my mind,
for the king has not come, nor has Kirīṭin.
"I have been born to many sorrows, O charioteer;
this is the sorrow, O driver, that Dharmarāja has gone away, leaving me in the midst of enemies."
Whether he is living or not, I do not know; nor do I know Bibhatsu—that is my extreme sorrow today.
Thus, I [face] the enemy host, which is like a fierce fire.
Filled with supreme joy, I shall destroy them;
having slain these who have gathered here in the midst of battle,
I shall be delighted along with you today.
Having inspected all my quivers and arrows,
[I shall consider] what might remain of the shafts on my chariot,
and how many arrows I have left at this very moment.
"O Viśoka, look at my quivers;
how many arrows remain to me? What is their species, and what is their measure?"
"Having understood this clearly, tell it to me, O Sūta:
how many thousands or how many hundreds [of years] are there? Viśoka said:
"O charioteer, tell me quickly;
having understood everything thus, I shall speak today, O hero, that which brings about the fulfillment of your purpose."
The Kaikeyas, Kāmbojas, Surāṣṭras, and Bāhlikas;
the Mlecchas, Suhmas, and the Parataṅkaṇas; and the Madras, Vaṅgas, Magadhas, and Kuṇindas.
The Ānartakas, Āvartakas, and the mountaineers—
all of them, having taken up their excellent weapons, surrounded you again and again and then roared aloud.
Upon this chariot of yours were twelve thousand sharp and well-polished broad-headed arrows (bhallas).
Viśoka said:
O hero, there were ten thousand arrows of the six types,
as well as ten thousand kṣuras and bhallas,
and two thousand nārācas, O hero.
And there were exactly three *pradaras*, ten *vatsadantas*, and twelve *karṇins*; and six hundred *ardhacandras*, O Pārtha.
Seven of the most excellent *vipāṭha* arrows,
thirty and ten *śilīmukha* arrows,
and thirty small *ayomukha* arrows.
There remains a store of weapons belonging to the sons of Pāṇḍu,
which would not fit upon a cart drawn by six oxen;
ten thousand missiles, O son of Pāṇḍu, remain yours.
This six-bull cart shall carry spears,
mallets, pikes, and javelins;
do not fear the depletion of these weapons.
Knowing this, O wise one, release even a thousand [of them];
you possess the power of maces,
swords, and arms, so conquer your enemies swiftly, O hero of a thousand powers.
Bhīma said:
"O Śoka-less one, let the Siddhas proclaim my vow this very day throughout all the worlds!"
Either Bhīmasena shall not be released alive from the battle,
or he alone shall conquer his enemies in combat;
let this be the one thing desired by us.
May the gods accomplish all this for me. O charioteer,
look now at this [chariot] being struck by the swift, high-velocity arrows released by Bhīma,
which are shattering the kings.
With fierce arrows, the battle took on a terrible form;
with the sun obscured, it became like the realm of death.
This was realized this very day by the kings.
O charioteer, it shall come to pass that even the children will know this: either Bhīmasena will be overwhelmed in battle,
or he alone will conquer the Kurus in combat.
"Let all the Kurus rush forth in battle, or let the worlds proclaim my fame down to the children;
I alone shall strike them all down."
Let all those who desire the highest merit for their actions strike Bhīmasena;
may the gods accomplish that for me alone.
May Arjuna, the slayer of enemies, come here today like Śakra swiftly summoned to a sacrifice;
may he come here on his chariot with Keśava as his charioteer.
Indra was summoned at the sacrifice by sheer force. Behold, behold my strength, O Viśoka;
the strength of my enemies has been shattered on all sides.
Behold all these various sounds as they are released;
likewise, the powerful sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are fleeing. Behold this army of the Bharatas being torn asunder!
Why are these lords of men fleeing?
Clearly, the wise Savyasācin, the foremost of men,
is swiftly shrouding this army with his arrows.
"O Sūta, surely Dhanañjaya is approaching;
therefore, this army of the Bharatas is being broken.
Behold, O Viśoka, the banners fleeing!"
Behold these elephants, horses, and throngs of foot-soldiers in battle, O charioteer, as well as these shattered chariots struck by arrows and spears, and the car-warriors themselves.
And yet this Kaurava army is being constantly replenished,
even though it is being slaughtered in great numbers by Dhananjaya’s arrows, which possess a force like that of thunderbolts.
Devoured by arrows with feathers of gold,
these chariots, horses, and elephants fled,
trampling the throngs of foot soldiers.
All the Kauravas, utterly bewildered,
fled like elephants terrified by a forest fire,
crying out "Alas! in the battle, O Viśoka.
The lordly elephants let out great roars.
Viśoka said:
"O Bhīma, do you not hear him here?"
Today, as the exceedingly terrible *gāṇḍīva* bow is being drawn by the enraged Pārtha,
has the tip of its string not slipped off your ears?
O Pāṇḍava, all your desires have been fulfilled;
the ape-bannered one is seen amidst the elephant host,
like lightning flashing from a dark cloud.
Thus I beheld that quivering bow being brandished by Dhanañjaya;
for that monkey was indeed seen on all sides.
Having ascended the top of Dhanañjaya’s banner,
terrifying the multitudes of elephants in the fray,
I am afraid of him even upon seeing him with my own eyes.
And this variegated diadem of Dhanañjaya shines exceedingly;
this divine jewel has the luster of the sun.
And look at this resplendent Devadatta, situated upon the crown; it is formidable, shining like a white cloud, and possesses a magnificent sound.
Behold, O Pārtha, standing at the side of Dhananjaya in battle, that one of great strength, terrible and resplendent, the slayer of his enemies.
Behold the divine conch Pāñcajanya of Janārdana, who holds the reins in his hand as he plunges into the army of the enemy.
Behold the discus of Janārdana, radiant as the sun, with a hub of diamond and edges like razors, standing at his side;
behold it, glowing with the brilliance of fire.
O hero, behold the discus standing at the side of Dhananjaya, the son of Pṛthā— increasing the fame of Keśava, and ever worshipped by the Yadus.
Likewise, O son of Kuntī, behold on the chest of Kṛṣṇa the highly precious Pāñcajanya conch, which has the color of a lotus filament, and the Kaustubha gem.
And behold this garland of victory,
O Bhīmasena,
blazing like a flash of lightning from a dark cloud.
The terrible sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow being drawn by Dhanañjaya at the proper time is heard; it is not heard from this [other] one.
"Are you deaf, O Pārtha? These trunks of great elephants, resembling straight *sarala* trees,
are being severed by razors and fall down."
Furthermore, by that diadem-wearing Arjuna,
the riders were cut down with arrows like mountains by thunderbolts;
likewise, [he struck] Kṛṣṇa’s Pāñcajanya conch.
O son of Kuntī, behold upon your chest this highly precious Kaustubha gem, possessing the hue of the moon,
and this blazing garland of victory.
Surely Pārtha, the foremost of chariot-warriors, is approaching,
putting this army of the enemies to flight with these black-darted arrows that have the hue of white clouds.
The best of chariot-warriors, with his precious horses,
[overwhelms] the chariots, horses, and throngs of foot-soldiers; behold how they fall, torn asunder by his arrows.
Behold these four hundred chariots destroyed by your younger brother, who possesses the splendor of the king of the immortals, like great forests felled by the wind of Suparṇa.
In battle, Kirīṭin [Arjuna] struck down seven hundred elephants along with their horses and drivers using great arrows,
as well as numerous foot soldiers, cavalrymen, and charioteers.
"Here comes the mighty Arjuna to your presence, striking down the Kurus like a wondrous planet;
your desires are fulfilled, for your enemies have been slain."
"May your strength and your life-span increase for a long time.
Bhīma said:
"I give you fourteen excellent villages."
O charioteer, you have brought pleasant news; I am well-pleased.
Give me a hundred female slaves and twenty chariots, O Viśoka, since you have informed me of Arjuna.
08,055.001 Saṃjaya said: 08,055.001a Having heard the rattling of the chariot and the lion-roar in the battle, Arjuna said to Govinda: "Urge the horses forward quickly."
Victory to the Lord of the World, the knower of dharma, the King of Dharma! May Keśava now grant auspiciousness to the Pāṇḍavas; may the Diademed One, whose steed is great victory, prevail!
"May the two sons of Mādrī become the burners of the forest that is the enemy host.
Having heard Arjuna’s words, Govinda said to Arjuna:
"I shall go very quickly to where Bhīma is stationed."
He was approaching on horses the color of snow and conch shells,
harnessed with networks of gold, pearls, and gems,
holding his thunderbolt and desiring to slay Jambha.
Like the fierce-tempered Indra for victory,
the multitudes of chariots, horses, elephants, and infantry [advanced] with the sounds of arrows and the clatter of rims and hooves.
Making the earth and the quarters resound,
those enraged lions among men advanced for victory;
and between them and Pārtha, there was then a great [encounter].
A righteous battle that destroys the sins of the body,
such as was fought by the Asuras for the sake of the three worlds against the god Viṣṇu, the foremost among victors.
And the single one, adorned with a diadem and garlands, cut down that diverse multitude of weapons belonging to Trailokyanātha and Cakrapāṇi.
With sharp razors, crescent-headed arrows, and other keen shafts, they cut their heads, arms,
umbrellas, yak-tail fans, and banners into many pieces.
Horses, chariots, throngs of foot-soldiers,
and elephants fell upon the earth in many forms and distorted shapes,
like forests shattered by the wind.
Great elephants, covered with golden nets,
were equipped for battle with banners and victory-flags,
and were bristling with gold-feathered arrows.
The elephants there, being torn apart by Balarāma, shone like mountains ablaze,
resembling burnt bamboos consumed by a forest fire.
Having torn asunder the elephants, chariots,
and horses with his excellent arrows, which were like the thunderbolt of Vāsava,
he proceeded swiftly with the intent to slay Karṇa.

Just as Marutvān in ancient times during the shattering of Bala’s strength, so that tiger among men, the subduer of foes, entered the army of the Sūtas with his mighty arms, like a makara entering the ocean.
O King, seeing him, your men— accompanied by chariots and infantry,
and consisting largely of elephant-riders and horsemen— rushed toward the son of Pāṇḍu.
As they charged at Pārtha, a tremendous clamor arose.
Like the roar of the waters of a surging ocean,
those great car-warriors, like tigers themselves,
rushed toward that tiger among men in battle, casting aside all fear for their lives.
As they rushed forward there, discharging showers of arrows,
Arjuna scattered that army like a great wind disperses the clouds.
Those strikers, having united with their ranks of chariots, [assailed] Arjuna.
Having advanced, those great archers pierced him with sharpened arrows,
with spears, javelins, shafts, *kuṇapa*-missiles, and *kuru-mudgara* clubs;
with tridents, three-pronged lances, iron maces, *bhiṇḍipāla* slings, and battle-axes.
With clubs, mallets, swords, spears, and likewise with maces, with iron bars, sharp-edged spears, bludgeons, and battle-axes—
hurled by great warriors along with gravel, *japā* flowers, and dust.
[He was assailed] with the falling of Indra’s thunderbolts, with nets, snares,
and thorns; with showers from blazing peaks, with stones, wooden stakes,
great hailstones, lovely [traps], and destructive magnets.
Accompanied by their hosts with corrupted wheels, elephants, and horses, and carrying concealed weapons,
tens of thousands of excellent kings from various lands and Mlecchas advanced toward Arjuna and Keśava as they emerged alone from the camp.
Then Arjuna dispatched thousands of chariots, elephants,
and horses toward the abode of Yama with his arrows;
being slaughtered in battle by the shafts released from Pārtha’s bow, they fell.
Whenever fear arose, those great car-warriors would take cover here and there;
Arjuna, with his sharpened arrows, sent four hundred of those striving heroic mahārathas to the abode of Yama.
Being struck in battle by sharp arrows of various descriptions,
they abandoned Arjuna and fled in all directions out of fear. A great clamor arose from them as they fled at the head of the army.

"May you be blessed; like a great flood breaking against a mountain, that army was shattered and put to flight by Arjuna with his arrows. O noble one, having routed it, Pārtha advanced toward the divisions of the Sūtas."
A great roar arose from him as he indeed faced his enemies;
as he rushed toward Karṇa, there was a mighty sound of chariots,
like that of Garuḍa swooping down in ancient times for the sake of seizing serpents.
Upon hearing that sound, the mighty Bhimasena became exceedingly joyful, longing for the sight of Pārtha;
as soon as he heard that Pārtha was approaching, the powerful Bhimasena [rejoiced].
Having risked his life, O great king, he crushed your army. Resembling the force of the wind and equal to the wind in speed,
the powerful Bhīma, the son of the Wind-god, moved about like the wind itself.
O Indra among kings, O lord of the people, being thus afflicted by him, your army,
O great king, wandered about like a shattered ship upon the ocean.
Then Bhīma, displaying his lightness of hand, [assailed] that army.
He struck chariot against chariot and horse against horse;
likewise, he brought elephants and the best of men to their destruction by means of elephants and men respectively.
Having lifted up an elephant, Bhīma rushed toward another elephant.

Like Hanumān [shaking] a mountain, he struck him with that which was joined with a great medicinal herb; enraged, he struck him as a mountain strikes a great mountain. Having uprooted a certain elephant’s tusk, he struck the elephant with that very tusk.
Just as in former times Kumbhakarṇa, having encountered Airāvata in battle,
seized two elephants with his hands and slew them with blows—
so did he [the son of Rāvaṇa] strike down chariots, horses, and the best of kings, like the Pāṇḍava possessed by a spirit.
With fierce arrows, he cut them down, intending to send them to the abode of Yama.
There, O Bhārata, seeing Bhīma’s superhuman strength,
the warriors in battle were terrified, as if at the end of an eon by Time itself.
O Bhārata, seeing those of terrible strength thus afflicted by Bhīmasena,
King Duryodhana,
that great archer, spoke these words to his soldiers and warriors, O bull of the Bharatas.
He commanded them all in battle, saying, "Slay Bhīma!
When he is slain, I consider the entire army to be already destroyed without exception.
And having received that command from your son, the kings—
They completely covered Bhīma from all sides with showers of arrows.
In that battle, O great king, there were likewise mighty archers among men,
as well as numerous elephants and men, O King, who were greedy for victory.
O Indra among kings, chariots and horses surrounded Vṛkodara; O best of the Bharatas,
that hero, surrounded on all sides by those heroes,
shone like the moon amidst the stars.
Just as the moon, encircled by a halo, shines in its full splendor,
so did that best of men shine in battle,
O great king; for he was indistinguishable from Vijaya himself.
There, all those kings, their eyes red with rage, cruel and desirous of slaying Vṛkodara, unleashed showers of arrows upon him. He,
however, pierced that great army with his straight-jointed arrows.
Bhīma emerged from the battle like a fish from its net in the water, O Bhārata,
having slain ten thousand elephants that did not retreat,
as well as two hundred thousand men and two hundred more.
Having slain five thousand horses and a hundred chariots,
Bhīma caused a river with mud of blood to flow;
it had blood for its water, chariots for its eddies, and was teeming with elephants for its crocodiles.
It had men for its fish and horses for its crocodiles; its moss and water-grass were hair;
it carried away many jewels and severed the great lordly elephants that were its arms; it had thighs for its alligators, marrow for its mud, and was strewn with skulls for its stones.
With bows for its reeds, arrows for its water-weeds, maces and iron clubs for its banners;
adorned with swans, umbrellas, and standards, with excellent turbans for its foaming crests; possessing necklaces for its lotus-beds and the dust of the earth for its garlanded waves.

In an instant, that tiger among men caused that river to flow toward the abode of Yama— a stream characterized by noble conduct yet exceedingly difficult for the timid to cross, filled with throngs of warriors in battle.

Just as the fierce Vaitaraṇī river is difficult to cross for those of unrefined souls, so did Bhīma set in motion that terrible, impassable river which increases the fear of cowards and carries away heroic warriors.
Whichever way that best of chariot-warriors, the son of Pāṇḍu, advanced,
in those very directions he struck down warriors by the hundreds of thousands.
Having thus witnessed the feat performed by Bhīmasena in the battle—
O great king, Duryodhana spoke these words to Śakuni:
"Victory in battle, O maternal uncle! Subdue the mighty Bhīmasena;
for when he is conquered, I consider the mighty son of Pāṇḍu already defeated."
Then, O great king, the powerful son of Subala set forth for the great battle, joined by his brothers and surrounded by them;
having encountered Bhima of terrible prowess in that conflict.
The hero restrained him, as the shore restrains the ocean;
though being warded off by Bhima with sharp arrows,
he turned back upon hearing the words of his sister’s son, Śakuni, who was most deceitful.
O Indra among kings, Śakuni dispatched gold-feathered arrows, whetted on stone, into his left side between the breasts.
Having pierced the golden armor of that high-souled one, the arrows [entered].
O great king, those clad in garments of heron feathers and peacock plumes sank down. Deeply pierced in battle, O Bhārata, Bhīma suddenly dispatched a gold-adorned arrow toward the son of Subala.
O King, as that terrible arrow approached, Śakuni, the scorcher of his enemies,
who was skilled of hand and possessed of great strength, cut it into a hundred pieces.
When that [arrow] had fallen to the ground, O lord of the people, Bhīma became enraged.
As if laughing, he severed the bow of Saubala with a broad-headed arrow. Casting aside that broken bow, the powerful son of Subala swiftly took up another bow and sixteen broad-headed arrows.
O great king, with those straight-knotted broad-headed arrows,
he struck Bhīma’s charioteer with four and Bhīma himself with five;
with one he cut down the standard, and with two the umbrella, O lord of the people.
With four arrows, the son of Subala pierced the four horses;
then, O great king, your son, the lord of the earth, was delighted and said, "Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Slay Bhima with your sharp arrows!"
"This very one of wicked soul constantly oppresses us;
crush him, O mighty-armed one, and having slain him, be at peace.
Thereupon, O great king, the powerful Bhīmasena became enraged.
In that battle, he hurled an iron spear with a golden shaft;
released from Bhīma’s arm, it fell swiftly upon the chariot of the high-souled son of Subala, flickering like the tongue of a serpent.
Then, O lord of the people, assuming a furious form, he seized that very spear adorned with gold and hurled it at Bhīmasena. Bhīma, filled with supreme indignation, warded off that spear.
He released showers of arrows at all the vital spots of Śakuni;
that evil-minded son of Subala, afflicted by Bhīmasena’s shafts,
fell upon the seat of his chariot while all the kings looked on.
Having pierced the left arm of the high-souled Pāṇḍava,
it fell from there to the ground like lightning fallen from the sky.
Then, O great king, a cry was raised on all sides by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But Bhīma could not endure that lion-roar of those swift warriors;
quickly taking up his strung bow, O Indra among kings, that great car-warrior covered them with arrows in what seemed like a mere moment.
Having disregarded the army of Saubala in battle, that mighty hero,
O lord of the people, having slain his four horses and his charioteer as well, quickly cut down the standard with a broad-headed arrow, displaying his prowess.
Leaving his chariot whose horses had been slain, that best of men quickly stood firm,
stretching his bow with eyes red with rage and panting;
and with many arrows, O King, he assailed Bhīma from all sides.
But having repelled him with speed, the powerful Bhīmasena,
filled with rage, cut his bow asunder and pierced him with sharp arrows.
Thus deeply pierced by his mighty enemy, that crusher of foes—
Then, O lord of men, he fell to the ground with but little life remaining.
Then, O ruler of the people, perceiving him to be overwhelmed, your son carried him away from the field of battle on his chariot while Bhīmasena looked on.
When that tiger among men was stationed upon his chariot, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra turned their backs and fled in all directions, terrified by the great fear born of Bhīma,
O King, once the son of Subala had been defeated by the archer Bhīmasena.
Broken by great fear, your son Duryodhana fled on swift horses toward his maternal uncle, looking back with longing;
and seeing the king with his back turned, O Bhārata, the troops [followed suit].
Abandoning their duels on all sides,
they fled away; seeing all those great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side turning their backs,
Bhīma rushed toward them with speed, scattering many hundreds of arrows.
Being slaughtered by Bhīma, O King, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra turned their backs and,
having reached Karṇa in the battle, stood all around him;
for he, possessed of great heroism and immense strength, became their island of refuge.

O King, O tiger among men, just as sailors whose ship has been wrecked find relief upon reaching an island when their time comes, so too did your men, O bull of the Bharatas, find solace upon encountering Karṇa.
For those sinking in the bottomless depths, Karṇa then became an island; O King, having found refuge, they stood there, filled with mutual joy,
and gathered for battle, making death their only point of return.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Then, when the armies had been broken by Bhīmasena in battle,
what did Duryodhana say, or indeed what did the son of Subala say, O Sañjaya?"
Whether it be Karṇa, the best among victors, or my own warriors in battle— Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, the son of Droṇa, or even Duḥśāsana—
I consider this prowess of the son of Pāṇḍu to be most extraordinary.
That the son of Rādhā alone, in battle, exerted himself against all my warriors and fulfilled his vow toward those combatants—
Karna, the destroyer of enemies, has done this for all the Kurus as well.
"O Sañjaya, for all the Kurus and Yaudheyas, Karṇa— indeed the slayer of enemies— is their refuge, their armor, their foundation, and their hope for life.
Having seen that army shattered by the son of Kuntī of immeasurable splendor..."
What did Karṇa, the son of Rādhā and the charioteer’s son, do in battle? Or what did my invincible sons, or the kings who were great car-warriors, do?
Tell me all of this, for you are skilled, O Saṃjaya.
Saṃjaya said:
"O great king, in the afternoon, the powerful son of the Sūta slaughtered all the Somakas while Bhīmasena looked on."
The exceedingly powerful Bhīma also crushed the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons. Then Karṇa said to Śalya, "Lead me toward the Pāñcālas," having seen his own force being routed by the wise Bhīmasena.
Karna said to the charioteer, "Carry me toward the Panchalas alone.
Then Shalya, the King of Madra, possessed of great strength, urged on the swift white horses toward the Chedis, the Panchalas, and the Karushas.
Having entered that army, Śalya, the crusher of enemy forces,
joyfully guided the horses wherever he wished, for he was their leader.
That chariot resembled a cloud and was covered with tiger skins.
O lord of the people, upon seeing him, the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas were struck with terror.
Then, in that great battle, the roar of his chariot arose,
sounding like the thundering of a rain-cloud or like a mountain being split asunder.
Then Karna, with hundreds of sharp arrows drawn back to his ear,
struck the Pandava army by the hundreds and thousands.
As he was thus performing superhuman deeds in battle, [the Pandavas beheld him].
The great car-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas, those mighty archers,
surrounded him— namely Śikhaṇḍin, Bhīma, Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata,
Nakula, Sahadeva, the sons of Draupadī, and Sātyaki.

Desiring to kill the son of Rādhā, they surrounded him with showers of arrows. Then the heroic Sātyaki, that best of men, struck Karṇa in the battle on the region of the collarbone with twenty sharpened shafts.
Śikhaṇḍin pierced Karna in battle with twenty-five arrows, Dhṛṣṭadyumna with five,
the sons of Draupadī with sixty-four, Sahadeva with seven,
and Nakula with a hundred shafts.
But the mighty Bhīmasena, enraged in battle, pierced the son of Rādhā in the region of the collarbone with ninety straight-knotted arrows.
Then the son of Adhiratha, laughing, brandished his excellent bow.
The exceedingly powerful one released sharpened arrows, afflicting him;
Rādheya pierced each of those with five arrows.
Then that bull among men, having cut off Sātyaki’s bow and his standard, [proceeded].
Then he struck him between the breasts with nine arrows;
but Bhīmasena, enraged, pierced him with thirty shafts,
O Sire, and cut down Sahadeva’s standard with a broad-headed arrow.
The scorcher of foes struck the charioteer with three arrows,
and that bull among men deprived the sons of Draupadī of their chariots;
in the mere twinkling of an eye, it was like a marvel.
Having turned them all away with straight-jointed arrows,
that hero struck down the Pāñcālas and the great car-warriors of the Cedis.
O lord of the people, while being slaughtered in battle, the Cedis and Matsyas—
Rushing toward Karṇa alone, they assailed him with volleys of arrows;
but the great car-warrior, the son of the Sūta, struck them down with sharp shafts.
Terrified in battle, they fled like deer frightened by a lion.

Then, laughing, that hero conquered those Pāṇḍavas in battle. O Bhārata, I have witnessed this great marvel regarding Karṇa: how the powerful son of a Sūta, alone in the fray, [overcame] those heroes.
He fought in battle against those great car-warriors who were striving,
and he engaged those archers who were fighting with their utmost power.
O great king, he warded off the sons of Pāṇḍu with his arrows in battle. There, O Bhārata, all the gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis were delighted by the dexterity of the high-souled Karṇa.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, those great archers, honored that best of men,
Karṇa— the most excellent of chariot-warriors and the foremost of all bowmen.
Then, O Great King, Karṇa consumed the army of the enemy.
The solitary hero, the great archer, who swept away obstacles, crushed the advancing army of the Pañcālas with his sharp arrows,
like a great blazing fire kindled in the summer heat consumes a forest thicket.
Being slaughtered by Karṇa here and there, the Pāṇḍava troops fled in terror from the battle upon seeing the mighty Karṇa;
a great cry of distress arose there among the Pañcālas in that great conflict.
"Let them be slain by sharp arrows released from the excellent bow of Karṇa!
At that sound, the great army of the Pāṇḍavas was terrified;
there, the enemies perceived Karṇa alone as their warrior in battle.
There, the son of Rādhā, the crusher of enemies, performed a supreme marvel,
which all the Pāṇḍavas together were unable even to look upon;
it was like a torrent that, upon encountering a great mountain, is shattered to pieces.
In that same way, O King, the Pāṇḍava army, having encountered Karṇa,
was torn asunder; and Karṇa too, blazing like a smokeless fire in battle, stood consuming the great host of the Pāṇḍavas, O mighty-armed one.
And with his arrows, O great king, that hero swiftly severed the heads of the warriors— heads adorned with trembling earrings— as well as their ears, arms,
elephant tusks, sword hilts, swords, banners, spears, horses, and elephants.
O King, Karṇa, adhering to the vow of a warrior, cut into a hundred pieces various chariots, banners, fans, axles, shafts, yokes, traces, and diverse wheels.

There, O Bhārata, the earth became impassable, mired in flesh and blood by the elephants and horses slain by Karṇa; and both the uneven and the level ground was covered with the corpses of fallen horses and foot-soldiers.
Neither by chariots nor by elephants could anything be discerned;
the warriors could not distinguish their own from the enemy in that terrible darkness of arrows when Karṇa’s weapon had expanded.
O great king, those striving mahārathas among the sons of Pāṇḍu were repeatedly covered in battle by the gold-adorned arrows released from the bow of the son of Rādhā.
O great king, even as they strove, the great car-warriors were broken apart,
just as an enraged lion drives away herds of deer in the forest;
so did he put to flight the enemy, including the foremost chariot-warriors of the Pañcālas.
But the highly illustrious Karṇa, in that battle, drove those warriors here and there,
driving back that army like a wolf among herds of cattle;
and seeing the Pāṇḍava host with its backs turned, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [rejoiced].
Those great archers approached, uttering terrible cries;
for Duryodhana, O king of kings, filled with supreme joy,
being greatly delighted, caused various musical instruments to be played on all sides.
The Pāñcālas too, those great archers and best of men, though repeatedly broken,
returned to the fight like heroes who have made death their only means of retreat.
Against those heroes who had rallied in battle, the son of Rādhā, the scorcher of his enemies, [advanced].
O Great King, that bull among men shattered [the enemy] many times over.
There, O Bhārata, twenty Pāñcāla chariot-warriors were slain by Karṇa along with their mounts; out of wrath, more than a hundred Cedis were also destroyed.
O Bhārata, having rendered the floors of the chariots empty, the backs of the horses devoid of riders,
the shoulders of the elephants manless, and the foot-soldiers scattered in flight,
that scorcher of foes became as difficult to behold as the sun at midday.
The cruel son of the Sūta, possessing a body like that of Time the Destroyer, moved about.
O great king, having thus slain those men, horses, chariots, and elephants, the great archer Karṇa, the slayer of enemy hosts, stood firm.
Just as the mighty Time stands after having destroyed the hosts of living beings,
so did that great car-warrior stand alone after having slain the Somakas.
There we beheld the wonderful prowess of the Pāñcālas.
Even while being struck by Karṇa, they did not abandon the front of the battle:
King Duḥśāsana, Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat,
Aśvatthāman, Kṛtavarman, and Śakuni the son of Subala.
They slaughtered the Pāṇḍava army by the hundreds and thousands;
and the two sons of Karṇa, O Indra among kings, those brothers of true prowess,
being powerful, destroyed the Pañcālas here and there.
Then a fierce and great slaughter occurred in that battle;
likewise, the heroic Pāṇḍavas, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin,
and the sons of Draupadī, filled with rage, struck down your army.
"Thus did this destruction of the Pāṇḍavas occur here and there,
and likewise that of your own men in battle upon encountering the mighty Bhīma.
Saṃjaya said:
But Arjuna, O great king, having arrayed his army in various formations and seeing the son of the Suta highly incensed in that great battle,
Phalguna then struck down the Kaurava forces one by one.
Having witnessed the fury of the Sūta’s son in that great battle,
[the earth] was made a river of blood, carrying flesh, marrow,
and bones; it had human heads for its stones and elephants and horses for its banks.
It was strewn with heaps of heroes' bones and resounded with the cries of crows and vultures; it possessed parasols like swans and rafts, swept away the trees that were the warriors,
contained necklaces like lotus-pools, and was foamy with excellent turbans.
Equipped with bows, arrows, and banners, filled with men, beasts, and skulls, crowded with shields, armor, and whirlpools,
it was exceedingly difficult to cross for those seeking victory and utterly impassable for the timid.
Having brought that river to them, Bībhatsu, the slayer of enemy heroes,
addressed these words to Vāsudeva, O bull among men:
"O Kṛṣṇa, there is seen the banner of the Sūta’s son in battle."
"Moreover, Bhīmasena and these other great chariot-warriors are fighting [the enemy].
These Pāñcālas are fleeing, O Janārdana, terrified of Karṇa.
There is King Duryodhana with his radiant white umbrella."
Charging the Pāñcālas broken by Karṇa, he shines greatly;
and Kṛpa, Kṛtavarman, and the mighty son of Droṇa—
these, protected by the Sūta’s son, guard the king.
"If they are not slain by us, they will cause the Somakas to be slaughtered.
Here is Śalya, skilled in managing the reins, sitting upon the seat of the chariot;
O Kṛṣṇa, he looks most magnificent as he drives the chariot of the Sūta’s son."
Then this thought arose in me: "Drive this great chariot there;
I shall by no means return from the battle without having slain Karṇa. Otherwise, Rādheya [will slay] the Pārthas and the Sṛñjaya mahārathas."
"O Janārdana, you shall leave them without remainder in battle while we both look on.
Thus addressed by Pārtha, O King, Keśava, filled with haste,
then quickly set out toward your army with his chariot.
O King, at that great battle,
the mighty-armed Hari, having set out with Savyasācin against the great archer Karṇa in a single combat, proceeded swiftly on his chariot by the command of the Pāṇḍava.
Encouraging the Pāṇḍava armies on all sides with his very chariot,
the roar of that Pāṇḍava’s chariot resounded in battle like the thunderbolt of Vāsava or like a mighty torrent, O noble one.
Then, O noble one, the roar of that Pāṇḍava’s chariot arose like the crashing of mountains by the discharge of Vāsava’s weapon;
with that great sound of the chariot, the Pāṇḍava of true prowess [advanced].
Vijaya, whose nature is immeasurable, advanced against your army. Upon seeing him approaching with his white horses and Kṛṣṇa as his charioteer,
and beholding the banner of that high-souled one, the King of Madra spoke to Karṇa.
"Here comes that chariot with white horses and Kṛṣṇa as its charioteer, O Karṇa,
whom you are asking about— he who slays his enemies in battle. There stands the son of Kuntī, grasping his bow Gāṇḍīva."
If you slay him today, it will be for our supreme welfare.
O Karṇa, he comes seeking to seize you, striking down excellent chariot-warriors;
O son of Rādhā, go forth against that descendant of Bharata without faltering.
Casting aside his compassion and maintaining his composure while recollecting the weapon of Bhṛgu,
and remembering the application of sight and fist-strikes taught by Rāma,
Dhanañjaya, desiring victory, advanced against the great chariot-warriors.
In the science of horses, in battle, and in strength, Hari is no match for me;
O Karṇa, he will not defeat me, especially in a mace-duel.
My bowstring is adorned with the moon, stars, and sun as its banners, and is fitted with small bells.
"Behold, O Karṇa, this [standard] of Arjuna is like lightning in the sky. There,
upon the tip of Pārtha’s banner, the terrifying monkey is seen looking in all directions, increasing the fear of those who behold him."

This discus, mace, conch, and the Śārṅga bow of the Lord Kṛṣṇa are visible upon the chariot of the Pāṇḍava as he drives his horses. This is the Gāṇḍīva bow emitting its twang as it is drawn by Savyasācin.
These sharp arrows, released by those skilled with their hands, slay the enemies;
this earth is strewn with the heads of kings who did not flee, their faces resembling the full moon and their large, long, copper-hued eyes wide open.
These arms, resembling iron clubs and smeared with fragrant unguents,
are being struck down along with their weapons as they were raised by those intoxicated by battle;
likewise, horses have their tongues and eyes forced out by their riders in the heat of the fray.
Having fallen and being struck down,
these elephants from the Himalayas, resembling mountain peaks,
lie exhausted upon the earth; with their trunks severed by Pārtha, they fall like mountains.
These chariots, shaped like cities of the Gandharvas, with their lords slain,
fall down like the celestial palaces of the gods when their merit is exhausted;
behold the army utterly thrown into confusion by Kirīṭin.
Like a lion amidst thousands of various beasts,
this army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons is being torn asunder on all sides;
out of fear of Arjuna, who swiftly slaughters his many enemies, it flees in haste.
Avoiding all the troops, Dhanañjaya indeed hastens; I believe it is for your sake, judging by how his body is swelling with energy. For Pārtha, eager for battle, cannot be held back by anyone.
For, without you, while Vṛkodara was being tormented by the fire of his wrath,
and seeing Dharmarāja deprived of his chariot and severely wounded,
as well as Śikhaṇḍin, Sātyaki, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna the son of Pṛṣata— [he would have been overcome].
Having observed the sons of Draupadī, as well as Yudhāmanyu and Uttamaujas,
and the two brothers Nakula and Sahadeva,
Pārtha, the scorcher of foes, approaches you on a single chariot with his entire host.
With eyes red with rage, he is furious and desires to slay all archers;
he will undoubtedly charge at us in haste, abandoning his troops. O Karṇa, go against him yourself, for there is no other archer [capable of this].
I do not see anyone else in this world besides you who could hold back the enraged Arjuna in battle, just as the shore holds back the tide;
he who might restrain the furious Arjuna, who resembles the surging ocean, just as the shoreline resists the sea.
"I see no protection for him, neither from behind nor from the sides;
he advances against you all alone—behold the fulfillment of your own purpose! For you are capable of overcoming the two Kṛṣṇas in battle within this conflict."
"O son of Rādhā, this burden is yours; go forth against Dhanañjaya!
For you alone have been appointed by Bhīṣma, as well as by Droṇa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛpa—turn back that Pāṇḍava, the equal of Savyasācin."
"O Karna, ward off Savyasācin as he approaches in this great battle;
slay Dhananjaya, who is like a licking serpent, like a bellowing bull, and like a tiger poised to spring."

These great car-warriors of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s side, these lords of men, are fleeing swiftly in battle out of fear of Arjuna, showing no concern for one another. Indeed, among those who are thus fleeing in combat, there is no other man [who can stop them].
"O hero, son of a Sūta, there would be no one to remove this fear except for you.
All these Kurus, O tiger among men, having reached you as their island in this battle, stand here seeking refuge from you."
O Rādheya, summon that same fortitude with which you conquered the Vaidehas, Ambaṣṭhas, Kāmbojas, Nagnajits, and the Gāndhāras— those who are so difficult to defeat in battle—
and then go forth against the Pāṇḍava.
O mighty-armed one, standing firm in great manliness, go forth to meet Vāsudeva of the Vṛṣṇi clan, who is being cheered by Kirīṭin;
just as in the past, the great conquest of the quarters was achieved by you alone.

Having conquered the lord of Kaliṅga, you brought his queen here; likewise, having defeated Jarāsaṃdha, you brought Duryodhana’s queen. Relying on that very same courage, slay Dhanañjaya, the son of Pṛthā.
Karna said:
"O Shalya, you appear to me now as being established in your true nature and highly esteemed; O mighty-armed one, you seem to me even more fearless than Dhananjaya."
"Behold today the strength of my arms; behold also my training.
Alone today I shall slay the great army of the Pāṇḍavas, as well as those two tigers among men, the two Kṛṣṇas—I tell you this as the truth."
Without slaying those two heroes in battle, I shall not depart by any means;
either I shall sleep having been slain by them, for victory in battle is uncertain,
or else I shall have achieved my purpose, being either the slayer or the slain.
"Either slain I shall go, for victory in battle is never certain;
or, having accomplished my purpose, I shall depart, or being killed, I shall attain heaven.
Śalya said:
The great chariot-warriors declare this Karna, the foremost of car-fighters, to be invincible in battle;
how much more so when he is alone and protected by Krishna?
Who here would venture to conquer him?
Such a one has never before existed in the world; as far as we have heard, there has never been a superior chariot-warrior like him.
Today, while you look on, I shall slay that Dhananjaya in battle with full success;
I shall fight against such a son of Pṛthā as he.
Behold my prowess in this great battle:
this hero among chariot-warriors, the son of the Kuru king, moves upon his chariot drawn by swift horses.
"He will lead me into this distress today;
with the end of Karṇa, you all have reached your end. Thus spoke that hero among chariot-warriors as he approached the excellent chariots.
The prince of the Kauravas, with his swift horses,
will today swiftly lead me to my end;
even Karna would be capable of this at the conclusion of it.
The prince’s hands were free from sweat,
unwavering, calloused, and large; he was firm with weapons, skillful, and swift of hand.
There is no warrior equal to the son of Pāṇḍu;
having overwhelmed those many kings, he receives as if they were but one those arrows feathered with vulture plumes.
Those unerring arrows fall for the distance of a *krośa*;
what warrior on earth is his equal? Seizing and releasing [his weapons] in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Possessing prowess equal to that of Purandara himself,
their unerring arrows fall at a distance of one *krośa*;
there is no one who is the equal of the Pāṇḍava.
The prince [Arjuna] greatly pleased others with his bow,
while Keśava greatly pleased others in combat with the discus;
thus the son of Pāṇḍu gratified the sacrificial fire.
The energetic Kṛṣṇa, the second atiratha,
obtained the discus there, as did the high-souled Pāṇḍava Savyasācin, who received the bow Gāṇḍīva.
The mighty-armed one of undaunted spirit [mounted] a preeminent chariot yoked with white horses and endowed with a beautiful sound,
as well as two divine quivers of inexhaustible capacity.
And from the sacrificial fire, he obtained divine weapons;
with these, he slew the Daityas in Indra’s world, as well as all the innumerable Kālakeyas.
There he obtained the conch Devadatta;
who indeed on earth could surpass him?
And he also gratified Mahādeva.
Then, through direct and fair combat, that high-souled one obtained the most terrible Pāśupata,
the great weapon capable of destroying the three worlds.
The world-protectors, having gathered together individually,
gave him immeasurable weapons,
with which that lion among men swiftly slew those [enemies] in battle.
Having defeated all of us— the assembled Kālakhañja Asuras as well as those gathered in the city of Virāṭa— with but a single chariot;
He seized that wealth of cattle in the midst of the battle and took away the garments from the great chariot-warriors;
such was he, endowed with the quality of heroic prowess.
"I choose Kṛṣṇa as my second for battle; O Śalya, I know that he himself is the supreme challenge for all the world."
It is protected by Keśava of infinite prowess, by Nārāyaṇa the peerless;
its virtues cannot be recounted even in ten thousand years.
It is impossible for all the worlds combined to describe the greatness of the high-souled Viṣṇu, the victorious son of Vasudeva, who holds the conch, the discus, and the sword in his hands.
Fear and trembling indeed arise within me upon seeing the two Krishnas united on a single chariot;
for Partha is exceedingly superior to all archers in battle.
Nārāyaṇa is peerless in battle with the discus;
such are the Pāṇḍava and Vāsudeva. Indeed, you might move from your own country, but not these two Kṛṣṇas.
Karṇa said:
"What is the use of this description of the King of Madra and Arjuna?
Why do you try to frighten me today in battle, when I am vigilant?"
Indeed, you are not able to frighten me like a captive; rather, you praise his very virtues,
for that Phalguna is endowed with prowess in battle.
Just as Guptaka was slain today by Keśava in battle,
even so shall I slay him while you look on;
remain silent and urge on the horses for now.
Seeing the two Krishnas united on a single chariot,
great joy arises within me today;
for both are heroes, accomplished, and firm in their mastery of weapons.
These two great chariot-warriors, endowed with robust frames— such heroes among men, having met together,
