have fallen from their station, possessing the forms of divine youths.
Whether it be Agni and Anila, Indra and Bṛhaspati,
Yama and Antaka, or Śaśin and Pūṣan;
whether it be Bhaga, Aṃśa, Mitra, Varuṇa, or the two Aśvins.
Neither the hosts of Maruts nor the Vasus, together with Indra— whether acting individually or united— were able by force to conquer Arjuna and Acyuta in battle.
Such are Phalguna and Vāsudeva;
who else indeed, O Śalya, other than I, could withstand them?
But as for the desire that I have today, O Śalya—
O Lord of Madra, this battle against the Pāṇḍava will not take long; it shall happen quickly—
extraordinary, wonderful, and of incomparable form.
The fortune of all the Vṛṣṇi heroes is established in Kṛṣṇa;
the victory of all the sons of Pāṇḍu is established in Pārtha. Both those tigers among men stand upon the same chariot.
"O Śalya, it is truly well-born of me that I have these two as my adversaries;
indeed, before long, quickly drive this chariot of mine forward, and I shall attack them both."
"Behold, in this very moment, the two Kṛṣṇas have been slain!
Or else, let me be slain in battle by those two enemies! I shall either strike these two down in combat;"
"Either they will slay me today, O Kṛṣṇas," so saying to Śalya, Karṇa, the slayer of enemies,
roared in battle like a thundercloud.
"Behold, in this very moment, the two Kṛṣṇas have been struck down!
Either they shall be slain by me in battle, or I shall be slain by my enemies!
Speaking thus, that great car-warrior suddenly—
Then the Sūtaputra rushed toward the Pāṇḍava;
having approached, he was greeted by your son,
and having met with him, he spoke to the heroes of the Kurus.
Both the mighty-armed Kṛpa and Bhoja,
as well as the King of Gāndhāra along with his younger brother,
and the preceptor’s son as well as his own younger brother— these he addressed.
Then there were foot soldiers,
elephant-riders, and others; likewise, your son and the son of the preceptor [Droṇa] were there, along with infantry, elephant-riders, elephants, and chariots.
"By obstructing and charging at Acyuta and Arjuna from all sides,
quickly cause them both to be joined with exhaustion, so that they may be severely wounded by you."
"Today I shall slay these lords of the earth with ease.
Having said, "So be it," those most heroic warriors, desiring to kill Arjuna, rushed forward in haste.
And those great car-warriors, acting under Karna’s command, struck Dhananjaya with arrows in battle,
just as the great ocean of abundant waters swallows the rivers and streams.
In whatever manner Arjuna devoured them in battle,
he was not seen by his enemies as one who was aiming those excellent arrows, nor even as one releasing them.
Neither taking up his arrows, nor drawing them back,
nor releasing them could he be seen by his enemies; yet Dhananjaya was seen rending [the foe] with those very shafts.
Slain, men, horses,
and elephants fell before the beautiful circle of the Gāṇḍīva, which emitted rays of arrows and possessed a splendor like the sun at the end of a Yuga.
The Kauravas were unable to look upon his victory, just as people with diseased eyes cannot look upon the sun,
as he discharged those excellent arrows by means of the great chariot-warriors.
Laughing, Pārtha cut them down with showers of arrows;
moreover, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, drawing his bow into a full circle, struck those multitudes of shafts.
Just as the sun, possessing fierce rays and situated in the midst of pure white light,
easily draws away masses of water,
so too did Arjuna, having discharged his multitudes of arrows.
O lord of kings, he consumed your army;
Kṛpa, as well as Bhoja and your own son himself, rushed toward him while discharging arrows.
The great car-warrior, the son of Droṇa, covered him with arrows like clouds shrouding a mountain— desiring to slay the son of Pṛthā, whose prowess is irresistible.
Just as moths seek to destroy a great-flamed fire, so did those skilled warriors, with great effort, discharge their excellent arrows in that great battle against those who were already enraged.
The son of Pāṇḍu, acting with haste, cut them down with arrows;
he pierced him in the chest with three by three. He [Kṛtavarman], with the circle of his bow drawn wide by the Gāṇḍīva...
Scorching his enemies, Arjuna shone like the sun with his fierce rays of arrows; he appeared just like the sun situated between the months of Śuci and Śukra while surrounded by a halo.
Then the son of Droṇa pierced Dhanañjaya with ten foremost arrows, Acyuta with three,
his four horses with four, and likewise the ape with one.
He covered him with excellent iron arrows;
likewise, as he was quivering with his bow drawn,
[the other] struck off the head of the charioteer with three razor-sharp arrows.
With four arrows Dhananjaya struck down the horses, and with three the standard; he brought down the chariot of Drauni. Then that mighty one [struck] the bow of Drona’s son.
Having severed it with a broad-headed arrow, he caused it to fall.
Filled with rage, [he struck] that [bow], which was adorned with gold like a thunderbolt and possessed the luster of the coils of Takṣaka.
He took up another bow with a firm string,
like a preeminent great serpent descending from a mountain;
and having scattered his own weapons upon the ground, he stood there.
Having strung his bow, the one of superior merit,
the son of Droṇa, from close range pierced with excellent arrows those two best of men who were equal in their vehicles and unconquered.
Kṛpa, Bhoja, and likewise your son,
like clouds pouring rain upon one who dispels the darkness,
fell upon that bull among the Pāṇḍavas in battle with numerous arrows.
Great chariot-warriors, standing at the forefront of the battle,
possessed of great strength and free from fear on the field of combat— there,
O Pārtha, was Kṛpa with his bow and arrow.
With his arrows, he who possessed the prowess of a thousand arms struck the horses, the banner, and the charioteer,
just as the wielder of the thunderbolt once struck Bala.
In that great battle, his weapons having been struck down by the arrows of Pārtha and his banner crushed,
Kṛpa was held at bay by thousands of arrows.
Just as the son of Pṛthā first [acted] against your son with arrows,
so did he cut down the banner and the bow of the roaring one.
The powerful warrior then struck down Kṛtavarman’s beautiful horses and cut down his standard, along with its horses, driver, bow,
and banner.
Hurrying, he struck down elephants, horses, and chariots;
then that vast army of yours was scattered,
like a dam breached by water.
Then Keśava, with Arjuna’s chariot, quickly caused his enemies to turn away in distress;
then Dhananjaya proceeded with great haste.
Others, desiring to fight, pursued him with chariots well-yoked and their banners raised high, just as they had once pursued Śatakratu when he was slaying Vṛtra.
Then, having advanced and warded off those enemies,
the great car-warriors— Śikhaṇḍin, Sātyaki, and Yama’s son (Yudhiṣṭhira)— rushed toward Dhananjaya’s chariot with sharpened arrows.
Tearing [each other] apart, they let out a most terrifying roar;
then, filled with rage, they struck one another with arrows that were straight-flying and well-sharpened.
The Kuru heroes, together with the Sṛñjayas, fought like the gods of old fought against the foremost of the deities,
desiring victory and eager for the attainment of heaven.
Elephants, horses, and chariots fell, O scorcher of foes;
they roared loudly and struck each other with great force,
each shooting well-aimed arrows at the others individually.
O King, when the ten directions and the sky were shrouded in darkness by the arrows of those great-souled and preeminent warriors in that great battle against one another, they did not shine forth.
The radiance of the sun was shrouded in darkness,
and a blinding gloom of arrows was created by those great-souled ones;
then, afflicted by the shafts, the quarters of the sky did not shine forth.
Saṃjaya said:
O King, Dhananjaya, desiring to rescue the son of Kuntī who was being assailed by the foremost forces of the Kurus and was as if sinking, rushed toward Bhīma.
O Bhārata, having crushed the army of the Sūta’s son with his arrows,
Dhanañjaya dispatched the enemy heroes to the realm of death. Then, his nets of arrows covered the sky in every direction.
Others were likewise seen slaughtering your army;
filling the sky, which was frequented by flocks of birds, with his arrows,
O great king, Dhanañjaya became the destroyer of the Kurus.
Then, with broad-headed arrows, razor-sharp shafts, and stainless iron bolts,
Pārtha mangled their limbs and severed their heads.
With their bodies cut apart, divested of armor, and headless, they lay scattered on all sides.
The field was completely covered by warriors who had fallen and those still falling—
chariots, horses, men, and elephants struck by Dhanañjaya’s arrows;
it was strewn with those mangled, pierced, and shattered, their limbs and body parts severed.
O King, the field of battle became as difficult to traverse, as treacherous, and exceedingly terrible and hard to behold as the great Vaitaraṇī river;
it was covered with bodies, both those whose life-force had departed and those still possessing it.

The earth became strewn with chariots whose poles, wheels, and axles were broken, some deprived of horses and others still yoked to them; with chariots whose drivers were slain or whose drivers remained,
and with horses whose riders had perished or who were otherwise riderless.
The earth was strewn with chariots whose poles, wheels, and axles were shattered;
and there lay excellent, ever-maddened elephants, clad in golden armor and equipped with golden ornaments,
their riders still holding their positions.
Enraged, four hundred great warriors sent by their furious commanders advanced toward Arjuna; struck down by Kirīṭin with showers of arrows,
they fell like the peaks of a great mountain, complete with their living creatures, cast down.
The earth was strewn on all sides with excellent elephants resembling clouds and shedding rut-fluid, pierced by the arrows of Dhanañjaya;
Arjuna’s chariot advanced like the sun breaking through the clouds.
With slain elephants, men, and horses; with chariots shattered in many ways;
with weapons, banners, and armor cast aside; and with those once skilled in battle now deprived of life—the path was indeed strewn by Phalguna with their discarded weapons.

And he made the great Gāṇḍīva bow vibrate with a most terrible sound, like the horrific crash of a thunderbolt or the roar of a rain-cloud in the sky. Then the army, struck by Dhanañjaya’s arrows, was torn asunder.
Like a great ship tossed by a mighty wind upon the ocean,
your army was utterly consumed by arrows of various forms discharged from the Gāṇḍīva, which resembled blazing brands, firebrands, and thunderbolts.
Like a bamboo forest blazing at night upon a great mountain,
so did your vast army quiver, tormented by arrows;
crushed, scorched, and destroyed was your host by Kirīṭin.
Slain and struck down by arrows, fleeing in all directions like herds of deer in a great forest consumed by a forest fire,
the Kurus turned back, scorched by Savyasācin.

For when the mighty-armed Bhīmasena had been left behind in that battle, the entire Kuru army became agitated and turned its back in retreat. Then, while the Kurus were broken, the unconquered Bībhatsu—
Having approached Bhīmasena, he stayed with him for a moment. Having met with Bhīma and consulted with him, Phalguna informed him that Yudhiṣṭhira was free from arrows and his pain had ceased.
Then, permitted by Bhīmasena, Dhanañjaya set forth,
O Bhārata, making the earth and the sky resound with the roar of his chariot. Thereupon, he was surrounded by ten formidable bulls among enemies.

O Bhārata, Dhanañjaya was assailed by your younger sons, beginning with Duḥśāsana; those cruel men, with their bows drawn, seemed to dance as they struck him with arrows like firebrands against an elephant.
Madhusūdana, with his chariot, placed them to the left; for he considered them already dispatched to Yama by Kirīṭin. Then those heroes fled as Arjuna’s chariot turned its back upon them.
As they were charging, Pārtha swiftly struck down their banners, chariots, bows, and arrows with iron shafts and crescent-headed missiles; then,
with ten other broad-headed arrows, he felled their heads.
With eyes bloodshot with rage and lips bitten,
those faces shone upon the ground like clusters of stars in the sky;
then, with ten high-velocity broad-headed arrows (bhalla), he struck ten Kauravas.
Having pierced those adorned with golden armlets with gold-feathered arrows, the slayer of enemies advanced.
Sañjaya said:
As he proceeded on his swift horses, he whose banner bore the foremost of monkeys—
Ninety chariot-warriors of the Kurus,
those heroes who had taken terrible oaths regarding the world of Brahmā,
rushed forward for battle; those tigers among men surrounded Arjuna, that tiger among men, in the fray.

Kṛṣṇa dispatched white horses of great speed, adorned with golden ornaments and covered with nets of pearls, toward Karṇa’s chariot. Then Dhananjaya proceeded toward Karṇa’s chariot, slaying his enemies.
Striking with showers of arrows, the chariots of the Saṃśaptakas advanced;
but Arjuna, with his sharpened shafts, slew all those ninety rushing heroes along with their drivers, bows, and banners.
Slain by the various kinds of arrows discharged by Kirīṭin, they fell down like Siddhas with their celestial chariots falling from heaven upon the exhaustion of their merit.
Then, O best of the Kurus, the Kurus, along with their chariots, elephants, and horses, [were overwhelmed].
Immediately becoming enraged in the battle with a desire to slay their enemy,
they fearlessly advanced against Phalguna, the best of the Bharatas.
He was exerting himself, having released his weapons, and had raised up his excellent elephants.
Dhananjaya overwhelmed the great army of your sons; meanwhile, the Kuru great-archers covered the joy of the Kurus with spears, double-edged swords, iron clubs, darts, maces, scimitars, and arrows.

The son of Pāṇḍu dispersed that extensive shower of weapons raised by the Kurus with his arrows, just as the sun dispels darkness with its rays. Then the Mlecchas [advanced] with thirteen hundred rutting elephants standing ready.
At the command of your son, they struck Pārtha from the side;
with barbed arrows, reed-shafted shafts, iron bolts, lances, spears,
spikes, kampanas, and bhindipālas, they afflicted Pārtha as he stood upon his chariot.

Smiling, Phalguna cut down that shower of weapons discharged by the Yavanas mounted on elephants with sharp *bhalla* arrows and crescent-shaped shafts. Then, he struck all those elephants with great arrows of various forms.
Like mountains with their banners and riders, he shattered them as if with thunderbolts;
those great elephants, covered with gold-feathered arrows and adorned with golden garlands, fell slain like mountains ablaze with fire.
Then, O lord of the people, there arose the great roar of the Gāṇḍīva bow,
along with the sounds of men, elephants, and horses groaning and crying out.
And the elephants, being struck, O King, fled in every direction.
And horses, their riders slain, galloped in all ten directions; and chariots, O great king, deprived of both warriors and steeds,
were seen by the thousands like cities of the Gandharvas.
O Great King, horsemen were seen fleeing here and there,
while men, elephants, and horses were crying out and making distressing noises;
they were seen fallen right where they stood, struck down by the arrows of Pārtha.
At that moment, the strength of the Pāṇḍava’s arms was revealed,
as he alone conquered in battle the horsemen, elephants, and chariots;
and those [foes], O King, though unengaged, turned back toward the field of combat.
Men, *nāgas*, and chariots, roaring, rushed toward Arjuna. Then, O bull of the Bharata race, O King, Bhīmasena saw that the Diademed One (Arjuna) was surrounded by a great threefold force.
O King, leaving behind a few of your chariots that had survived the slaughter,
he rushed with speed toward the chariot of Dhanañjaya.
Then that army, mostly slain and distressed, fled away.
Seeing that Arjuna had gone toward his brother, Bhīma—
unperturbed and mace in hand— routed the high-speed horses that remained after being slain by Arjuna in that great battle.
O Bhārata, seeing Bhīma with mace in hand at that time, the Bhāratas thought him to have arrived like Death himself with staff in hand;
he was as exceedingly fierce as the Night of Doom, devouring men, elephants, and horses.
Then Bhīma swiftly hurled that most terrible mace, capable of shattering walls, towers, and city gates, against the men, elephants,
and horses, aiming specifically at each elephant, horse, and rider, O Bhārata.
O noble one, she struck down many horses and horsemen;
the Pāṇḍava, with his mace, crushed those men and horses clad in bronze and iron armor,
and they fell dead with a great noise.
In an instant, the enraged Bhīma sent them indeed to the abode of Yama.
Then he, who delights in battle, struck down the elephant division;
with his mace, he scattered them in the fray like Antaka himself bearing the staff.
O King, with ease, through their training and their strength, they slaughtered intoxicated elephants equipped with armor, along with their riders and banners;
those elephants looked magnificent even as they were being slain in the great battle.
Crying out loudly like winged mountains,
they fell swiftly upon the earth in battle, oppressed by Bhīmasena,
like mountains whose wings have been severed in due time by the thunderbolt.
Biting the earth with their teeth, they lie there drenched in blood;
their heads, bones, and feet shattered, they become food for the hosts of flesh-eaters—
those who feed on flesh and fat, now satiated by blood, meat, and marrow.
Even as she devoured bones, she stood there, as difficult to behold as the Night of Doom;
having slain ten thousand horses and many foot soldiers,
Bhima, enraged and mace in hand, rushed hither and thither.

Then, O Bhārata, seeing Bhīma with mace in hand, your warriors thought that the God of Death had arrived with his staff raised. Like an infuriated elephant in rut, the son of Pāṇḍu was filled with rage.
He entered the elephant division like a sea-monster entering the ocean. Having plunged into the elephant host and seized his great mace,
the enraged Bhīma in an instant sent them to the abode of Yama.
We beheld intoxicated elephants, clad in armor, accompanied by their riders and banners, falling like winged mountains. Having slaughtered that elephant division, the mighty Bhīmasena—
Mounting his own chariot once more, he followed behind Arjuna. O great king, the enemy host— mostly turned away in flight, demoralized, and slain— largely lay prostrate, still encased in their armor.
Seeing that army hesitating, lacking courage, and standing still,
Arjuna covered them with life-scorching arrows;
men, horses, chariots, and elephants were overwhelmed in battle by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Covered with volleys of arrows, they shone like *kadamba* trees with their filaments;
then, in that great battle, there arose the cry of distress from the Kurus as they were being slain by the hundreds with Arjuna’s sharp shafts.
As the lives of chariots, horses, and elephants were being taken by the arrows of Arjuna,
O great king, a great cry of distress arose among the Kurus upon seeing the shafts of the Diademed One (Kiritin) destroying men, horses, and elephants.
Uttering cries of "Alas! Alas! and huddling closely together, your army then whirled about like a circle of firebrands. Then that great battle of the Kurus took place.
For there was no chariot, rider, horse, or elephant there that remained unpierced;
then the vast army of the Kurus was utterly destroyed by arrows.
There was not a single chariot, steed, man, or elephant there that was not pierced through.

O best of the Bharatas, that army of yours, its armor shattered by arrows and drenched in its own blood, was set ablaze like a forest of blossoming *aśoka* trees. It was being slaughtered by sharp shafts.
Having encountered Phalguna, the scorcher of enemies, they did not abandon the battle;
there we beheld the wonderful prowess of the Kauravas,
O Lord, in that they did not desert Partha in the fray even while being slaughtered.
Seeing that prowess of Savyasācin there, all the Kurus became hopeless for Karṇa’s life;
indeed, the rain of arrows from Pārtha was unbearable in battle.
Realizing this, the Kurus turned back, defeated by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Abandoning Pārtha in the battle while being struck down by his arrows,
they fled in fear in all directions and cried out to the son of the Sūta.
Pārtha rushed toward them, scattering many hundreds of arrows,
gladdening the Pāṇḍava warriors led by Bhīmasena;
but your sons, O great king, fled toward the chariot of Karṇa.
Then, for those sinking into the bottomless depths, Karṇa became their island. For the Kurus, O great king, like venomless serpents,
sought refuge with Karṇa alone out of fear of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Just as all beings, O Bhārata, being afraid of death, take refuge in dharma— provided they have performed meritorious deeds—
so too, O lord of men, do your sons seek refuge with Karṇa, the great archer.
They huddled together out of fear of the high-souled Pāṇḍava.
To them—drenched in blood, fallen into perilous positions, and afflicted by arrows—Karṇa said, "Do not fear; indeed, [the enemy] is on my flank."
Seeing his army shattered by the might of Pārtha,
Karṇa stood there, stretching his bow with the intent to slay the enemy;
the invincible son of Adhiratha, having stretched his great bow.
Seeing those Kurus fleeing, Karṇa, the best among wielders of weapons,
reflected and set his mind on the slaughter of Pārtha, sighing heavily; then that bull-like son of Adhiratha drew his great bow.
As Savyasācin looked on, he charged once more against the Pāñcālas;
then, in an instant, the kings, their eyes resembling blood,
showered Karna with floods of arrows, just as clouds rain upon a mountain.

Like a great cloud covering a mountain with torrents of rain, he shrouded [the enemy] with showers of arrows. Then, O noble one, those thousands of arrows released by Karṇa deprived the Pāñcālas— foremost among those who possess life— of their lives.
He took away the lives of the Pāñcālas, just as the sun, the dispeller of darkness, takes away the gloom;

then, O lord of the people, a great battle ensued between the Pāñcālas— those slayers of enemies who fought for the sake of their allies— and the son of the Sūta, as they were being slaughtered by him.
08,060.001 Saṃjaya said: 08,060.001a Then, O King, when the Kurus had fled, Karṇa [advanced] with his chariot-fleet and his white horses.
The son of the Sūta scattered the sons of the Pañcālas with great arrows, like the wind dispersing masses of clouds; having struck down the charioteer from his chariot with the Añjalika weapon, he—
He slew Janamejaya’s horses,
and with broad-headed arrows he struck down Śatānīka and Sutasoma,
while also cutting their bows asunder.
Then he pierced Dhṛṣṭadyumna with six arrows and slew his right horse in the battle;
having killed Satyaki’s horses, the Sūta’s son—
When the prince was slain,
Ugradhanvā, the commander-in-chief of Kaikeya’s army, rushed toward Viśoka, the son of Kaikeya.
With arrows of extremely fierce velocity,
he deeply pierced Suṣeṇa, the son of Karṇa;
with three crescent-headed shafts (*ardhacandra*), he cut off [his arms].
Violently struck in the arms and the head, Karṇa fell from his chariot to the earth, lifeless,
like a *śāla* tree hewn down by axes.
Suṣeṇa, the son of Sūta, having slain the horse with straight-flying arrows, covered the hero of the Śini clan with sharpened shafts,
appearing as if he were dancing.
Struck by the arrows of Śaineya, Karna— his mind overwhelmed with rage at the death of his son— fell,
desiring to slay the bull of the Shinis.
Saying, "You are slain, O descendant of Śini!
he released an arrow capable of overcoming enemies;
Śikhaṇḍin cut that arrow of his asunder.
And with three by three arrows he struck Karṇa; having severed Śikhaṇḍin’s bow and standard with two shafts, he struck that well-born man.
The fierce one pierced Śikhaṇḍin with six arrows;
Dānta cut off the head of Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s son,
and then he struck Sutasoma with an arrow.
Then, O Bhārata, other hosts of Pāñcāla charioteers, difficult to shake, gathered together against that high-souled son of Adhiratha who was armed with a sharpened weapon.
For an echo indeed arises in the sky and vanishes; yet those who are preeminent in the bow are likewise preeminent on the chariot,
even as that tumultuous clamor rages on.
When Dhṛṣṭadyumna had been slain there, Kṛṣṇa said,
"O lion among kings, go, O Pārtha, so that the Pāñcāla line may no longer exist; slay Karṇa!"
Then, laughing, that hero among men, the mighty-armed one, desiring to protect them from fear, quickly approached the chariot of the son of Adhiratha with his own chariot.
Struck down by that leader of chariot-divisions, who,
having stretched the Gāṇḍīva bow of fierce sound,
struck it violently with his palm against the bowstring.
Suddenly creating a darkness with his arrows,
he struck down elephants, horses, chariots, and men;
the delighted parrots flew forth through the sky.
Birds fell from the mountain caves as the diadem-wearer,
expanding with his circular bowstring,
descended during the Raudra moment.
Bhimasena followed him on his chariot,
protecting that peerless hero, the Pandava, from behind;
those two princes, swift on their chariots, [proceeded].
While Karna and Yuyutsu were being pursued by the enemies,
the son of the Suta, crushing the Somakas, waged a great battle in that interval.
He struck down multitudes of chariots, horses, and elephants,
and covered the quarters with his arrows;
[so did] Uttamaujas and Janamejaya.
And the enraged Yudhamanyu and Śikhaṇḍin,
together with the son of Pṛṣata, roared as they struck Karna with arrows while pressing him hard.
Those five Pāñcāla chariot-warriors,
rushing toward Karṇa, the son of Vikartana,
were unable to dislodge him from his chariot despite their handsome forms.
With his arrows, he cut down their bows, banners, horses, and charioteers, as well as their quivers and pennants, as if his senses were mastered through fortitude.
With his arrows, he cut down their banners, horses, charioteers, pennants, quivers,
and bows; then he struck them with five shafts each.
Then Karṇa roared like a lion as he discharged and struck down those arrows,
his hand holding the bowstring and shafts amidst the thunderous twang of his bow.
"The earth, along with its mountains and trees, would be shattered"—
thinking thus, the people despaired.
With a bow resembling the rainbow of Śakra...
Discharging arrows with great intensity,
the son of Adhiratha shone in battle like the sun-god encircled by a halo, with its blazing circles of rays.
He pierced Śikhaṇḍin with twelve sharp arrows, then Uttamaujas with six,
and pierced Yudhāmanyu with three swift shafts.
O noble one, in that great battle, those five great car-warriors— the two sons of Somaka and Pārṣata— were defeated by three each at the hands of the Suta’s son.
Those crushers of enemies stood motionless,
like the objects of the senses when overcome by one who has mastered his self; then, as they were sinking into the ocean that was Karṇa, [the son of Subhadrā spoke].

Just as merchants whose ships have wrecked in the ocean might be rescued from the sea by means of boats, so did the sons of Draupadī rescue their maternal uncles from the ocean by means of well-prepared chariots.
Then the bull of the Śinis, having cut down the many arrows dispatched by Karṇa with his own sharp shafts,
pierced Karṇa himself with keen iron arrows.
Then Kṛpa, Bhoja, your son, and Karṇa himself struck your eldest son with eight sharpened arrows.
That best of the Yadus fought with those four,
just as the lord of the Daityas fought with the lords of the quarters; he held a bow that was drawn to its full extent and emitted a twanging sound.
With his bow drawn taut, raining down immeasurable showers of arrows,
that Sātyaki became utterly invincible,
like the sun situated in the midst of the sky.
Once again, having mounted their chariots and being well-armored,
those subduers of foes protected the hero of the Śinis.
Having come together in that great battle, the Pāñcāla chariot-warriors [stood guard].
Then there occurred an exceedingly fierce battle between your enemies and your soldiers, like that of the hosts of Maruts against Śakra in the subduing of his foes.
It was like the destruction of chariots, horses,
and elephants that occurred between the gods and the asuras in ancient times; chariots, elephants, cavalry, and even infantry were likewise destroyed.
Enveloped by various kinds of weapons, they wandered about;
struck down by one another, they stumbled, shrieked in agony, and fell lifeless.
When Bhīma had thus departed, your son,
the younger brother of the king, rushed after him scattering arrows; Vṛkodara then swiftly charged toward him.
Like a lion pouncing upon a great ruru deer, he rushed forward;
then there occurred between those two a superhuman battle, like two men gambling with their very lives as the stake.
With their mutual wrath firmly fixed upon one another,
like Śambara and Śakra in their fierce intensity, they struck with well-sharpened arrows capable of ending the body.
They struck each other violently,
like two great elephants in rut with minds possessed by passion, fighting over a female elephant.
Then, having observed those two looking at one another, Bhīma— both being equally brave and accompanied by their charioteers— said, "Go toward Duḥśāsana!"
"O Duḥśāsana, go toward Vṛkodara!
Impelled by their respective charioteers,
those two chariots suddenly met one another.
Armed with various weapons and bearing variegated banners and standards,
Bhīma was like Bala and Śakra in battle in the heavens of old.
"By good fortune, Duḥśāsana, you are seen today! You shall now repay the debt, together with its interest and principal— that which was long ago proclaimed by me to you in the assembly hall."
"Take from me [this wealth] by means of your touch upon Kṛṣṇā.
Thus addressed,
the high-souled hero Duḥśāsana then spoke these words.
I remember everything and do not forget it;
listen, Bhīmasena,
as I recount it, for I have long remembered my own origin.
When they dwell in houses made of lac for days and nights,
devoid of trust, wandering in search of prey,
they are everywhere rejected.
Remembering [the Dharma] day and night out of great fear, they are deprived of enjoyments and pleasures as they wander through forests and mountain caves.
Having entered the city of the King of Pañcāla,
you have entered into some kind of illusion,
since Phalguna has been chosen by Kṛṣṇā for you.
Having combined their evils, they then committed that ignoble deed consistent with the mother’s own nature;
she was seized by those five who had conspired together.
And while they were not feeling shame toward one another,
Sañjaya was summoned by the son of Subala into the assembly hall to recall [the events] there.
"You have been made slaves along with Kṛṣṇā.
Thus addressed by your son,
whose mind was so youthful, Vṛkodara also—
Then Vṛkodara, seizing his bow and knitting his brows upon his forehead, his eyes blazing with rage like copper, acted with haste toward your son.
With two razor-sharp arrows, he cut down both the bow and the standard;
with another feathered shaft, he pierced his forehead and struck off the charioteer’s head from his body.
Taking up another bow,
that prince struck Vṛkodara with twelve straight-flying arrows while he himself controlled the horses.
And he again showered Bhīma with arrows;
then [he discharged] an arrow radiant as the rays of the sun,
adorned with gold, diamonds, and the finest jewels.
He released [the weapon] that was as unbearable as the fall of Mahendra’s thunderbolt, capable of rending formidable limbs;
by it, Vṛkodara’s body was pierced through.
Felled with his body collapsing as if life had departed,
he stretched out his arms and clung to the excellent chariot; then, regaining consciousness once more, he let out a roar.
Saṃjaya said:
He encountered the fierce prince Duḥśāsana,
who had treated him with deceitful treachery.
There, Prince Duḥśāsana performed a difficult feat,
fighting in the tumultuous fray as he opposed Bhīmasena in battle.
Just as Jambha severed the bow of Śakra of noble prowess with a razor-sharp arrow, he likewise cut Bhīma’s bow and pierced his charioteer with six arrows.
Having done that, the swift prince pierced Bhīma with nine arrows,
and then he quickly struck him with many more.
The high-souled one [pierced] Bhīmasena with excellent arrows;
then the swift Bhīmasena, filled with rage,
hurled a fierce *śakti* at your son.
Seeing that most terrible weapon falling upon him like a blazing meteor, your high-souled son [faced it] with arrows drawn back to his ear.
The son [of Drona] cut [him] with ten arrows;
seeing that most difficult feat accomplished,
all the warriors, filled with joy, offered him their praise.
Then your son once again swiftly pierced Bhīma deeply with an arrow;
Bhīma, in turn, quickly grew enraged at him.
Beholding him with rage, he blazed up intensely:
"O hero, I have been pierced by you today most severely;
endure now, in turn, the blow of my mace!"
Having spoken thus loudly, Bhīma, filled with rage,
then seized his terrible mace for the sake of slaughter and said,
"Today, O evil-souled one, I am the one!"
"I shall drink your blood in the midst of the battle! When he had spoken thus, your son hurled with great force that fierce spear, which was like Death itself.
Whirling his most terrible mace, Bhīma, his form overwhelmed with rage, hurled it;
it suddenly shattered that spear.
He struck your son on the head in battle;
then Bhīma, seizing his bow capable of bearing great weight, pierced the prince.

With fifty volleys of arrows, he pierced him in the center of the chest, just as one might strike a lordly elephant with goads; then, being deeply pierced, that great-souled one was deprived of his chariot.
Duḥśāsana struck Bhīmasena in battle,
slew his four horses,
and having cut the chariot pole, he cast it down once more.
Then the high-souled Vṛkodara, descending from his vehicle and standing upon the ground, dispatched his horses to the abode of Yama with his mace.
As he was pulling the chariot of the prince,
Duḥśāsana leaped down from that chariot and hurled a javelin of fierce velocity.
Pierced in the chest by him, the immeasurable Bhīmasena, out of wrath, hurled an immeasurable mace at him. Then Bhīmasena performed [deeds].
Constantly recollecting all his sufferings and repeatedly calling to mind his formidable vow, the prince sat down.
Reflecting with extreme rage out of anger,
that hero among men seized [his weapon], which possessed a velocity equal to the thunderbolt of Indra, for thirteen years.
Then, with his hand, the mighty Vṛkodara, in a fury,
brought the mace down violently upon the surface of the earth and struck it repeatedly.
With his body severely beaten and mangled,
Duḥśāsana indeed fell to the ground,
having been trampled by the prince in battle at the throat.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he spoke to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Tell me, what were you searching for when you came here again after having defeated us?"
Today, I shall drink this honey from the vessel of your belly— the wrath that I have long accumulated and now intensely kindled.
Thus spoke the impetuous Bhīmasena,
crushing Duḥśāsana by the throat;
thereupon Bhīmasena committed a cruel deed.
Having frustrated him, that powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra suddenly rushed forward by force,
displaying his enmity toward the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Bhima rushed toward your son,
just as a lion cub repeatedly pursues a deer in the forest;
thus did the powerful one charge at the mighty foe.
Having seized him with supreme force and repeatedly lifting him up, the hero then swiftly dashed him against the ground.
He drew his stainless sword from its scabbard and,
assuming a most terrible form, seized the trembling man by the throat.
Then, tearing open the chest of the great car-warrior Duḥśāsana— the punisher of his enemies— he appeared like Time and Death themselves.
Like a rutting elephant discharging its ichor,
he hurled a mace at him in that tumultuous fray; with it, he struck him back ten *dhanus* away.
Bhīmasena forcibly struck Duḥśāsana with that [mace];
struck by that swift mace, Duḥśāsana fell down trembling.
O lord of men, his horses and charioteer were slain,
and his chariot was pulverized by the falling [weapon];
his armor, ornaments, garments, and garlands were shattered.
Seeing Duḥśāsana writhing, afflicted by intense agony, all the Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas were delighted and let out lion-like roars.
Having thrown him down, Vṛkodara then roared with joy, making the quarters resound;
by that roar, all those standing nearby—
O descendant of Ajamidha, they fell down in a state of swooning confusion;
seeing your son unconscious, Bhima, who stood nearby,
felt distress in his mind and fell into the deepest anxiety.
"How can I drink the blood of an enemy who is unconscious—
of this ignorant, evil-minded betrayer of friends?
While Bhīma was reflecting thus, he then beheld him lying senseless.
He fanned him with a garment, and by that means he regained consciousness.
Seeing that he had returned to his senses, Bhīma, acting with contempt, stepped upon his chest with his foot;
then, appearing joyful, he spoke to him.
Bhīma also, swiftly alighting from his vehicle,
impetuously rushed toward Duḥśāsana;
then the powerful Bhīmasena, remembering [his vow], acted with speed.
While that most terrible and tumultuous conflict, incited by your sons out of rivalry,
was proceeding on all sides with the preeminent warriors at its core;
O King, beholding Duḥśāsana there,
the mighty-armed Bhīma, whose deeds are inconceivable,
then remembered the seizing of the Queen’s hair.
And even after reflecting deeply, he inflicted sufferings upon her who was innocent, though she had turned away from her husband while in her menses and had stolen his garment.
Bhīma blazed with wrath and indignation like a sacrificial fire sprinkled with clarified butter;
there he spoke to Karṇa and Suyodhana.
I shall slay Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and Kṛtavarman, as well as the wicked Duḥśāsana today;
let all the warriors protect themselves this day.
Having spoken thus,
the exceedingly powerful and impetuous Vṛkodara, desiring to slay him, suddenly rushed forward, displaying such prowess in battle.
Just as a lion seizes a great elephant, that solitary hero subdued Duḥśāsana in the presence of Suyodhana and the son of Adhiratha.
Leaping down from the chariot, he went to the ground;
having fixed his gaze upon him with great effort,
the high-souled Bhīma then spoke to him.
"How could you have insulted Draupadī by seizing her hair? Tell us quickly how you did it— how you, being joyful, spoke of her as 'Gaurī' along with Karṇa and Suyodhana!"
"Having observed them, O evil-minded one,
I shall go today to where the leader of the clan is.
Having heard those most terrible words of Bhīma, [he was struck with fear].
Beholding Bhīma in this manner, Duḥśāsana then spoke to Bhīma with a smile,
while the Kauravas and the Somakas looked on.
May this excellent arm of mine be yours once more;
having observed that he was the one who seized your kingdom,
you deceived him by means of the fraud of dice when he was assembled there.
As you behold that afflicted noble one, he— by means of this—
is like the lord of serpents, capable of bestowing wealth like cattle and yet a giver of poison.
Bhīma has made all eighteen [divisions] eaters of alms; therefore, exert yourself against him.
As for that hand of yours which was used to seize Draupadī by the hair—
let Duḥśāsana be pointed out to me, O sinner; which one of them shall I tear out?
This hand, shaped like an elephant’s trunk, which crushes the breasts of amorous women,
is Sañjaya;
it is the giver of a thousand cows and the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas.
Having heard these words, Bhīmasena, the subduer of enemies and one who is exceedingly intolerant,
drew his sharp, well-edged sword and raised his right arm.

O evil-minded one, those locks of hair belonging to Yājñasenī, which were purified at the final purificatory bath of the Rājasūya sacrifice— having seized them by the throat, he stood there trembling.
"Tell me, Bhīmasena, as you are asked, with which hand were they dragged down by you in battle? Thus addressed,
he then spoke with wrath.
Turning her eyes toward Bhīma, she said:
"This hand, which resembles the trunk of an elephant, which crushes full breasts,
which is the giver of thousands of cows, and which is the end-maker of Kṣatriyas— "
"O Bhīma, by him my hair was seized from Yājñasenī while the leaders of the Kurus and you, the members of the assembly, were looking on.
Having heard this, that son of a king—
As he was speaking thus in the battle, Bhīma forcibly seized his arm with both his own arms, pressed him against his chest,
and then roared loudly at all the warriors.
He said: "Let him who possesses both strength and noble lineage protect Duḥśāsana today as he is about to give up his life, now that his arms have been cast down."
O King, having swiftly seized that mighty warrior by the hand with his own hand in the heat of battle, the enraged hero suddenly tore him up.
In the midst of those heroes, he struck Duḥśāsana with [a weapon] resembling a thunderbolt;
having torn open the chest of him who had fallen upon the earth, [he drank his blood].
Then, O King, he drank his warm blood;
having struck him down and severed the head of your son with that sword.
Desiring to fulfill his vow,
the wise Bhīma drank his warm blood,
tasting it again and again while looking upon him.
Greatly incensed, he spoke these words:
"Of my mother’s breast-milk, or of honey and clarified butter, or of the drinking of refined honey-wine— [none of these can compare to this]."
Or from drinking the essence of divine water;
or from the foremost products churned from milk and curds;
or from whatever other drinks exist in the world.
This flavor is superior to all others— superior to those juices as sweet as nectar and ambrosia, and likewise to the charming essence of sugarcane.
"Today my blood has been shed by him," said Bhīma,
whose mind was overwhelmed with rage, as he addressed Duḥśāsana once more, that man of fierce deeds.
Seeing him lifeless, he laughed with a loud voice and said, "What indeed can I do? You have been spared by Death.
As he was speaking thus, the other rushed forward again.
Those who then beheld Bhīmasena leaping about with extreme joy after tasting his victory,
were themselves distressed by fear and fell down.
And those men who had not fallen there,
the weapons fell from their hands,
and out of fear they cried out loudly.
And those who had seen Bhīma there on all sides drinking that blood of the son of Duḥśāsana beheld it with eyes closed.
Overcome by fear, they all fled,
saying, "This is no human being!"—
thus spoke Saṃjaya.
Having drunk his blood and grasped his feet, O Bhārata,
when that form had been assumed by Bhīmasena and he saw that blood being consumed, [he was struck with wonder].
Afflicted by fear, they fled together with Citrasena, crying out to the Rakṣasa Bhīma;
Yudhāmanyu [pursued] the fleeing Citrasena.
The prince advanced against that great host and,
free from fear, pierced him with seven sharp, swiftly discharged arrows.
Treading upon him like a snake, the great serpent-like warrior, hissing and wishing to discharge the poison of his wrath,
turned back and pierced the son of Pañcāla.
With three arrows he also pierced the charioteer;
then, with an arrow that was well-feathered, well-jointed, and possessed of a very sharp point, the hero—
With an arrow drawn back to his ear and released with perfect concentration,
Yudhāmanyu struck off his head;
when his brother Citrasena had been slain, [the others fled].
Enraged and displaying his prowess, Karṇa rushed against that army of the Pāṇḍavas; he of immeasurable energy was then countered by Nakula.
Bhīma, having slain the intolerant Duḥśāsana right there,
filled his cupped hands once more with blood and, with a fierce roar,
spoke these words while the world’s heroes were listening:
Thus Vṛkodara, dancing about, spoke these words aloud:
"O lowest of men, here I drink the blood from your throat!
Speak now, you who are so enraged: 'Cow! Cow!'"
"Those who then dance before us, crying out again and again, 'O cow! O cow!', we dance back at them, crying out again and again, 'O cow! O cow!
[Yet] our bed is upon the edge of the abyss, and our food is the *kālakūṭa* poison."
The painful biting by serpents, the burning in the house of lac,
the loss of the kingdom through gambling, the dwelling in the forest,
and the most cruel seizing of Draupadī’s hair.
The weapons and missiles [used] in battles, the hardships within the household,
and the various kinds of suffering we endured in Virāṭa’s palace—
all this was due to the counsel of Śakuni Dhārtarāṣṭra and the son of Rādhā.

The sufferings we have experienced—you alone are indeed their cause. We know these things to be nothing but suffering; we have never known happiness, always due to the wickedness of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his sons.
"O King, having spoken these words, 'We have undoubtedly obtained these pleasures,' Vṛkodara, having achieved victory,
spoke again with a smile to Keśava and Arjuna, O Great King."
Smeared with blood, his mouth dripping gore,
Bhīmasena was exceedingly enraged and impetuous; then that great-souled one had his limbs drenched in blood.
With mace in hand, like Death himself at the time of the end,
terrifying the army of your sons,
he runs here and there across your host.
Then, O Bhārata, in an instant that most terrible battlefield of the Kurus became empty,
where Bhīmasena had drunk [the blood] in the midst of the fray.
Blazing with rage,
O King, having slain the mighty prince Duḥśāsana in battle, he—
his desires fulfilled and fierce with pride— was like a lion that has killed a rutting ruru deer.
Drenched in blood, O Great King, that scorcher of foes shone most brilliantly;
like a *kiṃśuka* tree in flower, he appeared even more red than red. With his body wet with blood, the terrible one, filled with rage, O King, spoke these words.
"Speak now, O evil-minded one, O cruel man, for you have fallen! Speak now, O evil-minded one, O cruel man;
for you are no longer the son of Drupada."
"O heroes, whatever was promised by me in battle regarding Duḥśāsana has indeed all been accomplished here today;
this very day I shall give you another second boon."
Having slaughtered Duryodhana like a sacrificial animal and having crushed the head of that evil-minded one with my foot,
I shall obtain peace in the presence of the Kauravas.
She who was without a husband has indeed become one with a husband;
those who were co-wives have become wives without rivals.
Let them behold the wondrous variety that exists in this world.
Those very sesame seeds that once grew in clusters,
if they have been processed and have passed away, what indeed is the wonder in this world of living beings?
Having spoken these words,
the exceedingly powerful and high-souled one, his limbs drenched in blood, rejoiced, roared loudly, and danced.
Just as the thousand-eyed Indra after slaying Vṛtra,
he beheld him dancing with a fierce form,
like Time itself at the end of all beings.
A great fear entered the son of Adhiratha, and your sons lost all hope of victory. Sañjaya said:
When Duḥśāsana had been slain, O King, ten of your sons— those great car-warriors,
heroes of immense prowess who never retreat in battle, and whose wrath was like a potent poison—
shrouded Bhīma with their arrows.
Kavacin, Niṣaṅgin, Pāśin, Daṇḍadhāra, Dhanurdhara,
Alolupa, Śala, Saṃdha, Vātavega, and Suvarcas—
these, having come together in a group, were emaciated by the calamity that had befallen their brother.
They obstructed the mighty-armed Bhīmasena with their arrows. Being hemmed in on all sides by those great car-warriors with their shafts,
Bhīma, his eyes bloodshot with rage, appeared like the wrathful God of Death himself.
Then, O King, Vṛkodara was surrounded by nine of your sons, the younger brothers of Duḥśāsana, who were harassers of their enemies;
but he [pierced] them with ten sharp, high-velocity broad-headed arrows each.
Arjuna, adorned with golden armlets, dispatched him to the abode of Yama with gold-feathered arrows.
When those heroes had been slain, your army fled in terror,
afflicted by fear of the Pāṇḍava, even as the Sūta’s son looked on.
Then, O great king, Karna entered the great battle,
having witnessed Bhīma’s prowess as if it were that of Death among living beings. But Śalya, the ornament of assemblies, who was cognizant of his outward appearance and inner state—
The subduer of enemies spoke these words to Karṇa at the opportune moment:
"Do not give way to distress, O son of Rādhā; this is not worthy of you.
These kings are fleeing, afflicted by the fear of Bhīmasena."

And Duryodhana was utterly bewildered, pained by the calamity that had befallen his brother; while the blood of Duḥśāsana was being drunk by the high-souled one, they were all deprived of their senses, their wrath overcome by grief.
Kṛpa and the others, along with the surviving brothers of Karṇa, were sitting on every side surrounding Duryodhana; meanwhile,
the Pāṇḍavas, led by Dhanañjaya, had achieved their aim.
The heroes have stood facing you alone for the sake of battle. Therefore,
O tiger among men, established in great manliness and placing the duty of a Kṣatriya before you, go forth against Dhanañjaya.
For the entire burden has been placed upon you by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
bear it, O mighty-armed one, according to your power and according to your strength.
In victory there would be great fame, and in defeat, heaven is certain.

"O son of Rādhā, your son Vṛṣasena, filled with rage while you were overcome by delusion, is charging against the Pāṇḍavas. Having heard these words of Śalya, who possesses immeasurable splendor, [Kṛṣṇa spoke].
In his heart, he formed a firm human resolve for battle. Then, filled with rage, Vṛṣasena rushed toward his enemy-slaying foe who was stationed upon his own chariot.
Vṛkodara, like Time itself with staff raised,
mace in hand, crushing your men—
Bhīma, the subduer of enemies, was advancing.
As he advanced fiercely, scattering arrows like the gaping-mouthed God of Death rushing forward,
the heroic Nakula charged at him.
In that battle, Jiṣṇu, desiring to slay Karṇa’s son who was exultant, pierced his enemy with arrows out of wrath,
just as Maghavan struck Jambha.
Then the heroic Nakula, with a razor-sharp arrow, cut down the standard— adorned with crystal and variegated conch shells—
and the beautiful bow of Karṇa’s son.
Then, taking up another bow very swiftly, the son of Karṇa pierced the Pāṇḍava with a broad-headed arrow bound with bands of Jāmbūnada gold.
Desiring to take vengeance for Duḥśāsana, that great archer Nakula struck him with divine and mighty weapons;
then the high-souled Nakula became enraged at him.
With arrows resembling great meteors,
he pierced him, and Karna’s son, skilled in weapons, likewise struck Nakula with divine missiles.
O King, from the impact of the arrows, from his own wrath,
and from the power of the *bhāsa* weapon itself,
the son of Karṇa blazed up excessively.
O King, Karṇa’s son, like a blazing fire fed by oblations of clarified butter, destroyed all of Nakula’s horses with his supreme weapons.
O hero among the Bharatas, there was then a most terrible battle between Karṇa, the whisperer, and the Pāṇḍava;
[the Pāṇḍava] [felled] the beautiful, white steeds of the delicate one born in Vanāyu.
The hero, the son of the Suta’s son, slew Nakula’s swift horses, which were adorned with gold,
upon the field of battle.
Then, descending from the vehicle whose horses had been slain,
he took up a beautiful shield marked with eight moons and grasped a sword as bright as the sky.
Floating like a bird,
he moved through the sky, traversing various paths and cutting down the courses of the best of men, horses, and elephants.
Then Nakula, acting with great speed, dispatched two thousand of his winged followers to Yama;
they fell to the earth, slaughtered by his sword.
Just as in the horse-sacrifice there were two thousand animals known to the slaughterers— men from various lands, well-supported, skilled in battle, and true to their word.
They were swiftly cut down by that single mongoose, like choice sandalwood trees sought after for their heartwood;
then, as Nakula was rushing toward him, he [the elephant] charged at him.
The son of Karṇa, suddenly rushing forward in battle, pierced him from all sides with many sharpened arrows, desiring to kill him who sought to slay him.
As Nakula moved upon the ground, those standing on their chariots surrounded him from all sides and assailed him with arrows;
being thus pierced by those shafts, Nakula—
He pierced the hero; being thus pierced,
the high-souled one, though protected by his brother Bhīma against great danger, became enraged and wrought a terrible deed there.
The son of Karṇa [beheld] him alone, scattering the foremost of men,
horses, elephants, and chariots,
as he sported with eighteen arrows.
He pierced the hero, who, being thus pierced, became enraged; O King, that powerful warrior was struck very deeply by Vṛṣasena in that great battle.
Then, desiring to slay him, that hero among men, the son of Pāṇḍu, rushed forward in battle against the son of Karṇa,
who was suddenly swooping down like a bird spreading its wings.
Just as one might scatter a hawk greedy for meat in the fray,
Vṛṣasena then covered Nakula of noble prowess with sharp arrows.
Rendering those showers of arrows futile,
he moved through various beautiful paths;
then, O lord of men, as he moved swiftly—
In that great battle, the son of Karṇa pierced Nakula’s variegated shield, adorned with a thousand stars, with his arrows, while Nakula struck back with his sword.
He [wielded] a sharp-edged, keenly whetted iron sword,
unsheathed, capable of bearing a heavy burden, most terrible, and the destroyer of the bodies of enemies.
As he brandished it like a serpent of fierce form,
the subduer of enemies swiftly cut that sword with six sharp, keen-edged arrows.
And again, with sharp yellow arrows,
he pierced him deeply in the center of the chest;
having performed that difficult feat beloved by the noble ones.
O King, scorched by arrows, the high-souled Nakula, having performed his duty in battle against other men, proceeded to the chariot of Bhīmasena.
His horses having been slain,
the son of Mādrī, tormented by the son of Karṇa,
leaped onto Bhīmasena’s chariot like a lion onto a mountain peak.
While Dhanañjaya was looking on,
he destroyed Bhīmasena’s chariot and indeed rained down a most terrible shower of arrows.
Then the high-souled hero Vṛṣasena, filled with rage,
rained down a net of arrows upon those two great car-warriors who had come together upon a single chariot.
As if piercing the two sons of Pāṇḍu with arrows,
when that chariot of the Pāṇḍava had been destroyed and his sword swiftly cut to pieces by shafts;
Enraged at Vṛṣasena, Bhīma and Arjuna rained down a most terrible shower of arrows;
then the son of the Wind-god spoke to Phalguna.
"Behold this mongoose as it torments him; and here is the son of Karṇa harassing us. Therefore, you must go forth against the son of Karṇa."
Having heard those words, Kirīṭin (Arjuna) approached the chariot of Vṛkodara,
which bore the banner of the monkey and was held by Keśava.
The fierce one urged his chariot toward Vṛṣasena;
then, perceiving Nakula to be without a bow, sword,
or chariot, afflicted by the enemy's arrows, and shattered by the weapons of Karṇa’s son—
With banners shaken by the wind, resounding with the prancing of their horses, and guided by excellent charioteers,
those chariots moved swiftly—
the five most eminent sons of Drupada, with the descendant of Śini as the sixth.
And the five sons of Drupada’s daughter, the subduers of enemies, bearing their weapons,
slaughtered your elephants, chariots,
men, and horses with arrows resembling the lords of serpents.
Then the foremost of your chariot-warriors rushed forward in haste against them:
the son of Hṛdika, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, and Duryodhana;
as well as Śakuni, Śuka, Vṛka, Krātha, and Devāvṛdha.
With chariots possessing the roar of elephants and clouds, and with bows,
those foremost among the best of men struck those eleven heroes with excellent,
choice, and supreme arrows and hemmed them in.
The Kuṇindas advanced against them with elephants of terrible speed, resembling mountain peaks and the color of fresh rain clouds—
well-equipped Himalayan beasts, fierce with rut.
Covered with golden nets by skillful warriors eager for battle, the elephants shone like clouds accompanied by lightning.
The son of Kuṇinda, with ten arrows made of great steel, severely afflicted Kṛpa along with his charioteer and horses;
then he was struck by the arrows of Śaradvat’s son.
Together with the elephant, he fell to the earth;
but the younger son of Kuṇinda struck him with iron *tomara* spears that resembled the rays of the sun.
Having shaken his chariot, he roared aloud;
then the lord of the Gāndhāras struck off his head.
When those Kuṇindas had thus been slain, [the battle continued].
Those great chariot-warriors of yours, appearing exceedingly joyful,
blew their conchs born of the salt waters with great force;
and with bows in hand, they advanced against the enemies.
Then there occurred once more an exceedingly fierce battle between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍus and Sṛñjayas,
with arrows, swords, spears, double-edged blades, maces, and axes.
Then, as men, horses, and elephants— slayers of one another— were thrown into great turmoil, chariots, horses, elephants,
and foot-soldiers fell upon the earth, struck down by each other.
Like clouds accompanied by lightning and thunder,
driven from all directions by fierce winds,
those great elephants were then struck down by Śatānīka.
Likewise, he struck down your chariots and throngs of infantry;
the Bhoja king slew the horses, and elephants fell,
their limbs severed by Kṛtavarman’s weapons.
Then other elephants, struck by the arrows of Droṇa’s son,
fell lifeless upon the earth, having been cast down along with their weapons, warriors, and banners.
Just as great mountains struck by a thunderbolt,
he— immediately following the younger brother of the King of Kuṇinda—
struck him between the breasts with excellent arrows.
His son pierced the body of his [the opponent's] son with sharp arrows, as well as that elephant;
that king of elephants, together with the prince—
Blood flowed profusely from him in all directions as he fell,
like a mountain of red chalk discharging water during the rainy season when struck by Indra’s thunderbolt.
The king of Aparāntaka, dispatched by the son of Kuṇinda,
struck down Śuka along with his charioteer, horses, and chariot;
then Krātha fell, pierced by arrows.
Like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, the lord of Kratha—
the invincible one— fell, his charioteer slain by arrows from the mountain-born [Durmukha] as he stood upon his elephant.
The arrow, released by Savājisūta, fell like a great tree struck down by a mighty wind;
Vṛka [struck] him who was mounted on an elephant and dwelling upon the king of mountains.
He pierced him violently with twelve arrows;
then, acting with haste, he struck down Vṛka— along with his horse and chariot— of great speed, with four arrows to his feet.
That king of the *nāgas*, along with his driver, fell down,
severely struck by the arrows discharged by Babhru,
at the place where the mighty Vṛka was stationed.
Struck by that preeminent elephant, the valiant one pierced it in return with twelve feathered arrows;
hit by those shafts, Vṛka fell to the earth.
Then that elephant [was struck] along with Babhru’s son by another son of the King of Kuṇinda,
Devāpṛthu [or Devāvṛdha], with his own elephant.
He [Sahadeva] afflicted him,
and that son of Devāvṛdha, being thus tormented and struck down by the son of Sahadeva, fell.
With his trunk as a goad,
the King of Kuṇinda led the elephant— who struck the enemy’s limbs— to the abode of Vaivasvata in battle to slay Śakuni.
He advanced with great speed, severely afflicting him;
then the lord of the Gāndhāras struck off his head. Thereupon, the great elephants were slain by Śatānīka.
Your horses, chariots,
and throngs of foot soldiers fell to the earth helpless and shattered, like trees struck down by the wind from Garuda’s wings.
Then, smiling, the son of Kuṇinda pierced the son of Nakula with many sharp arrows;
thereupon, the son of Nakula cut away his body [from the trunk].
Then, with a razor-sharp arrow, he struck the head of Śatānīka, whose face resembled a lotus; the son of Karṇa pierced Arjuna with three keen shafts.
With three arrows he struck Bhīma, with seven Nakula,
and with twelve shafts Janārdana;
such was the deed of him whose actions transcend those of men.
Having observed this, the Kurus were delighted and honored him;
for they, who knew Dhananjaya’s prowess,
considered that he had already been offered as a sacrifice into the fire.
Then Kirīṭin, the slayer of enemy heroes,
beholding that foremost of men, Nakula the son of Mādrī, whose horses had been slain in the midst of the world, [acted].
Beholding Kṛṣṇa severely wounded,
he rushed at Vṛṣasena in the battle,
as the latter stood then in front of the Sūta’s son.
As that fierce hero among men,
bearing thousands of arrows, was charging forward in the great battle with terrible form and speed—
The great car-warrior, the son of Karṇa, rushed against the best of the Kurus, who possessed a thousand streams of arrows,
just as Namuci once rushed against Indra in ancient times.
There in the battle, those two heroic great chariot-warriors, like elephants among men, facing one another,
discharged numerous volleys of arrows.
Then, appearing utterly bewildered,
the son of the Sūta’s son pierced Pārtha with one hundred and one wonderful arrows.
The one of great majesty let out a roar,
just as Namuci once roared after piercing Śakra;
again, Vṛṣasena [assailed] Pārtha with fierce [shafts].
He pierced him in the middle of the upper arms with arrows,
and likewise struck Kṛṣṇa with nine;
then he again struck Pārtha with ten sharp-pointed shafts.
Previously, having been pierced by Vṛṣasena with those arrows of great velocity, the white-horsed one was only slightly incited to fury for the sake of slaying him.
Then the son of Karṇa set his mind [on Arjuna];
thereafter, Kirīṭin, out of anger at the head of the battle,
knit his eyebrows into three lines upon his forehead.
The high-souled one, whose eyes were blood-red and who was the slayer of the enemy Antaka, swiftly released his arrows in battle, intent on the slaughter of Karṇa’s son.
Then, smiling broadly, he spoke to Karṇa,
Duryodhana, and all those headed by the son of Droṇa:
"I [shall slay] that fierce Vṛṣasena in battle."
O Karṇa, as you look on today in battle,
I shall send you to the world of Yama with my sharpened arrows,
even as the people describe it.
"All of you have slain this son of mine;
he was a single, swift chariot-warrior deprived of me. I shall slay him in your very presence."
"Let this son of yours, who is stationed on his chariot, be protected;
I shall slay this Vṛṣasena first,
and afterwards I will kill you as well when you are utterly bewildered."
"O Arjuna, today in the midst of battle, I shall slay that very root of this strife,
whose pride was born from his reliance upon Duryodhana."
"Today in battle, I shall forcibly slay you;
Bhīmasena himself shall be the slayer of this Duryodhana, the lowest of men, in combat."
"By whose misconduct this great destruction has occurred"—
having spoken thus and having wiped his bow,
he made Vṛṣasena his target in the battle.
The high-souled one released sharp-pointed arrows for the sake of slaying the Suta’s son in battle, O King,
and he pierced him with ten shafts.
Without hesitation at the vital points, Kirīṭin violently severed his bow and both arms,
and with four fierce razor-sharp arrows, he cut off his head as well.
Struck by Pārtha’s arrows, he fell from his chariot to the earth with outstretched arms and severed head—
like a massive tree in full bloom shedding its leaves.
Seeing his son, struck by arrows, falling from the chariot like a *śāla* tree blown down from a mountain peak by the wind, the son of a charioteer acted with swift resolve.
Tormented by the slaughter of his son, Sañjaya swiftly went by chariot toward the chariot of Kirīṭin with great speed.
Beholding him approaching like the ocean overflowing its shores—
roaring, possessed of a massive body, and difficult to restrain even by the gods—
the descendant of Daśārha, that bull among men, laughed and spoke to Arjuna.
"Behold, that chariot approaches with white horses and Śalya as its charioteer, with whom you must fight; be steadfast, O Dhanañjaya! Look, O Pāṇḍava, at this chariot of Karṇa, now fully prepared."
Yoked with white horses and joined by the son of Rādhā,
it was crowded with various banners and garlanded with networks of tiny bells;
it was like a celestial chariot being carried through the sky by pale steeds.
And behold the banner of the high-souled Karṇa, featuring an elephant’s girth,
resembling the bow of Indra and as if scraping the very sky.
Behold Karṇa approaching, desiring to do what is pleasing to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Releasing showers of arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of rain—
this is the King of Madra stationed at the front of the chariot,
restraining the horses of this son of Rādhā, who possesses immeasurable prowess.
Listen to the roar of the kettledrums and the harsh sound of the conchs;
O Pāṇḍava, listen everywhere to the various lion-roars,
which have drowned out all other great sounds by the immeasurable splendor of Karṇa.
Hear the sound of the bow being violently shaken;
these great car-warriors of the Pāñcālas, along with their hosts,
are being torn asunder like deer in the great forest upon seeing an enraged lion.
O Kaunteya, you ought to slay the son of the Sūta with every effort;
for no one else, O sinless one, is able to withstand the arrows of Karṇa—
not even the three worlds, including the gods, Asuras, and Gandharvas, along with all things mobile and immobile.
For it is well known to me that you are indeed capable of conquering in battle Bhīma,
the fierce Mahādeva, the three-eyed Śarva with matted hair;
yet you were not able even to look upon that Lord, much less to fight him.

By you, O Pārtha, Mahādeva himself— Śiva, the source of auspiciousness for all beings, the immovable Sthāṇu— was propitiated through battle, as were the gods who grant boons; it is by the grace of that trident-bearing God of gods that this has come to pass.
"O mighty-armed one, slay Karṇa, just as the slayer of Vṛtra slew Namuci.
Arjuna said:
"May it ever be well with you, O Pārtha; may you attain victory in battle."
"O Kṛṣṇa, victory is certain for me; there is no doubt in this, since you, the teacher of all the worlds, are pleased with me, O Madhusūdana. Urge on the horses, O Hṛṣīkeśa, my great chariot."
Phalguna will not return from the battle without having slain the enemy.
Today, behold Karna slain and torn to pieces by my arrows;
or else, O Govinda, you shall see me struck down by Karna’s shafts.
"This terrible battle, which will enchant the three worlds, has arrived;
people shall speak of it as long as the earth endures.
While speaking thus, Pārtha [then addressed] Kṛṣṇa, the one of unwearied deeds.
He quickly advanced on his chariot like one elephant against another;
then the immensely energetic Pārtha spoke again to Kṛṣṇa, the subduer of enemies:
"Urge the horses forward, Hṛṣīkeśa, for the time is passing away."
Thus addressed then by that high-souled Pāṇḍava,
Jayanta honored the Pāṇḍava and then urged on the horses, which were as swift as thought.
That chariot of the son of Pāṇḍu, swift as thought,
in an instant came to the front of Karṇa’s chariot;
then, seeing his own son before him...
When Karṇa heard that he had been slain by the one with white horses in battle,
the high-souled hero was seized by supreme fury and suddenly rushed toward Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
With a single arrow in that battle, Pārtha severed the head, both arms, and the bow of Vṛṣasena,
the king of Aṅga, and struck down his army.
With the fire of his wrath, he consumed the fourfold army.
Sañjaya said:
Having seen Vṛṣasena slain, [Duryodhana] was filled with grief and indignation.
Suddenly shedding the tears born of grief from his eyes, the powerful Vṛṣa,
Karna, rushed toward his enemies in his chariot;
with eyes copper-red from indignation, he challenged Dhananjaya to battle.
Those two chariots, brilliant as the sun and covered with tiger skins,
were seen there joined together like two suns meeting; they were mounted by the subduers of enemies, who possessed white horses and were resplendent like the sun and Puruṣa.
Those two great-souled ones shone like Bhaga and Mitra in the sky with four clouds as their chariots, or like the moon and the sun in the heavens;
seeing them, O noble one, all living beings were struck with wonder.
In that *Trailokyavijaya* battle, just like Indra and Virocana,
those two kings beheld the chariots of the monarchs rushing toward them with the thunderous roar of chariot wheels, bowstrings, and palms, as well as the sounds of arrows and conchs.
Seeing the two banners entangled—
the elephant-girth of Karṇa and the monkey of the Diademed One—
and seeing those two chariots closely joined, O Bhārata, the kings were filled with wonder.
They let out lion-like roars and uttered abundant cries of "Well done!
Hearing of that duel between the two, the warriors on all sides displayed the strength of their arms and likewise raised a great clamor.
Then the Kurus arrived there, accompanied by musical instruments,
gladdening Karṇa and blowing their abundant conchs;
they blew hundreds of thousands of conchs all around the son of Rādhā.
In that very manner, all the Pāṇḍavas, gladdening Dhanañjaya,
made all the directions resound with the blare of trumpets and conchs; with their lion-roars,
the slapping of arms, and shouts, a tumultuous din arose on every side.
And there was the roar of the arms of the heroes at the encounter between Karṇa and Arjuna;
seeing those two tigers among men, the best of chariot-warriors, standing upon their chariots with great bows grasped and armed with arrows, spears, and maces.
Clad in armor and girt with swords, with white horses and adorned with conchs,
those two great car-warriors were mounted upon the chariot of Kṛṣṇaśalya; equal in appearance,
they had the shoulders and arms of lions, red eyes, and wore golden garlands.
Equipped with bows, lightning, and banners, and resplendent with a full array of weapons;
attended by yak-tail fans and graced by white parasols;
endowed with excellent quivers, both were truly beautiful to behold.
With their limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, like two bulls in rut,
resembling the shoulders of lions, broad-chested and possessed of great strength,
they vied with one another, O King, each desiring the death of the other.
Charging at one another like two great bulls in a pen,
like two elephants in rut, or like two enraged mountains;
resembling venomous serpents and comparable to Yama, Kāla, and Antaka.
Like Indra and Vṛtra enraged, possessing the splendor of the sun and moon,
they were like two cruel great planets appearing at the end of an eon;
they were the offspring of gods, equal to gods, and like unto deities in form.
Like the sun and the moon meeting by chance,
those two powerful men, arrogant in battle and bearing various weapons in combat—
those tigers among men, rushing like two leaping tigers— he beheld them.
O lord of the people, supreme joy arose among your men;
yet doubt concerning victory arose in all living beings upon seeing those two tigers among men, Karṇa and Dhanañjaya, come together.
Both bore excellent weapons, both were seasoned by the toil of battle;
both were the best among those who wield missiles, both possessed the prowess of lions,
and both made the vault of heaven resound with the sound of their arms.
Both were renowned for their deeds and for their manly strength;
both were equal in battle to Śambara and the King of the Immortals (Indra),
as well as equal to Kārtavīrya and equal to the son of Daśaratha (Rāma) in combat.
Equal to Viṣṇu in prowess and equal to Bhava in combat,
O King, both were borne by excellent chariots drawn by white horses; their charioteers were likewise preeminent and possessed of great strength.
O great king, seeing those two illustrious great car-warriors,
a sense of wonder arose among the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with their forces, [advanced against] Karṇa.
They quickly surrounded the high-souled one who shines in battle;
likewise, the joyful Pāṇḍavas, led by Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
as well as the twins, Cekitāna, and the delighted Prabhadrakas, [surrounded him].
And those heroes from various lands, disciplined and delighting in battle—
all of them, joyful and united, surrounded Dhanañjaya,
those slayers of enemies, desiring to protect him with their foot-soldiers, horses, chariots, and elephants.
O King, intent upon Dhananjaya’s victory and likewise resolved upon the slaying of Karṇa,
all your warriors,
the strikers at the head of the army, led by Duryodhana, protected Karṇa in the battle.
They surrounded the high-souled Pārtha, who was peerless in battle.
O lord of the people, for your men in that conflict, Karṇa was the stake;
likewise, for the sons of Pāṇḍu, Pārtha was the stake in the fight.
Those very same courtiers were present there as spectators;
for them, as they placed their stakes, victory and defeat were certain.
The outcome of the game—whether victory or its opposite—depended entirely upon those two.
While we and the Pāṇḍavas stood at the forefront of the battle,
O great king, those two, both skilled in combat, stood facing each other in the fray,
enraged at one another and each desiring victory over the other.
Both of them desired to strike one another, like Indra and Vṛtra on all sides;
they assumed terrifying forms, like two great comets wreathed in smoke.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, there arose contentious disputes in the sky.

O noble one, there arose mutual dissensions among all beings regarding Karṇa and Arjuna; the quarters were divided and all the worlds were rent asunder. The gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas [were likewise divided].
At the encounter of Karṇa and Arjuna, they took up opposing sides; O lord of the people, the sky along with its stars was anxious on Karṇa’s account,
while the vast earth, O Bhārata, was on that of Pārtha, as a mother for her son.
O best of men, the rivers, the oceans, the mountains,
the trees, and the medicinal herbs all took refuge with Kirīṭin;
so too did the asuras, the yātudhānas, and the guhyakas, O scorcher of enemies.
Birds that move through the sky gathered from all sides around Karna, appearing joyful;
so too did the sages, the *cāraṇas*, and the *siddhas*.
All the jewels and treasures, the Vedas with the Purāṇas as the fifth,
along with the Upavedas, Upaniṣads, secret doctrines, and compendiums;
Vāsuki, Citrasena, Takṣaka, and Upatakṣaka.
Likewise, all the mountains and the sons of Kadrū along with their progeny—
those venomous and highly wrathful Nāgas— became subordinate to Arjuna.
These included the Airāvatas, the Saurabheyas, and the Vaiśāleyas, all of whom were powerful serpents.
These became small serpents from Arjuna’s side, while from Karṇa’s side came wild beasts,
predatory animals, auspicious beasts and birds,
auspicious domestic animals, as well as lions and tigers.
O King, all were fully intent upon the victory of Pārtha:
the Vasus, Maruts, Sādhyas, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and likewise the Aśvins.
Moreover, the two Aśvins, together with their beloved [wives], were devoted to Arjuna’s triumph.
Agni, Indra, Soma, Pavana, and the ten directions,
as well as dogs, jackals, birds, wild animals, domestic cattle, and likewise lions and tigers, all gathered around his ears.
Then the Vasus with Mahendra, the Maruts with Agni,
Agni (or Agnī), Rudra, Soma, Yama, and Vaiśravaṇa approached Dhanañjaya; the Ādityas were on the side of Karṇa.
O King, at that time, the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Sūtas, and those born of the intermixture of castes— among all living beings— sided with the son of Rādhā.
But the gods, together with the Pitṛs and their hosts, were on the side of Arjuna.
Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Varuṇa follow wherever Arjuna goes;
the Brahman, the Kṣatriya, the sacrifices, and the sacrificial fees all take refuge in Arjuna.
So too do the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, the flesh-eaters, and the beasts and birds.
The *rākṣasas*, along with aquatic monsters, and the jackals were on the side of Karṇa;
while the hosts of gods, brahmins, and royal sages were on the side of the Pāṇḍavas.
All the groups of celestial sages and brahmin sages, as well as those who move through the sky, [were likewise there].
O King, the Gandharvas headed by Tumburu followed Arjuna,
as did the Prāveyas along with the Mauneyas, the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases,
the Guhyakas, and the messengers of the gods, together with the radiant Apsarases.
We have taken refuge in the Diademed One; the delightful and holy fragrances have all taken refuge in his ears, while those odors that are unpleasant belong to those who are destined for destruction.
For those who are perishing, all things turn contrary and undesirable.

Those states that at the time of death quickly enter a man who is deluded and afflicted when the hour of death has arrived— those very states entered together into the ear of Karṇa, the son of the Sūta.

O best of kings, O tiger among men, in that ocean of battle there were vigor, splendor, success, great joy, truth, valor, contentment of mind, victory, and likewise bliss— such things as these were present there.
Auspicious omens entered Jiṣṇu in the battle;
the ṛṣis, together with the brahmins, attended upon Kirīṭin.
Then the Siddhas, along with the hosts of gods and the Cāraṇas, [did likewise].
Dividing into two groups, O Great King, those two best of men took refuge in various and excellent celestial chariots on all sides;
having ascended them, they approached for the single combat between Karṇa and Pārtha.
O great king, desiring to witness the encounter between Karṇa and Arjuna,
the gods, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas gathered in the sky; thus,
O Bhārata, all beings were divided into two groups.
While the hopes for victory were being entertained for both the son of Rādhā and Arjuna,
the sky then became crowded with tens of thousands of celestial chariots,
as well as with leaping beasts, wild animals, deer, elephants, chariots, and infantry.
Carried along by the clouds and the wind, the wise ones gathered together,
desiring to witness the encounter between Karṇa and Arjuna;
the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, and birds [all assembled].
O great king, the great seers learned in the Vedas, the ancestors who partake of the *svadhā* offerings,
