ascetic power, sacred knowledge, and medicinal herbs— each possessing various forms, garments, and splendors—
stood in the intermediate space, uttering loud cries.
Brahmā, together with the Brahman-sages and the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis),
remained in his divine vehicle and proceeded toward that place.
Seeing those two high-souled ones, Karṇa and Dhanañjaya, standing there together, he approached.
"Let Arjuna conquer Karṇa," Śakra himself said; "Let Karṇa conquer Arjuna," the Sun declared.
"Having slain Arjuna, let my son Karṇa be victorious in battle."
"Having slain Karṇa, let my son Dhanañjaya be victorious today"—
thus was the dispute between Sūrya and Vāsava,
as those two lions among men stood there, each taking his side.
For two sides there was a conflict between the gods and the asuras;
seeing those two great-souled ones, Karṇa and Dhanañjaya, come together,
the three worlds, along with the celestial rishis and cāraṇas, trembled.
All the hosts of gods and all beings whatsoever—where Pārtha was, there were the gods; where Karṇa was, there were the asuras.
These were the two wings of the two leaders of chariot-divisions, the heroes of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, O lord of the earth, Prajāpati quickly arrived there to witness that single combat between Karṇa and the son of Pāṇḍu in battle,
wondering whether Karṇa would conquer this earth.
Then Sañjaya said: "The Lord himself also had this doubt: 'Will Arjuna indeed master it all?'"
Having observed that great strength of those two, Prajāpati,
O King, seeing Devabhāga arrive,
spoke then even as the Self-born One looked on.
Both are great chariot-warriors (*atiratha*), heroes, both possessed of firm prowess;
both are equal in their deeds, resembling the wielders of the thunderbolt and the discus as their weapons. Oh, what a great battle will take place in the encounter between Karṇa and Arjuna!
"A most terrible conflict will arise, like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
Having seen this, the gods approached Prajāpati, the Self-Existent One, and asked:
"O Lord, who shall be victorious between these two warriors, the Kuru and the Pāṇḍava?"
"O God, let victory be equal for these two lions among men.
Having heard that, Maghavan prostrated before the Grandfather [Brahmā], saying:
"Let not the entire world perish through the destruction of Karṇa and Arjuna."
"O Self-Existent One, tell us the truth; O Lord, declare the victory of these two.
O Self-Existent One, speak those words so that the victory of both may be equal.
Thus did he, the best among the wise, address the Lord of Gods.
"Previously, the Blessed One declared that victory for the two dark ones was certain.

When he had spoken thus, O Great King, the Blessed One—Mahābrahmā Prajāpati—said this while their victory remained undecided: [08,063.049b–08,063.050a] "Victory is indeed certain for those two. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
"Both of these are indeed accomplished, and both are exceedingly powerful;
a battle between them will bring terror to the three worlds.
Thereupon, the thousand-eyed Indra urged Prajāpati to intervene.
"Let it be so; salutations to you! Be gracious to me, O Blessed One.
Then Brahmā and Īśāna spoke these words to the Lord of the Thirty-three:
"May victory be certain for the high-souled Vijaya."
By that Savyasācin, the eater of oblations (Agni) was gratified at Khāṇḍava;
and having reached heaven, you were assisted by him, O Śakra. Moreover, Karṇa is on the side of the Dānavas; therefore, his defeat must be brought about.

When this is done, the purpose of the gods will certainly be accomplished; and for all of them, O Lord of the Thirty-three, one's own duty is the most important. Moreover, the high-souled Phalguna is always devoted to truth and righteousness.
Victory will certainly be his; there is no doubt about this—
O Śatānīka, how could victory not be his who has gratified the Blessed One, the Great-Souled One whose banner bears the bull?
He whose chariot the Lord of the Universe, Viṣṇu himself, drives;
who is high-minded, powerful, heroic, skilled in weapons, and rich in asceticism;
and who, possessed of great splendor, maintains the science of archery in its entirety.
Pārtha is endowed with all virtues, for this is the work of the gods;
the Pāṇḍavas have been constantly and severely afflicted by forest exile and other hardships,
yet that bull among men is perfected and sufficient through his ascetic power.

Due to his greatness, he might even transgress what has been ordained by destiny; and if that were transgressed, the destruction of the worlds would become inevitable. There is no standing ground anywhere for the two Kṛṣṇas when they are enraged.

For these two bulls among men, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, are the ancient and most excellent of sages; they are the creators of both the non-existent and the existent. Unrestrained themselves, they are the restrainers of all, fearless subduers of their enemies.
But there is no one equal to these two, whether in heaven or among men;
for this has been followed by the three worlds together with the celestial sages and *cāraṇas*,
as well as all the hosts of gods and whatever beings exist.
By the power of these two, however, the entire world exists.
May this Karṇa, the bull among men, attain the foremost worlds;
may the hero Vaikartana be victorious, and may there be triumph for the two Kṛṣṇas.
May he attain the same world as the Vasus or the Maruts;
together with Droṇa and Bhīṣma, may he be honored in the heavenly realm.
For Pārtha has been afflicted in the forest for a long time, O Grandfather.
Therefore, Arjuna will conquer in battle, for he is superior through his ascetic power;
previously, it was declared by the Blessed One that victory for the two Kṛṣṇas is certain. Let it be so; salutations to you, O Lord; speak, O Grandfather.
Having heard those words of the thousand-eyed one, the Lord, the Master,
did not declare victory for either Karṇa or Kirīṭin as being equal;
therefore, Śakra departed with hope when the Grandfather remained silent.
"The victory of the son of Pāṇḍu and the slaying of Karṇa in battle"—
having been addressed thus by the two gods of gods, the thousand-eyed Indra spoke these words,
addressing all beings at the command of Brahmā and Īśāna.
"O worthy ones, you have heard what has been spoken by the two Blessed Ones for the welfare of the world;
that is so and not otherwise. Therefore, remain with your anger gone. Having heard these words of Indra, O noble one, all beings [responded].
O King, they were filled with wonder and paid homage to that;
they did not then declare victory for either of those two lions among men as being equal.
And likewise, from the sky, they released various kinds of fragrant flowers.
The gods showered rains of flowers and sounded celestial instruments;
desiring to behold the peerless duel between those two lions among men,
all the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas took their positions.
With eyes wide open in wonder, none perceived any other activity;
those two chariots, yoked with white horses, bearing great banners and making a mighty sound—
those very chariots of Karṇa and Arjuna, O King, upon which they stood, were filled with joy.
The heroes of the world assembled there blew their conchs individually:
Vāsudeva and Arjuna, those two heroes, as well as Karṇa and Śalya, O Bhārata.
Then that battle commenced, causing terror to the cowardly.
Like Śakra and Śambara vying with one another in prowess,
the two banners of those two, standing upon their chariots and adorned with garlands,
shone brilliantly like Rāhu and Ketu risen in the sky at the destruction of the world.
Encountering each other in battle, they both displayed their distinct forms in a fit of mutual rage.
Karna’s elephant-girth, resembling a venomous serpent, studded with the finest jewels, firm and radiant like the bow of Indra, shone brilliantly.

But the banner of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the best of monkeys, became terrifying with its gaping mouth; frightening [the enemy] with its fangs, it was as difficult to look upon as the sun. Desiring battle, it stood there as the standard of Pārtha.
He approached Karna’s standard and roared;
then, springing up with great speed, the monkey struck the girth with his claws and teeth,
just as Garuḍa strikes a serpent.
Adorned with small tinkling bells and made of iron like the noose of Death,
the elephant-girth, highly enraged, rushed toward the great monkey.
In that supreme duel between the two, a chariot-duel that had been staked as a wager, they fought on.
The two standards engaged in battle as the horses neighed back at the horses;
the steeds, vying with one another, neighed at the other steeds.
Then the lotus-eyed one pierced Śalya with arrows that were his very glances.
And he too gazed upon the lotus-eyed one in that very same way.
There, Vāsudeva defeated Śalya with the arrows of his eyes,
and Dhanañjaya, the son of Kuntī, also defeated Karṇa with his gaze.
Then the Sūta’s son, having addressed Śalya with a smile,
spoke these words out of affection, O King, beginning with words of conciliation:
"If Pārtha should ever slay me here in battle today..."
"O friend, tell me truly, what would be your answer then?
Śalya said:
"If you were slain, I would indeed slay both Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya."
"O Karṇa, if Śvetavāhana should slay you in battle today,
I myself shall slay both Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava with a single chariot.
Saṃjaya said:
In this very manner Arjuna addressed Govinda;
laughing at him, Kṛṣṇa spoke these supreme words to Pārtha:
"The sun might fall from its place, and the earth might shatter into many pieces."
Fire may become as cold as ice, yet Karna shall not slay you, O Dhanañjaya.
Even if it were somehow possible for the world to be overturned,
I would slay both Karna and Śalya with my own two arms in battle.

Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, Arjuna, whose banner bears the monkey, smilingly replied thus to Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds: "O Janārdana, even for me, these two— Karṇa and Śalya— are not enough."

Today in battle, you shall see Karṇa cut into many pieces by my arrows— along with his banners and standards, his chariot, horses, and Śalya; together with his parasol and armor, and his spears, arrows, and bow.
Today, behold him— along with his chariot, horses, spear, armor, and weapons—
as crushed like a tree in a trampling by an elephant. Today, widowhood has arrived for the wives of the son of Rādhā.
"O Mādhava, surely those women have seen evil omens in their dreams;
surely this very day you shall see the wives of Karṇa as widows. For my enmity toward her who formerly mocked Kṛṣṇā does not subside."
"O Govinda, having seen Kṛṣṇā brought into the assembly by that deluded and shortsighted man,
who mocked us and insulted us again and again,
today you shall see Karṇa destroyed by me."
Like a rutting elephant [trampling] a flowering tree,
today you shall hear those sweet words, O Madhusūdana:
"By good fortune you are victorious, O Vārṣṇeya," once Karṇa has been struck down.
"O Janārdana, today, filled with joy, you shall free yourself from your debt by consoling Abhimanyu’s mother, Kuntī, and your paternal aunt;
O Mādhava, today you shall console Draupadī, whose face is bathed in tears."
With words that were like nectar, [he addressed] Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma.
Saṃjaya said:
Then, by the hosts of gods, nāgas, asuras, and siddhas;
Frequented by hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, and apsarases, and graced by brahmarṣis, rājarṣis, and suparṇas,
the sky shone with a wondrous appearance.
All the men in the sky beheld him not crying out, but rather with charming sounds, accompanied by instrumental music, songs, hymns of praise, and dances.
Then the Kuru and Pāṇḍava warriors, filled with joy, beheld those [beings] standing in the sky, their forms wondrous to behold,
amidst the sounds of musical instruments, the rustling of wings, the clashing of weapons, and lion-like roars.
Making the earth and the quarters resound with their noise, they all struck down their enemies;
[the field] was crowded with tens of thousands of various horses, elephants, and chariots.
The battlefield, unbearable due to the falling of excellent swords, spears, and double-edged blades, frequented by the fearless and strewn with slain bodies, shone, dyed crimson with blood.
A battle took place between the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas,
just like that which occurred between the gods and the asuras; thus it proceeded when the destruction of those who wield weapons had begun.
Dhananjaya and the son of Adhiratha, both clad in armor,
covered each other, the quarters of the sky, and the army with sharp, straight-flying arrows.
Then, when darkness had been created by your arrows and those of the enemy, neither side could discern anything at all;
out of fear, they both sought refuge within their respective chariots.
Like two dispellers of darkness with rays extended across the sky,
they then warded off each other's weapons with their own weapons,
like the east and west winds.
Just as two dispellers of darkness shine exceedingly when the thick gloom has spread, so did they shine;
and they were urged on with the thought that they must not be spared.
Then your enemies and your own men stood surrounding those two great chariot-warriors on all sides,
like the gods and asuras surrounding Vasava and Sambara.
O Bhārata, amidst the resounding blasts of mṛdaṅgas, bherīs, paṇavas, and ānakas, as well as the blare of conchs,
those two best of men shone forth with lion-like roars.
Like the moon and the sun amidst a mass of clouds,
those two bulls among men then shone resplendent,
both standing in the center of the great circle of the bow.
Possessing great luster and possessing the radiance of thousands of arrows, they sought to consume the world with all its mobile and immobile beings;
in battle, they were as unbearable as two suns at the end of an eon.
Both were invincible and both were intent on the destruction of their enemies; those two skillful and foremost of heroes, desiring to slay one another, encountered each other in that great battle.
Then, like Indra and Jambha, Karṇa and the Pāṇḍava,
those two great archers discharged mighty weapons with terrifying arrows.
The two immeasurable heroes struck down men, horses, and elephants;
they slew one another with excellent arrows.
Then, tormented once more by those shafts, they fled in all directions.
Under the two best of men, those belonging to the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas—
along with their elephants, infantry, horses, and chariots— fled in all directions,
just as forest-dwellers flee out of fear of a lion.
Then Duryodhana, the Bhoja king, Saubala,
and Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat—
these five great chariot-warriors [confronted] Dhanañjaya and Acyuta.
With arrows capable of ending lives,
Dhanañjaya struck their bows, quivers, horses, standards, chariots, and charioteers with his shafts.
He cut them down evenly and struck them through with twelve excellent arrows, [piercing] the son of the Suta;
those five heroes were thus continuously deprived of their chariots.
With their bodies mangled by the force of Arjuna’s arrows,
the foot soldiers fled from there in great haste;
others climbed onto other chariots and went back toward him.
Then a hundred chariots and a hundred elephant-riders, all armed with weapons, rushed swiftly toward Nāgārjuna;
they were Śakas, Tukhāras, and Yavanas, along with their cavalry.
Together with the best of the Kambojas,
those desiring to slay him quickly severed with razor-sharp blades both the excellent weapons held in their hands and their heads.
Then, as they fought, Dhananjaya— that Savyasacin in battle— consumed that host of enemies, along with their horses, elephants,
and chariots.
And Dhanañjaya cut down elephants, horses, chariots, and charioteers there with razor-sharp blades; Kirīṭin struck off their heads with his arrows.
While Dhanañjaya was fighting there,
in an instant everything went to destruction;
then, in the sky, the sounds of celestial trumpets arose.
Accompanied by shouts of "Well done!", they were uttered by those who were thrilled;
showers of excellent flowers fell,
auspicious, fragrant, well-formed, and wafted by the wind.
O King, having witnessed that marvel witnessed by gods and men, all beings were struck with wonder:
"Aha! This most magnificent deed has been performed by Arjuna himself!"
When they beheld that solitary hero fighting against the great chariot-warriors— the gods and the foremost among kings—
they praised the great glory of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.
Your son and the Suta’s son, being of one mind, experienced neither distress nor amazement. Then the son of Droṇa spoke to your son:
Pressing hand against hand and consoling him, he said:
"Be gracious, Duryodhana; make peace with the Pāṇḍavas; enough of this opposition—fie upon war!"
The preceptor, equal to Brahmā and a master of great weapons, has been slain, as have those bulls among men headed by Bhīṣma. Yet I am unslayable, and so too is my maternal uncle.
Rule the kingdom for a long time together with the Pāṇḍavas;
Dhananjaya will remain restrained by me,
and Janārdana does not desire any conflict at all.
Yudhiṣṭhira is always devoted to the welfare of all beings,
as is Vṛkodara under his command, and likewise the twins;
and you, O Pārtha, along with them, are united with one another.
If you so desire, may the subjects attain auspiciousness;
let the remaining kings return to their own cities,
and let the soldiers be free from enmity.
O King, if you do not hear that the mighty Karna, the son of the Suta, has been slain,
you will lose your entire kingdom in its entirety.
O lord of men, if you do not listen to my words, you will surely go along the wondrous path of Karṇa—
scorched by grief once you have been slain by your enemies in battle.
And this has been witnessed by you along with the world:
what was accomplished by the single wearer of the diadem,
such as neither the Shatterer of Bala nor Antaka could ever do.
The venerable Pracetā is not the king of the Yakṣas;
for the compassionate Dharmarāja, having beheld his aged father and the illustrious Gāndhārī, will surely seek peace when entreated.
And your lord, the heroic Vipaścit, who possesses excellent intelligence and knows the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures, will grant you the kingdom as is appropriate;
that righteous soul will not pursue enmity toward his own kin, for there is no transgression against them.
Kṛṣṇa has no thought of conflict; he rejoices in his own kin—
both Bhīmasena and Arjuna, as well as the two sons of Mādrī, the Pāṇḍavas—
acting in accordance with the counsel of Vāsudeva and that of the wise Pāṇḍava.
Those tigers among men will abide by the weight of their word; therefore, O Duryodhana, protect yourself. The self is the vessel for everything;
exert effort to remain alive, for only while living does one behold prosperity.

"O Bhārata, may you be blessed; for it is while one is alive that sovereignty and prosperity are possible. Indeed, O Kauravya, for one who is dead there is no kingdom, much less happiness. Behold this worldly conduct as it has been established and set in motion."
Make peace with the Pāṇḍavas and preserve the remainder of your lineage.
O Kauravya, let that time not come when I must speak words of ill omen; O mighty-armed one, do as you wish, but do not disregard my words.
This is most righteous, exceedingly beneficial for both the king and his lineage;
for this is the supreme good for the prosperity of the Kuru dynasty,
bringing welfare to the subjects and happiness to the family, O son of Gāndhārī.

"Karna will indeed not defeat Arjuna, that tiger among men, in battle; for my mind is firmly resolved that he will prevail, provided his actions are beneficial and conducive to the future. O best of men, may these auspicious words of mine be pleasing to you."
Otherwise, O Indra among kings, there would be a very great destruction.
Moreover, Dhanañjaya is even greater than this in his virtues;
he will follow every word of mine.
He will likewise provide you with an escort;
be gracious, O King, for the sake of the world’s peace,
for the intense enmity toward your father has not yet been fully unleashed.
To slay that fierce and formidable enemy in battle,
even though it was thus beneficial and wholesome,
the virtuous Pāṇḍavas have today failed to accept what was revealed to them here.
I, too, always have the highest regard for you;
therefore, out of supreme friendship, I speak to you.
For I shall indeed restrain even Karṇa.
When you have become a friend,
the wise say that a friend is born with one; likewise, a friend is acquired through conciliation and wealth.
For I have previously declared, out of compassion and other virtues,
that the king is indeed your own body and the offspring of your body,
as well as all the other extensive manifestations of your qualities.
There was no archer equal to Dhanañjaya in this world, a master of the supreme weapons;
he whose friend was Viṣṇu had no cause for conflict.
O Suyodhana, today, having brought your battles to an end, remember first all those wondrous deeds of yours, every single one of which was marvelous.
"Do not cause the death of Karṇa’s sons; do not bring them to ruin. O great chariot-warrior, if you do not listen to me, you shall see the army of the Pāṇḍavas slaughtered in that manner."
Then, how will you not behold Arjuna moving about in battle, whose power is equal to Time itself,
the radiant sun of great splendor among the energetic?
Why do you not see that excellent weapon in battle? For once you have perished, the son of Dharma— honored by the heroes among men— will enjoy the kingdom upon this earth.
When addressed in this way by the son of the preceptor, how is it that he remains just as he was, so dejected? O friend, why do you yourself speak thus today?
From the side of Pārtha, who was filled with joy in battle,
Duryodhana— extremely weak, laughing, his arms cast loose, and impelled by the time of his miserable end— fell.
"I shall slay Vṛkodara along with his kinsmen in battle;
how could I, being prepared for this great conflict, feel fear? For the fourfold army has been brought under my control by my prowess."
All that exists is present in you and in the Pāṇḍavas by nature; O hero, they are your kinsmen,
so win them over again with conciliation and establish a firm alliance.
"O Indra among kings, if they were to enter into friendship with you once you are well-disposed toward them, you should certainly act accordingly.
Having been thus addressed by his friend with these beneficial words, [he...]
Reflecting thus and sighing, he spoke with a heavy heart:
"Friend, it is exactly as you have said;
now hear my words as I inform you."
"Who else is my constant companion in sorrow except for you,
my sole hero?
Having slain Duḥśāsana, he spoke these many words.
This evil-minded Vṛkodara has forcibly [seized her] like a tiger; that remains fixed in my heart,
and since it is not hidden from you, how can there be peace?
Nor could Arjuna withstand Karṇa in battle,
just as a fierce wind cannot move Mount Meru, the great mountain;
and my sons, the offspring of Pṛthā, will find no peace while I am present.
Having repeatedly considered this enmity with resolve,
O son of the preceptor, you ought to speak so that Karṇa may desist from it out of respect for you, O Acyuta.
Today Phalguna is overcome by great exhaustion;
Karna will now forcibly slay him,
and the earth itself shall tremble.
The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, might dry up;
even the greatest of mountains might float upon the vast waters;
yet Arjuna shall not defeat Karṇa in battle.
The non-existence of these— of water, earth, the sky, the wind, and the golden-seeded fire of most brilliant radiance— might indeed occur on all sides.
"And Arjuna shall not defeat Karṇa in battle.
Having spoken thus and having consoled him repeatedly,
your son gave instructions to his own soldiers.
"Striking down and rushing against these enemies,
why do you remain silent amidst the sound of arrows?
Sañjaya said:
Amidst the swelling roar of conchs and kettledrums,
those two foremost of men with white horses met—
one the son of Vaikartana, the Sūta’s son, and the other Arjuna.
O King, due to the evil counsel of your son,
those two were like venomous serpents emitting fire,
breathing forth enmity from their mouths.
Then those two illustrious ones blazed forth in battle like two sacrificial fires sprinkled with clarified butter,
like two rutting elephants from the Himalayas.
Like two elephants with tusks bared for the sake of a female,
those two heroes, Dhanañjaya and the son of Adhiratha, encountered each other with fierce speed.
Just as a cloud is met by another cloud,
or as one mountain might by chance encounter another mountain,
so too were the sounds of the bowstring, the palms, and the rims of the wheels.
Those two, raining down showers of arrows,
met like two oceans with waves of great crests stirred up by the wind of wrath, where arrows, missiles, spears, double-edged swords, maces, and scimitars were the serpents.
Just as two mountains move while remaining immovable,
so did those two advance like two oceans at the end of an eon,
with their horns, trees, creepers, and medicinal herbs flourishing.
Like two great winged mountains, or like two mighty peaks that have come loose from a vast range, they were exceedingly powerful and dwelt upon various lofty mountain heights.
Thus, as they struck one another with great weapons,
a massive clash occurred between them,
like that between the Lord of the Gods and Vairocana in ancient times.
With its elephants, drivers, and mounts mangled by arrows,
that river— difficult for others to endure, with brisk blood for its water—
abounded with lotuses, lilies, fish, and turtles.
Like two great lakes, resounding with flocks of birds and closely drawn together by the wind,
those two chariots, bearing their banners, came together.
Both were equal in prowess to Mahendra;
both were great chariot-warriors (mahāratha) resembling Mahendra himself;
and with arrows resembling the thunderbolt of Mahendra, they [fought].
Like Mahendra and Vṛtra, those two armies— both consisting of elephants, infantry, horses, and chariots, and adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments of various colors— assailed one another.
In that battle between Arjuna and Karṇa, those who had gone to the sky trembled and rose up in amazement,
their arms raised with fingers adorned by the thunderbolt-mark.
When the son of Adhiratha, desiring to slay him, rushed at Arjuna like one rutting elephant against another, the spectators, eager to see the sight, let out lion-like roars in delight.
Then, when the son of the Sūta [Karna] encountered Arjuna in the afternoon, a great clamor arose on all sides from both the Kurus and the Somakas.
In that great battle, he struck like a cloud against a mountain;
even so was the encounter of the two chariots in that great conflict, amidst the mire of blood and flesh.
There the Somakas shouted at the son of Pṛthā:
"Hurry, Arjuna, go and pierce Karṇa! Cut off his head; enough of this delay!"
Having placed their faith in the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra rather than in the kingdom,
many of our warriors there then said to Karṇa, "Go! Go!"
"O Karṇa, slay Arjuna! Then, clad in their bark garments, let the sons of Pṛthā go once more to the forest for a long time.
Thereupon, Karṇa first [attacked] Pārtha there.
He pierced him with ten great arrows;
Arjuna, exceedingly enraged, pierced him back in the armpits with ten sharp-pointed shafts.
Then Karṇa quickly pierced the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow with ten arrows first; thereafter, the diadem-wearing Arjuna struck him back.
Then, with eighteen well-aimed arrows,
Karna quickly struck Partha once more with ten shafts from his chariot.
And Pārtha, in turn, pierced him with ten sharp-pointed,
keen-edged arrows in the space between his armor straps; then, O Bhārata, in that battle, Karṇa—
In that terrible and excessive carnage of battle,
he struck Pārtha with nine sharp-pointed arrows,
like one striking a rutting elephant within its enclosure.
Then, in that battle, the high-souled son of the Suta, acting with great speed, struck Hari with two other razor-sharp arrows.
Just as Namuci once assailed the Lord of the Gods by force,
so did that son of Pāṇḍu strike Karṇa with five iron-tipped arrows drawn back to his ear.
Then those arrows of Pārtha, like the messengers of Death, drank his blood;
and Karṇa [assailed] Pārtha along with Vāsudeva.
O Bhārata, they covered each other with calf-toothed arrows;
the Sūta’s son and Arjuna hacked at one another with exceedingly sharp shafts.
Seeking each other's weakness in their clash, they both advanced with great joy toward that most terrifying encounter;
then Arjuna, the wielder of the formidable bow, loosed his arrows.
Having wiped both his arms and the Gāṇḍīva bow, he took up iron shafts,
reed-arrows, boar-eared arrows, razor-sharp arrows, as well as *sāñjalika*s and crescent-headed arrows.
O King, those arrows of Pārtha, entering Karna’s chariot from all sides, were scattered everywhere like flocks of birds with downward-turned faces at the end of the day.

O King, those whom Arjuna— the conqueror of his enemies— released against Karṇa with a frown and a sidelong glance, swiftly entered [him] like moths entering a tree for the sake of their own destruction.
The Suta’s son devoured with his own arrows those multitudes of shafts discharged by the Pāṇḍava, as they were shot one after another;
then Karṇa [took up] that which had been bestowed upon him by Bhārgava.
The Great-Souled One manifested the Brahma-weapon;
then that fierce weapon blazed forth,
possessing the radiance of the sun at the end of an eon.
Having struck Pātāla with that weapon,
Karṇa then slew the multitudes of men and elephants;
thereafter, he [discharged] the Agneya weapon, which torments the enemy.
Dhananjaya, the son of the Lord of the Gods, blazing at the forefront of the battle, released that supreme weapon at Karna;
then that excellent weapon burst into flames.
With the flames of the weapon of Sūra, the son of Mahendra, which issued forth excessively,
the earth, the atmosphere, the quarters, and the path of the sun [were filled].
Having covered his body, it became ablaze;
and all the warriors, their inner selves burning with pain, fled from there with their clothes scorched.
And a terrible sound arose there,
like that of a bamboo forest burning in the woods,
when Karṇa beheld the fire-weapon raised.
Then that powerful son of a Sūta, discharging that Vāruṇa weapon for the sake of pacification in the battle,
extinguished the fire with it.
With the cloud-weapon (*balāhakāstra*), the swift hero enveloped all the directions in darkness. Then [the mountains], whose slopes were like those of the earth-supporters (*dharitrīdhara*),...
Having been completely surrounded on all sides by water,
that exceedingly fierce fire was brought to a state of calm by them, despite its such nature, through their great force.
Just as all the quarters of the sky are pervaded by clouds,
so too were all the directions completely enveloped in darkness.
Covered by clouds, nothing at all could be seen;
then, he drove away those masses of clouds by means of the wind-weapon (samīraṇāstra) he had invoked.
Then he, the scorcher of his enemies, filled with great wrath, touched the string of the Gāṇḍīva and manifested the beloved weapon of the King of the Gods, the thunderbolt.
Dhanañjaya, the crusher of hosts of enemies,
then [discharged] razor-edged arrows, *añjalika*s, crescent-shaped arrows, iron shafts (*nārāca*), hollow reed-arrows (*nālīka*), and boar-eared arrows.
From the Gāṇḍīva bow there emerged thousands of extremely sharp arrows, equal in velocity to the thunderbolt;
those terrible shafts rushed about in every direction.
The arrows from Pārtha’s bow fell upon Karṇa’s chariot like flocks of birds with downward-turned faces at the end of the day,
swiftly seeking a tree as their dwelling for the night.
The son of the Sūta intercepted with his own arrows those volleys of shafts discharged by the Pāṇḍava as Dhanañjaya could not endure them.
On the field of battle, Vaikartana, whose actions were like those of Death himself and whose mind was overwhelmed with rage,
rose up like the radiance of light.
Just as the sun destroys [darkness] in an instant,
Karṇa, while still fighting, utterly destroyed all those multitudes of arrows belonging to Pārtha.
Those arrows of great power, well-sharpened, fletched with vulture feathers, and possessed of great speed, having reached Karna,
struck all his limbs as well as his horses.
Having swiftly pierced the bow, the chariot wheels, and the banner,
those exceedingly sharp arrows entered [the earth] like serpents terrified by Garuḍa.
Then Karṇa, his limbs covered with arrows and his body drenched in blood,
his eyes rolling in rage, drew back his bowstring—
which was firm and produced a sound like the roar of the ocean— until it was fully bent.
The high-souled Karṇa, having cut down the multitudes of arrows discharged by the Pāṇḍava that were aimed at Mahendra’s weapon, manifested the Bhārgava weapon.
Having neutralized the Pārtha weapon with his own weapon,
Karṇa, unable to endure it in that great conflict, struck down the multitudes of men, elephants, and horses.
The great car-warrior, the impetuous son of the Sūta, overcome with rage by the power of Bhārgava’s weapon, [slew] even the foremost warriors among the Pāñcālas.
Laughing, that hero among men pierced the two Kṛṣṇas in battle with well-aimed arrows;
then, O King, the Pāñcālas and the Somakas also [attacked].
Being afflicted in battle by Karṇa with showers of arrows,
they were overcome with rage; united together, they pierced the Sūta’s son from all sides with sharp shafts.
Having swiftly cut down those arrows with his own,
he violently overwhelmed the multitudes of chariots, elephants, and horses of the Pāñcālas with showers of shafts.
Agitating the battlefield in that encounter, the Sūta’s son caused them to fall; with their bodies pierced by Karṇa’s arrows, they fell lifeless, making loud sounds upon the surface of the earth.
Just as mighty elephants are struck down by an enraged lion, so too were the foremost of the Pāñcālas slain by him of terrible strength.
Then, O King, Karna shone forth amidst those powerful and rivalrous chief warriors,
vomiting forth arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of rain.
Thinking that victory belonged to Karṇa,
your men experienced supreme joy and let out lion-like roars;
for they all believed those two had been brought under his control.
"O Indra among the Kauravas, seeing that such prowess of the great car-warrior Karṇa— which was unbearable for his enemies— [the two] Kṛṣṇas were drawn by Karṇa."
But seeing that weapon destroyed by Karṇa in the midst of the battle, Dhananjaya,
unable to endure it in that great conflict, [acted].
Thereupon the high-souled Bhīmasena did not become angry;
instead, striking his hand with his hand, he spoke with his lips bitten, as if dancing while playing a musical instrument.
Then the impatient son of Vāyu, his eyes blazing with anger, struck his hand against his hand;
Bhīma spoke to Arjuna, who was true to his promise.
Then Bhīma, indomitable in spirit, being provoked, sighing with rising wrath,
and blazing with rage in that great conflict,
became incensed.
Rubbing his hand against his hand in rage, he,
filled with indignation, spoke these words to Pārtha:
"How indeed can this sinful man, who has strayed from dharma..."
O Jishnu, today in battle, the son of the Sūta has forcibly slain many of the foremost warriors of the Pāñcālas right before your very eyes.
How indeed could the son of a charioteer overcome you— O Kiritin— who were previously unconquered by the Daityas, the sons of Kalaka, and who have received the direct touch of Sthanu’s own arms?
With ten great arrows he pierced him first;
that he swallowed the multitudes of arrows discharged by you—
this appears to me today as a marvel.
Remember the suffering of Kṛṣṇā; recall the words she spoke— those words as sharp as bone-piercing thorns, so unpleasant to hear, calling you "barren sesame seeds."
This wicked son of a charioteer, devoid of fear,
now recalls all that evil; therefore,
O Savyasācin, quickly slay Karṇa in battle today.
O Kirīṭin, why do you practice equanimity?
This is not the time here today for indifference.
With that same fortitude by which you conquered all beings—
With that same fortitude with which you gave a mouthful of food to the fire at Khāṇḍava, slay the son of the Sūta;
as for him, I shall crush him with my mace.
Having approached Pārtha, that speaker of cruel words said,
"This man, ripened by time, shall not escape alive.
Then Vāsudeva also spoke to Pārtha:
Seeing his chariot-arrows being repelled,
Karna has crushed them all today with his own weapons; what is this, O Kirīṭin?
"O hero, why do you falter and not take up arms? These Kurus are shouting with great joy,
for they all have Karna at their head."
With such fortitude as yours, your weapon— which was being struck down by [his] weapons— destroyed that weapon of darkness,
just as the terrible Rākṣasas have been slain age after age.
The Asuras born of Dambha were slain in battles by that very fortitude;
with that same fortitude, O Kirīṭin, slay the son of the Sūta, who is arrogant with pride and whose prowess is at its height.
Having encountered Karṇa, the crusher of enemies,
in battle today, the son of Pṛthā will clearly manifest his capable weapon;
by means of this [weapon] with razor-sharp rims, he shall [strike him].
"By the Sudarśana discus released by me, forcibly sever the head of the enemy,
just as Śakra did to his foe Namuci with the thunderbolt."
O hero, having once again assumed that same steadfastness by which the Blessed One, appearing in the form of a Kirāta, was so greatly gratified by you;
Slay the son of the Sūta along with his followers;
then you shall possess the earth, girdled by the ocean,
complete with its cities, villages, and abundant wealth.
"Deliver [the earth] to the king, having slain the hosts of his enemies;
and may you attain incomparable glory from the son of Pṛthā.
Thus addressed, that great-souled one of exceeding strength—
Having placed Karṇa at their head,
all those heroes, having repelled your weapon upon the earth, roared and indeed set their minds on the slaughter of the Sūta’s son.
Exert yourself, O hero among the Bharatas!
These Sṛñjayas and Somakas are fleeing upon seeing Karṇa exultant in battle.
And seeing you as well declining,
urged on by Bhīma and Janārdana,
he then remembered his own nature and observed his true essence.
Knowing that the arrival of the Great-Souled One was for this purpose, he said to Keśava:
"I shall now manifest this fierce and great weapon."
For the welfare of the world and for the destruction of Sauti, may you,
the gods,
Brahmā, Bhava, and all those who know Brahman, grant me your permission.
Having spoken thus, the Pāṇḍava Savyasācin,
that one of immeasurable soul, paid homage to Brahmā and spoke these words regarding the irresistible Brahmā weapon: "So be it."
Having mentally prepared that which was to be employed,
Karṇa shone forth after striking him down,
releasing arrows like a cloud pouring down torrents of rain.
Having observed that weapon thus discharged by Karṇa into the midst of the battle against Kirīṭin,
the powerful and indignant [Arjuna] blazed with wrath.
Bhīma said to Arjuna, who was true to his promise: "Indeed,
people call you the knower of the great Brahmā weapon, which is supreme and must be mastered."
"O Kirīṭin, once again aim your weapons all around!"—
thus addressed, Savyasācin then aimed them toward all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
He of immense splendor covered [him] with arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva, which were like fierce serpents,
blazing and resembling the rays of the sun.
The bull among the Bharatas also discharged hundreds upon hundreds of arrows with swift velocity as if they were one;
in an instant, they shrouded Karna’s chariot.
Then there were tridents, axes, discuses, and hundreds of iron arrows, radiant as the fire at the end of an eon and the rays of the sun.
Then the warriors, most terrible, rushed forth;
they were struck down on all sides,
and the severed head of one was seen in the midst of the battle.
It fell from the body of another warrior;
out of fear, he too quickly fell to the ground,
while yet another fled upon seeing him fallen.
The sword of another warrior fell, severed from his arm which was like the trunk of an elephant; and the left arm of yet another, together with its shield, [fell].
Severed by a razor-edged arrow, he fell upon the earth;
in this manner, the one adorned with a diadem and garland destroyed all the foremost warriors as well.
With extremely terrible arrows that bring an end to the body,
the entire army of Duryodhana was likewise [destroyed] by Vaikartana in the midst of the battle.
Thousands of multitudes of arrows,
released with a roar, fell upon the son of Pāṇḍu like torrents of water discharged by the rain-cloud.
He of superhuman deeds and terrible strength, having struck Bhīmasena, Janārdana, and Kirīṭin each with three arrows;
Struck by Karna’s arrows, the diadem-wearing Arjuna let out a terrible roar with a mighty voice,
beholding Bhima and Janardana in that state.
Unable to endure this, Pārtha once again drew forth eighteen arrows;
having pierced Suṣeṇa with one arrow, he struck him down.
Then, with four well-aimed arrows he struck Śalya, and with three he struck Karṇa; thereafter, with ten well-released shafts,
he struck Sabhāpati, who was clad in golden armor.
That prince, with his head severed, his arms gone,
his horses slain, his charioteer lost, his bow broken, and his banner fallen— shattered, he then fell from the front of his chariot.
Like a *śāla* tree cut down by axes, he was struck again, pierced by Karṇa with three, eight,
two, four, and ten arrows.
Having slain four hundred armed elephants,
he destroyed eight hundred chariots,
and furthermore, a thousand horses along with their riders.
And eight thousand heroic foot-soldiers,
along with Karna— his charioteer, his chariot, his horses, and his banner—
he rendered invisible by means of his straight-flying arrows.
Then, being slaughtered on all sides by Dhanañjaya, the Kurus cried out to the son of Adhiratha:
"Release him! Pierce Arjuna quickly, O Karṇa!"
"Previously, he would slay all the Kurus with his arrows; yet,
though urged on with every effort, Karṇa released very many arrows only intermittently."
Those two, the foremost of all archers, smeared with blood and flesh, struck down the hosts of the Pāṇḍus and Pāñcālas, piercing their vital organs.
The two fierce and mighty warriors,
capable of withstanding all enemies and skilled in weapons, struck down the hostile army with great missiles against one another.
Then, having been freed from pain and deprived of the arrow by his friends— the most eminent of physicians— through mantras and medicinal herbs, he arrived in haste, desiring to see [the king].
08,065.030f*1063_18 Yudhiṣṭhira was there, clad in golden armor;
08,065.030f*1063_19 seeing the King of Dharma arrive there for battle, 08,065.030f*1063_20 all living beings rejoiced with joy.
Just as the moon, completely freed from Rāhu, rises stainless and whole,
so too [is he] by means of Nāsatya, Dasra, Atri’s son, and others.
Carrying the burden of the eight branches of medical science, with his bandage bound due to the lightness of his wounds,
he was like the Lord of the Gods whose limbs were wounded by the sons of Diti.
Then, having seen those two foremost warriors fighting—
the best of heroes and slayers of foes— the spectators, restraining their mounts, watched both Karṇa and Pārtha.
People stood on the heights and on the ground;
that tumultuous clash of the bowstring against the palm of the hand,
accompanied by well-released arrows, became a great uproar.
O King, as Dhananjaya and the son of Adhiratha thus struck one another with showers of arrows,
the bowstring was then suddenly pulled taut.
At that very moment, as the Sughoṣa bow of the Pāṇḍava was being severed, the Sūtaputra covered Pārtha with a hundred small arrows.
With sixty sharp iron arrows, polished with oil and fletched with the feathers of birds— resembling snakes that have cast their skins— he pierced Vāsudeva.
In that interval, the Somakas fled;
Pūṣan’s son pierced the son of Marut in his vital organs with tens of thousands of arrow-tips.
They covered Kṛṣṇa, Pārtha, and likewise the banner, as well as the younger sons of Pṛthā and the Somakas,
striking them down with sharpened arrows.
Like masses of clouds [obscuring] the sun in the sky,
the son of the Suta, skilled in weapons, checked those approaching warriors with numerous arrows.
Having neutralized all those weapons with his own,
he struck down their chariots, horses, and elephants,
as well as the foremost warriors of the army, O King.
Afflicting them with his arrows, the Suta’s son [struck them down];
with their bodies pierced and deprived of life,
they fell upon the surface of the earth, groaning under Karna’s shafts.
Just as a herd of horses is [routed] by an enraged lion,
so too were those of great strength and terrible power, as well as the other foremost Pāñcālas, [overcome] by him of mighty might.
In that interval, those powerful warriors, leaping forward toward Karṇa and Dhanañjaya,
were forcibly struck down by Karṇa with well-aimed arrows.
Considering the victory to be great,
your men struck their palms together and let out lion-like roars;
for they all believed those two had been brought under their control.
"Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna have been struck by Karṇa!"— thus they cried out. Then the wearer of the diadem (Arjuna), seizing the newly-strung,
very firm bow produced by the exertion of his own arms, [prepared for battle].
The great archer, acting with swiftness, took up the Gāṇḍīva bow in the mere twinkling of an eye; for him,
the snapping of the string and the fixing of the string were likewise instantaneous.
Due to his lightness of hand, the Suta’s son did not perceive Pārtha in battle as the slayer of his enemies; that,
O King, was a marvel that occurred there.
Then, having quickly loosened the bowstring and having warded off the arrows discharged by the son of Adhiratha,
Pārtha also swiftly fixed that string.
Having severed the bowstring of Adhiratha’s son,
Pārtha, though his body was wounded by Karṇa’s arrows, became highly incensed and received the Somakas back in battle.
Wiping his bowstring, he struck his arm-guard and in an instant created a darkness of arrows over Śalya,
Karṇa, and all the Kurus.
Kiritin pierced them all at once with his arrows; when darkness was created by that most swift weapon, even birds could no longer fly through the sky.
The wind, meeting with the immortals stationed in the sky who were watching on, carried away the arrows;
and Pārtha struck Śalya with ten shafts.
Laughing, he pierced Bhṛśa’s armor;
then, having struck Karṇa with twelve well-aimed arrows,
he pierced him again with seven.
Struck firmly by those feathered arrows of fierce velocity, propelled by the force of Pārtha’s bow,
his limbs were mangled and his body drenched in blood.
With his bow drawn, Karṇa shone like Rudra;
sporting then in the midst of the cremation ground during the Raudra hour, his limbs were drenched in blood.
Then, with three arrows, the son of Adhiratha pierced Dhananjaya, who resembled the lord of the thirty gods;
he [then] loosed five arrows that were like blazing serpents.
Desiring to slay Acyuta,
he discharged them; having pierced the armor of the Supreme Person, those well-aimed arrows fell, adorned with gold.
With great speed, those swift ones entered the earth with force;
having bathed there, they returned toward Karṇa.
With five well-aimed and swiftly discharged arrows, he [struck] them.
Then Dhananjaya cut each one of those great horses, which were the wings of Takshaka’s son, into three pieces; they fell to the earth.
Then he whose crown was adorned with a garland blazed up in anger like a fire consuming dry undergrowth,
beholding Kṛṣṇa thus with his limbs pierced.
With arrows released from his ears and arms drawn back to his ear,
he [assailed him] with those blazing shafts that bring an end to the body.
He pierced him in his vital spots, and he trembled from the pain;
yet, possessing extreme fortitude, he remained steadfast through his courage.
Then the Great-souled One manifested his arrows.
As if searching for the body of the Suta’s son,
those great arrows of yours, with their variegated golden shafts,
fell by the hundreds upon the earth.
Then, O King, with floods of arrows, the intermediate directions, the cardinal directions,
the radiance of the sun, and Karna’s chariot all became invisible when Dhananjaya was enraged.
Just as the sky is shrouded by frost and mist,
he [then addressed] all the wheel-protectors, foot-soldier guards, those who went before him, and those who protected his rear.
Terrified and being struck by the great arrows discharged from the hand of Pārtha, they fled;
then Arjuna, the foremost hero of the Bharatas, [acted].
The one of great majesty, the slayer in battle,
[encountered] those destroyers of enemies approved by Duryodhana— those who had gathered together, possessing excellent chariots, and being the very essence [of his forces].
In battle, Savyasācin, the bull among the Kurus, in an instant [overwhelmed] two thousand Kuru heroes, along with all their chariots, horses, and charioteers.
O King, that peerless hero led them to their destruction;
then your sons and the remaining Kurus fled, abandoning Karṇa.
Having scattered those who were slain and those wounded by arrows,
and while their sons and fathers were lamenting,
all the Kurus fled, utterly deprived.
Scorched by the arrows of Pārtha,
those most excellent warriors were then once again urged on by Suyodhana to follow Karna’s chariot.
"O Kṣatriyas, you are all most heroic and devoted to the duty of a warrior;
it is not fitting that [this should happen] in your presence."
Fleeing away from Karṇa,
even though they were being urged by your son and were being tormented by the arrows of Pārtha, they [departed].
Pale with fear, they did not remain at all;
in an instant, the intermediate points and the cardinal directions vanished.
Having looked in all directions, he saw them entirely empty.
O Bhārata, though deprived of the Kurus who were shattered by fear, Karṇa did not waver there;
he charged directly against Arjuna.
"Even so, O great car-warrior, the Sūta’s son [remained].
Then Sañjaya said:
"Thereupon, they retreated to a distance of just one arrow-shot."
The Kurus, their army broken and standing firm,
beheld on all sides Dhananjaya’s weapon being unleashed, flashing like lightning.
That weapon of Arjuna devoured the heroes;
likewise, the sky and the atmosphere resounded with an infinite roar as it was swiftly released by the enraged Pārtha.
In that great conflict for the slaughter of Karṇa,
Karṇa, having drawn his formidable bow with its firm string,
discharged volleys of arrows.
As he was discharging arrows with golden feathers that were burning the Kurus, the high-souled one [Arjuna] acted with great majesty by means of the weapon received from Rāma.
With the *ātharvaṇa* weapon, the destroyer of enemies,
he dispersed that *arjuna* missile as it was burning;
and with sharp arrows, he struck down Pārtha.
Then, O King, a truly great conflict arose between that Arjuna and the son of Adhiratha as they assailed one another with arrows.
Like two elephants with fierce blows from their tusks,
O King, the field of battle then became tumultuous, covered by a multitude of weapons.
Then Karṇa and Pārtha made that sky completely devoid of intervals with showers of arrows;
it became a great weapon consisting solely of a mass of shafts.
All the Kurus and Somakas saw [this],
and in that tumultuous darkness of arrows, they did not perceive any other being at that time.
Then, O King, those two heroes among men, the best of all archers,
having cast off their own bodies in that most terrible battle, [departed].
Having seen those two, who have attained great exertion and are difficult for enemies to overcome, now fully engaged with one another,
their eyes fixed upon each other's vulnerabilities.
The hosts of celestial sages and gandharvas, along with the yakṣas and the delighted ancestors, offered praises to the two of them as they were incessantly uniting, O King.
Discharging numerous arrows and displaying various wonderful maneuvers in battle,
those two preeminent archers were masters of weaponry.
As those two were thus fighting in the midst of the battle,
sometimes the son of the Sūta was superior,
and sometimes the diadem-wearing Pārtha was superior.
Then, having witnessed that combat in battle through the excellence of their vigor, weapons, perfect strength, and agility, those who were watching for each other's weaknesses [intervened].
Then, all the warriors were struck with amazement at that terrible and unbearable sight in battle, which could not be endured by others;
thereafter, the beings stationed in the intermediate space [beheld it].
O king, they praised both Karṇa and Arjuna;
filled with joy and affection, they spoke in groups, saying, "O Karṇa, well done! O Arjuna, well done!"
In that tumultuous clash, chariots, horses, elephants,
and throngs of foot soldiers made the earth tremble;
then, he who was reclining in the depths of the netherworld—
O King, at that time, the Naga Aśvasena, who had harbored enmity toward Arjuna, having escaped from the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest,
assumed great speed while remaining within the depths of the earth.
Then, having witnessed the clash between Karṇa and Arjuna, he leaped upward with great speed, thinking,
"This is indeed the right time for this evil-minded one."
O King, assuming the form of an arrow, he reflected upon the requital of Pārtha’s enmity and entered Karna’s quiver.
Then that mass of weapons became a dense web of spreading rays;
Karna and Partha [covered each other] with showers of volleys of arrows.
Then they both incessantly made that vast sky consist solely of a mass of their arrows;
all the Kurus and the Somakas were struck with terror.
In that tumultuous and exceedingly thick darkness created by the arrows, they saw nothing else at all as it fell;
then those two tigers among men, the foremost archers in all the world—
The two heroes, having cast off their lives in battle and succumbed to the exhaustion of combat,
were being fanned with divine palm-leaf fans by hosts of Apsarases stationed in heaven, while they looked upward and were sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Both had their faces wiped by the lotus-like hands of Śakra and Sūrya; yet,
when Karṇa could no longer distinguish himself from Pārtha and was firmly oppressed by Pārtha’s arrows, [he withdrew].
Then Karna, his limbs mangled by arrows,
set his mind upon that lone recluse;
then Karna fixed the enemy-slaying weapon.
A fierce, well-polished arrow, sharp as a serpent’s mouth and blazing,
which had been guarded for an exceedingly long time for the sake of Pārtha in battle.
Having drawn back his ear-to-ear bow, Karṇa released that great poison of an arrow, which was always honored and rested upon sandalwood powder, lying within a golden tube.
Desiring to take the head of Phalguna in battle, he aimed that fiercely wrathful, blazing arrow— born of the lineage of Airāvata— at one facing toward Pārtha.
That crusher of enemies swiftly released it;
thereupon the quarters and the sky blazed forth,
and terrible meteors suddenly fell.
But when that bow was fixed upon the serpent [missile],
all the worlds, including Śakra, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!",
yet the Sūta’s son did not perceive it.
Seeing the serpent, who had entered the arrow by the power of yoga,
the thousand-eyed Indra,
thinking "my son has been killed," became dejected with his limbs drooping.
Born from a lotus-flower, of noble nature, and self-conquered, he spoke to the Lord of the Thirty-three: "May fortune not fail you in victory.
That son of a charioteer [struck] him in the corner of the eye.
Out of rage, he joined his palms with his face turned downward;
he did not recognize that high-souled one who stood before him in battle,
fixed upon the corner of his eye.
Beholding Vaikartana with his arrow fixed, the high-souled King of Madra said to him:
"O Karṇa, this arrow shall not reach his neck."
"Having aimed it, fix an arrow capable of striking the head!
Then Karna, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke forcefully to Shalya as he fixed the shaft.
O Śalya, Karṇa does not fix an arrow twice;
those like me do not employ deceit.
When [the target] is reached, the son of Pṛthā remains humble, offering his own oblations.
Having thus spoken, Kṛṣṇa again fixed that arrow—
Balāhaka, which was honored by the rain-clouds— and discharged it.
"You are indeed slain, O Phalguna! he cried out.
Then Mādhava, seeing the serpent being joined by Karṇa, hurled a powerful shaft with great haste.
Having stepped upon the chariot with his feet by means of his strength, that best among the strong caused the horses to sink to their knees in the earth as the chariot was submerged;
then that arrow struck the diadem of that wise hero.
Released from Karna’s arm,
that most terrible arrow, resembling fire and the sun,
blazed in the sky as it was discharged from the bowstring.
Creating a parting in the sky with his fearsome form,
Mādhava, the enemy of Kaṃsa, beholding that blazing [weapon] in battle, acted with agility and haste.
Having crushed that excellent chariot with his feet, he forced it down into the earth by the measure of a cubit;
those horses, however, sank into the ground upon their knees.
Then that arrow struck the diadem;
seeing it approaching, blazing,
and coursing through the sky, the hero of the Vṛṣṇi clan [beheld it].
Suddenly pressing down on the wheel of the chariot,
the hero sank it five finger-breadths deep;
then, a great roar arose in the sky.
For the purpose of worshipping Madhusūdana,
divine words suddenly arose,
as did divine flowers and lion-like roars.
When the chariot had thus sunk into the earth due to the exertion of Madhusūdana,
that arrow then struck the crown.
Then [he gave] to that wise Arjuna the very firm bow named Indradatta, which was renowned throughout the earth, the sky, and the waters, and served as an ornament for his excellent limbs.
With the power of his supreme effort in discharging weapons and with his fury,
the son of the Sūta struck off the head,
which possessed the brilliance of the sun, the moon, fire, and the planets.
Adorned with nets of gold, pearls, and jewels,
it was built by the son of Bhuvana himself through asceticism and great effort for the sake of Purandara.
Of exceedingly precious form and terrifying to enemies,
it shone with extreme beauty and fragrance as the Lord of the Gods bestowed it upon the slayer of the foes of the gods.
With a gracious mind, he himself gave [the earrings] to Kirīṭin,
[earrings] which were sought by Hara, Varuṇa, Indra, Kubera,
and Yama with their supreme weapons: the Pināka, the noose, the thunderbolt, and the arrow.
Though he was being struck by the hosts of Rudra along with Pinākin,
who were aided by arrows resembling fire,
he was difficult even for the best of the gods to afflict.
O King, that evil-minded one, who had failed in his vow, was forcibly seized by the serpent Vṛṣa, which had long been held here by Āditya.
He struck Arjuna’s crown,
which was adorned with pure gold and jewels;
the powerful warrior snatched it from the head of Pārtha.
Covered with a golden net, making a beautiful sound and blazing intensely, that [arrow] fell to the earth;
it was the supreme arrow, whetted by the fire of poison.
The beloved,
supreme diadem of Pārtha, blazing and radiant with flames, fell down like the sun falling from the mountain of setting.
Then the serpent forcibly snatched away from Arjuna’s head his crown, adorned with many jewels,
like a mountain whose trees are well-grown with sprouts and flowers.
O Bhārata, just as the earth, the atmosphere, the heavens, and the waters appear distinct when separated by the wind, so too does Mahendra’s vajra shine like a supreme peak.
In that very way, a sound then arose throughout the worlds;
the people, becoming despondent, faltered as they tried to regain their composure.
Then, having fastened a white garment [around his head], he—
Standing with his own hair undisturbed,
Arjuna shone even without his diadem;
that dark-complexioned youth was like a mountain whose peak has been struck down.
He shone like the mountain of sunrise with its peak crowned by the sun of full, radiant rays;
then Arjuna [struck] Karṇa with straight, new [arrows].
With gold-feathered, very firm iron arrows,
resembling the staff of Yama or the fire-god Agni, he pierced him between the breasts,
just as the son of Agni [Skanda] shattered Mount Krauñca.
Then, having cast aside his quiver and that bow which resembled the bow of Śakra, the son of the Sūta stood firm, did not falter, and was not bewildered; he continued to exert himself.
Though struck down firmly and again and again from here and there,
Arjuna did not abandon him in his misfortune;
for the noble one, remaining steadfast in the vow of a man, sought to slay him.
Then the younger brother of Indra, out of agitation, said to him: "O Pāṇḍava, why do you act so recklessly?
Wise men never [trust] their enemies."
Even the very weak wait for a moment;
especially when enemies are in distress, a wise man,
having struck them down, attains both merit and fame.
Hasten, O Karṇa, to swiftly crush that lone hero who is ever your adversary,
before the son of the Sūta arrives in full strength.
"Penetrate this Namuci, just as Hari did! "So be it, O God," Janārdana replied in honor of the request; then Arjuna quickly pierced Karṇa.
Then the best of all the Kurus, acting with haste, struck him with the finest arrows,
just as the Lord of Heaven struck Śambara;
and Gokarṇā, sent by the son of the cowherd, was dispatched with a well-aimed shaft.

Having seen the crown of Gogataka— which was adorned with the word "go" (cow) as its very essence, well-fashioned, clearly manifesting the splendor of "go," and filled with the sound of "go"— he seized it; yet Gokarṇa,
the crusher of his enemies, did not fall under the power of death.
Then, impelled by Karṇa’s arms,
there arose a great cloud-like serpent, possessing a brilliance like that of fire or the sun,
which had long harbored enmity toward Arjuna.
Having reached the crown, it sprang up;
having seized Arjuna’s crown,
that great serpent, having long harbored enmity toward him, quickly [departed].
Just as Karṇa had discharged [the weapon] for the sake of slaying the son of Pṛthā,
the serpent, having observed him, returned toward Karṇa,
turning away from that kirīṭin.
Seeing that crown flying up,
the high-souled Pārtha spoke to Vāsudeva;
and having burned that [crown] adorned with gold, he—
Having pulled off Arjuna’s diadem,
he thought it was [Arjuna] himself and entered the quiver again;
then, questioned by Karṇa, he spoke this.
"O Karṇa, I have been spared by you because you did not perceive that my head had already been taken away by Arjuna;
seeing me now, release me quickly in battle!"
"I shall slay the enemy, both yours and my own"—
when he had spoken thus in battle, the Sūta’s son said to him, "Who are you, O one of such fierce form?"
Then that Naga, as if laughing at his own misfortune, fell down while looking at him; and Arjuna, acting with haste, said to him:
"Know that you have committed an offense against me."
"O Kṛṣṇa, today [I shall avenge] the enmity born from the slaughter of my mother. "I am a white elephant who has established enmity with Arjuna."
For even though his mother formerly leapt up into the sky,
and even if the Wielder of the Thunderbolt himself were his protector,
she nonetheless went to the abode of the King of the Dead.
O Karna,
one should not today, relying on the strength of another, desire victory in battle like a Naga-ear (Karṇa).
The elephant did not even take up a second arrow;
even if it were to kill a hundred Arjunas,
Karṇa spoke again to that elephant.
Then, in the midst of the battle, that best of the sons of the Sun, through his supreme effort and fury in discharging the serpent-weapon,
will slay Pārtha; go back with a peaceful mind.
Thus addressed by Karṇa in battle, O King, that lord of elephants was distressed and, unable to endure those words,
set out himself for the slaughter of Pārtha.
Having assumed the form of an arrow and desiring to strike Arjuna,
he then spoke to Vāsudeva:
"O Dāśārha, who indeed is this great serpent?"
"Do not despise me; follow my word this day.
I shall slay the enemy; release me. "I was not released by you because you were unwilling to make peace."
You have been deceived by that Kṛṣṇa as well;
yet, by the strength of my very arms,
you are capable of slaying even a hundred Arjunas in battle.
"Even here, you do not know my vow;
I shall declare it in the very presence of Kṛṣṇa:
today, having slain the Pāṇḍavas in battle..."
"Indeed, by my own prowess in battle, I shall slay him;
knowing this vow, let the Naga proceed."
"O Pāṇḍava, what vow did you make?
Having defeated me in battle, Karṇa shall send me to Yama."
O hero, although I knew this was for the sake of my friend— to set out tomorrow and proceed to his palace— nevertheless, you exerted yourself so that your body did not fall [in exhaustion].
Alas, if you had slain Pārtha at the head of the battle,
would I have been able to face the Kauravas? Or rather, am I not indeed capable against them?
"O Karna, I myself shall indeed slay the mighty Vāsudeva and Pārtha at once; of this there is no doubt. Then Kṛṣṇa spoke to Pārtha on the battlefield:
"O best of the sons of the Sun, slay that great *mahoraga* with whom you have a grudge; in the midst of your battle,
he has released a very firm serpent-weapon (*nāgāstra*) against your body."
Seeing him springing up, Kṛṣṇa, the best of men, spoke these words to Pārtha:
"O Pāṇḍava, look, look at this great serpent!"
"By you, however, this fierce weapon has been employed for the sake of slaughter.
Thus addressed by Madhusūdana,
the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— that formidable archer against his enemies— [acted accordingly].
"Who indeed is this serpent who has today come of his own accord into the mouth of Garuḍa?
Then the high-souled one spoke to Vāsudeva.
O descendant of Daśārha, who indeed is this elephant of mine today,
possessing such swift speed like an arrow released from a bow,
that comes of its own accord as if into the very mouth of Garuḍa?
Kṛṣṇa said:
"He who, as a wielder of the bow, gratified the Fire-god at Khāṇḍava with this [bow] of yours..."
With his body pierced by arrows while traveling through the sky, he assumed many forms; his mother was slain,
and it is he who indeed remembers that enmity toward you.
Today, O Pārtha, he comes toward you for slaughter,
like a blazing great meteor fallen from the sky;
behold him, the subduer of enemies, as he approaches.
Then Jiṣṇu, having avoided the remainder,
cut down the elephant with six sharp, well-edged arrows as it leapt obliquely through the air.
With its limbs severed, it fell to the ground;
and when that serpent had been slain by Kirīṭin,
the Lord himself [arose] from the surface of the earth.
In that very moment, the mighty-armed Puruṣottama quickly lifted that chariot up again with his two arms using ten arrows.
With arrows whetted on stone and fletched with peacock feathers,
Karṇa pierced Dhananjaya, that hero among men, as he was looking askance at him.
Then Arjuna, having discharged twelve sharp arrows released from a full draw, struck him with a steel shaft possessing a velocity like that of a venomous serpent.
Drawing it back to his ear,
that excellent wielder of variegated armor released the arrow, which,
being well-aimed, pierced through him as if casting out his very life-breaths.
Having drunk Karna’s blood, he entered the earth, smeared with the gore of his own arrows;
then Vṛṣa, provoked by the falling of those shafts, [rushed forward].
Like a great serpent struck by a staff,
the swift-acting warrior discharged his excellent arrows,
like a highly venomous snake emitting its supreme poison.
He struck Janārdana with twelve arrows and Arjuna with ninety-nine;
having covered them with vulture-feathered shafts, he overwhelmed them with his arrows.
Having pierced the Pāṇḍava again with a terrible arrow, Karṇa roared, laughed,
and bellowed in the battle.
Gladdening the Kurus,
that joy of his the Pāṇḍava could not endure; then,
knowing his vital spots, he pierced his very vitals.
With feathered arrows, he displayed prowess like that of Indra, just as Indra struck down Bala with his might;
then Arjuna [discharged] ninety-nine arrows.
He discharged arrows resembling the staff of Death at Karṇa;
his body severely afflicted by those shafts,
he trembled like a mountain split asunder by a thunderbolt.
Formerly, when his clan was being shattered by wrath,
his supreme ornament for the head was adorned with the finest jewels, excellent diamonds, and gold.
Cast down upon the earth by Dhananjaya with his feathered shafts, those two excellent earrings,
along with that great wealth crafted with effort by the finest artisans, fell away.
That radiant and supreme armor which had been fashioned for him over a very long period of time, the son of Pāṇḍu shattered into many pieces in an instant with his arrows.
With the edges of his earrings shattered by his arrows and severely wounded at that time,
he, whose ears were dripping with blood, shone forth.
Like the planet Mars appearing in the sky with its red hue,
he,
enraged, pierced that one who was deprived of armor with four excellent arrows.
Struck by his enemies, he was exceedingly distressed, like a sick man afflicted by wounds caused by bile, phlegm, and wind,
pierced by sharp arrows released from the circle of a great bow.
With great force, through skillful application of effort,
and with many excellent arrows, Arjuna swiftly struck Karṇa and pierced his vital organs.
Struck firmly by Pārtha with various sharp-pointed arrows of fierce velocity,
Karṇa shone like a mountain reddened by red chalk minerals.
O Bhārata, as if shedding blood like water from waterfalls, the Diademed One covered Karṇa, along with his horses and chariot, with calf-tooth-headed arrows.
With arrows gold-feathered and calf-tooth-tipped, he, whose chest was broad and full, covered all directions with every effort.
Covered all over, the son of Adhiratha shines like a mountain filled with blossoming aśoka, palāśa, and śālmali trees, and abounding in spandana and sandalwood.
O lord of the people, with his body pierced in many places by arrows, Karṇa shines in battle like a mountain whose peaks and valleys are covered with trees.
Just as Mahendra is adorned with beautiful *karṇikāra* flowers, so Karṇa,
discharging multitudes of arrows from his bow,
shines forth, possessing rays in the form of a web of shafts.
Like the sun facing the setting mountain, its orb crimson with red rays,
so too were the arrows released from the armpit of Adhiratha’s son.
The sharp-pointed arrows released from Arjuna’s arms, having reached all directions, destroyed Bāṇa’s shafts— which were like blazing great serpents— before they could reach their mark.
Then Karna, regaining his composure,
released arrows resembling enraged serpents and pierced Pārtha with ten shafts.
And [he struck] Kṛṣṇa with six arrows resembling enraged serpents;
then [he loosed] a great arrow, whose sound was like the thunderbolt of Mahendra,
and which was like the fire of serpent venom.
In that great battle, Dhanañjaya, desiring to hurl his iron spear— which was equal to a fierce and mighty weapon—
was like Time itself, O King, though invisible due to the Brahmins' curse.
Proclaiming the slaughter of Karṇa as an illustration, he said,
"The earth swallows the wheel," at that time when the moment of Karṇa's death had arrived.
The Brahma-missile, which even the high-souled Bhārgava had bestowed upon him, has vanished from his mind;
the earth swallows his left wheel.
O hero among men, O lord of men, when that time of slaughter arrived,
the chariot then reeled due to the curse of that best of Brahmins.
Furthermore, that terrible weapon which the high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu invoked does not manifest before him;
rather, the earth swallows his left wheel.
When his time had come and the Lord of Death stood before him,
O Bhārata, the chariot then began to reel due to the curse of that best of Brahmins.
Then he announced that his death had arrived and that his weapon was being destroyed by the curse of the foremost of the twice-born;
thereupon, his discus fell to the ground.
Distraught in battle, that son of a charioteer sank into the surface of the earth like an exceedingly tall sacrificial monument with its altar, though in full bloom.
When the chariot reeled due to the Brahmin’s curse,
when the weapon taken from Rāma no longer manifested its power,
and when the terrible serpent-mouthed arrow was severed;
At that, Karna despaired because of Partha,
unable to endure those calamities;
wringing his hands, he reproached himself.
"Dharma protects those for whom dharma is paramount";
so have the knowers of dharma always declared.
And we, too, shall constantly strive toward dharma.
I have composed this according to my ability and as I have heard it; yet even today, the Compassionate One does not protect his devotees,
for I believe that Dharma does not always provide protection.
Speaking thus, with his horses and charioteer stumbling, and shaken by the volleys of Arjuna’s weapons,
he faltered in his actions due to the blow to his vital organs.
Again and again he censured Dharma in the battle;
then, in that combat, he pierced him with three most terrible arrows,
and Karna then struck Pārtha in the hand with seven.
Then he pierced Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya between the breasts with most terrible arrows;
thereupon Arjuna, of fierce splendor, [discharged] seventeen straight-flying shafts.
He discharged terrible arrows, equal to Indra’s thunderbolt and resembling fire;
having pierced through them with fearsome speed, they fell upon the surface of the earth.
Thus shaken in spirit, Karṇa displayed his exertion by means of his spear.

Then, steadying himself with strength, he invoked the Brahmā weapon; and Arjuna, seeing that, likewise consecrated the Aindra weapon. Having consecrated the Gāṇḍīva bow, its string, and his arrows, Dhanañjaya [prepared for battle].

He released showers of arrows like Purandara pouring down rain. Then, arrows composed of fiery energy and possessed of great power issued forth from Pārtha’s chariot and appeared close to Karṇa’s chariot.
The great car-warrior Karṇa rendered those [arrows] discharged at him from the front futile.
Then, when that weapon had been neutralized, the hero of the Vṛṣṇis said:
"O Pārtha, discharge a supreme weapon; Rādheya is devouring your arrows."
Then Arjuna, having deliberated, discharged the Brahmāstra;
having covered Karna with arrows and caused him to reel, Arjuna—
whom Karna, enraged, cut the bowstring of with his well-sharpened shafts.
He cut off his second, third, fourth, and likewise the fifth;
then he cut off his sixth, seventh, and eighth; and the bull likewise cut off his ninth, tenth, and eleventh.

Karna did not perceive that his bowstring had been severed a hundred times and reattached a hundred times. Then, having fixed another string and wiped it with his hand, the son of Pandu covered Karna with thousands of blazing arrows.

In that battle, Karna did not perceive the severing of the bowstring nor its replacement due to his swiftness; it was like a marvel. With his own weapons, the son of Radha struck down the weapons of Savyasacin.
Displaying his own prowess, he exerted himself even more than Pārtha. Then Kṛṣṇa, seeing Arjuna oppressed by Karṇa’s weapon, said to Pārtha, "Employ the unsurpassed weapon."
Then, having consecrated with mantras another divine arrow made of diamond, resembling fire and like the venom of a serpent,
the diadem-wearing Dhanañjaya took up that fierce weapon, desiring to discharge it.
Then, in that great battle, the wheel of the son of Rādhā sank deep into the earth.
Thereupon, the son of Rādhā quickly descended from his chariot and, exerting himself,
grasped the wheel with both arms and strove to lift it up.
The earth, with its seven islands, mountains, groves, and forests,
was swallowed up and lifted four finger-breadths upward by Karṇa;
but Rādheya, his wheel having been seized, shed tears out of anger.
Seeing Arjuna so enraged, he spoke these words:
"O Pārtha, O great archer, wait for a moment!
And he said to Arjuna as well: "Be patient for a moment, O son of Pāṇḍu."

"Until I lift this wheel that has been swallowed by the earth's surface, O Pāṇḍava, you must observe the duty of a Kṣatriya; it behoves you to act. Having seen this wheel of mine thus swallowed in the midst [of the field] by fate,"
O Pārtha, abandon this treacherous intent practiced by cowards;
you ought not to follow a path trodden by the base. You are renowned, O son of Kuntī, as preeminent in the arts of war.
O Pāṇḍava, you ought to show even greater distinction toward one whose hair is disheveled, one who turns away, a Brāhmaṇa with palms joined in reverence,
one who has come for refuge, one who has laid down his weapons, and likewise one who is in distress, O Arjuna.

"O son of Kuntī, heroes do not strike in battle one who is without arrows, whose armor has fallen away, or whose weapons have been dropped or broken; nor do kings strike another king in such a state. Since you are a hero, O Kaunteya, therefore endure this for a moment."
"Heroes established in virtuous vows do not cast aside their weapons;
and you, O Pāṇḍava, are the greatest hero in the world and one of righteous conduct, well-acquainted with the laws of battle. Therefore, forgive me for a moment."
"O Dhananjaya, you who possess divine weapons, whose soul is immeasurable, and who are equal to Kartavirya in battle: as long as I lift this wheel from the earth,
you ought not to slay me while I stand on the ground, unarmed and stationed upon my chariot."
"O son of Pāṇḍu, I do not fear Vāsudeva or you;
however, remembering the duty of heroes, wait for a moment. For you are a scion of the Kṣatriyas and the enhancer of a great lineage."
"O Pāṇḍava, best among the wise, remember the instruction on Dharma and wait for a moment while I prepare my bow. Saṃjaya said:
Then Vāsudeva, standing upon his chariot, said:
"O son of Rādhā, by good fortune you remember dharma here! For the Pārthas are always devoted to dharma."
Therefore, he grants them prosperity;
yet those Kurus, having fallen away from dharma and being bound by greed, have indeed gone to their destruction.
Generally, those of base character, submerged in calamities,
blame fate rather than their own various misdeeds—
that they brought Draupadī, clad in a single garment, into the assembly hall.
When you, Suyodhana, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni the son of Subala were summoned there,
O Karṇa, righteousness did not occur to you.

When Śakuni, skilled in dice, defeated Yudhiṣṭhira— the son of Kuntī, who was ignorant of gambling, compassionate toward all creatures, and a man of honor— by means of deceit in the assembly hall, where had your sense of dharma gone then?

When, according to your own counsel, the king treated Bhīmasena with snakes and food mixed with poison, where had your dharma gone then? Or when he [plotted] against the Pārthas while they were sleeping in the house of lac at Vāraṇāvata?
