O son of Rādhā, you set fire [to the house]; where had your dharma gone then? And when the thirteenth year of forest exile had passed, O Karṇa, since you did not grant the kingdom, where had your dharma gone then?

O Karṇa, when you laughed in the assembly hall at Kṛṣṇā while she was in her menses and under the power of Duḥśāsana, where had your dharma gone then? When formerly those ignoble men were tormenting the innocent Kṛṣṇā...

"O Kṛṣṇā, the Pāṇḍavas have perished; they have gone to eternal hell. Choose another husband!"—speaking thus to her who moves with the grace of an elephant, you looked on with indifference, O son of Rādhā; where had your dharma gone then?

"O Karṇa, greedy for the kingdom, you again challenged the Pāṇḍava; having taken refuge with the King of Gāndhāra, where did your dharma go then? When many great chariot-warriors slew Abhimanyu in battle?"
When you surrounded the boy in battle, where had your dharma gone then?
If this dharma was not present there,
what was the point of parching your palate in every way?
"O Sūta, perform the religious rites this very day;
nevertheless, you shall certainly not be released today,
for Nala has been defeated at dice by Puṣkara."
Just as he regained his kingdom through valor,
so too have all the Pāṇḍavas, acting together and having cast off greed, obtained [their realm] through the strength of their arms.
Having slain their enemies who had grown powerful in battle,
they, together with the Somakas, shall obtain the kingdom;
for thus have the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra gone to destruction.
By those lions among men who are ever devoted to the protection of the Dharma.
Sañjaya said:
O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by Vāsudeva at that time, Karṇa—
Bowing his head in shame, he did not utter any reply;
instead, O Bhārata, with his lips quivering from rage, he raised his bow and,
possessing great speed and prowess, engaged Pārtha in combat.
Then Vāsudeva spoke to Phalguna, that bull among men:
"O one of great strength, pierce him with a divine weapon and bring him down.
When these words had been spoken by Vāsudeva to the son of Rādhā regarding the Pāṇḍava, [the latter acted].
A fierce rage took possession of him as he recalled those various deeds of Dhanañjaya. From all his pores, O Great King, rays of fiery energy burst forth due to his anger,
and it was like a marvel.

Beholding him, Karna then rained down upon Dhanañjaya with the Brahmā weapon; he again made an effort to discharge his chariot. Pārtha, for his part, overwhelmed him with showers of arrows using that very same Brahmā weapon.
Then, O King, Karṇa, his eyes reddened at the corners with rage, warded off that weapon with his own weapon; meanwhile, the Pāṇḍava struck him.
Thereafter, the son of Kuntī [discharged] another beloved weapon of Jātavedas (Agni).
Aiming it at Karṇa, he released it, and it blazed up violently.
Then Karṇa extinguished that fire with the Vāruṇa weapon,
and with clouds, he made all the quarters of the sky dark and overcast with gloom.
But the heroic son of Pāṇḍu, remaining unperturbed, then blew away those clouds with the Vāyavya weapon while the son of the Sūta looked on;
there, O Bhārata, the son of the Sūta beheld a marvel.
As each wheel sank into the earth,
he fought the Pandava of fierce impetuosity and pierced him with ten arrows.
Then, O King, having been deeply pierced by Karṇa in that battle, Arjuna, the hero among the Bharatas,
became intensely inflamed with rage.
Like a fire sprinkled with clarified butter in a sacrificial assembly,
the Suta’s son then took up a most terrible arrow, blazing like a flame, with the intent to slay the son of Pāṇḍu.
O King, as that worshipful arrow was being fixed upon the bow,
the earth, with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled;
a wind carrying grit blew, and the quarters of the sky were shrouded in dust.
And a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods in heaven, O Bhārata, upon seeing that arrow aimed by the Sūta’s son, O honorable one;
the Pāṇḍavas, their hearts despondent, fell into the deepest despair.
That arrow, released from Karna’s arm,
possessing a brilliance like Indra’s thunderbolt and a sharpened point,
reached the chest of Dhanañjaya.
Like a supreme serpent entering its anthill,
that high-souled one, deeply pierced in battle,
reeled with the Gāṇḍīva bow slipping from his loosened grasp.
Bībhatsu, the crusher of enemies,
trembled like the best of mountains during an earthquake;
and having found that opening, the great car-warrior Vṛṣa—
Desiring to lift the wheel that had sunk into the earth,
he leaped down from the chariot and, though possessed of great strength, was unable to seize it with his two arms due to fate.
Then the high-souled Arjuna, the wearer of the diadem, having regained consciousness, took up an arrow resembling the staff of Yama, blazing with light and joined with a *prāñjalika* head.
Then Vāsudeva also said to Pārtha:
"Sever the head of this enemy with an arrow before the bull [Duryodhana] mounts his chariot."
Having thus honored those words of his lord,
he then took up a blazing razor and struck the armpit, which was the color of the stainless sun.
When the great chariot’s wheel had sunk down,
he [pierced] that excellent elephant-girth,
which was polished with gold, pearls, gems, and diamonds, with his arrows.
Crafted with the utmost effort by master artisans over time, it is beautiful, radiant,
and ever provides strength to your army.
It is the terrifier of enemies, of praiseworthy form, renowned in the world as equal to the sun,
and in brilliance equal to fire, the sun, and the moon.
Then, with a sharp, gold-feathered razor-headed arrow, the diadem-wearing Arjuna,
exerting himself, struck down the banner of the son of Adhiratha as it blazed with splendor.
O noble one, through that banner, the high-souled son of Adhiratha, the great car-warrior, attained fame, righteousness, victory,
and all things dear to him.
Then the hearts of the Kurus fell, and a great cry of "Alas! Alas!
arose upon seeing that banner fallen upon the earth.
When it was swiftly cut down by the hero of the Kurus,
all those people among your own side, O Bhārata, no longer hoped for victory for the son of the Sūta.
Then, hastening for the sake of slaying Karṇa, Pārtha, the son of Pāṇḍu,
drew from his quiver the *añjalika* arrow, which resembled the thunderbolt of Mahendra, the fire, or the staff of Yama.
Like the most excellent ray of the thousand-rayed sun,
it cut to the very vitals, smeared with blood and flesh,
resembling both Vaiśvānara and the sun, and was most precious.
It was three cubits long, swift as a bird, moving straight with fierce speed, taking the lives of men, horses,
and elephants; it possessed a brilliance equal to the lightning of the thousand-eyed Indra.
Like a common flesh-eating beast, it was exceedingly difficult to endure;
resembling the Pināka bow, the Nārāyaṇa mace, and the discus,
it was terrifying and the destroyer of all living beings.
Pārtha, exceedingly joyful, seized that [weapon] which was like the power of the commander-in-chief of the lord of gods,
and which was difficult even for hosts of deities to withstand.
That great-souled one who is constantly honored,
who with his great bow would conquer the gods and asuras, and whom they indeed regard as preeminent in battle.
The entire world, with all its moving and non-moving beings, trembled;
"May the world be well! the sages cried out upon seeing that great arrow raised for battle.
Then the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva fixed that immeasurable arrow upon his bow,
having joined it with a supreme great weapon through his knowledge of mantras.
Drawing the Gāṇḍīva bow with a roar, he said:
"This great, peerless weapon, this arrow, has been held; it pierces the body and takes the life of the wicked."

"Austerity has been practiced by me and my gurus have been gratified; likewise, I have performed sacrifices for my friends and listened to the sacred teachings. By this truth, let this arrow be destroyed!"

The virtuous King of Dharma is well-armored against his enemy Karṇa; he is unconquered, righteous-souled, true to his promise, and devoted to compassion. He has conquered his senses and speaks the truth—therefore, slay this son of the Sūta.
Having spoken thus, Dhanañjaya released that terrible arrow for the slaughter of Karṇa,
like a fierce *kṛtyā* of the Atharva-Aṅgirasas.
Speaking thus, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, exceedingly joyful, said: "May this arrow of mine, blazing and unbearable even for Death himself in battle, bring me victory."
Desirous of slaying him, he who possessed a splendor equal to the sun and the moon brought Karṇa to his end by delivering him to Yama;
then that great arrow was released by the mighty one.
With that shower of arrows which brought victory, the one adorned with a diadem, appearing joyful, set ablaze the quarters and the sky.
Desiring to slay him, the assailant, having utterly bewildered many armies, fixed his enemy— who possessed a splendor equal to the sun and moon— upon his discus.
O King, with broad-headed arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva by Vijaya, Arjuna struck off the head of the Sūta’s son from the midst of his armor.
Severed by the one with joined palms, it fell swiftly; his body followed after, falling to the earth. Then Arjuna took off his head.
Just as Mahendra [struck] Vṛtra with his thunderbolt, O King, so did he then [strike him] with that most excellent arrow, the Añjalika,
empowered by great mantras.
Then, in the afternoon, Pārtha,
the son of Mahendra, severed the head of Vaikartana; severed by the *añjalika* arrow, it fell down.
Then his body fell down behind him,
possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun,
like the sun situated in the midst of the autumnal sky.
With that arrow, he struck off the head of Karṇa;
the commander’s noble head fell upon the earth like the sun with its crimson orb setting behind the western mountain.
That body of his, which was constantly filled with happiness,
was the very nature of that one of exceedingly noble deeds;
yet he abandoned that body with supreme effort.
Like a lord with great supernatural power entering his palace,
the tall body of Karṇa— bereft of armor and life, its limbs mangled by arrows— fell down along with his chariot.
With a bleeding wound from which liquid red chalk (gairika) flowed,
he was like the peak of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt; thus it was when Karṇa was struck down from his body.
O King, when Karṇa had been slain, all the human warriors beheld that wonder as a blazing radiance quickly penetrated the sky.
Then, seeing Karna struck down by Phalguna, the Pāṇḍavas, as well as Kṛṣṇa and Dhanañjaya, blew their conchs loudly.
Then, filled with joy, they quickly blew their conchs;
thereafter, having penetrated even into the sky, his blazing splendor entered the sun.
With its head severed in battle, Karna’s body fell, strewn with arrows;
seeing him slain and lying there, the Somakas gazed upon him.
Delighted, they raised a shout together with their armies; being exceedingly joyful, they struck their musical instruments,
waved their garments, and brandished their arms.
And the warriors of the king, cheering him on, approached Pārtha with great joy;
others, endowed with strength, even danced.
Embracing one another and crying out,
they spoke upon seeing Karṇa slain on the ground, pierced from his chariot by an arrow as he groaned.
Like a great fire cast away by a mighty wind at the conclusion of a sacrifice, Karna’s severed head shone brilliantly upon the bed at the end of the night.
Like the orb of the sun that has set,
his body, its head severed,
was drenched by the gushing torrents of blood.
Covered with Karna’s arrows, he shone like the sun when its rays have spread far and wide; indeed,
having scorched the Pāṇḍava army in battle, he blazed forth.
At the close of day, the sun that was Karṇa was driven to his setting by Kṛṣṇa, the Time-Being wearing a diadem, with arrows possessing a brilliance equal to fire.
O King,
that face of the Sūta’s son shone like a lotus whose stalk has been severed;
its every limb was covered with arrows, and it was drenched in a flood of blood.
The body of Karṇa shines like the sun with its own rays,
having scorched the enemy army with the blazing shafts for its beams;
now that sun-like Karṇa has been led to his setting by the powerful Arjuna, who acts as the god of death.
Just as the sun, setting, departs taking its radiance with it,
even so did Karna’s arrow depart, taking his life away in the afternoon of that day,
O Sire.
Severed by Añjalika in battle, the head fell with a loud thud;
directly above the enemy troops,
that arrow swiftly carried away Karna’s head, which fell with a great crash upon the ranks.
O best of the Bharatas, that head graced the earth like the sun descending upon the earth by its own will, O great king; and beholding it,
which had found rest after the crushing toil of battle—
With his lips bitten and his eyes distressed by blood,
the son of Rādhā sat upon the back of his excellent chariot;
for a moment, the sun became shorn of its rays.
Deprived of the son of the Sun, Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s army— silent of its musical instruments, its chief warriors slain, and its pride extinguished— no longer shines.
Like a host of planets deprived of the moon,
Sañjaya said:
"But seeing the heroic Karṇa fallen upon the earth..."
Seeing him lying on the ground, covered with arrows and his limbs smeared with blood, the King of Madra departed on a chariot whose banner had been severed.
When Karṇa was slain, the Kurus,
afflicted by fear and deeply pierced in battle,
fled while repeatedly looking back at Arjuna.
A great banner, blazing with its own form,
[was seen]. When Karṇa was slain, the Kurus, afflicted by fear and deeply pierced in battle by the arrows of the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, fled away.
Beholding Pārtha’s banner with its terrifying monkey,
which was the slayer of hostile armies, they fled in the ten directions;
once Karṇa had been slain, they ran away out of fear of Pārtha.
The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, pierced by arrows,
gazed repeatedly at the great banner of Arjuna, which blazed with glory.
His face was like that of the thousand-eyed one;
it was auspicious, resembling a thousand-petaled lotus,
like the sun with its thousand rays at the end of the day.
Thus his head fell upon the earth— Karna, broad-chested, lotus-eyed, with the luster of molten gold, who had been scorched by the arrows of Pārtha as he lay fallen on the ground.
Gazing repeatedly at his son, who was covered in dust and soiled, the sun, its rays dimmed, proceeds very slowly toward its abode. Sañjaya said:
But Śalya, having seen the forces crushed by arrows in the clash between Karṇa and Arjuna,
watched as Duryodhana approached.
O Bhārata,
when the great chariot-warrior Adhiratha’s son had been struck down, the standards were lowered by the Somakas and the Pāṇḍavas as they displayed the battlefield.
He departed swiftly in that very chariot,
treating the Sṛñjayas and Somakas with contempt;
for Śalya, once Karṇa had been slain by the Diademed One (Arjuna).
Beholding the army terrified and distressed in appearance, and seeing that the son of Adhiratha had been slain along with his follower,
he departed on his chariot whose equipment had been shattered.
Seeing that army with its chariots, horses, and elephants struck down, and the son of the Suta slain,
Duryodhana’s eyes became filled with tears.
Sighing again and again, appearing distressed,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"How indeed was the clash between Karṇa and Arjuna?"
On that fierce day, the appearance of the Kuru and Sṛñjaya forces as they fled,
mangled by arrows in the battle, was like that of one who has been consumed by fire.
But seeing the heroic Karṇa fallen upon the earth,
his body covered with arrows and smeared with blood,
like the sun resting upon the ground by chance;
Desirous of seeing him, they stood surrounding him;
some were thrilled, others terrified, dejected, or bewildered,
while others appeared as if overcome with grief.
Your enemies and your own men struck one another;
each became exactly as his innate nature dictated.
Their armor, ornaments, garments, and weapons were cast aside.
Hearing that Karṇa had been struck down by Dhanañjaya and deprived of his vital energy, the Kurus fled in utter confusion,
like cows whose bull has been slain.
And Bhīma, having let out a roar with a terrifying and mighty sound that made heaven and earth tremble,
slapped his arms and leaped about, dancing.
When Karṇa was slain, O King, terrifying the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra as well as the Somakas and Sṛñjayas,
they all blew their conchs and embraced one another.
Then, when the son of the Sūta had been slain, the Kṣatriyas, appearing joyful,
struck one another after having been violently crushed by Arjuna.
Karna was slain like an elephant by a lion;
that bull among men has fulfilled his vow,
and Partha has reached the end of his enmity.
Seeing him lying on the ground, the King of Madra,
struck with fear, retreated very swiftly with his chariot;
the lord of Madra was utterly bewildered in mind.
Having quickly approached Duryodhana on a chariot whose banner had been carried away,
he spoke these words to him who was afflicted by grief after conversing with him briefly.
With its foremost elephants, horses, chariots, and heroes shattered,
your army, having encountered one another and been struck down by the great warriors, resembles the realm of Yama.
O Bhārata, there has never been such a battle as that which took place today between Karṇa and Arjuna, with men, horses, and elephants resembling mountain peaks.
For the two Kṛṣṇas and all your other enemies have been seized by Karṇa upon encountering him;
yet that which is destiny has proceeded according to its own power.
That [power] protects the Pāṇḍavas and destroys us;
for all these heroes, who were intent on accomplishing your purposes, have been forcibly slain by our enemies.
Those heroes were equal in power to Kubera, Vaivasvata, and Vāsava, and likewise to the Lord of Waters,
in prowess, valor, and strength.
Endowed with various and vast floods of virtues,
those lords of men, who were nearly invincible, have been slain in battle by the Pāṇḍavas for the sake of your interests.
"Therefore, do not grieve for him, O Bhārata; this was ordained by destiny.
Success is achieved through the turn of time; success does not always come immediately.
Having heard these words of the Lord of Madra, [he remained silent].
Beholding his own [army] routed, Duryodhana, with a dejected mind and deprived of consciousness,
sighed again and again in a state of great distress.
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen the army being turned back by your son at that time, the Lord of Madra then—
With a terrified appearance and a bewildered mind,
he spoke these words to Duryodhana.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
But during that clash between Karṇa and Arjuna,
on that fierce day when they were scorched and fleeing, such was the appearance of the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas.
Saṃjaya said:
"O King, listen attentively as to what kind of great slaughter occurred when Bala was mangled by arrows."
A terrible slaughter of the best of men occurred in that battle among human bodies;
when Karṇa was slain, O King, Pārtha let out a lion’s roar,
and at that moment a great fear entered your sons.
Once Karṇa was slain, not a single one of your warriors had the inclination to rally the ranks or even to display prowess;
they were like boatless merchants stranded upon a fathomless sea when their ship has been wrecked.
O King, when the island had been destroyed by the Diademed One (Arjuna) and the Suta’s son was slain, those who desired the further shore in the shoreless sea became terrified and wounded by arrows;
like deer tormented by lions, they were without a protector and sought one.
Like bulls with broken horns or serpents with broken fangs,
we retreated at sunset, utterly defeated by Savyasācin;
our foremost heroes slain, we were shattered and mangled by his sharpened arrows.
O King, when the Sūta’s son was slain, your sons fled in fear;
deprived of their weapons and armor, all were bewildered, not knowing where to go,
trampling one another as they looked about, afflicted by terror.
Thinking, "Bībhatsu is rushing toward me alone, and Vṛkodara is rushing toward me alone," they fell down and fainted from agitation;
some great car-warriors [abandoned] their horses, others their chariots, and others their elephants.
Struck by the swift-footed, the infantry fled in terror;
chariots were crushed by elephants, horsemen by great car-warriors,
and throngs of foot-soldiers, afflicted by fear, were trampled by fleeing masses of horses.
Just as a caravan abandoned in the forest becomes beset by wild beasts and robbers,
so did your troops become when the Sūtaputra had been slain;
likewise, the elephants were deprived of their riders, and the men had their arms severed.
Seeing the entire world filled with Arjuna, they were overcome with fear;
beholding them all fleeing, afflicted by the terror of Bhīmasena, Duryodhana then said this to his charioteer: "Drive! and spoke as follows.

Pārtha, standing with bow in hand, will not bypass you; he is positioned at the very rear of the army, slowly urging on his horses. For there is no doubt that the son of Kuntī intends to fight me at the rear.
I would not venture to transgress [his command], just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore. Today, having slain Arjuna along with Govinda, the proud Vṛkodara,
and the remaining enemies, I shall attain freedom from my debt to Karṇa.
Having heard those words of the Kuru king, which were worthy of a hero’s purpose,
the charioteer slowly urged on the horses covered in gold.
But your foot soldiers, O honorable one, were deprived of their chariots, horses, and elephants.
Twenty-five thousand [warriors] stood ready for battle alone;
Bhīmasena, enraged, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the son of Pṛṣata,
surrounded them with a fourfold army and slaughtered them.
They all fought back against Bhīmasena and the son of Pṛṣata;
others there even called out the names of Pārtha and the son of Pṛṣata.
Then Bhīma became enraged by those who had confronted him in battle.
Descending swiftly from his chariot,

Vṛkodara, the son of Kuntī, who was observant of dharma, fought them while standing on the ground; relying on the strength of his own arms, he did not engage those who were on the ground while remaining in his chariot.
Grasping a massive mace encased in gold,
he struck down all your men like Death himself with staff in hand;
even the foot soldiers, filled with fury, cast away their very lives.
They rushed at Bhīma in battle like moths into a fire;
but having encountered Bhīmasena, those furious warriors, intoxicated by combat,
perished suddenly upon seeing him, like hosts of living beings before the God of Death.
With mace in hand, the immensely powerful Bhīma moved about like a hawk;
he slaughtered twenty-five thousand of your men. Having destroyed that army of men, Bhīma, whose prowess is truth, [remained].
Placing Dhṛṣṭadyumna at his front, that one of great strength stood once more;
and Dhṛṣṭadyumna also, the great crusher of enemy hosts,
the son of the King of the Pañcālas, was the foremost of bowmen in battle.
With sharp arrows, he slew twenty-five thousand chariots, horses, and foot soldiers who were scattered on all sides;
thus were your men cut down in battle by Dhṛṣṭadyumna with his shafts.
Twenty-five thousand foot soldiers met their end; having slain that army of men, the mighty Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
placing Bhīmasena at his head, soon reappeared.
Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna in battle— whose horses were the color of pigeons, who was enraged like the wrathful Destroyer at the end of time— your men fled in fear;
meanwhile, the heroic Dhanañjaya advanced against the division of chariots.

The two sons of Mādrī and the great car-warrior Sātyaki, filled with joy, rushed impetuously toward Śakuni, slaughtering the army of Subala’s son. Having struck down a great many of his horsemen with sharp arrows, they pressed on.
They rushed toward him with speed, and then a battle took place.
O Lord, Dhananjaya also, having approached your chariot-force,
drew his bow Gāṇḍīva, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Seeing the chariot with white horses approaching with Kṛṣṇa as its charioteer, and seeing Arjuna as the warrior, your men fled in fear—
deprived of their chariots and horses, and abandoned by their elephants.
Twenty-five thousand foot soldiers met their end; having slain that army of men, the great car-warrior Dhṛṣṭadyumna,
the son of the Pāñcāla king, remained a great car-warrior himself.
Placing Bhīmasena at the forefront, that illustrious wielder of the great bow, the slayer of hosts of enemies, soon came into view—
he whose horses were the color of pigeons and whose great banner bore the emblem of the *kovidāra* tree.

Seeing Dhṛṣṭadyumna’s chariot, they fled in great fear; however, the two illustrious sons of Mādrī, along with Sātyaki, having pursued the King of Gāndhāra, who was swift in the use of weapons, soon came into view.
O Sire, Cekitāna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the sons of Draupadī,
having slaughtered your vast army, then blew their conchs;
they all beheld your men fleeing with their backs turned.
Like bulls having conquered other bulls, they rushed forward, desiring to slay.
Seeing that remnant of your army turned away and standing firm,
Savyasācin then became powerfully enraged.
The valiant Dhanañjaya advanced against the division of chariots;
he drew his bow Gāṇḍīva, renowned throughout the three worlds,
and then, O King, he held back those thousands with his arrows.
Then, because of the rising dust, nothing at all could be seen;
when the world was turned into another state and the surface of the earth became a mass of arrows,
O Great King, all your troops fled in fear in every direction.
O lord of the people, while the armies were being broken, your son, the Kuru king, rushed against the enemies who were facing him. Then Duryodhana challenged all the Pāṇḍavas.
O best of the Bharatas, like Bali against the gods in ancient times,
they turned toward him and rushed at him together,
all discharging various weapons and reviling him again and again.
O king of kings, O lord of the people, Duryodhana also, remaining unperturbed and assuming a terrible form, scattered those enemies in battle with sharpened arrows;
there we beheld the wonderful prowess of your son.
Because all the Pāṇḍavas were unable to overtake him,
Duryodhana saw his own army, which had not retreated very far, mangled by arrows, even as he had set his mind on flight.
Then, O Indra among kings, your son, having steadied his mind,
spoke these words as if to gladden those warriors:
"I do not see any place on earth or among the mountains where [he might be]."
Wherever you go, the Pāṇḍavas will not slay you; what is the use of your flight?
Their force is small, and the two Kṛṣṇas are severely wounded.
If we all remain here, our victory will be certain.

If we depart and are scattered, the sinful Pāṇḍavas will pursue and slay us; death in battle is better for us. For those who fight according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, death in combat is a source of happiness.
The dead man knows no suffering; having passed away, he experiences infinity.
Listen, all you Kṣatriyas who have gathered here, as many as you are:
when Yama, the Ender, slays both the hero and the coward alike.

Who indeed, being a fool like me and bound by the vow of a kṣatriya, would not fight? You will fall under the power of the enraged Bhīmasena, your enemy; you ought not to abandon the dharma practiced by your ancestors.

For there is no dharma more sinful for a Kṣatriya than flight; O Kauravas, there is no path to heaven better than the duty of battle. All these warriors, slain before long, shall attain the celestial realm.
While his son was speaking thus, the soldiers, severely wounded,
fled in every direction without even heeding those words; they left him there,
silent in meditation, miserable, and deeply afflicted.
Ārtāyani spoke these words to the distressed man:
"Behold this fierce battlefield, overrun with men, horses, and elephants, and filled with heroes who have been slain."
With great elephants resembling mountains fallen— once cast down,
their vital organs pierced by arrows— and with them writhing and deprived of life;
With their machines, weapons, armor, and warriors utterly destroyed—
like great mountain kings struck by thunderbolts—
their rocks, wild animals, trees, and medicinal herbs were all shattered.

With others gasping, vomiting blood,
wretched, groaning with rolling eyes,
biting the earth, and piteously crying out;
Likewise, with elephant-riders, horsemen, and warriors cast away,
some with but little life remaining and others already lifeless,
and with throngs of heroic chariot-warriors hurled down by force.
With crushed men, horses, elephants, and chariots,
the earth was as difficult to behold as the great Vaitaraṇī river;
with elephants whose trunks and limbs were hacked off;
Trembling and fallen upon the earth,
with shattered teeth and vomiting blood,
they quivered in pain, crying piteously on the field of battle.
[The field was covered] by those who protected Suyodhana’s armor, weapons, and feet;
with quivers and banners strewn about;
and by [the bodies of] those who had been violently struck and were draped in golden nets.
The earth was covered by the feet of the drivers and warriors, as if the sky were shrouded by clouds, by great elephants,
and by illustrious infantry, chariot-fighters, and horsemen.
The earth was covered with foot soldiers who had been slain facing the enemy—
their armor, ornaments, garments, and weapons shattered—
resembling extinguished fires.
Struck by the blows of arrows, those of great strength lay fallen by the thousands,
their consciousness lost yet breathing again as they looked on.
The earth became as if covered by fires following them,
when the great heroes of the Kurus and Sṛñjayas were slain, their bodies pierced by the arrows of Karṇa and Arjuna.
By day, the earth was illuminated by arrows exceedingly radiant as they fell from the sky; by night, the heavens shone with those bright shafts like a cloudless firmament.
Indeed, those arrows were released from the arms of Karṇa and Arjuna.
Having torn through the bodies of serpents, horses, and men,
and swiftly casting out their life-breaths, they passed over the earth with their weapons, like great serpents entering their dwellings on all sides.
The path of Dhanañjaya and the son of Adhiratha became strewn with slain men, horses, and elephants in the battle, and with chariots shattered by arrows.
The earth became impassable for elephants and exceedingly difficult to traverse due to chariots and warriors crushed by excellent arrows, with their charioteers,
horses, weapons, and standards entangled together.
With weapons shattered, their seats cut away,
with wheels, axles, yokes, and triple-poles severed, with iron parts destroyed and their mechanisms released;
The earth was strewn with [arrows] whose feathers were destroyed, their nocks beautiful, their shafts shattered, yet adorned with jewels and gold— like the sky covered by autumnal clouds.
With swift,
well-equipped chariots whose masters had been slain,
being dragged along by [surviving] horses, and with multitudes of men, elephants, chariots, and horses;
Hurled with great speed and shattered into many pieces were iron clubs adorned with golden bands, battle-axes,
maces, iron pestles, and sharp-edged spears.
Stainless swords were drawn from their scabbards, maces bound with bands of Jāmbūnada gold,
and bows adorned with ornaments of golden armlets.
And there were arrows with variegated shafts made of gold, bright yellow double-edged swords unsheathed and stainless,
and spears along with swords that shone like gold.
Parasols, yak-tail fans, and conch shells;
garlands variegated with gold and the finest flowers; and rugs encircled by banners and cloth.
Diadems, garlands, and bright crowns; scattered fans and spread-out rugs; and necklaces with central gems of choice pearls.
Turbans, armlets, and excellent bracelets; neck-ornaments, golden coins, and gold threads;
the finest gems, diamonds, gold, and pearls.
Jewels and various auspicious objects,
limbs accustomed to extreme comfort,
and heads with faces resembling the moon.
Having renounced bodies, enjoyments, and possessions, as well as delightful pleasures,
and having attained great steadfastness in their own duty;
They have filled the worlds with their fame and departed from here for the heavenly realm, O King;
turn back, Duryodhana, let the soldiers go.
"Go to your camp, O King, bestower of honor;
for the sun, O Lord, is already hanging low.
You alone, O ruler of men, shall be the cause for returning here again."
Having spoken thus, Śalya fell silent;
Duryodhana, his mind overwhelmed by grief, cried out, "Alas, Karṇa! Alas, Karṇa!"
Afflicted, unconscious, with eyes streaming with tears, O King, he whose mind was intent on battle cried out,
"Alas Karna! Alas Karna!"
All those lords of men, headed by the son of Droṇa, having consoled him,
set out together while repeatedly gazing at Arjuna.
The great banner blazed with fame,
while the earth was drenched with blood born from the bodies of men, horses, and elephants.
Clad in red garments and garlands, adorned with gold,
she was like a radiant woman accessible to all,
yet her form was concealed by blood, O King.
Shining intensely during the Raudra moment,
the Kurus did not remain [in their positions] upon seeing them;
all those exiled ones were like the worlds of the gods.
O King, deeply distressed by the slaughter of Karṇa and crying out,
"Alas, Karṇa! Alas, Karṇa!",
they quickly departed for their camps.
Gazing at the sun turned crimson by the sharp,
gold-feathered arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva,
whose shafts were smeared with blood.
With his limbs covered by arrows, Karṇa shines upon the earth even though he is slain, like the sun garlanded with rays;
Karṇa’s body is drenched in blood.
The Blessed One Vivasvat, compassionate toward his devotees,
having touched [the world] with his rays, red as blood in form,
approaches the great ocean desiring to bathe.
Having reflected thus, the hosts of celestial rishis set out and departed for their respective abodes;
and having deliberated, the people dispersed.

Having heard of that wonderful battle between the two foremost heroes of the Kurus, which caused terror among living beings and made both the sky and the surface of the earth tremble at will, [the people were amazed].
Astonished by the deeds of Dhanañjaya and the son of Adhiratha,
the people then departed, praising that hero whose armor had been cut away by arrows and who lay slain upon the battlefield.
Even though Rādheya’s life had departed, Fortune did not abandon him;
all beings regarded that hero as if he were still alive— his body like refined gold, possessing a splendor equal to the blazing sun.
O Great King, even when the Sūta’s son was slain in battle,
all living beings were terrified, like other animals at the sight of a lion.
Although that tiger among men was dead, he appeared as if he were still speaking.
O King, even though that great-souled one was dead, there was no deformity whatsoever;
his face, wearing beautiful garments and possessing a lovely crown and neck,
possessed a splendor equal to the full moon.
O King, adorned with various ornaments and polished armlets of refined gold,
having showered volleys of arrows and scorched the enemy host,
he— like the glorious thousand-rayed sun— blazed forth, scorching all.
Karna, the son of Vikartana, has been slain along with his sons and his mounts;
the wish-fulfilling tree for the flock of birds seeking refuge has been felled.
The son of Vikartana lies slain like a tree still bearing its sprouts.
Resembling the finest gold and blazing like a fire,
that tiger among men was extinguished by the water of Pārtha’s arrows;
for just as a kindled flame is quenched upon encountering water.
In that same way, the fire of Karṇa’s prowess was extinguished in battle by the cloud that was Pārtha;
and having grasped radiant glory for himself upon the earth through fair combat,
he released showers of arrows and scorched the ten directions.
That tiger among men, together with his sons, was extinguished by the splendor of Pārtha;
yet, O King, having scorched the Pāṇḍavas and the Pañcālas with the energy of his weapons, he—
when entreated by supplicants— used to say only, "I shall give," and never, "I have not."
That bull among men, a virtuous man ever honored by the righteous, was slain in a duel— he,
that high-souled one, for whom everything was dedicated to the Brahmins and not for his own sake;
for whom there was nothing that could not be given to the Brahmins, even his own life.
Always beloved by men, a giver, and one who gave with affection, Priyadāna has gone to heaven. Consumed by the weapons of Pārtha, he has attained the supreme goal—
that son of yours who, relying upon him, had waged enmity, has now gone to the celestial realm.
Having taken away the hope for victory, the protection, and the armor of your sons,
once Karṇa was slain, the rivers no longer flowed and the sun went to its setting, turbid with grief.
And a planet, blazing with the color of the sun,
the son of Yama, rose up obliquely, O King;
then the sky split asunder and the earth roared.
Winds blew with excessive harshness,
the quarters of the sky blazed intensely with smoke,
and the great oceans were agitated and roared.
O noble one, the forests together with the mountain ranges shook, and the hosts of living beings were deeply distressed,
as Bṛhaspati oppressed Rohiṇī.
When Karṇa was slain, the quarters of the sky could no longer be distinguished; the heavens were shrouded in darkness and the earth trembled, as if it had taken on the hue of the moon and the sun.
A meteor, blazing with the brilliance of fire, fell down,
and the night-stalkers became filled with joy when Arjuna [beheld him] whose face was as radiant as the moon.
With a razor, he struck off Karṇa’s head;
then, repeatedly from the atmosphere, the heavens, and here on earth, there arose the cry of "Alas! Alas! from the people.
Having slain his enemy Karṇa in battle— Karṇa who was honored by gods, Gandharvas, and humans— Arjuna,
the son of Pṛthā, shone with supreme splendor.
Then, like the thousand-eyed Indra after slaying Vṛtra,
he [proceeded] in a chariot that rumbled like a mass of clouds and possessed the brilliance of the sun situated in the midst of an autumn sky.
With their banners flying and their standards making a terrifying sound,
shining like snow, the moon, conch shells, and crystal,
those two were like the mounts of Mahendra.
Possessing prowess equal to the strength of Mahendra,
they were adorned with gold, pearls, gems, diamonds, and coral,
and possessed incomparable speed.
Those two best of men, the crusher of the Pāṇḍavas and the Keśin,
who resembled fire and the sun,
shone resplendent on the field of battle, free from fear after their marriage.
Like Viṣṇu and Vāsava on a common chariot,
they then forcibly stripped their enemies of their luster with the sounds of bowstrings, palms, and wheel-rims.
Having completely subdued the Kurus with showers of arrows,
both the son of the Yadavas and the son of the Pandus— those whose banners bore the monkey and the king of birds— then [stood] together.
Forcefully blowing their resonant conchs,
which were covered with golden nets and produced a great sound, they struck terror into the hearts of their enemies.
Taking hold of those two excellent conchs, which were as white as snow, with their hands, the two best of men kissed them and blew them simultaneously with their beautiful faces.
The roar of both the Pāñcajanya and the Devadatta filled the earth, the intermediate space, the heavens, and the waters;
and all the Kurus, O best of kings, were struck with terror.
With the sound of their conchs, that of Śūra, Mādhava, and Arjuna,
those two caused the forests, mountains, rivers, and all directions to resound with the blast of their conchs.
Terrifying your son’s army,
those two heroes gladdened Yudhiṣṭhira;
then the Kurus fled with speed.
O descendant of Bharata, as soon as they heard the sound of the conch being blown,
the sons of Bharata abandoned both their lord, the King of Madra, and Duryodhana.
In that great battle,
the assembled hosts of beings then rejoiced at Dhananjaya and Janardana, who were both appearing exceedingly resplendent.
Just like two risen suns, those two scorchers of foes, Acyuta and Arjuna, though covered by Karna’s arrows, both shone brightly in the battle.
Having dispelled the darkness, they rose up like the stainless moon and sun garlanded with rays;
then, having left behind those multitudes of arrows, they arrived.
Those two lords, whose prowess was beyond compare even among their friends,
entered their own camp in comfort,
like Indra and Viṣṇu summoned by the members of the assembly.
They were honored with supreme prayers for victory and prosperity by the great ṛṣis, as well as by gods, gandharvas, humans, cāraṇas, yakṣas, and mahoragas.
Having slain Karṇa in that supreme battle,
Sañjaya then said:
"When Vaikartana Karṇa had been killed, the Kurus were oppressed by fear."
Glancing in all directions, they fled everywhere;
hearing that the hero had been slain by the enemies in the great battle,
all your men, bewildered by fear, scattered in every direction.
Then, O King, those warriors withdrew from all sides,
though they were being restrained by your son who was agitated by fear, O Bhārata;
and having ascertained their intention, O bull of the Bharatas, your son [acted accordingly].
Then, O King, with the permission of Śalya, he withdrew from the field,
surrounded by your great car-warriors who remained after the slaughter, O Bhārata;
and he fled in haste toward his camp.
Surrounded by a thousand Gāndhāras, Śakuni,
seeing the son of Adhiratha slain, fled toward the camp.
O King, Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, was surrounded by a division of elephants.
Like a massive cloud, he rushed toward the camp;
then the heroic Aśvatthāman, sighing again and again upon seeing the victory of the Pāṇḍavas, fled toward the camp itself.
Surrounded by the great remaining force of the Saṃśaptakas,
Suśarman also departed, O King, watching those who were overcome with fear;
and King Duryodhana too, distressed, having lost all his possessions.
Overcome with grief, reflecting deeply and despondent, Śalya, the best of chariot-warriors, proceeded toward the camp in his chariot whose banner was severed,
looking about in the ten directions.
Then many other great car-warriors of the Bharatas,
overcome by fear and deprived of their senses, fled from the battle with tearful throats, agitated by terror, trembling and utterly overwhelmed.
O best of the Kurus, seeing Karṇa struck down, all the Kuru warriors fled; some great car-warriors praised Arjuna, while others praised Karṇa, as they ran in fear toward every direction.
Among those thousands of warriors on your side in that great battle, O Great King,
there was not a single man who set his mind upon fighting;
once Karṇa was slain, the Kurus became hopeless.
O Lord, having gathered them together— regarding their lives, their kingdoms, their wives,
and their wealth— your son, filled with pain and grief, resolved with great effort to establish them in marriage.
O lord of the people, having received his command with their heads bowed,
those great car-warriors, pale-faced and dejected,
entered [their quarters] after having honored him in accordance with their respective ranks.
Being praised for their incomparable deeds,
the two of them, together with their circles of friends, then rejoiced like the Lord of the Gods and Keśava after subduing Bali.
08,069.001 Saṃjaya said: 08,069.001a When Karṇa had been thus struck down and your army had fled,
the descendant of Daśārha embraced Pārtha and spoke these words out of joy:
"O Dhanañjaya, Vṛtra was slain by the breaker of strength (Indra), and Karṇa has been slain by you.
Indeed, mankind will speak of the slaying of both Karṇa and Vṛtra;
Vṛtra was struck down in battle by the wielder of the thunderbolt, who possesses great splendor."
"Karna has been slain by you with your bow and sharpened arrows.
O son of Kuntī, let us report this valor of yours— renowned in the world and bringing fame— to the wise Dharmarāja."
By announcing the slaying of Karṇa in battle— a deed you have desired to accomplish for a long time— you shall attain freedom from your debt to Dharmarāja,
while this war between both you and Karṇa is indeed proceeding.
Having arrived earlier to witness the battlefield, that delighter of the Dharma,
because he was so severely and deeply pierced, was unable to remain in the fray;
thereupon, O bull among men, that king departed for his own camp.
When Arjuna had said "So be it," Keśava, the bull among the Yadus,
unperturbed, turned that chariot of the best of car-warriors.
Having thus spoken to Arjuna, Kṛṣṇa addressed the soldiers as follows:
O Govinda, he spoke these words to Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Yudhāmanyu, the two sons of Mādrī, Vṛkodara, and Yuyudhāna:
"Stand firm, facing the enemy; may it be well with you."
"As soon as it was announced to the king that Karṇa had indeed been slain by Arjuna, so must you [behave] toward those lords of men. Permitted by those heroes, he went to the royal palace."
Taking Pārtha with him, Govinda beheld Yudhiṣṭhira,
that tiger among kings, lying upon an excellent golden bed;
and both of them joyfully grasped the feet of the monarch.
Observing their great joy and their superhuman blows,
Yudhiṣṭhira, believing the son of Rādhā to have been slain, rose up;
having risen, that mighty-armed subduer of enemies did so again and again.
Out of affection, he embraced Vāsudeva and Arjuna once more;
then the joy of the Kurus questioned Vāsudeva, the descendant of Vṛṣṇi,
and the sweet-spoken Vāsudeva related to him everything exactly as it had occurred.
The joy of the Yadus related the death of Karṇa;
then Acyuta Kṛṣṇa, smiling slightly, spoke with joined palms to King Yudhiṣṭhira, whose enemies had been slain.

"By good fortune, O King, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, Vṛkodara the Pāṇḍava, yourself, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī are all well. You have been liberated from this hair-raising battle, which was a slaughter of heroes."
"O King, quickly perform the duties that follow this time.
The cruel Vaikartana, the son of a Sūta and possessor of great strength, has been slain.
By good fortune you are victorious, O Indra among kings; by good fortune you prosper, O Pāṇḍava."
That lowest of men who laughed at Kṛṣṇā when she was won at dice—
the earth now drinks the blood of that son of a Sūta;
O bull among the Kurus, your enemy lies there with his limbs mangled by arrows.
Behold him, O tiger among men, pierced in many places by arrows;
O mighty-armed one, rule this earth whose enemies have been slain. Being diligent together with us, enjoy abundant pleasures.
Saṃjaya said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Keśava,
Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with joy, honored the descendant of Daśārha in return.
"By good fortune! By good fortune! O Indra among kings, he spoke thus out of joy:
"O mighty-armed son of Devakī, this is not surprising in you;
for with you as his charioteer, what manliness Pārtha might not display today!"
"O mighty-armed one, it is no wonder that this has arisen from the grace of your arms.
Then the best of the Kurus, the upholder of dharma, raising his right arm adorned with an armlet, spoke to both Keśava and Arjuna, O Pārtha.
"The two gods Nara and Nārāyaṇa were indeed described by Nārada as the ancient and supreme persons (puruṣottama) engaged in the establishment of dharma;
and the wise Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana has told me this many times."
O mighty-armed one, the Lord recounted this divine story:
"By your power, O Kṛṣṇa, and by means of the Gāṇḍīva bow, Dhanañjaya conquers his enemies face-to-face and has never turned his back anywhere."
"Victory is indeed certain for us, and not defeat,
now that you have taken up the role of charioteer for Pārtha in battle—
[when] Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and the high-souled Kṛpa, son of Gotama [are present]."
"And many other heroes,
O Govinda, and those who were their followers, are all utterly destroyed once Karna has been slain by your intellect.
Having spoken thus, O Great King, he [ascended] that chariot adorned with gold.
Mounting a great chariot yoked with horses the color of ivory and with black manes,
that tiger among men, surrounded by his own forces,
then took leave of his beloved friends, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, both heroes.
Then, having arrived at that battlefield to witness many events,
he spoke to those two heroes, Mādhava and Phalguna;
he beheld Karṇa, that bull among men, lying on the field of battle.
The King of Dharma beheld Karṇa covered on all sides with filaments like a kadamba flower, and strewn with hundreds of arrows,
along with thousands of golden lamps soaked in scented oil.
Then, illuminated by lamps, he beheld the bull,
its armor shattered and pierced, torn apart by arrows,
and reduced to fragments on all sides by the shafts released from the Gāṇḍīva bow.
Seeing Karṇa slain along with his son, King Yudhiṣṭhira,
having gained full conviction after gazing upon this again and again,
praised both those tigers among men, Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava.
"Today, O Govinda, I am king upon the earth along with my brothers,
protected by you, our heroic and wise lord.
Having seen the son of Rādhā, that arrogant tiger among men, slain."
Today that evil-souled son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra will become hopeless,
both of life and of his kingdom, once the great car-warrior Karṇa is slain.
And through your grace, O bull among men, we too shall have achieved our purpose.
"You and the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, O victorious joy of the Yadus—by good fortune you are victorious, O Govinda; by good fortune Karna has been struck down.
Thirteen years have been spent in agonizing vigil."
"O mighty-armed one, by your grace we shall sleep happily tonight. Thus,
O king of kings, the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira, being greatly delighted, praised Janārdana and Arjuna in many such ways.
Saṃjaya said:
Having seen Karṇa slain along with his son by the arrows of Pārtha,
the upholder of the Kuru lineage considered himself as if born again.
And having approached Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, O great king,
all those kings of immense splendor then praised him;
he was surrounded by all his brothers, beginning with Bhīma.
Filled with joy, those great car-warriors—
Nakula, Sahadeva, Vṛkodara the Pāṇḍava,
and Sātyaki, O Great King, that foremost chariot-warrior of the Vṛṣṇis— cheered on the king.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and the Pāṇḍus, Pāñcālas,
and Sṛñjayas honored the son of Kuntī when the son of the Sūta had been slain. Having thus congratulated King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, they [departed].
Radiant with victory, having achieved their goal, skilled in battle and fierce strikers,
those great car-warriors— filled with joy and praising the two Kṛṣṇas, the subduers of foes, with words full of eulogy— returned to their own camp.
"Thus did this great and hair-raising destruction occur, O King, due to your own evil counsel; why do you grieve for what is past?
Vaiśampāyana said:"
"Thus it was; that battle was great and exceedingly terrible.
Upon hearing that unpleasant news, O King, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of the earth and descendant of Kuru, fell motionless upon the ground, overcome by supreme agony.
Likewise, Queen Gāndhārī, devoted to truth and perceiving the dharma,
lamented at length over the death of Karṇa in battle;
Vidura and Sañjaya likewise consoled the king.
While they were thus consoling the lord of the earth,
the royal women likewise raised up Gāndhārī. Then the king, considering fate to be supreme and that which was destined to be, [accepted his lot].
Suffering extreme agony, his mind was lost; though a great ascetic, his soul was overwhelmed by anxiety and grief, and being tormented by delusion, he knew nothing.
Comforted by those two, the king remained silent and unconscious.
Whoever should read this great battle-sacrifice of the two high-souled ones, Dhanañjaya and the son of Adhiratha,
shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice properly performed.
O Bhārata, one may attain that [merit] even by merely hearing it;
for the Lord Viṣṇu is the eternal Sacrifice (Makha),
whom fire, wind, moon, and sun carry.
Therefore, he who listens to this without malice and recites it shall conquer all worlds and become happy;
whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all acts of giving— [he shall obtain that].
A mortal who hears this narrative of Karṇa indeed obtains that fruit:
gold, clothing, grain, a cow with its calf, and sandals;
by means of that, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Rudras, and likewise the Vasus [are pleased].

All the sages, the ancestors, and likewise the two Aśvins have been honored. Whoever always listens with devotion to this unsurpassed narrative of Karṇa shall obtain the fourfold fruit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Those men who, having always attained devotion,
recite this meritorious and excellent compendium,
shall [prosper] in wealth, grain, and fame.
They rejoice; there is no doubt about this. Therefore, a man who is free from malice should always listen to it, and he shall obtain all happiness.
Viṣṇu, the Self-existent Lord, and Bhava—
whichever of these are pleased with that best of men,
for him the attainment of the Vedas is seen here in this world as the mark of a Brāhmaṇa.
In battle, strength belongs to the Kṣatriyas, and victory in combat; the Vaiśyas indeed have wealth as their primary concern;
and all the Śūdras obtain health in this world.
In the same way, the Lord Viṣṇu is eternal;
since that deity is celebrated here,
a man who is happy obtains his desires from him.

The merit one would gain from continuously giving away tawny cows with their calves for one full year is indeed equal to the merit of honoring the words of that Great Sage by listening to the Karṇa Parvan.
Reflecting upon the terrible slaughter of the Sūta’s son in battle,
and contemplating Arjuna’s victory in the fight again and again,
those great archers of the Pāṇḍavas, the subduers of their foes, took up their positions.
With hearts full of joy, having conquered their great chariot-warrior enemies,
all the Pāñcālas then approached Yudhiṣṭhira, who was seated there filled with delight, and honored him according to the prescribed rites.
But the highly illustrious Arjuna, quickly descending from his chariot,
joyfully pressed the feet of Dharmarāja. O great king, the powerful son of Dharma raised him up.
Smelling and touching the best of the Bharatas,
Nakula, Sahadeva, and Vṛkodara the Pāṇḍava embraced him; having saluted the great king, they also embraced Phalguna.
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Śikhaṇḍin, and those who were the chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas,
increased the joy of the king once the son of the Sūta had been slain.
Then, O great king, Kṛṣṇa and Sātyaki the Sātvata [did likewise].
When the son of the Suta had been slain, they both caused the king to rejoice;
and Vāsudeva, out of affection, spoke this to the son of Kuntī:
"Today, O King, all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been killed, along with their allied kings."
When Karṇa, the son of Vikartana, the foremost of chariot-warriors,
has been slain, even if all the three worlds together with Indra himself were to fight him,
that Sūta would still have been difficult to conquer; yet he has been destroyed by your wrath.
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja replied to Janārdana:
"By your grace, O Govinda, the highly illustrious Karṇa has been slain;
the Pāṇḍavas have attained victory, and our enemies have been destroyed."
For you alone are capable of protecting anyone from fear in battle;
you are the protector of this world and of the Pāṇḍavas at all times. Having obtained you, even Śakra rejoices eternally in heaven.
"You are the protector of the sons of Pāṇḍu, just as you are the protector of the entire world.
It is no wonder that victory belongs to them, O Lord, for they possess devotion toward you.
With you as our protector, O Govinda, we are truly well-protected in battle."
Just as the gods were [protected] by Indra in the past, and by you as well, O Janārdana, so shall I sleep happily today, O Kṛṣṇa; dwelling here, I shall obtain sleep throughout the night.
For my fear has departed today through your grace; of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by Pārtha, Keśava spoke to the son of Pāṇḍu: "O King,
we are indeed merely instruments for you in this attainment of joy,
since your brothers Bhīmasena and the others are heroes."
The kinsmen, possessing the prowess of Indra, headed by the son of Pṛṣata, as well as those led by the son of Pr̥ṣata, are likewise here.
You are indeed worthy to speak what is pleasant, for you always act for my benefit;
O best of men, you are dear to me because of these words.

Thus addressed, the King of Dharma, that tiger among men and lord of the earth, mounted his own gold-adorned chariot, which was yoked to horses the color of ivory with black manes, and set out surrounded by his own forces.
He set out toward the battlefield, which was full of many occurrences, to see it;
while those two heroes, the Pāṇḍava and the Mādhava, were conversing, he,
that bull among men, beheld Karṇa lying on the field of battle.

Seeing Karna slain along with his son, having been thoroughly crushed on all sides by arrows released from the Gāṇḍīva bow, King Yudhiṣṭhira praised both those tigers among men, the Pāṇḍava and the Mādhava.
"O Madhusūdana, today I am the king of the entire earth!
By good fortune you are victorious, O Govinda; by good fortune the enemy has been struck down.
Thus, O King, he praised Janārdana in many such ways.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and best of the Kurus, seeing Arjuna and Karṇa slain along with his son by the arrows of Pārtha,
that upholder of the Kuru lineage considered himself as if born anew.
Having approached Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and best of the Kurus,
those great car-warriors, filled with joy, offered their congratulations to the king.
Sañjaya said:
"Thus has this great destruction occurred, hair-raising and immense, O King, due to your evil counsel; it is by good fortune that you now grieve.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this unpleasant news, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the lord of the earth and scion of the Kuru race, fell motionless from his excellent throne onto the ground;
likewise did Queen Gāndhārī, who was devoted to truth and possessed divine vision.
Then Vidura and Sañjaya quickly comforted that king, and both of them consoled the lord of the earth;
likewise, Gāndhārī also comforted the best of kings.
He considered destiny to be supreme and that it was destined to happen thus;
O lord of the people, consoled by those two, the king remained silent.
Having spoken thus to the king, O best of monarchs, Sañjaya—
After the high-souled Karṇa had been slain, he returned once more to his camp.
O King, having seen Śalya killed, as well as King Suyodhana and very many warriors and soldiers by the thousands, [he entered].
O King, having likewise seen the Pāṇḍava army slaughtered during the night-attack by the son of Droṇa, with its horses,
men, and elephants slain on all sides in battle, Saṃjaya beheld them all destroyed.
Afflicted by grief and overwhelmed by fear, he departed for Hastināpura;
and when these many elephants and horses,
as well as the warriors born in various lands, had been slain, O Great King.
O Lord of the World, all that Kurukṣetra was empty,
for both the Pāṇḍavas and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had been slain in battle.
Sañjaya related to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra everything that had occurred according to the events of each respective region.
He reported all that had occurred exactly as it happened and according to the facts.
They announced that Karṇa had been struck down by the high-souled Phalguna.
Then those two went quickly to the place where the slaughter of heroes was taking place.
Hundreds of men returned from all sides with lamps in their hands;
and once again, O bull of the Bharatas, the son of Bharata reached his camp with his brothers,
after Yudhiṣṭhira had performed whatever duties remained to be done and was seated comfortably.
